In the absence of request it is not error to fail to charge on presumption as to continuance of insanity arising from judgment committing the defendant to the insane asylum. Harris, 155 Ga. 405, 409, 410 (2) (117 S. Ę. 460); Quattlebaum, 119 Ga. 433 (7) (46 S. E. 677).

Habitual insanity, when once proven to exist, will be presumed to continue, but this presumption is rebuttable. But continuous insanity can not be presumed from a mere temporary derangement. 

Dicken, 7 Ga. 484, 490; Humphrey, 46 Ga. App. 720, 722 (169 S. E. 53).

Insanity. The law of no civilized country holds idiots or lunatics responsible for their acts, either civil or criminal. Wilson, 9 

Ga. App. 274, 285 (70 S. E. 1128).

Definition of general insanity as total or partial impairment of intellect rendering the person unable to know right from wrong,upheld. Carr, 96 Ga. 284 (2) (22 S. E. 570).

An idiot is one "who hath no understanding from his nativity.' 

1 Blackstone, Comm. 304. He is a natural fool, or fool from birth. 

Battle, 105 Ga. 703, 708 (32 S. E. 160).

Intermittent insanity, caused by physical weakness or nervous disorder, is no excuse or justification for crime, unless it appears that at the time of the act committed the defendant was incapable

CRIMES 

19 of adjudging the quality of the act and of knowing whether it was right or wrong. Carter, 2 Ga. App. 254 (3) (58 S. E. 532).

If one has sufficient reason to distinguish between right and wrong, as to the act about to be committed, he is responsible. 

Otherwise not. Roberts, 3 Ga. 310.

If a man has sufficient reason to distinguish between right and wrong in relation to the particular act about to be committed, he is criminally responsible. Bridges, 43 Ga. App. 214 (158 S. E. 358); 

Hinson, 152 Ga. 243 (3) (109 S. E. 661).

The general test of sanity is the ability to distinguish between right and wrong. The only exception from this rule is in a case of one who can distinguish right from wrong, but who acts under a peculiar delusion, in consequence of which, and without criminal intent, his will is overmastered, and he commits the act. Carter, 2 

Ga. App. 254 (3) (4), 258, 259 (58 S. E. 922); Strickland, 137 Ga. 

115 (5) (72 S. E. 922).

The law of general insanity and the law of delusion should not be confused in charging the jury. Caison, 171 Ga. 1 (154 S. E. 337).

Delusions. Delusion, overmastering the will is an exception to the rule that one who knows right from wrong is responsible, where the criminal act is connected with such delusion. The reason for the rule is that there is no criminal intent in such cases. Roberts, 3 Ga. 310; Flanagan, 103 Ga. 619 (2) (30 S. E. 550); Allams, 123 

Ga. 500 (3) (51 S. E. 506).

Delusion as to the existence of a fact which would be immaterial if it did exist,-no defense. Choice, 31 Ga. 424, 478; Hill, 64 Ga. 

453, 454 (3).

Where appropriate and timely written request is presented, the Court should not restrict the charge to the right and wrong test, but should extend it to the test of intelligence and capacity or incapacity to form a criminal intent. Wilson, 9 Ga. App. 274 (2) (70 

S. E. 1128).

Where there is no evidence of delusion, Court should not charge on delusional insanity. Goosby, 153 Ga. 496 (2) (112 S. E. 467).

Drugs. Though mania or insanity is caused by drugs, if it is permanent and fixed in the character of the accused, so as to destroy the knowledge of right and wrong, accused is not responsible. 

Strickland, 137 Ga. 115 (1) (72 S. E. 922). 

Weak mind. Weak-mindedness is no defense. Goosby, 153 Ga. 

496 (1) (112 S. E. 467).

Weak-minded person would not be exempt from criminal responsibility if he could distinguish right from wrong, and understand that the act about to be committed is against the criminal laws, and that he is liable to be punished and held responsible for his acts. 

Bowden, 151 Ga. 336, 337 (4) (106 S. E. 575).

Evidence of weak-mindedness is not admissible, unless the accused was an idiot, lunatic, or insane person. Rogers, 128 Ga. 67 (1) (57 S. E. 227); Goosby, 153 Ga. 496 (1) (112 S. E. 467).

Lucid intervals. One adjudged insane is still responsible for his crimes committed by him during lucid intervals. Quattlebaum, 119 

Ga. 433 (6) (46 S. E. 677).

Burden of proof. The burden of proof rests upon the defendant to establish his insanity at the time of the trial. Carter, 56 Ga. 

463; Keener, 97 Ga. 388 (3) (24 S. E. 28).

Where in the trial of one charged with a crime he relies upon the defense of insanity, the burden is upon him to rebut the presumption of sanity by establishing his insanity by a preponderance of the evidence. Clark, 167 Ga. 341, 345 (145 S. E. 647); Currie, 153 Ga. 

178 (111 S. E. 727).

The burden of proof of insanity is linked with that of a criminal intent, and the presumption of the accused's innocence. The rule is now that if the jury entertain a doubt of the accused's guilt on the whole showing, including the question of insanity, they must give the benefit of that doubt to the accused, and acquit him. Goosby, 153 Ga. 496 (112 S. E. 467); Wilson, 9 Ga. App. 274 (70 S. E. 1128).

The evidence of insanity must be sufficient to the reasonable satisfaction of the jury. Hobbs, 8 Ga. App. 53, 54 (4) (68 S. E. 515); 

Bowden, 151 Ga. 336 (3) (106 S. E. 575).

Insanity must be proved by a preponderance of the evidence. 

Allams, 123 Ga. 500 (1) (51 S. E. 506). It is, therefore, error to charge the jury that the defendant must make good such defense to a reasonable certainty and to reasonable satisfaction of the jury. 

Currie, 153 Ga. 178 (2) (111 S. E. 727); Goosby, 153 Ga. 496, 497 (8) (112 S. E. 467).

Sanity need not be established to the exclusion of a reasonable doubt. Danforth, 75 Ga. 614, 615 (4). 

Criminal intent. An insane person can not have a criminal intent in a legal sense. Long, 38 Ga. 491, 507.

Jury. The question of insanity is for the jury. Wilson, 9 Ga. 

App. 274, 284 (70 S. E. 1128). See this case for full discussion of the law of insanity.

CRIMES 

21 Insanity is a question of fact and not of law. But the jury can not arbitrarily disregard the clearest and most convincing proof. 

Wilson, 9 Ga. App. 274, 287 (70 S. E. 1128). But see: Caison, 171 

Ga. 1 (154 S. E. 337).

Insanity after conviction. Where a person is convicted of a crime, and sentenced to serve a term in the penitentiary, or on the chain gang, and subsequently, but before performance of his sentence, he becomes insane, and is sent to the State sanitarium, he may, after being discharged as not insane, and in the absence of proof that he is in fact insane, be taken into custody and compelled to perform the unexecuted sentence. Talley, 141 Ga. 110 (80 S. E. 556).

Lunacy trial. Jurisdiction of ordinary. Ordinary has no jurisdiction to hold sanity trial, where the person to be examined is under arrest charged with a crime. McGriff, 135 Ga. 259 (1) (69 S. E. 

115). Writ of prohibition will issue to prevent ordinary from proceeding with such insanity hearing. (Id.) (2).

Evidence. Evidence of domestic difficulties is not admissible to establish insanity under an issue of insanity at the time of committing the offense. Carter, 56 Ga. 463 (5).

Evidence of general reputation of accused, before the commission of the crime, as to insanity,-not admissible. Brinkley, 58 Ga. 296 (1); Choice, 31 Ga. 424 (6).

A non-expert witness may give his opinion as to the sanity of another person, based upon his acquaintance and the manner, appearance, and conduct of such person, during the time that the witness has known him. Harris, 155 Ga. 405, 406 (4) (117 S. E. 460).

Sheriff's custody. It is immaterial, how court obtained jurisdiction of the person of the accused. A special plea of insanity must allege that the accused is insane at the time of the trial, although the accused was in actual custody of the court under a lunacy warwant, awaiting transfer to the State sanitarium. Humphrey, 46 Ga. 

App. 720 (169 S. E. 53). 

2. MUNICIPAL ORDINANCES. 

A writ of error will not lie in behalf of a municipal corporation to review a judgment sustaining a certiorari in a case of one convicted of the violation of a municipal ordinance. Manchester, 38 

Ga. App. 83 (142 S. E. 747).

One can not be lawfully convicted, in a municipal court, of the alleged offense of doing business in a designated city without a license, where there is no municipal ordinance of such city making it an offense to carry on business therein, for which license is required, without first obtaining such license. Thompson, 127 Ga. 53 (56 

S. E. 114).

The doing of a single act pertaining to a particular business will not be considered engaging in or carrying on the business; yet a series of such acts would be so considered. Lichtenstein, 34 Ga. 

App. 138, 140 (128 S. E. 704).

One can not be tried and convicted for an offense different from that for which he is prosecuted or called upon to answer. Nobles, 39 Ga. App. 814, 817 (148 S. E. 612).

One charged with the violation of a municipal ordinance is, equally with those charged with greater crimes, entitled to a fair and impartial trial. Nobles, 39 Ga. App. 814, 817 (148 S. E. 612).

Judicial notice of a municipal ordinance defining an offense may be taken by a recorder on a trial in the recorder's court, but not by any other than a municipal court; and when there is a petition for certiorari to review a conviction of one charged with violating such an ordinance, on the ground that it is contrary to the evidence, and the provisions of the ordinance are not set out so that the reviewing court may compare the evidence with the ordinance, the court can not determine whether the evidence fails to show a violation of the ordinance; and this is a sufficient reason for refusing to sanction the certiorari. Nobles, 39 Ga. App. 814 (148 S. E. 612).

Municipal ordinances and State offenses. A municipal corporation is without jurisdiction to try an offense covered by a State law. 

Lumpkin, 12 Ga. App. 111 (76 S. E. 1059).

A municipal ordinance, punishing an act made penal by a State law in existence or subsequently enacted, covering the same subject matter, must yield to the State law. Lanford, 147 Ga. 799 (95 

S. E. 688).

The fact that the accused was subsequently convicted in the State courts, for offenses against the State arising out of the same transaction which drew a conviction from a mayor's court, will not affect the right of the city to compel the performance of the sentence imposed by the mayor. Shuler, 126 Ga. 73 (e) (54 S. E. 965).

The General Assembly may, by express enactment, authorize the corporate authorities of municipalities to provide by ordinance for the punishment of an act which in its nature affects the health,

CRIMES 

23 peace, and good order of the community, notwithstanding that such an act has already been made penal under the general law of the State. An ordinance passed in pursuance of such authority does not provide for the punishment of an offense against the laws of the 

State. Littlejohn, 123 Ga. 427 (1) (2) (51 S. E. 390).

The charge of "keeping intoxicants for sale within the limits of a named town" in violation of an ordinance of that town, does not charge the commission of a crime punishable under the laws of the State. (This was held in 1905, and has to be construed in the light of the prohibition law as it then existed. In Barlow, 146 Ga. 805 (1) (92 S. E. 643), it was held that the Georgia Laws, 1915, Extraordinary Session, page 77, stated such an ordinance, and invalidated the same. See also Snipe, 147 Ga. 285 (93 S. E. 399) ; Lanford, 147 Ga. 799 (1) (2) (95 S. E. 688).) Little, 123 Ga. 503 (51 

S. E. 501).

Where a portion of a municipal ordinance is valid, the addition of certain other portions which may be invalid as undertaking to deal with matters punishable by a State law, would not prevent a conviction of one guilty of violating the valid portion. Fichtenberg, 126 Ga. 62, 63 (4) (54 S. E. 933).

Where the penal laws of this State provide for the punishment of an offense, which is punishable also by an ordinance of a municipality, the State law supersedes the city ordinance, and one convicted of a violation of such ordinance, and against whom a charge is pending for a violation of the State law, will be discharged on proper habeas corpus proceedings, since the conviction of the accused in the recorder's court is void. Mayo, 146 Ga. 650 (92 S. E. 59).

A plea of autrefois acquit is bad, where the accused was tried in a municipal court for the violation of a city ordinance and set up such plea of former jeopardy in the Superior Court. The same act may constitute an offense both against the penal laws of the State and against an ordinance of a municipal corporation, and both may punish for it without violating any constitutional principles. In such a case, "punishment for the same act is not necessarily punishment for the same offense," because "when committed in a city, and when of that class of acts which tend to disturb the local health, peace, and good order, and which therefore fall properly within the scope of municipal jurisdiction, an act punishable by the general law may, because of its more serious consequences in a city than elsewhere, constitute an additional offense, punishable by a munic-

ipal by-law as an offense against the city." The "same transaction test" is applicable only in courts of the same jurisdiction; and while it is possible for the legislature, by express grant, to confer upon. municipal courts the right to punish for violation of the general laws of the State, ordinarily they are not clothed with this power. 

For this reason, the same transaction test can not be applied to a judgment based upon a municipal ordinance, and the judgment of guilty in a city court; and the plea in bar in either court, based upon the fact that a transaction for which the offender has already been tried in one court or the other is identical in fact with that upon which he is again about to be tried, affords no ground of defense. A conviction in a mayor's court, under a municipal ordinance for disturbing the peace, will not protect the accused from a subsequent prosecution in the State court, for assault and battery, even though the identical transaction be involved in both cases. 

Nor will an acquittal in a State court on a charge of assault and battery protect the accused from a subsequent prosecution for disorderly conduct, under a municipal ordinance. (Italics by the 

Court.) Sutton, 4 Ga. App. 30, 32, 33 (60 S. E. 811).

Municipal ordinances dealing with the subject already dealt with by a criminal statute of the State, in order to make a new and different criminal offense, must not only introduce a new ingredient, but that new ingredient must be "an ingredient or concomitant essential to the preservation of the city's peace, health or good order, which is not included in the act or acts made criminal by the State law. Snipe, 147 Ga. 285, 286 (93 S. E. 399).

It is competent for the legislature to pass general laws conferring on all municipalities the power to pass ordinances similar to the general State laws, but this can not be done by a special law which in itself is repugnant to the provision of the Constitution, forbidding the passage of a special law in any case for which provision has been made by an existing general law. Lanford, 147 Ga. 799 (4) (95 S. E. 688); Aycock, 104 Ga. 533 (30 S. E. 815).

Where a municipal ordinance is objected to on the ground that it is superseded by a valid State law, it is the duty of the objector to point out the particular penal law of the State which supersedes the ordinance. Martin, 147 Ga. 575 (94 S. E. 998).

Presumption. When it is alleged that the defendant committed an offense, violating a municipal ordinance, in the absence of proof to the contrary the courts will presume that there existed at that

CRIMES 

25 time a legal ordinance defining, forbidding and punishing that act. 

Fountain, 2 Ga. App. 713, 716 (58 S. E. 1129). 

Certiorari. Where the city council conducts a trial of an alleged offender in accordance with the statute granting the city council a judicial authority to act as a police court, the trial is a quasi-criminal procedure, and the writ of certiorari lies to review the ruling and findings of such a corporation court. Gill, 118 Ga. 85 (44 S. E. 

830); Carr, 124 Ga. 116 (2) (52 S. E. 300).

The general rule applicable to criminal cases pertains to bills of exceptions to convictions for the violation of municipal ordinances. 

Barnett, 109 Ga. 166 (34 S. E. 322). 

3. CORPORATIONS. 

Whenever an indictment or special presentment against a corporation doing business in this State is returned, or filed in any court in this State having jurisdiction of the offense, the clerk of said court shall issue an original and copy notice to the defendant corporation of the filing of such indictment or special presentment, which copy notice shall be served by a sheriff upon any officer of such corporation to be found in his county; and if there be no such officer in his county, then upon any agent of such corporation; and the sheriff serving such copy notice shall make an entry of such service on the original notice and return the same to the court from which it issued, and such service shall be service upon the corporation, and the indictment or special presentment shall, upon the said return of said notice executed as provided in this section, stand for trial. On the trial, if the defendant corporation fails to appear, or appearing fails to plead, the judge shall cause to be entered a plea of not guilty, and the trial shall proceed as though the defendant had appeared and pleaded. Upon the conviction of any corporation in any such trial, there shall be rendered against it a judgment for the fine imposed, together with the costs of the prosecution, upon which judgment an execution shall issue against the property of the defendant. § 27-1001.

This section provides an exception to the general law, that defendants charged with crime are not served with process. They can not be arraigned in their absence. As a rule, jurisdiction over the accused is obtained by his presence. Wells, 121 Ga. 368, 370 (49 S. E. 319).

The method of serving corporations is an exclusive procedure, un-

www less it is waived by the corporation. Progress Club, 12 Ga. App. 

174, 180 (76 S. E. 1029).

Voluntary appearance by agent or attorney is a sufficient waiver of any defect in the service. Southern Railway Co., 125 Ga. 287 

Corporations can not be punished except by fines. Southern Railway Co., 125 Ga. 287 (54 S. E. 160).

In the absence of waiver of indictment by the corporation it can be tried for a crime by indictment or special presentment only. 

Progress Club, 12 Ga. App. 174 (76 S. E. 1029); Central Georgia 

Power Co., 12 Ga. App. 260 (77 S. E. 107); Brunswick-Oglethorpe 

Club, 12 Ga. App. 180 (76 S. E. 1034).

A corporation can be liable criminally for nonfeasance in neglecting to perform duties which it owes to the public. The Act requiring railroads to provide adequate water supply of pure drinking water for their passengers, held constitutional. Southern Railway Co., 125 Ga. 287 (54 S. E. 160). 

The name "The Piedmont Feed and Grocery Company" connotes a corporation, and an allegation in the indictment that it is a corporation is surplusage and need not be proved, unless the corporation entity of the company is an issue upon the defendant's trial. 

Hornsby, 49 Ga. App. 305 (1) (175 S. E. 399).

CRIMINAL PROCEDURE

a. THE WARRANT. 

PART II 1. ARREST. 

A Justice of the Peace, issuing a warrant, performs an act of a judicial officer and begins judicial proceedings, but such act is not an act of a court. Ormond, 120 Ga. 916 (4) (48 S. E. 383).

A mayor may issue a warrant against a violator of an ordinance. 

Williams, 121 Ga. 665 (2) (49 S. E. 732).

A person may be arrested under a warrant, that merely describes his person, the color of his eyes and hair, his complexion, height, weight, etc., where his name is unknown; and he may be indicted and convicted under such description. Wiggins, 80 Ga. 468, 470 (5 S. E. 503). 

A warrant may issue on Sunday. Weldon, 62 Ga. 449 (1). (1) Affidavit for Warrant.

A criminal warrant consists of the affidavit upon which it is based and the precept of the officer. Cox, 151 Ga. 632 (1) (107 S. E. 863).

The affidavit is a part of the criminal warrant, and imposes duties, in their nature judicial, upon the officer. Cox, 151 Ga. 632 (107 S. 

E. 863).

A warrant issued on an instrument purporting to be an affidavit, but not verified, is void. Wiggins, 14 Ga. App. 314, 315 (3) (80 

S. E. 724).

An affidavit, neither attested by an officer authorized to administer oaths, nor purporting to be sworn to in open court, is void as a basis of criminal proceedings. Gilbert, 17 Ga. App. 143 (2) (86 

S. E. 415).

Substantial compliance. A substantial compliance with the statute is all that is necessary for the validity of affidavits and warrants based thereon. Kumpe, 167 Ga. 284 (145 S. E. 509).

Essentials. For form of affidavit see § 27-104. 

It is not essential to the validity of an accusation that a warrant be issued on the same affidavit on which the accusation is based, or that the affidavit minutely describe the offense. Brown, 109 Ga. 570 (2) (34 S. E. 1031); McAlpin, 86 Ga. 271, 272 (12 S. E. 412).

The offense may be charged in general terms, or by name, in the affidavit, except in cases of larceny. Pye, 9 Ga. App. 397, 398 (71 

S. E. 594).

Affidavit not stating when and where the offense was committed is void. Thorpe, 68 Ga. 359, 367; Cox, 151 Ga. 632, 638 (107 S. E. 863). 

Affidavit for a criminal warrant may be based on knowledge and belief. Thomas, 91 Ga. 204, 207.

Where warrant for assault with intent to murder was based on an affidavit which omitted to state that the attack was made with a weapon likely to produce death, the warrant was still valid. Sasser, 73 Ga. 547 (1-a).

Where affidavit charges that the accused committed a misdemeanor, the accusation may charge the specific offense. Williams, 107 Ga. 693 (33 S. E. 641).

Commercial notary public. Whether affidavit made before a commercial notary public is sufficient as the basis of a warrant, without special statutory authority,-not decided. Mitchell, 126 Ga. 

84 (3) (54 S. E. 931). 

Constable as prosecutor. Where prosecutor is also constable, he is disqualified from executing warrant, based upon his own affidavit. 

Davis, 79 Ga. 767, 768 (4 S. E. 318).

Warrant as evidence. The presumption is that a warrant, apparently legal on its face, is legal. Warrant, apparently legal on its face, unaccompanied by affidavit, is admissible in evidence. Hilburn, 121 Ga. 344 (2) (49 S. E. 318); Rushing, 135 Ga. 224 (69 S. 

E. 171). (2) The Warrant.

An affidavit made, or warrant issued, for the arrest of an offender against the penal laws shall state, as nearly as practicable, the following facts, to wit: The offense, the county in which the same was committed, and the time when committed; and when the offense charged is a larceny, the ownership of the property alleged to have been stolen, or the person from whose possession it was taken, shall, as far as practicable, be stated in the affidavit and warrant. § 27103. 

For form of warrant see: § 27-105. 

Any judge of a superior, city, or county court, or justice, or any corporation officer clothed by law with the power of a justice, may issue his warrant for the arrest of any offender against the penal laws, based either on his own knowledge or the information of others given to him under oath. § 27-102.

29 Special warrant. No judicial officer, except a judge of the superior court, shall issue a special warrant, returnable only before himself; nor shall any judge issue such warrant out of his own judicial circuit. In such cases the warrant, though special, shall be treated as a general warrant. § 27-106. 

A justice of the peace can not issue special warrants, returnable only before himself, but a warrant issued by him must be made returnable before himself or "some other judicial officer." mond, 120 Ga. 916 (6) (48 S. E. 383). 

b. ARREST. 

Or- What constitutes an arrest. An actual touching with the hand is not essential to constitute a valid arrest. If the defendant voluntarily submits to be considered under arrest, or yields on condition of being allowed his freedom of locomotion, under the discretion of the officer, the arrest is complete. § 27-201.

Breaking open doors. In order to arrest under a warrant charging a crime, the officer may break open the door of any house where the offender is concealed. § 27-205.

Arrest and posse. Every officer is bound to execute the penal warrants placed in his hands, and to that end he may summon to his assistance, either in writing or verbally, any of the citizens of the neighborhood or county. As the posse of such officer, their acts shall be subject to the same protection and consequences as official 

An attempt by an officer to delegate his authority is distinguished from summoning one in his aid. Robinson, 93 Ga. 77, 85 (18 S. E. 1018).

One summoned in aid of an officer is entitled to the same protection as the officer himself, and he need not act in the actual presence of the officer. Robinson, 93 Ga. 77 (18 S. E. 1018).

A person orally summoned to assist an officer in making an arrest should give notice to the one about to be arrested of his authority, and if he has no warrant, he should inform the accused that it had been issued, and where it is. But where the accused knows, or has a reasonable ground to believe that such warrant is issued, a resistance on his part will not be excused by a failure to receive notice. Robinson, 93 Ga. 77 (18 S. E. 1018); Croom, 85 Ga. 718 (11 S. E. 1035).

The mere possession of a warrant does not authorize a private

citizen to make an arrest of the person named therein, unless such. person be properly deputized. Coleman, 121 Ga. 594 (49 S. E. 716).

A de facto marshal stands upon the same footing as to the right to make an arrest as one regularly appointed. McDuffie, 121 Ga. 

580, 583 (49 S. E. 708).

A private detective may arrest for a crime committed in his presence. DuPre, 153 Ga. 798, 819 (113 S. E. 428).

A night watchman of a railroad has only such rights to make an arrest as private citizens. Hickman, 142 Ga. 630 (83 S. E. 508).

Refusal to arrest. Refusal of an officer to execute a warrant is an indictable offense. Ormond, 120 Ga. 916, 917 (13) (48 S. E. 383). 

Arrest on Sunday. Arrests may be made on Sunday. Weldon, 62 Ga. 449 (1). 

Interference with officers.

It is an indictable offense to interfere with an officer in executing a warrant. Ormond, 120 Ga. 916 (13) (48 S. E. 383).

Appointment of peace-officers and detectives. No sheriff, mayor or other person authorized by law to appoint special deputy-sheriffs, constables, marshals, policemen, or other peace-officers, or detectives, to preserve the public peace or detect crime, shall appoint, as such special deputy, special constable, marshal, policeman, or other peace-officer or detective, any person who is not a citizen of this State, and no person shall assume or exercise such functions, powers, duties, or privileges incident and belonging to the office of special deputy-sheriff, special constable, marshal, or policeman, or other peace-officer or detective, without first having received his appointment in writing from the lawfully constituted authorities. 

of the State. § 26-4901. 

(1) Arrest by Private Persons. 

A private person may arrest an offender, if the offense is committed in his presence or within his immediate knowledge; and if the offense is a felony, and the offender is escaping, or attempting to escape, a private person may arrest him upon reasonable and probable grounds of suspicion. § 27-211. Delegal, 109 Ga. 518, 521 (35 S. E. 105).

A private person as well as an arresting officer may arrest an escaped felon without a warrant on a probable ground of suspicion. 

Johnson, 30 Ga. 426; Harper, 129 Ga. 770, 776 (59 S. E. 792).

A private person may arrest one who is indicted for a felony, even

CRIMINAL PROCEDURE 

31 though three years have elapsed between the return of the indictment and the arrest. Snelling, 87 Ga. 50 (13 S. E. 154).

It is the duty of a private person, who is present when a felony is committed, to apprehend the felon, with a view to taking him before a magistrate and, after a felony is committed, any private person may arrest the felon with the same view, upon a reasonable and proper ground of suspicion of his guilt. Long, 12 Ga. 233 (4). But a private person has no right to arrest another for violation of a municipal ordinance committed in his presence, unless the violation of that ordinance is a felony or a misdemeanor. Graham, 143 Ga. 

440, 441 (3-a) (85 S. E. 328).

There is a difference between the power of an officer and that of a private individual to arrest without a warrant. An officer may make an arrest without a warrant if the offense is committed in his presence, or the offender is endeavoring to escape, or for other cause there is likely to be a failure of justice for want of an officer to issue a warrant. A private individual can not make an arrest for a misdemeanor, unless the offense is committed in his presence or within his immediate knowledge. Delegal, 109 Ga. 518 (1), 521 (35 S. E. 105).

Unless properly deputized, a private citizen can not justify an arrest merely because he has in his possession a warrant for the arrest of the person sought to be taken. Coleman, 121 Ga. 594 (3) (49 S. E. 716).

The words "in his presence" and the words "within his immediate knowledge" are synonymous. Piedmont Hotel Company, 9 

Ga. App. 672 (72 S. E. 54).

A private detective who sees a crime committed stands substantially on the basis of an arresting officer. DuPre, 153 Ga. 798, 819 (113 S. E. 428).

The officer or agent of a railroad company, duly authorized to do so, has a right to arrest one who is stealing a ride on the train of said railroad company in violation of the statute. Summers, 118 

Ga. 174 (45 S. E. 27).

It is the duty of an arresting officer to disclose his official character to the person whom he is arresting when he has reason to believe that his official character is unknown to the person about to be arrested. Douglass, 152 Ga. 379 (3) (110 S. E. 168).

Where an official attempts to make an arrest under circumstances which would authorize a peace officer to arrest without a warrant, but would not authorize a private citizen to do so, the officer must

make his identity and official position known to the person about to be arrested, otherwise he would be placed in the same position as a private person. To make an arrest lawful under such circumstances, it is necessary that the person arrested should, in some way, have notice that he is arrested by lawful authority. He may have this notice from the fact that he knows the person making the arrest to be an officer, or by seeing his uniform or badge of office, or by being arrested while committing a breach of the peace, or other crime, or by the person making the arrest giving notice of his purpose and the reason for it, or by being immediately pursued from the scene of his crime. Franklin, 118 Ga. 860, 863 (45 S. E. 698).

If a warrant is shown authorizing the arrest, the presumption is that the arrest was made legally, and for a lawful purpose, and the burden of proof is upon the person asserting the contrary, but whoever arrests or imprisons a person without a warrant has the burden to justify it under one of the exceptions prescribed by law, and the burden of proving that a case lies within the exception rests upon the person making the arrest or inflicting the imprisonment. 

Piedmont Hotel Company, 9 Ga. App. 672, 680 (72 S. E. 51).

Where an innocent bystander is killed, the burden of proof of authority is upon the person attempting the arrest, where the attempted arrest was the cause of the death. McCrackin, 150 Ga. 

718, 723 (105 S. E. 487); O'Connor, 64 Ga. 125, 127. (2) Arrest Without Warrant.

An arrest for a crime may be made by an officer, either under a warrant, or without a warrant, if the offense is committed in his presence, or the offender is endeavoring to escape, or for other cause there is likely to be a failure of justice for want of an officer to issue a warrant. § 27-207. Thomas, 91 Ga. 204, 206 (18 S. E. 

305); Graham, 143 Ga. 440, 441 (2) (85 S. E. 328); Waters, 142 Ga. 

133 (1) (82 S. E. 535).

Crime committed in the officer's presence. An offense is being committed in the presence of the officer, where any of his senses affords him knowledge that the offense is being committed. Ramsey, 92 Ga. 53, 63 (17 S. E. 613). "In his presence" and "within his immediate knowledge" are synonymous. Piedmont Hotel, 9 Ga. App. 672 (4) (72 S. E. 51).

The crime may be committed in the officer's presence so as to authorize an arrest without a warrant whether he knew the full extent of it or not. Smith, 10 Ga. App. 36, 37 (72 S. E. 527).

CRIMINAL PROCEDURE 

33 Where an officer sees. gambling within a house, it is not only his right, but it is his duty to enter the house and make an arrest. Earl, 124 Ga. 28, 29 (2) (52 S. E. 78).

An officer may arrest one without a warrant for wife beating, if he arrives at the scene during the progress of or immediately after the beating, he being attracted thereto by the noise of the disturbance, or the outery of the woman. Ramsey, 92 Ga. 53 (4) (17 S. E. 613).

Though at common law, of which § 27-207 is a codification, an officer may arrest for breach of peace committed in his presence, without a warrant, the arrest must have been made within a reasonable time after the commission of the offense, that is, the officer must immediately set about the arrest, and follow up the effort until the arrest is made. There must be a continued pursuit from the time of the commission of the offense until the apprehension of the offender. Any delay for purposes foreign to the arrest will make the officer a trespasser. Yates, 127 Ga. 813 (56 S. E. 1017).

Where the officers went to defendant's residence for the purpose of arresting him, but did not actually do so until the defendant committed two crimes in their presence, the question of illegal arrest is not involved. Cumbie, 37 Ga. App. 9 (138 S. E. 524).

Using opprobrious words and abusive language to an officer, without provocation, constitutes commission of a crime in the officer's presence, and the officer may arrest such person without a warrant. 

Cumbie, 37 Ga. App. 9 (138 S. E. 524). The fact that the officer went to the place for the purpose and with the intention of making an illegal arrest-immaterial. 

Where officer neglects to make arrest for crime committed in his presence until after he has had ample time to have warrant issued, he can not then make an arrest without a warrant lawfully. Wiggins, 14 Ga. App. 314, 315 (5) (80 S. E. 724).

An officer has no authority, without a warrant, either upon suspicion or information that another is carrying a concealed weapon, to arrest the latter and search his person to ascertain whether he is violating the law. Even if such person is so violating the law, the offense is not, in legal contemplation, committed in the presence of the officer, and such arrest, search and seizure are unauthorized, and are, within the meaning of the Constitution, unreasonable. 

Hughes, 2 Ga. App. 29 (1) (58 S. E. 390); Pickett, 99 Ga. 12 (1) (25 S. E. 608).

An offender endeavoring to escape. An escaped convict may be recaptured by any officer without a warrant. Williford, 121 Ga. 

173 (1) (48 S. E. 962); Harper, 129 Ga. 770 (1) (7) (59 S. E. 792); 

Snelling, 87 Ga. 50 (13 S. E. 154).

An officer has no right to proceed to the extremity of shooting one whom he is attempting to arrest for the violation of a municipal ordinance, in order to prevent his escape, even though the offender can not be taken otherwise. Holmes, 5 Ga. App. 166 (2) (62 S. E. 716).

The right to arrest without warrant a suspected person apparently about to escape is broader in felony than in misdemeanor cases. 

Thompson, 4 Ga. App. 649, 652 (62 S. E. 99).

Where an offender is endeavoring to escape, or has escaped from lawful imprisonment, he may be recaptured without a warrant, regardless whether the offense is a felony or a misdemeanor. Maughon, 7 Ga. App. 660, 666 (67 S. E. 842); Brooks, 114 Ga. 6 (39 S. 

E. 877).

An arresting officer may recapture without a warrant one who deserted from the United States army. Huff, 149 Ga. 139 (99 S. E. 307).

Failure of justice for want of officer to issue a warrant. The mere possibility of there being a failure of justice does not authorize an officer to attempt an arrest for a misdemeanor without a warrant. There must be a likelihood of failure of justice, a probable ground for believing that there will be a failure of justice. Giddens, 152 Ga. 195, 198 (108 S. E. 788).

General. Where an arrest for a past offense is intended, and there is no present emergency, no want of time or opportunity for obtaining a warrant, why should a policeman be allowed to dispense with a warrant when other officers of the law could not? Any information as to the commission of the offense which would serve as a reasonable basis for making an arrest, would serve for suing out a warrant. Thomas, 91 Ga. 204, 207 (18 S. E. 305). The policeman could himself apply for a warrant and obtain it, if the injured party or other person giving information decline to do so, since. the affidavit required to obtain a warrant need not charge the offense absolutely and without qualification, but only to the best of the affiant's knowledge and belief. (Id.) 

A charge of the Court that "the law as a rule does not look with favor upon arrests made without a warrant" is erroneous. Where the law permits an arrest without a warrant, it does not apply,

CRIMINAL PROCEDURE 

35 where it does not permit it, such arrest is illegal. McPherson, 137 

Ga. 129, 131 (5-c) (72 S. E. 948).

Where there is time and opportunity to obtain warrant for a misdemeanor, an officer can not lawfully arrest without a warrant upon information. Thomas, 91 Ga. 204, 205 (18 S. E. 305).

The question whether an arrest is legal or illegal is for the jury, under proper instructions from the Court. West, 155 Ga. 482 (7) (117 S. E. 380).

Felonies. There is a distinction between the authority of an of ficer to arrest without a warrant in cases of felony and of misdemeanor. An officer may arrest one, without a warrant, on a reasonable suspicion of felony. Johnson, 30 Ga. 426 (2); Robinson, 93 

Ga. 77, 87 (18 S. E. 1018).

Where a person is arrested without a warrant on reasonable suspicion of having committed a felony, the arresting officer may subject him to a reasonable search. Thompson, 4 Ga. App. 649 (2) (62 S. E. 99).

Motive. An officer may lawfully arrest his bitterest enemy, or he may unlawfully arrest his best friend. The motive of the officer in making the arrest without warrant has no bearing on the question of legality of the arrest. McDuffie, 121 Ga. 580 (5) (49 

S. E. 708).

Police officers. The legality of an arrest is to be determined by the laws of the State of Georgia, as it is applicable alike to the 

State and municipal arresting officers. Jenkins, 3 Ga. App. 146 (2) (59 S. E. 435). Faulkner, 166 Ga. 645, 666 (144 S. E. 193).

A municipal officer has a right to arrest within the jurisdiction of a municipality, without a warrant, one who has violated an ordinance in his presence, or who is endeavoring to escape. King, 6 Ga. 

App. 332 (1) (64 S. E. 1001).

A police officer may make an arrest without a warrant for a crime committed in his presence, or if the offender is endeavoring to escape, or for other cause there is likely to be a failure of justice for want of an officer to issue a warrant. But there must be an offense actually committed by the party arrested. O'Connor, 64 Ga. 

125 (1); Dixon, 12 Ga. App. 17 (7) (76 S. E. 794).

As a general rule, a municipal peace officer in whose presence a town ordinance has been violated has no lawful authority, without a warrant, to arrest the offender, when he had ample time and opportunity since the commission of the offense to secure a warrant. 

Yates, 127 Ga. 813, 814 (5) (56 S. E. 1017).

Notice of official character. Where an officer is attempting to arrest without a warrant for an alleged misdemeanor, he must give notice of his official character, otherwise the person about to be arrested has a right to resist. Franklin, 118 Ga. 860 (2) (45 S. E. 698).

Posse. A member orally deputized by an officer as "posse" has the same protection as the officer. Phillips, 66 Ga. 755 (1); Robinson, 93 Ga. 77 (1) (18 S. E. 1018).

An officer may deputize another to serve process in his presence, but not otherwise. Hill, 8 Ga. App. 77 (1) (68 S. E. 614).

Peace officers ought to assist each other in making arrests and officer so assisting another is under the same protection as the one attempting to make the arrest. Harrell, 75 Ga. 842 (1).

Recapture. A bail may in person or by duly authorized agent recapture his principal. But the agent must be duly authorized, otherwise the arrest is unlawful. Coleman, 121 Ga. 594 (1) (2) (49 

S. E. 716).

To authorize the rearrest of one who has given bond for appearance to stand preliminary trial for the same offense, forfeiture of bond must be duly declared, and another warrant issued. Sherman, 2 Ga. App. 686 (2) (58 S. E. 1122).

De facto officers. A de facto officer lawfully holding over has the same authority to arrest without warrant as a de lege officer. 

Garrett, 89 Ga. 446 (1) (15 S. E. 533); McDuffie, 121 Ga. 580 (1) (49 S. E. 708).

Possession of warrant. Where the circumstances are such that a lawful arrest can not be made without a warrant, it must be in the possession of the officer, or of another in the neighborhood with whom he is acting in concert. Adams, 121 Ga. 163 (3) (48 S. E. 910).

Attempt to arrest a person, by bailiff on request of justice of the peace of another county, who said that he had issued a warrant against the person, unlawful. Luffman, 166 Ga. 296 (1) (143 S. E. 371).

Resisting unlawful arrest. No person should be punished for resisting or obstructing an illegal arrest. Prichard, 160 Ga. 527, 529 (128 S. E. 655).

Every man, however guilty, has a right to shun an illegal arrest by flight, without becoming thereby a fugitive. Thomas, 91 Ga. 

204, 206 (18 S. E. 805).

CRIMINAL PROCEDURE 

37 Every person has a right to resist an illegal arrest whether attempted by an officer or by a private individual, and, in resistance, may use as much force as is necessary for the purpose, and no more. 

Holmes, 5 Ga. App. 166 (1) (62 S. E. 716); Coleman, 121 Ga. 594 (6) (49 S. E. 716).

Where an officer attempted an illegal arrest, in furtherance of which he shot at the prisoner without justification, and defendant killed officer in resisting such attempted arrest, he is guilty of no offense. Perdue, 5 Ga. App. 821 (1) (63 S. E. 922).

The mere fact of an unlawful arrest will not authorize the killing of the officer. But, if in the progress of the transaction, the officer so acts as to excite in the person sought to be arrested a reasonable fear that a felony is about to be committed upon him, and such person acts under the influence of those fears and not in spirit of revenge, he may protect himself, although it may be necessary to slay the officer. In cases where the circumstances are not such as to justify the killing of the officer, they may be sufficient to reduce the homicide from murder to manslaughter. Norton, 137 Ga. 842 (3) (74 S. E. 759). 

Where an officer attempts an illegal arrest, he does so at his peril. 

Where a person sought to be arrested, resists the same upon the assumption that the arrest is illegal, he does so at his peril. Dixon, 12 Ga. App. 17 (9) (76 S. E. 794).

Excessive force used in repelling unlawful arrest is an unlawful attack. Coleman, 121 Ga. 594 (7) (49 S. E. 716).

Generally it is manslaughter to kill an officer to resist an unlawful arrest. Where the officer is shot, to prevent an illegal arrest, but not killed, prima facie such shooting is not assault with intent to murder, but shooting at another. Jenkins, 3 Ga. App. 146 (1) (59 S. E. 435); Thomas, 91 Ga. 204, 206 (18 S. E. 305); Porter, 124 

Ga. 297 (2) (52 S. E. 283).

One attempting an unlawful arrest, with intent to kill if necessary to make it effectual, and by show of a deadly weapon puts the deceased in fear of his life, and the deceased thereupon fired, he would be guilty of murder if he took the life of the person legally resisting an illegal arrest. Coleman, 121 Ga. 594 (5) (49 S. E. 716).

If an unauthorized person seeks to make an arrest, but does nothing to put the other in real or apparent danger of life, and if mere assault is met by drawing and firing a deadly weapon upon the person making the arrest, the latter may defend himself against

excessive and unjustifiable counter assault. Coleman, 121 Ga. 594 (8) (49 S. E. 716).

In prosecution of one charged with killing officer who was attempting to execute a warrant, warrant apparently legal on its face is admissible in evidence without preliminary proof of prior proceedings attending its issuance. Rushing, 135 Ga. 224 (1) (69 S. E. 171).

A person can use such force in resisting an arrest as is proportionate to that used by the arresting officer, even to the extent of taking his life, but the fact alone that the arrest is illegal does not authorize person about to be arrested to kill officer. However, where such killing is not done in the spirit of revenge, it is manslaughter and not murder. Wall, 153 Ga. 309, 310 (11) (112 S. E. 142).

Chastising prisoners. An officer can only use such force as is necessary to make the arrest effectual, and can not punish a prisoner for insolence. Moody, 120 Ga. 868 (48 S. E. 340).

Selection of judge to try the case. The arresting officer shall carry the prisoner before the most convenient and accessible judicial officer authorized to hear the cause, unless the prisoner shall desire otherwise; in which case, if there be no suspicion of improper motive, the arresting officer shall carry him before some other judicial officer. But in no case has a prisoner the right to select the justice before whom he shall be tried. § 27-208.

Officer may make arrest in any county. An arresting officer may arrest any person charged with crime, under a warrant issued by a judicial officer, in any county of the State, without regard to the residence of said arresting officer; and it is his duty to carry the accused, with the warrant under which he was arrested, to the county in which the offense is alleged to have been committed, for examination before any judicial officer of that county. The county where the alleged offense is committed shall pay the expenses of the arresting officer in carrying the prisoner to the county; and the officer may hold or imprison the defendant long enough to enable him to get ready to carry the prisoner off. § 27-209. Harris, 115 Ga. 767 (42 S. E. 71). 

c. PROCEDURE AFTER ARREST. 

Duty of person arrested. It is the duty of every person arrested under a legal process to quietly submit. The same rule applies where the offense is committed in the presence of the arresting officer. Dixon, 12 Ga. App. 17 (6) (76 S. E. 794).

CRIMINAL PROCEDURE 

39 Duty of person arresting. In every case of an arrest without warrant, the person arresting shall, without delay, convey the of fender before the most convenient officer authorized to receive an affidavit and issue a warrant. And no such imprisonment shall be legal beyond a reasonable time allowed for this purpose. § 27-212. 

The object of an arrest is to carry the prisoner before a magistrate. After a warrant has been issued and the accused has been placed under arrest, a reasonable time will be allowed by the presiding magistrate for making an investigation and procuring evidence in the case. Ocean Steamship Company, 69 Ga. 251, 252.

Temporary imprisonment for a reasonable time may be justified by the circumstances of the case. King, 6 Ga. App. 332 (2) (64 

S. E. 1001).

What constitutes a reasonable time is a question for the jury. 

Ocean Steamship Company, 69 Ga. 251 (9); Harris, 62 Ga. 290 (3). 

Detention over night is not illegal. Johnson, 46 Ga. 80, 84.

Imprisonment and detention of one under arrest beyond a reasonable time is not only illegal but renders the entire transaction, including the arrest, trespass ab initio. Piedmont Hotel Company, 9 Ga. App. 672 (6) (72 S. E. 51); Potter, 77 Ga. 419 (3 S. E. 94).

It is the duty of every person, making an arrest, to deliver the party arrested before an officer authorized to receive an affidavit and issue warrants. This duty is not discharged by delivering the prisoner to a policeman. Harris, 62 Ga. 290 (2); Ocean Steamship 

Company, 69 Ga. 251, 252 (9).

Escaped convict. An escaped convict, arrested on suspicion, can not be unreasonably detained, but must be brought before a magistrate in order that the ground of suspicion be judicially determined. 

Harris, 62 Ga. 290.

Duty of officer arresting. Every officer arresting under a warrant shall exercise reasonable diligence in bringing the person arrested before the person authorized to examine, commit, or receive bail. § 27-210.

What is reasonable diligence, depends upon the peculiar facts of the individual case. The exigencies of the particular case may authorize an officer to imprison the person arrested temporarily and for a reasonable time. King, 6 Ga. App. 332 (64 S. E. 1001); Moses, 6 Ga. App. 251 (64 S. E. 699).

While an officer has authority to imprison a person arrested, before commitment trial, he should not do so arbitrarily and without reasonable cause, but he should exercise reasonable diligence in

bringing the person arrested before a judicial officer, authorized to examine, commit, or receive bail. Moses, 6 Ga. App. 251 (64 S. E. 699). 

2. BONDS. 

S$ 27-901 to 27-906. 

Bail before conviction. An accused is entitled to bail as a matter of right and not as a matter of discretion in all criminal cases, less than capital felonies, before indictment and trial. Habeas corpus will lie where bail is wrongfully refused. Newsome, 151 Ga. 639 

Bail after conviction. Where the defendant was convicted of a felony and sued out a bill of exceptions, it is discretionary with the judge of the Superior Court whether or not bail would be granted. 

The judge has a right to refuse bail after conviction of a felony. 

Vanderford, 126 Ga. 67 (54 S. E. 822); Maddox, 18 Ga. App. 712, 713 (90 S. E. 377); Barnes, 24 Ga. App. 372, 373 (100 S. E. 788). 

Where the judge refused to grant bail, pending appeal, a bill of exceptions from this decision will not lie. Jernagin, 118 Ga. 307 (45 S. E. 411). Discretion of the Court in granting or refusing bond will not be disturbed or controled unless flagrantly abused, where the accused was tried and convicted. Lester, 33 Ga. 192. 

Terms of bail. Where bail is taken prior to a commitment hearing, in order to bind the defendant to appear subsequently before a trial court to answer an indictment for the offense stated in the bond, the condition of the bond should indicate such requirement. 

Fox, 34 Ga. App. 74 (128 S. E. 222).

The bond must show the cause of the arrest. But it need not describe the offense with such particularity as is required in indictments. The denomination of "accessory after the fact" is sufficient. Rogers, 138 Ga. 750 (1) (2) (75 S. E. 1130).

Purpose of bail. The purpose of a bond given in a criminal case is twofold: (1) To prevent punishing the accused before conviction, and (2) to secure his attendance at the time named in the bond. 

Roberts, 32 Ga. App. 339, 340 (123 S. E. 151).

Duty of bail. Failure of the accused to appear in accordance with the bond will not authorize punishment for contempt of court. 

Collins, 32 Ga. App. 450 (123 S. E. 723). 

Where bail is furnished a prisoner to answer one charge, such duty of bail to surrender includes the duty to surrender the prin-

CRIMINAL PROCEDURE 

41 cipal to answer another charge for a lesser offense contained in the greater. Wells, 121 Ga. 368 (5), 372 (49 S. E. 319).

Where the case was duly transferred from the Superior Court to the city court, the sureties were bound for the appearance of the accused in that court. Williams, 77 Ga. 4; Sampson, 147 Ga. 426, 

Before bail in a criminal case can be made liable, the record must show that the principal was called and did not appear. Park, 4 

Ga. 329 (2).

Where, as a matter of fact, the accusation against a principal under bond was called out of its order, and the State failed to announce ready, this is a matter of affirmative defense. Collins, 7 Ga. 

App. 653, 654 (67 S. E. 847).

The bail is not bound to produce his principal until a bill of indictment has been found, where it is conditioned for the appearance of a principal to answer a bill of indictment. Hudson, 91 Ga. 553 (18 S. E. 432).

Discharge of the sureties. Where a criminal recognizance has been forfeited, and a scire facias has issued, the securities of the bond have until the State case against the principal is called at the next term, to produce his body to answer to the charge against him. 

To enter the scire facias on another docket, call it and enter a judgment against the sureties before the call of the criminal case, is illegal. Boswell, 73 Ga. 63.

Where the principal is rearrested under an indictment of a higher grade of crime, growing out of the same transaction for which he was originally arrested, his surety is discharged. Benson, 19 Ga. 

App. 328, 329 (91 S. E. 491).

Where, pending an appeal from judgment on bond, the principal is tried and acquitted, the surety is discharged except for the payment of the costs. Williams, 77 Ga. 4.

Where principal is rearrested on a separate and distinct offense the surety is not discharged, unless custody of the principal by the 

State prevents the surety from producing him. Benson, 19 Ga. 

App. 328, 329 (91 S. E. 491). Distinguishing and modifying rule announced in Cooper, 10 Ga. App. 730 (73 S. E. 1101).

Where first bond was duly forfeited, and rule nisi issued, and scire facias served, and, before term of court to which scire facias was made returnable principal voluntarily appeared in sheriff's office in vacation, paid all costs, and tendered second bond, which was

accepted and approved by the sheriff, sureties on the first bond were discharged. Fleming, 10 Ga. App. 701 (73 S. E. 1074).

Surrender of the principal. The bail may surrender his principal in vacation, or in open court, discharging himself from any liability. Perkins, 1 Ga. App. 250 (1) (58 S. E. 133).

Where the security surrenders the principal, the attention of the court must be called to the presence of the principal, and the intention of the surety to surrender the principal must be understood. 

Perkins, 1 Ga. App. 250 (58 S. E. 133).

The highest evidence of the surrender of the principal by the security is an exoneratur entered upon the minutes. Perkins, 1 Ga. 

App. 250 (1-a) (58 S. E. 133).

A deputy sheriff may receive the surrender of the principal. 

Ward, 62 Ga. 267.

Payment of costs. After a judgment nisi and before final judgment, the payment of the costs is a condition precedent to the surrender of the principal. Ward, 62 Ga. 267.

A motion to vacate a judgment absolute upon the bond, on the ground that it is defective, does not require the payment of the costs. Hardwick, 30 Ga. App. 526, 528 (8) (118 S. E. 575).

Right of the accused to second term. There is no rule giving the defendant the right, as a matter of law, to forfeit his bond at the term of court to which it is made returnable. Roberts, 32 Ga. App. 

339, 342 (123 S. E. 151). 

Sunday. Bond for appearance may be assessed and given on

Sunday, the same being in favor of liberty and charity to a person. in distress. Weldon, 62 Ga. 449 (2). 

3. COMMITMENTS. 

§§ 27-401 to 27-424. 

Justice of the Peace has statutory power to hold a court of inquiry. Ormond, 120 Ga. 916 (48 S. E. 383).

The court of inquiry does not come into existence until a person is legally arrested and brought before the magistrate. Ormond, 120 Ga. 916, 920 (48 S. E. 383). 

Sundays. Court of inquiry can not be held on Sunday. Weldon, 62 Ga. 449 (1).

A magistrate holding inquiry on Sunday violates the penal laws. 

Hayden, 103 Ga. 431, 446 (30 S. E. 287).

CRIMINAL PROCEDURE 

43 

Municipal courts. Municipal courts may bind over offenders for violation of State laws. And this may be done in addition to punishing for violation of municipal ordinances. Newton, 114 Ga. 

833 (1) (40 S. E. 993); Parks, 115 Ga. 242 (41 S. E. 605); Johnson, 6 Ga. App. 779 (2) (65 S. E. 810).

Waiver. Where the defendant is arrested on a warrant issued by a magistrate, and, without demanding committal trial, enters into a bond for his appearance in a court having jurisdiction to try him for the criminal offense, the committal trial is waived. Hopkins, 5 Ga. App. 700 (63 S. E. 719).

Where a bond was taken by a justice of the peace, binding the obligor to appear at the Superior Court to answer a charge to be there preferred against him, it was not essential to a lawful forfeiture of the bond that it should be made to appear that there had been a committing trial or an express waiver thereof by the obligor. 

Bird, 128 Ga. 386 (1) (57 S. E. 777). The execution of such bond is an implied waiver of commitment trial before the magistrate, and such bond is good as a statutory bond, and may be forfeited in the 

Superior Court as such. (Id.)

Statement of defendant. Where the statute provides that the defendant's statement shall be reduced to writing by the magistrates, there is a presumption that such statement made at the committal trial has been reduced to writing. Parol evidence of such statement is inadmissible in the absence of evidence that no such writing was in fact made by the magistrate as provided by law. Oliver, 94 

Ga. 83 (21 S. E. 125); Leggett, 97 Ga. 426 (24 S. E. 165).

A statement made by the defendant at a commitment hearing is admissible against him upon his trial in the Superior Court. Statement reduced to writing at the commitment hearing is the best and highest evidence. Oliver, 94 Ga. 83 (21 S. E. 125); Daniel, 65 Ga. 

199; Dumas, 63 Ga, 600.

Examination of the accused. A justice of the peace has no right to examine the accused at the committal trial. The accused has a right to make such statement as he deems fit for his own defense. 

And where the magistrate, in violation of the law, examined the accused, evidence of such examination, and of what was then said, is inadmissible on the trial in the Superior Court. Cicero, 54 Ga. 156. 

Where committing magistrate assessed cost against the defendant, other than cost of his own witnesses, certiorari will lie to correct such judgment. Hyden, 40 Ga. 476.

Certiorari. Judgment of committing court that the defendant be bound over can not be reviewed by certiorari. Hyden, 40 Ga. 476. 

Binding over witnesses. Every citizen owes to the State the duty of giving in the courts of justice, when he is required to do so, testimony as to such matters as fall within his knowledge, where there is no exemption or privilege protecting the matters from disclosure. 

The courts, as an arm of the State, have the inherent power adequately to control, in the furtherance of justice, officers, parties, jurors, witnesses, and others connected with a pending case. A court, in order to secure the presence of a witness in a criminal case, and to prevent his leaving the jurisdiction of the court prior to the trial, may require that he shall give bail for his appearance, and, in default of his giving bail, cause him to be held in confinement. 

This power probably existed in the courts at common law. This requirement, being harsh and oppressive, should never be resorted to except in extreme cases. It is a matter, however, resting in the sound discretion of the court. Crosby, 8 Ga. App. 463 (69 S. E. 582). 

4. SOLICITOR-GENERAL. 

§§ 24-2908 to 24-2918. 

Disqualifications. Solicitor-general is disqualified, after his term of office expired, from appearing as counsel for a person against whom he has preferred an indictment. Gaulden, 11 Ga. 47.

Solicitor-general can not represent any person, either during or after his term, in a criminal or civil matter growing out of an indictment which he has preferred against him. Conley, 93 Ga. 823 (20 S. E. 762).

Solicitor-general is not disqualified to find indictment against one for receiving stolen goods, although he is attorney for the prosecutor, where no civil action against the defendant is pending at the time when the indictment is returned. Casper, 22 Ga. App. 126, 127 (95 S. E. 524), distinguishing Nichols, 17 Ga. App. 593 (87 S. E. 817).

Solicitor-general is not disqualified in prosecuting a director of a bank, though he be a depositor in the bank. Stapleton, 19 Ga. App. 

36 (1) (90 S. E. 1029); Spence, 20 Ga. App. 61 (1) (92 S. E. 555).

Where solicitor-general signed an indictment in his official capacity, and then signed the same as prosecutor, the indictment is not subject to a plea in abatement on this ground. Pinkney, 22 Ga. 

App. 105 (95 S. E. 539).

45 Where solicitor-general, in his private capacity as attorney at law, is counsel for the plaintiff in a suit for damages, and his fee is contingent or conditional, that is dependent upon his client's recovery of damages from the defendant, he is disqualified by interest from advising with the grand jury as to the finding of a true bill for perjury against a witness for alleged false testimony given by the witness in favor of the defendant in the damage suit, where that cause, at the time of the finding of the indictment, is still pending in the courts. Nichols, 17 Ga. App. 593 (87 S. E. 817).

A city court judge may appoint solicitor pro tem in the absence of a solicitor-general or where solicitor is disqualified. Horton, 11 Ga.

It is not required that the should reside in the circuit.

Solicitors pro tem are appointed for the term only. It is not the duty of a solicitor-general pro tem to represent the State in cases brought to the Supreme Court. Hackey, 15 Ga. 400.

Where solicitor pro tem was appointed in the city court, and a writ of certiorari sued out, which was sanctioned, notice thereof must be given to the solicitor-general. It is not sufficient that such notice was given to solicitor pro tem of the city court. Butts, 90 

Ga. 450 (16 S. E. 96).

Bill of exceptions should be served on the solicitor-general and not on the solicitor pro tem. Hackey, 15 Ga. 400; McColers, 74 Ga. 

411; Patillo, 49 Ga. 172, 173 (3). 

5. GRAND JURY. 

Qualifications of grand jurors. All male citizens of this State above the age of twenty-one years, being neither idiots, lunatics, nor insane, who have resided in the county for six months preceding the time of serving, and who are the most experienced, intelligent, and upright persons, as hereinafter provided, are qualified and liable to

serve as grand jurors, unless exempted by law: Provided, however, that county commissioners, tax receivers, tax collectors, members of the county board of education, county school commissioners, ordinaries, county treasurers shall be incompetent to serve as grand jurors during their respective terms of office. § 59-201. 

Depositors of bank serving on grand jury returning an indictment against a director of a bank-not disqualified. Stapleton, 19 Ga. 

App. 36 (1) (90 S. E. 1029); Bitting, 165 Ga. 55, 62 (139 S. E. 877). 

Person over sixty years of age is not disqualified to serve as a grand juror. Such exemption is a privilege and not bar to his qualifications. Loeb, 75 Ga. 258 (3); Jackson, 76 Ga. 551 (1).

The fact that a member of the grand jury which returned an indictment was a member of the coroner's jury who found that the defendant committed the homicide, disqualifies him. but is not good ground for plea in abatement. Objection should be made before bill is found. Betts, 66 Ga. 508, 509 (6); Lee, 69 Ga. 705 (1).

Where grand juror was removing from the county at the time he served on the grand jury, but has not established residence in the other county, he was qualified to serve. Shirley, 1 Ga. App. 143 (1) (57 S. E. 912).

Objection to grand juror. Demurrer is not the proper method of attacking an indictment on the grounds of the alleged disqualification of a grand juror. Motion to quash or plea of abatement is the proper remedy. Cooper, 106 Ga. 119 (1) (32 S. E. 23).

A special plea upon arraignment that one of the grand jurors who found an indictment was disqualified, is a good plea. Reich, 53 Ga. 

73 (2). But in Simpson, 110 Ga. 249 (1) (34 S. E. 204) the contrary rule is held.

Charge to the grand jury on the ground of disqualification must be made before indictment and the plea of abatement will not be sustained unless it appears that the defendant did not have an opportunity to object before the bill was returned. Folds, 123 Ga. 167 (2) (51 S. E. 305); Stapleton, 19 Ga. App. 36 (1) (90 S. E. 1029); 

Kato, 33 Ga. App. 342 (126 S. E. 266). See also Parris, 125 Ga. 777 (3) (54 S. E. 751); Mize, 135 Ga. 291 (69 S. E. 173).

Irregularity in the appointment of a jury commissioner to revise the list of jurors; omission of the jury commissioners to take and subscribe the oath as provided in the Code, before entering upon the discharge of their duties as commissioners; failure of the clerk of the Superior Court to certify the revised list of jurors, as provided in the Code; exclusion by the jury commissioners of certain

CRIMINAL PROCEDURE 

47 classes of persons (such as all persons over sixty years of age, all ministers of the gospel, all practicing physicians, all justices of the peace and notaries public and ex-officio justices of the peace, and constables, policemen and other arresting officers) from the jury box, failure of the clerk to take and subscribe the oath as prescribed in the Code; and disqualification of grand jurors to return a bill of indictment, on account of having served as jurors at preceding terms of the city court and the superior court of the county,are matters of objection in their nature propter defectum; and when relied on as grounds for showing illegality of the grand jury returning an indictment, all such objections should be made by a proper challenge to the array of the grand jurors before the indictment is found, where the illegality was known, or, if not known by the defendant or his attorney at law before indictment, by plea in abatement to the indictment. Where there is no such challenge or plea in abatement, such questions can not be raised for the first time. after verdict, by motion for a new trial. Lumpkin, 152 Ga. 229, 231 (7) (109 S. E. 664).

Where the accused did not have full notice or opportunity to challenge the grand jury on the ground of disqualification before the indictment is returned, he may do so later. Edwards, 121 Ga. 590, 591 (2) (49 S. E. 674); Parris, 125 Ga. 777 (3) (54 S. E. 751); Mize, 135 Ga. 291 (69 S. E. 173).

After verdict the burden is upon the accused to show that he had no opportunity to object to the disqualified grand juror before indictment. Parris, 125 Ga. 777 (4) (54 S. E. 751); Edwards, 121 Ga. 

590, 591 (2) (49 S. E. 674).

Number of grand jurors. A grand jury shall consist of not less than eighteen nor more than twenty-three persons. § 59-202.

The number of persons composing a grand jury being limited by law to twenty-three, the findings of a body, purporting to act as a grand jury, but consisting of more than twenty-three persons, are void. Evans, 17 Ga. App. 120 (86 S. E. 286). 

Witnesses before grand jury. Witness must be duly sworn in the particular case, before his testimony can be made the basis of an indictment. Lester, 77 Ga. 143; Switzer, 7 Ga. App. 7 (1) (65 S. E. 1079).

A plea in abatement showing that a witness was not sworn must also allege that the indictment was found solely upon the testimony of such witness. Lennard, 104 Ga. 546 (1) (30 S. E. 780).

IP

A substantial compliance with the form of oath given in the statute for the examination of witnesses before the grand jury on either an indictment or a presentment is sufficient. Where there is a substantial difference between the oath prescribed and the one given, it is a ground for quashing the indictment. The following form is prescribed: "The evidence which you shall give to the Grand Jury, on this bill of indictment (or presentment), as the case may be, (here state the case) shall be the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth-so help you God." Ashburn, 15 Ga. 246; Lester, 77 Ga. 

143, 147.

The solicitor-general may be compelled to give testimony upon the trial of a criminal case, as to how a witness was sworn before the grand jury. He is not privileged. Switzer, 7 Ga. App. 7 (2) (65 S. E. 1079).

While the failure to swear a witness before the grand jury might be a sufficient reason for quashing the indictment or presentment founded in part upon the testimony of such witness, if a proper plea in abatement is filed, it is no ground for objection after issue was joined. Nixon, 121 Ga. 144, 145 (4) (48 S. E. 966). 

Impeachment of proceedings. A grand juror can not be sworn to impeach the finding of the grand jury upon which he serves. 

Simms, 60 Ga. 145; Tanner, 163 Ga. 121, 128 (135 S. E. 917).

Grand juror illegally excused. The fact that certain grand jurors were excused without legal reason does not give the accused a ground for a new trial, nor for quashing the indictment, where eighteen jurors return an indictment. Cabaniss, 8 Ga. App. 129 (23) (68 

S. E. 849). 

Judge disqualified. Where the judge who administered an oath to the grand jury was disqualified to preside upon the trial of a particular case, the indictment was nevertheless valid. Cabaniss, 8 Ga. 

App. 129 (6) (68 S. E. 849).

Subpoena duces tecum. In a proper cause subpoena duces tecum may issue in a cause pending before the grand jury or to be brought before that body. Lester, 77 Ga. 143, 144.

Minutes of the grand jury. There is no law requiring the grand jury to keep minutes of its proceedings. Therefore the minutes of the proceedings do not preclude parol evidence as to what transpired in the grand jury room. Thompson, 18 Ga. App. 488 (89 S. 

E. 607).

CRIMINAL PROCEDURE 

49 Change of venue. Where certain investigation has been transferred from one county to another, on a change of venue, and the indictment did not recite such facts, such indictment was nevertheless valid, although it would be a better practice to show such change of venue upon the face of the indictment. Howell, 162 Ga. 

14 (134 S. E. 59); Sallette, 162 Ga. 442 (134 S. E. 68); Sallette, 35 

Ga. App. 658 (134 S. E. 203).

Knowledge of individual grand jurors. It is the duty of a grand juror to bring to the attention of his fellows any matter that has come to his knowledge or which might be given in charge. Groves, 73 Ga. 205 (1-a), 208. 

See also: Indictments, Presentments and Accusations. 

6. INDICTMENTS, PRESENTMENTS AND a. GENERAL. 

ACCUSATIONS. 

There is no difference between an indictment and a presentment, with respect to the requirements of the law in regard to trials under them. Groves, 73 Ga. 205 (1-b); Barlow, 127 Ga. 58, 60 (56 S. E. 131).

The form is substantially the same, whether the grand jury indicts or presents. Barlow, 127 Ga. 58, 60 (56 S. E. 131).

Indictment as evidence of guilt. An indictment is a mere charge or accusation by the grand jury, and is no evidence of guilt. Mc- 

Cray, 134 Ga. 416, 425 (68 S. E. 62).

Distinction between indictment and presentment. In an indictment the accusation is presented by the prosecutor, and in a special presentment it is preferred by the grand jury without a prosecutor. 

Barlow, 127 Ga. 58, 60 (56 S. E. 131).

A presentment is the notice which the grand jury, of its own motion, without the assistance of a prosecutor, take of the violation of law. Progress Club, 12 Ga. App. 174, 177 (76 S. E. 1029).

A special presentment is supposed to originate in the grand jury room, and is drawn by the solicitor-general at the suggestion of the grand jury. The solicitor-general's signature is not indispensable. 

He may authorize another to sign for him. Newman, 101 Ga. 534, 539 (28 S. E. 1005).

The word "indictment" marked on a special presentment does not change its character. Ivey, 23 Ga. 576 (1).

Special presentments are to be treated as indictments. Curtis, 48 

Ga. App. 135 (1) (172 S. E. 99).

Evidence of action of grand jury. The highest evidence of the action of the grand jury in the matter of "true bills" or "no bills' is the entry of their return upon the minutes of the court. Elliott, 1 Ga. App. 113, 114 (2) (57 S. E. 972)..

Two "no bills". Two returns of "no bill" by grand juries, on the same charge or accusation, shall be a bar to any future prosecution for the same offense, either under the same or another name, unless such returns have been procured by the fraudulent conduct of the person charged, on proof of which, or of newly discovered evidence, the judge may allow a third bill to be presented, found, and prosecuted. § 27-702. Elliott, 1 Ga. App. 113 (1) (57 S. E. 972).

Public officers. The grand jury may present public officers for misconduct in office. Groves, 73 Ga. 205 (overruling Hawkins, 54 

Ga. 654 (1)).

Former indictment as defense. The pendency of a former indictment, charging the same offense against the accused as that set out in the indictment upon which he is to be tried, affords no ground for a plea in abatement. Hurst, 11 Ga. App. 754 (76 S. E. 78). The same rule applies to accusations. (Id.)

Accusations. Accusations are not included in the terms "Indictments" and "Presentments." Progress Club, 12 Ga. App. 174, 177 (76 S. E. 1029).

Reconsideration by grand jury. After the grand jury has returned into court a true bill of indictment, and it is docketed, the court takes jurisdiction and the grand jury is without authority to recall the same, erase the entry of "true bill," and make an entry of "no bill." Gibson, 162 Ga. 504, 505 (134 S. E. 326); Gibson, 35 Ga. 

App. 658 (134 S. E. 327).

The grand jury has a right to reconsider its act of finding a "no bill," and to substitute the same with a "true bill." Fuss, 31 Ga. 

App. 147 (120 S. E. 37); McNeely, 25 Ga. App. 328 (1) (103 S. E. 189).

Where the grand jury has found a true bill and subsequently in the general presentments recommend that the indictment be nol prossed, it is within the discretion of the Court whether this recommendation will be followed. Edwards, 121 Ga. 590 (1) (49 S. E. 674).

Constitutional provision. There is no constitutional provision in this State giving the defendant the right to demand indictment by a grand jury as a condition precedent to his being put on trial in a

CRIMINAL PROCEDURE 

51 criminal case. In the Superior Court there is a uniform statutory provision for indictments in all cases. In city courts the general and special acts govern. Hopkins, 5 Ga. App. 699, 700 (63 S. E. 718). 

There is nothing in the Constitution of the United States, or the State of Georgia, guaranteeing one charged with a misdemeanor an indictment by a grand jury. Green, 119 Ga. 120 (2) (45 S. E. 990); 

Gordon, 102 Ga. 673 (29 S. E. 444).

Acts of legislatures creating city courts, and providing that an accused of a misdemeanor shall have no right to demand an indictment-are constitutional. Moore, 124 Ga. 30 (52 S. E. 81); Darden, 74 Ga. 842; Maples, 43 Ga. App. 295 (158 S. E. 762); Haire, 43 Ga. 

App. 105 (157 S. E. 909).

In county courts, upon a charge of misdemeanor, demands for indictments must be in writing. Oral demand is not sufficient. Shivers, 123 Ga. 538 (1) (51 S. E. 596).

Procedure before finding indictment. As a prerequisite to a valid testimony before a grand jury there must be before the grand jury some pleading, either in the form of a bill of indictment, or a special presentment, charging a named person with a specific offense, and upon which particular case the witness must be sworn. Switzer, 7 

Ga. App. 7, 11 (65 S. E. 1079).

A bill of indictment can not go before the grand jury without the endorsement of the prosecutor, who, in certain cases, may be liable for cost, or for damage, if the prosecution be malicious, and the judge of the Superior Court has no power to place an indictment before the grand jury. Thompson, 109 Ga. 272, 276 (34 S. E. 579).

The English practice of drawing an indictment was to engross the indictment first on parchment, called "bill," and place it before the grand jury, and after evidence was heard the grand jury endorsed it as a "true bill" or as a "non bill." But in this country the common practice is for the grand jury to investigate any alleged crime, no matter how, and by whom suggested to them, and, after determining that the evidence is sufficient to justify putting the party suspected of a crime on trial, to direct the preparation of a formal charge of indictment. Barlow, 127 Ga. 58, 59 (56 S. E. 131).

If an oath of the witnesses sworn before the grand jury is materially different from the one prescribed by the Code, the indictment or presentment should be quashed upon motion. Whether special presentment, or bill of indictment, the law prescribes the same oath

to be administered to the witness before the grand jury; and giving to each word in this oath its proper significance, the conclusion is irresistible that there can be no valid indictment or special presentment by the grand jury except in a particular case, charging a named party with a specified offense. To swear a witness generally is not sufficient. Switzer, 7 Ga. App. 7, 10, 11 (65 S. E. 1079).

The right to question a witness before the grand jury is limited to the special case upon which he is sworn, and the grand jury has no right to find any bill or to make any special presentment except upon the testimony of a witness sworn in a particular case in which the party is charged with a specified offense. Switzer, 7 Ga. App. 

7, 11 (65 S. E. 1079).

Sufficiency of evidence before the grand jury. Plea in abatement on the ground that there was not sufficient evidence before the grand jury to make out of prima facie case and to warrant an indictment is properly overruled. The courts will not test the sufficiency of the evidence before the grand jury. Powers, 172 Ga. 1 (157 S. E. 195).

Number of indictments adopted at once. It is not within the power of the grand jury to adopt on motion at one and the same time several indictments against different persons and for different offenses and without a separate hearing of testimony in each case. 

Evans, 17 Ga. App. 120 (3) (86 S. E. 286).

Failure of grand jury to act. The fact that the grand jury has made a return of a "no bill" or failed to find a bill of indictment against a person does not prevent the resubmission and finding another bill for the same offense by the same or another grand jury. 

McNeely, 25 Ga. App. 328 (1) (103 S. E. 189).

Returning bills. In Georgia bills are returned, whether they are "true bills" or "no bills." Barlow, 127 Ga. 58, 61 (56 S. E. 131).

The findings of the grand jury should be returned in open court, whether indictments or presentments. The proper practice is to return bills through the sworn bailiff, in open court. Danforth, 75 

Ga. 614; Sampson, 124 Ga. 776, 778, 779 (53 S. E. 332).
