Indictments returned to the clerk of the Superior Court, while court is not in session,-is defective, and a plea of abatement is the proper remedy. Sampson, 124 Ga. 776 (53 S. E. 332).

Solicitor-general has no legal authority to return to court a special presentment or indictment. Bowen, 81 Ga. 482 (8 S. E. 736).

CRIMINAL PROCEDURE 

53 

b. FORMAL REQUISITES. 

Sufficiency. An indictment, following substantially the language of the statute is sufficient. Lenhardt, 37 Ga. App. 41, 43 (138 S. 

E. 590).

One accused of a crime has a right, if he demands it by timely demurrer, to have an accusation perfect in form and in substance. 

Harris, 37 Ga. App. 113 (138 S. E. 922); Lanier, 5 Ga. App. 472 (2) (63 S. E. 536); Gazaway, 9 Ga. App. 194, 197 (70 S. E. 978).

The facts set forth in the indictment or accusation determine the offense charged therein. Crummey, 37 Ga. App. 149 (139 S. E. 131).

If, taking the facts alleged in the indictment as premises, the guilt of the accused follows as a legal conclusion, the indictment is good. 

Kidd, 39 Ga. App. 30 (146 S. E. 35); Chelsey, 121 Ga. 340, 342 (49 

S. E. 258); Newman, 63 Ga. 533, 534.

It is not the name, but the description of the crime which characterizes the offense charged. Accordingly, where the indictment designated the offense as a misdemeanor, and the acts therein charged constitute a felony, it will be considered as charging a felony. 

Pratt, 38 Ga. App. 114 (1) (142 S. E. 903); Crummey, 37 Ga. App. 

149 (139 S. E. 131); Cabaniss, 8 Ga. App. 129, 135 (68 S. E. 849).

The indictment need not name the crime by a specific name. If the description of the crime is sufficient, the indictment will be upheld. De Witt, 27 Ga. App. 644 (3) (109 S. E. 681).

Every indictment should be so definite in its allegations as to enable the person accused to prepare his defense. Burbank, 22 Ga. 

App. 646, 647 (96 S. E. 1043).

A defendant, who makes a timely objection, is entitled to have an indictment perfect as to the essential elements of time and place of the commission of the offense. Bailey, 65 Ga. 410, 411; Harris, 58 Ga. 332 (2), 333; Newsome. 2 Ga. App. 392, 394 (58 S. E. 672); 

Adkins, 103 Ga. 5, 6 (29 S. E. 432).

The requisite of a valid indictment, as to form, is that the offense with which the accused is charged be so stated as to give him ample opportunity to prepare for his defense. Dean, 9 Ga. App. 303, 304 (71 S. E. 597); Roughlin, 17 Ga. App. 205 (86 S. E. 452).

Every indictment will be deemed sufficiently technical and correct, which states the offense in the language of the Code, or so plainly that the nature of the offense charged may be easily understood by the jury. Camp, 3 Ga. 417 (1); Knowles, 166 Ga. 182 (1) (142 S. E. 676); Roughlin, 17 Ga. App. 205, 207 (86 S. E. 452); Cook, 22 Ga. App. 770 (1) (97 S. E. 264).

Every indictment is sufficiently technical if it states the offense so plainly that a man of ordinary capacity would readily understand it. Stephen, 11 Ga. 225 (17). It is sufficient if it describes the offense so plainly as to make it intelligible to the jury. Johnson, 8 

Ga. 453, 457.

The rule is not intended to dispense with the substance of good pleading, nor to deny to one accused of a crime the right to know enough of the particular facts constituting the alleged offense to be able to prepare for trial, nor to deprive him of the right to have an indictment perfect as to the essential elements of the crime charged. Brown, 116 Ga. 559, 562 (42 S. E. 795); Amorous, 1 Ga. 

App. 313 (57 S. E. 999); Burkes, 7 Ga. App. 39, 40 (65 S. E. 1091); 

Snell, 13 Ga. App. 158, 161 (79 S. E. 71).

If the nature and the circumstances of the charge can not be easily understood, a criminal accusation may be defective, even though it be stated in the precise language of the statute. Roughlin, 17 Ga. 

App. 205, 207 (86 S. E. 452).

An indictment should leave nothing to inference or implication, but should be plainly and easily understood. Locke, 3 Ga. 534, 539; 

Johnson, 90 Ga. 441 (16 S. E. 92).

An indictment need not specify the statute upon which it is founded. Crabb, 88 Ga. 584 (15 S. E. 455).

An indictment ought not be ambiguous. If really equivocal, it will be inadequate. Franklin, 85 Ga. 570, 572 (11 S. E. 876).

The description of the offense contained in the indictment must be complete. If an essential element of the offense is missing from the indictment, there can be no conviction. O'Brien, 109 Ga. 51 (35 S. E. 112).

No person can be convicted of any offense not charged in the indictment. Arnold, 30 Ga. 517; Tarpe, 95 Ga. 457 (20 S. E. 217); 

Goldin, 104 Ga. 549 (30 S. E. 749).

The mere characterization of an act which may be lawfully committed as unlawful does not suffice to so inform one accused of a crime of the nature of the offense with which he is charged as to enable him to prepare for trial. To charge that an act intrinsically lawful was done unlawfully without more, is not a statement of a fact, but a mere conclusion of the pleader. Dukes, 9 Ga. App. 537 

An indictment is not defective because it alleged that the crime was a "felony," whereas it was a "misdemeanor.' Lummus, 17 

Ga. App. 414 (1-a) (87 S. E. 147).

CRIMINAL PROCEDURE 

55 Verbal inaccuracies. Though, by reason of verbal inaccuracies, an indictment may be in part unintelligible, yet where, either by disregarding the unintelligible portion as surplusage, or by considering it along with the rest of what is said, the language of the indictment plainly, clearly, definitely, and accurately charges a particular offense, it is not subject to be quashed on demurrer. Mixon, 7 Ga. App. 805 (1) (68 S. E. 315).

Offense may be committed in several ways. One accused of an offense which may be committed in more than one way is entitled to a statement of the facts relied on to put him upon reasonable notice as to what he is called upon to meet. This is an exception to the rule that an accusation is considered sufficiently specific if it alleges the violation in the language of the Code. Langston, 109 

Ga. 153 (35 S. E. 166); Roughlin, 17 Ga. App. 205, 207 (86 S. E. 452).

Generic terms. Where the definition of the offense includes generic terms, it is not sufficient that the indictment shall charge the offense in the same generic terms as in the definition, but it must state the species; it must descend to particulars. Burkes, 7 Ga. 

App. 39, 42 (65 S. E. 1091); Roughlin, 17 Ga. App. 205, 207 (86 S. 

E. 452). 

Exceptions in the statute. Where the statute provides in general terms that the commission of a given act by any person shall constitute a penal offense, and then exempts a certain class of people, the indictment need not negative that the accused belong to the exempted class, this being a matter of defense. But where the statute. provides that the act is criminal only where it is committed by a special class of persons, the indictment must show that the accused belongs to the class of persons so specified. Kitchens, 116 Ga. 847 (43 

S. E. 256); Herring, 114 Ga. 96 (39 S. E. 866).

Where certain exceptions and provisos appear in the statute, the indictment must negative the same, otherwise it is fatally defective. 

But where such exception appears in the clause designating punishment, or where the statute indicates that the exception provides merely a defense, it need not be negatived in the indictment. Tigner, 119 Ga. 114 (1) (45 S. E. 1001); Oglesby, 121 Ga. 602 (2) (49 S. E. 

706); Dukes, 9 Ga. App. 537 (1) (71 S. E. 921).

As a rule, an exception, or proviso in the statute, which withdraws from the operation of the enacting clause defining the offense certain limited classes of persons or things, and which constitutes no part of the definition of the offense, need not be negatived in the in-

dictment, charging the accused in the language of the statute with a violation of its terms. Blocker, 12 Ga. App. 81 (1) (76 S. E. 784).

Accessories. In an indictment of an accessory before the fact it is not necessary to state the manner of committing the offense. 

Snell, 13 Ga. App. 158 (1) (79 S. E. 71).

Evidence. It is never necessary to allege in an indictment mere matter of evidence, or the details of the alleged offense, unless it alters the offense. Snell, 13 Ga. App. 158, 162 (79 S. E. 71); Minter, 104 Ga. 743, 748 (30 S. E. 989).

A defective indictment can not be helped out by evidence at the trial, nor aided by argument and inference. O'Brien, 109 Ga. 51, 52 (1) (35 S. E. 112).

Repealed statute. Where the statute has been repealed, the indictment must charge that the offense was committed prior to the repeal. Draper, 6 Ga. App. 12 (2) (64 S. E. 117).

Intent. Where there is not a complete act charged, but an attempt only, in which the intent is a material part of the crime, such intent must be charged in the indictment. Chelsey, 121 Ga. 340 (1) (49 S. E. 258). But where the act is completed, the law presumes the intent, and it need not be charged, unless the intent is a material and integral part of the crime. Chelsey, 121 Ga. 340 (49 S. E. 258); 

Wood, 46 Ga. 322.

Name and description of the accused. Where the true name of the accused is known it must be alleged in the indictment. The surname must be alleged and its omission from the indictment is fatal. 

Culpepper, 173 Ga. 799 (161 S. E. 623).

The sole object of the description of the accused in an indictment is to identify him as the one to be tried. Stinchcomb, 119 Ga. 442 (46 S. E. 639).

A person may be properly indicted under a name by which he is generally known and called, whether this be his true name or not. 

Wilson, 69 Ga. 224 (1); Roland, 127 Ga. 401, 402 (56 S. E. 412).

The surname of the defendant must be alleged in the charging part of the accusation, and its omission therefrom is a fatal defect. 

Culpepper, 173 Ga. 799 (1) (161 S. E. 623).

It is a better practice to set forth the full name of the accused. 

Eaves, 113 Ga. 749, 755 (39 S. E. 318).

It is no ground for complaint that the initials of the accused are stated instead of his Christian name, where such initials are true and correct. Eaves, 113 Ga. 749 (39 S. E. 318); Wiggins, 80 Ga. 468, 470 (5 S. E. 503).

CRIMINAL PROCEDURE 

57 

Where only the initials of the Christian name are known, it is better practice to allege in the indictment that the full name is to the grand jurors unknown. Wiggins, 80 Ga. 468, 470 (5 S. E. 503).

It is no ground for a plea of abatement that the initials of the defendant were transposed, the proper initials being used in different order, and a demurrer to such plea should be sustained. Timberlake, 100 Ga. 66 (27 S. E. 158).

Failure to designate a middle name or middle initial is immaterial. Veal, 116 Ga. 589 (4) (42 S. E. 705).

A person may be indicted under a warrant, that merely describes his person, the color of his eyes and hair, his complexion, height, weight, etc., where his name is unknown, and he may be indicted and convicted under such description. Wiggins, 80 Ga. 468, 470 

Color of the accused. An indictment against a Negro need not describe him as a colored person. Unless the color of the defendant is material to the issue, such as a charge of intermarriage between the races, it need not be alleged in the indictment. Taylor, 44 Ga. 263.

Residence of the accused. The residence of the defendant is wholly immaterial and need not be alleged in the indictment. Studstill, 7 Ga. 2, 15; Washington, 113 Ga. 698 (39 S. E. 294).

Names interchanged. Where, in drawing the indictment, the prosecutor's name is inserted, by mistake, for the one of the accused, the error is fatal. Culpepper, 173 Ga. 799 (161 S. E. 623).

Name of injured party. For the protection of the accused it is necessary that the person injured should be referred to by his correct name, if it be known, or by some name by which he is commonly known and generally called. Irwin, 117 Ga. 722 (2) (45 S. E. 59).

Where the person injured is known by two names in the community where he resides, either name may be alleged in the indictment. 

Hainey, 107 Ga. 711 (33 S. E. 418); Johnson, 46 Ga. 269; Jones, 63 

Ga. 456.

Where the name of the company imports a corporation, it need not be alleged in the indictment that it is in fact a corporation. 

Gray, 6 Ga. App. 428 (2-b) (65 S. E. 191).

Where the ownership of the goods stolen is laid in a partnership, the names of the partners must be alleged. Failure to do so is fatal. 

Buffington, 124 Ga. 24 (2) (52 S. E. 19).

The name of a corporation as laid in the indictment need not be proved verbatim et literatim. (Italics by the Court.) Identity is the important question. Jackson, 76 Ga. 551.

Where the name of the injured party is known, it must be alleged. 

But where it is unknown, the indictment may state that the true name is unknown to the grand jurors. In such case testimony showing the true name of the party is admissible. Nelms, 84 Ga. 466 (1) (10 S. E. 1087); Rouse, 4 Ga. 136, 141.

When only part of the name of the injured party is known, the indictment must give that part, stating that the balance is unknown. 

Eaves, 113 Ga. 749, 755 (39 S. E. 318).

Unless the evidence shows that the person designated in the indictment to have been injured was a different person from the one proven, the question of the identity is for the jury. McLain, 71 Ga. 

279; Robinson, 68 Ga. 833; Jones, 65 Ga. 147 (3).

The name by which the deceased person was generally known is the name which should be alleged in the indictment, though he might have had another name also. Jones, 65 Ga. 147 (3).

Misnomer. A plea of misnomer should state the true name of the accused, that he had never been known by any other name than that, and that he was not known and called by the name under which he was indicted. § 27-1505.

A plea of misnomer is fatally defective when it does not allege that the defendant was not known and called by the name under which he was indicted. Wilson, 69 Ga. 224, 234; Roland, 127 Ga. 

401, 402 (56 S. E. 412).

The rule of misnomer operates alike where a corporation is alleged. The true question is, does the indictment sufficiently describe the artificial person for identification. (1) (16 S. E. 205); Jackson, 76 Ga. 551, 567 (6). 

Rogers, 90 Ga. 463

Where an accused person is indicted with an alias under more than one name, a special plea of misnomer to be good must aver unequivocally that he has never been known by either of the names set out in the indictment, and that neither is his true name. Stinchcomb, 119 Ga. 442 (46 S. E. 639).

Where by mistake in drawing an accusation a named person is charged as the perpetrator of an offense instead of the person who in fact committed the same, such error is fatal and incurable, and the accusation is null and void. Culpepper, 173 Ga. 799 (161 S. E. 623). 41

CRIMINAL PROCEDURE 

59 99 Where the name of the defendant, as stated in the indictment, and the name of the defendant, as generally used, were "idem sonans, a plea of misnomer should be overruled. Roland, 127 Ga. 401 (56 

S. E. 412).

The question whether one name is idem sonans with another is not a question of spelling, but of pronunciation, depending less upon rule than upon usage. The term "idem sonans" does not mean that the names are pronounced precisely alike, but only that their pronunciations are so nearly alike that when one of them is uttered it may be readily taken for the other. Roland, 127 Ga. 401 (45 S. E. 412).

Under the doctrine of "idem sonans," if two names, although spelled differently, sound alike, they are to be regarded as the same. 

Great latitude is allowed in the spelling and pronunciation of proper names, and in all legal proceedings, whether civil or criminal, if two names, as commonly pronounced in the English language, are sounded alike, a variance in their spelling is immaterial. Webb, 149 Ga. 211 (1) (99 S. E. 630); Biggers, 109 Ga. 105 (34 S. E. 210); 

Washington, 113 Ga. 698 (39 S. E. 294).

The question of idem sonans may be determined either by pronunciation, or by spelling, or both. Lovett, 9 Ga. App. 232 (1) (70 S. 

E. 989).

Where the writing in the indictment is somewhat illegible or unintelligible, the ruling of the presiding judge that the name in which the accused is charged is the same as the one he admits to be his true name, is final, where it can be said that it reasonably represents the true name of the accused. Gunn, 10 Ga. App. 819 (74 S. E. 312). 

The following names have been held idem sonans: 

Hudson and Hutson,-Chapman, 18 Ga. 736 (1). 

Jeffers and Jeffries, Jeffries, 75 Ga. 230 (2). 

Biggers and Bickers,-Biggers, 109 Ga. 105 (34 S. E. 210). 

Surrens, Surrena and Serena,-Washington, 113 Ga. 698 (39 S. E. 294). 

Witt and Wid,-Veal, 116 Ga. 589 (3) (42 S. E. 705). 

Gittings and Giddans,-Woody, 113 Ga. 927 (39 S. E. 297). 

Lovett and Levatte,-Lovett, 9 Ga. App. 232 (1) (70 S. E. 989). 

Maria and Marie,-Watkins, 18 Ga. App. 500 (89 S. E. 624). 

Welch and Welsh,-Webb, 149 Ga. 211 (1) (99 S. E. 630). 

Ila and Ira,-Roberts, 40 Ga. App. 732 (1) (151 S. E. 240).

The rule of "idem sonans" is no longer the infallible test in settling the question as to variance between allegata and probata. "Identitate personae" and not "identitate nominis" is and should

always have been the true and only issue. Dees, 41 Ga. App. 321 (7-a) (152 S. E. 913); Roland, 127 Ga. 401, 403 (45 S. E. 412); Chapman, 18 Ga. 736.

Misnomer may be taken advantage of by a plea of abatement before arraignment. It is too late after conviction or a plea of guilty. 

Pulliam, 140 Ga. 864 (1) (80 S. E. 315). plea of misnomer.

Whether two names are idem sonans may be decided by the Court as a matter of law. This may be done where a demurrer is filed to a 

Veal, 116 Ga. 589 (3), 591 (42 S. E. 705). Or the Court may charge the jury that two names are or are not idem sonans, as a matter of law. Webb, 149 Ga. 211 (1) (99 S. E. 630).

The ruling of the Court upon a plea of abatement setting up "misnomer can not be made ground of a motion for a new trial. 

Wilkinson, 18 Ga. App. 330 (1) (89 S. E. 460). 

Indictment subject to two constructions. Of two permissible constructions the courts will adopt that which sustains rather than that which defeats the indictment. Franklin, 85 Ga. 570, 572 (11 S. E. 876). 

Venue. Where an indictment was headed: "State of Georgia,

Bacon County," this was sufficient to show the county for which the grand jurors were drawn and served, and of what county they were. 

Odum, 21 Ga. App. 310 (1) (94 S. E. 257); Reed, 148 Ga. 18 (1) (95 

S. E. 692); Stevens, 76 Ga. 96.

Formal parts. Where indictment reversed the wording of the statute and alleged that the grand jurors were "sworn, chosen and selected" for the county, the irregularity is immaterial. Wesley, 65 Ga. 731 (2).

An indictment should be "in the name and in behalf of the citizens of Georgia." If these words are omitted, on exception taken at the proper time, the indictment will be quashed. Horne, 37 Ga. 80 (1). 

The legislature has power to prescribe a particular form for an indictment by the grand jury. Hardin, 106 Ga. 384 (32 S. E. 365).

Names of grand jurors. The names of all grand jurors who pass upon the bill should be inserted in the body of the indictment. Williams, 107 Ga. 721 (1) (33 S. E. 648); Taylor, 121 Ga. 362, 364 (49 S. 

E. 303). A failure to comply with this rule requires that the indictment be quashed on motion. Willerson, 14 Ga. App. 451 (81 S. E. 391).

It is sufficient if the initials of the grand jurors are given. Minor, 63 Ga. 318 (1).

CRIMINAL PROCEDURE 

61 There is no statutory requirement that one of the grand jurors shall be designated as foreman. Taylor, 121 Ga. 362, 364 (49 S. E. 303).

Term of court. It is not necessary that an indictment or presentment shall show upon its face the term at which it is found. It is sufficient if this fact appears upon the back of the indictment or presentment, where the return of the grand jury is entered. Nixon, 121 Ga. 144 (1) (48 S. E. 966).

Signatures. There is no positive law requiring the foreman that he should sign an indictment. McAllister, 2 Ga. App. 656 (58 S. E. 

1110); But it is better practice. Barlow, 127 Ga. 58, 59 (56 S. E. 131).

An accusation in the county court must be signed by the prosecutor. Smith, 63 Ga. 168 (2).

Solicitor-general need not sign a special presentment, and at any event where his signature is placed there by his authority, it is sufficient. Newman, 101 Ga. 534 (4) (28 S. E. 1005).

An indictment, not signed by the solicitor-general is not subject to attack by the accused because not so signed. It is sufficient authentication of a paper, as an indictment, where the foreman of the grand jury signs it, and the words "True Bill" are entered thereon. 

White, 27 Ga. App. 769 (1) (109 S. E. 917). 

The prosecutor need not sign a special presentment. Switzer, 28 

Ga. App. 747 (2) (113 S. E. 55).

Conclusion. Where the formal conclusion "contrary to the laws of said State, the good order, peace and dignity thereof" is omitted, a special demurrer pointing out the defect should be sustained. 

Hardin, 106 Ga. 384 (32 S. E. 365).

Time. The time when the offense was committed is, as a rule, immaterial. It must have been before the indictment was found, and within the period of limitations. Hollingsworth, 7 Ga. App. 16, 18 (65 S. E. 1077).

The indictment must show upon its face that the crime was committed before it was found, and within the statutory period of time. 

The burden of proving these allegations is upon the State. Askew, 3 Ga. App. 79 (59 S. E. 311); Tharpe, 2 Ga. App. 649 (58 S. E. 1070).

However, a defect of this character must be taken advantage of before conviction. Motion in arrest of judgment will not lie. Adkins, 103 Ga. 5 (1) (29 S. E. 432).

The State, as a rule, is not restricted to the date alleged in the indictment; and a conviction for a crime is authorized, where the of-

fense is shown to have been committed on any day, prior to the affidavit upon which the indictment is based and the indictment which is within the statute of limitations. Cripe, 4 Ga. App. 832 (62 S. E. 

567); Wheeler, 4 Ga. App. 325 (61 S. E. 409); Shealey, 16 Ga. App. 

191, 192 (84 S. E. 839); Grayson, 39 Ga. App. 673 (148 S. E. 309).

An indictment must allege a certain time within the statute of limitations. Adkins, 103 Ga. 5 (29 S. E. 432).

Day and month must be alleged in addition to the year. Bailey, 65 Ga. 410; Braddy, 102 Ga. 568 (27 S. E. 670); Walker, 12 Ga. App. 

91 (76 S. E. 762).

Ordinarily when a month is referred to, it is presumed to be of the current year. Tipton, 119 Ga. 304 (46 S. E. 436); Givens, 105 Ga. 

843 (32 S. E. 341); Goldberg, 22 Ga. App. 122 (95 S. E. 541).

Where the date on which the offense is charged to have been committed is material to the issue, it must be proved as alleged. Green, 6 Ga. App. 324 (3) (64 S. E. 1121); Draper, 6 Ga. App. 12 (64 S. E. 117).

The day on which the offense was committed may be proved by circumstantial evidence. Tipton, 119 Ga. 304 (46 S. E. 436); Goldberg, 22 Ga. App. 122 (95 S. E. 541).

Place. The indictment must allege the county where the crime was committed. It must be the county of the prosecution. Conley, 83 Ga. 496, 497 (10 S. E. 123).

Where the caption in the indictment shows the county, a subsequent allegation that the crime was committed "in the county aforesaid" is sufficient. Thomas, 71 Ga. 44 (3).

As a rule no locality, except the venue, need be alleged. Hall, 120 Ga. 142 (2) (47 S. E. 519).

Where the character, description or location of the place is an essential element of the crime, it must be alleged with sufficient particularity. Burkes, 7 Ga. App. 39, 42 (65 S. E. 1091); Morrow, 17 

Ga. App. 116 (1) (86 S. E. 280).

If the criminality of the act depends upon the place where it is committed, the allegation of the place is material and a variance between the allegation and the proof is fatal. Johnson, 1 Ga. App. 

Description. The description of a thing must be always one of degree. Certainty to a reasonable intent is all that the law requires. 

Bone, 120 Ga. 866 (1) (48 S. E. 356).

Presumption. An indictment duly returned as true, with proper indorsement signed by the foreman of the grand jury, is presumed

CRIMINAL PROCEDURE 

63 to have been regularly found. Tanner, 163 Ga. 121 (1) (135 S. E. 917).

Surplusage. An indictment will be upheld, if otherwise sufficient, although it may contain unnecessary and immaterial allegations. 

Smith, 39 Ga. App. 552 (1) (147 S. E. 781).

Allegations in the indictment wholly foreign to any element in the offense charged may be disregarded as surplusage and need not be proved. The rule is otherwise as to averments which are descriptive of some element in the offense though more precise and detailed than absolutely necessary. Shrouder, 121 Ga. 615 (1) (49 S. E. 702).

Allegations in the indictment which are too general and indefinite to set forth a crime may be treated as surplusage, if there are other averments in the indictment which sufficiently allege the commission of the offense. Elsbery, 12 Ga. App. 86 (76 S. E. 779).

If evidence can be offered in support of an allegation in the indictment, the allegation can not be rejected as surplusage. Henderson, 113 Ga. 1148, 1149 (39 S. E. 446).

No averment can be rejected as surplusage which is descriptive either of the offense or of the manner in which it was committed. 

Henderson, 113 Ga. 1148, 1149 (39 S. E. 446).

All necessary allegations in the indictment must be proved as alleged, although they are unnecessarily minute in their description. 

Hightower, 39 Ga. App. 674 (2) (148 S. E. 300).

Averments or descriptions in an indictment, although not necessary in the first instance, must be proved as alleged, whenever a failure of the evidence to conform to the descriptive averments might put the accused again in jeopardy for the same offense. Often an indictment contains averments not required by way of description, but which, having been placed therein, become such a part of the indictment, as framed, that they may not be rejected as surplusage. If the entire averment of which the descriptive matter is a part may be omitted, or can be rejected as surplusage, the descriptive matter falls with it and need not be proved. Sparks, 48 Ga. 

App. 498, 504 (173 S. E. 216).

Duplicity. Separate and distinct offenses can not be embraced in one count in the same indictment. Mitchell, 6 Ga. App. 554 (1) (65 S. E. 361); Long, 12 Ga. 293.

Offenses of the same nature and differing only in degree may be joined in the same count of the same indictment. Mitchell, 6 Ga. 

App. 554 (1) (65 S. E. 361). Or in separate counts in the same

indictment. Long, 12 Ga. 293 (3); Thomas, 59 Ga. 784; Lampkin, 87 Ga. 516 (2) (13 S. E. 523); Harris, 1 Ga. App. 136 (1) (57 S. E. 937). 

Where the offense may be committed in one of several ways not repugnant to each other, a count is not demurrable because it charges that the act was done in several of the ways prohibited by the statute. Cody, 118 Ga. 784 (1) (45 S. E. 622).

The State can not be required to elect for which particular act it will ask a conviction, and proof of any one of the prohibited acts is sufficient to convict. Cody, 118 Ga. 784 (45 S. E. 622); 

Roddenberry, 37 Ga. App. 359 (2) (140 S. E. 386); Mills, 41 Ga. 

App. 834 (155 S. E. 104).

Where the various acts, taken together, will constitute but one offense, they may be charged in one count. Johnson, 125 Ga. 243 (54 S. E. 184); Alsobrook, 126 Ga. 100 (1) (54 S. E. 805); Lawrence, 10 Ga. App. 786, 788 (74 S. E. 300). 

See also: Joinder of Parties, Offenses, Counts.

Charging in the alternative. Where the descriptive terms relating to any material allegation are set forth in an alternative form, the indictment is fatally defective, and subject to demurrer. Jackson, 76 Ga. 551; Henderson, 113 Ga. 1148 (39 S. E. 446); Whitaker, 11 Ga. App. 208 (5) (75 S. E. 258).

Where the statute declares that a criminal act may be committed in various ways, using the word "or," the indictment may allege in a single count that the defendant did as many of the forbidden things as the pleader chooses, but it must employ the conjunction "and" where the statute has "or," without being double. In such cases proof of any one of the offenses will support a conviction. 

Southern Express Co., 1 Ga. App. 700 (4) (58 S. E. 67); Eaves, 113 

Ga. 749, 756 (39 S. E. 318).

Where the indictment charges the offense disjunctively, using the word "or," it is fatally defective. Sanders, 86 Ga. 717 (12 S. E. 

1058); Brand, 112 Ga. 25 (37 S. E. 100); Lawrence, 10 Ga. App. 

786, 788 (74 S. E. 300).

The rule above stated does not apply where the disjunctive, and all that follows it, can be rejected as surplusage. Henderson, 113 

Ga. 1148 (39 S. E. 446).

Where the word "or" is applied to amplify or explain the preceding phrase, it is permissible. Whitaker, 11 Ga. App. 208 (75 S. 

E. 258).

CRIMINAL PROCEDURE 

65 Second offenders. Where the accused is charged as a second offender of a felony, and the compulsory maximum sentence is demanded, the indictment should charge the former conviction and sentence. Reid, 49 Ga. App. 429, 430 (5) (176 S. E. 100). 

c. JOINDER OF PARTIES, OFFENSES AND COUNTS. 

Joinder of parties. Indictment against two persons jointly need not charge what particular part each played in the commission of the crime. It is a matter of evidence. Davis, 25 Ga. App. 532 (1-d) (103 S. E. 819).

Joinder of offenses. (1) The State may in a single county charge the accused with violating the statute in all of the ways set out in the statute, and a general verdict of guilty may be sustained upon proof of violation of the law in any one or more of the ways prescribed, but the verdict will be construed as convicting the accused of only a single offense, for which only a single punishment can be imposed. (2) The State may prosecute under an indictment containing several counts, charging a violation of any one of these provisions, viewed as distinct offenses, but varying in the details of the commission, and in that event, if it appears that but a single transaction is referred to, and that the several counts are introduced merely for the purpose of varying the details, a general verdict of guilty may be sustained as finding the defendant guilty of only a single offense, and only a single punishment can be imposed. (3) 

The State may prosecute under an indictment setting out in a number of separate counts violations of the various provisions of the prohibition law as distinct offenses. In that a general verdict of guilty will be construed as meaning guilty of all the offenses set out in all the counts, and can not be sustained unless the evidence is sufficient to support all the counts separately considered. But if conviction is sustainable, the trial judge may impose sentences upon each and every count, just as if it were a separate indictment. 

Under such an indictment the jury may acquit on some of the counts and convict on others. Tooke, 4 Ga. App. 495 (61 S. E. 

917); Hall, 8 Ga. App. 747, 750 (70 S. E. 211).

Misjoinder of offenses in an indictment is a defect of which the defendant can take advantage only by a demurrer specifically pointing out the defect. Boatwright, 26 Ga. App. 67 (1) (105 S. E. 381).

Every count in an indictment should charge the defendant upon its face with a distinct offense. Yet one count may refer to mat-

ters in another count, to avoid unnecessary repetitions. Durden, 29 Ga. App. 548 (116 S. E. 41); Pope, 41 Ga. App. 653 (154 S. E. 

194); Durden, 152 Ga. 441 (1-a) (110 S. E. 283).

The general rule is that a defendant can not be charged with separate offenses in the same indictment. Gilbert, 65 Ga. 449; 

Mitchell, 6 Ga. App. 554 (65 S. E. 326). This rule does not apply where the offenses charged in the separate counts of the same indictment are misdemeanors. Lynes, 46 Ga. 208; Bishop, 21 Ga. App. 

236 (1) (94 S. E. 49); Butler, 18 Ga. App. 201 (1) (89 S. E. 178).

Felonies and misdemeanors can not be charged in the same indictment. Especially is this true where the offenses are of different character. Doyle, 77 Ga. 513 (1).

Offenses of the same nature and differing only in degree may be charged in the same count. Offenses not of the same nature may also be charged in the same count, if they constitute but one transaction blended together by concurrent acts. Mitchell, 6 Ga. App. 

554 (65 S. E. 326); Butler, 18 Ga. App. 201 (89 S. E. 178); Warren, 32 Ga. App. 359 (123 S. E. 182); Gaulden, 41 Ga. App. 635 (1) (154 

S. E. 209).

Offenses, though not of the same nature, may be charged in the same count in the same indictment if they constitute but one transaction. Warren, 32 Ga. App. 359 (123 S. E. 182).

The test is whether or not the acts described in the indictment relate to but one transaction. Lepinsky, 7 Ga. App. 285 (66 S. E. 

965); Hall, 8 Ga. App. 747 (70 S. E. 211).

Two or more felonies may probably be charged in separate counts in one indictment, although the offenses be committed at different times and places and involve transactions with different persons, where the crimes charged, though differing in degree and varying in punishment to be inflicted for their perpetration, are of the same general nature, and the mode of trial is the same. Such an indictment is not subject to general demurrer; and it is within the sound discretion of the Court, to require or not to require the solicitor-general to elect upon which count he will proceed. Webb, 47 Ga. App. 505 (170 S. E. 827).

Where separate and distinct offenses are joined in one indictment, and those offenses are of such nature that on appeal, the Supreme Court would have jurisdiction of one charge, and the Court of Appeals of another, the indictment should be quashed on demurrer. 

Gilbert, 175 Ga. 276 (165 S. E. 120).

CRIMINAL PROCEDURE 

67 Where there are good and bad counts in the indictment the courts may strike the bad counts without quashing the whole indictment. 

Martin, 10 Ga. App. 795 (74 S. E. 304).

Verdict. Where the indictment lawfully charges the commission of distinct offenses of a similar nature, a general verdict of guilty is not good, unless the evidence sustains each count. Innes, 19 Ga. 

App. 271, 273 (91 S. E. 339).

Where the same offense is charged in different ways in the same indictment, a general verdict of guilty will be upheld. Innes, 19 

Ga. App. 271, 273 (91 S. E. 339); Parham, 3 Ga. App. 468 (60 S. 

E. 123).

Where the indictment charges in different counts the commission of the same offense in different ways, the verdict need not specify upon which count it was rendered. Fry, 141 Ga. 789 (82 S. E. 135).

Election. Where the various, counts are good, the State need not elect. Sims, 110 Ga. 290 (2) (34 S. E. 1020); Walker, 118 Ga. 772 (45 S. E. 621).

If upon the trial of a case it appears that the charge preferred by the State is duplicitous, the Court, after the evidence is closed, Thompson, 18 Ga. App. 488 (3) (89 S. E. 607). may require the State to elect upon which counts it will proceed. 

See also: Duplicity.

Lesser offenses included in the greater. Whenever an indictment charges a major offense and the evidence does not support it as to that offense, the jury may convict of any minor offense which is included in the major and to which the evidence applies,-upon the principle of "Omne majus continet in se minus." Mitchell, 6 Ga. 

App. 554, 556 (65 S. E. 326).

There may be a conviction of a lesser offense than that expressly named in the indictment, in some cases in which the lesser is not included in the greater offense, but where the language used in the indictment is sufficient to embrace the smaller offense. Goldin, 104 

Ga. 549, 550 (30 S. E. 749).

One indicted for one offense may lawfully be convicted for an attempt to commit the same offense, although the attempt is not charged in the indictment. Brownlow, 112 Ga. 405 (1) (37 S. E. 733).

Where the affidavit which formed the basis for the indictment was general, the indictment may charge a specific crime included within the offense named in the affidavit. Glass, 119 Ga. 299 (46 S. E. 435). 

See also: Specific Crimes.

d. DEMURRERS. 

Right of the accused to inspect indictment. The accused has a right to inspect the indictment or presentment before pleading thereto. Hatcher, 23 Ga. 307.

Motion to quash. Motion to quash indictment is a demurrer. 

Golden, 45 Ga. App. 501, 503 (165 S. E. 299).

Striking superfluous words. The Court may strike on demurrer superfluous words in an indictment, without amending the indictment. Brooks, 47 Ga. App. 226 (2) (170 S. E. 406).

Question of law. Whether or not a count of an indictment is sufficient is a question of law for the Court, and not for the jury. 

Bostock, 61 Ga. 635 (4).

Must be perfect. A demurrer, being a critic, should itself be free from imperfection. Boatwright, 26 Ga. App. 67 (105 S. E. 381). ·

Construction against the State. Upon a demurrer an accusation should be construed most strongly against the State. Gazaway, 9 

Ga. App. 194, 195 (70 S. E. 978). Contrary rule held: 

Ga. 536, 540 (35 S. E. 97); DeVere, 45 Ga. App. 330, 332 (164 S. E. 

485); Gilbert, 175 Ga. 276 (1) (165 S. E. 120). 

Green, 109

The language of an indictment is to be construed liberally in favor of the State. DeVere, 45 Ga. App. 330, 332 (164 S. E. 485).

General demurrer. The true test of the sufficiency of an indictment to withstand a general demurrer, or a motion to quash, is found in the answer to the question: Can the defendant admit the charge as made and still be innocent? If he can, the indictment is fatally defective. The mere characterization of an act, which may be lawfully committed, as unlawful, does not suffice to so inform the accused of the crime or the nature of the offense with which he is charged as to enable him to prepare for trial. The charge that an act intrinsically lawful was done unlawfully, without more, is not a statement of fact, but a mere conclusion of the pleader. Dukes, 9 Ga. App. 537 (2) (71 S. E. 921); Roughlin, 17 Ga. App. 205, 209 (86 S. E. 452).

If the indictment is fatally defective, the sufficiency of the indictment can be questioned by general demurrer or by motion in arrest of judgment. Woods, 10 Ga. App. 476, 478 (73 S. E. 608).

Special demurrer. Exceptions which go to the form of the indictment must be made by special demurrer or motion to quash. Smith, 17 Ga. App. 612 (1) (87 S. E. 846); Sanders, 118 Ga. 329 (2) (45 

S. E. 365); Foss, 15 Ga. App. 478 (1) (83 S. E. 880).

CRIMINAL PROCEDURE 

69 

Written demurrer.

General demurrer, based on defects for which a judgment should be arrested, may be presented by oral motion. 

Gilmore, 118 Ga. 299 (1) (45 S. E. 226).

Special demurrers, which go merely to the form of the indictment, must be in writing. King, 117 Ga. 39 (1) (43 S. E. 426).

Time of demurrer. General demurrer may be filed and insisted on at any time during the trial. Gilmore, 118 Ga. 299 (45 S. E. 226).

Special demurrer must be filed before pleading to the merits of the indictment. Scandrett, 124 Ga. 141 (2) (52 S. E. 160); Thomasson, 22 Ga. 499 (1); Jordan, 22 Ga. 545, 546 (3).

Waivers. A defect in the form of an indictment is waived by pleading to the merits thereof, although a timely objection should be sustained. Hardin, 106 Ga. 384 (32 S. E. 365); Lanier, 5 Ga. 

App. 472, 473 (63 S. E. 536).

All special demurrers should be insisted upon before pleading, otherwise the defects will be considered waived. Hill, 41 Ga. 484 (2); Spencer, 123 Ga. 133 (1) (51 S. E. 294).

Misnomer is considered waived unless objected to by timely plea, before arraignment. Pulliam, 140 Ga. 864, 865 (80 S. E. 315); 

Christopher, 16 Ga. App. 194 (84 S. E. 833).

One who waives the right to be tried upon an indictment or accusation perfect in form and substance, by failing to demur, and takes his chances on acquittal, will not be heard, after conviction, to urge defects in the indictment, unless the defects are so great that the indictment or accusation is absolutely void. Every defendant has a right to be tried upon an indictment or accusation perfect in form and substance. But this right must be insisted upon, otherwise it will be considered waived. Pence, 36 Ga. App. 

268 (1) (136 S. E. 821); Gravitt, 36 Ga. App. 301 (1) (136 S. E. 

829); Foy, 40 Ga. App. 617 (1) (150 S. E. 917).

Waiver of indictment. Where a defendant in a city or county court waives indictment, he can not withdraw such waiver, but must stand trial in city or county court upon an accusation. Butler, 97 Ga. 404 (23 S. E. 822); McConnell, 67 Ga. 633 (1). 

Where accused waived indictment, and went on trial in a city court, where he was convicted, and the case was carried to the Superior Court on certiorari, where the judgment was reversed and returned for new trial, the accused could not then withdraw his waiver, and demand an indictment. Brown, 89 Ga. 340 (15 S. E. 462).

Ground must be apparent. A demurrer as well as a motion to quash the indictment must be resting upon some matter apparent upon the face of the indictment or elsewhere in the record. Jackson, 64 Ga. 344, 346.

Constitutionality of statute. All questions of constitutionality of the statute the violation of which is charged should be raised by timely demurrer. Cohen, 7 Ga. App. 5 (3) (65 S. E. 1096).

Where a demurrer is based on a contention that the statute upon which the charge is based is void and unconstitutional, it should point out fully in what particular the statute violates the Constitution. Carr, 10 Ga. App. 21 (72 S. E. 516); Arthur, 146 Ga. 827 (92 S. E. 637); Harris, 147 Ga. 489 (1) (94 S. E. 572).

Specification of defect. A demurrer should distinctly specify the defect complained of. Field, 126 Ga. 571, 572 (55 S. E. 502).

A demurrer to an indictment alleging that the affidavit upon which the indictment is based charges no crime, ought to show how, or in what respect the affidavit is insufficient, otherwise there is no point presented upon which the reviewing court may decide. 

Lucas, 38 Ga. App. 449 (2), 451 (143 S. E. 924).

Demurrer on the ground that the affidavit on which the accusation was based was vague, and insufficient to put the accused on notice as to the nature of the crime charged,-is too general. Morgan, 38 Ga. App. 686 (1) (145 S. E. 521).

Ground of demurrer "that the acts charged to have been done by the accused do not constitute the commission of any offense for which the accused may be convicted and punished under any valid existing law of this State" is too vague to raise any point for decision. Demurrer must in itself be perfect and point out wherein and why the law which it attacks is invalid. Saunders, 172 Ga. 770, 772 (3) (158 S. E. 791).

Where an indictment is demurred to on the ground that felonies and misdemeanors are joined, the demurrer should state specifically what felonies and misdemeanors are charged. Boatwright, 26 Ga. 

App. 67 (105 S. E. 381).

Demurrer alleging that the indictment was duplicitous for the reason that two separate and distinct offenses were improperly joined therein should indicate what the two offenses were. Gatlin, 18 Ga. App. 9 (6) (89 S. E. 345).

Demurrer to evidence. A motion to quash the indictment on account of insufficiency of the evidence will not be entertained by the Court, the question being one of facts, for the consideration of the

CRIMINAL PROCEDURE 

71 jury. Cox, 3 Ga. App. 609, 610 (3) (60 S. E. 283); Scott, 6 Ga.

App. 567 (1) (65 S. E. 359). 

Cooper, 13 Ga. App. 686 (79 (2) (107 S. E. 621); Harrison,

Motion for new trial. Defect in the indictment can not be taken advantage of by motion for new trial. 

S. E. 764); Lawrence, 26 Ga. App. 607 

26 Ga. App. 645 (107 S. E. 90).

A judgment overruling a demurrer to an indictment can not be made a ground of a motion for new trial, but exception thereto must be taken either by bill of exceptions sued out within twenty days from the date of the judgment, or by exceptions pendente lite, on which error is assigned in the bill of exceptions. Long, 118 Ga. 319 (1) (45 S. E. 416); Wheeler, 4 Ga. App. 325 (6) (61 S. E. 409); 

Jones, 92 Ga. 480 (1) (17 S. E. 859). e. ACCUSATIONS.

Definition. The word "accusation" is a generic term, and generally includes "indictments" and "presentments." Gordon, 102 

Ga. 673, 679 (29 S. E. 444); Cleveland, 141 Ga. 829 (82 S. E. 243). 

The word "accusation" may also include a warrant. Cox, 152 Ga. 

532 (1) (110 S. E. 236).

Although the word "accusation" may include indictments and presentments, the reverse is not true. "Indictment" does not include "accusations." Progress Club, 12 Ga. App. 174, 177 (76 S. 

E. 1029).

General. An accusation in the City Court supplies the place of, and is governed by the rules that apply to indictments. Conley, 83 Ga. 496 (10 S. E. 123); Progress Club, 12 Ga. App. 174, 175 (76 S.

E. 1029). This rule is, however, subject to special restrictions. Flint, 12 Ga. App. 169, 172 (76 S. E. 1032).

An accusation, as used in reference to the form in which a charge is made in courts having jurisdiction over misdemeanors, is the equivalent of "information" at common law. Gordon, 102 Ga. 673, 679 (29 S. E. 444); Wright, 120 Ga. 670, 676 (48 S. E. 170).

A County Court accusation is not a bill of indictment, but something different therefrom both in form and in substance. Hudson, 91 Ga. 553 (18 S. E. 432).

There are certain offenders who can not be tried on accusations though only charged with misdemeanors. Corporations are such. 

Progress Club, 12 Ga. App. 174 (76 S. E. 1029).

Where the act creating the court provides that the accused charged with a misdemeanor shall have no right to demand an in-

dictment, such provision is valid and will be enforced. There is nothing in the Constitution guaranteeing a right to demand indictment by grand jury. Maples, 43 Ga. App. 295 (158 S. E. 762); 

Gordon, 102 Ga. 673 (29 S. E. 444).

Unless there is something in the charter to the contrary, it is not necessary that a person accused of a violation of a municipal ordinance shall be furnished with a written accusation or statement of the charge made against him. It is sufficient if he be informed of the charge and be given an opportunity to defend. Norris, 15 Ga. 

App. 511 (83 S. E. 866); Porter, 18 Ga. App. 33 (88 S. E. 744); 

Pearson, 124 Ga. 701, 711 (52 S. E. 751).

Formal requirements. The accusation should state that the State of Georgia, upon the information of the prosecutor, charges the defendant with the crime. Mere irregularity is not fatal. Mitchell, 126 Ga. 84 (54 S. E. 931); Dickson, 62 Ga. 583, 586.

It must appear that the offense was committed before the affidavit charging the same was made. Chambers, 85 Ga. 220 (1) (11 S. E. 653).

Affidavit. An accusation must state that it is based on the affidavit. Smith, 63 Ga. 168 (2).

Failure to state in accusation that it is based on an affidavit is immaterial, where the accusation shows upon its face that such affidavit was made. (Two justices dissenting.) Mitchell, 126 Ga. 

84 (6) (54 S. E. 931).

Void affidavit is a nullity, and the trial thereon is illegal. Such affidavit may be objected to at any time. Scroggins, 55 Ga. 380 (3).

Unless the statute creating the court provides to the contrary the affidavit may be signed before a commercial notary public. 

Shuler, 125 Ga. 778 (54 S. E. 689); Mitchell, 126 Ga. 84 (2) (54 

S. E. 931).

An affidavit neither attested by an officer authorized to administer oaths, nor purporting to be sworn to in open court, is void, as the basis of criminal proceedings. Gilbert, 17 Ga. App. 143 (2) (86 S. E. 415); Scroggins, 55 Ga. 380, 381.

An affidavit charging the defendant with a "misdemeanor" is sufficient, unless there is a clear contrary provision in the act creating the court. Hunter, 4 Ga. App. 579 (61 S. E. 1130); Lewis, 28 

Ga. App. 681 (113 S. E. 228).

Affidavit to be basis of an accusation need not describe the offense. It is sufficient if it names it. Murray, 30 Ga. App. 641 (1) (118 S. E. 760).

CRIMINAL PROCEDURE 

73 133 As the greater includes the less, if the affidavit is general, the accusation may charge a specific criminal act included within the offense named in the affidavit. Glass, 119 Ga. 299 (46 S. E. 435).

The accusation may be broader and more specific in the allegations of the offense than the original affidavit. Lepinsky, 7 Ga. App. 

285, 288 (66 S. E. 965).

The accusation may be more restricted, but it can not be broader, than the affidavit, nor can it charge an offense different from that described in the affidavit. Glass, 119 Ga. 299 (46 S. E. 435); Frazier, 11 Ga. App. 261 (75 S. E. 10).

That the affidavit upon which the accusation is based is defective, in not properly denominating or describing the offense charged, will not afford ground for quashing the accusation, if the identity of the transaction set forth in the affidavit with that charged to be a crime in the accusation is apparent. Crawford, 4 Ga. App. 789 (1) (62 S. E. 501). 

Where the affidavit charges the commission of a specific crime, the accusation must conform thereto. Glass, 119 Ga. 299 (46 S. E. 

435). The evidence must support both. Shealy, 16 Ga. App. 191, 192 (84 S. E. 839).

The affidavit for accusation need not minutely describe the offense. It is sufficient if it is specific enough to uphold a warrant. 

Dickson, 62 Ga. 583; Brown, 109 Ga. 570 (2) (34 S. E. 1031).

The accusation need not be based upon the same affidavit that the warrant is issued upon. Brown, 109 Ga. 570 (34 S. E. 1031).

Signature. The solicitor of the city court has a right to appoint an assistant. Where the solicitor has an assistant, the assistant may sign accusations. Christopher, 21 Ga. App. 244 (1) (94 S. E. 72).

The solocitor pro tem has the same right, when duly appointed, and has the right to represent the State in the court in which he is appointed, just as the regular solicitor. Horton, 11 Ga. App. 33 (74 

S. E. 559). 

Demand for indictment. Must be in writing. Shivers, 123 Ga. 

538 (51 S. E. 569).

Where the accused waived indictment, and demanded a trial by jury in the county court, the State is bound to try him in the county court, and can not remove the case into the Superior Court, where the charge is a misdemeanor. Cunningham, 80 Ga. 4 (5 S. 

E. 251).

Where new trial is granted in the county court, a waiver of indictment can not be withdrawn. But a waiver of trial by jury may be withdrawn. Brown, 89 Ga. 340 (15 S. E. 462).

Where, upon the trial of a case in the county court, the accused waived indictment and demanded trial by jury, the judge could withdraw the case from the jury at any time of the trial, when in his opinion the offense committed was a felony. He can, in such cases, bind the defendant over to Superior Court, even over defendant's protest. Cunningham, 80 Ga. 4 (5 S. E. 251).

An indictment can not be amended, except by the grand jury, before arraignment. Goldsmith, 2 Ga. App. 283, 285 (58 S. E. 486).

Matters of form may be amended by the solicitor-general, but not matters of substance. Hill, 41 Ga. 484; Dedge, 28 Ga. App. 558 (112 S. E. 155).

An accusation in the city court may be amended by the solicitor at any time before the defendant has pleaded thereto, or the jury has been selected, but it is not amendable thereafter. Smith, 17 Ga. 

App. 612 (1) (87 S. E. 846); Bishop, 22 Ga. App. 784 (97 S. E. 251). 

See also: Goldsmith, 2 Ga. App. 283, 285 (58 S. E. 486); Conley, 83 Ga. 496, 497 (10 S. E. 123).

The reason for the difference in rules of amending indictments and accusations is that the former are sanctioned by the oaths of the grand jurors, and the latter are preferred by the State's attorney. Goldsmith, 2 Ga. App. 283 (58 S. E. 486); Flint, 12 Ga. 

App. 169, 172 (76 S. E. 1032).

An amendment of an accusation must be supported by the affidavit of the prosecutor. Bishop, 22 Ga. App. 784 (1-a) (97 S. E. 251).

The proper procedure, in the city court, would be for the judge to sign a formal order amending the affidavit and accusation, but irregularity in the form and method of the amendment will not be considered error. Bishop, 22 Ga. App. 784, 785 (97 S. E. 251).

Interlineations and erasures. Interlineations or erasures in an indictment will not be fatal, unless it appears that the same have been made after the grand jury has acted upon it. The legal presumption is that they were made at the proper time by the proper authority. Jones, 99 Ga. 46 (1) (25 S. E. 617); Crawford, 4 Ga. 

App. 789 (4) (62 S. E. 501); Allen, 123 Ga. 499 (1) (51 S. E. 506); 

Cook, 119 Ga. 108 (2), 110 (46 S. E. 64); Gunn, 10 Ga. App. 819 (2) (74 S. E. 312).

Objection to interlineations or erasures should be made by plea in abatement. Gunn, 10 Ga. App. 819, 821 (74 S. E. 312).

CRIMINAL PROCEDURE 

75 

a. GENERAL. 

7. ARRAIGNMENT. 

§ 27-1404. 

Definition. The arraignment of the prisoner is nothing more than reading the indictment to him, and asking him in open court whether he is guilty or not guilty. Harris, 11 Ga. App. 137, 139 (74 S. E. 895); Horne, 27 Ga. App. 587 (109 S. E. 699); Fears, 125 

Ga. 739 (54 S. E. 667).

Matter of right. The prisoner is entitled to a formal arraignment as a matter of right, unless he waives it. Kincade, 14 Ga. App. 544 (81 S. E. 910).

Requirements. Upon the arraignment of a prisoner, the indictment shall be read to him, and he shall be required to answer whether he is guilty or not guilty of the offense charged in the indictment, which answer or plea shall be made orally by the prisoner, or his counsel. And if he shall plead "guilty," such plea shall be immediately recorded on the minutes of the court by the clerk, together with the arraignment; and the Court shall pronounce upon such prisoner the judgment of the law, in the same manner as if he had been convicted of the offense by the verdict of a jury; but, at any time before judgment is pronounced, the prisoner may withdraw his plea of "guilty," and plead "not guilty," and such former plea shall not be given in evidence against him on his trial. § 271404. 

Purpose of arraignment. The purpose of the arraignment is to form an issue between the State and the accused, which issue shall be tried. Bryans, 34 Ga. 323:

The purpose of the arraignment is to give the prisoner an opportunity to plead to the indictment. Tarver, 95 Ga. 222, 227 (21 S. 

E. 381).

The purpose of an arraignment is to give the prisoner an opportunity to demur to the indictment, or offer an objection to it. Lampkin, 87 Ga. 516, 524 (13 S. E. 523); Smith, 17 Ga. App. 612 (87 

S. E. 846).

The purpose of the arraignment is to identify the prisoner, as the party accused. Wells, 121 Ga. 368 (2) (49 S. E. 319).

Standing mute. If the prisoner, upon being arraigned, shall plead "not guilty," or shall stand mute, the clerk shall immediately record upon the minutes of the court the plea of "not guilty," together

with the arraignment, and such arraignment and plea shall constitute the issue between the prisoner and the State. § 27-1405. 

Standing mute is equivalent to pleading "not guilty." The clerk should record on his minutes that the defendant stood mute, or that he entered a plea of "not guilty." Failure of the clerk to so mark the record is not fatal, and the Court may order the same done nunc pro tunc at any time. Johnson, 7 Ga. App. 48 (2) (66 S. E. 

148); Kincade, 14 Ga. App. 544, 548 (81 S. E. 910).

Where the accused stands mute the Court should require the State to prove every material part of the crime, and charge the jury as if a plea of "not guilty" had been entered. Manchester, 171 Ga. 121 (155 S. E. 11).

Joint defendants. All of the persons charged in the indictment may be arraigned at one time. Rawlins, 124 Ga. 31, 43 (52 S. E. 1).

Prisoner must be present. The prisoner must be present at the time of the arraignment. Wells, 121 Ga. 368 (49 S. E. 319).

Waiver of right to arraignment. The prisoner may waive his right to formal arraignment. Tarver, 95 Ga. 222 (21 S. E. 381); 

Harris, 11 Ga. App. 137 (74 S. E. 895).

Pleading to the merits of the charge, either as a question of law or of fact, without objection, is an implied waiver of arraignment. 

Hudson, 117 Ga. 704 (45 S. E. 66); Kincade, 14 Ga. App. 544 (81 

S. E. 910).

Defendant will be held to have waived formal arraignment, unless, at the time of entering a plea of "not guilty," he called the attention of the Court to the fact that he did not intend to waive arraignment. Merely striking from the printed form of back of indictment the words "waives formal arraignment" will not entitle the accused, after verdict, to complain that he was not arraigned. Harris, 11 Ga. App. 137 (1) (74 S. E. 895).

When new trial is granted. Where new trial is granted, or mistrial declared, there need not be a second arraignment. Cogswell, 49 Ga. 103; Hayes, 58 Ga. 35; Atkins, 69 Ga. 595.

Where new trial is granted and arraignment has been waived. at the first trial, the prisoner is not entitled to another arraignment. 

Parker, 17 Ga. App. 252 (87 S. E. 705).

Plea as waiver. Where solicitor-general reads indictment to the accused and he pleads "not guilty," a formal arraignment is waived. 

Fears, 125 Ga. 739 (2) (54 S. E. 667); Horne, 27 Ga. App. 587 (1) (109 S. E. 699).

CRIMINAL PROCEDURE 

77 Issues of law and of fact. When arraigned, the prisoner may plead an issue of fact or an issue of law, or both. Issues of law are for the Court, issues of fact for the jury. Kincade, 14 Ga. App. 

544 (81 S. E. 910).

Where accused is present for other purposes. One present in court for the purpose of being tried under a criminal accusation may be placed on trial under another accusation charging an offense growing out of the same transaction and based upon a new affidavit, even though no warrant for the arrest of the accused was issued based upon the second affidavit. Harris, 11 Ga. App. 137 (3) (74

S. E. 895). 

Arrest of judgment. The omission of arraignment furnishes no ground in arrest of judgment. Bryans, 34 Ga. 323, 324.

Where accused not arraigned. When no arraignment had, and there was no waiver, express or implied, there is no issue before the jury. Bryans, 34 Ga. 323, 324. 

b. BENEFIT OF COUNSEL. 

Appointment of counsel. Where accused, because of poverty, can not employ counsel, or is unwilling to do so, Court will appoint one. 

Such counsel is under same responsibility as if employed, and receiving fee. Martin, 51 Ga. 567, 568; Delk, 99 Ga. 667 (1) (26 S. 

E. 752).

Where the accused requests the Court to appoint counsel before an indictment is returned, Court may do so. Charlon, 106 Ga. 400 (32 S. E. 347).

The accused is entitled to counsel as a matter of absolute and sacred right. McArver, 114 Ga. 514, 516 (40 S. E. 779). 

Counsel of choice. Where the accused is able and willing to employ counsel, he is entitled, as a matter of right, to a counsel of his own choice. Delk, 100 Ga. 61 (1) (27 S. E. 152).

Neglect of counsel. As a general rule, the neglect of counsel affords no ground for the granting of a new trial. Hudson, 76 Ga. 727. 

Counsel will do his duty. There is a presumption, in the absence of clear proof to the contrary, that the appointed counsel has done his full duty, unless the contrary appears by clear and satisfactory proof. Fambles, 97 Ga. 625 (2) (25 S. E. 365). 

Counsel presumed sufficiently experienced. Counsel appointed to represent the accused is presumed to be of sufficient experience and

legal attainment to satisfy the constitutional requirements of the benefit of counsel. Delk, 99 Ga. 667 (1) (26 S. E. 752).

Accused entitled to counsel at every stage of the trial. The constitutional guaranty of benefit of counsel extends to every important phase of the trial. Where the Court recharged the jury, defendant's counsel should have been present. Martin, 51 Ga. 568. 

Sufficiency of time. The right of counsel includes the right to a reasonable time for the preparation of the case. Blackman, 76 Ga. 288. 

Ten minutes are not sufficient for the preparation of a capital case. Where counsel was appointed and moved for a continuance on the ground of insufficiency of time during which to prepare for the case, this motion should be granted. Reliford, 140 Ga. 777 (79 S. E. 1128).

Court should allow counsel a reasonable time for consultation with the accused. Perryman, 114 Ga. 545 (1) (40 S. E. 746).

Where the accused and his counsel had ample time to prepare for trial upon a bill of indictment, but the bill was nol prossed, a motion for postponement upon the new bill, based on the same charge, on the ground that counsel did not have sufficient time to prepare for trial, is properly overruled. Jones, 115 Ga. 814 (2) (42 S. E. 271). 

See also: Continuances. 

Waiver of right to counsel. Right to counsel may be waived by the accused. Where the records show that the accused had no counsel, the presumption is that counsel has been waived. Gatlin, 17 

Ga. App. 406 (87 S. E. 151).

If the accused declines Court's offer to appoint counsel, his constitutional rights to such are waived. Stokes, 73 Ga. 816. 

Absence of counsel. Absence of counsel, where due to no neglect of the prisoner, entitles him to a postponement of the case. Delk, 100 Ga. 61 (1) (2) (27 S. E. 152). 

C. DEMAND OF ACCUSATION. 

Every person charged with an offense against the laws of this State shall be furnished, on demand, previously to his arraignment, with a copy of the accusation, and a list of witnesses on whose testimony the charge against him was founded. § 2-105. See also § 27-1403. 

The provisions of this law are mandatory and not directory. 

Moore, 25 Ga. App. 251, 253 (102 S. E. 916).

CRIMINAL PROCEDURE 

79 Demand necessary. Where no demand made, the accused is not entitled to a copy of the indictment and a list of witnesses. Fears, 125 Ga. 739 (3) (54 S. E. 667); Fears, 125 Ga. 740 (4) (54 S. E. 

661); Williams, 42 Ga. App. 225 (155 S. E. 511).

Incorrect list. Where incorrect list is furnished on demand, the proper procedure is to object to such witness. And the Court may exclude the witness so objected to. Moore, 25 Ga. App. 251, 254 (102 S. E. 916).

Incorrect list furnished on demand is no ground for setting aside judgment, nor for motion in arrest of judgment. Regopoulas, 116 

Ga. 596 (2) (42 S. E. 1014); Regopoulas, 115 Ga. 232 (2) (41 S. E. 619).

Omission of the witness' name from the list furnished on demand is no ground for mistrial, especially where testimony of such witness is stricken from the records. Moore, 25 Ga. App. 251, 254 (102 S. E. 

916). (One dissenting.) The rule laid down in the Regopoulas case is purely obiter and not binding.

Omission of the witness' name from the list furnished on demand is not valid ground for continuance by reason of surprise. Palmer, 23 Ga. App. 84 (97 S. E. 460).

Failure to except to a witness whose name does not appear on the list furnished on demand, is waiver of such rights. Dean, 43 

Ga. 218, 220.

Where right to copy exists. Right of the accused to be furnished with a copy of the accusation and a list of witnesses applies alike to felonies and misdemeanors. Bird, 50 Ga. 585, 587.

Right of accused to be furnished with a copy of the accusation and a list of witnesses does not apply in municipal courts, unless the charter, creating such court, expressly provides for the same. 

Venable, 7 Ga. App. 190 (2) (66 S. E. 489); Wynne, 10 Ga. App. 

818 (1) (74 S. E. 286).

What the list must contain. The list of witnesses need include only those who testified before the grand jury. It is no valid objection to a witness that his name does not appear on the list furnished on demand. Inman, 72 Ga. 269 (1); Echols, 101 Ga. 531 (29 S. E. 

14); Abbott, 11 Ga. App. 43 (4) (74 S. E. 621). 

d. PLEA OF "GUILTY." 

Must be scanned with great care. A plea of "guilty" is a confession of guilt, and as such must be scanned with great care, and received with caution. Griffin, 12 Ga. App. 615 (6) (77 S. E. 1080).

Must be voluntary. Plea of "guilty" ought never to be received unless freely and voluntarily made. Griffin, 12 Ga. App. 615 (3) (6) (77 S. E. 1080).

Misapprehension. Where plea of "guilty" is entered under misapprehension of its legal effect because of misrepresentations made or inducements held out either by the Court or by the counsel for the State, the prisoner ought to be allowed to withdraw such plea, even after sentence has been pronounced if he moves promptly upon discovery that he has been misled. Griffin, 12 Ga. App. 615 (6) (77 S. E. 1080).

Defendant's belief that he would be dealt with leniently is no ground to permit him withdrawal of plea after sentence. Foster, 22 Ga. App. 109, 110 (1) (95 S. E. 529). 

Where, after plea of "guilty" has been entered and sentence pronounced, in a criminal case, the accused at the same term files a written petition asking that judgment and sentence be vacated and that he be allowed to withdraw his plea and enter a plea of "not guilty," on the grounds that he entered his plea of "guilty" under misapprehension of facts of the case, and that he is really not guilty of the offense, and where the facts stated in the petition. sustain these allegations, it is error for the trial judge to dismiss the petition on general demurrer. Bell, 24 Ga. App. 533 (2) (101 

S. E. 695). 

Who may enter plea of "guilty." A plea of "guilty" may be entered by the accused or his attorney. Where entered by the attorney in defendant's presence, without his objection, it is binding upon the defendant. Bearden, 13 Ga. App. 264 (2) (79 S. E. 79). 

When plea of "guilty" may be withdrawn. Before judgment and sentence the accused may withdraw his plea of "guilty" as a matter of right. This rule is true, although all witnesses have been dismissed from court and sentence was deferred on defendant's request. Defendant's motive is immaterial. It is immaterial that it causes substantial hardship upon the State, or that material witnesses, non-residents of this State, have been dismissed. Nobles, 17 Ga. App. 382 (86 S. E. 1073); Woodward, 13 Ga. App. 130 (78 

S. E. 1009); Bearden, 13 Ga. App. 264 (1) (79 S. E. 79); Polston, 15 

Ga. App. 632 (2) (83 S. E. 1101).

After sentence the accused may withdraw his plea of "guilty" by permission of the trial court only. Such permission rests solely within the sound discretion of the Court, which will not be disturbed, unless abused. Bearden, 13 Ga. App. 264 (1) (79 S. E. 79); Sanders,

CRIMINAL PROCEDURE 

81 

18 Ga. App. 786 (2) (90 S. E. 728); Walker, 27 Ga. App. 269 (107

S. E. 898). 

When is judgment "pronounced." Judgment is pronounced, within the purview of this rule, whenever the accused is informed by the Court of the sentence to be entered against him. Griffin, 12 Ga. App. 615 (2) (77 S. E. 1080). 

Oral sentence is sufficient. Sanders, 18 Ga. App. 786, 788 (90 S. 

E. 728).

Right of accused absolute. Right of defendant to withdraw his plea of "guilty" and enter a plea of "not guilty" before sentence is pronounced, is absolute. It is not qualified nor limited. Fowler, 41 Ga. App. 333 (153 S. E. 90). 

Fraud. Where plea of "guilty" was entered as a result of fraud practiced upon the defendant, it is mandatory upon the judge to grant a withdrawal of such plea and enter a plea of "not guilty.” 

Griffin, 12 Ga. App. 615 (7) (77 S. E. 1080). 66 Where accused made an affidavit that he was fraudulently induced to plead guilty" by two other persons, under a promise that they would see that he got off with a light fine or sentence, supporting this plea by his own affidavit only, and they deny this under oath, it is not mandatory to grant a withdrawal of the plea. Jackson, 99 

Ga. 209 (25 S. E. 177).

The fact that two policemen told the defendant that if he enters a plea of "guilty" he would get off with a fine, is not such a fraud as would entitle him to withdraw his plea of "guilty" as a matter of right on the ground of fraud. Smith, 27 Ga. App. 270 (108 S. E. 121).

Several indictments. Where there are several indictments against the defendant and he plead "guilty" to one under the apprehension that he is pleading to the other, intending to plead "not guilty" to the one before the bar, he ought to be allowed to withdraw his plea. Davis, 20 Ga. 674.

Indictment containing several counts. A general plea of "guilty” to an indictment containing several counts is in effect a plea of "guilty" to all counts. Bishop, 21 Ga. App. 236 (4) (94 S. E. 49). 

Plea with recommendation. Where plea of "guilty" is entered to a felony with the recommendation that the accused be punished as for a misdemeanor, such recommendation may be disregarded by the Court as surplusage, and the plea dealt with as unconditional. Griffin, 12 Ga. App. 615 (3) (77 S. E. 1080). 1

Motion for new trial. One who entered a plea of "guilty" in a criminal case can not move for a new trial. Bearden, 13 Ga. App. 

264 (1) (79 S. E. 79).

Plea of "guilty" compared with conviction. A plea of "guilty" of one accused with a crime stands on the same footing and subjects him to the same punishment as a conviction. Jackson, 171 Ga. 

349 (1) (155 S. E. 466); Whitehead, 41 Ga. App. 466 (153 S. E. 428).

Record of plea as evidence. The record of a plea of "guilty" is prima facie evidence that such plea has been lawfully entered. 

In the absence of any evidence to the contrary an oral plea will be presumed. Jackson, 171 Ga. 349 (1) (155 S. E. 466). 

Waiver of Indictment. Plea in Vacation.

Be it enacted by the General Assembly of Georgia, and it is hereby enacted:

Section 1. Section 27-704, chapter 27-7 of title 27 ("Criminal 

Procedure") of the Code of Georgia of 1933, is hereby amended by adding at the end of said section the following: "Judges of the Superior Court may open their courts at any time without the presence of either grand jury or traverse jury to receive and act upon pleas of guilty in felony or misdemeanor cases, except those punishable by death or life imprisonment, when the Judge and the accused consent thereto, and the Judge may try the issues in such cases without a jury upon an accusation filed by the prosecuting officer where the accused has waived indictment," so that said section when amended shall read as follows: 

"27-704. Trial on accusation; waiver of indictment. In all misdemeanor cases and in felony cases other than capital felonies in which the defendants have been bound over to the Superior Court, or are confined in jail pending commitment trial, or are in jail, having waived commitment trial, the prosecuting officers of such court shall have authority to prefer accusations, and such parties shall be tried on such accusations; Provided, that parties going to trial under such accusations shall in writing waive indictment by a grand jury. 

Judges of the Superior Court may open their courts at any time without the presence of either grand jury or traverse jury to receive and act upon pleas of guilty in misdemeanor cases, and in felony cases except those punishable by death or life imprisonment, when the Judge and the accused consent thereto, and the Judge may try the issues in such cases without a jury upon an accusation filed by the prosecuting officer where the accused has waived indictment, and consented thereto in writing; and provided further that counsel

CRIMINAL PROCEDURE 

883 is present in court representing such defendant either by virtue of his employment or by appointment by the Court." 

Sec. 1A. All misdemeanor offenses may be tried in any county court, city court or Superior Court upon accusation without an indictment by the grand jury.

Sec. 2. All laws and parts of laws in conflict with this Act are hereby repealed. (Acts of 1935, p. 116.) 

e. PLEA IN BAR. 

When filed. Special pleas must be filed on arraignment and before pleading to the merits. Barlow, 13 Ga. App. 306 (79 S. E. 

93); Hall, 103 Ga. 403 (29 S. E. 915).

Special pleas will not be allowed after entering a plea of "not guilty." Wilkerson, 14 Ga. App. 475, 477 (81 S. E. 395); Reddick, 24 Ga. App. 776 (102 S. E. 132).

After the selection of the jury, (if the accused participated in the selection) and after the introduction of evidence has commenced, a motion to quash, or a demurrer is presented too late. Reddick, 24 Ga. App. 776 (102 S. E. 132); Reddick, 149 Ga. 822 (102 S. E. 347).

Question of venue. Question of venue may be raised by special plea in abatement, denying jurisdiction of the Court, or under the general issue. Knight, 15 Ga. App. 474 (2). (83 S. E. 797). 

See also: Demurrers. 

f. NOLLE PROSEQUI. 

The solicitor-general has authority, on the terms prescribed by law, to enter a nolle prosequi on indictments. § 24-2915. 

After an examination of the case in open court, and before it has been submitted to the jury, the solicitor-general may enter a nolle prosequi with the consent of the Court. After the case has been submitted to the jury, a nolle prosequi shall not be entered except by the consent of the defendant. § 27-1801.

Consent of Court. Consent of the Court to nolle prosequi is required. The solicitor-general can not enter such judgment without permission and consent of the Court. Statham, 41 Ga. 507 (1); 

Durham, 9 Ga. 306.

Consent of the accused. The consent of the accused is not required if the case has not been submitted to the jury, even after demurrer was filed to the indictment. Jones, 115 Ga. 814 (42 S. 

E. 271).

. 

If, after the jury is sworn, a nolle prosequi is entered, without the consent of the prisoner, it amounts to an acquittal, and bar to further prosecution. Reynolds, 3 Ga. 53 (2). (Distinguished in 

Franklin, 85 Ga. 570 (11 S. E. 876).)

Where case has gone to the jury, and afterwards nolle prosequi is entered without the consent of the accused, this amounts to an acquittal, and is a good defense on a subsequent charge for the same offense. This is true, although the first charge was for simple larceny and the second for burglary. Jones, 55 Ga. 625 (2) (3); 

Doyal, 70 Ga. 134; Jackson, 76 Ga. 551 (2).

The accused has no right to except to a nolle prosequi unless it is entered after the case has gone to the jury. Jackson, 76 Ga. 551 (2).. 

When case is submitted to the jury. The case is not submitted to the jury until after the jury have been impanelled and sworn. Fortson, 13 Ga. App. 681 (1) (79 S. E. 746).

Where jury have not been sworn, the case is not submitted to them, although they have been selected and taken their seats in the jury box. Fortson, 13 Ga. App. 681 (1) (79 S. E. 746).

Object of the law. The object of this act is to prevent entries of nolle prosequi by the solicitor-general without the sanction and approval of the judge, who presumably will not allow such entries to be made except for good reason, and an examination in open court is required in order that the judge may have lawful information upon which to base his action. Lewis, 101 Ga. 532 (28 

S. E. 970).

Minutes. The Court's consent must be recorded in the minutes with the Court's cognizance thereof. Statham, 41 Ga. 507, 511; 

Lascelles, 90 Ga. 347 (16 S. E. 945).

Mandatory. The provisions of the Code in reference to nolle prosequi are mandatory and not directory. Doyal, 70 Ga. 134.

Former jeopardy. That the previous indictment for the same offense has been nol prossed is not a good plea in abatement. Lascelles, 90 Ga. 347 (2) (16 S. E. 945).

After nolle prosequi is entered on an indictment, it will not support a plea of abatement to a subsequent charge, upon the ground that another indictment is pending. Jones, 115 Ga. 814 (5) (42 S. 

E. 271).

Where indictment has been nol prossed, the accused may be tried on a second indictment for the same cause, unless the first one was

CRIMINAL PROCEDURE 

85 nol prossed after the case has gone to the jury, and without his consent. In such event the accused has been placed in jeopardy once, and this would be a good defense. Doyal, 70 Ga. 134. 

Where nolle prosequi is

Nolle prosequi as termination of case. 

entered that particular case is terminated, with all of its incidentals, such as bond, etc. A new indictment is a new case. Lamp, 56 Ga. 

589 (1) (2). Sureties are discharged.

Several counts. Nolle prosequi as to some of the counts in the indictment does not work acquittal, but leaves the prosecution just as though such counts had never been inserted in the indictment. 

Carty, 26 Ga. App. 249 (1) (106 S. E. 11). 

Where new trial is granted. Where second trial is granted, the solicitor-general may, with the consent of the Court, enter nolle prosequi, before the case is submitted to the jury again. Lewis, 101 Ga. 532 (28 S. E. 970).

Appeal and collateral attack. A nolle prosequi terminates the case, and an appeal can not be entered in the same case from the overruling of a demurrer to the indictment. Jones, 115 Ga. 814 (42 

S. E. 271).

After an entry of nolle prosequi is made, it is conclusive. The higher courts will not review such entry to see whether or not it was expedient and proper. Jones, 115 Ga. 814, 817 (42 S. E. 271).

Nolle prosequi is conclusive and is not subject to collateral attack. Clark, 136 Ga. 812 (5) (72 S. E. 251); Lascelles, 90 Ga. 347 (16 S. E. 945); Bird, 53 Ga. 602. 

8. SETTLEMENT. 

All cases of indictments, or special presentments, shall be submitted to and passed upon by the jury, under the direction of the presiding judge, unless there is a settlement thereof between the prosecutor and defendant, which settlement shall be good and valid only by the approval and order of the Court on examination into the merits of the case. § 27-1701.

Offenses which can be settled. An offense against the person or property of a citizen, not punishable by fine and imprisonment, or a more severe penalty, may be settled by the prosecutor and offender, without an order or consent of the Court, where there is no indictment or special presentment. Goolsby, 53 Ga. 353 (2).

Assault and battery may be settled by consent of the Court. 

However, the Court has discretionary power to approve or refuse to permit the settlement. McDaniel, 27 Ga. 197.

Offenses which can not be settled. Trading with slaves is not such an offense against the person or property of the citizen as can be privately settled by the mere act of the parties. Dunn, 15 Ga. 419. 

Indictment for obstructing legal process can not be settled between the parties. Statham, 41 Ga. 507 (1).

Assault with intent to murder can not be compromised or settled between the parties. Stancel, 50 Ga. 152. 

Larceny of hogs can not be settled. Brown, 44 Ga. 300, 301.

Discretion of Court. It is not error for the presiding judge to refuse to allow an offender to settle a criminal cause of the grade in which he is vested with discretion to allow the settlement, or not. 

McDaniel, 27 Ga. 197. 

9. LIMITATIONS OF PROSECUTION. 

Indictment may be found and filed in the proper courts as follows: (1) For murder, at any time after the death of the person killed. (2) In all other cases where the punishment is death or perpetual imprisonment, within seven years next after the commission of the offense, and at no time thereafter. (3) In all other felonies, within four years next after the commission of the offense, and at no time thereafter. (4) In all misdemeanors, within two years after the commission of the offense, and at no time thereafter. 

If the offender shall abscond from this State, or so conceal himself that he can not be arrested, such time during which he has been absent from the State, or concealed, shall not be computed or constitute any part of said several limitations. 

Nor shall any limitation run so long as the offender or offense is unknown.
