If the indictment is found within the time limited, and for any informality shall be quashed or a nolle prosequi entered, a new indictment may be found and prosecuted within six months from the time the first is quashed or the nolle prosequi entered. § 27-601. 

Homicide. A homicide is not consummated until the death of the victim. Where an indictment is found for manslaughter, the

CRIMINAL PROCEDURE 

87. statute runs from the time of the death and not from the time the mortal wound was given. Reynolds, 1 Ga. 222, 228.

There being no statutory time of limitations for murder, one can be convicted of a lesser offense, when on trial for murder, although the statute of limitations has run against the lesser offense. Wall, 75 Ga. 474 (2); Reynolds, 1 Ga. 222; Jinks, 114 Ga. 430 (1) (40 S. 

E. 320); Troup, 17 Ga. App. 387 (2) (87 S. E. 157); Sikes, 20 Ga. 

App. 80 (92 S. E. 553).

The statute of limitations applies to the offense for which the defendant is indicted, and not to any offense included therein, of which he might be found guilty. Wall, 75 Ga. 474 (2); Jinks, 114 

Ga. 430. (1) (40 S. E. 320).

In an indictment for murder, the date of the death need not be alleged, to meet the requirements of the statute of limitations. Allegation of the date when the mortal wound was inflicted-is sufficient. Black, 14 Ga. App. 534 (3) (81 S. E. 588).

General. Law of limitations applies equally to indictments, presentments and accusations. Crawford, 4 Ga. App. 789, 797 (62 S. 

E. 501); Flint, 12 Ga. App. 169, 171, 172 (76 S. E. 1032).

The law of limitations does not apply to police courts of municipalities. Battle, 118 Ga. 242 (44 S. E. 994); Bell, 126 Ga. 443, 445 (55 S. E. 230). 

Where it does not appear that the municipal charter of an ordinance fixed a period of limitations, it will be presumed that there is no such limitation. It must appear, however, that the offense was committed after the passage of the ordinance making the act unlawful. Starling, 17 Ga. App. 336 (1) (86 S. E. 742).

A date prior to the indictment and within the period of limitation must be proved. Levan, 125 Ga. 278 (2) (54 S. E. 173).

Unless the question of time enters into the nature of the offense, the time of the commission of the offense need not be proved as alleged in the indictment. The State may introduce evidence to show that the crime was committed any time within the statute. 

Wingard, 13 Ga. 396; Davis, 105 Ga. 783 (32 S. E. 738); Pitts, 124 

Ga. 79 (1) (52 S. E. 147).

The issuance of a warrant does not arrest the running of the statute. The indictment must be found within the statutory period. 

Flint, 12 Ga. App. 169 (76 S. E. 1032).

Where crime barred. Where indictment shows upon its face that the crime is barred by the statute of limitations, a motion to arrest judgment will be sustained. McLane, 4 Ga. 335. IL

Exceptions. The statute of limitations is suspended during the time the accused conceals himself. Watkins, 68 Ga. 832. 

The statute of limitations does not begin to run in favor of the accused until his offense is known to the prosecutor, or to someone interested in the prosecution, or injured by the offense. An allegation in the indictment that the offense was unknown to the prosecutor until a certain date, sets presumptively the time when the statute of limitations begins to run. Brown, 6 Ga. App. 329 (2) (64 

S. E. 1001).

Indictment alleging that the offense and offender were "heretofore" unknown should also state the date when the offense became known. Failure so to allege is not fatal defect, but may be taken advantage of by special demurrer. Durden, 152 Ga. 441, 442 (2) (110 S. E. 283).

Where exception to the statute of limitations is alleged, the burden of proof is upon the State. Williams, 13 Ga. App. 338 (1), 340 (79 S. E. 207).

Where allegation in the indictment, showing exception to the statute of limitations, is denied, the State must prove it beyond a reasonable doubt. Hulsey, 11 Ga. App. 258, 259 (74 S. E. 1099).

Where the indictment relied on exception to prevent the bar of limitations, such exception must be alleged in the indictment and proved. Such exception can not be proved unless it is alleged. 

Hollingsworth, 7 Ga. App. 16 (1) (65 S. E. 1077); Bazemore, 34 

Ga. App. 773 (131 S. E. 177). But such exception need not be minutely described. It is sufficient if stated in the language of the Code. Cohen, 2 Ga. App. 689 (1) (2) (59 S. E. 4).

Where the indictment alleges that the offense and offender were unknown until after stated date, it is not defective for the reason that it does not state to whom they were unknown. Saunders, 43 Ga. App. 59 (158 S. E. 433).

An indictment for a misdemeanor, returned at the March Term of the court, 1913, which alleged that the offense was committed on Dec. 5, 1910, was not relieved from the bar of the statute of limitations by the following allegations: "This indictment is drawn in lieu of Indictment No. 2326, which was found true at the March

Term of said court, 1912, and which was quashed on demurrer of the defendant's counsel at the March Term of the court, 1913. Copeland, 14 Ga. App. 109 (80 S. E. 211).

CRIMINAL PROCEDURE 

89 Evidence of exception. The State is required to show only prima facie case of exception to limitations. Cohen, 2 Ga. App. 689 (1) 

The prima facie evidence to show exception to limitations must be of some probative value. Hollingsworth, 7 Ga. App. 16, 19 (65 S. E. 1077). 

Where the State shows that the offense was unknown to the prosecutor, it is prima facie sufficient to show that it was unknown. Cohen, 2 Ga. App. 689 (2) (59 S. E. 4).

In order to arrest the running of the statute of limitations, it is prima facie sufficient if the solicitor-general testifies that the offense was not known to him prior to the date alleged in the indictment. Taylor, 174 Ga. 52 (69) (162 S. E. 504).

Ordinarily where a month is referred to, it is presumed to be in the current year, unless from the connection it appear that another was intended. Tipton, 119 Ga. 304 (2) (46 S. E. 436).

Where an accusation was filed on March 16, 1912, charging that the offense was committed on March 16, 1910, it was not filed within two years after the commission of the offense. McLendon, 14 

Ga. App. 274 (80 S. E. 692).

Prima facie the term "recently" imports reference to a transaction in the immediate past. Proof that a store was recently burglarized must, in the absence of any further inquiry or evidence, be held to refer to point of time within four years. Hawkins, 17 

Ga. App. 315 (1) (86 S. E. 735).

Where the accused was openly on the streets of the city where the crime was committed, after the commission thereof, so that he could be seen and could have been arrested, his concealment is not proved. Harris, 10 Ga. App. 366 (73 S. E. 413).

Conflicting evidence. Where the evidence is conflicting, it is for the jury to determine whether the crime was committed within the statutory period of limitations. Durrence, 20 Ga. App. 192 (3) 

Where no exception to the rule as to limitation of prosecution is alleged, and the evidence is conflicting as to the date of the offense, some evidence showing that the statutory period expired between the date of the offense and the indictment, it is error for the Court to refuse to charge the jury, that if they should find that more than the statutory period expired between the time of the offense and the date of the indictment, they should acquit. Dunson, 25 Ga. App. 

172 (1) (102 S. E. 899).

Series of acts. Where the crime consisted of a series of acts, some within the statute and some without, evidence as to those without the statute are admissible to throw light on the intent. Mangham, 11 Ga. App. 427 (3) (75 S. E. 512).

Where the accused is on trial for a misdemeanor, the State may prove as many separate offenses within the statute of limitations, and of the kind charged in the indictment, as it can. Holmes, 7 

Ga. App. 570 (3) (67 S. E. 693).

On the trial of one for an illegal sale of intoxicating liquor it is error to admit in evidence a sale more than two years before the accusation. Erwin, 121 Ga. 580 (49 S. E. 689).

Abandonment of child. On the trial of a father for abandonment of a child, the crime is continuous, and will not be calculated from the time of the separation. Phelps, 10 Ga. App. 41 (72 S. 

E. 524). Bastardy.

On trial for bastardy, the statute of limitations begins to run from the time when the putative father refused to give bond and pay the expense as provided by law. Jones, 11 Ga. App. 

760 (2) (76 S. E. 72).

Offense before indictment returned. Evidence that the accused sold intoxicating liquors "within the last two years' does not show with sufficient certainty that the offense was committed before the indictment was found. Abbott, 11 Ga. App. 43 (2) (74 S. E, 621).

Indictment must state some date. The indictment must allege a certain time within the statute of limitations, and before the same was returned, but on the trial the date may be established by circumstantial evidence. Tipton, 119 Ga. 304 (1) (46 S. E. 436). 

See also: Specific Crimes. 

10. FORMER ADJUDICATION AND JEOPARDY. 

No person shall be put in jeopardy of life, or liberty, more than once for the same offense, save on his, or her own motion for a new trial after conviction, or in case of mistrial. Constitution of the State of Georgia, Article I, Section I, Paragraph VIII; § 2-108. 

When prisoner is in jeopardy. A prisoner is in jeopardy within the meaning of the Constitution, and can not be tried again, when in a court of competent jurisdiction, and upon a sufficient indictment, he has been arraigned, has pleaded, and the jury has been impaneled and sworn. Peavy, 153 Ga. 119 (1) (111 S. E. 420).

CRIMINAL PROCEDURE 

91 The jeopardy attaches when the jury is impaneled and sworn. 

Franklin, 85 Ga. 570, 571 (11 S. E. 876).

Where the first trial was before a court without jurisdiction to hear the case, a plea of former jeopardy upon a subsequent trial before a proper court is bad. The accused can not confer jurisdiction upon a court by consent. Where the Court has no jurisdiction, a judgment and a sentence is void. Barrs, 22 Ga. App. 642 (97 S. E. . 86); Walker, 22 Ga. App. 765 (97 S. E. 195).

Where a jury was discharged, after it has been impaneled and the defendant arraigned, but before introduction of evidence, the 

State may try the defendant again. Watkins, 60 Ga. 601 (1).

Where the jury dispersed before returning the verdict, purported verdict was a nullity, and the plea of former jeopardy upon a subsequent trial should be sustained. Hopkins, 6 Ga. App. 403 (1) (2) (65 S. E. 57).

If an indictment is so defective that it can not withstand a motion in arrested judgment, a plea of former jeopardy based thereon is bad. Conley, 85 Ga. 348 (1) (11 S. E. 659); Simmons, 106 Ga. 355, 358 (32 S. E. 339).

Where, after the defendant entered a plea of not guilty in a city court, and after the jury was selected and sworn, and during the examination of witnesses, the judge withdrew the case from the jury and bound the defendant over to the Superior Court for a felony, a plea of former jeopardy should be sustained in the Superior 

Court. Griffin, 28 Ga. App. 767 (113 S. E. 66).

Where, on a trial for murder, the jury returns a verdict of guilty of manslaughter, and the Court refuses to receive the verdict, declaring a mistrial, a plea of former jeopardy upon a subsequent trial is good. Register, 10 Ga. App. 623 (4) (74 S. E. 429).

Where a jury was selected, and the judge discovered that one of the jurors was disqualified, whereupon he declared a mistrial, without objection by the defendant, such mistrial will not support a plea of former jeopardy. Minyard, 17 Ga. App. 398 (1) (87 S. E. 

710); Walker, 19 Ga. App. 98 (2) (90 S. E. 1041).

Where a mistrial is improperly declared, a plea of former jeopardy should be sustained upon a second arraignment. Oliveros, 120 Ga. 

237, 238 (2) (47 S. E. 627).

Where the defendant consented that a case be tried before a judge and without a jury, and before introducing evidence to the merits of the case the judge disqualified himself, and secured another judge to hear the case, without objection from the defendant, a

plea of former jeopardy should not be sustained. Walker, 19 Ga.

App. 98 (2) (90 S. E. 1041). The rule would be different had the defendant objected. Oliveros, 120 Ga. 237 (47 S. E. 627).

Definition of former jeopardy. The principle of the common-law maxim, "Nemo debet vis vexari eadem causa," as applied to criminal prosecution, has been expressed in our Constitution in the following language: "No person shall be put in jeopardy of life or liberty more than once for the same offense, save on his own motion for a new trial, after conviction, or in case of mistrial." 

Liberty, as here used, is not confined to the detention of the person, but embraces every inalienable right of the citizen. It includes freedom of locomotion, freedom of contract, and freedom to do and perform all those things which are regarded as inalienable rights, and, as applied to male citizens who are otherwise qualified, it includes the right to vote and hold any office of honor or trust in this State. Jenkins, 14 Ga. App. 276 (5) (80 S. E. 688).

Burden of proof. The burden of proof is upon the defendant, where he pleads former adjudication. Mance, 5 Ga. App. 229 (1) (62 S. E. 1053).

Federal and State offenses. The same act may constitute two offenses, one against the State, and the other against the municipal government of the United States. In these cases conviction or acquittal in one case does not amount to such jeopardy as would prevent a trial in the other. Hood, 88 Ga. 405, 409 (14 S. E. 405); 

Cooley, 152 Ga. 469, 471 (110 S. E. 449); Fews, 1 Ga. App. 122 (58 S. E. 64); Tharpe, 24 Ga. App. 349 (100 S. E. 754). 

Motion for a new trial. Where the defendant moves for a new trial and such new trial is granted, upon appeal or otherwise, he forfeits his right of a plea of former jeopardy. Taylor, 110 Ga. 

150 (2) (35 S. E. 161); Pride, 125 Ga. 750, 751 (54 S. E. 688).

Where one is convicted of voluntary manslaughter upon an indictment for murder, and moves for a new trial, which is granted, he may again be tried for murder. Waller, 104 Ga. 505 (30 S. E. 

835); Brantley, 132 Ga. 573 (67 S. E. 810); Register, 12 Ga. App. 

1, 4 (76 S. E. 649).

One who on his own motion causes a verdict in a criminal case to be set aside may be subsequently tried upon a new indictment charging a different offense from that named in the old one, though some of the evidence material on the trial of the former may be

CRIMINAL PROCEDURE 

93 pertinent on the trial of the latter. Taylor, 110 Ga. 150 (2) (35 

S. E. 161).

An accused person can not set up former jeopardy upon an accusation which was quashed on a demurrer filed by himself, and this is true though the judge at the time the demurrer was submitted overruled it and allowed the case to proceed to the extent of introducing testimony, but afterwards recalled his original ruling and adjudged that the demurrer was good and the accusation insufficient in law. 

Brown, 109 Ga. 570 (34 S. E. 1031).

Pleas of former jeopardy. A plea of autrefois acquit is legally sufficient when it alleges that the offense in the second indictment is identical with the offense which was or could have been made subject of investigations under the first indictment, and further alleges acquittal under the first indictment in a court of competent jurisdiction. Hines, 41 Ga. App. 294 (152 S. E. 616).

A plea of former jeopardy must be in writing and filed before pleading to the merits of the indictment. Hall, 103 Ga. 403 (29 

S. E. 915); Yeates, 4 Ga. App. 573 (2) (62 S. E. 104); Sable, 14 

Ga. App. 816 (1) (82 S. E. 379).

The authorities are in conflict whether at common law the plea of autrefois convict must set out a valid judgment of conviction, or whether it is sufficient if a verdict of guilty on a valid indictment be shown. Under the practice prevailing in this State, it would seem that if the plea showed a valid verdict upon a good indictment, it would not be demurrable merely because it was not alleged that a valid judgment of conviction had been entered upon on the verdict. Jenkins, 14 Ga. App. 276 (4) (80 S. E. 688).

The plea of former jeopardy must allege that the offenses are identical, and must set out the result of a former trial. Lock, 122 

Ga. 730 (2) (50 S. E. 932).

Plea of former jeopardy is fatally defective where it does not set out a copy of the accusation on which the accused was previously tried. Whitley, 14 Ga. App. 577 (1) (81 S. E. 797); Thomas, 24 Ga. 

App. 350 (1) (100 S. E. 760).

A plea of former jeopardy must set out such a state of facts as will show that the former conviction or acquittal was for the same offense for which the defendant is about to be arraigned. Thomas, 24 Ga. App. 350 (1) (100 S. E. 760).

Courts do not take judicial cognizance of municipal ordinances. 

Where the plea of former jeopardy states that the defendant has been convicted in a municipal court, for the same offense, under a

municipal ordinance, such plea should have a copy of the municipal ordinance attached. Howell, 13 Ga. App. 74 (78 S. E. 859).

A plea of former adjudication, in order to present a question for decision, must be traversed or demurred to. Lovett, 80 Ga. 255 (4 S. E. 912). 

Whether a plea of former adjudication is good, is determined by what is known as the "same transaction" test. If the transaction for which one has been tried is the identical transaction for which he is again prosecuted, a plea of former jeopardy is available, no matter how the designation of the charge may be varied. Moore, 12 Ga. App. 576, 578 (77 S. E. 1132).

To entitle the accused to plead successfully a former acquittal the offense charged in the two prosecutions must have been the same in law and in fact; and while there is no infallible test that can be applied in all cases for determining the identity of the offense charged in the different indictments, it has been said that it is a rule of almost universal application that if the facts required to support a second indictment would have been sufficient, if proved, to procure a conviction under the first indictment, the offenses are. identical. The rule above referred to is that which is sometimes called "the same evidence test." There is also another rule, which declares that if the prosecution under the second indictment involves the same transaction which was referred to in the former indictment, and it was or might have been properly the subject of investigation under that indictment, an acquittal or conviction under the former indictment would be a bar to a prosecution under the last indictment. This rule is sometimes called "the same transaction test. The latter rule has been adopted and generally followed in this State. Gully, 116 Ga. 527, 529 (42 S. E. 790). 

Waiver. The defendant waives his right to a plea of former jeopardy where no timely plea is entered. Sable, 14 Ga. App. 816 (1) (82 S. E. 379).

Mistrial. After properly declared mistrial the defendant may be tried again. Nolan, 55 Ga. 521 (2). But there must be either a moral or a physical necessity for the mistrial, where it is entered without the consent of the accused. Nolan, 55 Ga. 521; Oliveros, 120 Ga. 237, 239 (47 S. E. 627).

Former indictment pending. The pending of a former indictment, presentment or arraignment for the same offense is no defense, unless there was a former jeopardy. Gray, 6 Ga. App. 428 (65 S. E. 191); Irwin, 117 Ga. 706 (45 S. E. 48).

CRIMINAL PROCEDURE 

95 Specific instances. A conviction of a minor offense is a full and complete acquittal of the major offense charged. Miller, 58 Ga. 200, 203 (2). 

Where a verdict in a criminal case is in legal effect an acquittal, the accused can not be again tried for the same offense, even though a new trial be granted upon his own motion. The exception in the 

Bill of Rights which prevents a plea of former jeopardy, where a new trial has been obtained at the instance of the accused, applies only where there has been a conviction. Ezzard, 11 Ga. App. 30 (2) (74 

S. E. 551).

Where the former conviction has not been appealed, but the sentence imposed has been carried to the court of review and such sentence has been reversed, without affecting the merits of the case, the prisoner can plead former jeopardy on the second trial of the same cause. A new trial is a re-examination of the facts in issue, and can not be had so long as the verdict remains unreversed. 

Reversal of the sentence does not affect the verdict. Jenkins, 14 

Ga. App. 276, 277 (7) (80 S. E. 688).

Where offenses of the same nature were committed at different instances, the first trial does not prevent a second prosecution. 

Gully, 116 Ga. 527, 529 (42 S. E. 790); McIntosh, 116 Ga. 543, 544 (42 S. E. 793).

Where, by oversight, or otherwise, the defendant is put on trial upon an indictment alleging the homicide of a living man, and, upon the mistake being discovered, a verdict of not guilty is entered, such acquittal can not be pleaded in defense to another indictment charging the same defendant with the homicide of another person, although it was the intention in the first instance to indict and prosecute for the killing of the person last mentioned, and no other transaction was contemplated in the original indictment and trial, by the grand jury, the prosecutor, or the State's counsel. 

Moody, 1 Ga. App. 772 (1) (58 S. E. 262).

Where a person has been put in legal jeopardy of conviction of an offense, which is a necessary element in, and constitutes an essential part of another offense, such jeopardy is a bar to a subsequent prosecution for the latter offense, if founded upon the same act. Bell, 103 Ga. 397 (2) (30 S. E. 294).

Where assault was committed on two different persons in connection with the same transaction, a conviction of assault upon one is no bar to a prosecution for the assault upon the other. 

Crocker, 47 Ga. 568, 570. 1

. 

Trial for an assault and battery is bar to an indictment for an assault with intent to rape, where both charges grew out of the same transaction. Bell, 103 Ga. 397 (3) (30 S. E. 294).

Estoppel by the State. Where the defendant files a special plea of former adjudication, based upon the ground that the two cases grew out of the same transaction, which is decided against him, the State is estopped from relying upon evidence as to matters which could have been adjudicated on the former trial. Mance, 5 Ga. 

App. 229 (2) (62 S. E. 1053). 

Former jeopardy on void accusation. A plea of former jeopardy can not be based on a trial under a void accusation, even though the accused consented that the trial proceed under it. Culpepper, 44 Ga. App. 351 (1) (161 S. E. 849). 

11. VENUE. 

All criminal cases shall be tried in the county where the crime was committed, except cases in the superior courts where the judge is satisfied that an impartial jury can not be obtained in such county. 

When he becomes thus satisfied, he may change the venue for the trial. § 27-1101. 

Miscellaneous. Proof of venue is essential to conviction. Smith, 105 Ga. 831 (31 S. E. 542).

Where the venue is not proved, a verdict of "guilty" is without evidence to support it, and a general assignment of error that the verdict is contrary to law and evidence is sufficient to raise the point. Smith, 118 Ga. 83 (1) (44 S. E. 827); Tipton, 119 Ga. 304 (46 S. E. 436); Brown, 123 Ga. 502 (51 S. E. 505).

The venue being an essential element of the crime, it must be established beyond a reasonable doubt. Jones, 113 Ga. 271 (1) (38 

S. E. 858); Smith, 118 Ga. 83 (1) (44 S. E. 827).

Where the venue is not sufficiently proved, a new trial will be granted. Clark, 110 Ga. 911 (3) (36 S. E. 297); Kolman, 124 Ga. 

63 (52 S. E. 82); Williams, 9 Ga. App. 169 (70 S. E. 891); Wade, 11 

Ga. App. 411, 414 (75 S. E. 494).

Where the facts are undisputed, the sufficiency of the venue is for the Court. Grady, 11 Ga. 253.

Circumstantial evidence which merely shows that it is possible that the crime was committed in the county of the trial is insufficient to show venue. Wilson, 6 Ga. App. 16 (64 S. E. 112).

CRIMINAL PROCEDURE 

97 

Hearsay is admissible to show county line. Wimbish, 70 Ga. 718 (3). 

Evidence of venue may be direct or circumstantial. Chambers, 85 Ga. 220 (11 S. E. 653); Dyer, 6 Ga. App. 390 (1) (65 S. E. 42); 

Wilson, 6 Ga. App. 16 (2) (64 S. E. 112).

Where the Court has county-wide jurisdiction, proof that the crime was committed in a certain city or town not sufficient to show venue, without evidence that it was in the county of the trial. 

Stringfield, 4 Ga. App. 842 (1) (62 S. E. 569); Wooten, 119 Ga. 745 (47 S. E. 193); Cooper, 106 Ga. 119 (32 S. E. 23); Willis, 43 Ga. App. 

394 (159 S. E. 141).

Where Court has county-wide jurisdiction, the evidence is sufficiently proved by testimony that the crime was committed in "this county." Switzer, 28 Ga. App. 747 (6) (113 S. E. 55).

Where there is slight evidence of venue, and none conflicting, venue is upheld. Johnson, 62 Ga. 299; Porter, 76 Ga. 658, 659 (2); 

Womble, 107 Ga. 666, 669 (33 S. E. 630).

Residence of the accused is irrelevant as to venue. Tarver, 123 

Ga. 494 (51 Š. E. 501). 

Residence of the victim of crime is-immaterial. Wade, 11 Ga. 

App. 411, 414 (75 S. E. 494).

Venue of crime committed by mail or telegram is the point where the matter was delivered and took effect. But it is also held that this rule does not apply where the matter was sent through the mail into Georgia from a point outside of the State. Rose, 4 Ga. App. 

588 (2-c) (62 S. E. 117); Rose, 133 Ga. 353 (65 S. E. 770); Carter, 143 Ga. 632, 633 (3) (85 S. E. 884) (Reversing Rose 4 Ga. App. 588 (62 S. E. 117)).

Evidence in homicide prosecution need not show where the deceased died, in order to give the Court jurisdiction. Roach, 34 Ga. 78. 

Larceny committed in one county and goods removed to another, accused may be tried in either county. Green, 114 Ga. 918 (2) (41 

S. E. 55); Morton, 118 Ga. 306 (2) (45 S. E. 395); McCoy, 123 Ga. 

143 (51 S. E. 279).

Where attempt is charged, venue is in the county where the crime, if perpetrated, must have been committed. Griffin, 26 Ga. 493, 494.

Where the evidence shows that the stolen animal was last seen in the county of the prosecution, it is sufficient to show venue. Dyer, 6 Ga. App. 390 (2) (65 S. E. 42); Cook, 9 Ga. App. 208 (1) (70 S. E. 1019).

Where check was given for goods in one county and payment stopped in another county, venue is in the county where check was given, if fraudulent intent then existed. Garner, 100 Ga. 257, 258 

Where evidence in trial for car-breaking did not show that the car was situated in the county of the trial, when broken into, new trial should be granted. Thomas, 8 Ga. App. 95 (68 S. E. 522); 

Howard, 3 Ga. App. 659 (60 S. E. 328); Williams, 105 Ga. 743 (31 

S. E. 749).

CHANGE OF VENUE. 

The defendant in any criminal case in the Superior Court may move, by petition in writing, for a change of venue, whenever, in his judgment, an impartial jury can not be obtained in the county where the crime was committed. Upon the motion it shall not be necessary to examine all persons in the county where the crime was committed, liable to serve on juries, but the judge shall hear evidence by affidavit or oral testimony, in support of or against the motion; and if, from the evidence submitted, the Court shall be satisfied that an impartial jury can not be obtained to try the case, the judge shall transfer it to any county that may be agreed upon by the solicitor-general and the defendant or his counsel, to be tried in the county agreed upon. If the county is not thus agreed upon, the judge shall select such county as, in his judgment, will afford a fair and impartial jury to try the case, and have it transferred accordingly. The judge of the Superior Court of the circuit in which the crime is alleged to have been committed may change the venue for the trial of said case, on his own motion, with or without petition, whenever, in his judgment, the accused party will be lynched, or there is danger of violence being attempted to be committed on said accused, if carried back, or allowed to remain in the county where the crime is alleged to have been committed. If a motion by petition shall be made by the accused for a change of venue, said judge shall hear the same in chambers, with or without the presence of the accused, at such time and place in the State as he may direct; and if the evidence submitted shall reasonably show that there is a probability or danger of lynching, or other violence, then it shall be mandatory on said judge to change the venue to such county as, in his judgment, will avoid such lynching. The petitioner shall have the right to except to the ruling of the Court at such interlocutory hearing and the bill of exceptions, when signed, shall operate as supersedeas in the trial of said case, until passed on by the Supreme

CRIMINAL PROCEDURE 

99 Court; Provided, that said prisoner shall present said bill of exceptions to the judge hearing said motion within six days after the refusal to grant said motion. Said bill of exceptions shall be filed in the office of the Superior Court of the county of the alleged crime, within two days after being signed by the judge; and said clerk shall transmit said bill of exceptions and the required record of said case as early as possible and not exceeding 10 days from the filing in said office, to the Supreme Court. Said case in the Supreme Court shall be heard as soon as possible, taking precedence of all other causes: Provided, that should the Supreme Court not be in session at the time said writ of error is received in said Court it shall be the duty of the clerk of said Supreme Court to at once notify the Chief Justice of said Court, or, in his absence or illness, one of the other Justices of said Court, of the receipt of said writ of error; and it shall be the duty of said Justice to at once convene said Supreme Court for the purpose of hearing said case, and said Supreme Court shall remand said case with directions or pass such final order as may be deemed proper and correct. § 27-1201.

Whenever a change of venue is had, the clerk of the court of the county from which the case has been transferred shall send to the Superior Court to which the case has been transferred a transcript of the order for the change of venue, the evidence before the court of inquiry, a list of all the witnesses subpoenaed in the case, and all other papers connected with the case. The clerk of the court of the county selected to try the case shall issue subpoenaes to said witnesses and such others as may be applied for by either party. 

If it should be made to appear to the judge of the Superior Court, presiding in the county to which the case has been transferred, that a fair and impartial jury can not be had therein, he shall, in the manner prescribed in the first section of this Article, transfer the case to some other county where a fair and impartial jury can be had to try it. § 27-1203.

General. The act of 1911 (Acts 1911, p. 74) added a new ground to the old law, for a change of venue, to wit, the danger of mob-violence, theretofore not existing, and provided in this latter case, that exceptions from the Court's ruling should operate as supersedeas. 

Coleman, 140 Ga. 619 (79 S. E. 543).

Where there is any evidence that the defendant can get a fair trial and that there is no danger of lynching, or other violence, dis-

cretion of the Court will not be disturbed. Currie, 25 Ga. App. 399 (103 S. E. 474); Barbee, 43 Ga. App. 577 (159 S. E. 745).

The refusal of the trial court to change the venue was upheld, although there was evidence of a danger of lynching. Wilson, 28 

Ga. App. 574 (1) (112 S. E. 295); Broxton, 24 Ga. App. 31 (99 S. E. 635).

But Court of Appeals held on conflicting evidence that the trial court abused its discretion by refusing to change the venue upon the ground that there was a danger of lynching. Balkman, 28 Ga. 

App. 39 (109 S. E. 925); Gordon, 47 Ga. App. 708 (171 S. E. 313).

Where the evidence of reputable citizens showed that there was danger of lynching, and there was no counter-showing, it was the duty of the Court to change the venue. Butler, 26 Ga. App. 435 (1) (2) (106 S. E. 744); Graham, 141 Ga. 812 (82 S. E. 282).

Change of venue in murder prosecution improperly denied, where the evidence was sufficient to reasonably show a danger of violence if the accused escaped the death sentence. Gordon, 47 Ga. App. 

708 (171 S. E. 313).

Discretion of the trial judge in granting or refusing a change of venue on conflicting evidence will not be disturbed, unless abused. 

Rawlins, 124 Ga. 31 (2) (51 S. E. 1); White, 100 Ga. 659 (1) (28 S. 

E. 423).

The power of discretion being coupled with a duty, the courts of review will correct any abuse of discretion by the trial judge. Kennedy, 141 Ga. 314, 320 (80 S. E. 1012); Newman, 143 Ga. 270 (84 S. 

E. 579).

Where evidence of reputable citizens shows danger of violence, and there is no counter-showing by the State, it is the duty of the judge to grant a change of venue, although his own opinion, after personal investigation, differs from that of the witnesses. Butler, 26 Ga. App. 435 (1) (2) (106 S. E. 744).

Procedure. The judge may order a change of venue, with or without an application therefor, on his own motion, without hearing testimony, or evidence. Ruffin, 28 Ga. App. 40 (4) (110 S. E. 311).

The issues raised by a petition for a change of venue are for the judge without a jury. 

Ruffin, 28 Ga. App. 40 (3) (110 S. E. 311); 

Howell, 162 Ga. 14 (1-a) (134 S. E. 59).

Upon an application for a change of venue, the merits of the charge laid in a bill of indictment are not in issue. Ruffin, 28 Ga. 

App. 40 (3) (110 S. E. 311).

CRIMINAL PROCEDURE 

101 A motion to change the venue, though sworn to, is not evidence, unless it is formally introduced in evidence. Rawlings, 33 Ga. App. 825 (127 S. E. 881). 

Appeal. A bill of exceptions to review a judgment refusing a petition for a change of venue must be tendered to the judge hearing the petition within six days after his refusal to grant the same. 

Waters, 32 Ga. App. 82 (122 S. E. 650).

Where a motion of defendant for a change of venue is overruled, defendant's sole remedy is a direct bill of exceptions to the Court of Appeals. He can not assign this as an error after verdict and judgment, on an exception pendente lite. Wilson, 173 Ga. 275 (1) (160 S. E. 319). 

Motion for a new trial is not a proper remedy against erroneous refusal to change venue. Williford, 121 Ga. 173 (48 S. E. 962).

Where an application for a change of venue is denied, the Court of Appeals, and not the Supreme Court, has jurisdiction, upon exceptions taken. Ruffin, 28 Ga. App. 40, 42 (110 S. E. 311); Ruffin, 151 Ga. 743 (108 S. E. 29); Wilson, 173 Ga. 275 (160 S. E. 319).

Where a change of venue is erroneously denied, and this ruling is subsequently reversed by the Court of Appeals, the judge of the lower court should be directed to change the venue, and not to grant a new hearing on the application. Kennedy, 141 Ga. 314, 319 (80 

S. E. 1012).

Where a judgment overruling a motion for a change of venue is reversed by the Court of Appeals, and a change of venue is ordered, the petitioner is bound by the decree and may not then demand to be tried in the orignal venue. Graham, 143 Ga. 440 (1) (83 S. E. 328).

Where a petition for a change of venue is granted, and the case is removed to another county, a subsequent indictment upon a different charge, is unaffected by the former change of venue. Ruffin, 28 

Ga. App. 40 (2) (110 S. E. 311).

Upon a change of venue the county from which the case is transferred loses all jurisdiction to try the accused upon the indictment so transferred, or upon any other indictment charging the same offense. Johnston, 118 Ga. 310 (45 S. E. 381).

Supersedeas. Bill of exceptions to refusal to grant a change of venue will not operate as a supersedeas where the ground of the motion is that an impartial jury can not be found in the county of the original venue. The law is construed to provide for a supersedeas only where the motion is based upon the existence of danger

or probability of lynching or other mob violence. Coleman, 140 Ga. 

619, 622 (79 S. E. 543).

Second change of venue. Where indictment is transferred from the Superior Court of one county to the Superior Court of another county, if impartial jury can not be obtained in the second county, or there is a danger of violence, the venue may be changed again. 

Ruffin, 28 Ga. App. 40 (5) (110 S. E. 311).

History. History and discussion of the law of change of venue. 

Kennedy, 141 Ga. 314, 319 (80 S. E. 1012); Bivins, 145 Ga. 416 (89 

S. E. 370); Coleman, 140 Ga. 619 (79 S. E. 543). 

12. DEMAND FOR TRIAL. 

Any person against whom a true bill of indictment is found, for an offense not affecting his life, may demand a trial at the term when the indictment is found; or at the next succeeding term thereafter, or at any subsequent term, by special permission of the Court, which demand shall be placed upon the minutes of the court; and if such person shall not be tried at the term when demand is made, or the next succeeding term thereafter, and at both terms there were juries impaneled and qualified to try him, he shall be absolutely discharged and acquitted of the offense charged in the indictment. § 27-1901. 

Where the demand has been entered, under this section, the State is bound either to discharge the accused or to try him during the term at which demand is made, or at the next succeeding term. 

Mager. 21 Ga. App. 139 (94 S. E. 82); Nix, 5 Ga. App. 835 (1) (63 

S. E. 926). 

There are no exceptions. This law is mandatory. Durham, 9 Ga. 306 (2). 

Waiver. This right may be waived by the accused. But the waiver must be by some affirmative act of the prisoner. Flagg, 11 

Ga. App. 37, 39 (74 S. E. 562).

Time of demand. Demand for trial can not be made until after indictment, presentment or accusation is found. Williamson, 1 Ga. 

App. 657 (2) (57 S. E. 1079); Flint, 12 Ga. App. 169, 171 (76 S. E. 1032).

Demand for trial may be made at any time during the term, subject to the rule that it must be made after indictment was returned, -but it must be made before the jury is discharged. Jordan, 18 Ga. 532 (1).

CRIMINAL PROCEDURE 

103 Presence of the accused. The accused must be present, in order to claim acquittal under this section, when his case is called. Moreland, 51 Ga. 192.

A voluntary absence of the defendant is a waiver of demand. Involuntary absence is not. Flagg, 11 Ga. App. 37 (2) (3) (74 S. E. 

562); Jackson, 26 Ga. App. 372 (2) (106 S. E. 210).

Even the fact that the defendant voluntarily absented himself from court is not sufficient to refuse him a discharge, unless it appears that the State called this case and the defendant failed to an- He is entitled to an opportunity to answer. Mager, 21 Ga. 

App. 139 (3) (94 S. E. 82). swer.

Voluntary absence of the accused at the third term is no reason for refusing his discharge and acquittal. Flagg, 11 Ga. App. 37 (3) (74 S. E. 562).

Qualified jury. It is a condition precedent to discharge, that a jury, qualified to try the case, must have been impaneled at both terms. This must affirmatively appear. Roebuck, 57 Ga. 154 (1) (2). 

The word "qualified" refers to the panel and not to the individuals. If array is not subject to challenge, the jury is qualified. 

Campbell, 6 Ga. App. 539, 541 (65 S. E. 307).

Adjourned term. An adjourned term is a regular term and not a special session. Where the defendant is tried at the adjourned term of the second term, the trial is timely. Carter, 14 Ga. App. 

242 (80 S. E. 533).

Term means regular term. Where special term is held after regular term, at which demand was made, this is not included in the provisions of the statute, and the State need not try the accused at such special term. Stripland, 115 Ga. 578 (41 S. E. 987).

Where the Court refused to discharge the accused on the second term on the ground that an adjourned term would be held, but such adjourned term was not held, the accused was entitled to be acquitted and discharged. Dublin, 126 Ga. 580 (55 S. E. 487).

While it is permissible to try the accused at an adjourned term, yet his rights can not be defeated by adjourning the second term until the next succeeding one. Nix, 5 Ga. App. 835 (2) (63 S. E. 926).

Entering demand on the minutes. To entitle the accused to be discharged, the demand must be entered on the minutes. Couch, 28 

Ga. 64. The purpose of this entry is to inform the State of the demand. Stripland, 115 Ga. 578, 581 (41 S. E. 987).

The demand for trial should be placed on the minutes, even though the accused absconded. Odum, 25 Ga. App. 746 (105 S. E. 54).

Where Court refuses to enter demand on the minutes, proper remedy is writ of error. Couch, 28 Ga. 64; Moore, 63 Ga. 165 (1). Contrary rule held: Sharpe, 10 Ga. App. 212 (73 S. E. 33); Bishop, 11 

Ga. App. 296 (75 S. E. 165), where it is held that writ of error is not the proper remedy, but exceptions pendente lite and assignment of error in bill of exceptions sued out after final judgment, is the proper procedure.

Transfer of case. The demand follows the indictment to whatever court it is transferred. Castleberry, 11 Ga. App. 757 (76 S. 

E. 74); Nix, 5 Ga. App. 835 (63 S. E. 926).

Where the demand was made in the Superior Court and the case was thereafter transferred to county court, which convened more than ten days after the transfer, the defendant should be tried at the first term of the county court, or be discharged. Brock, 18 Ga. 

App. 175 (89 S. E. 156).

Where a demand was made in the Superior Court at the term at which the indictment was found, and subsequently, during the term, the indictment was transferred to the city court for trial, the demand being made and the indictment transferred during a concurrent term of the city court, the next term of the city court, and not the concurrent term, was the "next succeeding term" after the demand, within the meaning of the law. Castleberry, 11 Ga. App. 757 (76 S. E. 74).

It is immaterial that the court to which the indictment was transferred was without authority to try the case. Brock, 18 Ga. App. 

175 (89 S. E. 156). 

Demand must be made where case is pending. 

Where the case is transferred from the Superior Court to the city court, demand made in the former is unavailing in the latter. Hunley, 105 Ga. 636 (31 

S. E. 543). Contrary rule held: Gordon, 106 Ga. 121 (32 S. E. 32). 

Mistrial. Benefit of demand is not lost by mistrial. Brown, 85 

Ga. 713 (2) (11 S. E. 831); Little, 54 Ga. 24.

Although the defendant was tried at the second term, where the trial resulted in a mistrial, and the case was never completed at that term, the accused is entitled to an acquittal. Nix, 5 Ga. App. 835, 837 (63 S. E. 926); Mager, 21 Ga. App. 139 (3) (94 S. E. 82).

Where, after demand, mistrial was ordered at the second term, the Court should order a new trial at the same term or discharge the prisoner. Little, 54 Ga. 24.

CRIMINAL PROCEDURE 

105 After appeal. Demand for trial is exhausted after conviction. If new trial is granted, a new demand must be made in order to operate in defendant's favor. Clay, 4 Ga. App. 142 (2) (60 S. E. 1028).

Motion for continuance. Motion to continue the case for the term, made by the prisoner, would be a waiver of his right under demand. 

Request to postpone temporarily will not waive such rights. Walker, 89 Ga. 482 (15 S. E. 553).

Continuance at the instance of one, not the accused, is no waiver. 

Campbell, 6 Ga. App. 539, 540 (65 S. E. 307). In this case the Court expressed an opinion (obiter) that if the accused had requested a postponement, though not a continuance, and by such postponement the State would be less ready to try the case, when called, it would be considered a voluntary waiver of the demand for trial, and the accused would not be entitled to a discharge, if not tried. 

Motion for discharge. The motion must affirmatively show that jurors were impaneled and qualified at both terms to try the case. 

It must also show that a qualified jury was impaneled at the time the demand was made. Woodall, 25 Ga. App. 8, 10 (1) (102 S. E. 913).

Order of discharge. Where demand for trial has regularly been made, and the accused is not tried at that or the subsequent term, and qualified jury were impaneled, the Court should enter a discharge upon the minutes in order to make the record complete. But the defendant's discharge is complete without such order. Order may be entered at any time nunc pro tunc. Collins, 7 Ga. App. 653 (2-b) (2-c) (67 S. E. 847); Thornton, 7 Ga. App. 752 (1) (67 S. E. 

1055). Discharge of the accused results automatically by operation of law, after adjournment of the second term of court. Bishop, 11 

Ga. App. 296, 297 (75 S. E. 165).

Duty of prisoner. It is not incumbent upon the accused or his counsel to make any further motion or demand at the second term, where a demand for trial has been entered at the previous term. The demand having been regularly and lawfully made, the accused may thenceforward rely upon his right to a discharge if the State fails to comply by the end of the second term with the demand already made; the only duty imposed upon him being that he be not voluntarily absent from the court, and that he shall have done no other act which in law would amount to a waiver of his demand. No formal order of discharge is necessary; acquittal results automatically, by operation of law, after the adjournment of the second term. 

Flagg, 11 Ga. App. 37, 39 (74 S. E. 562).

Where the Court, at the second term, inquired before discharging the jury, whether there was any other case pending, the accused was entitled to a discharge, although he did not respond to such inquiry. Dacey, 15 Ga. 286; Thornton, 7 Ga. App. 752 (2) (67 S. E. 

1055); Flagg, 11 Ga. App. 37 (1) (74 S. E. 562).

Joint defendants. Where two are jointly indicted, one may demand a trial. Jordan, 18 Ga. 532 (1).

Bar to future prosecution. Former discharge, under demand, is bar to future prosecution for the same criminal act, though under differently named offense. Holt, 38 Ga. 187.

This section refers to the identical charge only. Where a second charge is nominally the same, but substantially different from the one upon which demand was made, it was not covered by it. Brown, 85 Ga. 713 (3) (11 S. E. 831).

Insufficient evidence. The fact that the State failed to get sufficient evidence is no reason why the defendant should not be dis-. charged. Bishop, 11 Ga. App. 296, 297 (75 S. E. 165).

Purpose of the Act. The purpose of this section is to carry into effect the constitutional provision for speedy trial. Stripland, 115 

Ga. 578, 580 (41 S. E. 987); Bishop, 11 Ga. App. 296 (75 S. E. 165). 

13. TRIAL OF JOINT OFFENDERS. 

Where several defendants are jointly indicted, the Court may, on motion of the solicitor-general, order a severance. Stewart, 58 Ga. 577. 

The right of the defendants to be tried separately is not affected by a joint arraignment. They may be arraigned jointly and tried separately. Rawlins, 124 Ga. 31, 43 (8) (52 S. E. 1).

Demand for severance is too late after the evidence has been introduced. 

Trowbridge, 74 Ga. 431 (3).

By voluntary waiver persons indicted separately for the same offense may be tried together. Towns, 149 Ga. 613 (101 S. E. 678).

Evidence. Declaration of one defendant that he alone committed the offense, is not admissible on the trial of the other. Robison, 114 

Ga. 445 (2) (40 S. E. 253); Kelly, 82 Ga. 441 (2) (9 S. E. 171).

Where two offenders are jointly tried, competent evidence of the guilt of either offender is admissible, though it might be irrelevant as to the other. Johnson, 70 Ga. 725.

CRIMINAL PROCEDURE 

107 A witness jointly indicted with another is a competent witness against the other-on a separate trial. Williamson, 9 Ga. App. 442, 444 (71 S. E. 509).

Where two are tried jointly, and the right is reserved that each may testify for the other, one, who testified for the other may be impeached just as any other witness. McGruder, 71 Ga. 864 (2). 

Where two, jointly indicted, were tried jointly, without reserving the right to testify for each other, the wife of one was not a competent witness for the other. Trowbridge, 74 Ga. 431 (2).

Peremptory challenges. Where two or more persons are jointly indicted and put on trial for an offense for which one may be convicted and the other acquitted, each is entitled to the same number of peremptory challenges as if tried separately. This rule is applicable in misdemeanors as well as in felony cases. Nobles, 12 Ga. 

App. 355 (1) (77 S. E. 184).

Argument of counsel. Where two are tried together without objection, they have a right to only so much time for argument as a trial for a single defendant would permit. Bloodworth, 161 Ga. 332, 334 (131 S. E. 80).

Operation of conviction or acquittal. Where it takes two to commit a crime, the acquittal of one does not operate as an acquittal of the other jointly indicted with the first one, but tried separately. 

Rachels, 51 Ga. 374 (2); Lewis, 5 Ga. App. 496, 498 (63 S. E. 570).

Where two persons are indicted for a crime which does not require the joint act of both, one may be convicted, although the other is acquitted. A conviction of one does not raise a presumption of guilt of the other. Easterling, 12 Ga. App. 690 (3) (78 S. E. 140); 

Roane, 97 Ga. 195 (22 S. E. 374); Mixon, 123 Ga. 581 (7) (51 S. E. 580).

Election by the State. The State may elect which one of the joint defendants it will try first. Dixon, 12 Ga. App. 17 (1) (76 S. E. 

794). After electing, the State may withdraw the election, and try the other. (Id.) 

14. CONTINUANCES. 

All applications for continuances are addressed to the sound legal discretion of the Court, and, if not expressly provided for, shall be granted or refused, as the ends of justice may require. And in all civil and criminal cases in the courts of this State, the presiding judges may, in their discretion, admit a counter-showing to a motion for a continuance, and, after a hearing, may decide whether

the motion shall prevail. § 81-1419. Henry, 153 Ga. 412 (1) (112 S. 

E. 647); York, 42 Ga. App. 453 (156 S. E. 733).

In order to grant a new trial, it must affirmatively appear that the judge flagrantly abused his discretion. Edenfield, 26 Ga. App. 206 (1) (105 S. E. 732); Pope, 42 Ga. App. 680 (157 S. E. 211).

When continuance should be granted. Where showing for a continuance is complete, and there is no counter-showing, it is reversible error to refuse continuance. Andrews, 84 Ga. 82 (10 S. E. 503); 

Barnard, 73 Ga. 803.

Where a defendant is entitled to a continuance, the refusal thereof is a reversible error. Copenhaven, 14 Ga. 22 (1); Collins, 12 Ga. 

App. 635 (2) (77 S. E. 1079).

Although showing for continuance may not be complete, if the defendant is in fact entitled to a continuance, it should be granted. 

Battles, 9 Ga. App. 192 (70 S. E. 973); Jones, 125 Ga. 307, 309 (54 S. 

E. 122).

Where ground of motion for continuance is not stated when the motion is made, it is not an error to refuse the same. Delk, 99 Ga. 

667, 668 (4) (26 S. E. 752).

All grounds should be urged at once. All grounds for continuance existing at the time of the motion should be urged at once therein. It is not error to refuse to hear a second motion for continuance after the first one is overruled. Robson, 83 Ga. 166 (4) (9 S. 

E. 610).

Opinion of judge. Opinion of the presiding judge as to the guilt or innocence of the accused is no ground for depriving him of his right to continuance. Copenhaven, 14 Ga. 22 (4).

Who makes motion for continuance. Affidavit for continuance must be made by the defendant himself, unless good and sufficient reason is shown why he could not do so. Fogarty, 80 Ga. 450 (1) (5 S. E. 782); Moody, 54 Ga. 660 (2); Jarrett, 41 Ga. App. 838, 839 (1) (155 S. E. 49).

The judge is not required to hear a motion for continuance in the absence of the accused. Oglesby, 121 Ga. 602, 603 (9) (49 S. E. 706).

Discretion of the Court. The broad discretion of the Court looks to the attainment of justice and each case should be decided on its merits, without being interfered with by exact letter of law. Smith, 7 Ga. App. 252, 257 (66 S. E. 556).

Judge has discretion to either continue the case or postpone it until a later day in the term. Oglesby, 121 Ga. 602, 603 (49 S. E. 706).

CRIMINAL PROCEDURE 

109 A motion for continuance made at the term at which the indictment was found, while addressed to the sound discretion of the Court, stands upon different footing from such motion made at a subsequent term. Reasonable opportunity to prepare for one's defense should not be sacrificed in interest of speed. The Court's discretion should be liberally exercised in favor of the accused. 

Brooks, 3 Ga. App. 458 (3) (60 S. E. 211); Haines, 8 Ga. App. 627 (2) (70 S. E. 84); Patten, 10 Ga. App. 20 (72 S. E. 521); Moody, 54 

Ga. 660 (3); Malone, 49 Ga. 210 (4).

Delay. Where the application failed to show that it is not made for delay only, it should be overruled. Tomlin, 110 Ga. 268 (34 S. 

E. 845); Jones, 128 Ga. 23 (1) (57 S. E. 313). 

Cross examination. Conflicting ruling whether defendant making showing for continuance may be cross-examined by the State. 

Bishop, 9 Ga. 121 (6); Thompson, 24 Ga. 297 (3); Bell, 36 Ga. App. 

111, 112 (135 S. E. 521).

Where showing for continuance is made by another, the witness may be cross-examined. Fogarty, 80 Ga. 450, 453 (5 S. E. 782).

Information. Where affidavit for continuance was based on information, affidavit of such informant should be presented. Bradley, 128 Ga. 20 (1) (57 S. E. 237). 

Erroneous overruling of motion. was erroneously overruled, all else tory. Johnson, 16 Ga. App. 287, 288 (3) (85 S. E. 204). 

Where motion for continuance occurring at the trial is nuga- 

Surprise. Where the defendant is surprised by the testimony, which could not be anticipated, but which he could have disproved, if anticipated, his proper remedy is a motion for continuance, and not for a new trial. Sanders, 7 Ga. App. 603 (67 S. E. 696). 

a. INSUFFICIENT TIME TO PREPARE. 

Where counsel asked for a continuance on the ground that he had not had time to prepare for the case, the grant or the refusal of such request rests within the sound discretion of the Court. Renfroe, 8 Ga. App. 676 (1) (70 S. E. 70). And such discretion will not be disturbed, unless abused. Harris, 119 Ga. 114 (1) (45 S. E. 973); 

Nick, 128 Ga. 573 (1) (58 S. E. 48); Baker, 111 Ga. 141 (1) (36 S. 

E. 607).

Forcing one, indicted of an offense, peremptorily to a trial, immediately after appointing counsel to defend him, without giving counsel an opportunity to investigate the case, is error. McArver, 114 

Ga. 514 (40 S. E. 779).

Where counsel is appointed, Court should allow reasonable time for the preparation of the case. Hunt, 102 Ga. 569 (27 S. E. 670).

Where counsel appointed had no opportunity to confer with the accused, a motion for a postponement should be granted. Blackman, 76 Ga. 288; (distinguished in Walton, 79 Ga. 446 (1)).

Ten minutes time to prepare for trial on an appointed case is insufficient. 

Reliford, 140 Ga. 777 (79 S. E. 1128).

Lack of proper time to prepare can not be complained of in the absence of a motion for continuance. Lamar, 153 Ga. 216 (6) (111 

S. E. 914).

While ample time should be allowed one accused of a crime to prepare for his trial, it is the duty of the accused, who has given bond for appearance, to employ counsel and take any other steps essential to his defense, in advance of the term to which he is bound to appear. Walker, 11 Ga. App. 251 (1) (74 S. E. 1100); Stamper, 21 Ga. App. 798 (1) (95 S. E. 266); Hall, 22 Ga. App. 112 (1-b) (95 

S. E. 936). 

Imprisonment is no reason for not preparing defense. Revel, 26 

Ga. 275, 276 (2); Long, 38 Ga. 491 (3).

It is too late to complain after conviction that counsel did not have time to confer with the witnesses, where no such complaint or motion was made before the trial. Scott, 137 Ga. 337 (1) (73 S. E. 575).

The time to be allowed counsel to prepare for the trial is in the sound discretion of the trial judge and this discretion will not be disturbed, unless abused. Hulsey, 172 Ga. 797 (2) (159 S. E. 270); 

Hightower, 9 Ga. App. 236 (1) (70 S. E. 1022).

That case was called for trial immediately after indictment was returned does not in itself entitle the accused to a continuance, without a proper showing. In fact the accused has a right to demand trial immediately. Braxley, 17 Ga. App. 196 (1) (86 S. E. 425).

Constitutional guaranty. The constitutional guaranty of "benefit of counsel' means something more than the mere appointment of counsel by the Court to represent the accused. He is entitled to reasonable time for the preparation by such counsel to properly represent him on the trial. Reliford, 140 Ga. 777, 778 (79 S. E. 1128).

Insufficient time. Where the accused was arrested the afternoon before the trial, and his counsel was busy with other matters, not being able to confer with witnesses, a refusal to grant a postponement is a reversible error. Battles. 9 Ga. App. 192 (70 S. E. 973); 

Contrary rule held: Moody, 54 Ga. 660 (1).

CRIMINAL PROCEDURE 

111 Where counsel was appointed on the case, and trial forced within a short notice, continuance should be granted on motion. Cummings, 151 Ga. 593 (107 S. E. 771).

Nolle prosequi. Where the accused and his counsel had ample time to prepare for the trial upon a bill of indictment, but the bill was nol prossed, a motion for postponement upon the new bill, based on the same charge, on the ground that counsel did not have sufficient time to prepare for trial, is properly overruled. Jones, 115 

b. ABSENCE OR ILLNESS OF COUNSEL. 

What motion must show. Motion for continuance on the ground of absence of counsel, because of illness, must affirmatively disclose: (1) that absent counsel, where there is more than one, is the leading counsel; (2) that he is sick; (3) that motion is not made for delay only; (4) that movant expects to secure the services of the counsel at the next term. Wall, 126 Ga. 86 (1) (54 S. E. 815). 

Not favored. 

Continuance for absence of counsel not favored. 

Poppell, 71 Ga. 276 (2); Curry, 17 Ga. App. 377 (2) (87 S. E. 685); 

Caswell, 27 Ga. App. 78 (1) (107 S. E. 562).

Strict showing is required where ground of continuance is the absence of counsel. Caswell, 27 Ga. App. 78 (1) (107 S. E. 562). 

Leading counsel. Continuance will be granted for illness of leading counsel only. Cliett, 132 Ga. 36 (3) (63 S. E. 626).

The Court must determine who is the leading counsel. Smith, 78 

Ga. 71.

If there is more than one counsel, the Court shall, as between them, give him preference who was first employed. Smith, 78 Ga. 71, 74.

Illness. Motion to continue for illness of counsel is addressed to sound discretion of the Court. Especially is this true where counsel is in court and is urging the motion in person. Rawlins, 124 Ga. 

31, 33 (19) (52 S. E. 1); Brantley, 133 Ga. 264 (4), 365 (65 S. E. 

426); Jones, 128 Ga. 23 (3) (57 S. E. 313).

Illness of counsel contemplated by law is such physical condition resulting from sickness, malady, or disease, as would prevent counsel from properly attending to his duties. Mere indisposition is not sufficient. Rawlins, 124 Ga. 31, 54 (52 S. E. 1).

Physical inability of counsel is no ground for continuance, where it appears that the accused knew of his inability at the time he retained counsel. Curry, 17 Ga. App. 377 (3) (87 S. E. 685).

Leave of absence. Where leading counsel has leave of absence from Court, but there is another counsel in the case who is present when it is called, motion for continuance should be made. In the absence of such motion a new trial will not be granted, based on the aforestated facts. Childs, 18 Ga. App. 782 (5) (90 S. E. 723).

Withdrawal of counsel. Withdrawal of counsel, shortly before trial, leaving the accused unprepared, is ground for continuance or postponement. Jackson, 88 Ga. 784 (2) (15 S. E. 677); Jones, 65 

Ga. 506 (1). 

Conflicting engagements. Where counsel has conflicting engagement in the Court of Appeals, continuance is in the sound discretion of the trial judge. Hulsey, 172 Ga. 797, 804 (159 S. E. 270). 

Error of counsel. Where counsel believed in good faith, which was justified, that the case will not be called until a later time, postponement should be granted. Delk, 100 Ga. 61 (2) (27 S. E. 152). 

Denial of right of postponement. Where the accused is entitled to a continuance on account of providential absence of his counsel, the denial thereof is reversible error. Chivers, 5 Ga. App. 654 (1) (63 S. E. 703). 

c. ILLNESS OF THE ACCUSED. 

If a prisoner is forced to trial when he is too sick to have use of his faculties, a new trial will be granted. Frain, 40 Ga. 529, 530 (4).

Where the ground of the motion for continuance is that the accused is physically unable to go to trial, and the accused is present in court, the judge has sufficient opportunity to ascertain his physical condition, and a denial of the continuance will not be disturbed. 

Rowland, 125 Ga. 792 (1) (54 S. E. 694); Stovall, 106 Ga. 443, 444 (1) (32 S. E. 586); Cook, 27 Ga. App. 253 (1) (107 S. E. 897); Edenfield, 26 Ga. App. 206 (1) (105 S. E. 732); Switzer, 28 Ga. App. 747 (1) (113 S. E. 55).

Where medical opinion is conflicting as to defendant's physical condition and fitness to go to trial, the discretion of the trial judge will not be disturbed. McDaniel, 103 Ga. 268 (1) (30 S. E. 29); 

Oglesby, 121 Ga. 602 (5) (49 S. E. 706); Rawlins, 124 Ga. 31, 33 (18) (52 S. E. 1). 

d. PUBLIC EXCITEMENT. 

Generally public excitement is not a sufficient ground for a continuance. Thompson, 24 Ga. 297 (2); Hulsey, 172 Ga. 797 (1) (159 

S. E. 270); Woolfolk, 85 Ga. 69 (3) (11 S. E. 814).

CRIMINAL PROCEDURE 

113 To justify a continuance for public excitement, the defendant must show that the excitement is so strong that a fair trial can not be obtained. Davis, 33 Ga. 98 (5).

Under extraordinary circumstances public excitement may be sufficient ground for a continuance. Thomas, 27 Ga. 287; Maddox, 32 Ga. 581, 582.

A continuance will not be granted simply on the asseveration of the accused, without any supporting evidence, that because of public excitement he will not be able to have a fair trial. Taylor, 135 

Ga. 622 (70 S. E. 237); Hulsey, 172 Ga. 797, 803 (159 S. E. 270).

The publication of an article in a newspaper of wide circulation in the county and the State does not require a finding upon the part of the courts that an impartial jury could not be obtained at the time of the trial. Biggers, 171 Ga. 596 (156 S. E. 201); Hulsey, 172 

Ga. 797, 803 (159 S. E. 270).

The Court may refuse to hear evidence to the extent that a former jury was divided on the question of recommending the accused to the mercy of the Court. (Id.)

Prior to the Act of 1856 in relation to the qualification of jurors to serve on the trial of persons charged with felonies, the courts were inclined to listen favorably to applications for continuances on account of public excitement. Since that time, it is impossible that a party on his trial for such an offense, if he choose to avail himself of all his legal rights, can have an unfair trial, unless it be by the perjury of persons put upon him as jurors, or the palpable misconduct of the officers of the law. Thompson, 24 Ga. 297; Hulsey. 172 Ga. 797, 802 (159 S. E. 270).

Continuance on the ground of popular excitement is not essential to a fair trial, where an impartial jury is obtained. The law provides adequate remedies for a fair trial. Lovett, 60 Ga. 257 (1). 

e. ABSENCE OR ILLNESS OF WITNESSES. 

Requirements. In all applications for continuances upon the ground of the absence of a witness, it must be shown to the Court: (1) that the witness is absent; (2) that he has been subpoenaed; (3) that he resides in the county where the case is pending; (4) that his testimony is material; (5) that the witness is not absent by permission, directly or indirectly, of the applicant; (6) that he expects he will be able to procure the testimony of the witness at the next term of the court; (7) and that the application is not made for the purpose of delay, but to enable the party to procure the testimony

of the absent witness; (8) and must state the facts expected to be proved by the witness. § 81-1410.

Names of witnesses, places of residence, facts to be proved, and their materiality should be shown, as well as efforts made to obtain witnesses. Moore, 7 Ga. App. 77 (1) (66 S. E. 377).

Absence of witness. Where witness, whose illness was the ground of the motion for continuance, is in court, and is examined, the judge has the benefit of personal observation, and his discretion will not be disturbed. Boatright, 27 Ga. App. 292 (1) (2) (108 S. E. 130).

Motion for continuance must show diligence in procuring the witness. Jones, 125 Ga. 307, 308 (54 S. E. 122).

Where diligence to secure the witness is not shown, and there is another witness to prove the facts expected of the absent one, a continuance is properly refused. Parker, 3 Ga. App. 336, 339 (59 S. E. 823).

Witness subpoenaed. Accused moving for continuance on account of absence of witness must show that the witness was subpoenaed. Hooks, 16 Ga. App. 456 (1) (85 S. E. 613). Or some other effort made to have him in court. Williams, 13 Ga. App. 179 (2) (78 S. E. 1012).

Where witnesses resided in the county, subpoenas issued in ample time, placed into the hands of the proper officers, and they were absent, and there was no evidence that the subpoenas were served, -continuance should be granted. Watts, 14 Ga. App. 600 (81 S. 

E. 902).

Court has discretion to grant continuance for absence of witness, though witness has not been subpoenaed. Hobbs, 8 Ga. App. 53, 56 (68 S. E. 515); Paulk, 5 Ga. App. 567, 569 (63 S. E. 659).

Where defendant requests postponement until later day during the same term, in order that he may have time to subpoena witnesses, the Court may require him to state the names of the witnesses, their addresses, and the materiality of their expected testimony. Moore, 7 Ga. App. 77 (1) (66 S. E. 377).

It must affirmatively appear that the witness, for whose absence the continuance is requested, had been subpoenaed. Walker, 118 

Ga. 34 (4) (44 S. E. 850).

Where defendant has used due diligence to procure presence of witnesses, he is entitled to continuance, whether witness had been subpoenaed or not. Hobbs, 8 Ga. App. 53, 54 (2) (68 S. E. 515);

CRIMINAL PROCEDURE 

115 

Brooks, 3 Ga. App. 458 (60 S. E. 211); Chatfield, 10 Ga. App. 40, 41 

It is the duty of the accused to ascertain whether the witness had been subpoenaed. Plumer, 22 Ga. App. 269 (1) (95 S. E. 873).

Where the accused had not had sufficient time to have witnesses subpoenaed, he should be granted a continuance. Rumsey, 126 Ga. 

419 (1) (55 S. E. 167); Haines, 8 Ga. App. 627 (1) (70 S. E. 84).

Where failure to subpoena is due to fault of officers of the court, continuance should be granted. Thomas, 95 Ga. 484 (20 S. E. 315); 

Paulk, 5 Ga. App. 567 (1) (63 S. E. 659); Blackshear, 25 Ga. App. 

327 (103 S. E. 198); Smith, 25 Ga. App. 324 (103 S. E, 198).

Where subpoena was not issued until it was too late, continuance may be denied. Bone, 8 Ga. App. 373 (69 S. E. 37); Solomon, 10 Ga. 

App. 469 (1) (73 S. E. 623); Fitzgerald, 126 Ga. 556 (55 S. E. 482).

It is not due diligence to hand to the sheriff a subpoena for a witness, living in another county, on Friday, before the Monday on which the trial was scheduled to take place. Glover, 89 Ga. 391 (15 

S. E. 496).

Where the party is offered the machinery of the court,-an attachment, to compel the attendance of the absent witness, and the offer is declined, it is not error to refuse to continue the case for the term. Curtis, 48 Ga. App. 135 (2) (172 S. E. 99).

Residence of absent witness. One is a resident witness, who resides in the State, though he may be temporarily absent. Pyburn, 84 Ga. 193 (1) (10 S. E. 733).

Where witness is inaccessible, a continuance is properly refused. 

Power, 8 Ga. App. 408 (2) (69 S. E. 315); Howard, 7 Ga. App. 61 

Where witness resides beyond the jurisdiction of the court, it is not error to refuse a continuance, especially where no promise is shown by the witness. Tolbert, 12 Ga. App. 685 (7) (78 S. E. 131); 

Owens, 110 Ga. 292 (1) (34 S. E. 1015); Wall, 126 Ga. 86 (2) (54 S: 

E. 815).

Subpoenas for non-resident witnesses for the defendant need not be countersigned by the solicitor-general. Paulk, 5 Ga. App. 567 

Where the witness was a non-resident, or absent from the State, his absence was not sufficient ground for a continuance. Hays, 16 

Ga. App. 20 (1) (84 S. E. 497); Watts, 20 Ga. App. 182 (1) (92 S. E. 966).

Where there is no evidence that the absent witness is only temporarily beyond the limits of the State and that he would probably be present at the next term of the court, the continuance should not be granted. Fudge, 18 Ga. App. 312 (1) (89 S. E. 374).

Where the material witness is beyond the jurisdiction of the court (in the United States Army, overseas in war), continuance need not be granted on account of his absence. James, 23 Ga. App. 534 (1) (98 S. E. 737).

Where the witness has left the vicinity and is inaccessible, his absence is not a valid ground of continuance. Howard, 26 Ga. App. 

431 (106 S. E. 732). Materiality of expected testimony. Motion for continuance must show materiality of evidence expected to be produced by absent witness. Jones, 125 Ga. 307, 308 (54 S. E. 122).

Where materiality is shown and the motion is otherwise perfect, continuance should be granted. Collins, 12 Ga. App. 635, 636 (77 

S. E. 1079); Andrews, 84 Ga. 82 (10 S. E. 503); Ryder, 100 Ga. 528 (1) (28 S. E. 246).

The facts to which the witness would swear, if present, must be shown. Wiggins, 101 Ga. 502 (1) (29 S. E. 26); Moore, 7 Ga. App. 

77 (1) (66 S. E. 377); Dallas, 129 Ga. 602 (1) (59 S. E. 279).

The judge should believe the defendant. The judge should believe the defendant as to what the absent witness would swear to, except, perhaps, in a very unusual case. Varnadoe, 67 Ga. 768.

Inadmissible evidence to be proved by absent witness. Where absent witness' testimony would not have been admissible, because it is hearsay, or for other reasons, the continuance is properly refused. 

Ivey, 154 Ga. 63 (3) (113 S. E. 175); Jackson, 148 Ga. 519 (1) (97 S. 

E. 525); Medlin, 149 Ga. 23 (1-a) (98 S. E. 551).

Absence not by permission of the accused. Where affidavit does not state that the witness is not absent by consent of the defendant, or that a motion is not made for delay only, affidavit is defective. 

Polite, 78 Ga. 347 (2); Moody, 54 Ga. 660 (2); Parker, 3 Ga. App. 

336, 339 (59 S. E. 823).

Securing testimony at the next term of court. Motion must show that the absent witness is expected to testify at the next term of the court. Jones, 128 Ga. 23 (1) (57 S. E. 313); Clarke, 41 Ga. App. 556 

Where movant has not stated that he expected to have the testimony of the absent witness at the next term of court, it was proper

CRIMINAL PROCEDURE 

117 to refuse the continuance. Williams, 25 Ga. App. 380 (2) (103 S. 

E. 685).

Motion for delay only. Where counter-showing tends to establish the fact that motion is made for delay only, a refusal of a continuance is no abuse of discretion, although the motion was perfect in every respect. The credibility of the witnesses is for the judge in such cases. Kimberly, 4 Ga. App. 852 (1) (62 S. E. 571).

Facts to be proved by absent witnesses admitted. No continuance shall be allowed in any court on account of the absence of witness, or for the purpose of securing testimony, where the opposite party is willing to admit and does not contest the truth of the facts expected to be proved; and the Court shall order such admission to be reduced to writing. § 81-1411.

Where the State is willing to admit, and does not contest the truth of the testimony expected to be proved by the absent witness, and the Court orders such admission to be reduced to writing, a continuance should be denied. Parker, 81 Ga. 332 (3) (6 S. E. 600); 

Waters, 150 Ga. 623, 625 (7) (104 S. E. 626); Hayslip, 11 Ga. App. 

194 (74 S. E. 1006).

It is not sufficient that the State admits that the absent witness would swear to the facts as alleged in the motion. The State must admit the truth of the facts, and consent to the contents of such facts. Klugman, 43 Ga. 581 (1); Watson, 118 Ga. 66, 69 (2) (44 S. 

E. 803). 

Other witnesses swearing to the same fact. Continuance should not be denied because there are other witnesses who could testify to the same facts, when it appears that absent witness' testimony is important and material. Britt, 13 Ga. App. 698 (79 S. E. 859). Contrary rule held in Blount 18 Ga. App. 204 (1) (89 S. E. 78); Johnson, 155 Ga. 509 (1) (117 S. E. 434); Hewitt, 27 Ga. App. 676 (2) (109 S. E. 679).

Where the defendant moved to continue for the absence of one witness to prove alibi, when he had another witness to swear to the same facts, and Court overruled the motion, and on the trial the defendant used the witness present, and then State impeached such witness by two witnesses who swore that they would not believe him on oath, the Court should have granted either the motion to continue, or should have exacted a promise from the State, not to introduce evidence to destroy the credit of the witness present. Reid, 23 

Ga. 190 (1).

Where other witnesses are present who can testify to the same facts as the one for whose absence the continuance is requested, refusal of the request is not error. Jones, 125 Ga. 307, 308 (54 S. E. 

122); Salmons, 118 Ga. 763 (1) (45 S. E. 611).

But as a general rule a continuance should be granted on account of an absent witness, although there might be other witnesses present who can testify to the same transaction. Absent witness might be believed when present witnesses might be discredited. Hobbs, 8 

Ga. App. 53, 54 (2) (68 S. E. 515); Price, 7 Ga. App. 571 (67 S. E. 

679); Little, 121 Ga. 159 (48 S. E. 904).

Cumulative evidence. The case before the bar may be such that cumulative evidence is of the utmost importance. Reid, 23 Ga. 190, 192. 

It is not abuse of discretion to overrule a motion for continuance based on the absence of a witness who would give cumulative testimony as to the good character of the accused. Stevens, 49 Ga. App. 

248 (174 S. E. 718).

Absent witness brought to court. Refusal of continuance is no error, where Court had absent witness brought in, and such witness testified in the case. Renfroe, 8 Ga. App. 676 (1) (70 S. E. 70); 

Stewart, 58 Ga. 577 (2); Rawlins, 124 Ga. 31 (6), 42 (52 S. E. 1).

When motion should be renewed. Where continuance was requested on account of the absence of a witness, who was alleged to be ill, and the Court refused the continuance, sending an officer of the court to bring the witness to the trial, after such officer returned reporting that the witness was too ill to attend, defendant should move for a continuance, or, if the trial has commenced, for a mistrial. In the absence of such motion the right is presumed to be waived. Pressley, 132 Ga. 64 (1) (63 S. E. 784).

Counter showing. Counter showing may be made that the absent witness would not testify as alleged in defendant's motion. Williams, 69 Ga. 11 (2); Johnson, 65 Ga. 94 (1-a); Brown, 65 Ga. 332, 338. 

Where one swore that the absent witness declined and disclaimed any knowledge of the matter in question, denial of motion not error. 

Mosely, 74 Ga. 404 (1). Contrary rule held: Waldrup, 84 Ga. 113 (10 S. E. 597); Kennedy, 101 Ga. 559 (1) (28 S. E. 979).

Counter showing to the effect that the absent witness made a statement, not under oath, inconsistent with what movant expected to prove, insufficient. Cunneen, 95 Ga. 330 (1) (22 S. E. 538).

CRIMINAL PROCEDURE 

119 Where the testimony of an absent witness, relied upon to prove a certain defense, would not have been sufficient to prove such defense, refusal of continuance is no error. Wrenn, 12 Ga. App. 694 (1) (78 S. E. 202).

Inquiry as to other witnesses. On a motion for continuance on the ground of an absent witness, it is not proper to inquire on a counter showing as to what other witnesses will swear to. Johnson, 65 Ga. 94 (1-a).

Facts untrue. On a motion for continuance it is not permissible to show on a counter showing that the facts, which it is claimed the absent witness will swear to, are untrue. Williams, 69 Ga. 11 (2). 

Stenographic notes. Where stenographic notes are to be used of a former trial, for the purpose of impeaching witnesses, it is no error to refuse a motion for continuance on the ground that such notes were in a different county. Helms, 136 Ga. 799 (1) (72 S. E. 246).

Defendant misled by the State. Where the uncontradicted evidence shows that the defendant was misled by the statement of the solicitor-general to the effect that the accused need not have his lawyer and witnesses present, meaning that the case will not be called, -this is an exception to the rule laid down as to showing that the witnesses are not absent by the permission of the movant. Windom, 24 Ga. App. 385 (100 S. E. 753); Delk, 100 Ga. 61 (2) (27 S. E. 152). 

Witness in dying condition. Where the absent witness is in the last stages of consumption, it is not an abuse of discretion to deny a continuance based on the absence of such witness. Burnsed, 14 Ga. 

App. 832 (1) (82 S. E. 595).

The Court may deny a continuance where the absent witness is so gravely ill that his presence in court at any time in the future is problematical. McAllister, 17 Ga. App. 159 (1) (86 S. E. 412). 

Wrong witness subpoenaed. Where the sheriff subpoenaed a wrong witness, continuance should be granted, where motion otherwise complete. Brown, 8 Ga. App. 412 (69 S. E. 316).

Impeaching witness. Absence of an impeaching witness is a sufficient ground for continuance. Fox, 9 Ga. 373. Contrary rule held: 

Smith, 13 Ga. App. 32 (1) (78 S. E. 685); Ivey, 154 Ga. 63 (3) (113 

S. E. 175).

Postponement for attachment. Where a court continued the case for one day, instructing the accused to secure attachment for the absent witness, which the accused failed to do, he had no ground for complaint. Hickox, 26 Ga. App. 416 (1) (107 S. E. 81).

Accessories. It is no ground of a motion for continuance of a case against an accessory that the principal intends to file motion for new trial. Loyd, 45 Ga. 57, 58 (5). 

15. JURY. 

Parties entitled to full panels. In civil cases and cases of misdemeanors in the Superior Court, each party may demand a full panel of 24 competent and impartial jurors from which to strike the jury, and when one or more of the regular panel of traverse jurors shall be absent or for any reason disqualified, the presiding judge, at the request of counsel for either party, shall call the panel to be filled by tales jurors to the number of 24 before requiring the parties, or their counsel, to strike a jury. § 59-704.
