Juries to try misdemeanors; peremptory challenges. For the trial of misdemeanors, the solicitor and the accused may select either panel of the petit jury. If they shall not agree upon a panel, the 

Court shall have a panel made of the 24 petit jurors in attendance, of which the accused will have the right to challenge seven peremptorily, and the State five. The remaining 12 shall constitute the jury. § 59-707.

Panel of 48 jurors in felony trials; tales jurors. When any person shall stand indicted for a felony, the Court shall have impaneled 48 jurors, 24 of whom shall be taken from the two panels of petit jurors, from which to select the jury. When the regular panels of petit jurors, or either of them, can not be furnished to make up panels of 48 for the trial of felony, because of the absence of any of such panels, where they, or any part of them, are engaged in the consideration of a case, the presiding judge may cause said panels to be filled by summoning such numbers of persons, who are competent jurors, as may be necessary to make full the said panels. If the jury shall not be made up from said panel of 48, the Court shall continue to furnish panels, consisting of such number of jurors as the Court, in its discretion may think proper, until a jury shall be obtained. 

In making up said panel of 48 jurors, or successive panels of any number, the presiding judge may draw the tales jurors from the jury box of the county and order the sheriff to summon them, or he may order the sheriff to summon tales jurors from among persons qualified by law to serve as jurors. § 59-801.

In the trial of a criminal case, where the jurors present have all been put upon the defendant, and it becomes necessary to procure other jurors, it is entirely within the discretion of the presiding

CRIMINAL PROCEDURE 

121 judge to draw the tales jurors from the jury box, or to order the sheriff to summon them from among persons qualified by law to serve as jurors. Spence, 20 Ga. App. 61 (3) (92 S. E. 555).

Where a full panel of forty-eight jurors is put upon the prisoner, without any objection to the array, and, during the striking of the jury, some of the jurors are excused for cause, and some because of relationship, or because they are conscientiously opposed to capital punishment, there is no merit in the contention that the accused is entitled, before the panel is exhausted, to know the names of any of the jurors, or talesmen, whom the sheriff may have drawn. 

Chewning, 18 Ga. App. 11 (1) (88 S. E. 904).

Forty-eight names shall be drawn in felony cases, but if some of the jurors drawn are engaged, additional jurors may be drawn or summoned. Kelly, 14 Ga. App. 20 (2) (80 S. E. 24).

The number of the tales jurors summoned after the regular panel has been exhausted rests in the discretion of the Court. Cason, 134 

Ga. 786 (1) (68 S. E. 554).

It is illegal to draw a petit or tales juror from the grand jury box. A challenge to the array is the proper remedy. Pollard, 148 

Ga. 447 (4) (96 S. E. 997).

Where a mistrial has been declared, the same jurors are competent on the second trial. It is error to exclude them from the regular panel, without the consent of the accused. A challenge to the array on such ground should be sustained. Cunneen, 96 Ga. 406 

Where two or more are jointly indicted and put on trial for an offense for which one may be convicted and the other acquitted, each is entitled to the number of peremptory challenges as would be allowed him if the case against him had been tried separately. 

This rule is applicable for felonies as well as misdemeanors. Nobles, 12 Ga. App. 355 (1) (77 S. E. 184).

Where several defendants were tried jointly for a felony, they were not entitled to a panel of forty-eight jurors for each defendant from which to strike. Lynn, 140 Ga. 387 (2) (79 S. E. 29); Pope, 144 Ga. 165 (1) (86 S. E. 542).

The right to a full panel is a valuable right, and will be enforced by the courts. Forty-eight jurors are required in the first panel to try a felony case. Where a less number is furnished, the proper remedy is a challenge to the array. The failure so to challenge is waiver of the irregularity. Ivey, 4 Ga. App. 828, 831 (62 

S. E. 565).

It is within the Court's discretion, after the regular panel has been exhausted, whether it desires to wait for the return of the jurors engaged in another trial, or has other tales jurors summoned. Benford, 18 Ga. App. 14, 15 (3) (88 S. E. 747).

Where the Court directed that the jurors who served during the preceding week shall be placed on the panel as talesmen, it was error. Bridges, 103 Ga. 21. (2) (29 S. E. 859).

Talesmen must have the same qualifications as regularly drawn jurors. Ford, 12 Ga. App. 228 (3) (76 S. E. 1079).

It is no valid objection to a talesman that his name is not in the jury box, if he is otherwise qualified at the time of the trial to serve as a juror. McGuffie, 17 Ga. 497, 498 (5).

Where the Court directs the sheriff to summon tales jurors from persons authorized by law to serve as jurors, the law devolves upon the sheriff alone the duty of selecting the person so qualified whom he will summon, and it is error for the trial judge to indicate in any manner to him the persons whom he shall so summon. Bridges, 103 Ga. 21 (2) (29 S. E. 859).

Misdemeanor panels. In misdemeanor cases it is not necessary to formally put the array upon the accused. Fears, 125 Ga. 740 (3) (54 S. E. 661).

In a misdemeanor case, it is no valid cause of objection that the juror was absent at the time the jury was selected. In a misdemeanor case the practice of striking the jury from a list is a legal equivalent of challenging. O'Byrne, 29 Ga. 36 (1); Smith, 11 Ga. 

App. 89 (2) (74 S. E. 711).

The defendant is required to make the first strike in a misdemeanor trial. Nobles, 127 Ga. 212, 213 (2) (56 S. E. 125).

The judge should not generally excuse a juror because of private business, but if sufficient number remain, such excuse is no ground for a new trial. Especially is this true where no challenge to the array was filed. Cochran, 113 Ga. 736 (3) (39 S. E. 337); Ellis, 114 Ga. 36 (39 S. E. 881).

In misdemeanor cases the accused is not entitled to have the twenty-four jurors called separately, and require them to rise and remain standing until the next juror is called. Osborne, 27 Ga. 

App. 271 (1) (108 S. E. 81).

In misdemeanor cases the defendant is entitled to seven strikes and the State to five out of a panel of twenty-four, and the order of strikes should be alternated, the defendant beginning and concluding. Kelly, 19 Ga. 425 (2).

CRIMINAL PROCEDURE 

123 Where a juror in a misdemeanor case failed to answer his name, after the jury was stricken, the Court may order a re-strike of the jury. Clifton, 53 Ga. 241 (6); Garrison, 97 Ga. 215 (2) (22 S. E. 403).

Presumption. It is presumed, unless there is evidence or record to the contrary, that the panel was regularly put upon the prisoner. 

Ruden, 73 Ga. 567..

Waiver of panel. The omission to put the panel upon the prisoner is considered waived where no objection is entered. Inman, 72 Ga. 

269 (2); Ruden, 73 Ga. 567; Vaughn, 88 Ga. 731 (1) (16 S. E. 64).

A general statement of the defendant's counsel that the accused waives nothing, will cause a new trial, where the panel is not put upon the prisoner in a felony case. Cochran, 62 Ga. 731. But see 

Cumming, 155 Ga. 346 (2) (117 S. E. 378), where this case is distinguished. 

Where the defendant insists that the panel be put upon him formally, he should state to the Court that he does not waive his right thereto. Amerson, 18 Ga. App. 176, 177 (5) (88 S. E. 998).

If a panel of less than forty-eight is put upon the prisoner, and he does not challenge the array, but proceeds with the selection of the jury, he can not thereafter, as a matter of right, demand the filling of the panel. Ivey, 4 Ga. App. 828 (2) (62 S. E. 565).

Qualification of jurors; challenge for cause. The trial by a jury can not be too carefully guided, to protect it not only from unfairness, but also from any uncertainty on that score. Jurors should be above suspicion. Omni exceptione majores. Lyens, 133 Ga. 587, 600 (66 S. E. 792).

The fact that the juror did not know of his relationship disqualifying him to try the case will not prevent a new trial. Crawley, 151 Ga. 818 (3-b) (108 S. E. 238); Merritt, 152 Ga. 405, 406 (5) (110 S. E. 160). 

The prosecutor is incompetent to sit on the jury. Johnson, 8 

Ga. App. 841 (4) (70 S. E. 258).

Where the facts and the witness by whom they can be proved, to manifest the incompetency of a juror, come to the knowledge of the counsel for the accused, after the jury have been sworn, but before any further step in the trial had been taken, thè question of the jury's competency should then be raised and submitted to the Court. It is not sound practice for counsel to remain silent, take a chance of an acquittal, and then, after conviction, urge the juror's incompetency. Lampkin, 87 Ga. 516, 517 (7) (13 S. E. 523).

It is a good ground for a new trial that one of the jurors was disqualified, where the accused or his counsel had no knowledge of such disqualification until after the verdict. Perrett, 16 Ga. App. 

587 (1) (85 S. E. 820); Brown, 28 Ga. 439; Ledford, 75 Ga. 856 (1).

The general rule is that where the accused knew of the disqualification of the juror before the trial, and made no objection, he is presumed to have waived the disqualification. Miller, 139 Ga. 716 (2) (78 S. E. 181).

Where a juror has been set down as disqualified, from a misapprehension of his answer, it is competent for the Court to correct the mistake, whenever it is discovered, and restore the juror to the panel. Epps, 19 Ga. 102 (2).

Where the evidence is conflicting as to the cause of a challenge, the Court's discretion in sustaining or overruling the challenge is conclusive, and will not be disturbed by the reviewing courts. 

Buchanan, 118 Ga. 751 (8) (45 S. E. 607); King, 119 Ga. 426 (1) (46 S. E. 633); Smith, 2 Ga. App. 574 (59 S. E. 311); Dent, 43 Ga. 

App. 153 (2) (158 S. E. 62).

Before a new trial will be granted because of an error in the ruling of the judge, both error and injury must be shown. Where the trial court refused to purge the jury, as to qualification of the jurors, although timely demand was made, before a new trial will be granted, the accused must show that the failure of the Court. to purge the jury left anyone disqualified. Carter, 106 Ga. 372, 373 (6) (32 S. E. 345); Dees, 41 Ga. App. 321, 322 (1) (152 S. E. 913). 

Age. A juror over sixty years old is exempt from service but not disqualified. Staten, 141 Ga., 82 (80 S. E. 850). But in Thomas, 27

Ga. 287 (4) it was held that a juror may be disqualified and set aside for cause on the ground that he is over age, after the statutory questions have been propounded to him, provided that the State has not been prejudiced by the irregularity. 

The fact that a petit juror in a criminal case is over sixty years of age is no ground of challenge for cause. Staten, 141 Ga. 82 (80 S. E. 850).

An objection that the juror is under twenty-one years of age must be made by a challenge for cause. It is too late to make such objection after verdict. Shirley, 146 Ga. 9 (2) (90 S. E. 277).

Ministers of the gospel. The right to claim exemptions from jury service, allowed to a minister of the gospel, is a privilege to him

CRIMINAL PROCEDURE 

125 and affords no ground for a challenge. Smith, 11 Ga. App. 89 (1) (74 S. E. 711). 

Jury list. Where a juror's name does not appear on the jury list, a challenge for cause should be sustained. But after verdict the objection on such ground comes too late. Faulkner, 122 Ga. 28 (2) (3) (49 S. E. 747). 

Citizenship and residence of the juror. Non-residence of a juror is a defect which can be taken advantage of only by challenge. It is too late to object to a juror after verdict, although the defendant had no knowledge of his disqualification before that time. Epps, 19 Ga. 102, 103 (6); Costly, 19 Ga. 614, 628; Brown, 105 Ga. 640 (1) (31 S. E. 557).

It is sufficient if the juror is a resident and citizen of the county at the time of the trial. The length of residence is immaterial. 

Thomas, 27 Ga. 287.

Where the juror's house is on the county line, and he claims residence in the county of the venue, pays taxes there and votes there, he is qualified as a juror there. Chancey, 141 Ga. 54 (80 S. E. 287). 

Temporary residence in another county, without an intention of changing residence, and where the juror intends to return to his permanent residence, is no cause for a challenge. Sikes, 116 Ga. 

182 (1) (82 S. E. 346).

Before a juror can be challenged on account of foreign birth, it must also appear that he has not been naturalized. Jordan, 22 Ga. 

545, 546 (5); Johnson, 58 Ga. 491 (2).

Intoxication of jurors. Where the Court is satisfied by inspection that the juror is drunk, it may set aside such juror of its own motion. Thomas, 27 Ga. 287 (6).

Sanity of jurors. It is a good ground for a new trial that one of the jurors was mentally incompetent and that the defendant had no knowledge thereof before the trial. Wall, 126 Ga. 549, 550 (3) (55 S. E. 484).

Relationship. General. In criminal cases relationship by consanguinity or affinity within the ninth degree disqualifies. Crawley, 151 Ga. 818 (3) (108 S. E. 238); Perrett, 16 Ga. App. 587 (85 S. 

E. 820).

Disqualification on account of relationship is based upon the doctrine that a juror would naturally favor his own kinsman. 

Wright, 104 Ga. 174, 175 (30 S. E. 651).

Amendment of 1935. 

Section 1. Be it enacted by the General Assembly of Georgia, and it is hereby enacted by authority of the same, that from and after the passage of this Act, all judges, grand and trial jurors in the courts of this State, shall be disqualified to preside, act, or serve, in any case or matter, when such judge or juror is related by consanguinity or affinity to any party interested in the result of the case or matter, within the sixth degree, as computed according to the civil law, and relationship more remote shall not be a disqualification. 

Sec. 2. Be it further enacted by the authority aforesaid, that all laws and parts of laws in conflict with this Act be and the same are hereby repealed. (Acts of 1935, p. 396.)

Relationship to the prosecutor. Relationship within the ninth degree to the prosecutor disqualifies a juror. Smith, 2 Ga. App. 

574, 575 (59 S. E. 311).

Even where the prosecuting witness is not named in the indictment as such, if he in fact is the prosecuting witness, the juror related to him within the ninth degree is disqualified. Perrett, 16 

Ga. App. 587 (85 S. E. 820).

A juror related within the prohibited degree to any one who has contributed to the funds used for the prosecution, is disqualified. 

Lyens, 133 Ga. 587, 588 (4) (66 S. E. 792); O'Berry, 153 Ga. 644 (2) (113 S. E. 2). 

One related within the prohibited degree to the assaulted person, is incompetent as a juror upon the trial for the assault, although the assaulted party may not be the prosecutor. Perrett, 16

Where one contributes to a fund to be used in employing an attorney to aid the solicitor-general in the prosecution of a particular person for an alleged offense with which he is charged, and the attorney does render such aid upon the trial of the case, the person so contributing is to be considered as a voluntary prosecutor. 

Lyens, 133 Ga. 587 (4) (66 S. E. 792); O'Berry, 153 Ga. 644 (2) (113 S. E. 2).

One who is closely related to persons who assist the solicitorgeneral in striking the jury in a criminal case, is not incompetent to sit as a juror in that case. Caswell, 27 Ga. App. 76 (1) (107 

S. E. 560).

CRIMINAL PROCEDURE 

127 The fact that a juror is closely related to one acting as a partisan of the State in a criminal prosecution affords no ground for challenging such juror for cause. Atkinson, 112 Ga. 411 (37 S. E. 747).

It is competent to prove that one is in fact the prosecutor in a criminal case, although he may not nominally appear as such; and one who is actively engaged in any way in the prosecution of one accused of a crime is disqualified from sitting as a trior in the case, either as a judge or a juror. Johnson, 8 Ga. App. 841, 842 

A juror is not disqualified simply because he is related to a witness for the State. Hamlin, 27 Ga. App. 633 (1) (110 S. E. 421).

The fact that a peace officer swore out the warrant in order to hold the accused does not make him the prosecutor, where he did not appear on the indictment as the prosecutor, and where he swore that he was not partisan. Relationship to such officer does not disqualify. McKenzie, 28 Ga. App. 33 (7) (110 S. E. 248).

The nephew of a county commissioner is not a competent juror, if the uncle has taken part officially in promoting the prosecution, by voting county funds to pay a reward for the prisoner's apprehension, by aiding to employ counsel to prosecute, and by aiding in the prosecution of the case, the indictment being a special presentment of the grand jury. The uncle is to be considered as a volunteer prosecutor, no law requiring him to perform that function as a county commissioner. Dumas, 62 Ga. 58; Lyens, 133 Ga. 587, 

A juror is incompetent if related within the prohibited degree to a person beneficially interested in the result of the litigation, although not a party of record. McElhannon, 99 Ga. 672 (26 S. E. 

501); Fordham, 148 Ga. 758 (98 S. E. 267).

An employee of one who would be disqualified to serve as a juror on a case is not disqualified himself by reason of such employment. Campbell, 144 Ga. 224, 226 (87 S. E. 277).

On the trial of an officer of an insolvent bank, a juror who is related within the prohibited degree to a stockholder or depositor in the insolvent bank, is disqualified. Fordham, 148 Ga. 758 (98 

S. E. 267). But see Griffin, 18 Ga. App. 402, 403 (4) (89 S. E. 

625); Stapleton, 19 Ga. App. 36, 39 (14) (90 S. E. 1029) where it was held that relationship to a mere depositor of the bank does not disqualify the juror where an officer of the bank is on trial for the violation of the banking laws.

Rule of ascertaining relationship. In ascertaining the degree of relationship for the purpose of qualifying a juror, the rules of the civil law govern. Crawley, 151 Ga. 818 (3) (108 S. E. 238); Ethridge, 163 Ga. 186 (1) (136 S. E. 72). 

For diagram of relationship see Smith, 2 Ga. App. 574, 576 (59

S. E. 311). 

Relationship to the accused. A new trial will not be granted in a criminal case because of the relationship within the prohibited degree of a juror to the accused, although such relationship was unknown to the accused and his counsel until after verdict. Smith, 40 Ga. App. 515 (2) (150 S. E. 431); Durham, 41 Ga. App. 421 (4) 

Disqualification by affinity. Marriage does not establish a relationship between the relatives of the contracting parties. Miller, 139 Ga. 716 (78 S. E. 181); Cargile, 136 Ga. 55, 56 (5) (70 S. E. 873).

While marriage will relate the husband by affinity to the blood relations of the wife, it will not relate the husband to those merely related to the wife by marriage. Central of Georgia Railway Co., 25 Ga. App. 110, 113 (12) (103 S. E. 259). 

The groom and bride each come within

The circle of the other's kin; 

But kin and kin are still no more 

Related than they were before. 

Garner, 6 Ga. App. 788, 789 (9) (65 S. E. 842).

Marriage relates the husband to his wife's kindred, but does not relate any of his kindred to hers. Consequently, a man whose brother had married the prisoner's sister was not, for that reason, incompetent as a juror to try the prisoner for an offense. Burns, 89 Ga. 527 (1) (15 S. E. 748).

Specific instances. If the juror's great-grandmother and the defendant's great-grandfather were brother and sister, the relationship is not within the ninth degree. Clary, 8 Ga. App. 92 (1) (68 

S. E. 615).

The fact that the sister of the juror married the brother of the prosecutor's wife does not affect the competency of the juror. 

Miller, 139 Ga. 716 (3) (78 S. E. 181). 

The third cousin of the prosecutor is not a qualified juror. Ledford, 75 Ga. 856 (1).

A juror whose brother-in-law was first cousin of the mother of

CRIMINAL PROCEDURE 

129 the deceased,—not disqualified. Keener, 97 Ga. 388, 389 (2) (24 

S. E. 28).

Where the juror's father's great-great-grandmother was a sister of the grandfather of the murdered man, the relationship is within the ninth degree. Ethridge, 163 Ga. 186 (1-a) (136 S. E. 72).

A juror who married the widow of the prosecutor's uncle is not disqualified. O'Neal, 47 Ga. 229, 230 (2).

That the wife of the juror was the second cousin of the wife of the prosecutor is no disqualification. Baldwin, 120 Ga. 188, 189 

Where one spouse is deceased. The general rule is that a relationship by affinity is dissolved by the death of either party to the marriage, unless the deceased left a living issue. Miller, 97 Ga. 

653, 657 (25 S. E. 366).

A juror who is the first cousin of the deceased wife of the prosecutor is competent. Harnage, 7 Ga. App. 573 (3) (67 S. E. 694).

Where the deceased childless wife of the prosecutor was the sister of the juror's wife, the juror was not disqualified. Garner, 6 Ga. 

App. 788 (9) (65 S. E. 842).

Where it is necessary to show that there is a living issue of a marriage, in order to determine a disqualification, the burden of showing this fact affirmatively is on the objecting party. Miller, 97 Ga. 653 (3) (25 S. E. 366). 

Illegitimacy. Where the relationship between the prosecutor and the juror is within the prohibited degree and by blood, illegitimacy on the maternal side of one of the ancestors will not prevent the disqualification of the juror. O'Berry, 153 Ga. 644 (3) 

In a trial for murder an illegitimate third cousin of the slain man is disqualified to serve as a juror, although the relationship is on the paternal instead of the maternal side. Currie, 156 Ga. 85, 86 (5) (118 S. E. 724). (Two dissenting.)

Motion for a new trial. A motion for a new trial on the ground of disqualification of the juror will not be considered, unless supported by affidavit. Arnall, 14 Ga. App. 472 (2) (81 S. E. 366). 

Popular subscription. Where counsel for the prosecution has been obtained by popular subscription, a juror related within the prohibited degree to anyone contributing to such fund, is incompetent. Whitworth, 155 Ga. 395 (1) (117 S. E. 450). .

Challenge to the array. The accused may, in writing, challenge the array for any cause going to show that it was not fairly or properly impanelled, or ought not to be put upon him; the sufficiency of which challenge the Court shall determine at once. If sustained, a new panel shall be ordered; if not sustained, the selection of jurors shall proceed. § 59-803. 

A challenge to the array is an objection to all the jurors collectively, because of some defect in the panel as a whole. Bryan, 124 Ga. 

79 (1) (52 S. E. 298). It differs from a challenge to the poll in that the latter is an objection to a juror individually. Humphries, 100 Ga. 260, 262 (28 S. E. 25).

The sole remedy of objecting to the entire panel is by a written. challenge to the array. Ivey, 4 Ga. App. 828, 831 (62 S. E. 565); 

Williams, 31 Ga. App. 173 (3) (120 S. E. 131).

A challenge to the array, otherwise good, but objecting only to a part of the jurors, is defective. Eberhart, 47 Ga. 598 (2); Blackman, 80 Ga. 785 (2) (7 S. E. 626).

The rules of the challenge to the array apply to misdemeanors as well as to felony cases. Thompson, 109 Ga. 272 (34 S. E. 579); 

Whitworth, 155 Ga. 395 (117 S. E. 450).

The following have been held grounds for a challenge to the ar ray: Illegal selection of the panel. Carter, 143 Ga. 632 (85 S. E. 

884); Pollard, 148 Ga. 447 (96 S. E. 997). Unauthorized revision of the jury list. Carter, 17 Ga. App. 90 (2) (86 S. E. 287). Where the judge has established arbitrary rules for selecting the jurors and has selected the jury list arbitrarily, and there are jurors on the panel so selected by the judge, this is a good ground for a challenge to the array. Campbell, 48 Ga. 353 (2) (3). Where the sheriff who summoned the jury is also the prosecutor, a challenge to the array should be sustained. Phillips, 29 Ga. 105, 107. Where jurors were irregularly summoned, a challenge to the array is the proper remedy, and not a motion for a new trial. Dumas, 65 Ga. 

471, 472 (4); Dover, 109 Ga. 485 (1) (34 S. E. 1030).

The following have been held not to present a sufficient ground for a challenge to the array: The fact that the jurors were present and heard the evidence of the crime upon the trial of a co-defendant, upon a previous motion of a plea in abatement. The objection, if good at all, should be made to the poll. Jones, 90 Ga. 616 (1) (16 

S. E. 380); Robinson, 82 Ga. 535 (4) (9 S. E. 528); Brown, 97 Ga. 

215 (1) (22 S. E. 403); Harrell, 11 Ga. App. 407 (2) (75 S. E. 507).

The fact that the twelve members of the panel have served on

CRIMINAL PROCEDURE 

131 the trial and conviction of another for a similar offense growing out of the same transaction, and returned a verdict of guilty. 

Schnell, 92 Ga. 459 (1) (17 S. E. 966). That the array is composed of the same jurors who were put upon a co-defendant. Humphries, 100 Ga. 260 (2) (28 S. E. 25); Bryan, 124 Ga. 79 (2) (52 S. E. 

298); Edge, 8 Ga. App. 125 (1) (68 S. E. 623). 

Where there are individual jurors disqualified, the challenge should be made to the poll and not to the array. Thompson, 109 

Ga. 272 (2) (34 S. E. 579); Teal, 119 Ga. 102 (2) (45 S. E. 964); 

Nixon, 121 Ga. 144 (5) (48 S. E. 966); Rawlins, 124 Ga. 31, 33 (14) (52 S. E. 1).

It is not every defect that can be reached by a challenge to the array. It must appear that the right of the accused to a fair and impartial jury is affected. Governor, 5 Ga. App. 357 (63 S. E. 

244); Worley, 21 Ga. App. 787 (1) (95 S. E. 304).

The legal presumption is that the jury was summoned according to law, and this presumption remains until the contrary appears affirmatively. Wheeler, 42 Ga. 306, 308. Where the record is silent it will also be presumed that the panel was put upon the prisoner with the ordinary formality. Ivey, 4 Ga. App. 828, 830 (62 S. E. 565).

The only restriction upon the sheriff is that the talesmen selected by him should be qualified jurors. Cox, 64 Ga. 374, 375 (2).

A statement of counsel for the accused that he demanded all of his legal rights, and waived nothing, is not an equivalent of a challenge to the array. Schumpert, 9 Ga. App. 553 (1) (71 S. E. 879).

Exceptions. Where a challenge to the array was overruled, exceptions pendente lite proper remedy, unless bill of exception is presented to the Court within twenty days. Crawford, 49 Ga. App. 

801 (1) (176 S. E. 92).

Voir dire. On trials for felonies, any juror may be put upon his voir dire and the following questions shall be propounded to him, viz.: 

1. "Have you, from having seen the crime committed, or having heard any of the testimony delivered on oath, formed and expressed any opinion in regard to the guilt or innocence of the prisoner at the bar?" If the juror shall answer in the negative, the following question shall be propounded to him: 

2. "Have you any prejudice or bias resting on your mind either for or against the prisoner at the bar?" If the juror shall answer in the negative, the following question shall be propounded:

3. "Is your mind perfectly impartial between the State and the accused?" If the juror shall answer this question in the affirmative, he shall be adjudged and held a competent juror in all cases where the offense does not involve the life of the accused; but when it does involve the life of the accused, the following additional question shall be put to him: 

4. "Are you conscientiously opposed to capital punishment?"

If he shall answer this question in the negative, he shall be held a competent juror: Provided, nevertheless, that either the State or the defendant shall have the right to introduce evidence before the judge to show that the answers, or any of them, are untrue; and it shall be the duty of the judge to determine upon the truth of such answers as may be thus questioned before the Court. § 59-806. 

Misdemeanors. In misdemeanor cases the statutory questions prescribed in felonies, or such other questions as will test the juror's impartiality, may be asked, as a matter of right, when requested by a proper challenge to the poll. Jacobs, 1 Ga. App. 519 (2) (3) (57 

S. E. 1063).

In trials for misdemeanors there is no right to examine the juror upon his voir dire without first challenging him and assigning a cause of challenge. This must be done before the juror is sworn, unless the cause of challenge is unknown until afterwards. Schnell, 92 Ga. 459 (17 S. E. 966); Crew, 113 Ga. 645 (38 S. E. 941); Cook, 22 Ga. App. 770, 771 (5) (97 S. E. 264).

Where, in a misdemeanor case, the juror is challenged, it is within the discretion of the Court to specify what questions may be asked. 

Nobles, 127 Ga. 212 (1) (56 S. E. 125); Jacobs, 1 Ga. App. 519 (3) (57 S. E. 1063).

Where juror is challenged in a misdemeanor case, by timely and proper challenge when the panel is put upon the prisoner, it is the duty of the Court to subject the juror to such examination as will test his competency. Wells, 102 Ga. 658 (29 S. E. 442). 

What questions may be asked on voir dire. It is irregular and improper to ask any other questions than those authorized by statute. Williams, 3 Ga. 453 (3); Ford, 12 Ga. App. 228 (1) (76 

S. E. 1079). However, the Court may allow additional questions as a matter of discretion. Alford, 137 Ga. 458, 459 (3) (73 S. E. 375).

The solicitor-general may not ask any other question than the one authorized by statute, such as the juror's opinion of the prohibition law. But where such question is asked without objection by the

CRIMINAL PROCEDURE 

133 defendant, the irregularity is waived. Rothschild, 12 Ga. App. 728, 729 (3) (78 S. E. 201). 

Time of challenge. The defendant may challenge a juror for cause, after evidence has been introduced, where the moving party or his attorney had no knowledge of the disqualification before the acceptance of the juror. Wesley, 65 Ga. 731 (3); Lampkin, 87 Ga. 

516 (7) (13 S. E. 523); Norton, 137 Ga. 842 (6) (74 S. E. 759).

The Court may recall a juror, who has been challenged, after the jury has retired to consider of the verdict, and interrogate him as to his qualifications to serve. Norton, 137 Ga. 842, 843 (6) (74 

S. E. 759).

The oath. The oath may be administered to all jurors at once, before examination on voir dire. Roberts, 65 Ga. 430 (1).

Separate examination. In felony cases it is error to put two or more jurors at one time upon their voir dire. Each juror should be examined separately. Williams, 60 Ga. 367 (1); Wilkerson, 74 Ga. 

398. But failure to object will be considered waiver of irregularity. 

Wilson, 176 Ga. 198 (167 S. E. 111). 

Constitutionality. Upheld. Woolfolk, 85 Ga. 69, 71 (9) (11 S. 

E. 814).

Explaining questions. If the juror does not understand one of the statutory questions put to him on his voir dire, the Court may explain to him. Dumas, 65 Ga. 471, 472 (3).

Forming and expressing an opinion. To disqualify one from being a juror in a criminal case, he must have formed and expressed an opinion, either from having seen the crime committed or from having heard the testimony under oath. A man may form and express an opinion from rumor or from newspaper reports, and yet be qualified and competent as a juror, if the opinion has not become fixed and determined. West, 79 Ga. 773, 774 (4-a); Blackman, 80 

Ga. 785, 786 (3-a) (7 S. E. 626).

Mere former expression of opinion as to the guilt of the accused will not disqualify the juror, unless he has seen the crime committed or heard the testimony under oath, or is prejudiced or biased. 

Wilburn, 141 Ga. 510, 511 (3) (81 S. E. 444); Thomas, 144 Ga. 298 (2) (87 S. E. 8); Langston, 24 Ga. App. 316 (1) (101 S. E. 3); 

Story, 28 Ga. App. 109 (1) (110 S. E. 326).

While a juror who has served in the trial of a criminal case, and, from the testimony given at the trial, has formed and expressed an opinion as to the guilt or innocence of the accused, is disqualified

to sit as a juror on a subsequent trial of the same person for the same offense, yet, if he does so sit, a new trial will not be granted solely for that reason, unless it is affirmatively made to appear that the accused and his counsel exercised due diligence to discover who constituted the first jury. Wilcox, 19 Ga. App. 83 (1) (90 S. E. 1032).

Where a juror has served on other juries at the same term and convicted other defendants of the same offense in cases involving the same transaction on the same evidence, a challenge to the juror should be sustained, and overruling such challenge is reversible error. This is true, although the juror qualified by his own answer to the usual questions propounded. Smith, 16 Ga. App. 299 (1) (85 S. E. 207).

The fact that the juror who sits on the case has heard the testimony on a former trial against the accused, does not disqualify him, without the juror having formed and expressed an opinion as to the guilt or innocence of the prisoner, from having heard the testimony on the former trial. Johnson, 21 Ga. App. 497 (8) (94 

S. E. 630).

A juror who states upon oath in answer to the questions propounded to him by the statute, that he has formed and expressed an opinion from hearsay, is not an impartial juror. Hudgins, 2

Ga. 173, 175. (But see headnote (1) where it is held that a juror, who has formed and expressed an opinion from mere rumor is not incompetent.) But see Anderson, 14 Ga. 709 (2); Ray, 15 Ga. 223 (2); Myers, 97 Ga. 76 (3) (25 S. E. 252), where it was held that the definite and unalterable formation and expression of an opinion based upon rumors is a good ground for a challenge. See also 

Fogarty, 80 Ga. 450 (10) (5 S. E. 782); McDuffie, 90 Ga. 786, 791 (2) (17 S. E. 105); Hinkle, 94 Ga. 595 (1) (21 S. E. 595), where it was held that where the opinion of the juror is based upon rumors, or newspaper reports, and he swears upon his voir dire that he can give the prisoner a fair trial, he is not disqualified.

Where the juror has heard the evidence under oath on the first trial, and has expressed a decided opinion, he can not render himself competent by swearing that he could give the prisoner a fair and impartial trial. McGuffie, 17 Ga. 497, 512.

Jurors who have served upon the trial of another defendant charged with a similar offense, the principal witness for the State being the same, are disqualified. Roberts, 4 Ga. App. 378 (2) (61 

S. E. 497).

CRIMINAL PROCEDURE 

135 A juror who has served on the jury which convicted one jointly accused with the defendant for the identical offense, involving the same transaction, is incompetent to serve, although he testified on his voir dire that he was impartial. McKay, 6 Ga. App. 527 (65 

S. E. 306).

A juror is not disqualified by hearing the evidence without forming or expressing an opinion. Robinson, 82 Ga. 535 (4) (9 S. E. 

528); Ford, 164 Ga. 638, 641 (139 S. E. 355).

Prejudice and bias. Prejudice imports the formation of fixed anticipatory judgment as contradistinguished from those opinions which may yield to evidence. Temples, 15 Ga. App. 115, 122 (82 S. E. 777). 

Bias means a leaning toward one of the parties rather than the other. Temples, 15 Ga. App. 115, 122 (82 S. E. 777).

Prejudice does not necessarily denote an ill feeling, and may indicate only prejudgment; and bias is a mere leaning to one side of the issue, rather than the other. Rowe, 15 Ga. App. 660 (84 S. E. 132).

The prime test of the disqualification of jurors is the probability of interest, prejudice, or bias, as ascertained and determined by the application of the Court's judicial knowledge of the particular facts which may indicate prejudice or bias, or the absence thereof. 

Rowe, 15 Ga. App. 660 (84 S. E. 132).

It is no valid cause for a challenge, without more, that the juror stated upon a previous trial of the same cause that he was biased. 

Chapman, 148 Ga. 531 (3) (97 S. E. 546).

The fact that the juror, together with many others, signed petition to the Court asking for a special session of the Court, will not alone disqualify him, if otherwise he is impartial and has neither prejudice nor bias resting upon his mind. Hicks, 126 Ga. 80 (1) (54 S. E. 807).

Where the evidence clearly shows that the juror is partial, and biased, an objection to him should be sustained. Carter, 154 Ga. 359 (1) (114 S. E. 194). 

The jurors should come to the consideration of a case (especially when it is a criminal one) free from even a suspicion of prejudgment or fixed opinion upon any material fact in the issue to be tried, as to the parties, the subject matter, or the credibility of the witnesses. Smith, 16 Ga. App. 299 (1) (85 S. E. 207).

Capital punishment. Where a juror answers that he is opposed to capital punishment in most instances, he is disqualified. Mickens, 149 Ga. 185 (1-a) (99 S. E. 779).

Where a juror answers to the questions on the voir dire that he is opposed to capital punishment in cases depending upon circumstantial evidence, he is disqualified. Smith, 146 Ga. 76 (1) (90 

S. E. 713).

Where the juror answers to the question on his voir dire that he is opposed to capital punishment where the defendant is a woman, he is incompetent, although he also states that as a general rule he is not opposed to capital punishment. Abbott, 24 Ga. App. 367 (1) (100 S. E. 759). 

Challenge. Judge as trior. Where the competency of a juror is challenged, the trial judge is the sole trior. Frank, 141 Ga. 243, 247 (18) (80 S. E. 1016); Crawley, 151 Ga. 818 (2-a) (108 S. E. 238).

While the finding of the Court when sitting in lieu of common law triors, as to the competency of jurors, is not subject to review, a challenge for principal cause being considered a question of law, the judgment of the trial court thereon may be reviewed. Smith, 16 Ga. App. 299 (2) (85 S. E. 207).

Discretion of the trial judge, sitting as trior of the juror's qualification, will not be disturbed, upon conflicting evidence, unless manifestly abused. Hall, 141 Ga. 7 (1) (80 S. E. 307); Lee, 144 

Ga. 831 (1) (88 S. E. 206); Chapman, 148 Ga. 531 (6) (97 S. E. 

546); Taylor, 13 Ga. App. 689 (2) (79 S. E. 862).

Where the Court sets aside the juror, after having interrogated him, on the ground that he is incompetent to try the case, in the absence of timely objection any error in such ruling is considered waived. Gunter, 19 Ga. App. 772 (2) (92 S. E. 314).

Where a juror has answered the questions on his voir dire satisfactorily, and the Court is made trior of his competency, evidence of his incompetency must be introduced before the juror can be asked the statutory questions on his voir dire again. Chapman, 148 Ga. 531 (4) (97 S. E. 546).

An affidavit of a third person that the juror has formed and expressed an opinion adverse to the prisoner will not outweigh a sworn answer of the juror on his voir dire qualifying himself. 

West, 79 Ga. 773 (4) (4 S. E. 325); Blackman, 80 Ga. 785 (3) (7 

S. E. 626).

A juror who answers all statutory questions on his voir dire so as to qualify him, is prima facie competent; and if the defendant

CRIMINAL PROCEDURE 

137 objects to his competency, he must try him and prove him incompetent. Dumas, 63 Ga. 600 (3).

Where the challenge is for cause, the question before the Court is a question of law. Where the challenge is for favor, the question is one of fact. But the Court decides both questions, and such decision is not subject of review. Turner, 114 Ga. 421 (2), 423 (40 S. E. 308).

Juror who has answered his voir dire questions, and is put upon the Court as a trior, and testified that he had no fixed opinion that would not yield to testimony, without regard to anything that he might have heard, was competent. Spence, 20 Ga. App. 61 (4) (92 

S. E. 555); Blackman, 80 Ga. 785 (3) (7 S. E. 626).

The finding of the trial court that the juror who was accused of expressing an opinion that the defendant was guilty, was impartial, will not be reversed if there is any evidence to support the conclusion. Brown, 13 Ga. App. 144 (1) (78 S. E. 868).

Motion for a new trial. Upon a motion for a new trial, alleging that the juror has prejudged the case, where the evidence is conflicting, the judge is the sole trior of the issue. Smith, 170 Ga. 

234 (4) (152 S. E. 482). The same rule applies where the juror is charged with being prejudiced or biased. Bradberry, 170 Ga. 859 (6) (154 S. E. 344); Patterson, 41 Ga. App. 375 (1) (153 S. E. 201); 

Patterson, 42 Ga. App. 288 (155 S. E. 922).

In order to secure a new trial for favor of the juror, both the accused and his counsel should show that they did not know of the disqualification before the trial, and, where the defendant had more than one counsel, that each of his counsel was ignorant thereof. 

Durham, 70 Ga. 264, 265 (12-a); Widincamp, 135 Ga. 323 (3) (69 

S. E. 535).

Where a juror has prejudged a case, and this fact was unknown to the prisoner or his counsel, a new trial should be granted. Jordan, 119 Ga. 443 (4) (46 S. E. 679); Glover, 128 Ga. 1 (4) (57 S. 

E. 101); Sasser, 129 Ga. 541 (15) (59 S. E. 255).

The presumption that a juror is competent is rebutted whenever the circumstances or influence by which he is environed and may likely be affected are not in dispute and are such that inherent probabilities, according to universal human experience, compel the conclusion that he is more likely to lean toward one side of the issue than toward the other. Temples, 15 Ga. App. 115, 116 (3) (82 S. E. 777). 

Where the juror contradicts the affidavit showing his bias, a new

trial will not be granted on that ground, where the presiding judge refused the same. Gore, 155 Ga. 642, 643 (4) (118 S. E. 40).

Where the juror dies between the trial and the hearing upon the motion for a new trial, the judge may take into consideration his answer upon the voir dire. Crawley, 151 Ga. 818 (2-a) (108 S. E. 238).

Where the juror put upon the prisoner served as a grand juror when the bill was returned, in order to secure new trial or mistrial, it must appear that the fact could not have been discovered by the accused or his counsel by the exercise of ordinary diligence, before the jurors were accepted. This is true although the middle initials were stated differently in the bill of indictment from what appeared on the list of jurors. Jones, 95 Ga. 497 (1) (20 S. E. 211); 

Britt, 112 Ga. 583 (1) (37 S. E. 886); Sapp, 116 Ga. 182 (1) (42 

S. E. 410); Massey, 124 Ga. 24 (1) (52 S. E. 78); Cargill, 12 Ga. 

App. 574 (1) (77 S. E. 832); Rogers, 42 Ga. App. 407 (156 S. E. 323).

To disqualify a juror who tried the case and swore that he had not formed and expressed an opinion, and had no bias or prejudice, and was perfectly impartial, there should be the affidavits of at least two witnesses, or what is equivalent thereto, against such oath of the juror; otherwise it is but oath against oath, and the verdict will not be set aside on the ground of the incompetency of the juror. Myers, 97 Ga. 76, 95, 96 (25 S. E. 252).

Where the disqualification of the juror is not discovered until after the trial, it is a ground for a new trial. Ray, 15 Ga. 223 (2); 

Anderson, 14 Ga. 709 (2); Myers, 97 Ga. 76 (2) (25 S. E. 252).

Additional questions. Under the practice in this State of trying the competency of jurors, only the statutory questions can be asked in the first instance. If the juror answers the statutory questions satisfactorily, and is pronounced prima facie competent, and the parties put him before the Court as trior, aliunde evidence of the untruthfulness of the answer must be offered, and it is not competent to propound questions to the juror himself to show his incompetency. It is within the province of the Court to permit a further examination of the juror himself in rebuttal of the testimony offered to show his incompetency. At common law a challenge for principal cause was tried by the Court on the testimony of the juror to the exclusion of other evidence, and if found true, the juror was incompetent per se. If the challenge was to the favor, as for undue influence or prejudice, the challenge was tried

CRIMINAL PROCEDURE 

139 by two triors under the direction of the Court, on the testimony other than that of the juror; and where the common-law practice prevails, substantially the same distinction is preserved. Polk, 148 Ga. 34 (2) (95 S. E. 988).

Where a juror on his voir dire has so answered the statutory questions as to prima facie qualify himself, it is not error to exclude other questions to test his impartiality, where the juror is not put on trial. Brown, 141 Ga. 5, 6 (5) (80 S. E. 320); Duncan, 141 Ga. 

4 (1) (80 S. E. 317); Polk, 148 Ga. 34 (1) (1-a) (95 S. E. 988).

Who may propound questions. The questions on voir dire may be propounded by the stenographer. West, 79 Ga. 773, 774 (4 S. 

E. 425).

Waiver. The right to have the jurors put upon their voir dire may be waived by the defendant, and where a jury is selected without any request being made by the defendant or his counsel to have the jurors put upon their voir dire, his right is thereby waived. 

Smith, 168 Ga. 611, 615 (148 S. E. 531).

When the accused waives his right to have the questions on voir dire asked separately, he may still object to a juror for cause, when the juror is put upon him. Jackson, 103 Ga. 417, 418 (2) (30 S. 

E. 251).

Peremptory challenges. Every person indicted for a crime or of fense which may subject him to death or imprisonment in the penitentiary for not less than 4 years may peremptorily challenge 20 of the jurors impanelled to try him, and every person indicted for an offense which may subject him to imprisonment in the penitentiary for any time less than 4 years may peremptorily challenge 12 of the jurors impanelled to try him; and the State shall be allowed one-half the number of peremptory challenges allowed to the prisoner. § 59-805.

Where joint defendants are tried together for an offense of which each might be convicted, each is entitled to the full statutory allowance of peremptory challenges. Cruce, 59 Ga. 83, 84 (2).

Where the defendants are jointly tried for an offense of which one only could not be convicted, such as affray, they must unite their challenges. Hawkins, 13 Ga. 322, 324.

Where the defendant requests a ruling on the total number of challenges he is entitled to, before the first juror is put upon him, it is the duty of the judge to determine the same. Cumming, 99 

---

Where two are jointly tried for a felony, and neither waives his peremptory challenges, the State is entitled to one-half of the whole number of challenges allowed to both. Butler, 92 Ga. 601 (1) (19 

S. E. 51); Rawlins, 124 Ga. 31, 33 (15), 48 (52 S. E. 1).

Where State waives strikes, the accused is entitled to the statutory strikes only and can not demand the unused strikes of the 

State. Epps, 2 Ga. App. 153 (1) (58 S. E. 381).

Where the juror is put upon a defendant, by whom he is peremptorily challenged, he is not so disqualified that he could not be again put upon the defendant at a subsequent trial for the same offense under the same indictment. Esa, 146 Ga. 17 (90 S. E. 278); 

Esa, 19 Ga. App. 14 (2) (90 S. E. 732).

Where indictment contained two counts, charging defendant with two distinct and separate offenses, of the same nature, the accused is not entitled to full number of peremptory challenges on each count. Vismore, 41 Ga. App. 544 (1) (153 S. E. 776); Slicer, 172 

Ga. 445, 446 (3) (157 S. E. 664); York, 42 Ga. App. 453, 454 (3) (156 S. E. 733). 

16. EVIDENCE. 

Editor's note. The subject of Evidence is one of the most extensive and voluminous in the criminal law. It is impossible to embrace this subject within the limits of a general brief, which is intended, primarily, to be used for quick reference in the court room. For this reason the most important chapters of Criminal Evidence are stated only, pertaining to such subjects as are restricted to criminal law. 

For further information on various rules of evidence the reader is referred to the chapters on the various specific crimes. a. Alibi. b. Witnesses. c. Res Gestae. 

d. Dying Declarations. 

e. Confessions. 

f. Illegally Obtained Evidence. 

g. Prisoner's Statement. 

General. 

Shifting of burden of proof. Whenever in a criminal case the evidence takes such a turn as to throw upon the defendant the burden of explaining some fact or of justifying conduct, he does not have to carry this burden by making proof beyond a reasonable doubt. He has carried it sufficiently if, under his proof, taken in

CRIMINAL PROCEDURE 

141 connection with the other evidence in the case, there is a reasonable doubt in the minds of the jury as to his guilt. Blandon, 6 Ga. App. 782 (2) (65 S. E. 842). 

Evidence of acts barred by statute of limitations. Where the of fense consists of various acts committed during a period of time, some of which is barred by the statute of limitations, and others within the statute, evidence of the acts so barred is nevertheless admissible to show design and intent. Mangham, 11 Ga. App. 427, 438 (3) (75 S. E. 512).

Crime subsequent to affidavit for warrant. Evidence tending to show the commission of the offense at a time subsequent to the date of the affidavit upon which the accusation was founded should be excluded. Shealey, 16 Ga. App. 191 (84 S. E. 839). Note: The word 

"admissible" in the headnote is apparently an error. "Inadmissible" was intended. a. ALIBI. General.

Two branches. There are two branches of the rule controlling alibi in this State. The first is, that, to overcome proof of guilt strong enough to exclude all reasonable doubt, the onus is on the accused to verify his alleged alibi, not beyond a reasonable doubt, but to the reasonable satisfaction of the jury. The second is, that, nevertheless, any evidence whatever of alibi is to be considered on the general case with the rest of the testimony, and if a reasonable doubt of guilt is raised by the evidence as a whole, the doubt must be given in favor of innocence. Raysor, 132 Ga. 237, 238 (63 S. E. 

786); Harrison, 83 Ga. 129 (9 S. E. 542); Wafford, 163 Ga. 304, 306 (136 S. E. 49).

Definition. Alibi, as a defense, involves the impossibility of the prisoner's presence at the scene of the offense at the time of its commission. Williams, 123 Ga. 138 (3) (51 S. E. 322). "The defendant has set up the defense of alibi. Alibi, as a defense, involves the impossibility of the prisoner's presence at the scene of the crime, at the time of its commission, and the range of the evidence in respect to time and place must be such as to reasonably preclude the possibility of his presence. When a defendant sets up a defense of alibi, the burden is on him to establish his defense of an alibi to the reasonable satisfaction of the jury, and it is the duty of the jury to consider the evidence on the question of alibi along with all other evidence introduced in the case, and if all the

evidence so considered creates in the minds of the jury a reasonable doubt as to the guilt of the prisoner, then it is their duty to acquit him, the law being, before they can convict him they must believe him guilty beyond a reasonable doubt." Smith, 3 Ga. App. 803 (61 

S. E. 737); Quarles, 37 Ga. App. 520 (6), 521 (140 S. E. 788).

It is to be borne in mind, not only that there are cases in which the defendant might be guilty of a crime without being actually present, but also that, where an alibi is insisted upon as a defense, this fact is to be measured by a rule different from that employed in determining the effect of testimony by the State. The State must satisfy the jury that the defendant committed the act charged against him, beyond a reasonable doubt. The defendant, to disprove the State's case, has only to reasonably satisfy the jury that he was absent. As pointed out in Smith, 3 Ga. App. 803 (61 S. E. 737), this rule is perhaps incongruous, and yet it is well established by the decisions of the Supreme Court. Hobbs, 8 Ga. App. 53, 58 (68 S. E. 515).

Alibi and mistaken identity. Alibi and mistaken identity are virtually the same defense, in some cases, and there is no error in failure to charge alibi, without proper request. Glover, 7 Ga. App. 628 (2) (67 S. E. 687).

Where a defendant, charged with committing murder by administering poison, introduced evidence for the purpose of proving that he was not present at the time and place when the State contended that he bought the poison, was proper for consideration under the plea of not guilty, but did not set up a distinct defense of alibi. Williams, 123 Ga. 138 (4) (51 S. E. 322).

Burden of proof. The burden of proving alibi is upon the defendant. Copeland, 33 Ga. App. 150, 151 (125 S. E. 728); Eugee, 159 

Ga. 604 (13) (126 S. E. 471).

Alibi, as a defense should be established to the reasonable satisfaction of the jury, and not beyond a reasonable doubt. Moss, 43 

Ga. App. 109 (3) (158 S. E. 461).

Alibi should be established by a preponderance of evidence, or greater weight. Copeland, 33 Ga. App. 150, 151 (125 S. E. 728).

Evidence. Evidence must be such that it was impossible for defendant to have been at the scene of the crime when it was committed. Collier, 154 Ga. 68 (6) (113 S. E. 213); Eugee, 159 Ga. 604 (13) (126 S. E. 471).

Time of offense placed by State's evidence as coincident with another event, evidence of alibi need only relate to time and place of such event. Fortson, 125 Ga. 16 (1) (53 S. E. 767).

CRIMINAL PROCEDURE 

143 Defendant contending he was in another town with friend at time car with whisky was seized, friend corroborating his statement, evidence of officer that he could recognize only defendant's friend in car authorized jury to reject testimony of friend. Bray, 26 Ga. App. 

620 (2) (106 S. E. 800).

Sufficiency of evidence of alibi is question for jury. Prater, 16 

Ga. App. 296 (3) (85 S. E. 204). 

Proper cross-examination of witness as to alibi. Stephens, 16 Ga. 

App. 144 (3) (84 S. E. 560).

Conflict of alibi. Where there is conflicting evidence, some tending to show that defendant was at one place at the time the crime was committed, and some tending to show that he was at another place at the same time, both places being some distance from the scene of the crime, and where the defendant insisted that he was at one of the places stated, it is error to restrict the consideration of evidence to the place stated by defendant. Vincent, 145 Ga. 293 (89 S. E. 203). 

New trial on newly discovered evidence of alibi. Cumulative evidence to prove an alibi, even if newly discovered, is not cause for new trial. Henderson, 36 Ga. App. 303 (1) (136 S. E. 333).

Alibi must be complete before new trial will be granted on newly discovered evidence of alibi. Where it conflicts with evidence introduced by defendant on trial, no new trial will be granted. Johnson, 128 Ga. 102, 110 (57 S. E. 353).

Where defendant was not informed of the testimony of a witness connecting him with the crime, the name of this witness not being on the indictment, witness not having appeared before grand jury, evidence of alibi held sufficient ground for new trial. Saylors, 9 Ga. 

App. 227 (3) (70 S. E. 975).

Strong evidence of alibi may authorize a new trial, even though newly discovered evidence is something like, but not quite, cumulative. Fellows, 114 Ga. 233 (39 S. E. 885).

When law of alibi should be charged. Court should charge jury on alibi, even without request, alibi being main defense. Holland, 17 Ga. App. 311 (1) (86 S. E. 739); Mosley, 165 Ga. 290, 291 (140 

S. E. 754).

Court should charge alibi, where defendant was near the scene of the crime, but not in position to commit the crime. Mosley, 165 

Ga. 290, 291 (140 S. E. 754).

When law of alibi need not be charged without request. Charge on alibi in absence of request is required only where defense of alibi 11.

is sustained or evidence on such issue is close. Holliday, 23 Ga. 

App. 400 (3) (98 S. E. 386); Barrett, 32 Ga. App. 30 (122 S. E. 645).

Where the defense of alibi is set up by defendant's statement alone, a charge thereon is not necessary, in the absence of a timely written request. Barrett, 32 Ga. App. 30 (1) (122 S. E. 645); Reed, 15 Ga. App. 435 (1) (83 S. E. 674). This latter rule applies, even though witness for State admitted facts tending to sustain such defense. Sheffield, 15 Ga. App. 514 (3) (3-a) (86 S. E. 285).

Where evidence construed most favorably for defendant did not reasonably exclude possibility of presence of defendant at the scene of homicide, no error for Court to fail to charge law of alibi. Mathis, 153 Ga. 105 (2) (111 S. E. 567).

Failure to charge upon second branch of rule of alibi requires new trial. Henderson, 27 Ga. App. 628 (110 S. E. 522); Brooks, 25 Ga. 

App. 739 (1) (105 S. E. 42).

Failure to charge upon second branch of rule of alibi no error, in absence of request, where the Court has fairly and correctly charged the doctrine of reasonable doubt. Mitchell, 37 Ga. App. 55 (138 S. 

E. 525).

Where the question of personal identity and the fact of alibi are virtually the same defense, the omission of the Court to instruct separately on alibi is not error. Glover, 7 Ga. App. 628 (2) (67 S. E. 687).

Where evidence in support of an alibi is not of clear and strong probative value, law of alibi need not be charged, without request. 

Throckmorton, 23 Ga. App. 112 (3) (97 S. E. 664).

If evidence warrants it, refusal to give charge, if requested,error. Montford, 144 Ga. 582 (5) (87 S. E. 797).

Error to charge law of alibi, where it is not involved. Daniels, 23 Ga. App. 762 (2) (99 S. E. 312).

Where charge is such, that it might be understood by the jury to relieve State of the burden of proving the defendant's connection. with the crime beyond a reasonable doubt, judgment will be reversed. Raysor, 132 Ga. 237 (63 S. E. 786); Brooks, 25 Ga. App. 

739, 741 (105 S. E. 42).

Instruction that alibi, as a defense, should be established to reasonable satisfaction of jury, and not beyond reasonable doubt, held not error. Cade, 41 Ga. App. 378 (1) (153 S. E. 76).

It is especially important for one on trial for a crime that the jury be instructed that testimony relating to alibi should be considered along with other evidence and that if, upon consideration of all the

CRIMINAL PROCEDURE 

145 testimony, including that upon the subject of alibi, the jury is not satisfied of defendant's guilt beyond a reasonable doubt, he is entitled to acquittal. Wafford, 163 Ga. 304 (136 S. E. 49).

Not error to give this section in toto in charge. Collier, 154 Ga. 

68 (5), 79 (113 S. E. 213).

Not error to charge on alibi, although defendant did not set it up as a defense, where defendant denied having been present when crime was committed. Taylor, 155 Ga. 785 (118 S. E. 675).

Charge that defendant pleads what is known as plea of alibi, that is to say that he was not at the place where the crime was alleged to have been committed, and that alibi as a defense involves impossibility of prisoner's presence at scene of the offense at the time of its commission, and that the range of evidence in respect to time and place must be such as to reasonably exclude possibility of presence, and that the evidence of alibi must satisfy minds of the jury that the accused was at a place where it was impossible for him to have committed the alleged crime, fully instructed jury upon subject of alibi as a defense. Goolsby, 24 Ga. App. 330, 331 (3) (100 S. E. 

678).

Court is not required, in absence of request, to charge jury upon alibi, but if Court does so, instruction must be correct. Incompleteness of charge on alibi (by omitting second section) requires reversal where jury could have been impressed with belief that if alibi were not established to their reasonable satisfaction it could not be considered for any other purpose. Moody, 17 Ga. App. 121 (1) (86 

S. E. 285); Wafford, 163 Ga. 304, 307 (136 S. E. 49).

Inaccurate instruction cured by general charge. Mack, 7 Ga. App. 

97 (2) (66 S. E. 282). 

Inapplicable instruction on alibi, favorable to defendant, not ground for new trial. Gullatt, 14 Ga. App. 53 (8) (80 S. E. 340).

Instruction that defendant sets up among other defenses defense of alibi, "that he attempts to show that he was at some other place at the time that the crime was committed" is erroneous on ground that it discredits his defense of alibi. Smiley, 156 Ga. 60 (5) (118 

S. E. 713).

Error to charge that defendant must establish defense of alibi to jury's satisfaction and to a reasonable certainty, because it has been held that the term "to a reasonable certainty" is the equivalent of "beyond a reasonable doubt." Dedge, 153 Ga. 176 (1) (111 S. E. 547).

Error to charge that defendant must establish defense of alibi beyond a reasonable doubt. Evans, 13 Ga. App. 700 (2) (79 S. E. 916). 

b. WITNESSES. 

Who decides competency of witness. The competency of a witness is a question of law, for the Court to decide. The credibility of the witness is for the jury. Reece, 155 Ga. 350 (1-b) (116 S. E. 631).

Husband and wife. A wife is an incompetent witness against her husband upon his trial under a criminal prosecution, except for offenses committed or attempted to have been committed upon her person, and in case of abandonment of his child. Grier, 158 Ga. 321 (2) (123 S. E. 210).

Husband and wife are incompetent to testify for or against the other spouse, either as to direct or circumstantial evidence. Ector, 10 Ga. App. 777 (74 S. E. 295).

Upon the trial of the husband for the killing of his child, the wife is not competent to testify, although it is alleged that the child was. accidentally killed, the accused having intended to kill his wife. 

Grier, 158 Ga. 321 (2) (123 S. E. 210).

Bigamy. In charge of bigamy, the woman, who, the uncontradicted testimony shows, married the defendant while he had living, undivorced spouse, is not a wife and is competent to testify. Dickerson, 30 Ga. App. 352 (118 S. E. 67).

The second marriage of a bigamist is void and does not render the woman incompetent witness against him on a criminal trial. Johnson, 61 Ga. 305 (1); Wrye, 95 Ga. 466 (1) (22 S. E. 273); Murphy, 122 Ga. 149 (2) (50 S. E. 48). 

Cohabitation. Cohabitation under a promise of marriage, but without marriage, does not render the woman or the man incompetent for or against the other party. Hill, 41 Ga. 484 (6).

Question whether witness is husband or wife. The witness may testify that she is not the wife of the accused. Hoxie, 114 Ga. 19 (2) (39 S. E. 944).

Where there is a conflict whether a woman, offered as a witness, is the wife of the accused, she may be permitted to testify, and the Court may leave the question of her competency to the jury, under proper instructions. Moore, 25 Ga. App. 251 (4) (102 S. E. 916).

Where in the trial of a criminal case a female witness was offered by the State, and her competency as a witness was challenged on the ground that she was the wife of the accused, and she was thereupon. interrogated as to her matrimonial status, and she testified in sub-

CRIMINAL PROCEDURE 

147 stance that she was married to the accused about two years before the trial, but that she has been married previously to another named person, and that this person to whom she had previously been married was still living and she had never been divorced from him, and this testimony was uncontradicted, it was not error for the Court to rule that she was a competent witness and to permit her to give evidence upon material issues involved in the criminal case. Jeems, 141 Ga. 493 (1) (81 S. E. 202).

Accomplices and joint defendants. The wife of an accomplice is a competent witness to testify to any fact in a criminal proceeding not against her husband, if he be not on trial and not affected by such testimony. Askea, 75 Ga. 356 (3).

The State may sever on trial for the purpose of obtaining testimony of the wife or husband of a joint defendant. Williams, 69 Ga. 

11, 13 (15) (15 S. E. 17); Whitlow, 74 Ga. 819 (2).

Where several defendants are jointly indicted, and jointly tried, for the commission of an offense, the wife of one may testify for or against the others, but not for or against her husband. Faulkner, 43 Ga. App. 763 (160 S. E. 117). Contrary rule held: Evans, 46 Ga. 

App. 342 (167 S. E. 724). 

Privileged conversations overheard by others. Conversations between husband and wife may be testified to by one who overheard them. Knight, 114 Ga. 48 (1) (39 S. E. 928); Ford, 124 Ga. 793 (53 

S. E. 335); Williams, 139 Ga. 591 (1) (77 S. E. 818).

On trial of husband, conversations between him and his wife may be testified to by one who overheard them, although they were intended to be confidential. Hudson, 153 Ga. 695 (1) (113 S. E. 519).

Declarations of wife, made under such circumstances as to be a part of the res gestae, that she killed the deceased, are admissible, and not subject to the objection that it is permitting the wife to testify for her husband. Reece, 155 Ga. 350 (2-b) (116 S. E. 631).

Where the accused was charged with larceny from the house, and the nature of the testimony against him required, upon his part, a satisfactory explanation of his possession of the property alleged to have been stolen, it is error to admit, over timely objection, testimony, as to a statement of the wife of the accused, made in his presence, which imputed to him an explanation of his possession contradicting the explanatory statement which he has just made on the trial; and it is also error to admit testimony to the effect that the accused and his wife disputed over the purport of his previous statement. The wife is incompetent to testify either for or against her

husband; and this rule applies as well to statements of the wife which would ordinarily be admissible as part of the res gestae as to any other statements which might be elicited from her, were she by law a competent witness. Wicker, 14 Ga. App. 665 (1) (82 S. E. 

58). Contrary rule held: Dunham, 8 Ga. App. 668 (3) (70 S. E. 111).

Where the wife makes a statement in the presence of her husband and a third person, which would implicate her husband in the crime, and the husband makes no denial thereof, the third person may testify as to these statements, although she is incompetent to testify. 

But such statements, to be admissible, must be a part of the res gestae, or where the circumstances require a denial. Otherwise they are not admissible. Bowen, 36 Ga. App. 666, 667 (137 S. E. 793).

After marital relation is terminated. Communications from husband to wife are protected from disclosure even after that relation has terminated. Lingo, 29 Ga. 470 (3).

Papers belonging to wife. Papers belonging to the wife and in her custody can not be produced by compulsory proceeding to be used as evidence for the State on the trial of her husband. Farmer, 100 Ga. 41 (1) (28 S. E. 26).

Where offense is committed against the wife. On a charge for an offense against the wife, she is competent to testify against her husband but not in his favor. Bryant, 43 Ga. App. 85 (157 S. E. 923).

Where defendant's wife is warned by the presiding judge that she may refuse to testify, upon the trial of her husband for pointing pistol at her, and she testifies, the accused can not complain, although on cross-examination she stated that she did not want to testify, and did not want her husband punished. Walls, 24 Ga. 

App. 697 (102 S. E. 43).

Who may object. The Court may interpose ex mero motu to prevent violation of the rule of competency of husband or wife as a witness for or against the other spouse. Goodrum, 60 Ga. 509. 

Attorney and client. Communications between attorney and party, in anticipation of employment, are privileged. Haywood, 114 Ga. 111 (3) (39 S. E. 948).

An attorney is not competent to testify that the accused intended to include certain matters in his statement to the jury at a former trial, but omitted it upon the advice of his counsel. Lewis, 91 Ga. 

168 (4) (16 S. E. 986). 

Communications between attorney and client are excluded as a

CRIMINAL PROCEDURE 

149 matter of public policy. Testimony of client as to advice given him by counsel is incompetent, and, on timely motion, should be excluded. Braxley, 17 Ga. App. 196, 197 (14) (86 S. E. 425).

An attorney is both, competent and compellable to testify for or against his client, as to any matter or thing, knowledge of which he may have acquired in any other manner than by virtue of his relations as attorney, or by reason of his anticipated employment as attorney. Bracewell, 21 Ga. App. 133 (2) (94 S. E. 91).

Where writing is in possession of the accused or his attorney, and it is competent evidence, secondary evidence is admissible, as the accused can not be compelled to produce it. A notice to produce is unnecessary. Moore, 130 Ga. 322 (4) (60 S. E. 544); Kinard, 1 Ga. 

App. 146 (4) (58 S. E. 263); Crawford, 4 Ga. App. 789, 799 (62 S. E. 

501); Kinsey, 12 Ga. App. 422 (1) (77 S. E. 369); Nalley, 11 Ga. 

App. 15 (5) (74 S. E. 567).

Certified copies of duly recorded instruments shown to be in possession of the defendant or his attorney, are admissible in evidence against him, in a criminal case, as against the objection that the original is the highest evidence, unless he voluntarily offers to produce the original. Kinard, 1 Ga. App. 146 (4) (58 S. E. 263).

Where, in a criminal case, the existence and the contents of a writing, shown to be in the possession of the accused or his attorney, are material, parol evidence of its contents is admissible. Kinsey, 12 Ga. App. 422 (1) (77 S. E. 369).

The relation of attorney and client does not exist between the solicitor-general and the prosecuting witness for the State, and therefore communications between such witness and the solicitor-general are not confidential, and on the trial of the defendant are admissible in evidence to prove contradictory statements. Vernon, 49 Ga. 

App. 187 (1) (174 S. E. 548).

Minors. A test, which the law of this State prescribes, as to the competency of a child of tender years to be a witness, is the knowledge by the child of the nature of an oath, and when an examination by the Court shows that the child has no such knowledge, it is error to permit the child to testify, over proper objection. Horton, 35 Ga. App. 493 (133 S. E. 647). 

The competency of a child of ten years is for the Court. Beebee, 

The child should be examined by the Court before permitted to testify. Where an examination is denied, and the child is permitted to testify, it is error, although at a former trial examination was

held and the child admitted as a witness. Young, 122 Ga.

725 (1) (50 S. E. 996). 

The better practice is for the Court to examine a child, offered as a witness, before permitting it to testify, especially where the child is objected to. But a failure of the Court to conduct a preliminary examination of a child offered as a witness is not ground for a new trial, where subsequently the child proved competent as a witness, during the examination before the jury. Webb, 7 Ga. App. 35 (1) (66 S. E. 27).

A failure of the Court to examine the child, who is offered as a witness, is not a reversible error, unless the child is objected to. 

Mills, 104 Ga. 502 (1) (30 S. E. 778).

Discretion of the Court. Where the judge examined the child and found it either competent or incompetent, it must be a flagrant case of error to warrant a reversal. Peterson, 47 Ga. 524 (2); Beebee, 124 Ga. 775 (1) (53 S. E. 99); Young, 125 Ga. 584 (4) (54 S. E. 82).

Where the evidence is conflicting, the mental competency of a child is for the Court. Ravenel, 153 Ga. 130 (5) (111 S. E. 643).

Although a child, eight years old, on a preliminary examination, held for the purpose of testing his competency as a witness, stated that he did not know what an oath was, yet, where he also stated that he knew what it was to "go up in the court-house and swear: you have to tell the truth," that "the law would punish him if he told a story," and "that he was bound to tell the truth when sworn," and the examination as a whole disclosed such a degree of intelligence and knowledge on the child's part as to satisfy the judge of his competency, the ruling of the trial judge permitting the child to be examined as a witness concerning the facts in issue, will not be disturbed. Minton, 99 Ga. 254 (1) (25 S. E. 626).

An examination for the purpose of testing the competency of a child of tender years to testify as a witness, which develops nothing except that he does not know his age, but does know his father's name and the number and names of the days of the week, and can count thirty-two, is not sufficiently comprehensive to authorize a conclusion that such child understands the nature of an oath. 

Gaines, 99 Ga. 703 (1) (26 S. E. 760).

Question for the jury. Where the Court decided, that child is competent to testify, it is error to instruct the jury that they may disregard his testimony altogether if they thought from the preliminary examination that he was incompetent on account of his youth. 11

Child held competent. Child seven years old held competent where a trial judge examined her and found her competent. Johnson, 61 Ga. 35.

A boy of ten years of age is a competent witness if he understands the nature of an oath. Moore, 79 Ga. 498 (3) (5 S. E. 51).

Insane person. Where a witness is objected to on the ground that she was mentally incapable of giving testimony, and there was evidence to the contrary, it was no error to permit the witness to testify. Ravenel, 153 Ga. 130 (5) (111 S. E. 643).

The fact that there is evidence that the person offered as a witness was insane, or previously adjudged insane, and now in the sanitarium, does not of necessity render him incompetent as a witness. 

The evidence may show that a lunatic has lucid intervals; and it is for the jury to say whether the occurrence to which the witness testified occurred in a lucid interval, and it is also for their determination whether or not the witness, though formally adjudged a lunatic, is sane at the time of testifying. Conoway, 171 Ga. 782 (3) (156

Child only witness. Where the only witness against the accused is a child seven years old, the crime not being such as would require two witnesses for a conviction, the defendant can be convicted upon the sole testimony of the child. LaFray, 48 Ga. App. 133 (172 S.

The accused.

The accused is not a competent witness on his own criminal trial and can not be sworn. King, 24 Ga. App. 49 (1) (99 S. E. 784).

The constitutional provision against compelling the accused to be a witness against himself should be liberally construed by the Court in favor of the accused, and they should not permit any first or doubtful step which may invade his rights in this respect. Underwood, 13 Ga. App. 206 (78 S. E. 1103).

1 

The Fifth Amendment of the Constitution of the United States to the effect that no one shall be compelled in any criminal case to be a witness against himself, has no application to prosecution in State courts. Wilburn, 141 Ga. 510 (2-b) (5-c) (81 S. E. 444).

A defendant in a criminal case can not be required to give evidence against himself, either by act or by word. Blackwell, 67 Ga. 76 (1). 

Where the body of a man, apparently murdered, is found by a roadside, and two persons were arrested and placed in jail charged with murder, and were subsequently taken thence in custody before the coroner's jury, summoned to hold an inquest on the body, and, without being informed that they were not compelled to testify, were sworn and examined as witnesses, not on their own motion but on that of the coroner and his jury, in regard to the homicide and their connection with it, when, on a subsequent trial under an indictment charging them with murder, confessions or inculpatory statements elicited on their examination before the coroner's jury-were not admissible against them. Adams, 129 Ga. 248 (58 S. E. 822).

It does no violence to the constitutional prohibition against compelling a person, accused of a crime, to give testimony tending in any manner to criminate himself, for an officer to whose custody such a person is committed to take from the person of the accused any article of apparel which may be material as evidence upon his trial; and if such officer, under such circumstances, take the shoes of the prisoner and compare them with certain tracks found near the scene of the alleged homicide, he may testify to the result of the comparison, notwithstanding an objection upon the ground that the evidence was illegally obtained. Myers, 97 Ga. 76, 77 (6) (25 S. E. 252).

Witnesses. The constitutional provision against self-incriminating means that when one is sworn as a witness, he shall not be compelled to testify to facts tending to criminate himself; it does not prevent the introduction in evidence of clothing or articles taken from the person arrested. Drake, 75 Ga. 413 (2); Evans, 106 Ga. 

519, 521 (32 S. E. 659).

Where a witness is willing to give incriminating testimony, it is optional with him. Wilburn, 141 Ga. 510, 511 (4) (81 S. E. 444).

Protection against self-incrimination is a personal privilege, and another can not take advantage thereof. McCray, 134 Ga. 416, 417 (8) (68 S. E. 62).

It is for the witness, and not for the Court, to determine whether his answer to the propounded question would incriminate him. Empire Life Insurance Co., 12 Ga. App. 380, 383 (2) (77 S. E. 209).

A witness can not, without being in contempt of the Court, stand in silence, not claiming his privilege and permitting the Court to pass upon it, and refuse to testify at all. He may decline to answer any question having a tendency to incriminate him, and he will be protected if he insists on his right to decline to answer. Pledger, 77 Ga. 242, 248 (3 S. E. 320); Empire Life Insurance Co., 12 Ga. 

App. 380, 383 (77 S. E. 209).

Where the witness was informed by the Court that he need not answer questions tending to criminate him, and with full understanding of the meaning of this rule and the consequences his answer may have, he gives testimony, such testimony is admissible against him on a subsequent trial. Davis, 122 Ga. 564 (2) (50 S. E. 376).

Where the witness refuses to answer a pertinent question on crossexamination, because tending to criminate himself, the whole testi-

mony must be excluded. McElhannon, 99 Ga. 672 (2) (26 S. E. 

501); Young, 65 Ga. 525 (2); Pinkard, 30 Ga. 757 (2); Hays, 16 Ga.
