The Court may instruct a witness, in a proper case, that he need not answer questions tending to criminate himself, unless he desires to do so. Lauchheimer & Sons, 126 Ga. 261 (4) (55 S. E. 55).

The failure of the Court to caution a witness that he need not answer the question tending to criminate him is not a ground for setting aside the verdict. Dunn, 99 Ga. 211 (2) (25 S. E. 448). The

Court is not bound to caution the witness that he may refuse to answer a question if the answer would tend to criminate him. The witness is presumed to know the law. Moore, 130 Ga. 322 (2) (60 

S. E. 544). 

Motion for new trial. Where four are accused jointly, and one convicted, but made a motion for a new trial, he can not be compelled, upon the trial of the others, to give evidence tending to criminate him. Stallings, 136 Ga. 131 (2) (70 S. E. 1015).

Gaming. A witness is compellable to give evidence on a trial for gaming, although he has criminally participated in the game. 

Wheatley, 114 Ga. 175 (39 S. E. 877). See also: Gaming.

Separate examination. In all cases either party has the right to have the witnesses of the other party examined out of the hearing of each other. The Court will take proper care to effect this object as far as practicable and convenient, but any mere irregularity shall not exclude the witness. § 38-1703.

The right of sequestration of witnesses may be invoked by the

The judge may separate the witnesses at his option, even without request. Meeks, 51 Ga. 429 (3).

It is within the discretion of the trial judge to sequester an officer of the court, or to allow him to remain in the court room. Askew, 3 Ga. App. 79 (3) (59 S. E. 311).

Prosecutor, or other witnesses. Prosecutor may be permitted to remain in the court room throughout the trial. If he testifies, his presence may be considered by the jury upon the credibility of his

Intermingling with sequestered witnesses. It is error to permit persons actively interested in the result of the case (such as the prosecutor) to intermingle with witnesses who have been ordered to be sequestered, there being a probability that their testimony may be influenced and moulded to the prejudice of the parties to the cause. The prosecutor, real or nominal, may not be present when the solicitor-general examines the witnesses privately. Hightower, 14 Ga. App. 246, 247 (4) (80 S. E. 684).

Juror as witness. A witness may be called out of the jury-box and sworn in by either party. Williams, 42 Ga. App. 225 (155 S.

How convicts may be produced as witnesses. The courts of this 

State have inherent power to cause the production in court of a convict serving a penal sentence in the State penitentiary or county chain gang, whenever his presence is needed for a lawful purpose. 

Flagg, 11 Ga. App. 37 (74 S. E. 562).

A statement by the presiding judge in a criminal case, that he would not approve an application to the governor for a certain wit-

ness then confined in the penitentiary, is no ground for exception where it appears that such application was never prepared or presented to the judge for approval. Mehaffey, 114 Ga. 852 (40 S. E. 993). 

It is the duty of the Court to order service of process against a witness in prison. Roberts, 72 Ga. 673. (Old rule.)

In order for a defendant in a criminal case to take the benefit of the Acts of 1883, touching the production of convicts in the penitentiary, as witnesses, application must first be made to the governor as the act prescribes. The observance of that requirement is necessary, and its omission is more than failure on a mere technicality. 

Roberts, 94 Ga. 66 (21 S. E. 132).

If the law of compulsory process for witnesses applies where the person desired as a witness is imprisoned as a convict in the penitentiary, it imposes no absolute duty on the judge of the Superior Court to direct or require that the order for producing the convict shall be executed at the expense of the public, even though the applicant for the order be unable from poverty to defray the expense, and even if the judge in the exercise of his discretion might, if he thought proper, make the county chargeable therewith. The constitutional right to have compulsory process issue for witnesses does not include any right of having them brought into court at public expense; and no such right has been expressly conferred by statute, except by the Acts of 1883, under which the right is not unconditional, but limited by the sound discretion of the judge, to be exercised on the special facts of the case. Roberts, 94 Ga. 66 (21 S. E. 132).

c. RES GESTAE. 

Definition. Declarations accompanying an act, or so nearly connected therewith in time as to be free from all suspicion of device or afterthought, are admissible in evidence as part of res gestae. § 38-305. Hunter, 147 Ga. 823 (2) (95 S. E. 688).

Acts and circumstances forming a part or continuation of the main transaction are admissible as res gestae. Floyd, 143 Ga. 286 (2) (84 S. E. 971).

Declarations to be a part of the res gestae must be contemporaneous with the main fact, but to be contemporaneous they are not required to be precisely concurrent in point of time. If the declara-

CRIMINAL PROCEDURE 

157 tions spring out of the transaction-if they elucidate it—if they are voluntary and spontaneous, and if they are made at a time so near to it as to preclude reasonably the idea of deliberate design, then they are to be regarded as contemporaneous. Mitchum, 11 Ga. 615 (5). 

To except a statement from the rule which excludes hearsay, it must not be merely contemporaneous with the act, but also "free from all suspicion of device or afterthought.” What the law altogether distrusts is not after-speech but after-thought. That the declarations shall appear to be spontaneous is indispensable, and it is for this reason alone that they are required to be speedy. There must be no fair opportunity for the will of the speaker to mould or modify them. His will must have become and remained dormant, so far as any deliberation in concocting matter for speech or selecting words is concerned. His declarations must be the utterance of human nature, of the genus homo, rather than of the individual. 

If the state of his mind be such that his individuality is for the time being suppressed and silenced, what he says is regarded by the law as in some degree trustworthy. Although this statement may have been made within a minute after the shooting, the manner in which it was made was indicative of at least some degree of afterthought. Lyles, 130 Ga. 294, 300 (60 S. E. 578).

The res gestae of a transaction is what is done during the progress of it, or so nearly upon the actual occurrence as fairly to be treated as contemporaneous with it. No precise point of time can be fixed a priori where the res gestae ends. Each case turns on its own circumstances. Indeed the inquiry is rather into events than into the precise time which has elapsed. Hall, 48 Ga. 607, 608; O'Neal, 172 Ga. 526 (1) (158 S. E. 51).

An inquiry as to whether a particular saying constitutes a part of the res gestae of the transaction turns on the particular circumstances of each case, and is directed rather to the spontaneity of the events related, than the precise time which may have elapsed between the main fact and the statements made in reference to it. 

Cobb, 11 Ga. App. 52, 53 (5) (74 S. E. 702).

Although the time which elapsed between the crime and the declaration was short, where the manner of its delivery and the beneficial evidence it contained could not but raise a suspicion of device or afterthought, such evidence should be excluded. Sullivan, 101 Ga. 800, 802 (29 S. E. 16).

The question whether a statement is admissible as part of the res gestae is a question for the Court. Rouse, 135 Ga. 227 (2) (69 

S. E. 180).

Bystander. An exclamation of a bystander, who saw the commission of the offense, may in some cases be admissible, as part of the res gestae, but not where it was merely an expression of opinion. Harnage, 7 Ga. App. 573 (4) (67 S. E. 694); Smith, 10 Ga. 

App. 36, 37 (2) (72 S. E. 527); Hill, 17 Ga. App. 294 (1) (86 S. E. 657). 

Evidence of silence of the accused, when charged with the commission of the crime by a declaration of a bystander immediately after a crime was committed,-admissible. Clark, 117 Ga. 254 (3) (43 S. E. 853).

Declarations by the wife or mother of the accused. Although the wife of the accused is not a competent witness, declarations made. by her in his presence, requiring an answer from him, and forming a part of the res gestae-admissible. Dunham, 8 Ga. App. 668 (3) (70 S. E. 111).

Declarations by the mother of the accused, made by her in his presence, requiring an answer from him, and forming a part of the res gestae-admissible. Chapman, 40 Ga. App. 725 (4) (151 

S. E. 410).

Declaration of victim. Saying of the deceased within five or ten minutes after he was shot that the accused shot him,-admissible. 

O'Neal, 172 Ga. 526 (1) (158 S. E. 51).

Declaration of the deceased ten or fifteen minutes after the crime was committed, to hospital physician, describing the offense, not admissible. Hunter, 147 Ga. 823, 825 (2) (95 S. E. 688).

Declarations by the deceased, made a few minutes after the crime was committed, when all parties have left the scene, and he has been removed to a place two hundred fifty yards distant, not admissible in favor of the defendant. Ratteree, 53 Ga. 570, 572.

Declaration of the deceased that the defendant shot him, made immediately after the crime,-admissible as part of the res gestae and in corroboration of the dying declaration. Kirk, 73 Ga. 620, 621 (5); Dumas, 65 Ga. 471 (2).

Exclamation of the deceased, as he fell from the fatal wound: "Oh Lord, my poor wife and children"-admissible to show condition of mind or motives of the deceased. (One dissenting.) Goodman, 122 Ga. 111 (2) (49 S. E. 922).

159 Dying declaration may contain a conversation, which, although not admissible as dying declaration, may still be admissible as part of the res gestae. Bush, 109 Ga. 120 (3) (34 S. E. 298); Cason, 134 

Ga. 786 (5) (68 S. E. 554).

Child. In determining whether a declaration is part of the res gestae, the age of the child may be considered. Although the child may be too young to be a witness, declarations, part of the res gestae, may be admitted. Grant, 124 Ga. 757 (4), 759 (53 S. E. 

334); Berry, 9 Ga. App. 868 (1) (72 S. E. 433).

Declaration of the accused. Prisoner's statement, sometime after the crime, not admissible in his favor. Hall, 48 Ga. 607; Lyles, 130 

Ga. 294, 300 (60 S. E. 578); Park, 126 Ga. 575, 576 (8) (55 S. E. 

489); Warrick, 125 Ga. 133 (4) (53 S. E. 1027).

Statements by the accused, just after he was shot down by members of the posse while fleeing from the place of the homicide, made in answer to questions of what he was doing there, and whose was the gun he held,-admissible as part of the res gestae. West, 155 Ga. 482 (2) (117 S. E. 380).

Complaints made by the accused to a physician as to his own injury, not admissible. Westmoreland, 45 Ga. 225 (4).

Conspiracy. Where there is evidence of a conspiracy, evidence relating to occurrences and declarations of alleged conspirators, pending the conspiracy,-admissible as part of the res gestae. West, 153 Ga. 327 (112 S. E. 150).

Evidence that one jointly accused with the defendant called at the time the shooting was committed: "Pour it into him"-admissible against the defendant as part of the res gestae. Swain, 149 Ga. 629, 630 (2) (101 S. E. 539).

Acts of other violence. Evidence of acts of violence by the accused against others, at the time the crime was committed,-admissible as part of the res gestae, to throw light on his state of mind and to illustrate his intention at the time of the crime. Carter, 15 

Ga. App. 343 (1) (83 S. E. 153). 

Where the defendant fired at two persons, and killed one, evidence of the fact that he shot at the other also,-admissible as part of the res gestae. Glover, 137 Ga. 82 (1) (72 S. E. 926).

Declarations of the accused held admissible in his favor. The 

State having proved that the accused killed his wife by shooting her, disappeared for a few minutes and then returned, made manifestations of grief and said that he shot her by accident and would

not have done so for the world, it was competent for him (the accused) to prove that he acted consistently with this theory by going in search of an officer, overtaking him and surrendering himself, saying at the time of the surrender, and as explanatory thereof, that he has killed his wife by accident, the interval between the killing and the surrender not exceeding twenty or thirty minutes according to the indications of the evidence, though the precise time did not definitely appear. His mere declaration, made subsequent to his arrest, to the effect that the killing was accidental and that he desired to return to see the body of his wife, was inadmissible; nor was the statement of the officer to other officers in turning over the prisoner to them admissible in evidence, such statement consisting of repetition of what the accused has said on surrendering himself. Boston, 94 Ga. 590 (1) (20 S. E. 98).

Where it appeared that immediately after the shooting a witness went to the defendant, who was still standing at the scene of the shooting, and walked a few steps away with him, and asked him why he shot, and he then and there said that he shot unintentionally, this statement being made in less than two minutes from the time of the shooting, all circumstances tending to negative premeditation, it should have been admitted in evidence as part of the res gestae. Darby, 9 Ga. App. 700 (2) (72 S. E. 182).

Saying of the deceased before the homicide. Where it appeared that the defendant and the deceased lived together as husband and wife; that the deceased was jealous on account of defendant's attention to another woman, and had quarreled with the accused; that on the night of the homicide the deceased left her home saying that there were two persons down the alley, the accused and his sweetheart, and that she is going to see about it; and that she was found dead the next day in the alley, her statement was admissible as part of the res gestae. Thomas, 67 Ga. 460 (3). 

d. DYING DECLARATIONS. 

Definition. Dying declarations, made by any person in the article of death, who is conscious of his condition, as to the cause of his death, and the person who killed him, are admissible in evidence in a prosecution for the homicide. § 38-307. 

Dying declarations constitute one of the exceptions to the rule which rejects hearsay evidence; it is founded on the necessity of the case, and for the reason that the sanction under which these declarations are made, in view of impending death and judgment, when

CRIMINAL PROCEDURE 

161 the last hope of life is extinct, and when the retributions of eternity are at hand, is of equal solemnity as that of statements made under oath. Still it must be admitted that great caution should be observed in the use of this kind of evidence. Dying declarations are admissible only when made by a person in the article of death, and who is conscious of his condition, and then only in the case of prosecutions for homicide, and for the sole purpose of showing the cause of death and the person who committed the act. The necessity for this great caution, not only in the admission, but in the use, of this kind of testimony, is enforced by judges and writers who have dealt with the subject. It is to be observed that, although there may have been an utter abandonment of all hope of recovery, it will often happen that the particulars of the violence to which the deceased has spoken are likely to have occurred under circumstances of confusion and surprise calculated to prevent their being accurately observed. The consequences, also, of the violence may occasion an injury to the mind, and an indistinctness of memory as to the particular transaction. The deceased may have stated his inferences from facts concerning which he may have drawn a wrong conclusion, or he may have omitted important particulars, from not having his attention called to them. Such evidence, therefore, is liable to be incomplete. He may naturally, also, be disposed to give a partial account of the occurrence, although possibly not influenced by animosity or ill will. But it can not be concealed, that animosity and resentment are not unlikely to be felt in such situation. The passion of anger, once excited, may not have been entirely extinguished, even when all hope of life is lost. Such considerations show the necessity of caution in receiving impressions from accounts given by persons in dying state, especially when it is considered that they can not be subjected to the proper cross-examination; a power quite as necessary for securing the truth as the religious obligation of an oath can be. The security also, which courts of justice have in ordinary cases for enforcing truth, by the terror of punishment and the penalties of perjury, can not exist in this case.

Dying declarations are liable to be misunderstood and misreported, from inattention, from misunderstanding, or from infirmity of memory. . . This extract, which furnished a brief but accurate and comprehensive summary of the law, shows, even in cases where all the preliminary requirements are fully met, as clearly as anything can, not only the unreliable and unsatisfactory character of such proof, but its dangerous effect, from the fact of

the undue importance that juries are almost sure to give it, and should impress us with caution not only in its introduction, but in its application and use when admitted. Mitchell, 71 Ga. 128, 141. 

Note: See this case for a full and complete review of the law of dying declarations. Also, Coart, 156 Ga. 536, 544 (3) (119 S. E. 723).

When a dissolution is approaching, and the dying man has lost hope of life, and his mind feels the full consciousness of his condition, the solemnity of the scene gives to his statement the sanctity of truth, and such dying declarations, when made, should be admitted in evidence and considered by the jury under the charge of the Court upon the law applicable to them. Hill, 41 Ga. 484 (4).

Necessity of the case. Dying declarations, when the jury is satisfied that they are such, are founded on the necessity of the case and the reason that, being made in view of impending death and judgment, when hope of life is extinct and when retributions of eternity are at hand, they stand on the same plane of solemnity as statements made under oath,—and the Court may so charge the jury. 

Summerour, 172 Ga. 560, 561 (158 S. E. 327).

The common-law rule was that dying declarations were admitted with great caution and only from necessity. Now they may be proved though there may be abundant evidence as to the homicide. 

Battle, 74 Ga. 101 (1). 

Hearsay evidence. Dying declarations constitute exceptions to the rule which rejects hearsay evidence. Ransom, 23 Ga. App. 364 (1) (98 S. E. 255); Mitchell, 71 Ga. 128 (2).

Charge of Court. The Court may state to the jury why dying declarations are admissible. McArthur, 120 Ga. 195 (1) (47 S. E. 

553); Summerour, 172 Ga. 560, 561 (158 S. E. 327).

In the absence of appropriate written request, the Court need not charge the law of dying declarations, where the State does not rely for conviction upon such dying declarations solely. Thomas, 150 Ga. 269 (1) (103 S. E. 244).

It is error to charge the jury that dying declarations are admitted on the theory that a person is as "sure" to tell the truth when in the article of death as under oath. Darby, 16 Ga. App. 171 (3) (84 S. E. 724).

Dying declaration sole evidence. In a proper case conviction may be had upon the sole evidence of dying declaration, although it be unreasonable, and made while the deceased was in an in-

CRIMINAL PROCEDURE 

163 toxicated condition and under the influence of drugs. Stiles, 154 

Ga. 86, 94 (113 S. E. 208).

Articulo mortis. As a prerequisite to the admission of dying declarations to the jury it must appear, prima facie, that the deceased was in articulo mortis at the time the declaration was made. 

Mitchell, 71 Ga. 128; Hawkins, 141 Ga. 212 (2) (80 S. E. 711); 

Darby, 9 Ga. App. 700, 701 (2) (7 S. E. 182).

The actual period of survival after making the declaration is not controlling. The question does not depend upon the length of time between the declaration and the death of the declarant, but upon declarant's mind at the time of the declaration, and his belief that he is in a dying condition. Johnson, 169 Ga. 814 (3-b) (152 S. E. 76).

Although the deceased died two months after the declaration, if other requirements are satisfied, the declaration is admissible. Johnson, 169 Ga. 814, 815 (3-d) (152 S. E. 76).

Where deceased died five days after declaration, it was held admissible. Bryant, 80 Ga. 272 (1) (4 S. E. 853). Apparently contrary rule held: Taylor, 120 Ga. 857 (1) (48 S. E. 361).

Consciousness of the deceased. To render admissible one's dying declarations as to the cause of his death and the person who killed him, they must be made by the declarant in the article of death, and he must be conscious of his condition. Johnson, 169 Ga. 814 

Consciousness on the part of the deceased that he was dying and was in extremis may be inferred, not only from his statement, but also from the nature of the wound and other circumstances. Johnson, 169 Ga. 814 (3-a) (152 S. E. 76).

If the declarant was in fact in article of death and the circumstances indicate that he must have known it, it is proper for the declarations, made by him, to be admitted, with instructions to the jury that they find whether such statements were made consciously in articulo mortis. Green, 154 Ga. 117, 118 (6) (113 S. E. 536).

It is not necessary that the person whose statements are sought to be introduced should express himself as believing that he is in dying condition. Consciousness of his condition may be inferred from the nature of the wound or from other circumstances. Jones, 150 Ga. 775 (1) (105 S. E. 495); Bryant, 44 Ga. App. 781, 782 (3) (163 S. E. 219).

The opinion of a physician, that the deceased knew of his dying declaration at the time the declaration was made, is insufficient as

a foundation for the introduction of such declaration. Darby, 16 

Ga. App. 171, 172 (6) (84 S. E. 724).

If the deceased realized that he was mortally wounded, he knew that he was in articulo mortis. Davis, 120 Ga. 843 (3) (48 S. E. 305).

A dying declaration is admissible, where the deceased knew that he was dying, although others, including the attending physician, thought the wound to be slight, and the deceased died five days later. Bryant, 80 Ga. 272 (1) (4 S. E. 853).

Dying declarations of one deprived of full consciousness so as to be unable to give an intelligent account of the facts connected with the homicide-not admissible. Mitchell, 71 Ga. 128. 

It does not matter how, and by what means, the deceased became conscious that he was dying. Smith, 9 Ga. App. 403 (2) (71 S. E. 606).

Where the deceased stated that he was going to die "if they did not do something for him," his declaration is not admissible. 

Howard, 144 Ga. 169 (1) (1-a) (86 S. E. 540).

Remarks and statements of the deceased, illustrating that he was conscious of his condition, are admissible, although they do not relate to the cause of the death. Lyens, 133 Ga. 587, 597 (60 

S. E. 792).

Prima facie evidence. Where dying declarations are sought to be admitted, the Court must first determine from preliminary evidence whether prima facie they are competent as such and were under circumstances entitling them to admission. Swain, 149 Ga. 

629, 630 (4) (101 S. E. 539).

Slight preliminary proof is sufficient to admit dying declarations. 

Childs, 18 Ga. App. 782 (1) (90 S. E. 723); Moody, 1 Ga. App. 772, 773 (6) (58 S. E. 262).

Where the statement of the deceased is admitted as dying declaration, the jury should be instructed that such evidence is admitted only upon prima facie proof of verity and that it is in the province of the jury to determine whether the statement is in fact a dying declaration. Knight, 12 Ga. App. 111 (2) (76 S. E. 1047).

It is generally reversible error for the Court to omit to charge that the alleged dying declarations must not be considered by the jury, unless they are satisfied from the evidence that such declarations were made when the declarant was in the article of death. 

Knight, 12 Ga. App. 111 (2) (76 S. E. 1047).

Whether or not a dying declaration was made, whether the de-

CRIMINAL PROCEDURE 

165 ceased was in the article of death, and knew of it,—is a question of fact for the jury. Hawkins, 141 Ga. 212 (3) (80 S. E. 711); 

Williams, 148 Ga. 483 (2) (97 S. E. 77).

Preliminary proof to show that the deceased was conscious of his condition, and was in articulo mortis, is necessary. But prima facie evidence is sufficient. Darby, 16 Ga. App. 171 (3) (84 S. E. 

724); Faulkner, 166 Ga. 645, 661 (144 S. E. 193); Gibbs, 41 Ga. App. 

574 (3) (153 S. E. 613); Johnson, 169 Ga. 814, 815 (3-c) (152 S. E. 

76); Best, 26 Ga. App. 671, 672 (2) (107 S. E. 266).

Where there is no positive evidence that the deceased was conscious of his condition, the declaration is not admissible. Darby, 16 Ga. App. 171 (3) (84 S. E. 724).

The foundation for a dying declaration may be laid by witnesses other than the one to whom the declaration was made. One witness may testify to the condition of the deceased, and the other to his statement. Smith, 8 Ga. App. 680 (3) (70 S. E. 42).

What may be proved. Dying declarations should be limited to the cause of the death and the person who killed the declarant. 

Harris, 142 Ga. 627, 629 (83 S. E. 514).

In a trial for murder, dying declarations are admissible to prove any relevant fact embraced in the res gestae of the killing. Wilkerson, 91 Ga. 729 (3) (17 S. E. 990); Bush, 109 Ga. 120 (3) (34 

S. E. 298); Harris, 142 Ga. 627, 629 (83 S. E. 514); Taylor, 120 Ga. 

Immaterial or irrelevant matter in dying declaration is no ground for excluding the whole declaration. Brown, 8 Ga. App. 382 (2), 385 (69 S. E. 45).

Dying declarations, to be admissible, must consist of a statement of a matter of fact, and declaration, which amounts to merely an expression of an opinion, is not admissible. White, 100 Ga. 659, 665 (28 S. E. 423).

It is error to admit laudatory remarks by the deceased, of himself, such as "You know I always do what the white folks told me." 

Hawkins, 141 Ga. 212 (4) (80 S. E. 711).

Where it is manifestly impossible that the deceased could have seen his assailant or known certainly who he was, a mere expression of opinion as to who he was is not admissible as a dying declaration; but where want of knowledge does not appear either from the statement itself, or from other evidence in the case, it must be presumed that the declarant stated a fact within his knowledge. In these circumstances it is a question for the jury whether the declara-

tion represented the knowledge of the deceased or merely his opinion. Strickland, 167 Ga. 452, 457 (145 S. E. 879).

All vague and indefinite expressions, all language that does not distinctly point to the cause of the death and its attending circumstances, but requires to be aided by suppositions or inferences in order to establish facts tending to criminate the respondent—are inadmissible. Mitchell, 71 Ga. 128, 147. 

Objections to testimony as to an alleged dying declaration, that declarant has said: "I know the man, but I can not call his name, and that therefore declarant did not know the person who killed him, is not supported where there is other evidence disclosing the identity of the individual referred to by the declarant. Odom, 13 

Ga. App. 687 (2) (79 S. E. 858). 

Must be on trial for the killing. Dying declarations are not admissible in evidence, even where every prerequisite is in evidence, except where the defendant is on trial for the killing of the declarant. Miliken, 8 Ga. App. 478 (1) (69 S. E. 915). 

Where two persons are killed. Where two persons are killed in the same fight, the dying declarations of one are not, as such, admissible on the trial of the slayer for the murder of the other. 

Taylor, 120 Ga. 857 (2) (48 S. E. 361); Miliken, 8 Ga. App. 478 (1) (69 S. E. 915); Westberry, 175 Ga. 115 (1) (164 S. E. 905). 

Credibility. Credibility of dying declarations should be determined by the rules used in determining credibility of witnesses. 

The declarant may be impeached as any other witness, and upon request the Court should so charge the jury. Hall, 124 Ga. 649 (2) (52 S. E. 891); Robinson, 10 Ga. App. 462 (1) (73 S. E. 622).

Impeachment. The character of the deceased is admissible to impeach the dying declaration. By the same rule, contradictory statements are admitted to impeach the declaration. Battle, 74 Ga. 

101 (2); Perry, 102 Ga. 365, 375 (4) (30 S. E. 903); Redd, 99 Ga. 

210 (1) (25 S. E. 268).

It is admissible to show that the deceased made statements conflicting with the dying declaration. One dying declaration is admissible to impeach the other. Pyle, 4 Ga. App. 811 (4) (62 S. E. 540).

Where the accused introduced evidence of dying declarations of the deceased to show his innocence, the State can impeach these with other inconsistent dying declarations. Johnson, 169 Ga. 814, 

---

CRIMINAL PROCEDURE 

167 Accomplices. On the trial of one accomplice, dying declarations, incriminating the other accomplice admissible. Harris, 142 Ga. 627 (2) (83 S. E. 514). 

Declarations in defendant's favor. The declarations can be used by the accused in his favor as well as by the State to show his guilt. Johnson, 169 Ga. 814, 815 (4) (152 S. E. 76).

Dying declarations tending to show that the injury was accidental-admissible for the accused. Flannigan, 135 Ga. 221 (2) (69 S. E. 171).

On the issue of self-defense against a deadly assault by the deceased, the latter's dying declaration that he caught the accused in adultery with his wife is a declaration as to the cause of his death, and-admissible. Wilkerson, 91 Ga. 729, 739 (17 S. E. 990).

Constitutionality. The admission of dying declarations does not contravene that provision of the Constitution of the United States which provides that the accused shall be confronted with witnesses against him. Jones, 130 Ga. 274 (3) (60 S. E. 840).

Dying declarations in writing. Where dying declaration has been taken down in writing, read to the deceased, understood by him, intended by him as his dying declaration, it is admissible, whether signed or not. Where immaterial or irrelevant matter is contained in such writing, such matter should be stricken and the balance read to the jury. Freeman, 112 Ga. 48 (2) (37 S. E. 172); Perry, 102 Ga. 365 (2) (3) (30 S. E. 903); Mixon, 7 Ga. App. 805 (5) (68 

S. E. 315).

Voluntary and involuntary declarations. It is immaterial whether the dying declaration is voluntarily offered by the declarant, or elicited by question propounded by others. Smith, 9 Ga. App. 403 (2) (71 S. E. 606); Brinson, 22 Ga. App. 649, 650 (97 S. E. 102). 

Great caution in receiving dying declarations. Even though all the conditions laid down by law for the admissibility of dying declarations be satisfied, still the declaration should be received by the jury with great caution. Smith, 9 Ga. App. 403 (2) (71 S. E. 606).

The jury should be instructed, where the evidence authorizes such instruction, that dying declarations should be received with great caution, and the bias, the feeling, and the physical and mental condition of the declarant, as well as the credibility of the alleged declaration should be weighed by them. Knight, 12 Ga. App. 111

(2) (76 S. E. 1047). 

Failure so to charge, on request, is reversible error. Denton, 6 Ga. App. 3 (63 S. E. 1132).

The injunction that dying declarations must be received with great caution, is directed to the juries, rather than to the judges. 

Carter, 2 Ga. App. 254, 258 (58 S. E. 532). 

But see: Robinson, 17 Ga. App. 751 (3) (88 S. E. 410); Williams, 148 Ga. 483 (3) (97 S. E. 77), where it is held that it is not incumbent upon or proper for the Court to charge the jury that great caution should be observed in the use of dying declarations. 

e. CONFESSIONS. 

Highest Evidence. A confession, free and voluntarily made by the defendant, is direct evidence of the highest character, and, when corroborated by proof of the corpus delicti, is sufficient to authorize a conviction. Berry, 48 Ga. App. 303 (1) (172 S. E. 647); Calvin, 118 Ga. 73, 74 (44 S. E. 848); Phoenix, 113 Ga. 424, 431 (38 S. E. 

992); Mercer, 17 Ga. 146 (2); Cook, 11 Ga. 53, 59.

Not favored. The law does not favor convictions based upon confession, and least of all upon implied confessions. Graham, 118 

Ga. 807 (1) (45 S. E. 616).

Definition. The admission of the main fact in a charge of crime, without exculpatory explanation, amounts to confession. Adams, 47 Ga. App. 444 (3) (170 S. E. 525).

Admissions usually refer to civil cases; confessions to criminal. 

§ 38-401. 

Acquiescence, or silence, when the circumstances require an answer or denial or other conduct, may amount to admission. § 38-409. 

When an admission is given in evidence, it is the right of the other party to have the whole admission and all the conversation connected therewith. § 38-410.

A confession is a voluntary admission of guilt. An admission, as applied to a criminal case, is a statement by the defendant of a fact or facts, pertinent to the issue and tending, in connection with proof of other facts or circumstances, to prove the guilt of the accused, but which is of itself insufficient to authorize conviction. An admission is a circumstance which requires the aid of further testimony to generate a reasonable conclusion of guilt. The nearer an admission approaches the completeness of a plenary confession of guilt without attaining thereto, the more likely is any reference

CRIMINAL PROCEDURE 

169 in the charge to the subject of confession to confuse the jury and harm the defendant. Ransom, 2 Ga. App. 826 (2) (59 S. E. 101).

A confession is a voluntary statement made by a person charged with the commission of a crime, wherein he acknowledges himself guilty of the offense charged. A statement which admits the commission of an act, but which also gives a legal excuse or justification, is not a confession. Owens, 120 Ga. 296 (2) (48 S. E. 21); 

Reed, 15 Ga. App. 435, 436 (2) (83 S. E. 674); Easterling, 24 Ga. 

App. 424, 425 (100 S. E. 727).

In an incriminatory statement only one or more facts are admitted. In a confession the entire criminal act is confessed. Owens, 120 Ga. 296, 298 (48 S. E. 21).

An acknowledgment, in order to be a confession, must admit every essential element necessary to make out a case against the accused. Hart, 14 Ga. App. 714, 715, 716 (3) (82 S. E. 164).

Direct and circumstantial evidence. Confession of facts directly admitting the commission of the crime is direct evidence, but a confession of facts from which an inference of participation arises is circumstantial evidence. Hart, 14 Ga. App. 714, 716 (82 S. E. 164). An incriminatory admission is not a confession of guilt, but is only a circumstance from which guilt may be inferred. Confession is direct evidence, but incriminatory admissions can logically be considered as indirect or circumstantial evidence only. Kinard, 19 Ga. App. 624, 625 (3) (91 S. E. 941).

Confession must be voluntary. To make a confession admissible, it must have been made voluntarily, without being induced by another, by the slightest hope of benefit or remotest fear of injury. 

Incriminatory admissions and confessions are not admissible, if there is any evidence, arising from the testimony as to the circumstance under which the alleged confession was made, that the making of the confession was induced by the slightest hope of benefit, or the remotest fear of injury. King, 155 Ga. 707 (118 

S. E. 368); Johnson, 1 Ga. App. 129 (1) (57 S. E. 934).

Statements of an incriminatory character, made by one accused of a crime, are admissible, if freely and voluntarily made, though they were elicited by trick, artifice or deception. Hudson, 153 Ga. 

In order for hope of benefit or fear of injury to render confession inadmissible, such hope or fear must be induced by another. וי

Where hope or fear originated in the defendant's own mind from seeds of his own planting, and under such hope and fear defendant made the confession, this will not exclude the confession as evidence. 

Hill, 148 Ga. 521 (4) (97 S. E. 442); Jones, 18 Ga. App. 310 (1) (89 S. E. 347).

Where confessions were freely and voluntarily made, they will not be excluded because the defendant was placed into the sheriff's car, handcuffed, with two other men in the car, and taken to the home of the deceased. Bradberry, 170 Ga. 859 (4) (154 S. E. 344).

Where evidence accompanying testimony of confession by the accused demanded the finding that the confession was not made voluntarily and without inducement of hope of benefit or fear of injury, it is error to admit such testimony over objection, or to refuse to exclude it on motion. In such case it should not go to the jury. 

Thomas, 169 Ga. 182 (149 S. E. 871).

Where evidence of a confession is offered by the State, and there is no objection by the defendant upon the ground that it was not freely and voluntarily made, the evidence is admissible. Washington, 24 Ga. App. 65 (3) (100 S. E. 31).

The objection that the confession was not freely and voluntarily made must be timely. It is too late after verdict. McDuffie, 17 Ga. 

App. 342 (2) (86 S. E. 821).

Where the State's evidence shows that the confession was not freely and voluntarily made, the Court should not let it go to the jury. Hawkins, 6 Ga. App. 109 (1) (64 S. E. 289).

Confessions held admissible. A voluntary confession or incriminatory admission is not inadmissible merely because it was made pending an illegal arrest. Ivey, 4 Ga. App. 828 (3) (62 S. E. 565).

Defendant's statement on a former trial is admissible in its entirety, or parts thereof. Medlin, 149 Ga. 23 (2) (98 S. E. 551).

Statements based on memoranda, or testimony given while intoxicated, or testimony given upon suggestion of a leading question, are treated as dubitable, and may under circumstances be excluded. 

Wilson, 19 Ga. App. 759, 768 (92 S. E. 309).

Confessions or admissions by the accused are admissible against him in evidence, although they were coupled with offer of compromise and settlement, or made for that purpose. Futch, 43 Ga. 

App. 782 (1) (159 S. E. 888). 

Where admissions were made before a coroner's jury, they are admissible in evidence on trial, if freely and voluntarily made. 

Wright, 141 Ga. 475 (1) (81 S. E. 214).

CRIMINAL PROCEDURE 

171 The mere fact that the accused was in custody, or under arrest at the time the confession was made, did not render it incompetent, if in fact it was made voluntarily within the legal meaning of the term. The fact alone that the confession was made at night, in the woods, where the accused was handcuffed, and in the presence of officers, is no cause for its exclusion. Wilburn, 141 Ga. 510, 511 

The fact that the admission was made after three hours of grilling does not show that it was not freely and voluntarily made. King, 28 Ga. App. 751, 753 (113 S. E. 107).

The fact that a person who was with the sheriff struck the accused over the head with the butt of a pistol will not render the confession inadmissible, the confession being made subsequent to his being struck, and to the sheriff while not in company with the person who struck him. Bonner, 152 Ga. 214, 219 (3) (109 S. E. 291).

A statement of an officer to one accused of a crime, that it would be better for him to tell the truth about the case, does not necessarily, as a matter of law, render inadmissible as evidence a confession of guilt. If the inducement is sufficient by possibility to elicit an untrue confession of guilt, then the confession is to be rejected, otherwise it is to be admitted under proper instructions from the Court. Wilson, 19 Ga. App. 759, 760 (4) (92 S. E. 309).

Where a witness stated to the defendant that the co-defendant had owned up and that the defendant might as well own up,—this was not sufficient to exclude a confession. Nix, 149 Ga. 304, 306, 307 (1) (100 S. E. 197).

The fact that the accused was scared after being taken into custody, without more, is not sufficient to exclude his confession. 

Shivers, 17 Ga. App. 334 (1) (86 S. E. 734).

Confession admitted, although the sheriff has struck the accused on the head with handcuffs, when he jerked away, causing blood to flow, there being no promises or threats made. Sledge, 24 Ga. App. 

698 (102 S. E. 31). 

Confessions held not admissible.

Statements based on memo randa, or testimony given while intoxicated, or testimony given upon suggestion of a leading question, are treated as dubitable, and may under circumstances be excluded. Wilson, 19 Ga. App. 

759, 768 (92 S. E. 309).

Offer of money with which to pay a fine is a sufficient induce-

1 ment to require exclusion of a confession. Lee, 168 Ga. 554, 560 (148 S. E. 400).

Where confession was made by the accused under promise of the solicitor-general to carry over the case in order to enable the accused to raise money to pay his counsel and pay his fine, such confession was not voluntarily made, and a timely objection thereto should be sustained. Smith, 41 Ga. App. 341 (152 S. E. 916). 

Where the prosecutor offered to settle the case as an inducement, if the accused confessed and returned the stolen goods, such confession is not admissible. Byrd, 68 Ga. 661 (2); Frain, 40 Ga. 529 (3). 

The following has been held to be sufficient to exclude a confession: "It will be best for you to come on and tell the truth. The man wants his goods back. Come clear and tell the truth.' Morris, 33 Ga. App. 53 (125 S. E. 508). "I came to arrest you. You shan't be hurt if you own up." 

Earp, 55 Ga. 136. "If you know anything, it may be best for you to tell it." Green, 88 Ga. 516 (15 S. E. 10). "If you don't confess to me, you will have to confess to the 

Justice of the Peace." Johnson, 76 Ga. 76 (2). "If you are guilty, you better go to the prosecutor. They will be lighter on you." Smith, 125 Ga. 252 (54 S. E. 127).

Surrounding circumstances. The surroundings by which the declarant may be environed, or the acts of the parties, may be more ominous and more potential in inducing a confession than the use of threats. Moon, 12 Ga. App. 614 (4) (77 S. E. 1088); Irwin, 54 

Ga. 39; Burns, 61 Ga. 192 (2).

Religious influence, promise of secrecy, collateral benefit. Confessions made under promise of secrecy, or religious influence, or promise of collateral benefit,-admissible. Wilson, 19 Ga. App. 

759, 768 (92 S. E. 309); Woolfolk, 85 Ga. 69, 72 (12) (11 S. E. 814); 

Stafford, 55 Ga. 591, 592 (3). 

Artifice, trick, or deception. Statements of an incriminatory character, made by one accused of a crime, are admissible, if freely and voluntarily made, though they were elicited by trick, artifice or deception. Hudson, 153 Ga. 695 (3) (113 S. E. 519).

Question for the jury. Where a considerable time has elapsed between the offer of inducement to confess and the making of the 7745

CRIMINAL PROCEDURE 

173 confession, the question whether or not the confession was induced, or was free and voluntary, is for the jury. Elder, 143 Ga. 363 (2) (85 S. E. 97); Jackson, 172 Ga. 575 (158 S. E. 289); Cantrell, 141 

Ga. 98 (4) (80 S. E. 649).

Where the confession is prima facie admissible, whether it was freely and voluntarily given is a question for the jury. Cantrell, 141 Ga. 98 (4) (80 S. E. 649).

Preliminary hearing. The Court should conduct preliminary hearing to determine whether confession or admission was freely and voluntarily made, before admitting such evidence, where such preliminary hearing is demanded by the accused. Hawkins, 8 Ga. 

App. 705 (2) (70 S. E. 53).

Preliminary hearing as to the admissibility of confessions should not be held in the presence of the jury. The better practice is, and impartial justice demands, that the jury should retire while preliminary hearing is held. Hall, 65 Ga. 36 (1). (Contrary rule held: 

Holsenbake, 45 Ga. 43, 44 (2).)

When, after a proper preliminary examination as to their free and voluntary nature, confessions are adjudged competent and received in evidence, there is no room for any question touching the propriety of having conducted the preliminary examination in the presence of the jury. Fletcher, 90 Ga. 468 (1) (17 S. E. 100); 

Griner, 121 Ga. 614 (3) (49 S. E. 700).

Where the preliminary examination of witnesses offered by the State to show a confession, shows that the confession was freely and voluntarily made, without being induced by the slightest hope of benefit or remotest fear of injury, such evidence is prima facie admissible. Bradberry, 170 Ga. 859 (4) (154 S. E. 344).

Where, in the absence of the jury, the State makes out a prima facie case for admission or confession, the Court need not, before allowing it to go to the jury, hear the defendant's evidence tending to show coercion or improper inducement. Wilburn, 141 Ga. 

510 (5-d) (81 S. E. 444).

Where confessions are prima facie admissible, and the accused contends that they were not made freely and voluntarily, the burden of proof is on the defendant, to show that the confessions were improperly induced. Eberhart, 47 Ga. 598, 599 (7); Bradberry, 170 

Ga. 859 (4) (154 S. E. 344); Duren, 21 Ga. App. 524 (3) (94 S. E. 902).

The whole confession must be admitted. Where a witness for the State testified that the accused had admitted a crime, counsel

of the defendant is entitled to elicit on cross-examination all of the statements made by the accused in connection with that admission. He is entitled to a full and complete cross-examination. Richards, 152 Ga. 207 (4) (108 S. E. 800).

Where a confession is shown, it is error to admit part of the confession and exclude the balance. Where confession of matters harmful to the defendant is admitted, the whole confession should be given, including such statements as tend to explain the transaction. Peterson, 47 Ga. 524 (3). This rule applies, unless the matter to be shown is wholly immaterial and disconnected from the confession. Brown, 119 Ga. 572, 575 (46 S. E. 833).

Where incriminatory statements are testified to, and the witness refuses to answer some questions pertaining to the entire conversation, upon the ground that it may incriminate him, the whole conversation should be excluded. Young, 65 Ga. 525 (2).

Confession alone insufficient to convict. Confession alone, uncorroborated by other evidence, will not authorize conviction. Simmons, 18 Ga. App. 104 (3) (88 S. E. 904); Hart, 141 Ga. 672, 673 (5) (81 S. E. 1108).

The sufficiency of corroboration of a confession is for the jury. 

Hinson, 152 Ga. 243 (1-a) (109 S. E. 661); Peterson, 19 Ga. App. 

144 (91 S. E. 223).

Conviction of a crime may be sustained upon the free and voluntary confession, though the same be not otherwise corroborated than by proof of the corpus delicti. Chancey, 141 Ga. 54 (5) (80 S. E. 

287); Snow, 14 Ga. App. 489 (1) (81 S. E. 363); Walker, 26 Ga. 

App. 70 (1) (105 S. E. 717). Proof of corpus delicti either by direct or circumstantial evidence is a sufficient corroboration of a confession. Sutton, 17 Ga. App. 713, 714 (88 S. E. 122); Peterson, 19 Ga. App. 144 (91 S. E. 223).

A confession may be corroborated by the proof of the corpus delicti. But in no case can the corpus delicti be said to be established where both the identity of the dead body and the fact that the death was due to a criminal act are created solely from facts furnished by the confession sought to be corroborated. Clay, 176 

Ga. 403 (168 S. E. 289).

The corpus delicti need not be proved by evidence wholly independent of the confession. Wilburn, 141 Ga. 510, 513 (10) (81 

S. E. 444).

The corroboration of a confession need not show the guilt beyond a reasonable doubt. It is sufficient if it tends materially to cor-

CRIMINAL PROCEDURE 

175 roborate the confession and connect the defendant with the crime. 

Douglas, 6 Ga. App. 157, 158 (64 S. E. 490).

Two independent confessions, without corroborating circumstances, such as the corpus delicti, are insufficient to convict. Bines, 118 Ga. 320, 327 (45 S. E. 376).

In a homicide case the proof of the corpus delicti must not only show that a person has been killed, but must also identify the person shown to have been killed as the one whose death is the subject of inquiry. These elements of the corpus delicti must appear from some form of proof other than extrajudicial confessions or admissions alone; but if the defendant in his statement made on the trial of the case admits them, the State is not required to make further proof of them. Wall, 5 Ga. App. 305 (1) (63 S. E. 27).

Even if incriminatory admissions, supplemented by other circumstances, be equivalent to a confession, evidence that the accused confessed the commission of an offense would not be sufficient to authorize a conviction, unless all the facts essential to establish that the alleged offense was in fact committed are satisfactorily proved. Harvey, 8 Ga. App. 660 (1) (70 S. E. 141); Davenport, 12 

Ga. App. 102 (76 S. E. 756).

Failure to charge, that a confession, alone, uncorroborated by other evidence, will not justify a conviction,-is error, even in the absence of a request. Lucas, 110 Ga. 756, 757 (4) (36 S. E. 87).

Proof of possession of the stolen goods by the defendant is sufficient corroboration of a confession. McDuffie, 17 Ga. App. 342, 343 (3) (86 S. E. 821).

Evidence on the trial for larceny, that cotton was stolen, and that the basket in which it was stolen was later found where accused said he put it, is sufficient corroboration of a confession. 

Perdue, 24 Ga. App. 50 (99 S. E. 797).

Proof that the accused exhibited money to witness will not suffice to corroborate a confession that he killed the deceased for the purpose of robbery and took the money from his person, where there is no evidence that the deceased had in fact any money about his person at the time of the homicide. Langston, 151 Ga. 388 (a) (106 S. E. 903).

Confessions should be received with care. All confessions should be received with care and caution, on account of their transmission through one or more channels, with constant liability of mistakes. in the transmission as to what was said. Calvin, 118 Ga. 73, 74 (44

S. E. 848). The witness is liable to misunderstand the language of

the one making the confession. Minton, 99 Ga. 254 (3) (25 S. E. 626).

Where the State relies upon admission for conviction, and there is issue of fact whether the admissions were freely and voluntarily made, if the Court charges on the subject of admissions, it is error to fail to charge § 38-420, that all admissions should be scanned with care, and confessions of guilt should be received with great caution, even in the absence of request. Persons, 27 Ga. App. 

592 (3) (109 S. E. 533).

In the absence of special request to do so, the Court need not charge the jury that all admissions should be scanned with great care, and confessions should be received with great caution. Cantrell, 141 Ga. 98 (2) (80 S. E. 649); Cooper, 16 Ga. App. 539, 540 

Inculpatory and exculpatory statements. Where the defendant admits the perpetration of the crime, but, in connection with such admission, gives explanation justifying or excusing his commission of the offense, it is error for the trial judge to refuse a timely written request to charge that such admission, with such explanation, would not create a presumption that the accused was actuated by malice. Manning, 153 Ga. 184 (2) (111 S. E. 658).

A statement which admits the commission of an act, but which also gives a legal excuse or justification, is not a confession. Reed, 15 Ga. App. 435, 436 (2) (83 S. E. 674).

Statements made by the defendant that he killed the deceased because of certain facts, which, if true, furnish no legal excuse or justification therefor, amount to confessions. Thompson, 147 Ga. 745 (2) (95 S. E. 292). 

Where the defendant admits the killing but claims justification, the law of confession is not involved. Harris, 152 Ga. 193 (6) (108

S. E. 777). 

A charge in substance that when a killing is shown, the law presumes malice, and the burden is on the prisoner to justify or mitigate the homicide, is erroneous in a case where the proof of the homicide is derived through an admission of the defendant, which, itself presents matters of exculpation. Wall, 5 Ga. App. 305 (2), 306 (63 S. E. 27).

Exculpatory statements by the accused are inadmissible where they are not in immediate connection with the confession. Woolfolk, 85 Ga. 69, 72 (13) (11 S. E. 814).

Ordinarily the jury, in considering an admission which is partly

CRIMINAL PROCEDURE 

177 inculpatory and partly exculpatory, may believe it in part and disbelieve it in part; and this rule is especially true where the admission is made by the defendant in his unsworn statement on the trial. However, where the State must rely upon the defendant's admission alone for essential elements of its case, this rule does not apply to the extent that a verbal segregation of what the defendant has said be permitted. If the main fact is admitted with a qualifying exclusion of a necessary ingredient of the crime charged, the crime is not confessed. The qualification is a part of the admission, and both must be considered in interpreting the meaning of the statement. It would be manifestly unfair to hold a person criminally bound by a statement which admits the commission of an act and in the same breath legally justifies or excuses the same. 

Owens, 120 Ga. 296, 297, 299 (48 S. E. 21); Wall, 5 Ga. App. 305, 308 (63 S. E. 27).

Independent facts discovered by confession. Independent facts discovered in consequence of an incriminatory statement made by the prisoner are admissible in evidence against him, unless it appears that criminal violence was used in procuring such incriminatory statements, or making the discovery. And where such independent facts are admissible, so much of the prisoner's acts and declarations as are necessary to account for the discovery and explain the manner of it are admissible for that purpose. They count for nothing as incriminatory statements or confessions, if obtained under constraint, and as such are to be wholly disregarded. Goolsby, 133 Ga. 427 (1) (66 S. E. 159); Rusher, 94 Ga. 363 (1) (21 S. E. 593); 

Wilson, 19 Ga. App. 759, 768 (92 S. E. 309); Underwood, 13 Ga. 

App. 206, 212 (78 S. E. 1103).

Where, in a chain of evidence fixing unmistakable guilt on the accused, there is one link consisting of his own incriminatory admission leading to the discovery of other independent circumstantial evidence, the incriminatory admission, together with the circumstances, should go before the jury, even though the admission was induced by promise of immunity from prosecution. Garnett, 10 

Ga. App. 109 (3) (72 S. E. 951).

Admissions by silence. The sayings of other persons are admissible against a party, when made in his presence, and if it affirmatively appears that he assented to them by silence, or in some other way. Williamson, 29 Ga. App. 283 (1) (114 S. E. 919). It must affirmatively appear that the accused was present and must have

heard such inculpatory statements, before they are admissible. 

Jones, 65 Ga. 147 (2); Simmons, 115 Ga. 574 (41 S. E. 983).

The circumstances must require an answer, or denial, before such statements are admissible, and it must so appear affirmatively. 

Lumpkin, 125 Ga. 24 (53 S. E. 810).

It need not affirmatively, or positively, appear that the defendant heard the statement. Watson, 136 Ga. 236 (1), 238 (71 S. E. 122).

Where evidence is conflicting, whether the defendant heard the inculpatory statement made by another in his presence,-is for the jury. Moye, 66 Ga. 740 (2).

A statement made by the accused's wife, in his presence, and in the presence of others, is not admissible, unless the statement was such as required an answer, or denial. Bowen, 36 Ga. App. 666 (137 S. E. 793); Nunn, 143 Ga. 451 (2) (85 S. E. 346).

Ground of admission of the statement of third person in the presence of the accused is that the omission to controvert the statement affords basis for the inference of its truth. Such statement is admissible in evidence to show that it calls for an answer and to show the acquiescence of the accused. Thomas, 143 Ga. 268, 270 

While under arrest and confronted by another in the presence of the arresting officer, silence by the accused is as consistent with the theory that the accused prefers to exercise his right to await trial by proper tribunal as it is of consciousness of guilt. Johnson, 151 Ga. 21, 24 (105 S. E. 603).

Evidence as to declaration of a bystander accusing the defendant of the commission of the crime is admissible where the defendant hears it but fails to deny or explain such declaration. Thurman, 14 Ga. App. 543 (3) (81 S. E. 796); Gates, 20 Ga. App. 171, 172 (1) (92 S. E. 974). 1 Conspiracy. Acts and sayings of alleged co-conspirators, in attempting to carry out the terms of the alleged conspiracy, or made during the pendency of the criminal project-admissible. Baker, 17 Ga. App. 279 (1) (86 S. E. 530). See also: Accessories.

A confession of one joint offender or conspirator, made after the enterprise is ended, is admissible only against himself. § 38-414; 

Gray, 13 Ga. App. 374 (79 S. E. 223); Brandon, 169 Ga. 808 (1) (151 

S. E. 493); Gibbs, 144 Ga. 166 (2) (86 S. E. 543).

Evidence as to admissions of guilt involving the defendant, made by a co-defendant and co-conspirator after the termination of the

CRIMINAL PROCEDURE 

179 conspiracy, but in the presence of the accused, and stated by the accused, freely and voluntarily, to be true,-admissible. Gunter, 19 

Pleas of guilty of two defendants, jointly indicted with the accused, on trial of the accused, should not be admitted in evidence against the person on trial. Gray, 13 Ga. App. 374 (79 S. E. 223).

On the trial of the accessory, incriminatory admissions made by the principal may be admitted in evidence to show principal's guilt, but not against the accessory. Gullatt, 14 Ga. App. 53 (3) (80 S. 

E. 340).

The language of the Code "after the conspiracy is ended," necessarily makes admissible any statements made by any of the conspirators until the ultimate purpose of the conspiracy has been accomplished. Hence, where the killing is only an incident in carrying out a purpose to accomplish some further object, it would seem to follow from the wording of the statute, that where an enterprise has not ended, because the real purpose of the conspiracy has not been achieved prior to the completion of the enterprise, statements made even after such a killing and until the purpose of the conspiracy has fully been accomplished, would be admissible on the trial of any one of those engaged in the conspiracy. Rawlings, 163 Ga. 406, 421 (136 S. E. 448).

Declarations of one conspirator that he alone committed the crime are not admissible in favor of the other. Parks, 24 Ga. App. 

243, 244 (100 S. E. 724); Robison, 114 Ga. 445 (2) (39 S. E..862).

Testimony at former trial. What a witness voluntarily testified at a former trial of another, may be given in evidence against him. 

Burnett, 87 Ga. 622 (4) (13 S. E. 552).

Unsworn pleadings. Unsworn petition, plea or answer in a civil case is not admissible as confession. Farmer, 100 Ga. 41 (3) (28

S. E. 26). Where in such civil case the pleadings were signed by counsel, they are not admissible, unless it is shown that counsel was expressly authorized to sign them. (Id.) 

Testimony at coroner's inquest. Where the body of a man, apparently murdered, is found in the roadside, and two persons were arrested and placed in jail, charged with murder, and were subsequently taken thence in custody before the coroner's jury summoned to hold an inquest on the body, and, without being informed that they were not compelled to testify, were sworn and examined as witnesses, not on their own motion, but on that of the coroner or the jury, in regard to the homicide and their connection with

it, on a subsequent trial under an indictment charging them with murder, confessions or inculpatory statements elicited on their examination before the coroner's jury were not admissible against them. Adams, 129 Ga. 248 (58 S. E. 822). Under similar circumstances, same rule held, although the witness was not under arrest. 

Standifer, 24 Ga. App. 329 (2) (100 S. E. 775).

Charge. Failure to charge the law of confessions is not error in the absence of appropriate, timely, written request. Keen, 43 Ga. 

App. 331 (158 S. E. 611); Story, 145 Ga. 43 (2) (88 S. E. 548).

Proof of inculpatory statement does not authorize charge of the law of confessions. Easterling, 24 Ga. App. 424 (100 S. E. 727); 

Reed, 15 Ga. App. 435, 436 (2) (83 S. E. 674); Fletcher, 43 Ga. App. 

405 (159 S. E. 126).

Where there is evidence tending to show confession, it is not error to charge the law of confessions. Leverett, 23 Ga. App. 141 (2) (98 S. E. 115). But where there is no evidence of a confession, charging the law of confessions is a reversible error. Thomas, 143 

Ga. 268 (3) (84 S. E. 587); Chislon, 19 Ga. App. 607 (1) (91 S. E. 

893). Charge on confession is error where there is no confession but incriminatory admission only. Phillips, 27 Ga. App. 1 (2) (107 

S. E. 343); Beasley, 28 Ga. App. 564 (112 S. E. 168).

Burden of proof. Where in a criminal case a confession is shown to have been freely and voluntarily made, the burden is then on the defendant to show that the same was not so made. Bradberry, 170 Ga. 859 (4) (154 S. E. 344). 

f. ILLEGALLY OBTAINED EVIDENCE. 

Legal arrest. Where the arrest is legal, a search of the prisoner's person is legal, and evidence so obtained is admissible. Thompson, 4 Ga. App. 649, 652 (62 S. E. 99); Woolfolk, 81 Ga. 551, 552 (6) (8 S. E. 724).

Illegally obtained evidence. When admissible. Where evidence is incidentally disclosed by an unlawful search or seizure, it is not thereby necessarily rendered inadmissible; but where the sole object of the search and seizure was to obtain that very evidence, and the defendant was thus involuntarily compelled (in obedience to the will and act of another) to reveal the evidence of a crime, which he would not have disclosed but for the fact that his volition was nullified and supplanted by that of another, who enforced disclosure, the evidence so obtained should not be received against the accused on his trial. Wright, 9 Ga. App. 266 (2) (70 S. E. 1126).

CRIMINAL PROCEDURE 

181 Incriminating evidence taken from the person of the accused by the person arresting him illegally is nevertheless admissible. Calhoun, 144 Ga. 679 (1-b) (87 S. E. 893); Cooper, 14 Ga. App. 464 

The manner in which the evidence was obtained does not affect its probative value. Nowell, 18 Ga. App. 143 (3) (88 S. E. 909).

Where a defendant in a criminal case voluntarily exhibited a scar on his head to sustain his defense, there was no error in requiring him to allow it afterwards to be examined by a physician who was put on the stand in rebuttal. Gordon, 68 Ga. 814 (3).

Where two were indicted jointly, but tried separately, the defendant can not object to testimony against him, on the ground that it was obtained by illegal search and seizure of the other person jointly indicted with him. Jones, 4 Ga. App. 741 (62 S. E. 482).

A letter written by the prisoner while in jail, containing incriminating admissions, is admissible in evidence against him, although he gave the letter to the sheriff to mail, and the sheriff opened and kept it. Sanders, 113 Ga. 267 (1) (38 S. E. 841).

Evidence obtained by illegal search and seizure of a person under an unlawful arrest is not admissible against him, but evidence obtained by illegal search of the premises or property is admissible. 

Upon request to review and overrule this rule the Supreme Court adhered thereto, although the rule is different in Federal Courts. 

Lester, 155 Ga. 982 (4) (118 S. E. 674). 

Where the officer produced a pistol out of defendant's pocket, such evidence is admissible. Dozier, 107 Ga. 708 (1) (33 S. E. 

418); Springer, 121 Ga. 155 (2) (48 S. E. 907).

Where the defendant. though under illegal arrest, consents to be searched, evidence found by such search is admissible against him. 

Byrd, 10 Ga. App. 214 (2) (73 S. E. 34). 

When inadmissible. It is only when by unlawful search and seizure, under an illegal arrest, the defendant is compelled to furnish incriminating evidence that such evidence is not admissible. Smith, 3 Ga. App. 326 (2) (59 S. E. 934); Evans, 106 Ga. 519 (32 S. E. 659).

Evidence of guilt which the defendant, directly or indirectly, is compelled to disclose by unlawful search and seizure of his person under an illegal arrest, is not admissible. Jackson, 7 Ga. App. 414 (2) (66 S. E. 982); Hammock, 1 Ga. App. 126 (2) (58 S. E. 66).

But if the premises or belongings are searched by another, although without a vestige of authority, the evidence thus disclosed may be

used against the accused. The criterion is, who furnished or procured the evidence? Glover, 4 Ga. App. 455 (3) (61 S. E. 862).

Where an arresting officer, after making an illegal arrest, forcibly and violently, against his utmost resistance, took keys from defendant's pocket and by using such keys obtained evidence against him, the evidence was inadmissible. Underwood, 13 Ga. App. 206 (78 S. E. 1103).

Evidence that witness forcibly placed defendant's foot in certain tracks near the scene of the burglary, and that they were the same size, not admissible. A defendant can not be compelled to criminate himself by acts or words. Day, 63 Ga. 667 (2).

It is error to admit testimony of a certain witness for the State to the effect that the foot of the accused fitted certain tracks, the conformability of the defendant's foot to the tracks being material evidence in the case. The admission of this evidence violates the constitutional guaranty that no person shall be compelled to give testimony tending in any manner to criminate himself, unless under the circumstances the placing of the foot in the tracks by the defendant is voluntary; for, though no physical force is used in placing the foot in the track, where the defendant is at the time in custody of the sheriff and handcuffed and surrounded by companions of the sheriff, and the command from the sheriff, directing the prisoner to put his foot in the tracks, is a virtual coercion, it can not be said that his acts are voluntary. Elder, 143 Ga. 363 (1) (85 S. 

E. 97).

In order that the evidence be shown inadmissible on the ground that the accused was compelled to give evidence against himself, compulsion must be shown, as would rob the prisoner of volition. in the matter. Thompson, 4 Ga. App. 649 (3) (62 S. E. 99).

Burden of proof. Where it is claimed that the accused was compelled to furnish evidence against himself, the burden of showing that the arrest was legal is upon the State. Testimony of a witness that the arrest was under a warrant is insufficient to show that the arrest was lawful. Sherman, 2 Ga. App. 148 (1) (58 S. E. 393). 

g. PRISONER'S STATEMENT. 

General. In all criminal trials, the prisoner shall have the right to make to the Court and jury such statement in the case as he may deem proper in his defense. It shall not be under oath, and shall have such force only as the jury may think right to give it. They may believe it in preference to the sworn testimony in the case. 

The prisoner shall not be compelled to answer any questions on

CRIMINAL PROCEDURE 

183 cross-examination, should he think proper to decline to answer.

§ 38-415. 

Admission by statement.

Where the defendant made an admission of a fact in his statement, such admission is direct evidence, and the State need not prove such fact by any other evidence. 

Dumas, 62 Ga. 58, 59 (3).

Right to make a statement. The right of a defendant in a criminal. case, to make to the Court and jury such statement in the case as he may deem proper in his defense, should not be abridged in any case. Skinner, 13 Ga. App. 370 (2) (79 S. E. 177).

If the defendant sees fit to make no statement, he is acting within his rights, and such failure should not be considered for or against him. Stephens, 21 Ga. App. 151 (2) (94 S. E. 69).

Statement as evidence. The statement of the defendant is not evidence. Bragg, 15 Ga. App. 623 (4) (84 S. E. 82). It is not governed by rules controlling the admissibility of evidence. Fite, 16 Ga. App. 22 (1) (84 S. E. 485).

The statement of the defendant should not be curtailed either by ruling or by interruption, merely because the facts stated are irrelevant and do not present a valid defense in law. (Italics by the 

Court.) Fite, 16 Ga. App. 22 (1) (84 S. E. 485).

The statement of the accused can not lay the foundation for introducing evidence in his favor which would otherwise be inadmissible. Brooks, 150 Ga. 732 (3) (105 S. E. 362); Wiggins, 16 Ga. 

App. 477 (85 S. E. 674).

The Court may interrupt the defendant in his statement and instruct him to refrain from relating irrelevant matter. Vincent, 153 Ga. 278, 279 (4) (112 S. E. 120); Chance, 31 Ga. App. 543 (1) (121 S. E. 139); Bird, 26 Ga. App. 47, 49 (105 S. E. 456).

Long, rambling statement of irrelevant matter may be curtailed by the judge. Long, 118 Ga. 319 (4) (45 S. E. 416); Sutton, 2 Ga. 

App. 417, 418 (3) (58 S. E. 545).

Where counsel asked questions of the accused which were held by the Court out of order and illegal, the accused had nevertheless a right to incorporate in his statement matter so suggested by the questions asked. Walker, 116 Ga. 537, 540 (42 S. E. 787).

Restriction or interruption of defendant's statement because it presents facts, which, under the rules of evidence, are irrelevant and constitute in law no valid defense-improper. Richardson, 3 

Ga. App. 313 (2) (59 S. E. 916). But wholly immaterial matter is

not permissible. King, 9 Ga. App. 609 (71 S. E. 943); Montross, 72 

Ga. 261, 262 (4); Tiget, 110 Ga. 244, 245 (2) (34 S. E. 1023).

Accused as a witness. While the defendant, in a criminal case, may make to the jury a statement in his own behalf, not under oath, which may be received in whole or in part by the jury in preference to the sworn testimony, he is not a competent witness in the case, and can not be sworn as such. While he may be cross-examined, not under oath, if he consents thereto, an offer by his counsel to put him under oath and permit him to be cross-examined may be properly rejected by the Court. King, 24 Ga. App. 49 (1) (99 S. E. 784).

It is error for the Court to ask a prisoner questions during his statement or after he has finished. Hackney, 101 Ga. 512 (2) (28 

S. E. 1007); Robinson, 82 Ga. 535 (15) (9 S. E. 528).

Where the Court permitted counsel for the accused to ask questions of him, this did not entitle the State to cross-examine the prisoner, although such permission was given under condition that a cross-examination will be allowed. Walker, 116 Ga. 537 (1) (42 

S. E. 787).

Where the Court asked prisoner questions, his answering them is no waiver of his rights to be free of examination. Hackney, 101 

Ga. 512 (2) (28 S. E. 1007).

Where the accused has submitted to cross-examination, and the State cross-examined him, the Court is not bound to allow an examination by his own counsel. Lindsay, 138 Ga. 818, 819 (8) (76 S. 

E. 369).

Matter of permitting counsel to question defendant when making a statement rests within sound discretion of the Court. This discretion should be sparingly exercised. Whitley, 14 Ga. App. 577 (6) (81 S. E. 797).

Offer by counsel to have defendant cross-examined does not impose the duty upon the State to do so. King, 24 Ga. App. 49 (1) (99 S. E. 784).

Where counsel for the defendant desires to make a suggestion as to some matter omitted by the defendant in making his statement, he should make a request or motion addressed to the presiding judge in open court, asking permission to make the suggestion. 

Story, 145 Ga. 43 (1) (88 S. E. 548).

The Court may refuse to permit counsel for the accused to call his attention to certain facts omitted from his statement, or to ask any question of the accused. Clark, 43 Ga. App. 384 (2) (159 

S. E. 135).

CRIMINAL PROCEDURE 

185 Supplementary statements. The Court may refuse to allow the accused to make an additional statement. Clark, 43 Ga. App. 384 (2) (159 S. E. 135).

Second statement to the jury can not be made as a matter of right by the accused. It is within the discretion of the Court. 

Cason, 28 Ga. App. 550 (2) (112 S. E. 290).

Second statement is not allowed, as a matter of right, even where the State, after the first statement, has strengthened its case by additional evidence. Knox, 112 Ga. 373 (1) (37 S. E. 416); Jones, 12 Ga. App. 133 (2) (76 S. E. 1070).

It is no abuse of discretion to refuse to allow supplementary statement, although the State introduced evidence after the first statement was made, which was in rebuttal. Fairfield, 155 Ga. 

660 (4) (118 S. E. 395).

The Court may restrict defendant's supplementary statement to rebuttal only. Ray, 42 Ga. App. 420, 421 (156 S. E. 646).

Where the State introduces evidence of confession for the first time after the accused has made his statement, it is error to refuse to permit the accused to make supplementary statement in rebuttal of the alleged confession. Timmons, 13 Ga. App. 376 (79 S. 

E. 216).

After the defendant made his statement and rested his case, admission of evidence not in rebuttal of defendant's statement is a matter of sound discretion of the Court. Moore, 151 Ga. 648, 649 (4) (108 S. E. 47).

After both sides have closed, the Court may still permit the State to reopen and introduce witness in rebuttal of the prisoner's statement. Wilson, 80 Ga. 357 (2) (9 S. E. 1073).

Documentary or real evidence. Defendant may not read letters. to the jury in his statement. If he desires to corroborate his statement by documentary evidence, the writing should have been introduced in evidence in the usual and regular way. Allen, 150 Ga. 706 (3) (104 S. E. 369).

The attorney for the accused may not read to the jury a written statement prepared. Brown, 10 Ga. App. 50 (5) (72 S. E. 537).

The accused may not read or tender documents in his statement without proving that they are genuine. He may, however, state their substance. Woodard, 5 Ga. App. 447 (4) (63 S. E. 573); 

Gaston, 9 Ga. App. 824 (2) (72 S. E. 285).

The Court may refuse to allow defendant, while he is making a statement to the jury, to refresh his memory from newspaper

articles, or exhibit newspaper articles to the jury. Saunders, 172 

Ga. 770, 777, 778 (17) (158 S. E. 791); Theis, 45 Ga. App. 364 (164) 

S. E. 456).

The fact that the defendant in his statement identified certain articles will not entitle him to introduce them in evidence. Register, 10 Ga. App. 623 (3) (74 S. E. 429).

Failure to make a statement. Solicitor-general may not refer to the fact that the defendant has not made a statement. Yet, where such reference is made, the Court may, in the charge, make harmless, by proper admonition. Saffold, 11 Ga. App. 329 (4) (75 S. E. 

338); Tolbert, 12 Ga. App. 685 (4) (78 S. E. 131); Robinson, 82 

Ga. 535 (9) (9 S. E. 528); White, 43 Ga. App. 96 (3) (157 S. E. 919). 

Failure of the accused to make a statement to the Court and jury is ground for a new trial only where he was prevented from doing so by the Court. Dyson, 72 Ga. 206. 

Weight of statement.

There is no presumption of law one way or other respecting the truth of the prisoner's statement. Cornwall, 91 Ga. 277, 278 (5) (18 S. E. 154).

Defendant's statement need not be corroborated. Walker, 120 

Ga. 491 (1) (48 S. E. 184).

Where evidence and statement conflict, latter must yield to former. 

Brown, 60 Ga. 210, 212; O'Connor, 64 Ga. 125 (3).

It is the jury's prerogative to accept defendant's statement as a whole, reject it as a whole, or believe it in part. In the exercise of this discretion they are unlimited. French, 43 Ga. App. 97, 98 (5) (157 S. E. 902); Plemmons, 43 Ga. App. 344 (3) (158 S. E. 

630); Smallwood, 17 Ga. App. 516 (2) (87 S. E. 761).

The credibility of the defendant's statement is for the jury. 

Webb, 18 Ga. App. 44 (2) (88 S. E. 751).

Time of statement. The accused has a right to make his statement at any time after the State has rested, and before the case has gone to the jury. King, 99 Ga. 52 (2) (25 S. E. 613).

Statement in behalf of another. The accused has a right to make his statement in his own behalf only. Where the State has nol prossed the prosecution of one of several co-defendants, the Court may withdraw from the jury the statement made by that defendant. Williams, 107 Ga. 721, 722 (2) (33 S. E. 648). 

Argument of counsel. Making an unsworn statement in not introduction of such evidence as will deprive the accused of opening and closing. Farrow, 48 Ga. 30 (3); Seyden, 78 Ga. 105, 106 (4).

CRIMINAL PROCEDURE 

187 Though defendant need not make a statement whatever, insufficiency of his statement may nevertheless be considered by the jury. Clonts, 18 Ga. App. 707 (2) (90 S. E. 373).

While the State has no right to comment on defendant's failure to make a statement, counsel for the State may discuss any feature of the defendant's statement in argument to the jury. Frank, 141 

Ga. 243, 246 (13) (80 S. E. 1016); Coleman, 15 Ga. App. 338 (2) (83 S. E. 154).

Prejudicial remarks by the Court. Remarks of the judge to the accused: "If you are not through, go ahead if it takes the balance of the afternoon" are prejudicial and error. Cook, 40 Ga. App. 

125, 127 (2) (149 S. E. 79).

Prejudicial remarks made by the Court to the accused while making his statement are no grounds for a new trial. Mistrial should be moved for. Howard, 27 Ga. App. 313 (2) (108 S. E. 115).

Statement as subsequent evidence. Statement of the accused may be admitted in behalf of the State upon a subsequent trial. Morgan, 28 Ga. App. 358 (2) (111 S. E. 72).

Where the accused made a statement at the commitment trial, which was reduced to writing, parol evidence thereof is not admissible unless the writing is lost or destroyed. The presumption is that such statement has been reduced to writing. Leggett, 97 Ga. 

Testimony of joint defendant. Where several defendants are jointly on trial, the testimony of one of the joint defendants, received without objection by the State, and under oath, should be treated as evidence so far as it refers to the other defendants. 

Staten, 140 Ga. 110 (2) (78 S. E. 766).

Rebuttal. The State has a right to contradict the prisoner's statement by repeating the same testimony which was already submitted. 

McKinne, 81 Ga. 164, 165 (9 S. E. 1091).

Charge of the Court. It is a better practice to omit in the general charge any reference to the rule that the defendant may not be cross-examined as to his statement. However, generally such charge is not ground for a new trial. Cargile, 137 Ga. 775 (2) (74 S. E. 621).

Where the defendant made no statement in his behalf, it is error for the Court to charge the law on defendant's statement. Mason, 19 Ga. App. 623 (1) (91 S. E. 922). Contrary rule held: Stephens, 21 Ga. App. 151, 152 (2) (94 S. E. 69).
