Where the accused has made a statement, the Court should charge the rule of law touching such statement. Failure so to do is reversible error, even in the absence of a request, unless it appears from the facts in the case that no harm resulted to the defendant. 

Bryant, 23 Ga. App. 3 (1) (97 S. E. 271).

Court may charge the jury that if defendant failed to tell the truth in his statement he incurred no penalty by such failure. But it is better practice to confine the charge to the statute. Darden, 171 Ga. 160, 161 (5) (155 S. E. 38); Kirby, 43 Ga. App. 102 (6) (158 S. E. 438); Bates, 18 Ga. App. 718, 724 (4) (90 S. E. 481).

Where the accused made no statement, the Court need not charge the jury, without request, that they should not hold that against him. Grant, 42 Ga. App. 438 (2) (156 S. E. 642).

Where the Court properly charged the jury on the law of reasonable doubt, a doubt which springs from the evidence or want of evidence, it is not error to fail to charge that reasonable doubt may be created by defendant's statement as well as sworn testimony. 

Williams, 170 Ga. 886 (2) (154 S. E. 363).

It is error to use language in the charge calculated to impress the jury that they ought to be cautious in giving credit to the statement of the accused. Alexander, 114 Ga. 266 (1) (40 S. E. 231).

Charging the law of prisoner's statement by merely reading the appropriate section of the Code is sufficient. In fact it is the better practice. McDonald, 129 Ga. 452 (2) (59 S. E. 242).

It is error for the Court to charge the jury that if the evidence left their minds in doubt or did not satisfy them, they might consider the statement of the accused. Pease, 63 Ga. 631.

It is error to charge in a criminal case that the jury should not discredit sworn evidence in the case entirely, in order to believe defendant's statement in preference thereto. The credit to be given the statement is entirely within the province of the jury. Hayden, 69 Ga. 731, 732 (4).

It is error to charge the jury not to consider such part of defendant's statement as is based on hearsay. Stanley, 9 Ga. App. 

141 (3) (70 S. E. 894).

Where the Court omitted in his charge to the jury to instruct them upon the subject of the defendant's statement, but recalled the jury before they made their verdict and instructed them upon that subject, the omission to charge in the first instance is not ground for a new trial. Loyd, 150 Ga. 803, 804 (9) (105 S. E. 465).

Charge that it is for the jury to determine whether the defend-

CRIMINAL PROCEDURE 

189 ant is guilty under the evidence, is not error on the ground that it excluded from the jury's consideration the defendant's statement. 

O'Berry, 153 Ga. 880, 881 (8) (113 S. E. 203); Loyd, 26 Ga. App. 

259 (4) (106 S. E. 601).

Where the statement of the accused is in direct conflict with the testimony of the State's witnesses, and the statement, if true, demands his acquittal, it is reversible error for the Court, even in the absence of a written request, to fail to instruct the jury that they may believe the statement in preference to the sworn testimony in the case. Bullard, 31 Ga. App. 559 (1) (121 S. E. 130); 

Strickland, 41 Ga. App. 493 (1) (153 S. E. 432).

Charge that the jury may believe defendant's statement in preference to sworn testimony "provided they believe it to be true" is not erroneous. Gailliard, 16 Ga. App. 195 (2) (84 S. E. 837).

Theory of the case raised by defendant's statement. Issue raised by defendant's statement alone should be charged when properly requested. Dozier, 12 Ga. App. 722 (78 S. E. 203).

If the theory raised by defendant's statement alone is given in charge, it should fully cover it. Ragland, 111 Ga. 211 (1) (36 S. 

E. 682); Hart, 28 Ga. App. 258 (1) (110 S. E. 745).

It is not error for the Court to fail to charge on the theory of defense raised solely by defendant's statement, in the absence of written request. Hart, 28 Ga. App. 258 (1) (110 S. E. 745); McLendon, 172 Ga. 267 (2) (157 S. E. 475); Saunders, 43 Ga. App. 59, 60 (7) (158 S. E. 433).

While the Court is not required to charge on any theory of the defense arising solely from the statement of the accused, it is not error for the Court to charge on any principle which is pertinent under the statement of the accused. Taylor, 155 Ga. 785, 786 (1-a) (118 S. E. 675).

Where there is some evidence to corroborate defendant's statement, the Court should charge the jury on the theory thereof, even without a request. Reed, 15 Ga. App. 435 (1) (83 S. E. 674).

Where the theory raised solely by defendant's statement is the only defense in the case, it is error for the judge to fail to charge upon such theory, though not requested. Thornton, 18 Ga. App. 

744, 745 (90 S. E. 489). 

Erroneous ruling cured by statement. Where the Court erroneously admitted certain evidence, but subsequently the defendant in his statement to the jury, admitted the facts so proved, any

error the Court made in admitting the evidence became harmless. 

Vinson, 45 Ga. App. 219 (164 S. E. 208). 

17. ARGUMENT OF COUNSEL. 

§ 27-2201. 

Order of argument. After the testimony shall have been closed on both sides, the State's counsel shall open and conclude the argument to the jury, except that, if the defendant shall introduce no testimony, his counsel shall open and conclude after the testimony on the part of the State is closed. § 27-2201. Hargrove, 117 Ga. 706 (1) (45 S. E. 58); Freeney, 129 Ga. 759 (2) (59 S. E. 774).

The right to open and conclude is a substantial and valuable right. 

But it may be waived. Garrett, 21 Ga. App. 801, 802 (95 S. E. 301).

Testimony, as used in this section is synonymous with "evidence." 

Hargrove, 117 Ga. 706 (1), 708 (45 S. E. 58).

Where the accused introduced no evidence, his counsel is entitled to open and conclude, though he offered testimony which was rejected by the Court. Haywood, 14 Ga. App. 114 (1) (80 S. E. 213).

Where evidence has been introduced on behalf of the accused, and heard or examined by the jury, and counsel for the State therefore has had the opening and conclusion of the argument, counsel for the accused can not, as a matter of right, withdraw the evidence, and thus regain the right to open and conclude. Freeney, 129 Ga. 759, 760 (3) (59 S. E. 774); Daniels, 8 Ga. App. 469, 470 (4) (69 S. E. 588).

If the prisoner introduced evidence, no matter for what purpose, he loses his right to open and conclude. Downing, 66 Ga. 110 (1).

On a trial for murder the defendant is not entitled to open and conclude by admitting the homicide and offering to prove his justification. Mize, 135 Ga. 291, 292 (2) (69 S. E. 173).

Defendant, who, after the testimony of a witness for the prosecution has been concluded, and the witness has retired from the witness stand, calls, and examines the witness, is not entitled to open and conclude the argument, unless, for some reason addressed to the discretion of the Court, he has been granted permission to ask further questions in order to complete cross-examination of the witness. 

Dunn, 18 Ga. App. 95 (3) (89 S. E. 170).

Where the accused is entitled to the opening and closing, and after opening the State announced, without previously having given

CRIMINAL PROCEDURE 

191 notice to that effect, that it did not care to argue the case, defendant's counsel was entitled to complete his argument within the time limit provided by law, and the refusal thereof is reversible error. Porter, 6 Ga. App. 770 (1) (65 S. E. 814); Grant, 97 Ga. 789 

Where joint defendants are tried jointly, one introducing evidence, the other not, the State has the right to conclude. Hawkins, 13 Ga. 322, 324; Cruce, 59 Ga. 83, 84 (3).

The prisoner's statement is not such evidence as will lose him the right to open and close. Farrow, 48 Ga. 30; Seyden, 78 Ga. 105, 106 

Extension of time. 

Where counsel desires an extension of time for his argument, he must make a showing as provided by the Code. 

Otherwise the refusal of the Court to grant such extension is not reviewable. Bloodworth, 161 Ga. 332, 346 (131 S. E. 80).

Character of the accused. Unless the defendant puts his character in issue, the State's counsel may not comment thereon in his argument. Garrett, 21 Ga. App. 801, 802 (8) (95 S. E. 301).

Comment on statement of the accused. The solicitor-general is not permitted to refer to the fact that the defendant has not made a statement, but he may properly comment upon the fact that the accused has failed to adduce testimony in rebuttal of evidence introduced by the State, tending to show his guilt. Saffold, 11 Ga. App. 

While the failure of the defendant in a criminal case to make to the Court and jury a statement in his own behalf is not a matter which counsel for the State has the right to comment upon in his argument to the jury, yet, where the defendant does make a statement and therein fails to deny a material fact brought out in the testimony for the State, such an omission of the accused to make a denial is a legitimate subject matter of comment before the jury. 

The accused has the right to rest his case upon the evidence; and the fact that he does so can not be argued to his disadvantage; but if he undertakes to make a statement at all, counsel have a right to comment not only upon the statement as made, but upon any omission of the accused to deny a material fact brought against him in the testimony. Tolbert, 12 Ga. App. 685, 686 (4) (78 S. E. 131).

The effect of improper argument of counsel as to the failure of the accused to make a statement to the jury and the Court may be 

---

obviated by appropriate charge by the Court. White, 43 Ga. App.

Prejudicial argument of counsel. Counsel should not in their argument state prejudicial facts not appearing from the evidence, or not fairly deducible therefrom. Where, in a criminal case, a verdict of acquittal is authorized, and prejudicial argument is made by the State's attorney, it is error, requiring a new trial; to decline to rebuke counsel and instruct the jury to disregard the prejudicial remarks, when timely objection to such remark has been made. Martin, 10 Ga. App. 798 (74 S. E. 306); Cliett, 46 Ga. App. 315 (167 S. 

E. 610).

It is not error to refuse to declare a mistrial when the argument of counsel, though illogical, is not otherwise prejudicial to the rights of the opposing party. Sable, 14 Ga. App. 816, 817 (2) (82 S. E. 379). 

It is not only the privilege of the Court, but its solemn duty to interrupt counsel, when misstating the testimony to the jury. Grady, 11 Ga. 253.

The Court may interrupt the argument of counsel and correct a misstatement of the evidence, provided that, in ruling upon the question, neither the language nor the manner of the Court is prejudicial to the rights of the accused. Green, 43 Ga. 368 (4); Wilson, 58 Ga. 328; Wheeler, 4 Ga. App. 325 (3) (61 S. E. 409).

It is improper for the solicitor-general in the progress of the trial of a criminal case, in the presence of the jury, to make statements of facts bearing on the case, outside the evidence and calculated to injure the accused. Such statement should be met with prompt rebuke on the part of the presiding judge, should be clearly and distinctly excluded from the consideration of the jury; and in cases where it is not probable that the injury done can be eradicated, a mistrial should be granted on motion. Hunter, 133 Ga. 78, 79 (9) (65 S. E. 154).

Rebuke. Refusal to rebuke solicitor's unauthorized and prejudicial remarks, error. Cliett, 46 Ga. App. 315 (167 S. E. 610). 

See also: Mistrials.

Quotations. Counsel may quote from memory, or even read brief extracts of literary or historical matter to illustrate and make effective a discussion of the facts. But nothing which performs the office of evidence can be used in argument. Quattelbaum, 119 Ga. 433 (5) (46 S. E. 677).

193 

18. CHARGE OF THE JURY. 

§§ 81-1101 to 81-1104. 

Request for written charge. Where a written charge is requested, and the Court gives additional charge orally, it is a reversible error, although the additional charge was given upon the request of the jury for further instructions. Willis, 89 Ga. 188 (1) (15 S. E. 32).

The principal object in requiring the charge to be reduced to writing is to prevent dispute between the judge and counsel as to what was the charge. Walker, 8 Ga. App. 214, 217 (68 S. E. 873).

Where request is made to reduce the charge to writing, it is not a lawful reason for refusing the same, that the judge did not have time to write out the charge. If necessary, the judge should take a recess until he can write out the charge. Homer, 6 Ga. App. 667, 669 (65 S. E. 701).

After a written charge, the Court may not instruct the jury orally as to the form of the verdict. Burns, 89 Ga. 527 (3) (15 S. E. 748); 

Walker, 10 Ga. App. 85 (3) (72 S. E. 531).

In order that the oral statement of the Court may be ground for a new trial, it must appear that the oral statement was a part of the charge. Walker, 10 Ga. App. 85 (3) (72 S. E. 531); Dowling, 7 Ga. 

App. 613 (67 S. E. 697); Willis, 89 Ga. 188 (15 S. E. 32).

An oral charge of the Court is not equivalent to a written charge, although the stenographer was ordered to take it down. Brindle, 17 Ga. App. 741 (88 S. E. 460).

It is mandatory upon the judges of the respective courts to give written charges, when properly requested to do so. Brindle, 17 Ga. 

App. 741 (88 S. E. 460); Strickland, 6 Ga. App. 536 (1) (65 S. E. 300).

The rule as to written charges on request applies to every court where charges are allowed, and in all cases. Homer, 6 Ga. App. 667, 669 (65 S. E. 701).

Where the Court, instead of writing out the Code section applicable, made a notation: "Here the Court reads Named Section of the 

Code of 1910"-it was a reversible error, unless it is written so plainly that it is easily understood just what section or parts of section were read. Burns, 89 Ga. 527 (3) (15 S. E. 748); Walker, 8 Ga. 

App. 214 (2) (68 S. E. 873); Whitaker, 11 Ga. App. 208, 209 (11) (75 S. E. 258). But the judge, instead of copying into his charge the Code section which he submits to the jury may read to them verbatim from the Code itself, noting accurately in written charge the

sections so read. Burns, 89 Ga. 527 (3) (15 S. E. 748); Walton, 17 

Ga. App. 375 (86 S. E. 1072).

Requests for a written charge must be made before the argument begins. Ashley, 23 Ga. App. 93 (1) (98 S. E. 185); Sherwood, 33 

Ga. App. 49 (2) (125 S. E. 512).

Where a written charge is requested, a failure to file the same is a reversible error, unless the verdict was demanded by the evidence. 

Forrester, 6 Ga. App. 829 (65 S. E. 1063).

The charge written out should be filed, as soon as delivered, with the clerk of the court. (Italics by the Court.) Ashley-Price Lumber Co., 23 Ga. App. 93 (1) (98 S. E. 185). But see Sherwood, 33

Ga. App. 49 (2-a) (125 S. E. 512), where it was held that there is no requirement that the written charge be filed at once. If it is filed in time to make it accessible to all interested parties, the requirement of the statute is complied with.

Where it does not appear from the bill of exceptions that the written charge was filed below, the Court of Appeals will not order it sent up. Crawford, 19 Ga. App. 97 (1) (90 S. E. 1043); Perdue, 17 

Ga. App. 299 (1) (86 S. E. 661).

The manner of charging. The accused is not entitled to an elaboration of the abstract law upon a single phase of the case in the charge to such an extent as will give it undue prominence. Harrell, 121 Ga. 607 (5) (49 S. E. 703).

The prisoner is entitled to have his statement to the jury considered by them in its entirety, unaffected by any disparagement of it by the Court or intimation to the effect that it is in part unworthy of belief. Field, 126 Ga. 571, 572 (4) (55 S. E. 502); Roberson, 14 

Ga. App. 557 (81 S. E. 798).

The controlling issue in the case must not only be submitted to the jury with such appropriate instructions as will call their attention to the existence of such issue, but the charge of the Court must further contain such clear, apt, and definite exposition of the specific principles of law applicable to the case as will enable the jury to deal with the real issue in the case and to properly decide it. And this is true whether a specific request be made or not. Glaze, 2 Ga. 

App. 704 (2) (58 S. E. 1126).

When a judge undertakes to charge the law on any subject, he must charge all upon the subject that is material and applicable to the case. Harper, 17 Ga. App. 561 (1) (87 S. E. 808).

The Court should explain to the jury the meaning of technical terms used in the instructions, but a failure to do so will not gen-

CRIMINAL PROCEDURE 

195 erally require a new trial. Weldon, 21 Ga. App. 330, 331 (1-e) (94 

S. E. 326); Pickens, 132 Ga. 46, 47 (63 S. E. 783).

A correct statement of law embraced in a charge to the jury is not erroneous because the Court failed in the same connection to give to the jury other appropriate instructions. Woodall, 7 Ga. App. 

245, 246 (66 S. E. 619); Crone, 22 Ga. App. 636 (1) (97 S. E. 83); 

Powers, 138 Ga. 624 (4) (75 S. E. 651).

The charge should not be misleading. Holland, 3 Ga. App. 465, 466 (5) (60 S. E. 205); Manson, 14 Ga. App. 837 (2) (82 S. E. 763).

It is the duty of the trial judge in a criminal case to state the contentions of both the State and the defendant. Wilensky, 15 Ga. 

App. 360 (2) (83 S. E. 276).

Whenever the judge is not required, without appropriate and timely written request, to state the theory of the defense, still, when he undertakes to do so, he must state it correctly. Key, 21 Ga. App. 

300 (94 S. E. 283).

While it is the duty of the Court, without request, to present the particular defense upon which the defendant in a criminal case relies, it is not necessary, in the absence of a request, to refer specifically to the particular testimony upon which the defense is based, or to inform the jury of the defendant's specific contentions. Weldon, 21 Ga. App. 330 (1-a) (94 S. E. 326); Groves, 8 Ga. App. 690, 691 (2) (70 S. E. 93).

The Court in his instructions to the jury should be careful to guard against using abstract legal quotations and sententious judicial utterances in such manner as to make them misleading. Holland, 3 Ga. App. 465, 466 (5) (60 S. E. 205).

Every part of the charge of the Court must be construed in the light of the whole. Williams, 125 Ga. 265 (54 S. E. 166); Suple, 133 

Ga. 601 (66 S. E. 919); Ford, 9 Ga. App. 851, 853 (72 S. E. 442); 

Mixon, 15 Ga. App. 252, 253 (3) (82 S. E. 935).

The judge should not give a charge which is argumentative. 

Johnson, 148 Ga. 546, 547 (4) (97 S. E. 515).

A charge that the credibility of a witness is a matter solely for the jury, but that the jury should not disregard the testimony of a witness simply because he is a colored man, that it is possible for a person of a colored race to tell the truth as anyone else, and it is not against his credibility that he is a colored man, not argumentative. 

Cooley, 22 Ga. App. 263, 264 (2) (95 S. E. 871).

The tone of voice or emphasis of the trial judge in instructing the jury is not reviewable. Williams, 170 Ga. 886 (3) (154 S. E. 363).

Purpose of the charge. The office of a charge by the Court is to give to the jury such instruction touching the rules of law pertinent to the issue involved in the pending trial, as will enable them to intelligently apply thereto the evidence submitted, and from the two constituents, law and facts, make a verdict. Nelson, 124 Ga. 8, 9 (52 S. E. 20).

Inappropriate subjects. Rules of evidence, especially addressed to the discretion of the Court, are not appropriate subject matter of instructions to the jury. Harris, 2 Ga. App. 406 (2) (58 S. E. 669).

Metaphor, epigram and unique felicities of expression are not usually desirable in charge. Plainness, clearness, and the proper statement of the law relevant to the issues in the case in hand are rather to be sought. Leonard, 133 Ga. 435, 437 (66 S. E. 251).

In charging the jury in a criminal case, a charge that invokes any authority other than the law is inappropriate. It is error to charge the jury in such manner as would propose the Gospel as criterion. 

Braxley, 17 Ga. App. 196, 198 (10) (86 S. E. 425).

A language which would be appropriate in a headnote, headline, or in an opinion by a reviewing court may be improper when embodied in a charge to the jury. Smalls, 6 Ga. App. 502 (1) (65 S. 

E. 295); Mixon, 123 Ga. 581 (5) (51 S. E. 580); Leonard, 133 Ga. 

435 (3) (66 S. E. 251).

Charge without request. The Court, whether requested or not, should give to the jury appropriate instructions on every substantial issue in the case presented by the evidence, and a failure to do so is a cause for a new trial. The controlling issues of the case should be charged, even though not requested. Dorsey, 126 Ga. 633 (55 S. E. 479); Walker, 122 Ga. 747 (2) (50 S. E. 994); Holland, 17 

Ga. App. 311 (85 S. F. 739); McLendon, 14 Ga. App. 737 (4) (82 S. 

E. 317).

A failure of the Court to give in charge the law as to the weight of a confession of guilt, without timely written request is no ground for a new trial. Scarboro, 24 Ga. App. 27 (6) (99 S. E. 637); Mitchell, 24 Ga. App. 135 (1) (99 S. E. 889).

The Court need not give in charge the law as to the weight of evidence of good character, without timely, appropriate and written request. Scarboro, 24 Ga. App. 27 (6) (99 S. E. 637).

Where there is only one defense on which the party relies, a failure to instruct the jury as to the evidence supporting the defense, so specifically that the jury will not only be required to pass upon it, but will be enabled to do so intelligently, under pertinent rules of

CRIMINAL PROCEDURE 

197 law and evidence, practically withdraws that defense, and to that extent prejudices the defendant's right to a fair and impartial trial. 

Thompson, 16 Ga. App. 832, 833 (4) (84 S. E. 591).

Where one defense is mainly relied upon, and evidence is introduced to sustain it, it is a reversible error to omit such defense from the charge, even without a request. (Italics by the Court.) Reed, 15 

Ga. App. 435 (83 S. E. 674).

The failure to give in charge to the jury instructions not demanded by the evidence is no cause for a new trial, unless requested by appropriate, timely, written request. Cooper, 119 Ga. 752 (3) 

The trial judge is not obliged to charge, in the absence of a timely, written request, as to any collateral matter. Patterson, 134 

Ga. 264, 267 (67 S. E. 816); Watson, 136 Ga. 236, 240 (71 S. E. 122).

While it is the duty of the Court without request to present the particular defense upon which the defendant in a criminal case relies, it is not necessary, in the absence of a request, to refer specifically to the particular testimony upon which the defense is based, or to inform the jury of the defendant's specific contentions. 

Groves, 8 Ga. App. 690, 691 (2) (70 S. E. 93); Weldon, 21 Ga. App. 

Where there is some evidence to show the existence of a certain state of facts, it is not error for the Court to charge the jury in reference thereto simply because the great preponderance of evidence tends to show that the supposed state of facts did not in truth exist. 

Lyles, 130 Ga. 294, 295 (8) (60 S. E. 578).

The general rule is that instructions by the Court to the jury must be warranted by the evidence. A charge without evidence to support it is erroneous. Therefore, it is proper to refuse a request to charge a principle of law not applicable to the evidence. Stephens, 139 Ga. 594 (4) (77 S. E. 875); Harris, 142 Ga. 627, 629 (83 S. E. 

514); Curry, 17 Ga. App. 377, 378 (7) (87 S. E. 685).

Where the accused in a criminal case exercises his right to make a statement to the jury, it is the duty of the presiding judge to instruct the jury substantially in the terms of the statute touching the prisoner's statement. Where, however, the statement neither admits nor denies guilt, and the evidence for the State is uncontroverted, the omission of such charge is not reversible error. McLane, 20 Ga. 

App. 825 (1) (93 S. E. 558).

Omission to charge the jury that they may believe the defendant's statement in preference to the sworn testimony is reversible error. 

Fields, 2 Ga. App. 41 (4) (58 S. E. 327).

The failure to charge a theory of the case not presented in the evidence, but only in the statement of the accused, is not a ground for a new trial, in the absence of timely, appropriate, written request. Lampkin, 145 Ga. 40 (6) (88 S. E. 563).

Where the theory raised solely by the defendant's statement is the only defense in the case, it is error for the judge to fail to charge upon such theory, though not requested. Thornton, 18 Ga. App. 

744, 745 (90 S. E. 489).

In the absence of a timely and appropriate request, the failure of the Court to give instructions applicable to isolated facts and circumstances relied upon by a party to sustain his contentions is not error. Partee, 19 Ga. App. 752, 753 (5) (92 S. E. 306).

In the courts of this State, the juries, and not the judges, sum up the evidence. The judge in his charge to the jury should refer to the evidence only so far as is necessary to present the leading issue in the case, leaving the minor contentions to the jury. Nelson, 124 

Ga. 8, 9 (52 S. E. 20).

Request to charge. Where the general charge covers substantially all of the issues with sufficient fullness, and fuller and additional instructions are desired, they should be requested as provided by law. Hollis, 13 Ga. App. 307 (2) (79 S. E. 85); Dent, 14 

Ga. App. 270 (2) (79 S. E. 85); Jones, 15 Ga. App. 641 (2) (83 S. E. 

1099); Conley, 21 Ga. App. 134 (2) (94 S. E. 261); Mobley, 41 Ga. 

App. 379 (2) (153 S. E. 202).

In order to consider a request to charge, it must appear that it was presented in writing, and also that it was tendered to the Court before the jury retired to consider of the verdict. Johnson, 21 Ga. 

App. 497 (6) (94 S. E. 630); Stephens, 22 Ga. App. 123 (2) (95 S. E. 

537); McLeod, 22 Ga. App. 241 (6) (95 S. E. 934); Waller, 23 Ga. 

App. 156, 157 (97 S. E. 876).

Refusal to charge matter requested orally is no error. Richardson, 18 Ga. App. 755 (2) (90 S. E. 487).

It must appear that the written request was presented to the Court before the jury retired to consider their verdict. Brown, 24 

Ga. App. 268 (3) (100 S. E. 452); Macon, 24 Ga. App. 337 (1) (100 

S. E. 785).

Where counsel desires a modification of the charge already given, he should make a request in writing. Malone, 77 Ga. 767 (2-a).

CRIMINAL PROCEDURE 

199 A request to charge may be made at any time before the jury retires for the consideration of the cause. Brooks, 96 Ga. 353 (4) (23 

S. E. 413).

The rule is well settled that the request to charge must be presented in writing, and that an oral request can not be considered. 

Greene, 11 Ga. App. 257 (2) (74 S. E. 1101); Woods, 101 Ga. 526 (2) (28 S. E. 970). The fact that the judge has been in the habit in the past to consider oral requests to charge is immaterial. Campbell, 124 Ga. 432 (4) (52 S. E. 914).

Where the general charge covered the issue presented in the written request either literally or in substance, it is not error to refuse the written request. Davis, 153 Ga. 669, 677 (13) (113 S. E. 11); 

Danzley, 25 Ga. App. 170 (3) (102 S. E. 915).

When error to refuse a written request. Where the requests to charge were directed to the gravamen of the offense charged, the failure to give them as requested, or the substance thereof, is ground for a new trial. Formby, 14 Ga. App. 596 (4) (81 S. E. 799).

The law assumes that injury is done to the defendant where appropriate, timely and written request is refused. Terry, 17 Ga. 204 (2). 

Requested charge must be charged at least in substance. It is not enough if by inference it may be covered by some other charge, unless the inference is plain and noticeable. Wood, 48 Ga. 192, 193.

A refusal of an appropriate request in a close and doubtful case is cause for a new trial. Roberts, 114 Ga. 450 (1) (40 S. E. 297).

When not error to refuse a written request. A written request to charge must be wholly correct. Loeb, 6 Ga. App. 23 (3) (64 S. E. 

338); Wall, 126 Ga. 86 (54 S. E. 815).

A refusal to give a written request to charge is not error unless the charge requested is itself an accurate statement of the law of the subject. Moody, 1 Ga. App. 772, 773 (3) (58 S. E. 262).

Where the request to charge is not strictly accurate in its term, the Court may refuse it, and correctly charge the legal principle involved. Hunter, 133 Ga. 78 (2) (65 S. E. 154).

Request to charge matter not pertinent should be refused. Davis, 153 Ga. 669, 679 (15) (113 S. E. 11).

Argumentative matter or matter containing an expression of opinion should not be charged, though requested. Davis, 153 Ga. 669, 679 (17) (18) (19) (113 S. E. 110).

Where there are several written requests to charge the jury, each

involving the same principle, giving one is sufficient. Hammack, 52 

Ga. 397, 398 (3).

A request must be a legal, appropriate and correct statement of the law and applicable to the case. Green, 124 Ga. 343, 344 (8) (52 

S. E. 431); Johnson, 59 Ga. 142 (2).

A request to charge the jury, the whole of which is not pertinent and legal, should be denied. Pool, 87 Ga. 526, 527 (3) (13 S. E. 556).

Where several requests for instructions are made en bloc and by reference to Code sections only, and some of these were not appropriate or adjusted to the evidence, they may be refused, nor could they be properly treated as written requests for definite instructions. 

Conley, 21 Ga. App. 134, 135 (6) (94 S. E. 261).

It is not error to refuse a request to charge a series of propositions presented en bloc, where some of the instructions were not sound, or inapplicable to the case. Woodard, 18 Ga. App. 59 (2) (88 S. E. 

825); May, 24 Ga. App. 379, 380 (10) (100 S. E. 797).

The requested instructions need not be given in the identical language of the written request, if the matter and principle embraced therein is correctly and amply presented in the charge of the Court. 

Napper, 123 Ga. 571 (2) (51 S. E. 592).

Misleading, verbose, confusing and prolix requests should not be granted. Brinkley, 58 Ga. 296 (2). 

Erroneous request granted. Where the defendant requested an erroneous charge, he can not complain thereof after conviction. 

Coleman, 141 Ga. 737 (4) (82 S. E. 227); Coleman, 141 Ga. 731, 732 (4) (82 S. E. 228); Meyers, 169 Ga. 468 (3) (151 S. E. 34); Norris, 40 Ga. App. 232 (149 S. E. 158).

The judge may add to requested charge. The Court may make written addition to the request of counsel and read them both. 

Jones, 63 Ga. 456 (2).

Where the judge gives to the jury the charge as requested in writing, he may add comments that are pertinent and correct. Waller, 23 Ga. App. 156 (1) (97 S. E. 876); Brantley, 28 Ga. App. 536 (1) (112 S. E. 170). 

How a requested charge should be given. Where a request to charge is submitted in writing, the charge should be so worded as to make it appear that it is the Court's charge to the jury and the law of the case. Blandon, 6 Ga. App. 782 (3) (65 S. E. 842).

It is not a reversible error for the Court to state to the jury that the charge is given upon request by the defendant, although the bet- 11

CRIMINAL PROCEDURE 

201 ter practice would be to omit any reference to the fact that such charge has been requested. Hamilton, 129 Ga. 747 (1) (59 S. E. 

803); Jordan, 14 Ga. App. 429 (1) (81 S. E. 359).

While it is not a good practice for the Court to inform the jury that the charge is given upon request, it is not ground for a new trial. Hamilton, 129 Ga. 747 (1) (59 S. E. 803). But see Blandon, 6 Ga. App. 782 (3) (65 S. E. 842) where a contrary rule was held.

In giving a 'requested charge, it is sufficient if the Court reads the requested instruction and tells the jury that it is given in charge or that it is the law. Brantley, 28 Ga. App. 536, 537 (2) (112 S. E. 170).

Written form of verdict. The Court may prepare a written form of verdict, provided that the correct form of each verdict is submitted to the jury, which they may lawfully return, and in such manner that it could not have influenced the jury. Park, 126 Ga. 575 

Expression of opinion. The provision of the Code declaring that it is error for the judge, in his charge to the jury, to express or intimate an opinion as to what has or has not been proved, is mandatory, and a charge which discloses the opinion of the judge on the issue of fact can not be treated as harmless. Henderson, 14 Ga. 

App. 672, 674 (82 S. E. 61).

A charge containing an expression of opinion on the facts proved is ground for a new trial. Pitts, 15 Ga. App. 436, 437 (2) (83 S. E. 

673); Darby, 16 Ga. App. 171 (3) (84 S. E. 724); Suddeth, 112 Ga. 

407 (3) (37 S. E. 747). It is even error to violate the spirit of this section. Cook, 40 Ga. App. 125, 126 (149 S. E. 79).

There is a difference between telling the jury that a thing has or has not been testified to and telling them that such a thing has or has not been proved. Fair, 171 Ga. 112 (155 S. E. 329).

Stating the contention of the parties, supported by the evidence, is not an expression of opinion. Hawkins, 141 Ga. 212, 213 (6) (80 

S. E. 711); Linder, 17 Ga. App. 310 (1) (89 S. E. 741).

Stating an admitted fact does not constitute an expression or intimation of opinion. Swain, 162 Ga. 777, 789 (135 S. E. 187).

Where there is no dispute about a fact in evidence, the judge may state so. McCloud, 166 Ga. 436, 437 (3), 444 (143 S. E. 558); 

Thomas, 27 Ga. App. 38 (3) (107 S. E. 418).

Where there is nothing in the evidence or the defendant's statement to dispute the fact that a crime was committed, and the defense is that the accused did not participate in it, the judge may as-

sume that the crime was in fact committed, without violating the rule against expressing an opinion. Pruitt, 36 Ga. App. 736 (1) (138 S. E. 251). 

To assume that an important fact in the case has been admitted, and to so instruct the jury, where no such admission was made, is a reversible error. Duke, 43 Ga. App. 428 (158 S. E. 919).

On a trial for perjury (or false swearing) it is error to charge the jury that a lawful oath or affirmation was administered to the accused; that said statement alleged in the indictment was material to the issue. Pope, 43 Ga. App. 175, 176 (3) (158 S. E. 350).

Using the word "crime" by referring to homicide is no error on the ground that by so using it the judge expressed an opinion,where otherwise the law is correctly stated. Wilson, 152 Ga. 337, 

A charge that flight unexplained is a circumstance pointing to defendant's guilt is an unauthorized expression of opinion. Kettles, 145 Ga. 6 (3) (88 S. E. 197).

Assuming in a charge to the jury that certain facts were admitted, where no such admissions were made, is a reversible error. Cooper, 2 Ga. App. 730 (2) (59 S. E. 20).

It is error to charge that the accused has attempted to prove an alibi. Kimbrough, 101 Ga. 583 (2) (29 S. E. 39).

A statement of the Court in the hearing of the jury that he would direct a verdict of guilty if the accused did not introduce evidenceis reversible error, however conclusively the evidence establishes the guilt of the accused. Barge, 3 Ga. App. 20 (59 S. E. 192).

The trial judge may state, in colloquy with counsel in the case, whether or not a certain witness has been on the stand, or give his recollection as to whether or not the witness testified to some particular fact. The judge must say, when there is a dispute among counsel, what the witness said on the stand, but must not express an opinion as to the truth of the testimony. Stapleton, 19 Ga. App. 

36, 38 (11) (90 S. E. 1029).

The trial judge should not, in the hearing of the jury, make any remark tending to compliment or disparage a witness. Cole, 6 Ga. App. 798 (1) (65 S. E. 839). 

Reprimanding a witness by the judge for the violation of the rules. of procedure and disobedience of instructions is no ground for a new trial where the jury is instructed not to be influenced thereby. 

York, 42 Ga. App. 453, 466 (156 S. E. 733).

Whether the judge, by the language used in his charge, has vio-

CRIMINAL PROCEDURE 

203 lated the provisions of the Code by intimating or expressing an opinion as to what has or has not been proved, will be determined in the light of the entire context. Weldon, 21 Ga. App. 330, 331 (1-g) (94 

S. E. 326); Washington, 24 Ga. App. 65, 66 (4) (100 S. E. 31).

The Court may call to the jury's attention the gravity of the charge, where an expression of opinion is carefully avoided. Lyles, 130 Ga. 294 (5) (60 S. E. 578); Weldon, 21 Ga. App. 330, 331 (1-f) (94 S. E. 326).

When expression of opinion is no error. The rule against expression of opinion does not refer to statements made by the judge to the grand jurors, in the presence of the petit jurors. Long, 25 Ga. 

App. 22 (1-a) (102 S. E. 359).

A statement by the Court that a letter offered, which was entirely irrelevant, had no probative value, is not an unlawful expression of an opinion by the Court. Tanner, 163 Ga. 121, 122, 129 (135 S. 

E. 917).

An expression or intimation of opinion by the Court, when not flagrant, is not a violation of the law, where made during a discussion with counsel as to the admissibility of some testimony, or merits of a motion, or in explaining his ruling, or similar matters, during the progress of the trial. York, 42 Ga. App. 453, 457 (21) (156 S. 

E. 733).

Where an objection is made to the evidence offered, the judge has a right, if he deems proper, to give the reason for his decision, and the objection; and such reason, so given, if pertinent to the objection made, does not constitute an expression of opinion. Reed, 163 

Ga. 206, 213 (135 S. E. 748); Brown, 40 Ga. App. 546 (1) (150 S. E. 460).

The judge may properly admonish the jury as to the propriety and importance of agreeing on a verdict, and urge them to agree upon a verdict consistent with their consciences, care being taken not to suggest what verdict is proper, or to give instructions having a tendency to coerce the jury into agreeing upon a verdict. Yancy, 173 Ga. 685 (5-b) (160 S. E. 867).

Where a particular act is established by uncontradicted evidence, it is not error for the judge to assume or intimate that the fact has been proved. Denmark, 44 Ga. App. 157 (2-c) (161 S. E. 286).

A new trial will not be granted because the judge, after a verdict has been returned, and before passing sentence, stated from the bench that he thought the verdict was "eminently correct." Such expression did not disqualify the judge from passing upon defend-

ant's motion for a new trial. Plummer, 27 Ga. App. 185 (2) (108 

S. E. 128); Jackson, 15 Ga. App. 179 (2) (82 S. E. 771).

Expression of an opinion on the merits of the case, after verdict. and while imposing the sentence, is no error. Gray, 6 Ga. App. 428 

An expression of an opinion in pronouncing a sentence is not ground for a new trial, though the jury was subsequently polled, recharged, sent back, and again returned a verdict of guilty. Battise, 124 Ga. 866 (1) (53 S. E. 678).

Where judge interrogates witnesses. It is not only the privilege but also the duty of the Court, to propound such questions to the witness as will tend to elicit the truth, provided that the manner and the form of the questions do not convey any intimation of an opinion. Nelms, 18 Ga. App. 92 (3) (88 S. E. 917); Hays, 16 Ga. 

App. 20, 21 (6) (84 S. E. 497); Cox, 13 Ga. App. 687 (1) (79 S. E. 

909); Murphy, 13 Ga. App. 431 (79 S. E. 228).

Where the Court asked the witness a pertinent question, without intimating or expressing an opinion, the fact that the answer was detrimental to the accused, was no ground for a new trial. King, 22 Ga. App. 641 (1) (97 S. E. 81).

The utmost caution should be used by the judge to avoid impressing the jury by the examination, and when the questions suggest to the jury the inference that the Court entertains an opinion unfavorable to the innocence of the accused, the effect may be as prejudicial as the direct expression of an opinion. Nobles, 13 Ga. App. 710 (1) (79 S. E. 861); Cox, 13 Ga. App. 687 (1) (79 S. E. 909).

It is almost an intellectual impossibility for a judge to engage in examination of a witness on vital questions of the case on trial, without in some manner and to some extent indicating his own opinion. 

Every practitioner knows how eagerly alert jurors are to every utterance on the bench, and how sensitive is the mind of the juror to the slightest judicial expression. Therefore, while the trial judge has the right to ask questions of the witnesses whenever necessary to bring out the truth of a case, it is not his duty to do so; and, in exercising the right he should be careful not to intimate any opinion. upon the facts, or use any expression calculated to prejudice the rights of either party. Spivey, 38 Ga. App. 213, 216 (143 S. E. 450).

Remedy where Court expresses an opinion. Mistrial is the proper remedy where the Court expressed an opinion. In the absence of such motion, the error can not be urged on a motion for a new trial. 

Williams, 42 Ga. App. 225 (3) (155 S. E. 511); Gilbert, 27 Ga. App.

CRIMINAL PROCEDURE 

205 

604 (4) (109 S. E. 697); Durham, 28 Ga. App. 464 (1) (111 S. E. 

701); Adams, 171 Ga. 90, 91, 92 (8) (154 S. E. 700).

Where the judge makes prejudicial remarks to counsel in the hearing of the jury, counsel should either move for a postponement, in order that other jurors may be impaneled, or, if the jurors have actually been selected and impaneled to try the particular case, motion should be made to have a mistrial declared. Rogers, 18 Ga. 

App. 332 (1) (89 S. E. 460); Stapleton, 19 Ga. App. 36, 38 (13) (90 

S. E. 1029); Waldermar, 21 Ga. App. 504 (1) (94 S. E. 624); Grigg, 22 Ga. App. 637 (2) (96 S. E. 1049).

Where no motion for mistrial was made on account of prejudicial remarks by the Court, the Court of Appeals has nothing to pass upon. McCarty, 23 Ga. App. 79 (4) (97 S. E. 446).

Curing error in charge. Where the Court erroneously instructs the jury, and later specially calls their attention to the error, correcting the same, the original error is cured. Dotson, 136 Ga. 243 (71 S. E. 164). 

Erroneous charge; correct verdict. If the trial judge should erroneously charge the jury as to the law, and the jury should nevertheless find the correct verdict, the verdict will stand. In other words, the validity of the verdict is to be tested, not by the law as given in charge, but by the law as it is. Spence, 7 Ga. App. 825, 827 (68 

S. E. 443). 

Reviewing erroneous charge. Where only part of the charge is sent up to the reviewing court by bill of exceptions, and such part is found erroneous, it will be presumed that the erroneous instruction has been corrected in other parts of the charge. Mixon, 15 Ga. 

App. 252 (3) (82 S. E. 935).

Recharge. The judge may recall the jury and give additional charge. Davis, 122 Ga. 564 (50 S. E. 376).

The judge may recall the jury of his own motion, and over the objection of either party, and withdraw the instructions erroneously given, or give additional instruction erroneously omitted. Patterson, 122 Ga. 587 (1) (50 S. E. 489).

The Court may recall the jury where they have been out for a considerable length of time, and warn them that mistrials are a serious matter and in many ways hinder justice. Yancy, 173 Ga. 

685, 686 (5-c) (160 S. E. 867).

Where the jury requests a recharge, the Court need not charge again the whole law of the case. It is sufficient if charge is given on

the point requested by the jury. O'Shields, 55 Ga. 696, 697 (4); 

Kimberly, 4 Ga. App. 852, 853 (4) (62 S. E. 571).

Where the jury requests a recharge on any point, it is the duty of the Court to do so, and the consent of the accused is unnecessary. 

Phelps, 75 Ga. 571 (4).

Where the Court covers a pertinent issue on the recharge upon which he failed to instruct the jury in his original charge, with or without request to do so, the original error is cured. Wallace, 126 Ga. 749 (1) (55 S. E. 1042). 

The failure to give an additional charge to the jury can not be taken advantage of by exception to the correct charge given. 

Booker, 16 Ga. App. 280 (3) (85 S. E. 255).

The absence of the accused during the recharge is no ground for a new trial, unless the absence was caused by an act of the Court. 

Davis, 122 Ga. 564 (3) (50 S. E. 376).

When a jury, on the trial of a criminal case, have retired to consider of the verdict, and have been called back by the Court to be recharged, it is the right of the defendant to have his counsel present, and he does not lose this privilege unless by a clear and distinct waiver thereof. Martin, 51 Ga. 567.

The presence of the counsel is no substitute for that of the accused, and the presence of the accused is no substitute for the presence of counsel. Both should be present. Wilson, 87 Ga. 583, 584 

19. VERDICTS. 

Fixing punishment in felony cases. The jury in their verdict on the trial of all felony cases not punishable by life imprisonment shall prescribe a minimum and maximum term, which shall be within the minimum and maximum prescribed by law as the punishment for said crime, and the judge in imposing the sentence shall commit said convicted person to the penitentiary in accordance with the verdict of the jury; provided that in cases of pleas of guilty, then the presiding judge shall have the right to prescribe such minimum and maximum term as he may see fit. The Prison Commission shall fix rules by which said convict, after serving the minimum sentence, may be allowed to complete his term without the confines of the penitentiary upon complying with said rules. § 27-2502.

The jury may fix the same minimum and maximum punishment. 

Powell, 25 Ga. App. 329 (5) (103 S. E. 111); Johnson, 154 Ga. 806 (1) (115 S. E. 642); Loyd, 150 Ga. 803, 804 (10) (105 S. E. 465).

CRIMINAL PROCEDURE 

207 Where the jury fixes the term of punishment in a felony charge at "three years," the reasonable construction of the verdict is "not less than three years nor more than three years," and such construction will be upheld. Johnson, 154 Ga. 806 (2) (115 S. E. 642).

A charge omitting to instruct the jury that they should fix a minimum and a maximum punishment is erroneous. Butt, 150 Ga. 302 

Constitutionality of the Indeterminate Sentence Act upheld. 

Johnson, 169 Ga. 814 (1) (152 S. E. 76).

Where the jury returned a verdict recommending the accused to mercy, but failing to fix a minimum and a maximum punishment, whereupon the Court sentenced the prisoner to the minimum and maximum provided in the Code, the conviction was upheld. Oliver, 173 Ga. 892 (161 S. E. 828). Contrary rule held in Mitchell, 34 Ga.

App. 505 (130 S. E. 355) where the Court did not impose a minimum punishment and a new trial was granted. See also: Hollis, 48 Ga. 

App. 672 (1) (173 S. E. 179).

Where several defendants are jointly indicted for a crime, the jury may set the minimum and maximum punishment within the limits prescribed by law. There is no rule requiring the jury to set the punishment precisely the same for all joint defendants. Thompson, 160 Ga. 520 (5) (128 S. E. 756). 

Reducible felonies. All felonies, except treason, insurrection, murder, manslaughter, assault with intent to rape, rape, sodomy, foeticide, mayhem, seduction, arson, burning railroad bridge, train wrecking, destroying, injuring, or obstructing railroads, perjury and false swearing, shall be punished by imprisonment and labor in the penitentiary for the terms set forth in the several sections of the Code, prescribing the punishment of such offenses; but on the recommendation of the jury trying the case, when such recommendation is approved by the judge presiding on the trial, such crimes shall be punished as misdemeanors. If the judge trying the case sees proper, he may, in his punishment, reduce such felonies to mis demeanors. § 27-2501. 

See also: Specific Crimes.

The recommendation of the jury is merely advisory. The judge may follow it or disregard it. The judge may reduce the punishment to misdemeanor of his own motion. Durden, 152 Ga. 441, 442 (3) (110 S. E. 283).

The refusal of the trial judge to follow the recommendation of the jury that the accused be punished as for a misdemeanor is not

cause for a new trial, as such recommendations are entirely subject to the approval of the Court. Daniel, 118 Ga. 16 (1) (43 S. E. 861).

A new trial is not required by affidavits of the jury that they would not have agreed to the verdict of guilty if they had not thought that the recommendation to mercy, which was a part of their verdict, would be followed by the Court. Turner, 20 Ga. App. 

Where upon the trial of one, charged with a felony, the jury returned a verdict: "We, the jury, find the defendant guilty of a misdemeanor," such verdict is a nullity. Smith, 117 Ga. 16 (43 S. E. 

440); Wells, 116 Ga. 87 (42 S. E. 390).

The Indeterminate Sentence Act of 1919 did not repeal § 27-2501 of the Code. Thompson, 151 Ga. 328 (1) (106 S. E. 278); Durden, 152 Ga. 441 (110 S. E. 283). 

Where § 27-2501 is applicable, the trial judge should never fail to charge the jury as to their right to recommend a misdemeanor punishment, and that such recommendation will be effectual if approved by the Court. Taylor, 110 Ga. 150 (10) (35 S. E. 161); Thompson, 151 Ga. 328 (1) (106 S. E. 278). A request so to charge is unnecessary. Taylor, 14 Ga. App. 492 (81 S. E. 372); Frazier, 15 Ga. App. 

Failure to charge as to the jury's right to recommend misdemeanor punishment is not a reversible error where the jury in fact returns such recommendation. Ripley, 7 Ga. App. 679 (1) (67 S. E. 834).

The trial judge should inform the jury in plain, unmistakable language that the recommendation will not be effective unless it met with the Court's approval. Frazier, 15 Ga. App. 365 (1) (83 S. E. 

273); Braxley, 17 Ga. App. 196, 198 (13) (86 S. E. 425).

Where the accused is on trial for a felony, the judge, in charging upon the right of the jury to recommend punishment as for a misdemeanor, is not required to instruct the jury what the punishment for a misdemeanor is. Cade, 41 Ga. App. 378 (2) (153 S. E. 76).

After a verdict of guilty has been returned, the judge may hear additional evidence to determine whether a recommendation for misdemeanor punishment should be followed. Elzie, 21 Ga. App. 

501 (3) (94 S. E. 627).

Jury as judges of law and facts. No principle of law is founded upon better reason or has been more strictly adhered to than that the jury are the proper judges of the weight and sufficiency of the testimony and of the credibility of witnesses, and a verdict will not

CRIMINAL PROCEDURE 

209 be disturbed if there is any evidence to support it. Burse, 41 Ga.

Although the jury are the sole judges of the law as well as of the facts in all criminal cases, they are not authorized to get the law except through the Court, and may not reject the law, as charged, because they conscientiously differ from the Court. Edwards, 53 

Ga. 428, 429, 433.

The rule that the jury are the judges of the law does not mean that they might do as they please, or might disregard the charge of the Court. Brown, 40 Ga. 689.

It is the duty of the judge to charge the law in criminal cases, and the duty of the jury to accept the law given them in charge as correct. If the Court commits an error, it can be corrected. But the jury must accept the law it is given in charge. Darsey, 136 Ga. 

501, 504 (71 S. E. 661).

The failure to charge the jury that they are the exclusive judges of the law and the facts is not a reversible error in the absence of a proper request. Brantley, 154 Ga. 80, 81 (6) (113 S. E. 200); Webb, 149 Ga. 211 (2) (99 S. E. 630); Pope, 28 Ga. App. 568 (4) (112 S. E. 169).

If the trial judge should erroneously charge the jury as to the law, and the jury should nevertheless find the correct verdict, the verdict will stand. In other words, the validity of the verdict is to be tested, not by the law as given in charge, but by the law as it is. 

Spence, 7 Ga. App. 825, 827 (68 S. E. 443).

The jury have in their power to find a verdict of not guilty, and the judge can not properly refuse to receive it because it may not accord with his charge, or the evidence. Darsey, 136 Ga. 501, 504 (71 S. E. 661).

The jury may legally acquit the defendant as to some of the counts and convict as to others. Tooke, 4 Ga. App. 495, 496 (3-d) (61 S. E. 917).

Construction of verdicts. In the construction of the verdict the accusation must be considered. Dunbar, 21 Ga. App. 502, 503 (94 

S. E. 587).

A verdict is to be given a reasonable intendment, and, when ambiguous, may be construed in the light of the issues actually submitted to the jury under the charge of the Court; and if, when so construed, it expresses with reasonable certainty a finding supported by the evidence, it is to be upheld as legal. Barbour, 8 Ga. App. 27 (68 S. E. 458).

A verdict will be construed in the light of the maxim: "Id certum est quod certum reddi potest.' Espy, 19 Ga. App. 743 (1) (92 S. 

E. 229).

Verdicts are to have a reasonable intendment, and are to receive. a reasonable construction, and are not to be avoided unless from necessity. Dunbar, 21 Ga. App. 502, 503 (94 S. E. 587).

Several counts in one indictment. Where offenses of different grade are joined in the same indictment, a general verdict of guilty means guilty of the highest offense. Dean, 43 Ga. 218, 219; Estes, 55 Ga. 131; Barksdale, 24 Ga. App. 115 (1) (100 S. E. 45); Tanner, 24 Ga. App. 132 (1) (100 S. E. 44).

Where several misdemeanors, which though of the same general character, are separate and distinct offenses, are joined in different counts of the same indictment, a general verdict of guilty is to be construed as a conviction on all the counts. Driver, 112 Ga. 229 (37 

S. E. 400); Bishop, 21 Ga. App. 236 (3) (94 S. E. 49).

Where an indictment in different counts charges different misdemeanors, which relate to but one offense, one transaction, stating the different counts with variations of details, so that the indictment, as pleading, may adapt itself to the different phases which may appear in the proof at the trial, a general verdict of guilty, without a specification as to the count upon which it is returned, is sufficient, if any one of the counts is sustained by the evidence. 

Dohme, 68 Ga. 339 (2); Williams, 107 Ga. 693 (2) (33 S. E. 641).

Where the indictment charges several different and distinct transactions, though of a kindred nature, a general verdict of guilty is not sustainable, unless the proof is such as to uphold a conviction of each and every offense alleged. Driver, 112 Ga. 229 (4) (37 S. 

E. 400); Sewell, 23 Ga. App. 765, 766 (5) (99 S. E. 320); Innes, 19 

Ga. App. 271 (1) (91 S. E. 339).

A general verdict of guilty upon an indictment in two counts, each charging the violation of a different penal statute, can not be sustained where there is no evidence to support a conviction upon both counts, unless that count was withdrawn from the consideration of the jury. Jones, 27 Ga. App. 600 (110 S. E. 37); Williams, 27 Ga. App. 609 (110 S. E. 37); Brooks, 27 Ga. App. 629 (109 S. E. 548).

A general verdict of guilty on an indictment charging the violation of the same statute in different ways, is lawful, if there is evidence to sustain either count. Hetrick, 27 Ga. App. 671 (2) (109 

S. E. 528).

CRIMINAL PROCEDURE 

211 Where the defendant was charged on two counts, but the evidence only authorized conviction on the second count, the error in the verdict finding him guilty on both counts was cured, where the judge, during the same term, and before the defendant had begun to serve his sentence, struck the sentence under the first count. Perry, 25 

Ga. App. 481 (103 S. E. 719).

Where the crime charged has two grades, a general verdict of guilty will be construed as finding the defendant guilty of the higher charge, and the proof should support the verdict of the higher grade. However, where the only issue submitted by the 

Court to the jury is whether or not the defendant is guilty of the lower grade of crime, because the State abandoned the charge of the higher grade, the general verdict of guilty will be construed as guilty of the lower grade. Davis, 47 Ga. App. 706 (171 S. E. 401).

Where the defendant is charged on two counts, and the Court submits to the jury one of the counts only, thereby impliedly instructing them not to consider the other count, and the jury brings a verdict of guilty on both counts, the proper construction of such verdict is guilty of the count submitted by the Court to the jury. Vinson, 45 Ga. App. 220, 221 (3) (164 S. E. 209).

When one is tried for the violation of two laws, one of which is void, a general verdict of guilty is illegal. Douglas, 14 Ga. App. 

612, 614 (3) (81 S. E. 803).

Where there are two counts in an indictment, one good and one fatally defective, and the Court overrules a demurrer to the defective count, a general verdict of guilty will be reversed. Sutton, 122 

Ga. 158 (3) (50 S. E. 60).

A plurality of counts may be caused by charging the same transaction as having been committed in a number of different ways, or by charging a number of distinct transactions of the same general character. If caused in the former way, a general verdict will be upheld if any one of the counts is supported by evidence. If caused in the latter way, a general verdict will not be upheld, unless there is sufficient proof to justify a conviction under each and all of the counts. Tooke, 4 Ga. App. 495 (3) (3-b) (3-c) (61 S. E. 917).

The State's counsel, or the judge, may withdraw the count unsupported by evidence from the jury, in which case a general verdict of guilty will relate only to the counts submitted to the jury. 

Waver, 108 Ga. 775 (33 S. E. 423); Hall, 43 Ga. App. 224 (158 S. E. 357).

Joint indictments of two defendants. Where two parties are jointly indicted for an offense which does not require the concerted

action of both, but may be separately committed by either, a verdict finding one of the defendants guilty, if supported by the evidence,is authorized. Easterling, 12 Ga. App. 690 (2) (78 S. E. 140).

Where several were jointly indicted, and only one tried, a general verdict of guilty means the defendant on trial. Davis. 153 Ga. 154 (1) (112 S. E. 280). 

Special verdicts. A special verdict is returned when the jury find certain facts to exist, and leave the Court to determine whether or not, according to the law which controls these facts, the prisoner is guilty. Dunbar, 21 Ga. App. 502 (94 S. E. 587); Isom, 83 Ga. 378, 379 (9 S. E. 1051).

Where the verdict applies directly to the offense charged, but stops short in its finding of the requisite facts to constitute that offense, the verdict is equivalent to an acquittal. Dunbar, 21 Ga. App. 

502, 503 (94 S. E. 587); Couch, 28 Ga. 367.

Forms of verdicts. The judge may write out every form of verdict adaptable to the case, and have the jury write on the bill of indictment the one they find. Loyd, 150 Ga. 803, 804 (8) (105 S. E. 

465); Meyers, 169 Ga. 468 (5) (151 S. E. 34); Loyd, 26 Ga. App. 259 (8) (106 S. E. 601).

Charge as to the form of the verdict, if the accused is found guilty, is error, where no form of acquittal is given. Kearney, 101 Ga. 803 (7) (29 S. E. 127). But where form of verdict is not given for a conviction, omission to give form of verdict for acquittal is no error. 

Howell, 124 Ga. 698 (9) (52 S. E. 649).

Repugnant acts charged jointly. Where accusation refers to two repugnant acts in two counts, involved in the same transaction, and the same evidence is relied on, a general verdict of guilty (meaning guilty on both counts) can not be had. B'Gos, 43 Ga. App. 379 (159 

S. E. 137).

Where the defendant is charged with transporting liquor, and with possessing liquor, in two separate indictments, relating to the same transaction, and the same evidence is relied on, verdict of guilty of transporting liquor is repugnant to one finding him not guilty of possessing it. One can not transport something he does not possess. Davis, 43 Ga. App. 122 (157 S. E. 888).

Guilty means the highest grade charged. Upon the principle of a verdict of guilty means guilty of the highest grade charged, a verdict of "guilty of manslaughter" in a murder trial means "guilty of voluntary manslaughter." Smith, 109 Ga. 479 (1) (35 S. E. 59).

And upon the same principle, a verdict of "guilty of involuntary

CRIMINAL PROCEDURE 

213 manslaughter" means "in the commission of an unlawful act." 

Thomas, 121 Ga. 331 (2) (49 S. E. 273).

Defective verdicts. Where a verdict is not in a proper form, the 

Court should charge the jury to return to their room and bring back a verdict in proper form, instructing them what the form should be. 

Lambert, 17 Ga. App. 348 (1) (86 S. E. 782); Cook, 26 Ga. 593 (5).

Objection to the form of the verdict, or a question of nullity of the verdict, can not be raised by motion for a new trial. Harrison, 26 

Ga. App. 58 (2-a) (105 S. E. 614); Green, 26 Ga. App. 109, 110 (9) (105 S. E. 634).

Erasures by the jury. Erasures made by the jury do not void the verdict if their finding is clearly visible. Pippin, 172 Ga. 224 (157 

S. E. 185).

Verdicts on Sunday. It is lawful to receive a verdict in a criminal case on Sunday. Where the case has gone to the jury before

Sunday, it is not legally nor morally wrong to receive the verdict on 

Sunday. Henderson, 84 Ga. 159 (2) (10 S. E. 734); Rawlins, 124 

Ga. 31, 33 (22) (52 S. E. 1).

Polling the jury. The prisoner has a right to demand the polling of the jury, and a refusal to comply with such a demand is a reversible error. Williams, 63 Ga. 306; Russell, 68 Ga. 785, 788.

Where the Court erroneously refused a motion to poll the jury, and the jury was discharged, and dispersed, and mingled with the crowd, it is too late to cure the omission to poll by re-assembling the jury for that purpose. Russell, 68 Ga. 785, 788.

On demand made for the polling of the jury, the legality of the verdict is only completed by the poll. Russell, 68 Ga. 785, 788.

The proper time to demand the polling of the jury is after publication of the verdict, before the jury dispersed, and before sentence is pronounced. McCullough, 10 Ga. App. 403 (6) (73 S. E. 546).

Where jury dispersed prior to returning the verdict into court, thus depriving the defendant of his right to poll the jury, the verdict is void. Hopkins, 6 Ga. App. 403 (1) (65 S. E. 57).

It is too late to poll the jury after sentence has been pronounced. 

Robinson, 109 Ga. 506 (8) (34 S. E. 1017).

In polling the jury, the only inquiry is whether the juror consented to the verdict. Parker, 81 Ga. 332 (5) (6 S. E. 600).

The practice of polling the jury is to begin with the reading of the verdict and calling the juror's attention to it, and then asking each juror seriatim the question: "What say you, Mr. Juror; is this your

verdict or is it not?" Black, 31 Ga. 641 (7); Campbell, 62 Ga. 86, 87 (7).

Where it appears that the verdict is not the unanimous conclusion of the jurors, it should be rejected. Ponder, 11 Ga. App. 60 (74 S. 

E. 715).

Where juror answered that his consent to the verdict was not freely and voluntarily made, the jury should be sent back. A motion for mistrial is not the proper remedy. Macon Railway and 

Light Co., 121 Ga. 443 (5), 444 (49 S. E. 282).

A verdict will not be rejected because one of the jurors, upon being polled, answered that he agreed to it reluctantly. Parker, 81 

Ga. 332 (5) (6 S. E. 600).

A juror who has agreed to a verdict may dissent from it at any time before it has been received by the Court. Ponder, 11 Ga. App. 

60 (74 S. E. 715).

A prisoner may waive his right to poll the jury. Such waiver can be express or by implication. A failure to demand that the jury be polled is waiver. Russell, 68 Ga. 785, 788.

Concealing first verdict on second trial. Where a defendant was convicted, and a new trial was granted, and, before the jury had retired to consider of the verdict in the second case, the defendant made a motion to have a paper pasted over the first verdict, in order to conceal it from the jury, it was reversible error to overrule such motion. Morris, 49 Ga. App. 138 (174 S. E. 385).

It is not good ground for a motion for a new trial that the verdict of the jury in a former trial was not concealed from the jury of the second trial, where no request was made to detach or conceal the same. Ellard, 46 Ga. App. 345 (167 S. E. 783). 

20. MISTRIALS. 

To justify a grant of a mistrial without the consent of the accused, there must be either a moral or a physical necessity. Oliveros, 120 

Ga. 237, 239 (47 S. E. 627).

Where the trial judge expressed an opinion as to the weight of evidence, he was not authorized to grant a mistrial of his own motion over the objection of the accused. Oliveros, 120 Ga. 237 (47 S. 

E. 627). 

One can not invoke an erroneous ruling and afterwards take advantage of the error thus committed. The party at whose instance a mistrial is declared can not take advantage of any error com-

CRIMINAL PROCEDURE 

215 mitted by the granting of a mistrial. Nixon, 121 Ga. 144, 145 (3) (48 S. E. 966).

When during the trial of a capital case the presiding judge leaves the court room, even for a few minutes, during the prosecuting attorney's argument to the jury, without suspending the trial, and at the conclusion of that argument, the defendant's counsel makes a motion for a mistrial because of such absence, the motion should be granted. Moore, 29 Ga. App. 274 (115 S. E. 25).

A motion for a mistrial is not an appropriate remedy when, upon a poll of the jury, the party against whom the verdict was rendered. contended that it appeared from the answer of one of the jurors that it was not his verdict. Whidby, 21 Ga. App. 146 (1) (94 S. E. 55).

It is not error to decline to declare a mistrial because a witness accused the defendant of having told "an absolute lie"; the jury being instructed by the judge that this statement was improper and should not influence them. Whitman, 39 Ga. App. 547 (3) (147 S. 

E. 798).

Mistrial for remarks of judge. Without a motion for a mistrial, questions propounded by the trial judge to a witness are not cause for a new trial. Whitener, 39 Ga. App. 676 (148 S. E. 305). Prejudicial remarks of the judge in the presence and hearing of the jury on the trial of a criminal case are not cause for a new trial when there was no motion for a mistrial on account of them. Davis, 40 

Ga. App. 123 (4) (149 S. E. 51). But it was held in Cook, 40 Ga. 

App. 125 (1) (149 S. E. 79) that a motion for a mistrial is not required before a violation of the law against that section of the Penal Code prohibiting the judges from expressing an opinion can properly be made the basis of a motion for a new trial. Note: For full discussion, see dissenting and concurring opinions, Campbell, 155 

Ga. 127, 128 (116 S. E. 807). See also: Charge of the Jury. 

Mistrial for improper argument of counsel. A statement by the prosecuting attorney in his argument to the jury, expressive of his opinion of the defendant's guilt, should be construed to mean that the testimony led him to this conclusion. What the law condemns is the injection into the argument of extrinsic and prejudicial matters which have no basis in the evidence. (Italics by the Court.) 

Mitchell, 38 Ga. App. 360 (2) (144 S. E. 14).

The use of unfair or improper language by an attorney in arguing a case will not be held cause for a new trial when it is certain that no injury could possibly have resulted therefrom to the losing

party. Hoxie, 114 Ga. 19 (39 S. E. 944); Lee, 116 Ga. 563, 568 (42 

S. E. 759).

The matter of ordering a mistrial for improper argument of counsel is very important, and should be liberally exercised in all cases where counsel abused their privilege of argument by prejudicing the case of the opposite party. However, it is a matter largely within the discretion of the Court; and unless it is apparent that a mistrial was essential to the preservation of the right of a fair trial, the discretion of the Court will not be interfered with. Manchester, 171 Ga. 121, 132 (155 S. E. 11).

The justices of the Supreme Court were equally divided in their opinions as to whether the following remarks of the solicitorgeneral were so prejudicial that a new trial should have been granted: "It would be useless to convict this man and recommend the accused to the mercy of the Court with any assurance that he would serve for life; for statistics show, but I can't quote statistics, but I will say it is a matter of general information that probably half or a great per cent of the life convicts either succeed in making an escape or are pardoned by some over-sympathetic Governor." 

Biggers, 171 Ga. 596, 600 (156 S. E. 201).

Improper argument of counsel for the prosecution is not cause for a new trial where the verdict is demanded by the evidence. 

Bedsole, 32 Ga. App. 792 (124 S. E. 812); Hager, 71 Ga. 164, 167.

When evidence is offered and its admissibility is challenged, counsel may state the reason why such testimony should be allowed; and if what he says is in good faith and not calculated to prejudice the jury, it affords no ground for declaring a mistrial. 

Walker, 124 Ga. 97, 98 (5) (52 S. E. 319).

Misconduct of spectators. It is not necessarily a ground for a mistrial that one of the spectators, who was related to the injured. party, made an exclamation at the trial tending to discredit defendant's statement. Esa, 19 Ga. App. 14 (3) (90 S. E. 732).

Where the accused is on trial for bigamy, when his first wife improperly interferes with his right to make a statement to the jury, by inserting remarks, a mistrial should be granted. Robinson, 6 

Ga. App. 696, 697 (4) (65 S. E. 792).

Where a young woman demonstrated against the defendant in the presence of the jury, but the trial judge certified that it was not of such a character as even to attract the attention of the jury, a mistrial was not required. Sullivan, 121 Ga. 183, 186 (48 S. E. 949).

CRIMINAL PROCEDURE 

217 Improper remarks by the sheriff in the presence of the jury are not a sufficient ground for a mistrial where the judge admonished the jury to disregard it. Rawlins, 124 Ga. 31, 32 (9) (52 S. E. 1).

The mere fact that a woman in the court room burst out crying and sobbing loudly and was removed by the sheriff by order of the Court, is no ground for a mistrial. Clements, 123 Ga. 547 (2) 

Departure of a juror. It is not error to overrule a motion for a mistrial, made on the ground that one of the jurors was allowed to leave the jury room, it appearing that the juror was wanted as a witness in another case, and that from the time he left the jury room until he returned, he was accompanied by a bailiff, and it not appearing that any harm was done to the complaining party. May, 120 Ga. 497 (1) (48 S. E. 153).

Appeal. An order declaring a mistrial is not such final order as will authorize a writ of error. Starnes, 138 Ga. 341 (75 S. E. 104).

The ruling of the Court refusing a motion for a mistrial, made by the defendant in a criminal case, is not the subject matter of direct exceptions, unless exceptions pendente lite were made to the same, duly filed, or in a direct bill of exceptions, tendered within twenty days after the ruling complained of. Jones, 135 Ga. 357 

Absence of the accused. The involuntary absence of the accused from the trial at the time when the solicitor-general addresses the jury is a ground for a new trial, notwithstanding the fact that the judge was unaware of the prisoner's absence. Pierce, 47 Ga. App. 

830 (171 S. E. 731). 

21. SENTENCE.

Alternative sentence. The better practice in regard to sentences for misdemeanors is for the Court to state clearly and definitely the sentence to imprisonment in jail, if any, or to service on the chain-gang, or both; and then to provide, if an alternative sentence is to be passed, that either the imprisonment in jail or service on the chain-gang, or both, as the Court may prescribe, is to be discharged or relieved by payment of a fine of a stated amount. Dixon, 149 Ga. 86, 87 (99 S. E. 34). 

Concurrent or consecutive sentences. Where two sentences are imposed upon conviction of separate misdemeanors at the same term of the court, and the judge so moulds each of the sentences as

to allow the defendant to serve the same as probationer outside of the confines of the place of detention, the sentences will run concurrently. Shamblin, 148 Ga. 592 (1-a) (97 S. E. 520).

Where the accused is found guilty of more than one offense, and the imprisonment under one sentence is to commence at the expiration of the other, the sentences must so state, else second punishment will be executed concurrently, and the defendant will be discharged on the expiration of the longer term. Shamblin, 148 Ga. 

592 (1) (97 S. E. 520). But this rule has no application in a case where the different sentences were imposed by different courts. 

Hightower, 121 Ga. 159 (1) (48 S. E. 969); Sullivan, 156 Ga. 706 

Change of sentence. The trial judge has no right to change or modify the original sentence after the adjournment of the term at which it was rendered. Shaw, 148 Ga. 589, 590 (1) (97 S. E. 520).

After the accused has begun serving his sentence, it can not be modified or set aside, even during the term of the court where it was brought. Rutland, 14 Ga. App. 746 (82 S. E. 293).

Where one, convicted of a misdemeanor, was sentenced at the term at which the trial took place to serve a term in the chain-gang, and carried the case by a writ of error to the Court of Appeals, where the judgment of the lower court was affirmed, the trial court was without authority at the subsequent term, upon making the judgment of the appellate court the judgment of the trial court, to modify and change the sentence formerly imposed. Porter, 148 Ga. 

261 (1) (96 S. E. 426).

Suspension of sentence. Neither the judge of the Superior Court nor that of the city court have authority to suspend the sentence imposed by them, except through a supersedeas pending appeal. 

Hancock, 140 Ga. 688 (1) (79 S. E. 558); Cook, 146 Ga. 704 (1) (92 

S. E. 212); Wimbish, 170 Ga. 64 (1) (152 S. E. 97); Scott, 170 Ga. 

368, 369 (1) (153 S. E. 25).

Excessive punishment. While the sentence is within the limits fixed by the statute, it is no ground for a new trial that the sentence is excessive, or cruel and unusual within the meaning of the constitutional prohibition. Bellinger, 116 Ga. 545 (3) (42 S. E. 747); 

Rogers, 11 Ga. App. 814 (2) (76 S. E. 366).

Misdemeanor cases. The Court has the power in misdemeanor cases to pass upon the defendant a sentence of both, twelve months in the chain-gang and to impose a fine of not exceeding one thou-

CRIMINAL PROCEDURE 

219 sand dollars. The Court, therefore, could do less than both, and could do so without giving the defendant an election as to paying or refusing to pay the fine. Dickson, 36 Ga. App. 341, 343 (136 S. 

E. 537).

Restitutions. There is no provision in the penal law to make restitution to the party injured. That part of a sentence which directs that the accused make restitution in addition to a fine, is void. Ray, 40 Ga. App. 145 (2) (149 S. E. 64).

Female convicts. Where a female is convicted of a misdemeanor, or pleads guilty to such charge, the judge may, in his discretion, sentence her to serve a term in the women's prison on the State farm. Conley, 161 Ga. 462 (1) (131 S. E. 168). 

Valid verdict; illegal sentence. An illegal sentence upon a valid and lawful verdict is not a valid ground for a new trial. Morris, 44 Ga. App. 765 (162 S. E. 879). 

22. ARREST OF JUDGMENT. 

A motion in arrest of judgment differs from a motion for a new trial, in this: The former must be predicated on some defect which appears on the face of the record or pleading, while the latter must be predicated on some extrinsic matter. It also differs from a motion to set aside a judgment, in this: The motion in arrest of judgment must be made during the term at which the judgment was obtained, while a motion to set it aside may be made at any time within the statute of limitations. § 110-703.

Defects in the pleadings. A judgment can not be arrested or set aside for any defect in the pleading or record that is either cured by verdict, or amendable as a matter of form. Spence, 7 Ga. App. 

825, 826 (68 S. E. 443).

A judgment based upon a void affidavit and accusation in the city court may be arrested. Edmondson, 123 Ga. 194 (51 S. E. 301).

All exceptions which go merely to the form of an indictment shall be made before trial; and no motion in arrest of judgment shall be sustained for any matter not affecting the real merits of the offense charged in the indictment. § 27-1601. Hatcher, 18 Ga. 460, 465; Martin, 115 Ga. 255 (41 S. E. 576).

Where the indictment is absolutely void, a motion to arrest judgment should be sustained. Sims, 37 Ga. App. 819 (142 S. E. 464).

Upon a motion in arrest of judgment one may take advantage of

any non-amendable defect appearing upon the face of the record. 

Gilbert, 17 Ga. App. 143 (1), 144 (86 S. E. 415).

Common law. At common law a motion to set aside a judgment could be predicated upon any irregularity in the judgment, whether appearing upon the face of the record, or not. Regopoulas, 116 

Ga. 596, 597 (42 S. E. 1014). (Distinguishing Fannin vs. Durdin, 54 Ga. 476.)

Defect in verdict. A motion in arrest of judgment is the proper procedure where the verdict is for some offense not covered by the charge made in the indictment. Spence, 7 Ga. App. 825, 826 (68 

S. E. 443).

If a verdict, when construed with the indictment, does not find the defendant guilty of any offense, the judgment should be arrested. Lanier, 5 Ga. App. 472, 476 (63 S. E. 536).

Where the indictment and the trial were for a misdemeanor and the verdict was for a felony, the judgment should be arrested. Allen, 86 Ga. 399 (12 S. E. 651).

Where the indictment was for a felony, and the verdict is for "We, the jury, find the defendant guilty of a misdemeanor," the judgment ought to be arrested. Wells, 116 Ga. 87 (2) (42 S. E. 390).

The law does not require the jury to find a verdict in the language of the Code, and the failure of the jury to do so is not a good ground for arresting the judgment. Camp, 25 Ga. 689, 693.

It is not a good ground for arresting the judgment that the verdict is not signed. Roberts, 14 Ga. 18.

Presumptions. On the hearing of a motion in arrest of judgment, the Court looks only at the indictment and the verdict, the presumption being that the evidence lawfully authorized the verdict. 

And the Court is not at liberty to look to the evidence, although it is incorporated in the records. Watson, 116 Ga. 607 (6) (43 S. 

E. 32); Gates, 95 Ga. 340, 342 (22 S. E. 836); Herron, 93 Ga. 554 (19 S. E. 243); Sessions, 3 Ga. App. 13, 15 (59 S. E. 196).

Motion for a new trial distinguished. If the verdict is contrary to the charge of the Court for any reason, or is without evidence to support it, it is ground for a new trial, and not for arrest of judgment. Spence, 7 Ga. App. 825, 826 (68 S. E. 443).

Material variance between the allegations in the indictment and the proof is no ground for an arrest of judgment. A motion for a new trial is the proper remedy. Seals, 107 Ga. 713, 714 (33 S. E. 392).

CRIMINAL PROCEDURE
