Rule 39. Applications for a new trial on newly discovered evidence are not favored. Great care should be taken in the preparation of the ground of a motion for a new trial on account of newly discovered evidence. The essentials of such a ground are: (a) Affidavits of witnesses by whom new facts are to be proved should be produced, or satisfactory reason given for their nonproduction. 

Burge v. State, 133 Ga. 431, 432 (66 S. E. 243). (b) It must appear that the newly discovered evidence is not merely cumulative. Burge v. State, supra. (c) It must appear that the evidence is not solely to impeach the credit of the witness. Burge v. State, supra. (d) It must appear that the evidence was discovered by movant after the rendition of the verdict against him. Burge v. State, supra. (e) 

That the evidence was newly discovered, not merely that a certain named witness was newly discovered. Burgess v. State, 93 Ga. 304 (20 S. E. 331); Jinks v. State, 117 Ga. 714, 716 (44 S. E. 814). (f)

It must appear by the affidavit of the movant and of each of his counsel that the affiant did not know of the existence of the alleged newly discovered evidence before the trial and before the verdict, and that it could not have been discovered by the exercise of ordinary care. The affidavits showing diligence should not state conclusions, but should set out what was done by the movant and his counsel to discover the new evidence. Taylor v. State, 132 Ga. 235, 237 (63 S. E. 1116); Patterson v. Collier, 77 Ga. 292 (3 S. E. 119); Tyre v. State, 35 Ga. App. 579 (134 S. E. 178), and cit. (g) It must appear that the probable effect of the new evidence, if another trial be had, will be to produce a different verdict. Burge v. State, supra. 

But see "ultimate criterion," Todd v. Jackson, 24 Ga. App. 519 (101

S. E. 192). (h) It must appear that the evidence is material to the issues involved. (j) If the newly discovered evidence is that of a witness, affidavits as to his residence, associates, means of knowledge, character and credibility must be adduced, and the names of the "associates" must appear in the affidavits. Burge v. State, supra; Ivey v. State, 154 Ga. 63 (113 S. E. 175); Tyre v. State, supra. (k) The affidavits must be properly entitled in the cause, or otherwise identify the case. Hill v. McBurney Oil & Fertilizer Co., 112 

Ga. 792 (38 S. E. 42, 52 L. R. A. 398). (1) The affidavits must be made a part of the record, and the better practice is to attach them

CRIMINAL PROCEDURE 

237 to the ground and make them a part thereof by direct reference thereto. Follow the rules laid down touching this matter in Glover v. State, 128 Ga. 1 (57 S. E. 101). 24. COURTS. (See Specific' Chapters.)

SPECIFIC CRIMES

PART III 1. ABANDONMENT OF CHILD. 

§ 74-9902. (Misdemeanor.) charge and accuse. Indictment. .with the offense of a misdemeanor, for that the said.................did on the................day of………………………………….. 

19...., in the county of.......... willfully and voluntarily abandon his child (or children), to wit: leaving it (them) in a dependent condition, contrary, etc..

Willful abandonment must be charged, and that the child was left in dependent condition. McDaniel, 78 Ga. 188.

Defendant's relation as father is sufficiently indicated, if the name of the accused denotes a person of masculine gender, and if the child is described as his child. Child presumed to be the offspring of his body and lawfully begotten. Rimes, 7 Ga. App. 556 (67 S. E. 223).

Indictment need not allege the way in which child was left in dependent or destitute condition, nor what dependency consisted of. 

Woodard, 18 Ga. App. 59 (88 S. E. 825).

Sex. Sex of child immaterial. Need not be alleged in the indictment. Woodard, 18 Ga. App. 59 (88 S. E. 825). General. 

Child. Imports legitimate child. Woodard, 18 Ga. App. 59 (88 

S. E. 825). 

Father. Must be shown that the accused was in fact the father of the child, and the child, alleged to have been abandoned, is his child, because under the terms of the Code the father is the only person punishable for the abandonment. Rimes, 7 Ga. App. 556, 557 (67 S. E. 223).

It is not a valid defense that the father was less than seventeen years old when he married the mother of the child. Smith, 42 Ga.

Where the defendant denies paternity of the child, it is error to exclude testimony of wife's reputation for lewdness. Mims, 43 Ga. 

App. 100 (4) (157 S. E. 901); Wash, 41 Ga. App. 451 (153 S. E. 376).

Defendant's denial of paternity is inadmissible in the absence of evidence sufficient to rebut the presumption of paternity arising from the marriage relation. Jackson, 1 Ga. App. 723 (58 S. E. 272).

Common law marriage is recognized. Wynne, 17 Ga. App. 263 (86 S. E. 823).

Mother is competent witness to prove not only the abandonment but also the marriage. Cunningham, 13 Ga. App. 80 (78 S. E. 780).

Actual desertion. Absence of the father necessary to constitute the crime of desertion, but absence alone will not be sufficient until, and without, the child becoming dependent. Brown, 122 Ga. 568, 570 (50 S. E. 378); Phelps, 10 Ga. App. 41 (72 S. E. 524).

Actual desertion is essential, followed by refusal and failure to support the child; absence of either would prevent the offense from being made out. Gay, 105 Ga. 599, 605 (31 S. E. 569); Phelps, 10 

Ga. App. 41 (72 S. E. 524).

Father can be guilty of this offense, although the children may have continued to occupy the same dwelling as the father. Goffe, 14 Ga. App. 275 (3) (80 S. E. 519).

Father may be guilty, though he lawfully leave, children later becoming dependent and destitute and he fails to support them. 

Brown, 122 Ga. 568 (50 S. E. 378).

Unborn child. Father can not be guilty of this offense, until child is born. Indictment charging the father with abandoning his minor child "not yet born" is demurrable. Shelton, 19 Ga. App. 618 (91 

S. E. 923). But abandonment may begin before the child is born, if continued after birth. Crow, 96 Ga. 297 (22 S. E. 948); Bull, 80 Ga. 

704 (6 S. E. 178); Smith, 42 Ga. App. 419 (1) (156 S. E. 718); 

Chandler, 38 Ga. App. 362, 364 (144 S. E. 51); Campbell, 20 Ga. App. 

190, 192 (92 S. E. 963).

Dependent and destitute condition. OLD RULE: Old rule is that the indictment must charge, and the evidence bear out, that the child was left in dependent and destitute condition. Using the word "or" instead of "and" is a fatal error. Jemmerson, 80 Ga. 111 (5 S. 

E. 131).

NEW RULE: It is sufficient if the child is left in dependent condition. It is surplusage to allege destitute condition. The offense is fully consummated if father abandons child in dependent condition. 

Mixon, 34 Ga. App. 782 (131 S. E. 367). (The word "destitute" has been omitted by the Acts of 1907, p. 574.) 

Wants of child provided. OLD RULE: If, notwithstanding the desertion, the wants of the child be provided for by others, the statutory crime of desertion is not made out. Mays, 123 Ga. 507 (51 S. 

E. 503); Williams, 126 Ga. 637 (55 S. E. 480).

SPECIFIC CRIMES 

241 

NEW RULE: The fact that the mother supplied the food, shelter and clothing is no legal defense to an accusation against the father for abandonment of the child. Chandler, 38 Ga. App. 362, 364 (144 

S. E. 51); Campbell, 20 Ga. App. 190, 192 (92 S. E. 963); Daniels, 8 

Ga. App. 469 (2) (69 S. E. 588).

All children abandoned are considered to be in dependent condition when the father does not furnish sufficient food and clothing for the need of his children. Cleveland, 7 Ga. App. 622 (67 S. E. 696). 

Relation between father and mother. Separation of the father from the child does not bring about the question of how and in what manner such separation was brought about. It doesn't involve the question whether the father went away voluntarily from the place where the child has formerly been. It does not involve the question of whether the mother of the child took the child with her, away from the place where the father was. It does not involve the question of who, if either of the parents, were in fault in bringing about such separation between the father and the child. The conduct of the mother, no matter what it may be, in coming or going, can in no manner relieve the father of his duty to furnish food, shelter, and clothing for the minor child. The question to be considered by the jury is, whether the father separated from the minor child? If so, then did he fail to support its needs? Chandler, 38 Ga. App. 362, 364 (144 S. E. 51).

Unfriendly relations of father and mother-inadmissible. Daniels, 8 Ga. App. 469 (3) (69 S. E. 588).

Mother's misconduct and refusal to live with the father-no defense. Chandler, 38 Ga. App. 362, 364 (144 S. E. 51); Moore, 1 Ga. 

App. 502 (3) (57 S. E. 1016); Towns, 24 Ga. App. 265 (1) (100 S. E. 

575); Parrish, 10 Ga. App. 836 (74 S. E. 445).

It is immaterial what the relations between father and mother of the child are. It is entitled to support. In other words the conduct of the father and the mother does not affect the rights of the child to maintenance and support. If the father of the child is not satisfied, he may go to court to determine the custody thereof. Mobley, 41 Ga. App. 379 (153 S. E. 202).

Demand. Demand on father for support of the child need not be shown. Floyd, 17 Ga. App. 265 (86 S. E. 460).

Alimony. A judgment for alimony is not necessarily bar to a prosecution for abandonment, even if such judgment is partially satisfied. King, 12 Ga. App. 482 (77 S. E. 651).

Venue. In a prosecution of a father for the offense of abandoning his minor child, and leaving it in a dependent condition, the venue of the offense is in the county where the state of the child's dependency upon others began on account of the father's failure to support the child. Rogers, 27 Ga. App. 180 (1) (107 S. E. 889).

Foreign State. Where a man voluntarily, willfully, and permanently separated himself from his wife and minor child while the family was living in Pennsylvania, but the state of dependency of the child did not begin until after the child and the mother had returned to Georgia, and made Cherokee County, Georgia, their place of residence, the crime of abandonment was committed in Cherokee 

County. Garrett, 41 Ga. App. 545 (153 S. E. 628); Sikes, 37 Ga. App. 

164 (139 S. E. 87)-However, dependency must occur in Georgia.

Where a father abandoned his child in the State of Alabama, and came to Georgia five or six years before the finding of an indictment against him, and the mother of the child subsequently moved into this State (Georgia), bringing the child with her in a dependent and destitute condition, and notified the father, and requested him to support them, which he refused to do, this did not authorize his conviction, unless he received them and recognized them in some way as his family after they have come into this State. Jemmerson, 80 Ga. 

111 (5 S. E. 131); Nunn, 39 Ga. App. 643 (148 S. E. 165)—Where wife went to Alabama, for her confinement, but retained her residence in Georgia, and returned to Georgia, where child was left dependent, father guilty of abandonment. Fry, 36 Ga. App. 312 (136 

S. E. 466).

Former jeopardy. When accused was convicted once, he can not be again convicted though his abandonment be willful and continuous, unless it be shown that he has returned to the discharge of his parental duty to the child and has again deserted it. Gay, 105 Ga. 

599 (31 S. E. 569). But plea of acquittal on former trial for abandonment held properly overruled in prosecution for abandonment occurring since acquittal, although defendant has not returned to his family. Meadows, 43 Ga. App. 225 (158 S. E. 765).

Statute of limitations. The crime of abandonment begins and continues as long as there is a failure on the part of the father to perform his parental duty, and consequent dependence of the child. 

The continuing dependency of the child vitalizes the offense, and the fact that the absence, and even the dependency, began more than two years prior to the accusation affords no ground for the interposition of the statute of limitation. Phelps, 10 Ga. App. 41 (72 S. E. 524).

SPECIFIC CRIMES 

243 Abandonment is a continuing offense, at least until the defendant has once been convicted thereof. Lomax, 44 Ga. App. 500 (4) (162 

S. E. 395). 

2. ABORTION. 

(Misdemeanor.) (See also: Assault With Intent to Murder. § 26-1101.) Indictment. did willfully administer (employ instrument) to one...... being then and there a pregnant woman, medicine and drugs with intent thereby to produce the miscarriage and abortion of said............., and said medicine or drugs not then and there having been advised by two physicians to be necessary to preserve the life of said.

Not demurrable for failure to set forth the character of instrument, or how it was used, or on what part of the woman's body it was used. Snell, 13 Ga. App. 158 (79 S. E. 71); Herndon, 38 Ga. 

App. 117, 119 (142 S. E. 695). 

General. "Pregnant woman" distinguished from "woman pregnant with child." A woman who carries a foetus in her womb is pregnant, whether the foetus is living or dead. A woman pregnant with child is a woman, who is pregnant with an unborn child so far developed as to be quick, so far developed as to move in the mother's womb. Wilbanks, 41 Ga. App. 268, 272, 273 (152 S. E. 619); 

Hunter, 29 Ga. App. 366 (115 S. E. 277); Summerlin, 150 Ga. 173, 176 (103 S. E. 461). Code calls for "pregnant woman," and if the act of defendant was done not on the ground of removing a dead foetus, but to prevent the natural result of sexual intercourse, defendant guilty, although foetus was dead. Wilbanks, 41 Ga. App. 

268, 273 (152 S. E. 619). (This decision seems to hold that defendant charged with violating § 26-1101 can be found guilty of abortion.)

Defendant can be guilty without absolute knowledge that child was "quick." Barrow, 121 Ga. 187 (7) (48 S. E. 950).

Acts and sayings of one accomplice during the pendency of the common criminal act are admissible against the other. Barrow, 121 

Ga. 187 (2) (48 S. E. 950); Tate, 41 Ga. App. 300, 304 (152 S. E. 609).

Illicit relation between co-defendant and the female, on proof of conspiracy to destroy the result of such relation, admissible to show.

motive of crime. Barrow, 121 Ga. 187 (3) (48 S. E. 950); Gullatt, 14 

Ga. App. 53 (5) (80 S. E. 340).

Consent of female no defense, nor that purpose of crime was to conceal her shame by the operation. Barrow, 121 Ga. 187 (6) (48

S. E. 950). 

No error to admit acts and sayings of one conspirator against the other, during the pendency of criminal act, even before such conspiracy is established in court. Barrow, 121 Ga. 187 (48 S. E. 950); 

Tate, 41 Ga. App. 300, 304 (152 S. E. 609); Wall, 153 Ga. 309, 317 (112 S. E. 142); Cook, 22 Ga. App. 770, 779 (97 S. E. 264).

Woman consenting to abortion is not an accomplice. (Dictum.) 

Stone, 118 Ga. 705, 709, 710 (45 S. E. 630). 

Prior attempt at abortion may be shown. Sullivan, 121 Ga. 183 (1) (48 S. E. 949); Frank, 141 Ga. 243, 264, 265, 295 (80 S. E. 1016).

Attempt to produce abortion. Circumstantial evidence upheld. 

Rosette, 5 Ga. App. 492 (63 S. E. 513).

Character of female and proof that female upon whom abortion was performed is a lewd woman, not admissible. Gullatt, 14 Ga. 

App. 53 (7) (80 S. E. 340).

The female upon whom a criminal abortion has been performed is not an accomplice with the perpetrator of the offense, and can not be indicted for the offense. Gullatt, 14 Ga. App. 53 (9) (80 S. E. 340).

Defendant's efforts to cause abortion relevant as tending to show carnal intercourse, on trial for seduction. Odum, 21 Ga. App. 310 (2) (94 S. E. 257); Parker, 11 Ga. App. 251 (2) (75 S. E. 437).

Evidence, although slight, sufficient. Gardner, 94 Ga. 403 (20 S. 

E. 132).

Evidence not sufficient to convict. Brown, 125 Ga. 8 (53 S. E. 767).

Distinction between the offenses described in §§ 26-1101 and 

26-1102 should be charged. Barrow, 121 Ga. 187 (8) (48 S. E. 950).

Evidence that accused furnished room, in which crime of abortion was to be performed, with knowledge, at the time it was furnished, that criminal abortion was to be performed, did not render him an accessory before the fact. Snell, 13 Ga. App. 158, 165 (79 S. E. 71).

Evidence that accused, charged as accessory before the fact, was acquainted with female upon whom criminal abortion was performed, and has been seen in her company a short time prior to the crime, admissible. Gullatt, 14 Ga. App. 53 (2) (80 S. E. 340).

In prosecuting accessory, evidence as to the pregnancy of female, admissible. Gullatt, 14 Ga. App. 53 (2) (80 S. E. 340).

SPECIFIC CRIMES 

245 Declaration of woman to defendant as to pregnancy and age of foetus, admissible, to show motive and defendant's knowledge of pregnancy. Sullivan, 121 Ga. 183 (1) (48 S. E. 949).

Evidence, on trial for abortion, that defendant committed same offense on a different woman several years before, not admissible. 

Hunter, 45 Ga. App. 512 (165 S. E. 314). 

See also: Homicide and Foeticide. 

3. ACCESSORIES. 

§§ 26-601, 26-602, 26-603, 26-604, 26-605, 26-606, 26-1104, 26-4601, 26-4602, 26-4603, 26-4604. 

Punishment. Accessory before the fact, except where otherwise provided, shall receive the same punishment that is prescribed for the principal in the first degree.

Accessory after the fact, except where otherwise provided, shall be punished as for a misdemeanor.

Receiving and harboring guilty persons, if crime punishable by death or confinement and labor in the penitentiary: Not less than one, nor more than three years in the penitentiary. 

Harboring convicts: If felony convict: Not less than one nor more than four years in the penitentiary. If misdemeanor convict: As for misdemeanor. 

Compounding crimes: Felony: Not less than one nor more than five years in the penitentiary.

Compounding penalties: Misdemeanor. 

Advisers to kill infant: Accessory before the fact;

same punishment as principal. 

a. INDICTMENT. 

charge and accuse.. before the fact to...for that the said...... .a certain.. .with the offense of accessory being absent at described as... the time of the commission of the crime, did procure, counsel, and command one..... and of the value of................Dollars, to unlawfully take and carry away, with intent to steal the same, contrary, etc. . . . (Approved: Riggins, 116 Ga. 592, 593 (42 S. E. 707).) Joint: in the name and in behalf of the citizens of Geor- .with the offense of accessory before being absent at the gia, charge and accuse....... the fact to murder, for that the said..... time of the commission of the crime aforesaid, in the manner and form aforesaid, by said…………………………………….., did yet then and there unlawfully, feloniously, willfully and of malice aforethought procure, counsel and command the said to commit the crime of murder, as aforesaid. And the jurors aforesaid, upon their oaths aforesaid, do

say that... -" being absent at the time of the commission of said. crime of murder, did then and there unlawfully, feloniously, willfully, and of malice aforethought procure, counsel, and command the said......... ..to commit the said crime in manner and form afore- (Approved: Rawlins, 124 Ga. 31, 35 (52 S. E. said, contrary 1).) 

Indictment charging that one being absent "did procure, counsel and command" the crime to be committed-sufficient. Need not allege how he did it. Rawlins, 124 Ga. 31 (4) (52 S. E. 1); Snell, 13 

Ga. App. 158 (1) (79 S. E. 71); Golding, 30 Ga. App. 30 (4) (116 S.

E. 881). "Procure, counsel, and command" as used in indictment, means also "incite, encourage, cause." Snell, 13 Ga. App. 158, 167 (79 S. 

E. 71); Gullatt, 14 Ga. App. 53 (80 S. E. 340).

Principal and accessory before the fact may be charged in the same count. Rawlins, 124 Ga. 31 (52 S. E. 1); Bishop, 118 Ga. 799 

Where the indictment charges the accused in different counts of murder, as principal in the first degree, principal in the second degree, and accessory before the fact, state is not obliged to elect on which count it will try him. Stewart, 58 Ga. 577 (3); Freeman, 35 

Ga. App. 223 (1) (132 S. E. 782); Fry, 141 Ga. 789 (82 S. E. 135).

Name of principal, if known, must be alleged; if unknown, it must be so alleged, and proof of the crime by anyone will suffice. Simmons, 4 Ga. 465; Whitehead, 41 Ga. App. 466 (153 S. E. 428).

Indictment should allege that principal has been tried and convicted; name, if known, must be alleged, and proved. Jordan, 56 

Ga. 92; Roberts, 18 Ga. App. 529 (89 S. E. 1055); Whitehead, 41 Ga. 

App. 466 (153 S. E. 428); Indictment may allege, however, that principal offender can not be taken so as to be prosecuted and convicted. Smiley, 23 Ga. App. 317 (98 S. E. 125); Rogers, 138 Ga. 750 

Principal and accessory after the fact can not be jointly indicted, where prosecution is for receiving stolen goods. Smiley, 23 Ga. 

App. 317 (98 S. E. 125).

Indictment as principal does not warrant conviction as an accessory before the fact. Hately, 15 Ga. 346 (2); except in misdemeanors. Loeb, 6 Ga. App. 23, 27 (64 S. E. 338).

Indictment as principal does not warrant conviction as an accessory after the fact. McCoy, 52 Ga. 287 (3); Lanier, 141 Ga. 17 (2), 19 (80 S. E. 5).

SPECIFIC CRIMES 

247 On indictment as accessory one can not be convicted on proof that he was "aiding and abetting AT the fact." Riggins, 116 Ga. 592 (42 S. E. 707).

Misdemeanors. 

There are no accessories in misdemeanors.

All who procure, counsel, command, aid, or abet the commission of a misdemeanor are regarded by the law as principal offenders, and may be indicted as such. The indictment may be joint against all those connected with the criminal enterprise, or it may be several against any one of them. Loeb, 6 Ga. App. 23 (64 S. E. 338); Blalock, 40 Ga. App. 242, 245 (149 S. E. 297); Davis, 40 Ga. App. 164, 165 (148 S. E. 918); White, 43 Ga. App. 748 (1) (159 S. E. 897).

Whether the indictment is joint or several, any particular defendant accused therein of having committed the misdemeanor may be convicted by proof either that he directly and personally enacted the criminal transaction, or that he procured, counseled, commanded, aided or abetted the criminal transaction of another, who was the direct and immediate actor. Loeb, 6 Ga. App. 23 (1-b) (64 

S. E. 338).

Insufficiency. Although the indictment is insufficient to charge defendant as an accessory, nevertheless, if the allegations are sufficient to charge another crime, it will be so treated. The true character of an accusation is not fixed by the denomination given it by the pleader, but by its allegations. McKissick, 11 Ga. App. 721 (1) (76 S. E. 71). 

Indictment, charging "accessory after the fact," nothing more appearing, charges misdemeanor. Rogers, 138 Ga. 750 (2) (75 S. 

E. 1130). 

b. GENERAL. 

Misdemeanors. There are no accessories in misdemeanors. All participating are principals. Loeb, 6 Ga. App. 23 (1) (64 S. E. 338); 

Blalock, 40 Ga. App. 242, 245 (149 S. E. 297); Davis, 40 Ga. App. 

164, 165 (14 S. E. 918); White, 43 Ga. App. 748 (1) (159 S. E. 897).

Who is an accessory. §§ 26-601 and 26-602 should be construed together; and, so construed, one who aids and abets the commission of a crime by knowingly contributing to its commission would seem to "procure" its commission, in the meaning of this section. Snell, 13 Ga. App. 158, 167 (79 S. E. 71).

Participation in felonious design necessary to render one an accessory. Mere presence and participation in general transaction not sufficient. Fudge, 148 Ga. 149 (2) (95 S. E. 980); Gower, 166 Ga. 

500 (3) (143 S. E. 593).

One can be both, accessory before and after the fact.

Minor, 58 Ga. 552 (5). 

Difference between receiver of stolen goods and accessory after the fact. Receiver of stolen goods is not an accessory after the fact. 

Springer, 102 Ga. 447 (1) (2) (30 S. E. 971).

If an act which constitutes one a technical accessory has by statute been made an independent crime, he thereby becomes a principal of such new offense, and the law applicable to the trial of accessories does not apply. Stone, 118 Ga. 705 (1) (45 S. E. 630). Suborner of perjury is not an accessory. Stone, 118 Ga. 705 (2) (45 S. E. 630).

One may be an accessory before the fact to the crime of arson. 

Smith, 46 Ga. 298. To an attempt to commit arson. Howard, 109 

Ga. 137 (1) (34 S. E. 330).

Incest. Female accessory. Coercion no excuse, unless it amounts to rape. Raiford, 68 Ga. 672; Taylor, 110 Ga. 150 (5) (35 S. E. 161); 

Yother, 120 Ga. 204 (47 S. E. 555); Jennings, 13 Ga. App. 678, 680 (79 S. E. 756).

One acting under duress, if there is a present and immediate danger of life or member, or there is a reasonable cause to believe this to be the case, and an actual belief, is no accessory. Burns, 89 Ga. 

527 (5) (15 S. E. 748); Pirkle, 11 Ga. App. 98 (2) (74 S. E. 709).

One who is present at a still when whiskey is being made, and who personally assists, is guilty of making whiskey, even though hired. Thomas, 24 Ga. App. 350 (1) (100 S. E. 760); Lindsay, 32 

Ga. App. 74 (1) (2) (122 S. E. 649); Robinson, 43 Ga. App. 129, 130 (157 S. E. 884).

One who in Barrow County procures an agent to go to Hall County and there to buy and bring whiskey in Gwinnett County, wherein agent is intercepted and arrested with whiskey on return journey, is guilty as an accessory. Jackson, 154 Ga. 544 (114 S. E. 811).

Although ordinary is guilty of embezzlement, yet where he is indicted as an accessory to larceny in procuring another to commit theft of county property left in his charge, conviction upheld. 

Groves, 76 Ga. 808 (1).

One incapable of committing the crime in question, can still be accessory, and may be convicted for assisting. There are many of fenses, which can only be committed by particular classes of the community; bigamy by married persons, rape, seduction and bastardy by males; larceny after trust by bailees; embezzlement by officers, etc. Bishop, 118 Ga. 799, 801 (45 S. E. 614); Bartlett, 27 Ga. 

App. 7 (1) (107 S. E. 347).

SPECIFIC CRIMES 

249 Although under § 26-2803 only officers or employees can be principals in the first degree to the crime of embezzlement, others disconnected with the company may be guilty as principals in the second degree, or as accessories before or after the fact. Bishop, 118 

Ga. 799 (3) (45 S. E. 614).

Traps. When one is informed that another intends to commit an offense against him or his property, the law permits him to afford opportunities for its commission, and lay traps which may result in the detection of the offender. To this end he may employ another to act with the intending criminal, and be present with him at the time the crime is to be committed; and if the intending criminal does himself acts which would constitute the offense, he will not, when charged with the crime, be protected from punishment by reason of the fact that, at the time the criminal act was performed by him, another, who was there with the knowledge, consent, and approval of the victim, and even by his direct employment, aided in and encouraged its perpetration. In such a case, however, it must appear that the person charged with the offense did himself everything necessary to make out a complete offense against the law. Nothing that was done by the person present with the knowledge and consent of the victim will be imputed to the accused; and if, in order to constitute the offense, it is necessary that something done by such person shall be imputed to the accused, then the prosecution will fail. Or, if it appears that the intent to commit the crime did not originate with the accused, but was suggested by the person present with him, with the knowledge and approval of the victim, the prosecution will likewise fail. Arrington, 48 Ga. App. 64, 69, 70 (171 S. E. 874). 

City ordinance. Accessories, in violating city ordinance, punished as principals. (Misdemeanor.) Raoul, 15 Ga. App. 212 (82 

S. E. 763); White, 43 Ga. App. 748 (1) (159 S. E. 897).

Applicable to every felony. Every statutory felony, when incorporated in the body of the criminal law, becomes subject to existing regulations as to accessories, indictment, evidence, and procedure. 

Bishop, 118 Ga. 799 (1) (45 S. E. 614) ; Bartlett, 27 Ga. App. 7 (1) (107 S. E. 347). 

Principal's guilt. To convict accessory, principal must be proved guilty beyond reasonable doubt. Rawlins, 124 Ga. 31 (20) (52 S.

E. 1). Any evidence is admissible, which would be admissible if the principal were on trial. (Id.) Whitehead, 41 Ga. App. 466, 468 (153 S. E. 428). 

Defendant can waive conviction of principal and go to trial on

charge preferred against him. Ford, 162 Ga. 422 (4-c) (134 S. E. 

95). Waiver can be express or implied. (Id.) Perry, 41 Ga. App. 

651 (154 S. E. 211).

Conviction of the principal is admissible in evidence against the accessory, and even raises a presumption of the principal's guilt. 

Such presumption is not conclusive and may be attacked. Cantrell, 141 Ga. 98, 103 (80 S. E. 649). "Conviction" of principal does not necessarily mean sentence. 

Cantrell, 141 Ga. 98 (8), 104 (80 S. E. 649).

Requirement that principal shall be convicted before trial of accessory is complied with by showing conviction of any one of three alleged principals. Braxley, 17 Ga. App. 196 (3) (86 S. E. 425).

Requirement is complied with, where one of several principals has pleaded guilty at such time as permits submission of proof of conviction. Braxley, 17 Ga. App. 196 (3) (86 S. E. 425).

A plea of guilty stands upon the same footing as a conviction by a jury, and has the same force and effect as a verdict of guilty. 

Whitehead, 41 Ga. App. 466 (a) (153 S. E. 428). That principal pleaded guilty after commencement of trial of accessory, no cause for complaint. Perry, 41 Ga. App. 651 (1) (154 S. E. 211); Cantrell, 141 Ga. 98 (1), 104 (80 S. E. 649).

Parol evidence of the principal's conviction, although irregular, not being best and highest evidence, if admitted without objection, satisfactory. Martin, 95 Ga. 478 (2) (20 S. E. 271).

Not good ground for continuance, that there is a conviction of the principal, but that the principal intends to make a motion for new trial. Loyd, 45 Ga. 57 (5).

The requirement that the guilt of the principal must be shown before accessory is prosecuted, is not satisfied by showing that the principal has been prosecuted and acquitted because he was incapable of committing a crime. (Child under ten years of age.) 

Edwards, 80 Ga. 127 (1) (4 S. E. 268).

Charge. The Court is not required to charge the jury as to the guilt of the principal, in prosecution as an accessory, where evidence conclusively showed guilt of principal defendant. Gullatt, 14 Ga. 

App. 53 (11) (80 S. E. 340).

Accused, charged with being present, aiding and abetting another who fired the fatal shot, desiring more specific instructions as to necessity of believing such other guilty beyond reasonable doubt as condition precedent to conviction of accused, should have made

SPECIFIC CRIMES 

251 appropriate request thereof. Johnson, 148 Ga. 546 (3) (97 S. E. 515). 

Error to charge that defendant would be guilty as an accessory after the fact if he concealed the crime or harbored the criminal to prevent the arrest. The language of the law is, "conceals it from the officers of the law and harbors." (See § 26-604.) Loyd, 42 Ga. 221. 

Error to charge that the defendant would be guilty as an accessory if he aided and abetted in the killing of the deceased. It should have been confined to the aiding and abetting the co-defendant, charged as the principal. Brown, 17 Ga. App. 300 (4) (86

S. E. 661). 

The Court was requested to charge that, as all of the defendants were accused as principals, defendant on trial could not be convicted as an accessory. In the general charge the Court instructed. the jury that defendant could not be convicted unless he was present and actually participated. This was sufficient. Carter, 106 Ga. 

372, 375 (32 S. E. 345).

Verdict. In misdemeanor cases the general verdict of "guilty" is the proper form, regardless whether defendant is charged as a principal or accessory. Littlefield, 22 Ga. App. 782 (2) (97 S. E. 

259); Sudan, 34 Ga. App. 146 (128 S. E. 692).

On the trial of a defendant indicted as a principal he can not be convicted as being an accessory after the fact. McCoy, 52 Ga. 

287; Lanier, 141 Ga. 17, 19 (80 S. E. 5).

Detective, procuring through an agent, another to commit crime of larceny from the house of article under value of fifty dollars for the purpose of claiming reward for detection, convicted as principal. (Misdemeanor.) Slaughter, 113 Ga. 284 (1) (38 S. E. 854); Mitchell, 20 Ga. App. 778 (93 S. E. 709).

General authority by an employer to his clerk to sell unlawfully, will render him responsible for any single sale made by the clerk under such authority. Faircloth, 73 Ga. 426 (1) (2).

Conspiracy. Common law offense of conspiracy has not been incorporated in the Code, yet conspiring with another to commit an offense may be an element in the guilt of one charged as an accessory before the fact. Bishop, 118 Ga. 799 (3) (45 S. E. 614).

Punishment. The fact that the principal has been punished as for misdemeanor does not require similar punishment for the accessory. Snow, 5 Ga. App. 608, 610 (63 S. E. 651); Morris, 84 Ga. 

7 (10 S. E. 368).

c. AIDING AND ABETTING. 

Definition. "Aid” is a plain homely word, with a meaning well and generally understood. "Abet" smacks more of technical terminology, but it is almost synonymous with "aid." The two words together comprehend all assistance given by acts, words, or encouragement, or by presence actual or constructive. Loeb, 6 

Ga. App. 23, 30 (64 S. E. 338).

In criminal law the word "abet" means to encourage, or set another on to commit a crime. To abet another to commit a crime is to command, procure, or counsel him to do it; and presence and participation are necessary to constitute one an abettor. Brooks, 128 Ga. 261, 263 (57 S. E. 483).

The above definition explained and distinguished. Cain, 41 Ga. 

App. 333, 337 (153 S. E. 79).

Aiding and abetting to compound a felony. Hays, 15 Ga. App. 

386 (1) (4) (83 S. E. 502); Hays, 142 Ga. 592 (83 S. E. 236).

Facts constituting aiding and abetting. If a man should willingly go into an unlawful enterprise and engage in it or abet in it, though he himself might not point a gun or pistol, yet if he was a well-wisher to it, took part in it, and aided in it, he would be just as guilty as the man who pointed the pistol. Pirkle, 11 Ga. App. 

98, 101 (74 S. E. 709).

Felony; aiding, abetting; principal in second degree. In murder, where principal committed the actual killing, evidence that the accomplice was present, aiding and abetting, sufficient to justify conviction as principal in second degree. Lewis, 136 Ga. 355 (2) (71 S. E. 417); Robinson, 158 Ga. 47, 50 (122 S. E. 886). But it is error to charge that if one defendant was present and committed the actual criminal act, and the co-defendant was present and knew about the crime to be committed, he, the co-defendant, would be a principal in the second degree. Mere knowledge, without participation, aiding and abetting, not sufficient. Bryant, 15 Ga. App. 

535 (2) (83 S. E. 795). However, circumstantial evidence of common design sufficient. Hines, 16 Ga. App. 411 (85 S. E. 452).

Mere presence and participation in the act of killing a human being is not conclusive evidence of consent and concurrence in the perpetration of the act by a defendant sought to be responsible for the homicide as aiding and abetting the actual perpetrator, unless such defendant participated in the felonious design of the person killing. Brooks, 128 Ga. 261 (57 S. E. 483). Distinguished in Tanner, 161 Ga. 193, 198 (130 S. E. 64).

SPECIFIC CRIMES 

253 Keeping watch, while other perpetrators are committing the crime, and holding the horse and buggy so that the confederates might escape, makes one principal in second degree. Sufficient aiding and abetting. Pirkle, 11 Ga. App. 98, 101 (74 S. E. 709). The one keeping guard will be guilty of murder, if murder ensues. 

Berryhill, 151 Ga. 416 (1) (107 S. E. 158); Thompson, 166 Ga. 758, 775, 776 (144 S. E. 301).

Manslaughter. The killing was not reduced from murder to manslaughter merely because the man who fired the gun and the man who aided and abetted the act might have thought that the gun "would not kill a man that far.' Burnett, 160 Ga. 593, 599 (128 

S. E. 796).

Husband. In this State the husband is the head of the family, and where intoxicating liquors are kept in the house occupied by himself and his family, he is guilty of aiding and abetting in the commission of a misdemeanor, if he knowingly allows such liquors to remain there, irrespective of who owns them or who puts them there. And this is true although the husband has deeded the premises to his wife, previously. Buchanan, 34 Ga. App. 155 (1) (128 S. E. 686); Isom, 32 Ga. App. 75 (1) (122 S. E. 722).

Pilot car. Can not condemn car acting as pilot to other cars hauling liquor, on theory that there was an aiding and abetting, without proving that pilot car contained liquor also. Underwood, 29 Ga. App. 479 (115 S. E. 919).

Murder. Concealing the crime and the body. Where A, knowing that B is guilty of murder, assists B in concealing the crime and the body of the murdered person, A is not thereby guilty of "receiving, harboring, or concealing" the murderer, within the meaning of § 26-4601. Heath and Washington, 160 Ga. 678 (128 S. E. 913), and also 34 Ga. App. 218 (128 S. E. 914). 

d. CONSPIRACY. 

Definition. A conspiracy may be defined as a combination or agreement between two or more persons to do something that is unlawful. ... The existence or non-existence of a conspiracy, or common intent, may be established by proof of acts and conduct as well as by proof of express agreement. In other words, in order to make out conspiracy, it is not necessary to prove that there was an express agreement. West, 155 Ga. 482, 485 (117 S. E. 380). See this decision for full charge on conspiracy, approved by Supreme Court.

Where a conspiracy is shown, the act of one becomes the act of all, in so far as the furtherance of the conspiracy is concerned; and each is as fully responsible for the acts of the others in carrying out the common purpose as if he himself had committed the act. 

Langston, 42 Ga. App. 484 (1) (156 S. E. 632). This rule applies equally in the prosecution of resulting crime and resulting tort. 

Hill, 19 Ga. App. 334 (91 S. E. 434).

Conspiracy formed in one county and larceny in another, responsibility of conspirator who remained in first county while larceny is being committed, not lessened. Danzley, 25 Ga. App. 170 (11) (102 S. E. 915). 

The acts and sayings of one accomplice during the pendency of the common criminal enterprise are admissible against the other. 

Though evidence is objectionable because conspiracy was not proved, if it be afterwards shown, it renders the evidence competent. 

Tate, 41 Ga. App. 300 (5) (152 S. E. 609). Acts and conduct of one accomplice during the pendency of the wrongful act, not only in its perpetration, but also in its subsequent concealment, are admissible against each other. Ethridge, 163 Ga. 186 (11) (135 S. E. 72).

Acts and declarations of a co-defendant or alleged conspirator are admissible against the other only when made and done during the pendency of the criminal enterprise and in furtherance of its object. The declarations and conduct of one joint conspirator, made after the enterprise is ended, are inadmissible except against the person making them, and against others must be rejected as narrative merely of past occurrences. Wall, et al., 153 Ga. 309 (2-a) (2-b) (112 S. E. 142); Tanner, 161 Ga. 193 (1) (130 S. E. 64).

Evidence of conspiracy. Conspiracy may be shown by circumstantial evidence. Darr, 44 Ga. App. 201 (1) (160 S. E. 824). 

e. EVIDENCE. 

Guilt of principal. To show principal's guilt, any evidence that would be admissible against principal is admissible against accessory. Rawlins, 124 Ga. 31 (20) (52 S. E. 1); Whitehead, 41 Ga. App. 

466, 468 (153 S. E. 436).

Record of conviction of principal conclusive evidence of conviction and prima facie evidence of his guilt. Studstill, 7 Ga. 2 (4); accessory may show that principal, although convicted, is innocent. 

Anderson, 63 Ga. 675 (3); Snow, 5 Ga. App. 608 (2) (63 S. E. 651).

Where record of principal's conviction is introduced, error not to charge the jury that such record is to be taken only as evidence of guilt of principal and that the guilt of the accessory has to be

SPECIFIC CRIMES 

255 established independently. Such record is no evidence against the accessory. Thompson, 16 Ga. App. 832 (3) (84 S. E. 591).

On trial of alleged accessory, the free and voluntary declarations and admissions of the principal, are admissible to show his (principal's) guilt; but neither declarations, nor admissions of an alleged principal which merely tend to incriminate the alleged accessory are admissible against the latter, if made after the completion of the criminal enterprise. Howard, 109 Ga. 137 (4) (34 S. E. 330); Gullatt, 14 Ga. App. 53 (3) (80 S. E. 340).

Plea of guilty of principal does not raise any presumption of the guilt of accused as accessory before the fact, but is competent to prove that such plea has been entered as showing the guilt of the principal. Cantrell, 141 Ga. 98 (1) (80 S. E. 649); Whitehead, 41 

Ga. App. 466, 468 (153 S. E. 428).

In misdemeanors, testimony of accomplice need not be corroborated. Birdsong, 120 Ga. 850 (1) (48 S. E. 329).

Evidence showing accused guilty as absolute perpetrator, in felony, indictment charging him as an accessory before the fact, conviction not warranted. Riggins, 116 Ga. 592 (42 S. E. 707). 

Motive. Admissible to show that alleged accessory had a motive for desiring the crime to be committed and that he attempted to induce another than principal to commit it. Howard, 109 Ga. 137 (3) (34 S. E. 330); Pope, 171 Ga. 655, 659 (156 S. E. 599).

Res gestae. What was said to a thief at the time of the larceny is admissible against his accessory after the fact, as part of the res gestae. Parsons, 43 Ga. 197 (2). 

Murder. Slight corroborating evidence, held: First, insufficient; later, sufficient. Insufficient: Bivins, 144 Ga. 340 (87 S. E. 285). 

Sufficient: Bivins, 147 Ga. 229 (1) (93 S. E. 213). 

f. ACCOMPLICES. 

Who is an accomplice? The test for determining whether a witness is an accomplice is, "Could the witness himself have been indicted for the offense, either as a principal or as accessory?" Stone, 118 Ga. 705 (3) (45 S. E. 630).

Measured by the rule of determining an accomplice, a witness for the State, who was seven years old, could not have been indicted for the crime, and was not an accomplice. LaFray, 48 Ga. 

App. 133 (172 S. E. 115).

Participation in commission of the same criminal act, and in the execution of a common intent is necessary to render one criminal, in a legal sense, an accomplice of another, and if between two per-

sons who may be engaged in a criminal enterprise, in the execution of which two separate offenses may be committed, there is not this concurrence of act and intent, though each may commit a crime, neither is, in a legal contemplation, an accomplice with the other. 

Springer, 102 Ga. 447 (1) (30 S. E. 971); Sellers, 41 Ga. App. 572, 573 (153 S. E. 782).

Not necessarily an accomplice, who was at or near the crime, and concealed it, if he did not aid, abet, procure or participate in it. Lowery, 72 Ga. 649 (1); Allen, 74 Ga. 769 (1); Gower, 166 Ga. 

500 (3) (143 S. E. 593).

One informed of another's intent to commit a crime, and afterward concealing it, is not an accomplice. Bradley, 2 Ga. App. 622 (1) (58 S. E. 1064).

Question for jury. Where there is a conflict of evidence as to whether witness is an accomplice, question for jury under proper instructions. Suddeth, 112 Ga. 407 (2) (37 S. E. 747).

One is not an accomplice if evidence fails to prove him to be one, although jointly indicted with principal. Walker, 118 Ga. 

757 (1) (45 S. E. 608); Gower, 166 Ga. 500 (3) (143 S. E. 593).

Neither joinder of witness in indictment, nor plea of guilty by him make him necessarily an accomplice. It is for the jury to decide, from consideration of testimony wherein he admits presence but denies participation. Hargrove, 125 Ga. 270 (1) (54 S. E. 164); 

Hays, 9 Ga. App. 829 (1) (72 S. E. 285); Powell, 14 Ga. App. 484 (3) (81 S. E. 396); Sellers, 41 Ga. App. 572, 573 (153 S. E. 782).

In his instruction to the jury the Court properly left to them the determination of the question whether certain of the defendants were accomplices. Pruitt, 36 Ga. 736; Hargrove, 125 Ga. 270 (54 

S. E. 164).

Where evidence is conflicting as to whether one is an accomplice or not, and the question is left to the jury, they should be distinctly informed as to what is necessary to constitute one an accomplice. 

Suddeth, 112 Ga. 407 (37 S. E. 747).

Conflicting testimony. Uncorroborated testimony of one, who admitted and afterward denied complicity, could be accepted as sufficient corroboration, if jury so find. Ware, 18 Ga. App. 107 (89 

S. E. 155).

Burden of proving witness accomplice is on the party alleging it for the purpose of invoking rule. Hargrove, 125 Ga. 270, 274 (54 S. E. 164).

SPECIFIC CRIMES 

257 Receiver of stolen goods. The principal thief is not an accomplice of the receiver of stolen goods. Birdsong, 120 Ga. 850 (1) (48

S. E. 329). Nor is the receiver of stolen goods an accomplice of the principal thief. Bradley, 2 Ga. App. 622 (1-b) (58 S. E. 1064); 

Goodbread, 29 Ga. App. 195, 198 (115 S. E. 44). But receiver of stolen goods might be found in addition an accomplice. Question for jury. Wilson, 8 Ga. App. 816 (2) (70 S. E. 193).

An accessory after the fact is not an accomplice. Lowery, 72 Ga. 

649, 654; Allen, 74 Ga. 769; Springer, 102 Ga. 447, 452 (30 S. E. 971); 

Walker, 118 Ga. 757 (45 S. E. 608); Bradley, 2 Ga. App. 622 (1-a) (58 S. E. 1064).

Abortion. Female not an accomplice, as she can not be indicted. 

Gullatt, 14 Ga. App. 53 (9) (80 S. E. 340).

Seduction. Seduced woman is not an accomplice of the seducer. 

Washington, 124 Ga. 423 (1) (52 S. E. 910).

Liquor. The buyer of liquor is not an accomplice of the seller. 

Gamble, 4 Ga. App. 845 (1) (62 S. E. 544).

Larceny. Fact that stolen automobile was brought to the home of witness, who allowed conspirators to leave it there, but who advised them to take it back to owner and who promptly notified sheriff, did not warrant charge upon question as to whether or not witness was an accomplice. Danzley, 25 Ga. App. 170 (12) (102 

S. E. 915).

Corroboration of accomplice. In felony cases testimony of accomplice must be corroborated. § 38-121. Jennings, 13 Ga. App. 

678, 680 (79 S. E. 756). In misdemeanors testimony of an accomplice need not be corroborated. Davis, 23 Ga. App. 5 (1) (97 S. E. 263).

Amount of corroboration. Corroborating facts should relate to some material matter in issue, and should in some way connect the accused with the crime and point to his guilt. But it is not necessary that they point with such force as to authorize verdict of guilty independent of testimony of accomplice. Childers, 52 Ga. 

106; Partee, 67 Ga. 570, 571; Goodbread, 29 Ga. App. 195 (4) (115 

S. E. 44).

Corroborating testimony must connect defendant with the crime independently from testimony of the accomplice. Thompson, 25 

Ga. App. 29 (102 S. E. 453).

Corroboration in every material particular-not required. Goodbread, 29 Ga. App. 195 (4) (115 S. E. 44).

Not required that this corroboration shall of itself be sufficient to warrant a verdict. Evans, 27 Ga. App. 316 (2) (108 S. E. 129); 

Goodbread, 29 Ga. App. 195, 198, 199 (115 S. E. 44); Whaley, 177 

Ga. 757 (171 S. E. 290).

It is not sufficient corroboration of an accomplice that the witness corroborated the accomplice as to the time, place and circumstances of the transaction, if there is nothing except the statement of the accomplice to show any connection of the defendant with the crime. 

Brewer, 47 Ga. App. 759 (17) (171 S. E. 454).

The rule is well settled that the testimony of an accomplice in a felony case must be corroborated by some independent fact or circumstance, which, taken by itself, leads to the inference not only that the crime has been committed but that the defendant is implicated in its commission. Proof of the corpus delicti, independently of the evidence of the accomplice, is corroborative of the guilt of the accomplice, but does not at all corroborate his testimony as to the guilt of another. Sanders, 46 Ga. App. 175 (1) (167 S. E. 207); 

Whitehead, 46 Ga. App. 176 (167 S. E. 204).

Slight evidence from extraneous source identifying accused as participator in criminal act, sufficient. Evans, 78 Ga. 351; Evans, 27 Ga. App. 316 (2) (108 S. E. 129); Little, 31 Ga. App. 145 (120 

S. E. 33); Williams, 40 Ga. App. 217 (2) (149 S. E. 292).

Corroboration need not necessarily extend to main or vitally controlling question. Duncan, 97 Ga. 180 (2) (25 S. E. 182).

Corroboration of accomplice must be by other evidence which independently of the testimony of accomplice, directly connects the accused with the crime. Reversible error to charge that "unless such testimony was corroborated by other evidence which in connection with the testimony of the accomplice, connected the accused with the crime," the accused can not be convicted. Allen, 40 Ga.

App. 657 (150 S. E. 863). Facts which create merely a grave suspicion of the defendant's guilt are insufficient to corroborate the testimony of the accomplice. Even where the facts in proof so far agree with the evidence of the accomplice as well-nigh to convert a grave suspicion against the accused into a moral conviction of his guilt, yet if these facts, considered entirely apart from and independently of the evidence of the accomplice, fail in themselves, and without regard to the testimony of the accomplice, to connect the accused with the commission of the crime, a conviction is unauthorized. Jolly, 41 Ga. App. 494 (1) (153 S. E. 432). (Italics by the Court.)

SPECIFIC CRIMES 

259 Sufficiency of corroboration is for jury. Walters, 41 Ga. App. 

570 (2) (153 S. E. 925).

Corroborating testimony may be direct or circumstantial. Goff, 37 Ga. App. 471 (140 S. E. 793).

Circumstantial evidence. Where corroborating evidence is circumstantial, and not inconsistent with innocence, it will be disregarded and will not be considered sufficient corroboration to convict. Smith, 5 Ga. App. 833 (63 S. E. 917).

The conviction being dependent upon the evidence of an accomplice, and there being no corroborating circumstances which in themselves and independently of the testimony of the accomplice directly connect the accused with the crime, it was error to overrule his motion for new trial. Scott, 32 Ga. App. 52 (122 S. E. 

647); Goff, 37 Ga. App. 471 (140 S. E. 793).

Corpus delicti. Proof of the corpus delicti alone not sufficient corroboration. Altman, 5 Ga. App. 833 (63 S. E. 928); Smith, 7 Ga. 

App. 781, 783 (68 S. E. 335).

Time, place and circumstances. It is well settled that corroboration as to time, place, and circumstances will not alone suffice. 

Childers, 52 Ga. 106; Lynch, 158 Ga. 261 (123 S. E. 289).

Misdemeanor. In misdemeanor jury may believe uncorroborated testimony of accomplice, even though impeached, in preference to many witnesses. Allen, 39 Ga. App. 642 (5) (148 S. E. 167); Dobbs, 44 Ga. App. 749 (1) (162 S. E. 845).

Confession. Confession of accused sufficient corroboration. Hugle, 147 Ga. 35 (2) (92 S. E. 646). 

Confession is direct evidence. Mitchell, 18 Ga. App. 501 (4) (89 

S. E. 602).

Proof that defendant has made contradictory statements, not sufficient corroboration. Roddenberry, 37 Ga. App. 359 (3) (140 S. E. 386).

Where defendant was previously confronted with accomplice, and accomplice stated that defendant was guilty, defendant's failure to deny it was sufficient corroboration. Holt, 28 Ga. App. 758 (113 

S. E. 105). 

Witness swearing that he and accused jointly committed the crime, can not be corroborated by showing that witness had previously pleaded guilty. Branson, 99 Ga. 194 (24 S. E. 404).

Accomplice dead. The testimony of an accomplice, since deceased, given upon a trial in a court of inquiry, may be proved on the final trial of the same case, by any one who heard it, and who

professes to remember the substance of the entire testimony. 

Hardin, 107 Ga. 718 (1) (33 S. E. 700).

Incest. On trial for incestuous adultery, evidence of the woman's pregnancy is not sufficient corroboration. Taylor, 110 Ga. 150 (5) 

Burglary. Independent evidence of defendant's recent possession of stolen goods, if sufficiently identified, sufficient corroboration, unless satisfactorily explained. Johnson, 92 Ga. 577 (4) (20 

S. E. 8); Chance, 33 Ga. App. 137, 138 (125 S. E. 730).

Tracks. Corroboration by tracks not sufficient, where it is not shown that tracks corresponded with tracks of defendant. Even though defendant had a deformed foot, and tracks showed corresponding irregularity. Lawson, 21 Ga. App. 140 (94 S. E. 52); 

Welborn, 25 Ga. App. 245 (103 S. E. 193).

Wife of accomplice. The wife of an accomplice is a competent witness to testify to any fact in a criminal proceeding not against her husband, if he be not on trial, and not affected by such testimony. Askea, 75 Ga. 356 (3).

Testimony of two or more accomplices. One accomplice can' corroborate another. Williams, 31 Ga. App. 293 (1-a) (120 S. E. 550).

Supreme Court overruling Williams, 31 Ga. App. 293 (1-a) (120 

S. E. 550): In felony cases the testimony of one accomplice can not be corroborated by other accomplices, no matter how many there may be, if there be no other evidence establishing the fact that the accused participated in the crime. Williams, 159 Ga. 728 (126 

S. E. 844). 

Supreme Court overruling Williams, 159 Ga. 728 (126 S. E. 844):

One may be legally convicted of a felony other than treason, or perjury, where the only evidence directly connecting him with the offense charged is the testimony of an accomplice, and where the only corroboration is the testimony of another accomplice. Pope, 171 Ga. 655 (156 S. E. 599); Pope, 42 Ga. App. 680 (157 S. E. 211).

Charge. In a felony case where an accomplice testifies, and where the testimony of another witness, who is not an accomplice, directly connects the defendant with the perpetration of the offense charged, the failure of the Court to charge, without request, upon the subject of corroboration of an accomplice, is not error. Wood, 29 Ga. 

App. 179 (114 S. E. 586). Not error to fail to charge the law as to corroboration of accomplice,-without request. Durham, 41 Ga.

g. VENUE. 

Accessories and accomplices are indictable and triable in the county where the principal crime was committed. Welch, 49 Ga.
