h. ACTS, CONDUCT, AND DECLARATIONS. 

Acts, conduct, and declarations of one conspirator pending the wrongful act, not alone in its actual perpetration, but also in its subsequent concealment, are admissible against another conspirator. (Italics by the Court.) Grace, 49 Ga. App. 306 (4) (174 S. E. 384). 

4. ADULTERATION. 

§§ 42-9901, 42-9905. 

Food, Liquor, Drugs. 

(Obstructing inspectors.) (Misdemeanor.) Indictment: 

did then and there unlawfully and with force and arms, sell adulterated food (liquor, or drugs); in that the said .....sold to......... -a portion of an animal, to wit, a cow, unfit for food, not manufactured, and said portion of said cow being a product of a diseased cow, and being that of a cow that had died otherwise than by slaughter, contrary, etc.

Not subject to demurrer, because of failure to show compliance with statutory provisions as to examination of food by or under the direction of the State chemist, notice to the defendant, determination by the commissioner of agriculture that the provisions of the pure food law had been violated, etc. Evitt, 23 Ga. App. 532 (1) (98 S. E. 737).

Not subject to demurrer because of failure to show how, or in what way the portion sold was unfit for food, or was diseased, or what kind of product of the diseased cow was sold. Evitt, 23 Ga. 

App. 532 (1) (98 S. E. 737). 

5. ADULTERY AND FORNICATION. 

§ 26-5801. 

(Misdemeanor.) a. INDICTMENT. 

Indictment approved in Griffin, 30 Ga. App. 185 (117 S. E. 470) : charge and accuse. .with the offense of

adultery and fornication; for that the said accused did on the........ day of in the year of 19., in the county aforesaid, unlawfully have sexual intercourse with, and did also live in a state of adultery with... they not being then and there lawfully intermarried, and he, the said.. then and there a married (man), and she, the said.. being then and there a married (woman), contrary, etc. 

Indictment in four counts: (1) . . . for that the said.. being in said county, on the........day of19, being then and there an unmarried (man), did then and there unlawfully and with force and arms commit fornication by cohabiting and having sexual intercourse with who was then and there an unmarried (woman), and did also live in a state of fornication with the said one.......... -" contrary, etc. (2) . and the jurors aforesaid, in the name and in behalf of the citizens of Georgia, further charge and accuse upon their oath, as aforesaid, ...with the offense of adultery, for that the said....... in said county, on the........day of................19...., being then and there a married (man), did then and there unlawfully and with force and arms commit adultery by cohabiting and having sexual intercourse with, and did also live in a state of adultery with.... who was then and there a married (woman), they not being then and there lawfully intermarried, contrary, etc. . (3) being then and there a married (man) did then and there unlawfully and with force and arms commit adultery and fornication by cohabiting and having sexual intercourse with, and did also live in a state of adultery and fornication with one..... trary, etc. who was then and there an unmarried (woman), con- (4). being then and there an unmarried (man) did then and there unlawfully and with force and arms commit adultery and fornication by cohabiting and having sexual intercourse with, and did also live in a state of adultery and fornication with one... trary, etc. who was then and there a married (woman), con- State not required to elect, where indictment was for adultery and fornication on four counts. Sutton, 124 Ga. 815 (53 S. E. 381).

Both parties joined in indictment. Indictments for adultery and fornication, or adultery or fornication, can not be found jointly

SPECIFIC CRIMES 

263 against the man and the woman charged; and an indictment against both will be quashed on demurrer before trial. Foster, 41 Ga. 583.

Indictment for adultery and fornication against one person is proper; offense joint, but remedy several. Wasden, 18 Ga. 264 (1).

Denomination of crime. Indictment need not denominate offense as adultery and fornication, if criminal acts, sufficient to constitute that crime, are alleged. Disharoon, 95 Ga. 351 (1) (22 S. E. 698); 

McGouldrick, 20 Ga. App. 185 (2) (92 S. E. 953); Alexander, 122 

Ga. 174 (50 S. E. 56).

Living in adultery and adultery charged in one count. Indictment charging in a single count adultery and fornication by the perpetration of a single act of intercourse, and by living together in a state of adultery and fornication, charges but one offense, and is not subject to demurrer on account of duplicity. Heath, 91 Ga. 126 (16 S. E. 657); Griffin, 30 Ga. App. 185 (1) (117 S. E. 470). 

Allegation of marriage. Indictment need not allege whether man and woman single or married. (Better practice to make allegations.) Hopper, 54 Ga. 389; Boggs, 11 Ga. App. 92 (1) (74 S. E. 716). 

Single act of adultery. Indictment charging living in adultery not supported by evidence of single act of adultery. (Better practice to make two counts.) McLeland, 25 Ga. 477; Lawson, 116 Ga. 

571 (42 S. E. 752).

The same rule applies to "living in a state of fornication." Winkles, 4 Ga. App. 559 (1) (61 S. E. 1128). Proof of merely one act, or occasional acts, of incontinuance, is not sufficient. (Id.) 

Seduction. Indictment charging married man with offense of seduction upon virtuous unmarried female, by other fraudulent means than by promise of marriage, was, against general demurrer, sufficient to charge statutory offense of adultery and fornication, although not sufficient to charge seduction, on special demurrer. 

McGouldrick, 20 Ga. App. 185 (1) (2) (92 S. E. 953).

Surplusage. The allegations in the indictment that the woman was taken "into the State of Tennessee to a hotel and a room in Soddy, Tennessee," might have been omitted from the indictment, but when inserted therein they become material and relevant, and could not be rejected as surplusage, and in absence of proof the verdict is not supported by evidence. Hightower, 39 Ga. App. 674 (148 

S. E. 300). (See leading case: Fulford, 50 Ga. 591.)

Husband and wife. Affidavit for warrant or accusation. Although by statute persons accused of adultery and fornication must

be severally indicted, and although the acquittal of one will not operate to acquit the other, the wife of the man participating in such criminal offense is not competent to testify against the woman accused thereof, since the man must be guilty if the guilt of the woman be established. Howard, 94 Ga. 587 (20 S. E. 426); Smith, 14 Ga. 

App. 614 (81 S. E. 912).

It follows that the wife can not make an affidavit which furnishes the basis for a warrant, or sign an accusation, charging another woman with adultery committed with the husband. Smith, 14 Ga. 

App. 614 (81 S. E. 912). Where such facts appear upon the face of the indictment or accusation, plea in abatement is proper remedy. 

Error to strike plea in abatement. Bell, 14 Ga. App. 809 (3) (82 

S. E. 376).

But whether an accusation in the city court charging a married man with adultery, is or is not invalid because it is founded upon affidavit made by his wife, yet where it does not appear on the face either of the affidavit or the accusation that the prosecutrix is the wife of the accused, the objection to the accusation can not be made by demurrer, before trial, or by motion in arrest of judgment after conviction. Starke, 97 Ga. 193 (23 S. E. 832).

Although husband is not competent to make an affidavit as basis for the prosecution of another man for adultery with affiant's wife, and although an affidavit charging the accused in this case with the crime stated was made by the husband and a warrant issued thereon, the accusation on which the accused was tried was based on a subsequent affidavit made by another person, who, with the solicitor of the city court in which the case was tried, signed the accusation as prosecutor, and it was held that the accusation was good. Batchelor, 41 Ga. App. 843 (155 S. E. 58).

Time of offense. Indictment charging the offense to have been committed on a certain day, and "on divers days before and after that time", avers the time with sufficient certainty. The words "on divers days before and after that time" can be rejected as surplusage. Cook, 11 Ga. 53.

Offense may be charged to have been committed on any day previous to the finding of the bill of indictment, and may be proved at any time within the period of limitation. Cook, 11 Ga. 53. 

b. GENERAL. 

Offenses distinguished. If one of the parties married, and the other single, both are guilty of adultery and fornication; if both married, each is guilty of adultery; if both single, each is guilty of

SPECIFIC CRIMES 

265 fornication. Bigby, 44 Ga. 344; Kendrick, 100 Ga. 360 (28 S. E. 120).

Adultery not shown without proof that both are married. Tison, 125 Ga. 7 (53 S. E. 809).

Rape distinguished. The offense of adultery and fornication is not included in the crime of rape; and under an indictment for rape the defendant can not be convicted of the lesser offense of fornication and adultery. Speer, 60 Ga. 381; Smith, 161 Ga. 421 (4) (131 

S. E. 163).

Gist of action for rape is the forcible attack, against the will. In adultery or fornication consent of both parties is the gist of the of fense. Holland, 161 Ga. 492 (138 S. E. 503). Arrest of judgment is the proper procedure. Holland, 161 Ga. 492 (138 S. E. 503).

Consent of female. Conviction of adultery and fornication can not be obtained where it appears that the female did not consent. 

The crime of adultery and fornication necessarily involves the idea of consent; and while consent in some instances may be procured by force, yet where force is used in the inception of the offense it must be at least shown that consent was finally induced thereby. Nephew, 5 Ga. App. 841 (63 S. E. 930).

Seduction and fornication distinguished. Seduction is based on confidence and affection, which engagement has engendered, whereas intercourse upon mere prospect of engagement or promises to marry is fornication. Morris, 14 Ga. App. 395, 398 (81 S. E. 257).

One charged with seduction may be convicted of the lesser crime of fornication. Roberts, 40 Ga. App. 732 (2) (151 S. E. 240). This is true, though it is not alleged that the defendant was a single man. 

Hopper, 54 Ga. 389.

Indictment charges seductión, and that one party is married, other unmarried, verdict of guilty of adultery and fornication sustained. Disharoon, 95 Ga. 351 (22 S. E. 698); Shattles, 17 Ga. App. 

259 (86 S. E. 463). 

Assault: Assault not justified, because parent suspected that victim was about to seduce daughter or commit fornication. Jordan, 14 Ga. App. 429 (3) (81 S. E. 359).

Charge of Court. Error to charge that if the jury believes the parties were found on the bed together; that there was no one present in the room; that the woman was a prostitute; and that the defendant was frequently in the habit of visiting her house, the jury was bound to find the defendant guilty. Ells, 20 Ga. 438.

Marriage as bar to punishment. "It shall be, at any time, within the power of the parties to prevent or suspend the prosecution and the punishment by marriage, if such marriage can be legally solemnized." § 26-5801. Where a man was convicted of fornication, and then lawfully married the woman with whom the offense was committed, but was afterward sent to the chain-gang in accordance with the sentence, based on the verdict of conviction, there was no error in discharging him from custody under a writ of habeas corpus. Cox, 133 Ga. 682 (66 S. E. 799). 

Marriage to another. 

Where the female married another man, this constitutes no defense. Morris, 14 Ga. App. 395 (1) (81 S. E. 257).

Sexual capacity. Sexual capacity of a mature male of the human species is presumed and the burden of showing incapacity is upon him who asserts it. Gardner, 81 Ga. 144 (7 S. E. 144); Ward, 14 

Ga. App. 110, 113 (80 S. E. 295). 

c. EVIDENCE. 

Competency of witnesses. On the trial of a woman accused with adultery and fornication, the wife of the man participating in such criminal act is not competent to testify against the accused woman. 

Smith, 14 Ga. App. 614 (81 S. E. 912); Bell, 14 Ga. App. 809 (82 S. 

E. 376). On the trial of a man accused with adultery and fornication, the husband of the woman participating in such criminal act is not competent to testify against the accused man. Batchelor, 41 Ga. 

App. 843 (155 S. E. 58). The reason for this rule is stated in Howard, 94 Ga. 587 (20 S. E. 426). The woman is necessarily guilty as well as the man. 

Proof of criminal act. On the trial of one indicted for fornication, evidence that the accused, an unmarried woman, was seen in bed in the same room with an unmarried man, who just got out of bed and was still in his nightclothes, is sufficient to warrant a finding that the sexual act was performed. Seats, 122 Ga. 173 (50 S. E. 65).

The rule is well settled that illicit intercourse may be inferred from the presence of a man at a house of ill fame, or from his exclusive presence in a closed room with a woman of an established reputation for lewdness. Long, 5 Ga. App. 176, 177 (62 S. E. 711).

Evidence, that accused, a married man, and a married woman, not his wife, were together late at night in same room, without any light, and that both had off their clothes, and that such woman was in bed when witness called-sufficient to sustain conviction. Ram-

SPECIFIC CRIMES 

267 sey, 16 Ga. App. 218 (84 S. E. 984); Batchelor, 41 Ga. App. 843 (155 

S. E. 58); Cummings, 14 Ga. App. 441 (81 S. E. 366).

If the defendant and the other party were seen in bed together, that alone would authorize conviction. Radford, 7 Ga. App. 600 (67 

S. E. 707); McArthur, 19 Ga. App. 747 (92 S. E. 234).

Evidence that woman lived in accused's house, gave birth to children while there and that defendant had told witnesses that his wife was an invalid and he was a healthy man, not sufficient to convict. 

Moore, 8 Ga. App. 113 (68 S. E. 616).

Man and woman sleeping in one room house,-sufficient to convict, although there seems to be sufficient justification. Eldridge, 97 Ga. 192 (23 S. E. 832); Starke, 97 Ga. 193 (23 S. E. 832). (In latter case see dissenting opinion.)

Man, traveling with child and nurse, all occupying the same room; not sufficient to convict without more. Lightner, 126 Ga. 563 (55 S. E. 471). On similar facts conviction upheld. Conner, 3 Ga. 

App. 475 (60 S. E. 111).

Collection of cases showing circumstances that warranted conviction of adultery or fornication. Johnson, 119 Ga. 446 (46 S. E. 634).

Church committee was appointed to investigate the accusation against defendant. On trial for adultery and fornication it was error to admit that "from the investigation made by them they thought there was something in it." Webb, 6 Ga. App. 353 (1) (64 

S. E. 1001). 

Testimony that "they looked mighty embarrassed"-admissible without stating the evidence thereof, which may be indescribable. 

Glover, 15 Ga. App. 44 (5) (82 S. E. 602).

Evidence showing that if the offense was ever committed, it was committed after indictment found, insufficient to support conviction. 

Davis, 92 Ga. 458 (17 S. E. 336).

Consent of female. Where evidence conflicting as to whether or not female consented, conviction authorized. Avery, 12 Ga. App. 

562 (77 S. E. 892).

Although female resisted, if, afterwards she consented, although consent was given under duress, offense is fornication, or adultery, but not rape. Mathews, 101 Ga. 547 (29 S. E. 424); Wade, 37 Ga. 

App. 121 (138 S. E. 921).

Accomplice. A woman who knowingly and willfully consents to an incestuous act of sexual intercourse is an accomplice of the man, and her uncorroborated testimony is not sufficient to sustain a verdict. Solomon, 113 Ga. 192 (38 S. E. 332); Brown, 18 Ga. App. 30 (88 S. E. 710). But where the crime is not incestuous, and the charge

is adultery and fornication, this being a misdemeanor, all parties are principals, and the testimony of the other party to the alleged offense need not be corroborated. Britt, 24 Ga. App. 324 (100 S. E. 

796); Mitchell, 81 Ga. 458 (8 S. E. 444).

Confession. Sufficiently corroborated by proof that defendant and the woman lived together as man and wife, and for some months slept together in a room with one bed. Wooster, 21 Ga. App. 287 (94 S. E. 279); McArthur, 19 Ga. App. 747 (92 S. E. 234). 

Single act. Living in adultery not shown by one act, or occasional acts of adultery. Lawson, 116 Ga. 571 (42 S. E. 752); Winkles, 4 

Ga. App. 559 (1) (61 S. E. 1128). Living in a state of fornication not shown by one act, or occasional acts for fornication. Singletary, 7 Ga. App. 699 (67 S. E. 1046).

Living in state of adultery may be proved on trial for adultery, though they are different offenses. Radford, 7 Ga. App. 600 (1) (67 

S. E. 707).

Other acts of intercourse. In a prosecution against a man for fornication or adultery, testimony that the female with whom the intercourse is alleged to have taken place had intercourse with another man is immaterial, even though the female herself is a witness for the State. Connell, 9 Ga. App. 818 (72 S. E. 304).

Evidence of illicit intercourse admissible, although it was barred by statute of limitations, where defendant was tried on other acts with same woman. This, to show that the illicit relation continued to a period within the statute. Taylor, 110 Ga. 150 (4) (35 S. E. 161).

Competent to show illicit relation between the man and the woman in another county, prior to indictment. Nobles, 127 Ga. 212 (3) (56 

S. E. 125); Huckeba, 24 Ga. App. 333 (5) (100 S. E. 757).

Illegally obtained evidence. Evidence obtained by placing searchlight through broken window, admissible, although in violation of the constitutional right of the accused to be protected from an illegal search. Leatherman, 11 Ga. App. 756 (1) (76 S. E. 102).

Good character of other participant. Since adultery is necessarily a joint offense, one on trial for that offense may introduce proof of the good character of the other alleged participant. 

Glover, 15 Ga. App. 44 (2) (82 S. E. 602).

Reputation of woman as a prostitute, and of house as a bawdy house-admissible. Sutton, 124 Ga. 815 (3) (53 S. E. 381); O'Neil, 15 Ga. App. 487, 494 (83 S. E. 861).

SPECIFIC CRIMES 

269 Variance in name. Conviction approved, although there was some question as to the identity of the other party. Held: That identity is question for the jury, where the slightest evidence of identity present. Walker, 14 Ga. App. 587 (81 S. E. 797); Watkins, 18 Ga. 

App. 500 (89 S. E. 624); Roberts, 40 Ga. App. 732 (1) (151 S. E. 240).

Divorce. Conditional divorce, granted in another State, which was not yet absolute at the time the alleged misconduct occurred,inadmissible. Jackson, 21 Ga. App. 823 (1) (95 S. E. 631).

Circumstantial evidence sufficient to convict. Johnson, 119 Ga. 

446 (46 S. E. 634); Eldridge, 97 Ga. 192 (23 S. E. 832). (See dissenting opinion); Cummings, 14 Ga. App. 441 (81 S. E. 366); O'Neil, 15 Ga. App. 487 (83 S. E. 861); Shattles, 17 Ga. App. 259 (86 S. E. 

463); Britt, 24 Ga. App. 324 (3) (100 S. E. 796). 

Echols, 119 Ga.

Circumstantial evidence insufficient to convict. 

307 (46 S. E. 409); Weems, 84 Ga. 461 (11 S. E. 501); Lightner, 126 

Ga. 563 (55 S. E. 471); Winkles, 4 Ga. App. 559 (61 S. E. 1128). (This is a strong case for the State, but reversed); Moore, 8 Ga. 

App. 113 (68 S. E. 616); Seckinger, 11 Ga. App. 797 (76 Š. E. 167); 

Glover, 15 Ga. App. 44 (1) (82 S. E. 602); Phillips, 17 Ga. App. 824 (88 S. E. 716); Hales, 34 Ga. App. 693 (131 S. E. 542); Coleman, 37 

Ga. App. 606 (141 S. E. 431); Durden, 42 Ga. App. 345 (156 S. E. 

294); Thompson, 5 Ga. App. 7 (62 S. E. 571); Long, 5 Ga. App. 176 (62 S. E. 711).

Marriage. 

Proof necessary. Although there be no affirmative allegation in the indictment that the parties are married or single, proof thereof is necessary and admissible. Bennett, 103 Ga. 66 (29 S. E. 919); 

Shattles, 17 Ga. App. 259 (86 S. E. 463).

In indictment for fornication, absolutely necessary to prove that at the time of the offense both parties were unmarried. Bennett, 103 Ga. 66 (29 S. E. 919); Neil, 117 Ga. 14 (1) (43 S. E. 435); Shattles, 17 Ga. App. 259 (86 S. E. 463).

Marriage of both parties must be shown by competent evidence to convict either of adultery; burden of showing marriage is upon the State. Tison, 125 Ga. 7 (53 S. E. 809).

The testimony of a witness that the accused "claims to be a married man"-hearsay, and incompetent. Tison, 125 Ga. 7 (53 S. E. 809).

Presumption of marriage. There is no presumption of law, or fact, that a man or woman is married or single. Neil, 117 Ga. 14, 15 (43 S. E. 435); Shattles, 17 Ga. App. 259, 260 (86 S. E. 463).

Parol evidence of marriage. Upon a trial of one charged with adultery and fornication, admissible, and not subject to the objection that the marriage certificate is the best and highest evidence. 

Walters, 23 Ga. App. 666 (99 S. E. 138).

Insufficient to show marriage. Evidence that the accused woman said that she was married, and about a year before the criminal act lived with a man, who has since left for parts unknown. Craft, 13 

Ga. App. 79, 80 (78 S. E. 776); Zackery, 6 Ga. App. 104 (64 S. E. 

281). (But in Cook, 11 Ga. 53 (6) the old rule is stated, that marriage can be proved by admissions of the defendant. But see Wooster, 21 Ga. App. 287 (94 S. E. 279). Corroboration necessary.)

Circumstantial evidence of marriage. In a prosecution for adultery, the fact that the alleged participants were, respectively, a married man and a married woman, may be shown, either directly or circumstantially. The fact of the marriage may be at least prima facie shown by any of the following methods: By proof of the general repute in the family; by proof of general reputation in the community; by proof of the fact that a man or woman, as the case may be, lives together with a person of the opposite sex as his or her spouse, with general recognition in the community of their being married to each other. Miller, 9 Ga. App. 827 (72 S. E. 279). 

Cohabitation. Mere reputation, unsupported with proof of cohabitation, is by itself insufficient to establish marriage. Zackery, 6 Ga. App. 104 (2) (64 S. E. 281). 

Proposal of marriage. That defendant proposed marriage and was engaged to the female with whom he was alleged to have had sexual intercourse, is prima facie evidence that he was single. Shattles, 17 Ga. App. 259 (86 S. E. 463).

Spouse to prove marriage. Question discussed, but not decided, whether husband or wife of one with whom adultery is charged to have been committed is a competent witness to prove the fact of marriage. Thomas, 115 Ga. 235, 237 (41 S. E. 578).

Re-opening case to prove marriage. The re-opening of a case for the purpose of introducing additional material evidence after the testimony has closed is a matter within the discretion of the trial court. It is not an abuse of discretion, in a case in which there is direct proof that the defendant was guilty of unlawful sexual intercourse, to reopen the case for the purpose of supplying proof of the

SPECIFIC CRIMES 

271 necessary allegation of the indictment, as to whether the parties were married or unmarried, as alleged. Chatman, 8 Ga. App. 842 (70 S. E. 188); Odum, 21 Ga. App. 310 (94 S. E. 257). 

Variance. Where indictment charges accused, a married man, with committing adultery with a named woman, alleged to be married, and the proof shows that she was not married, a verdict finding accused guilty of adultery is contrary to law. The proof in such case shows that the accused is guilty of adultery and fornication. 

Kendrick, 100 Ga. 360 (4) (28 S. E. 120). And so where the indictment charges the accused with the offense of adultery and fornication, with an unmarried woman, and the evidence shows that she was at one time a married woman, and there is no legal testimony that her husband was dead at the time of the offense, a verdict of guilty is not warranted. Williams, 86 Ga. 548 (12 S. E. 743). Indictment. the...........day of.. to wit,. of..... 6. AFFRAY. § 26-5303. 

(Misdemeanor.) 

for the said............in the county aforesaid, on 

19......did fight together in a public place, ((in a public square (or street) in the city -)) to the terror of the citizens and disturbance of public tranquility, contrary, etc. . . .

Public place. Where persons are accused of an affray and there is no evidence that the fighting occurred at a public place, a verdict of guilty is contrary to law. Gamble, 113 Ga. 701 (39 S. E. 301).

If within sight or hearing of a road used by the public, conviction can be had. (Id., 703.) General rule: Place must be one to which public are at the time privileged to resort without an investigation.

Conviction. Where two are indicted, conviction can not be had against one and not against the other. The successful defense of one inures to the benefit of the other. Hawkins, 13 Ga. 322 (1); 

O'Quinn, 39 Ga. App. 829, 831 (148 S. E. 618). 

Violence. Use of profane language not sufficient to convict.

There must be some overt act, like drawing a razor, making a threatening gesture with a plank, and taking hold of each other. Blackwell, 119 Ga. 314 (46 S. E. 432).

Self-defense. When two or more persons were on trial for an affray, which occurred at a place of worship, and the defense was that the defendants were repelling an unlawful assault and battery

made upon them, it was error to charge the jury that the right of self-defense extended only to the right of defending against a felonious assault. Regardless of the place, defendants had a right to defend themselves against an assault, assault and battery, and even to resent the use of opprobrious words and abusive language, provided in so doing they did not exceed the proper measure of resistance. Bracewell, 10 Ga. App. 830 (74 S. E. 440).

Aiding and abetting. One who aids and abets is guilty as principal. Hawkins, 13 Ga. 322; O'Quinn, 39 Ga. App. 829 (148 S. E. 618).

Striking the jury. If two or more are tried for affray, they are entitled to only seven strikes, if tried together. Hawkins, 13 Ga. 

322, 324 (1); O'Quinn, 39 Ga. App. 829 (148 S. E. 618). 

See also: Assault, Riot. 

7. ARSON.

S$ 26-2201 to 26-2211. 

Punishments according to Acts of 1924. 

Arson of dwelling or outhouse: Not less than two nor more than twenty years in the penitentiary. Where arson produces death, or maiming of any person, punishment as for murder.

Arson of buildings not dwellings: Not less than one nor more than ten years in the penitentiary. Where arson produces death, or maiming of any person, punishment as for murder.

Burning goods, etc., to defraud insurer: Not less than one nor more than five years in the penitentiary.

Attempt to burn property: Not less than one nor more than two years in the penitentiary. 

Arson is not a reducible felony. 

a. INDICTMENT.

For full and approved indictment, joint, principal, accessories, etc., see Tate, 41 Ga. App. 300, 301 (152 

S. E. 609); Golden, 45 Ga. App. 501 (165 S. E. 299). 

Attempt: Maner, 45 Ga. App. 594 (165 S. E. 305).

In an indictment for arson, ownership of the property was properly laid in one to whom a deed conveying the property destroyed by fire was executed for the purpose of indemnifying him against loss by reason of having become surety on a bond, where the bond was still in force at the time the fire occurred. Kinsey, 12 Ga. App. 422 (2) (77 S. E. 369). 

The allegation in the indictment descriptive of the house that was maliciously set fire to and burned, that it was "an occupied dwelling house" is sufficiently proved by evidence that the accused (four persons) lived in the house prior to and up to the night in which it was burned, and that immediately upon setting fire to the house they fled therefrom. Williams, 11 Ga. App. 416, 417 (3) (75 S. E. 442).

In a trial for arson the allegation of title or occupancy need not be proved with the same degree of fullness as would be necessary in an action involving title or right of possession. Morgan, 120 Ga. 

499, 502 (48 S. E. 238); Rice, 16 Ga. App. 128 (3) (84 S. E. 609); 

Golding, 30 Ga. App. 30, 32 (116 S. E. 881).

The offense of arson is not so much against the property interest in the house as it is against security of the house, and an allegation of ownership in the indictment is sustained by proof of occupancy by the alleged owner under a claim of title. Rice, 16 Ga. App. 128 (3) (84 S. E. 709); Golding, 30 Ga. App. 30, 32 (116 S. E. 881).

An indictment which states the offense of arson in the language of the Code is sufficient. Hester, 17 Ga. 130.

An indictment for arson charging burning of an outhouse, need not state whether or not the same was located in a city, town or village. Smith, 64 Ga. 605 (3); Carter, 106 Ga. 372 (1) (32 S. E. 345); 

Golding, 30 Ga. App. 30, 32 (116 S. E. 881).

Indictment need not charge whether offense was committed in the daytime or at night. Brightwell, 41 Ga. 482. 

Outhouse embraces any house not dwelling. Carter, 106 Ga. 372, 373 (32 S. E. 345).

In an indictment for arson with intent to defraud insurance company, the naming of a certain insurance company was not necessary, and proof that the storehouse was insured in a different company from the one alleged in the indictment was not a fatal variance. 

Golden, 45 Ga. App. 501 (165 S. E. 299); Maner, 45 Ga. App. 594 (2) (165 S. E. 305). 

b. GENERAL. 

Corpus delicti. In case of arson, the corpus delicti consists of two fundamental facts: First, the burning of the house described in the indictment; and second, the fact that a criminal agency was the cause of the burning. West, 6 Ga. App. 105 (1) (64 S. E. 130); Williams, 30 Ga. App. 255 (117 S. E. 825). Without these two essential facts no crime is made out. (Id.); Davenport, 12 Ga. App. 102, 103 (76 S. E. 756).

Presumption. Presumption is that burning was the result of accidental or providential cause, rather than of criminal design. Sims, 14 Ga. App. 28 (79 S. E. 1133); Sevier, 17 Ga. App. 277 (86 S. E. 533).

Burden of proof is upon the State. Notwithstanding the fact that it may be difficult to convict of the offense of arson, the rule that upon the prosecution devolves the burden of showing that the burning was the result of criminal design is inflexible. Sevier, 17 Ga. 

App. 277 (86 S. E. 533).

Where nothing appears but the burning, burden is upon the State to overcome presumption that burning occurred from providential or accidental cause. Rice, 16 Ga. App. 128 (2) (84 S. E. 609). It

SPECIFIC CRIMES 

275 must appear from the evidence, either direct or circumstantial, to a reasonable and moral certainty that the house was burned by some criminal agency. Sims, 14 Ga. App. 28 (79 S. E. 1133).

House. A freight car body, which has been detached from the wheels, and placed upon permanent posts near a railway track at a station, and to which a platform has been attached, thus constituting a structure to be used as a "freight warehouse," and which is used for this purpose only, is a "house" within the meaning of these sections. Carter, 106 Ga. 372 (2) (32 S. E. 345).

The word "outhouse," as used in the Code, is applied to a structure not located in a city, town, or village, and embraces a house of any description which is not a dwelling house, though not appurtenant to any other building. Carter, 106 Ga. 372 (3), 375 (32 S. E. 

345); Watt, 61 Ga. 66.

Whether the outhouse burnt be in a city, town, or village, or not, does not affect the legal character of the offense. It affects the punishment only. Carter, 106 Ga. 372 (1), 373, 374 (32 S. E. 345); Golding, 30 Ga. App. 30, 32 (116 S. E. 881).

Burning a hole through the door or attempting to burn one through the floor of a guard house in an incorporated town, merely for the purpose of effecting an escape, is not arson. Jenkins, 53 Ga. 

33; Washington, 87 Ga. 12 (1) (13 S. E. 131).

War. Where, during a war, a private burnt a house of another, by the command of his superior officer in the usual course of prosecuting war, he could not be convicted of arson. Clark, 37 Ga. 191.

Charge. Failure to charge that every fire is presumed to be accidental, until contrary appears, not error in absence of request. Sutton, 17 Ga. App. 713 (4) (88 S. E. 122, 587); Robinson, 18 Ga. App. 

394 (89 S. E. 434).

Charge that a number of small houses so close together that the burning of one would endanger the others was a village, no error. 

Kinsey, 12 Ga. App. 422 (77 S. E. 369). 

c. EVIDENCE. 

Corpus delicti of arson may be established by circumstantial evidence provided circumstances are sufficient to exclude every other reasonable hypothesis than that of willful and intentional burning, and are so strong as to rebut presumption that fire was of providential or accidental origin. Robinson, 18 Ga. App. 394 (89 S. E. 434); 

Wade, 16 Ga. App. 163 (84 S. E. 593).

Circumstantial evidence held sufficient to sustain a conviction for arson: Westbrook, 91 Ga. 11 (16 S. E. 100); Brown, 6 Ga. App. 356

(64 S. E. 1109); Dixon, 11 Ga. App. 367 (75 S. E. 266); Williams, 11 

Ga. App. 416 (75 S. E. 442); Rice, 16 Ga. App. 128 (84 S. E. 609); 

Sutton, 17 Ga. App. 713 (88 S. E. 122, 578); Harris, 17 Ga. App. 723 (88 S. E. 121); Ware, 18 Ga. App. 107 (89 S. E. 155); Abdallah, 20 

Ga. App. 618 (93 S. E. 260); Hill, 27 Ga. App. 611 (110 S. E. 629); 

Edge, 44 Ga. App. 760 (162 S. E. 862).

Circumstantial evidence held insufficient to sustain a conviction for arson: Ragland, 2 Ga. App. 492 (58 S. E. 689); Matthews, 10 Ga. 

App. 302 (73 S. E. 404); Davenport, 12 Ga. App. 102 (76 S. E. 756); 

Sims, 12 Ga. App. 551 (77 S. E. 891); Sevier, 17 Ga. App. 277 (86 S. 

E. 533); Ivey, 27 Ga. App. 777 (110 S. E. 324).

Confession. Corpus delicti must be proved. Confession alone not sufficient. Sims, 14 Ga. App. 28 (79 S. E. 1133); Moon, 12 Ga. App. 

614 (77 S. E. 1088).

Confession and circumstantial evidence sufficient. Sutton, 17 Ga. 

App. 713 (3) (88 S. E. 122, 587). 

Ownership. Allegation of ownership sustained by proof of occupancy by alleged owner under claim of right. Harrell, 121 Ga. 607, 608 (49 S. E. 703); Rice, 16 Ga. App. 128 (3) (84 S. E. 609).

Where indictment charged arson by burning the property of Mrs. 

G. Bevill, and the evidence disclosed that the property has been deeded to Roxie S. Bevill, whose husband was G. Bevill, the jury was authorized to find that the property belonged to the person named in the indictment. Weaver, 116 Ga. 550 (1) (42 S. E. 745).

Where the indictment charged that house was the property of and in possession of a certain person, and the proof showed the actual possession was held by the tenant of that person, there was no material variance. Harvey, 67 Ga. 639 (2).

Circumstances. Evidence of bad feeling between owner of building and defendant admissible. Hammack, 52 Ga. 397 (1).

Where one is detected in the act of putting oil on house, and accused fled after detection, it is for the jury to say whether he desisted from repenting or detection. Weaver, 116 Ga. 550 (2) (42 S. 

E. 745).

Where the creating an opportunity to commit larceny from one building seems to have been the motive for setting fire to another on the same premises, evidence of the larceny is admissible against the prisoner on his trial for the arson. Jones, 63 Ga. 395.

In prosecution for burning church with intent to defraud insurance company, Court did not err in admitting in evidence insurance policy of certain company which covered the property burned. Tate, 41 Ga. App. 300 (2) (152 S. E. 609).

277 In prosecution for burning church with intent to defraud insurance company, receipt given to insurance company by trustees of church-admissible. Tate, 41 Ga. App. 300 (152 S. E. 609). 

Testimony of the bookkeeper of the defendant's landlord to the effect that the defendant had got considerably behind in payment of his rent, is admissible, the indictment alleging that defendant committed the acts alleged therein to defraud an insurance carrier. 

Maner, 45 Ga. App. 594 (165 S. E. 305).

Financial condition of the defendant may be shown to the jury to illustrate his intent. Maner, 45 Ga. App. 594 (2) (165 S. E. 305). 8. ASSAULT.

a. SIMPLE ASSAULT. 

Indictment. charge and accuse. the offense of assault, for the said.. day of.............. ..with ..on the........ 

19......, in the county aforesaid, in and upon one ....in the peace of said State then and there being, unlawfully and with force and arms did attempt to commit a

violent injury, upon the person of...... etc. contrary, Where the presentment charged the offense substantially in words which are found in approved common law precedents, as well as precedents which have been approved and followed in this country. for more than a hundred years, indictment good. Sims, 118 Ga. 761 (45 S. E. 621).

That accusation charges assault without specifying any act or acts constituting the same, is not good ground for arresting judgment. 

Scott, 35 Ga. App. 591 (134 S. E. 335). 

Indictment for assault held defective in particular instance. 

Gober, 7 Ga. App. 206 (66 S. E. 395).

General. There is no such crime as an attempt to make an assault. Wilson, 53 Ga. 205.

Mere preparation to commit a violent injury upon the person of another, or a mere threat to do so, unaccompanied by physical effort to do so, will not justify a conviction for assault. Mere words or threat, unaccompanied by some physical effort to commit a violent injury upon the person of another, will not justify a conviction for assault. Penny, 114 Ga. 77 (39 S. E. 871); Fennell, 164 Ga. 59, 64 (137 S. E. 762).

There need not be an actual present ability to commit a violent injury upon the person assailed, but if there be such a demonstration of violence, coupled with an apparent ability to inflict the injury, so as to cause the person against whom it is directed reasonably to fear the injury, . .the assault is completed, though the assailant may never have been within actual striking distance of the person assailed. Thomas, 99 Ga. 38, 44 (26 S. E. 748). While a mere threat or menace to commit a violent injury upon the person of another is not sufficient to constitute an assault, yet where the threat or menace is accompanied by an apparent attempt to commit such injury, and its consummation is prevented, either by the act of the person upon whom the assault is threatened or by the interposition of a third party, the violence has commenced and the assault is complete. Rutherford, 5 Ga. App. 482 (1) (63 S. E. 570); 

Smith, 147 Ga. 682 (1-a) (95 S. E. 223).

In every assault there must be an intention to injure. The test is: 

Was there a present purpose of doing a bodily injury? Edwards, 4 

Ga. App. 167, 169 (60 S. E. 1033); Godboult, 38 Ga. App. 137, 138 (142 S. E. 704).

To constitute an assault no actual injury need be shown, it being only necessary to show an intention to commit an injury, coupled

SPECIFIC CRIMES 

279 with an apparent ability to do so. Thomas, 99 Ga. 38 (26 S. E. 748) ; 

Dorsey, 108 Ga. 477, 479 (34 S. E. 135); Godboult, 38 Ga. App. 137, 138 (142 S. E. 704).

Where there is opportunity but no intention shown, conviction illegal. Godboult, 38 Ga. App. 137, 138 (142 S. E. 704). 

Accident. Accident which negatives intent is a good defense. 

Conoly, 10 Ga. App. 822 (74 S. E. 285). 

Calling one "damn rascal" and picking up rocks, and drawing arm back as if to throw, but not throwing rocks, is not an assault. 

Bowden, 27 Ga. App. 768 (109 S. E. 915); Penny, 114 Ga. 77 (39 S. 

E. 871). .

The fact that the person, in committing the assault, was also guilty of riot, or was also guilty of violating § 26-1703 making it unlawful to shoot at a dwelling house, does not render conviction. for assault illegal. It being reasonably inferable from the evidence that the person who shot at the house did so with knowledge that the prosecutor was therein, and shot toward him with the intention. of either injuring him or frightening him, this is sufficient to characterize the act as an assault. Smallwood, 9 Ga. App. 300 (2) (70 S. 

E. 1124); Edwards, 4 Ga. App. 849 (62 S. E. 565); Gazaway, 34 Ga. 

App. 442, 444 (129 S. E. 888). 

To shoot at another with a gun at a distance of twenty steps, is an assault, even if the gun be loaded with powder only. Crumbley, 61 Ga. 582 (2); Clark, 84 Ga. 577 (10 S. E. 1094). 

Drawing back with bottle in hand, in striking distance, causing reasonable fear of injury, question of apparent ability is for the jury. Robinson, 118 Ga. 750 (45 S. E. 620). 

To shoot in the direction of another, not to hit him, but only "to bluff or scare him," does not, without more, make an assault. Edwards, 4 Ga. App. 167 (60 S. E. 1033).

Raising stick and running after another person, assault, if there was an intention to strike. Thomas, 99 Ga. 38 (2) (27 S. E. 748).

To constitute an assault no actual injury need be shown, it being only necessary to show an intention to commit an injury, coupled with an apparent ability to do so. Thomas, 99 Ga. 38 (27 S. E. 38); 

Godboult, 38 Ga. App. 137, 138 (142 S. E. 704).

Evidence as to various acts of violence committed by the accused against other persons or things, at the identical time he was charged of committing the assault for which he was prosecuted, was admissible as part of the res gestae, to throw light on his state of mind and to illustrate his intention at the time of the assault. Carter, 15 

Ga. App. 343 (1) (83 S. E. 153).

Repentance and abandonment of criminal intent. When a man has an intent to commit a certain crime, and does an act concurrent with the intent sufficient to constitute a lesser crime of the same nature, and repents and desists from his first intention, he is still indictable for his first offense. If, however, he abandons his evil intention at any time before so much of the act was done as constitutes a crime, such abandonment takes from what has been done its indictable quality. Young, 82 Ga. 752 (1) (9 S. E. 1108). 

Negro boy followed white girl and said "Stop." When she ran, he ran after her. These facts warrant conviction for assault. Bryant, 36 Ga. App. 113 (136 S. E. 111).

Consummation of act. Where evidence shows no assault other than one consummated by a complete battery, a verdict of simple assault is not lawful. Jackson, 38 Ga. App. 138 (142 S. E. 694); Jackson, 132 Ga. 546, 547 (64 S. E. 653); Kennedy, 10 Ga. App. 794 (74 

S. E. 95); Brooking, 33 Ga. App. 49 (125 S. E. 504).

No person shall be convicted of an assault with intent to commit a crime, or of any other attempt to commit an offense, when it shall appear that the crime intended, or the offense attempted, was actually perpetrated by such person at the time of such assault, or in pursuance of such attempt. § 27-2508. Rich, 160 Ga. 513 (128 S. E. 666). 

b. ASSAULT UNDER COLOR OF OFFICE. 

A policeman may use all the force that was necessary to effectuate the arrest and overcome resistance. Burns, 80 Ga. 544 (2) (7 S. E. 

88); Elmore, 15 Ga. App. 461, 462 (83 S. E. 799).

An officer of the law can not justify an assault, or assault and battery upon his prisoner, on the ground that the beating was provoked by the use of opprobrious words or abusive language since that section of the Code applies between private persons, not between public officers and those in their custody. Burns, 80 Ga. 544 (7 S. E. 

88); Elmore, 15 Ga. App. 461, 462 (83 S. E. 799).

Insolence from a colored prisoner to a white policeman is no excuse for beating the prisoner with a club. Policemen shall do right, not less towards one color than another, in so far as it depends upon this Court to administer the rules of law to their conduct. (Id.) 

Moody, 120 Ga. 868 (3) (48 S. E. 340). 

Resistance to arrest.

Resistance to an arrest may begin in the use of words which import defiance, and indicate a purpose to use violence if necessary, the words being followed up by the actual use of violence. After the use of such words, the officer may in-

SPECIFIC CRIMES 

281 stantly employ such degree of force as is necessary to reduce the party to submission and accomplish the arrest. Ramsey, 92 Ga. 53 

It is the duty of every person arrested under legal process to quietly submit . . and in case the offender refuses to submit, the officer has a right to use such force as is necessary to accomplish the arrest. Dixon, 12 Ga. App. 17 (6), 18 (76 S. E. 794).

Resistance to an illegal arrest is no violation of law, provided the force offered in resistance does not exceed what is necessary and proper to that end, under the circumstances. Dixon, 12 Ga. App. 

17 (8), 18 (76 S. E. 794); Perry, 8 Ga. App. 181 (68 S. E. 864).

Convicts. Corporal punishment of a convict by a warden, administered when the circumstances are not of a character sufficient to authorize such punishment, is an assault. Westbrook, 133 Ga. 578 (2) (66 S. E. 788). 

c. ASSAULT-OBSTRUCTING LEGAL PROCESS. 

d. ASSAULT-OBSTRUCTING ORDER OR SENTENCE AFTER TRIAL. 

Indictment. charge and accuse.. .with the offense of obstructing legal process (or misdemeanor), for that the said.. ..did, on the........day of…………….. .19......, in the county of.............., unlawfully and with force and arms, knowingly and willfully obstruct and oppose... legal con- stable (or sheriff) of said county of, in his attempt to execute the judgment and order, the same being a lawful process, of (name the court and its authority), rendered and framed by the magistrate (or judge) at the... ..Term, 19., of...... court in and for said..... (district and) county, in the case then and there tried and determined of............... versus.. same being a (possessory warrant) proceeding for the said (magistrate).. the recovery of....... then and there awarding. ing the said.. ment by delivering said.. and ordering and directto execute and enforce said judg- ..to said..... the execution of said order by said.......... (constable or sheriff) was obstructed and opposed by said defendant, as aforesaid, contrary. . . (Approved: Gibson, 118 Ga. 29, 30 (44 S. E. 811).)

An indictment charging the violation of this section must disclose the officer alleged to have been obstructed and by what authority he attempted to execute legal process, as well as the nature of the proc-

ess he was attempting to serve, or show otherwise that the officer was authorized to execute process. Paschal, 16 Ga. App. 155 (84 S. E. 

725); Evans, 29 Ga. App. 204 (114 S. E. 812); Prichard, 34 Ga. App. 

181 (129 S. E. 12).

Where indictment or accusation fails to disclose the official character of the officer, and the nature of the process, motion in arrest of judgment will be upheld. Hunter, 4 Ga. App. 579 (2) (61 S. E. 

1130); Evans, 29 Ga. App. 204 (114 S. E. 812).

Indictment need not set out specific acts by which defendant forcibly obstructed and opposed the execution of process. Paschal, 16 Ga. App. 155 (4) (84 S. E. 725).

General. Process must bear upon its face evidence of its official character. Short, 79 Ga. 550 (4 S. E. 852).

Obstructing de facto officer is a violation of this section just as a de lege officer. Andrews, 45 Ga. 154.

Merely refusing, upon the demand of a levying officer, to unlock a door of the house, in order to enable him to enter the same for the purpose of levying a lawful process upon goods therein contained, is not a violation of this section. Vince, 113 Ga. 1070 (39 S. E. 435).

But there is a dictum in this case to the effect that had the accused shut the door and locked it to prevent an entrance by the officer, the case would have been different.

It is a misdemeanor to obstruct any officer in executing any lawful order of Court, whether it has been reduced to writing or not. Gibson, 118 Ga. 29, 30 (44 S. E. 811).

Forcible resistance is necessary to sustain indictment of this offense. Raines, 13 Ga. App. 693 (79 S. E. 860). Neither threats alone, unaccompanied by any fear, or apparent intention to execute them, nor even the doing of an act which impedes, delays, or defeats the execution of the process with which the officer is armed, but without resisting him, is sufficient to constitute the offense of obstructing legal process. Hutchinson, 9 Ga. App. 62 (70 S. E. 352); Raines, 13 

Ga. App. 693 (79 S. E. 860).

Declaration, by defendant, that a summons for a named person could only be served on his dead body, not sufficient to convict, and a demurrer to such an indictment should be sustained. Hutchinson, 9 Ga. App. 62 (70 S. E. 352).

Removing property levied on by sheriff is not a violation of this section. Davis, 76 Ga. 721.

No excuse that deputy sheriff, who attempted to execute process, did not file official oath or give bond. Stephens, 106 Ga. 116 (2) (32 S. E. 13).

SPECIFIC CRIMES 

283 One can not be convicted of this offense, unless he knew at the time the offense was committed the official character of the person attempting to make the arrest, and also knew that the officer was endeavoring to execute a lawful process. McLendon, 12 Ga. App. 

691 (78 S. E. 139).

Resisting attempts of a municipal officer to effect an arrest outside of the corporate limits will not amount to an assault, since municipal officers have no authority to make arrests anywhere except within the corporate limits. Blair, 90 Ga. 326 (17 S. E. 96).

Where an officer illegally endeavored to compel accused to go with him until a relative, against whom the officer had a warrant, is found, raising a stick in striking position is justified, although otherwise it might be assault. Shubert, 127 Ga. 42 (55 S. E. 1045).

Evidence. Where indictment charged obstructing legal process, in that defendant obstructed deputy sheriff in serving search warrant authorizing searching dwelling house of defendant, and to support allegation search warrant, in which appeared that defendant's name has been erased and that of another inserted, was offered in evidence, and there was no evidence or explanation of such change, or that the paper has been altered since sheriff has attempted to execute it, allegation of indictment was not supported by evidence, and it was error to allow search warrant to go to jury. Alexander, 23 

Ga. App. 546 (2) (99 S. E. 58). 

e. ASSAULT AND BATTERY. 

Indictment. charge and accuse. the offense of assault and battery, for the said......... with on the..............day of……………………………. 19...., in the county aforesaid, then and there unlawfully and with force and arms, in and upon one...

in the peace of said State then and there being, did make an assault and him, the said.. and with force and arms did beat, contrary, etc.

did attempt to commit a violent injury on the person of ..and the said. there unlawfully beat the said............ etc. ...then and etc. did unlawfully make an assault upon the person of one ...and then and there beat him with.. 

Badger, 5 Ga. App. 477 (63 S. E. 532).

Where the indictment charges the offense substantially in words. which are found in approved common law precedents, as well as precedents which have been approved and followed in this country

for more than a hundred years, indictment good. Sims, 118 Ga. 761 (45 S. E. 621).

Where the indictment charges "assault and battery" the law supplies the definition of the offense. Omission of the word "unlawfully" not fatal. Badger, 5 Ga. App. 477 (63 S. E. 532).

General. An infant of sufficient age and discretion to be responsible for a crime, who causes injury to another by throwing a stone at him, may be convicted of assault and battery, though the stone was thrown in sport or play, and though he acted without malice or anger. Hill, 63 Ga. 578.

Man laying his hand upon a girl in a lustful way, but without intent to attempt to have sexual intercourse with her, is guilty of assault and battery. Yarbrough, 17 Ga. App. 828 (88 S. E. 716).

It is assault and battery for a man, without some innocent reason or excuse, to put his arm around the neck of another's wife against her will. Goodrum, 60 Ga. 509; Yarbrough, 17 Ga. App. 828, 830 (88 S. E. 716). The definition of battery is the unlawful beating of another. To beat, in the legal sense, is not merely to whip, wound, or hurt, but includes any unlawful imposition of the hand or arm.

The slightest touching of another in an anger is battery. (Id.) 

A mother who has the right to control and correct her child may authorize another, in her presence, to chastise the child for disobedience; and if he does so in a proper manner, he is not guilty of an assault and battery upon the child. Harris, 115 Ga. 578 (41 S. E. 983). 

A father is guilty of assault and battery, who punishes his own child, a girl of ten years of age, by whipping her with a saw twentytwo inches long and three-fourths of an inch wide, if there was no good reason for the same, and under such circumstances one blow is unlawful. Neal, 54 Ga. 281. 

Where two attacked a man, one hitting him with a gun stock, the other shooting him with a pistol, and there was no evidence of conspiracy between the two, and the assaulted man afterwards died, and there was no evidence that he died from the injury inflicted upon him with the gun stock, defendant who struck the deceased with the gun stock can be convicted for assault and battery, if there was no intention to kill. Baynes, 135 Ga. 219 (69 S. E. 170).

Automobiles. An assault and battery may be committed by striking another with an automobile intentionally, or by driving the machine so recklessly as to justify a jury in finding that there was a reckless disregard of human life and safety. . . . The same is true where, under like circumstances, the automobile is driven against

SPECIFIC CRIMES 

285 another vehicle in which persons are riding, whereby the collision occasions bruises, blows, and similar physical injuries to persons in the vehicle so struck. Tift, 17 Ga. App. 663 (1) (88 S. E. 41).

Where there is a lack of either actual or legally imputable intention to do a certain act, there may be an absence of criminal responsibility, and the act be attributable to misfortune or accident. Carbo, 4 Ga. App. 583 (2) (3) (62 S. E. 140); Tift, 17 Ga. App. 663 (6) (88 

S. E. 41).

Collision of driver, inexperienced, and just learning how to drive, will not authorize conviction. Thomas, 36 Ga. App. 662 (137 S. E. 916). f. WHIPPING WIFE. Indictment. charge and accuse. offense of misdemeanor, for the said. day of............... ..with the .on the........

Hammond, 28 Ga. App. 680 (113 S. E. 221).)

Where upon an indictment for an assault with intent to murder the defendant was found guilty of the offense of whipping his wife, the judgment should be arrested, as whipping one's wife is a distinct statutory offense, and such offense was not charged in the indictment. Manigault, 53 Ga. 113. (Distinguished in Hammond, 28 

Ga. App. 680 (113 S. E. 221).)

Where the indictment charges that the accused did "unlawfully whip and beat" his wife, a verdict supported by evidence is not contrary to law "for the reason that a man can not be convicted of an assault and battery on his wife." Hammond, 28 Ga. App. 680 (113 

S. E. 221).

On an indictment charging a husband of whipping, beating and cruelly maltreating his wife, there is no error in allowing several witnesses to testify to several distinct beatings, within two years prior to the indictment. In such cases the State is not bound to elect one of these transactions upon which to rely. Memmler, 75 Ga. 

576; Mills, 41 Ga. App. 834, 835, 836 (155 S. E. 104).

The wife is a competent witness against her husband, where he is charged with whipping his wife, and if she testifies for her husband, and the State does not object, she may be cross-examined and impeached as any other witness. Memmler, 75 Ga. 576; Stevens, 76 

Ga. 96.

Evidence of third party as to statements of a wife that her husband had just beaten her, made in the presence of the husband without denial on his part, and under such circumstances that his silence amounted to admission, is admissible on the trial of the husband for wife beating, where wife declines to testify. Joiner, 119 Ga. 315 (46 S. E. 412).

Confession sufficiently corroborated by wife's cries, calling a policeman, showing him swollen eye, etc. (Id.)

Where a husband and wife were living separately, the wife suing for a divorce, and he found her in a compromising situation with another man, and assaulted and beat her, it was not error for the Court to charge the jury that "if they believe, from the evidence, that the defendant caught his wife under such circumstances that showed she was about to commit adultery, and that he interposed and prevented it, and if they believe further that he assaulted and beat her under such circumstances, it would be for the jury to say as to whether in such a case the defendant would be justified, or not, in what he did." Baird, 9 Ga. App. 232 (70 S. E. 990).

While a husband is authorized to use such force as may be necessary to repel a felonious assault by his wife upon him or his property, he is not justified under any circumstances in striking his wife either by way of chastisement or in resentment of a past injury consisting of an assault upon him or his property; and this is true although the assault may have been in the immediate past. Lawson, 115 Ga. 578 (41 S. E. 993).

Intent to kill. A specific intent to kill is an essential ingredient of the offense of assault with intent to murder, and the indictment

should allege such intent. Wright, 168 Ga. 690 (1) (148 S. E. 731).

This is true where the accused (charged with assault with intent to murder) injured a person by striking him with an automobile while operating it in a reckless and unlawful manner. Neese, 40 Ga. App. 

503 (150 S. E. 451); Springer, 37 Ga. App. 154 (139 S. E. 159).

A reckless disregard of human life may be equivalent of a specific intent to kill. Looney, 41 Ga. App. 495 (153 S. E. 372); Chambliss, 37 Ga. App. 124 (139 S. E. 80).

Driving automobile while under the influence of an intoxicant. 

Starnes, 45 Ga. App. 238 (164 S. E. 89).

An assault with intent to murder may be committed without a weapon likely to produce death, and indictment need not charge the use of a weapon likely to produce death. Wright, 168 Ga. 690 (2) (148 S. E. 731).

Indictment, not alleging intent to kill, fatally defective. Such intent is not alleged by alleging "malice aforethought." Minge, 45 

Ga. App. 197 (164 S. E. 68).

Where indictment alleges assault with intent to murder with a firearm, which is a weapon likely to produce death, it is not necessary to allege that the same was loaded with powder and ball. 

Parker, 95 Ga. 482 (22 S. E. 276).

An indictment which charged that the accused committed an assault with intent to murder "with certain pieces of iron in his hand, ," but which fails to describe the manner of the assault or the character of the pieces of iron, is lacking in the requisite particularity; and appropriate demurrer should be sustained. Walker, 124 

Ga. 440 (52 S. E. 738).

It is essential, where the instrumentality of some physical agency is alleged, that the indictment should describe the manner of its use with sufficient particularity to put the accused on notice as to the nature of the assault which is charged. Walker, 124 Ga. 440, 441 (52 S. E. 738).

That an indictment for assault with intent to murder with a pocket knife did not allege the use made of such weapon, is not good in arrest of judgment. Ash, 56 Ga. 583.

The act of maliciously putting poison into a well, with the intent that the water thereof shall be drunk by another, and that he shall in this manner be killed, does not, without more, constitute the offense of assault with intent to murder, when the person, whose death was intended never in fact drank of the water after the poison had been introduced into the same. Peebles, 101 Ga. 585 (28 S. E. 920); 

Leary, 14 Ga. App. 797 (2) (82 S. E. 471).

SPECIFIC CRIMES 

289 Where indictment charges assault with intent to murder by administering poison, it must be alleged in what manner the poison was administered. Johnson, 90 Ga. 441 (16 S. E. 92); Johnson, 92 

Ga. 36 (17 S. E. 974).

Joinder. Counts for an assault with intent to murder by shooting with a pistol, and for shooting at another with a pistol, may be joined in the same indictment. Adams, 52 Ga. 565. General.

No person shall be convicted of an assault with intent to commit a crime, or of any other attempt to commit an offense, when it shall appear that the crime intended, or the offense attempted, was actually perpetrated by such person at the time of the assault, or in pursuance of such attempt. § 27-2508.

On the trial of one indicted for assault with intent to murder by the use of a deadly weapon, the burden is on the State to show (1) the assault, (2) the deadly character of the weapon, (3) the intent to take life, and (4) the commission of assault under such circumstances that, had death ensued, the party making the assault would have been guilty of murder. McLane, 20 Ga. App. 825 (2) (93 S. E. 558). 

Where one shoots another with a pistol, inflicting a wound which causes a disease from which the wounded person dies, on his trial for murder the crime of assault with intent to murder is not involved. Clements, 141 Ga. 667 (4) (81 S. E. 1117).

To constitute the offense of assault with intent to murder it must appear that the circumstances connected with the assault were such, that had death ensued the accused would have been guilty of murder. Jackson, 51 Ga. 402.

All ingredients of murder, except death of the party, must be present at the time the party is injured. Whitsett, 115 Ga. 203 (41 

S. E. 699); Benton, 9 Ga. App. 291 (1) (71 S. E. 8); Looney, 41 Ga. 

App. 495, 497 (153 S. E. 372).

In a case where, if death had ensued, the defendant would only have been guilty of manslaughter, he can not be convicted of an assault with intent to murder, and the Court should so charge the jury on request. Elliott, 46 Ga. 159; Kimball, 112 Ga. 541 (37 S. E. 886).

Assault with intent to murder may be defined as an assault without justification and without any circumstances of mitigation, made by one person upon another, with a weapon in its nature likely to produce death, with a specific intent to take the life of the person assaulted. Killian, 19 Ga. App. 750 (1) (92 S. E. 227). Malice, either

express or implied, essential. Reddick, 11 Ga. App. 150 (74 S. E. 901). 

Intent. An intent to commit the crime of murder is necessary element to constitute the offense of assault with intent to murder. An assault may be made with a deadly weapon and with malice and at the same time there may have been no intent to kill. Whether there was an intent to kill is a question for the jury. Lanier, 106 Ga. 368, 370 (32 S. E. 335); Autrey, 24 Ga. App. 414 (100 S. E. 782).

Specific intent to kill may be inferred by jury from the circumstances as well as the direct evidence of the case. Lovett, 9 Ga. App. 

232 (70 S. E. 989); Belote, 41 Ga. App. 346, 348 (152 S. E. 911).

The specific intent to kill unjustifiably constitutes legal malice, whether death results or not. Thomas, 37 Ga. App. 823 (2) (142 S. 

E. 312).

There is no legal presumption, that if an assault is made with a weapon likely to produce death, the assault is made with intent to murder. Patterson, 85 Ga. 131 (11 S. E. 620); Lanier, 28 Ga. App. 

97 (2) (110 S. E. 682).

Where one is indicted as a principal in the second degree, for assault with intent to murder, he can not be convicted unless he participated in the murderous design, since the intent to murder is necessary. Kimball, 112 Ga. 541 (37 S. E. 886); Wright, 168 Ga. 

690, 691 (148 S. E. 731).

Where death ensues, there is a presumption that there was an intent to kill. But this presumption does not exist where the victim survives. Wright, 168 Ga. 690, 692 (148 S. E. 731).

Overt act. In order to convict one of assault with intent to murder, it is essential that an overt act be committed. Where one attempted to make an assault with a pistol, but the pistol caught in the lining of his coat, this alone is insufficient. Burton, 109 Ga. 134 (34 S. E. 286). 

Deadly weapon. The words "deadly weapon" include all means or instrumentalities by which assaults with intent to murder may be made. Wright, 168 Ga. 690 (1-d) (148 S. E. 731). It has been held that the following weapons are likely to produce death: A knife, Ward, 56 Ga. 408. A pocket knife, Chisholm, 41 Ga. App. 

311 (152 S. E. 907). A rock, Samuels, 103 Ga. 3 (29 S. E. 427). 

A champagne bottle, Wilson, 33 Ga. 207. A stick, Boatwright, 89 

Ga. 140 (15 S. E. 21). An automobile, Sudan, 41 Ga. App. 828 (155 S. E. 102); Chambliss, 37 Ga. App. 124 (137 S. E. 80). Shotgun, rifle, Burney, 22 Ga. App. 622 (97 S. E. 85). Soda-water bottle,

SPECIFIC CRIMES 

291 

Watson, 21 Ga. App. 637 (94 S. E. 857). It is not indispensable to prove the precise weapon set forth in the indictment. It is sufficient if both were weapons likely to produce death, and were capable of inflicting the same character of injury. Trowbridge, 74 

Ga. 431 (4-a); Watson, 21 Ga. App. 637 (94 S. E. 857); Burney, 22 

Ga. App. 622 (97 S. E. 85).

Where the indictment charged the commission of assault with intent to commit murder by using a weapon likely to produce death, the proof must show that such was the character of the weapon. 

This may be done by producing the instrument itself, or showing the effect of it, or other satisfactory evidence, but it must be done in some way. Paschal, 68 Ga. 818; Breedlove, 24 Ga. App. 592, 593 (101 S. E. 709); Paschal, 125 Ga. 279 (54 S. E. 172).

Where it is shown that the defendant fired a pistol which discharged a bullet that entered and went through the forearm and lodged in the back of the prosecutor, the jury are authorized to find that such a pistol was one likely to produce death in the manner in which it was used, without the pistol being exhibited or testified about. Dixon, 49 Ga. App. 76 (2) (174 S. E. 176).

An assault with intent to murder may be committed without the use of a weapon that would be likely to produce death. Monday, 32 Ga. 672; Paschal, 125 Ga. 279 (54 S. E. 172).

Whether a pistol used as a club is a weapon likely to produce death is a question for the jury. Prior, 41 Ga. 155.

Rocks. Where one was indicted for the offense of assault with intent to murder a named person with a rock; and upon the trial the evidence tended to show that the accused wantonly threw a rock, likely to produce death if hitting a person in a vital spot, into a street railroad car occupied by a number of persons, one of whom was the person alleged to have been assaulted and the rock came near striking, and it did not appear that the accused intended to hit any particular person, the evidence did not warrant conviction for assault with intent to murder. Crime was "rocking a passenger train." § 26-7308. Bray, 118 Ga. 786 (45 S. E. 598).

Poison. Though poison introduced into the stomach is not, strictly speaking, a "weapon," an assault with intent to murder may be thus committed. Johnson, 92 Ga. 36 (17 S. E. 974); Brown, 88 Ga. 257 (14 S. E. 578).

Where one is indicted jointly with others for murder, and it appears upon the trial that there was an actual homicide committed by another of the defendants than the one on trial, it is not com-

petent, under that indictment, to convict the defendant on trial of a separate and independent "assault with intent to murder" which may have been committed upon the person slain, immediately before the firing the fatal shot, with which he was in no way connected. Smith, 127 Ga. 262 (56 S. E. 360); Driskell, 20 Ga. App. 

173 (92 S. E. 1007).

Killing of an officer. Generally the killing of an officer or other person to prevent an illegal arrest is not murder, but manslaughter. 

Consequently, shooting at him for the same purpose without killing him is prima facie not an assault with intent to murder. Thomas, 91 Ga. 204 (18 S. E. 305).

In the absence of notice to the defendant that the person pursuing him was an officer or had a warrant for his arrest, a verdict finding him guilty of assault with intent to murder is contrary to law and the evidence. Davis, 79 Ga. 767 (4 S. E. 318); Giddens, 154 Ga. 54, 57 (113 S. E. 386).

If a marshal of an incorporated town, or his deputy, attempts to arrest disorderly persons, and such persons act in concert in making resistance, and one of them, with the consent and approbation of the others, attempts to kill the marshal or his assistant by using a weapon likely to produce death, all of the rioters may be guilty as principals of an assault with intent to murder. Garrett, 89 Ga. 

446 (15 S. E. 533).

Statute of limitations. There being no statute of limitations for the offense of murder, one charged with that crime may be found guilty of assault with intent to murder, although indictment returned twenty-one years after the commission of the alleged offense. 

Troup, 17 Ga. App. 387 (87 S. E. 157).

Indictment for stabbing should allege that stabbing was not committed in self-defense or under circumstances of justification.

293 Accusation charging cutting "with a knife or other like instrument"-defective on special demurrer. Henderson, 113 Ga. 1148 (39 S. E. 446).

General. Under an indictment for stabbing the accused can be lawfully convicted of assault and battery, in case where there is evidence of assault and battery independently of the stabbing. Sessions, 115 Ga. 18 (41 S. E. 259).

In order to convict one of assault by stabbing, it is not necessary to prove that it was intentionally done. Criminal negligence will take the place of intent. Wallace, 95 Ga. 470 (20 S. E. 250). 

Scissors held to be "instrument of like kind" with "a sword, dirk, or knife." Jury could determine from common knowledge and experience. Norwood, 3 Ga. App. 325 (2) (59 S. E. 828).

To constitute stabbing the knife need not enter further than to penetrate the skin and draw blood,-certainly, half an inch or even the eighth of an inch, would be deep enough. Ward, 56 Ga. 408 (2). 

Where indictment charges cutting and stabbing with a razor, evidence of cutting and stabbing not supported where not shown that it was with a razor or similar instrument. Mays, 39 Ga. App. 

498 (147 S. E. 403).

Defendant not necessarily guilty of stabbing, if offense would have been voluntary manslaughter, if death had ensued. Burris, 2 Ga. App. 418 (2) (58 S. E. 545). 

Stabbing justified where it was to prevent illegal arrest.

Dorsey, 

If the defendant had killed the person stabbed and crime would have been justifiable homicide, the stabbing would also be justifiable. 

Therefore justification not limited to self-defense. Baldwin, 75 Ga. 

482, 489; Edmondson, 1 Ga. App. 116 (57 S. E. 947). 

Opprobrious words will not justify stabbing. Ward, 56 Ga. 408 (3). 

Unless great disparity of strength, assault with fist will not justify stabbing. McEvoy, 123 Ga. 506 (51 S. E. 500).

Where offense is not alleged and shown to be a felony, city court has jurisdiction. Norwood, 3 Ga. App. 325 (3) (59 S. E. 828).

One indicted for stabbing may be convicted of assault and battery. Sessions, 115 Ga. 18 (41 S. E. 259). This is the law only where there is evidence authorizing such conviction of assault and battery. (Id.)

Charge. On a trial for assault with intent to murder, it was error to omit to charge the jury as to the lesser offense of stabbing, it appearing that if the assault was committed it was made with a knife. Lewis, 14 Ga. App. 503 (81 S. E. 378); Seay, 39 Ga. App. 

694, 696 (148 S. E. 284).

No error to state to the jury that the crime of stabbing is only a misdemeanor. Harris, 18 Ga. App. 752 (3) (90 S. E. 491). 

k. ASSAULT WITH INTENT TO RAPE.

E. 814).) 

Including battery: Add to above: "did make an assault, and her, the said.................., did then and there beat, wound, ill-treat 

(See also Mitchell, 6 Ga. App. 554 (65 S. E. 326).)

If a battery is inflicted as a part of the felony of assault with intent to rape, it is necessary to charge it; otherwise the defendant could not be convicted of assault and battery. Mitchell, 6 Ga. App. 

554, 556 (65 S. E. 326).

Female. An indictment for assault with intent to commit rape is sufficient if it shows the sex of the person assaulted by other words of the indictment, without the use of the term "female." Joice, 53 

Ga. 50.

Battery. An indictment for assault with intent to rape should allege a battery, as no conviction can be had for assault and battery unless it is alleged in the indictment. Goldin, 104 Ga. 549 (30 S. E. 749).

A charge in the indictment for assault with intent to rape that the accused "did feloniously assault and attempt. . . to ravish and carnally know" the female, necessarily implies that the act was done forcibly and against her will. Jackson, 114 Ga. 861 (1) (40 

S. E. 989). General. 

Assault with intent to rape is not a reducible felony. Atkins, 29
