SPECIFIC CRIMES 

295 In order to authorize a conviction for the offense of assault with intent to rape, the evidence must show beyond all reasonable doubt, (1) an assault, (2) an intent to have carnal knowledge of the female, and (3) a purpose to carry into effect this intent with force and against the consent of the female. If any of these three elements is lacking, the offense is not made out. Dorsey, 108 Ga. 477 (1) (34 S. E. 135); Green, 42 Ga. App. 437 (156 S. E. 637).

No actual touching of the woman's person is necessary to complete the assault. There need be nothing more than the intention to accomplish sexual intercourse presently by force, and the active prosecution of that intention until a situation of immediate, present danger to the woman is produced. Jackson, 91 Ga. 322, 329 (18 

S. E. 132).

While every rape necessarily includes battery, there may be an assault with intent to rape without committing a battery upon the female assaulted. Where battery is not charged in the indictment, and evidence shows assault and battery without intent to rape, defendant must be acquitted. Goldin, 104 Ga. 549 (30 S. E. 749); 

Davis, 41 Ga. App. 466 (153 S. E. 428).

Conviction for assault, assault and battery, or assault with intent to rape may be had in prosecution for rape. Sills, 36 Ga. App. 

103 (135 S. E. 758).

Overt act, amounting to an assault, with intention to have carnal knowledge of the female forcibly and against her will, necessary to convict. Gaskin, 105 Ga. 631 (31 S. E. 740).

On account of the provision of § 27-2508, a prisoner can not be convicted of simple assault where the only assault committed is consummated by battery. An assault with intent to rape may be committed without a battery, and an indictment for this offense need not charge battery; and under an indictment for this offense which does not charge battery, the defendant can not be convicted of assault and battery. It follows that if the indictment be for assault with intent to rape and does not charge a battery, and the proof shows a mere assault and battery, without an intent to rape, the defendant can not be convicted of any offense. Owens, 9 Ga. App. 

441 (71 S. E. 680).

Where State's evidence made out a case of assault with intent to rape, and accused relied upon the defense of alibi, assault or assault and battery not involved. Langston, 23 Ga. App. 82 (4) (97 S. E. 444).

To sustain a verdict of assault with intent to rape, evidence should

be as clear as to convict of rape, so that verdict of assault with intent to rape in rape prosecution will not be sustained by evidence of improper exposure of female patient's person by her doctor, under false statement of the necessity therefor. Nichols, 72 Ga. 191 (1). 

Where the evidence is conclusive that the carnal knowledge was realized, a verdict finding the prisoner guilty of assault with intent to rape is contrary to law. Kelsey, 62 Ga. 558; Rich, 160 Ga. 513, 514 (128 S. E. 666).

Race and social standing properly considered on the question of intent to rape. Dorsey, 108 Ga. 477 (2) (34 S. E. 135); McCullough, 10 Ga. App. 403 (1) (73 S. E. 546); McCullough, 11 Ga. App. 

612 (76 S. E. 393).

The mere solicitation by a man of a woman to go with him into the woods, though intended as a proposal to her to have sexual intercourse with him, and accompanied by a seizure of her hand, will not warrant a conviction for assault with intent to rape, where the evidence shows that there was no intention to have sexual intercourse by force and against her will. Tiller, 101 Ga. 782 (29 

S. E. 424); Bennett, 21 Ga. App. 505 (94 S. E. 626).

Attempting to have sexual intercourse with female under fourteen years of age constitutes assault with intent to rape. Todd, 25 

Ga. App. 411 (4) (103 S. E. 496); Suggs, 24 Ga. App. 323 (1) (100 

S. E. 778).

Even though child under age of fourteen consented, crime can be committed. Suggs, 24 Ga. App. 323 (1-b) (100 S. E. 778).

Any physical contact, or "laying on his hand," upon the child under fourteen, if in lust and with intent to have carnal knowledge of her, sufficient to authorize conviction for assault with intent to rape. Williams, 15 Ga. App. 306 (2) (82 S. E. 938).

An assault with intent to induce consent to sexual intercourse of a female child under the age of consent is not an assault and battery, but assault with intent to rape, just as the completed intercourse with such child would be rape. Gibson, 10 Ga. App. 117 (72 S. E. 944).

Where evidence shows that assault was committed upon the woman to obtain her consent, conviction for assault with intent to rape not supported. Sutton, 123 Ga. 125 (51 S. E. 316); Byfield, 33 Ga. App. 275 (125 S. E. 905). 

Boy under fourteen presumed incapable of committing rape. 

State must prove capacity. Gordon, 93 Ga. 531 (21 S. E. 54); Bird, 110 Ga. 315 (35 S. E. 156).

SPECIFIC CRIMES 

297 Upon the trial for assault with intent to rape, where evidence shows offense was either assault with intent to rape or assault and battery, verdict for mere assault not supported by evidence. Simmons, 36 Ga. App. 309 (136 S. E. 330).

Assault with intent to rape may be committed by two persons. 

Griffin, 37 Ga. App. 188 (139 S. E. 105).

Where there is no evidence showing that the accused intended to have sexual intercourse with the female forcibly and against her will, a verdict of guilty of assault with intent to rape is error. 

Joice, 53 Ga. 50; Green, 42 Ga. App. 437 (156 S. E. 637).

Evidence showed no greater offense than an attempt to commit fornication, without the element of attempt with intent to rape. 

Morrow, 13 Ga. App. 189 (1) (79 S. E. 63).

Desisting from purpose. If the intention to commit the crime of rape was present at the time the female was first assaulted, defendant is guilty of assault with intent to rape, distinguished from further effort, on account of resistance, inability to overcome the resistance, or from fear, does not relieve him from guilt. Taylor, 50 Ga. 79; McCullough, 11 Ga. App. 612, 614 (76 S. E. 393).

If the defendant, at the time of the assault, intended to desist as soon as he ascertained that the woman assailed would not consent, he can not be convicted of assault with intent to rape. McCullough, 11 Ga. App. 612 (1) (76 S. E. 393).

Evidence. The intent may be inferred from the actions of the defendant. Thus where the evidence showed that late in the evening, near dark, a girl twelve years of age was passing along a byway going to the house of a neighbor, that defendant, a grown man and a stranger, rushed out of the woods on the roadside, seized and squeezed her hand, clasped her in his arms, and was bearing her to the woods, saying that he was going to "take her off" and upon her crying, that he was going to take her off and kill her; and that upon her threatening him with her father, he put her down and ran, it was held that these facts warranted a verdict of assault with intent to rape. Ware, 67 Ga. 349.

Defendant attempting to force female with a pistol and threats, guilty of assault with intent to rape, although it was near public road and houses. Watkins, 68 Ga. 832; Brittain, 41 Ga. App. 577 

Negro man with pistol springing from concealment in lonely place at late hour, accosting white woman with "I have got you where I wanted you for a long time" and pursuing her until aid

reached-not sufficient to show guilt. Dorsey, 108 Ga. 477 (34 S. 

E. 135). (See full discussion and dissenting opinion.) 

Negro attacking white girl by the neck and legs, after dark,not sufficient to convict of assault with intent to rape, unless specific intent is shown. (Dorsey, 108 Ga. 477 (153 S. E. 622), cited with approval.) Little, 42 Ga. App. 222 (155 S. E. 352). 

Where evidence shows that sixteen year old white girl is alone and unprotected on the street at night, and colored boy of approximately the same age steps in front of her, stops, and orders her to go into a vacant lot, and tells her that he will shoot her heart out if she doesn't go, and will shoot her if she hollers, conviction for assault with intent to rape authorized. Brittain, 41 Ga. App. 577 (2-a) (153 S. E. 622). 

Where a man under the incitement of lust, and with the intention of gratifying it by force, enters the bedroom of a virtuous woman at a late hour of the night and gets upon the bed in which she is sleeping, within reach of her person, for the purpose of ravishing her, he commits an assault upon her, although he may not actually touch her, being prevented from so doing by her outcry. Jackson, 91 Ga. 322 (18 S. E. 132); Carter, 35 Ga. 263. 

Where a man hailed a woman walking along a pathway, and holding something in his hand and saying he had plenty of money, told her to go into a gully, and on her retreating drew a pistol and, advancing upon her, ordered her to turn back, and she escaped by flight, conviction authorized. Watkins, 68 Ga. 832.

Where there is slight evidence that the purpose of the accused was to commit rape, conviction upheld, although appellate court is of the opinion that no such purpose existed. Williams, 15 Ga. App. 

306 (82 S. E. 938).

That the female is a prostitute, or that she is a woman of ill fame, may be shown to affect her credibility as a witness and to throw light on the question of consent. Camp, 3 Ga. 417; Rudulph, 16 

Ga. App. 353, 354 (85 S. E. 365); Smiley, 156 Ga. 60, 61 (118 S. 

E. 713). 

Specific acts of lewdness not admissible. Camp, 3 Ga. 417; Clarke, 41 Ga. App. 556 (153 S. E. 616). 

Corroboration of prosecutrix not essential. Williams, 31 Ga. 

App. 173 (5) (120 S. E. 131). This rule was not changed by the act of the General Assembly approved July 31, 1918 (Ga. L. 1918, page 259), § 26-1304.

Defendant may be convicted of assault, though person assaulted

General. Assault with intent to rob may be committed in three ways: (1) By unlawfully and maliciously assaulting another with any offensive or dangerous weapon or instrument, with intent to commit robbery upon such person; (2) By menaces, demanding any money, goods or chattels of or from any other person, with intent to commit robbery upon such person; (3) By any forcible or violent manner, demanding any money, goods or chattels of or from another person, with intent to commit robbery upon such person. Erwin, 117 Ga. 296 (43 S. E. 719).

p. DEFENSE TO ASSAULT. 

Self-defense. The broadest statement of the rule of self-defense is that given by Blackstone: "Of the first sort, or that which arises from the sole act of the injured party, is the defense of one's self, of the mutual or reciprocal defense of such as stand in the relation of husband and wife, parent and child, master and servant. In these cases, if the party himself or any of these his relations, be forcibly attacked in his person or property, it is lawful for him to repel force by force, and the breach of peace, which happens, is chargeable upon him only, who began the affray." Cole, 2 Ga. App. 734, 736 (59 S. E. 24). § 26-1016, relating to justifiable homicide is not applicable to cases of homicide or assault with intent to murder, where the defense relied upon is self-defense. Ripley, 7 Ga. App. 679 (2) (67 

S. E. 834); Ward, 25 Ga. App. 296 (3) (103 S. E. 726).

Regardless of the character of the place (church), the defendants would have the right to protect themselves against an assault, or assault and battery, or even to resent the use of opprobrious words and abusive language, provided in so doing they did not exceed the proper measure of resistance. Bracewell, 10 Ga. App. 830 (1) (74 S. E. 440).

Where the doctrine of reasonable fear is invoked as a defense by one charged with an assault with intent to murder with a deadly weapon, it is essential for the defense to show that the attack was necessary, or apparently necessary, to prevent the commission of a felony upon the person making it. The danger must be urgent and pressing at the time of the assault, or it must appear that the danger was so urgent and pressing at the time, that it was necessary for the person to assault the other. Martin, 36 Ga. App. 288 (3)

SPECIFIC CRIMES 

305 (136 S. E. 324); Newman, 60 Ga. 609; Love, 14 Ga. App. 49 (80 

S. E. 209).

The circumstances must be such as to excite the reasonable fears of a rational mind, and the person assaulting must act under the influence of such fears, and not in a spirit of revenge. Frazier, 112 

It is not necessary that it appear that it was absolutely necessary to make the assault in order to save life. Heard, 114 Ga. 90 (3) (39 S. E. 909).

While provocation by mere words, threat, or menaces will not reduce the crime of assault with intent to murder to the statutory offense of shooting at another, yet if such words, threats or menaces were sufficient to arouse a reasonable fear on the part of the accused that his life was in danger, and he shot under the influence of this fear, the shooting would be justifiable. Phillips, 11 Ga. App. 

262 (75 S. E. 14). 

Merely biting another's finger does not justify the latter in taking the life of his assailant, or in making an assault with intent to kill him. Love, 14 Ga. App. 49 (2) (80 S. E. 209).

When a man goes to another to assail him or demand explanation or in anger, and the party puts his hand in his pocket, it is an unauthorized presumption that he has a concealed weapon that he is about to draw and use. One must depend on something more substantial, even in appearance, than this without the existence of threats. Mitchell, 41 Ga. 527 (4), 537.

Merely drawing a pistol in a quarrel, though done by the person who began the quarrel, will not deprive him of the right to use it in self-defense against a deadly attack upon his own life. But drawing a pistol with intent to attack his adversary's life, or under circumstances calculated to excite in the adversary the fears of a reasonable man that an immediate attack on him was intended, would outlaw the right of self-defense in the other. Fussell, 94 Ga. 

78 (1) (19 S. E. 891).

The law will not hold him guiltless who creates the necessity to kill another by provoking an attack in order to afford himself a pretext for slaying his assailant, but one who has provoked the difficulty may defend himself against violence on the part of the one provoked, if the violence against which he defends is disproportionate to the seriousness of the provocation, or greater in degree than the law recognizes as being justifiable under the circumstances. 

Reddick, 11 Ga. App. 150 (5) (74 S. E. 901).

Where defendant was not a trespasser upon the premises of the prosecutor, and prosecutor struck defendant first with a plank, and defendant thereupon struck prosecutor with fist, conviction unauthorized. Arthur, 9 Ga. App. 298 (70 S. E. 1127).

Disparity of physical qualities. Unless there be a great superiority in physical strength of an assailant who strikes another a blow with his fist, or ill health in the assailed at the time, or other circumstances producing relatively great inequality between them. in combat, the assailed can not justifiably resent the blow by stabbing the assailant. Morgan, 119 Ga. 566 (46 S. E. 836); McEvoy, 123 Ga. 506 (51 S. E. 500).

Defense of family. If a man takes the life of another who attempts the seduction of his wife, under circumstances of gross and direct aggravation, it is for the jury to find whether the case stands upon the same footing of reason and justice, as other instances of justifiable homicide enumerated in the Code. Biggs, 29 Ga. 723 (3); Rossi, 7 Ga. App. 732 (2) (68 S. E. 56).

When the injured husband meets one, the next morning, who has attempted, over-night, the violation of his marriage bed, and fires upon him, it is right and proper to give in evidence the previous occurrence, as a justification or excuse for the act. Biggs, 29 Ga. 723 (4). 

While the right of husband and wife, and parent and child, to defend one another is fully recognized, some cases hold that one can not defend another where the latter himself would not be authorized so to do; others rule that if one brings on a difficulty, or is in a position where it would be murder for him to kill his assailant, the relative would be guilty of a similar offense if under these circumstances he should interpose and kill the blameless opponent. Alexander, 118 Ga. 26, 27 (44 S. E. 857); Kimberly, 4 Ga. 

App. 852 (2) (62 S. E. 571).

In a prosecution for assault and battery, it is not competent for the defendant to show, that prior to the assault, and not contemporaneously therewith, the prosecutor or person assaulted had committed an injury upon the person, family, or property of the defendant. Cole, 2 Ga. App. 734 (59 S. E. 24). 

Parents may protect their children. Parker, 37 Ga. App. 84 (139 

S. E. 94).

A brother has a right to defend the reputation of his sister, and where he has made an assault and battery upon one assailing in his presence his sister's character for chastity, modesty and vir-

SPECIFIC CRIMES 

307 tue, question of justification is for the jury. Farmer, 7 Ga. App.

688 (1) (67 S. E. 834). 

Brother has a right to defend brother. Swain, 15 Ga. App. 445 (83 S. E. 642); Warnack, 3 Ga. App. 590, 596 (60 S. E. 288); Maryland Casualty Co., 45 Ga. App. 173 (164 S. E. 80).

Where grand juror asked lawful question in good faith, there is no right by relative of witness to assault grand juror. Nobles, 12 

Ga. App. 355 (77 S. E. 184).

Brother has no right to assault stepfather for chastising child brother, where stepfather had mother's permission, even where he is cruelly and inhumanly beating the child, unless a felony was committed, or about to be committed. Mosley, 11 Ga. App. 1, 6 (75 S. E. 569).

Parents have the authority to use necessary force to protect their daughters from seduction and debauchery, but may not assault an apparent suitor merely on the assumption that he may prove to be a seducer, unless the known facts and circumstances at the time are sufficient to legitimately induce this conclusion. Jordan, 14 Ga. 

App. 429 (3) (81 S. E. 359). 

No error to fail to charge that one brother may protect another, in absence of timely and appropriate request. Thurmond, 41 Ga. 

App. 431 (153 S. E. 384).

Defense of property and possession. One on trial for the offense of assault with intent to murder can not rely upon the theory of defense set forth in § 26-1013, to wit, forcible attack on or invasion of the property or habitation of the accused, unless it appears that the attempt to kill was necessary to prevent such forcible invasion or attack. If the difficulty was caused by a matter wholly independent of and disconnected from the invasion, the mere fact that the person assaulted entered the habitation of the assailant would be no defense. Love, 14 Ga. App. 49 (3) (80 S. E. 209).

Even a trespasser, where he is rightfully ordered to leave a building by one having the premises in charge, is entitled to be allowed such a period of time as is necessary to enable him to make his exit from the room or building he is ordered to vacate. The amount of time reasonably necessary to enable such a trespasser to effect his departure may be varied by circumstances and is a question for the jury. Hollis, 13 Ga. App. 307 (3) (79 S. E. 85).

If one whose premises are invaded by a riotous mob, who lay siege to his habitation and continue their rioting, shoots into the mob and wounds one of its members, he does not commit the offense

of assault with intent to murder; and this is true irrespective of any racial difference between the parties. Rhodes, 10 Ga. App. 68 (72 S. E. 518).

In a prosecution for assault and battery, it is not competent for the defendant to show, as justification, that prior to the assault, and not contemporaneously therewith, the prosecutor or person assaulted had committed an injury upon the person, family, or property of the defendant. Cole, 2 Ga. App. 734 (59 S. E. 24).

Opprobrious words and abusive language. At common law opprobrious words and abusive language did not justify an assault. Haygood, 137 Ga. 168 (73 S. E. 81).

Opprobrious words may justify simple assault, or assault and battery, but will not justify an attack with a deadly weapon made in a manner likely to produce death. Mathews, 125 Ga. 50 (54 S. E. 

192); Crawley, 7 Ga. App. 95 (66 S. E. 273).

If one, out of resentment of the use of opprobrious words by another, makes an attack upon him with a deadly weapon, the latter may repel the attack with all necessary force, even to the extent of using deadly weapon. Crawley, 7 Ga. App. 95 (66 S. E. 

273); Reddick, 11 Ga. App. 150 (5) (74 S. E. 901).

The law will not hold him guiltless who creates the necessity to kill another by provoking an attack in order to afford himself a pretext for slaying his assailant. Reddick, 11 Ga. App. 150 (5) (74 S. E. 901). 

Assault must not be disproportionate. Bedford, 5 Ga. App. 461 (63 S. E. 515); Sutton, 2 Ga. App. 659 (58 S. E. 1108).

Opprobrious words can not be used as defense, if they were provoked by defendant's use of similar language. Sutton, 2 Ga. App. 

659 (58 S. E. 1108). If defendant first used abusive language, or opprobrious words, then defendant would not be justified in assaulting prosecutor for the use of similar language. Folds, 23 Ga. 

App. 147 (97 S. E. 872). 

Sufficiency of provocation is question for the jury. Amerson, 18 

Ga. App. 176 (88 S. E. 998); Moore, 102 Ga. 581 (27 S. E. 675).

Insulting language and gestures used by a child nine years old to an adult furnish no justification for an assault and battery of the child by the adult. McKinley, 121 Ga. 193 (1) (49 S. E. 917).

Circumstances which arouse passion must be grave and serious. 

Berry, 105 Ga. 683, 689 (31 S. E. 592).

The opprobrious words must have been used in the presence of the defendant, at the time of the assault, and not previously. Hay-

SPECIFIC CRIMES 

309 good, 137 Ga. 168 (73 S. E. 81); Haygood, 10 Ga. App. 394 (73 S. 

E. 423).

Insulting words used to daughter of the accused, while he was absent, on the evening prior to the assault and battery, are no excuse, and inadmissible. Walker, 117 Ga. 323 (43 S. E. 737).

In prosecution for assault and battery the accused can not give in evidence as a justification opprobrious words or abusive language written or published of him by the person upon whom he made the assault and battery. Haygood, 10 Ga. App. 394 (73 S. E. 423); 

Haygood, 137 Ga. 168 (73 S. E. 81).

Retaliation. But though the law will not justify an assault made in retaliation of a wrong which has been completed, still, in mercy to the frailty of human nature, the gravity of the offense may be mitigated where the assault can be attributed to an impulse of passion supposed to be uncontrollable. 

Jury is the exclusive arbiter. Wimberly, 12 Ga. App. 540, 544 (77 S. E. 879). 

Accident. Accident is a good defense. (74 S. E. 285). 

Conoly, 10 Ga. App. 822

Former jeopardy. Prosecution in municipal court under municipal ordinance is irrelevant, and no defense. DeGraffenreid, 72 Ga. 

212; Butler, 10 Ga. App. 463 (73 S. E. 685). 

q. EVIDENCE. 

On the trial of one indicted for assault with intent to murder by the use of a deadly weapon, the burden is on the State to show: (1) The assault, (2) the deadly character of the weapon, (3) the intent to take life, (4) the commission of the assault under such circumstances that, had death ensued, the party making the assault would have been guilty of murder. McLane, 20 Ga. App. 825 (93 

S. E. 558).

Upon the trial of one accused of an offense in the perpetration of which malice is an essential ingredient, evidence as to the conduct and saying of the accused shortly after he made the assault may be admissible to characterize the quo animo with which the deed was committed. Davis, 11 Ga. App. 804 (76 S. E. 391).

Since the indictment was for assault with intent to murder, evidence tending to show prior quarrels between the parties and prior acts of violence on the part of the accused toward the prosecutor was admissible for the purpose of showing motive and malice. 

Smallwood, 9 Ga. App. 300 (70 S. E. 1124); Davis, 40 Ga. App. 

123 (149 S. E. 51).

On the trial of a woman charged with assault with intent to murder testimony of the person assaulted that at a time, several weeks before, the accused had a quarrel with her over her husband -is admissible, to show the animus and motive. Jackson, 18 Ga. 

App. 683 (90 S. E. 368); Belote, 41 Ga. App. 346 (2) (152 S. E. 911).

Evidence as to various acts of violence committed by the accused against other persons or things, at the identical time he was charged with committing the felonious assault for which he was prosecuted, was admissible, as part of the res gestae, to throw light on his state of mind and to illustrate his intention at the time of the assault. 

Carter, 15 Ga. App. 343 (1) (83 S. E. 153).

On the trial for an assault made when the assaulted man was in conversation with a woman, with whom the accused was intimate, evidence that a month or two before the accused threatened to kill this man if he ever caught him at his "girl's" house again, was admissible to show motive. Early, 14 Ga. App. 467 (81 S. E. 385).

There being no evidence that the person shot made an assault upon the person shooting, on the trial of the latter for assault with intent to murder, evidence of uncommunicated threats against the accused, made by the other party-inadmissible. Cargill, 12 Ga. 

App. 574 (77 S. E. 832); McKinney, 119 Ga. 467 (46 S. E. 719); 

Rouse, 135 Ga. 227 (69 S. E. 180).

Where there is no evidence that the prosecutor attempted to make an assault upon the defendant at the time the latter shot, evidence as to the violent character of the prosecutor-inadmissible. 

Wimberly, 13 Ga. App. 671 (79 S. E. 767).

The charge in the indictment that the assault was made with a shotgun, and that it was "a weapon likely to produce death," was sufficiently proved by showing the wounds, how they were made, and that the weapon used was in fact a shotgun, and was loaded with shot. Prater, 16 Ga. App. 296 (85 S. E. 204).

Where the indictment charges the commission of an assault with intent to murder by using a knife such as was likely to produce death, the proof must show that it was a weapon of this character. 

This may be done by producing the knife, or introducing other satisfactory evidence to establish the facts, but not by evidence which falls short of the character of proof which will justify an inference by the jury that the knife used was in truth a deadly weapon. Paschal, 125 Ga. 279 (54 S. E. 172).

Where one was charged with an assault with intent to murder "A," and it appeared that the defendant had fired into a house in which "A," "B," "C" and "D" were living; that one shot

SPECIFIC CRIMES 

311 came near "B" and another within eighteen inches of "A," there was sufficient evidence to support a conviction. Tipton, 119 Ga. 304 (6) (46 S. E. 436).

Where defendant is charged with assault and battery, evidence that he entered the house of the prosecutrix, although forbidden to go there, and began to curse and abuse her; and that she thereupon picked up a bed slat and hit him two licks, when he grabbed up a hoe and tried to hit her a severe blow, but that he was prevented from completion of the act by a third person, conviction for assault sustained by evidence. Price, 118 Ga. 60 (44 S. E. 820).

While the prosecutor was engaged in an altercation with another person, he was fired on by two bystanders. Although it was not absolutely certain which one of the shots took effect, conviction upheld. Hopkins, 119 Ga. 569 (46 S. E. 835).

An accusation against "A," for the offense of assault and battery charged that said defendant "did unlawfully and with force and arms assault and beat the person of 'B' with a pocket knife.” The undisputed evidence showed that "A" tore "B's" clothes and held him with his left hand, but did not strike him with a knife, which was in his right hand. Such evidence did not authorize conviction. 

Fulford, 50 Ga. 591; Johnson, 127 Ga. 277 (56 S. E. 420).

Prior quarrel between same parties admissible to show malice and motive. Smallwood, 9 Ga. App. 300 (70 S. E. 1124). 

r. CHARGE. 

Where on a trial for assault with intent to murder, there is no evidence except that defendant was guilty as charged, or justified, it is error to charge the jury that defendant may be found guilty of assault and battery, or shooting at another. Robinson, 118 Ga. 

45 (44 S. E. 804); Fitzgerald, 136 Ga. 163 (71 S. E. 128). But see Hopkins, 119 Ga. 569 (46 S. E. 835).

Upon a trial for assault with intent to murder, where the evidence tended to show that there was a mutual combat between the parties, the law of manslaughter was involved, and should have been charged without request, as bearing upon the question of whether the accused shall be convicted of the lesser offense than charged. Kimball, 112 Ga. 541 (37 S. E. 886).

Where evidence plainly shows assault with intent to kill (either maliciously or in self-defense) charge on assault and battery unauthorized. Howard, 2 Ga. App. 830 (59 S. E. 89).

One accused of the offense of assault with intent to murder may defend upon two theories of self-defense,-that applicable to cases.

of mutual combat, and that of reasonable fears where there is no mutual combat. If in his statement to the jury the accused relies upon the latter theory, it is error for the judge, if he charges at all upon the statement as to this defense, to fail to charge upon the subject of reasonable fears. Stephens, 118 Ga. 762 (3) (45 S.

E. 619). 

An instruction touching the law of self-defense, though not strictly accurate, will not be ground for a new trial, where, from defendant's statement, the shooting was not justifiable. Rawls, 124 

Ga. 11 (3) (52 S. E. 72).

On trial for assault with intent to murder, where the question of reasonable fear is involved, the defendant is entitled to have the question of existence and reasonableness of his fear determined by the jury in the light of all the words, threats and menaces, and other attendant circumstances, and the Court should so charge. Clay, 124 

Ga. 795 (1) (53 S. E. 179).

Where on the trial of a criminal case the judge tells the jury that the evidence tends to prove a mutual combat between the parties, such charge amounts to an expression of an opinion, and is error. 

Stephens, 118 Ga. 762 (45 S. E. 619). 

A charge in the following words: "Before you are authorized to acquit the defendant you must be satisfied from the evidence that the defendant was justified in all that he did" is too broad and in the absence of any explanation appearing in the record, will necessitate the grant of a new trial. Brewster, 63 Ga. 639.

When a charge of a graver character includes minor offenses, if the evidence will justify or require a verdict finding defendant guilty thereof, it is the duty of the judge to instruct the jury as to the principles applicable to the lesser offenses. Fields, 2 Ga. 

App. 41 (3), 45 (58 S. E. 327); Sutton, 123 Ga. 125 (51 S. E. 316); 

Smalls, 6 Ga. App. 502 (2) (65 S. E. 295); Ripley, 7 Ga. App. 679 (3) (67 S. E. 834); Autrey, 24 Ga. App. 414 (4) (100 S. E. 782).

An erroneous instruction to the jury will not work a reversal, if the verdict as rendered makes it manifest that the finding of the jury was in no wise affected thereby. Tinsley, 4 Ga. App. 611 (3) (62 S. E. 93); Wall, 69 Ga. 766 (2).

The failure to charge the jury in effect that the specific intent to take human life is necessary in the offense of assault with intent to murder, will require reversal, where the trial results in a verdict of guilty of assault with intent to murder, and the evidence does not demand a finding that the assault was made with the specific intent to take life. McLane, 20 Ga. App. 825 (2) (93 S. E. 558).

SPECIFIC CRIMES 

313 

Where the sayings and conduct of one assaulted do not, as a matter of law, justify the assault, it is not error to so instruct the jury. Nobles, 12 Ga. App. 355 (2) (77 S. E. 184).

Where defense is accident or misadventure, and evidence warrants it, it must be charged. Conoly, 10 Ga. App. 822 (74 S. E. 285). 

s. VERDICTS. 

It is an elementary principle of criminal procedure that no person can be convicted of any offense not charged in the indictment. 

There may, of course, be a conviction of a lesser offense than that expressly named in the indictment, where the former is necessarily included in the latter, and also in some cases in which the lesser is not included in the greater offense, but where the language used in the indictment is sufficient to embrace the smaller offense. Goldin, 104 Ga. 549, 550 (30 S. E. 749).

Under an indictment for assault with intent to murder a verdict for simple assault may be rendered. Smallwood, 9 Ga. App. 300 (1) (70 S. E. 1124); Butler, 10 Ga. App. 463 (73 S. E. 685).

Where under the uncontradicted evidence the accused is guilty of the offense of shooting at another, if not of the graver offense of assault with intent to murder, a verdict of guilty of the former offense will be upheld. Ridgley, 124 Ga. 454 (52 S. E. 761).

Where the evidence shows no assault other than one consummated by a complete battery, a verdict for simple assault is not lawful. Harris, 3 Ga. App. 457 (60 S. E. 127); Jackson, 38 Ga. App. 

138 (142 S. E. 694).

One accused of stabbing can be convicted of assault and battery where there is evidence of assault and battery independently of stabbing. Hollis, 13 Ga. App. 307 (79 S. E. 85).

In prosecution for rape conviction may be had for assault, assault and battery, or assault with intent to rape. Sills, 36 Ga. App. 

103 (135 S. E. 758). Where assault with intent to rape is charged, no conviction can be had for assault and battery, unless indictment charges battery. Davis, 41 Ga. App. 466 (153 S. E. 428).

Where the indictment charges rape, and there is no evidence of an assault, except a complete rape, verdict of guilty of assault with intent to rape is not authorized. Welborn, et al., 116 Ga. 522 (42 

S. E. 773); Rich, 160 Ga. 513, 514 (128 S. E. 666).

Under an indictment for assault with intent to murder, defendant may be convicted of stabbing, or assault and battery, if the evidence warrants it. Malone, 77 Ga. 767 (4-a); Bolton, 37 Ga. App. 515 (140 S. E. 924).

Where the person assaulted is badly cut and stabbed with a knife, Court's refusal to charge that defendant may be convicted of assault and battery is correct. Turner, 78 Ga. 174 (3-a).

On an indictment for stabbing, the jury may find the defendant guilty of assault and battery. Rives, 74 Ga. 375.

On an indictment charging assault with intent to murder, verdict of guilty of pointing pistol at another is upheld. Jenkins, 92 

Ga. 470 (1) (17 S. E. 693); Livingston, 6 Ga. App. 208, 210 (64 S. 

E. 709).

On an indictment charging assault with intent to murder by shooting another with a pistol, verdict finding defendant guilty of shooting at another upheld. Parker, 95 Ga. 482 (2) (22 S. E. 276); 

Johnson, 29 Ga. App. 659 (116 S. E. 226).

On a charge of assault with intent to murder the defendant can not be convicted of "whipping his wife." Manigault, 53 Ga. 

113. (Distinguished in Hammond, 28 Ga. App. 680 (113 S. E. 221).)

SPECIFIC CRIMES 

315 of the child does not amount to allegation that defendant was the father of the child. Stone, 24 Ga. App. 67 (1) (100 S. E. 21).

Indictment charging defendant is the putative father of child is not sufficient. Must allege that he is father. Hudson, 104 Ga. 723 (30 S. E. 947); Taylor, 133 Ga. 638 (66 S. E. 792).

Indictment need not allege that mother of bastard is single woman. Smith, 28 Ga. 19.

The charge is not complete until indictment, presentment or accusation is returned. Williamson, 1 Ga. App. 657 (57 S. E. 1079).

Motion for new trial should be granted where it does not appear upon the face of the indictment that defendant was required to give bond. Motion in arrest of judgment not proper remedy. Martin, 127 Ga. 39, 40 (56 S. E. 79).

General. Procedure being statutory, it must be strictly construed. Craft, 21 Ga. App. 258 (1) (94 S. E. 281).

The whole purpose of the statute is to indemnify the county against any expense that might be imposed upon it by having to take care of a pregnant woman who is a pauper during the time she lies in, and the child after it is born. Martin, 127 Ga. 39, 40 (56 S. E. 79).

The question of the probability of the child becoming chargeable to the county is not involved in the trial of an indictment for bastardy. Two questions are involved: Whether the defendant is the father of the bastard; and whether he refused to give bond in the terms of the law, that is in the manner pointed out by law, when called on to do so. Kennedy, 9 Ga. App. 219 (3) (70 S. E. 

986); Watts, 12 Ga. App. 350, 353 (77 S. E. 206).

The offense of the father is not that of being the father of a bastard child, but the statutory offense of bastardy, which is prima facie shown by the refusal of the putative father, when brought before the magistrate to give the required bond for the maintenance and education of the child. Watts, 12 Ga. App. 350, 352 (77 S. E. 206).

Failure to give bond when required to do so is equivalent of refusal. Rudulph, 16 Ga. App. 353 (5) (85 S. E. 365).

Though it must appear that defendant has refused or failed to give security for maintenance and education of child, before he can be convicted of bastardy, reason of failure or refusal is immaterial. 

Rudulph, 16 Ga. App. 353 (4) (85 S. E. 365).

In order for the defendant to be convicted of bastardy, it was necessary for the jury to arrive at the conclusion that he was the

father of the bastard child to which the prosecutrix had recently given birth. Bullard, 14 Ga. App. 478, 479 (81 S. E. 369).

Jurisdiction. The jurisdiction is in the county where bastard is likely to become chargeable, and not where the child was begotten, or born. White, 40 Ga. App. 264 (149 S. E. 304); Davis, 58 Ga. 

170 (4).

If a bastard child be born in Florida, and its mother subsequently removed to Georgia, the putative father of the child may be prosecuted for bastardy in Georgia. Jones, 11 Ga. App. 760 (3) (76 S. E. 72).

Statute of limitations. In a prosecution for bastardy the statute. of limitations begins to run from the refusal of the putative father to give the bond and pay the expenses as required by law. Jones, 11 Ga. App. 760 (2) (76 S. E. 72).

Presumptions. Children born during wedlock or within the usual period of gestation thereafter are presumed to be legitimate and children of husband. But presumption may be rebutted, and will be so held, where the proof to the contrary is clear. Jones, 11 Ga. 

App. 760 (1) (76 S. E. 72); Mims, 43 Ga. App. 100 (1) (157 S. E. 901). 

Preliminary trial. A proceeding to require security of the putative father of a bastard may be taken before a commissioned notary public he being ex officio justice of the peace. Childers, 3 Ga. App. 

449 (60 S. E. 128).

No law in this State confers jurisdiction to proceed against the father of the bastard upon a "justice court," presided over by two justices of the peace, but the jurisdiction belongs to a temporary court consisting of one justice of the peace only. Renew, 79 Ga. 

162 (4 S. E. 19).

While in many jurisdictions a proceeding for bastardy may be commenced by affidavit of some public officer, in Georgia it can be instituted only by affidavit of the mother of the bastard. Craft, 21 

Ga. App. 258 (2) (94 S. E. 281); Watts, 12 Ga. App. 350 (77 S. E. 

206). Judgment based on other affidavit null and void. (Id.) 

Bond. Expenses incurred by woman in supporting self and child after institution suit on bastardy bond and before trial, recoverable, although third persons contributed thereto. Graves, 35 Ga. App. 

418, 419 (133 S. E. 267).

Where child has been born and mother has recovered from her confinement before bastardy proceedings are begun, bond required by law is simply bond to indemnify county against possible charge 11

Mother need not appear before magistrate. Watts, 12 Ga. App.

Date of offense need not be stated. It is only necessary to state the name of the father. Watts, 12 Ga. App. 350, 352 (77 S. E. 206). 

Failure to direct to what magistrate warrant is returnable is no defect. Tolbert, 12 Ga. App. 685 (78 S. E. 131).

The duties of the justice of the peace are at end and his jurisdiction terminated so far as any further investigation of the case is concerned when he has required bond. Williamson, 1 Ga. App. 657 (57 S. E. 1079).

Father can not legally be convicted for failure to give bond "for the expense of lying in with child, boarding, nursing, and maintenance, while the mother is confined." Sullivan, 114 Ga. 520 (40 S.

Nelms, 84 Ga. 466, 467 (10 S. E. 1087).

Not necessary to allege time and place of prior marriage. Where so alleged it is surplusage and need not be proved. Murphy, 122 Ga. 

149 (50 S. E. 48); Dunson, 25 Ga. App. 172 (2) (102 S. E. 899).

Knowledge that the lawful husband or wife is alive is an essential element of the crime of bigamy and must be charged in the indictment. Where not charged, such defect is fatal, and not cured by verdict. Herrin, 27 Ga. App. 189 (107 S. E. 779). 

Indictment need not negative dissolution of former marriage. 

Oliver, 7 Ga. App. 695 (2) (67 S. E. 886).

Indictment must allege that first marriage was lawful or must set out facts tending to show this. King, 40 Ga. 244 (1).

Indictment must allege that defendant had a lawful wife at the time he married another. King, 40 Ga. 244.

General. Single man can be convicted as principal in the second degree. Boggus, 34 Ga. 275. 

Marriage may be legal without license. Minshew, 25 Ga. App. 

240 (102 S. E. 906).

It is the contract of marriage, entered in a formal way, which the law forbids. The gist of the crime is the fact that defendant, knowing his lawful wife (or husband) to be alive, has gone through a formal marriage. Allen, 17 Ga. App. 431, 433 (87 S. E. 681); Mc- 

Bride, 16 Ga. App. 240, 245 (85 S. E. 86).

Cohabitation with second woman not necessary to constitute the crime. Pitts, 22 Ga. App. 247 (2) (95 S. E. 935); Pitts, 147 Ga. 801 (2) (95 S. E. 706). 

The offense is complete upon the second marriage. (Id.) 

Prima facie case. In a prosecution for bigamy the State makes out a prima facie case by proving the first marriage, and that while the first spouse was living the defendant contracted a second marriage, knowing that the first marriage has not been dissolved by death or divorce; and the knowledge need not be shown by direct evidence, but may be inferred from circumstances. The de- fendant may rebut the prima facie case by showing five years' ab-

SPECIFIC CRIMES 

321 sence and no information of the fate of the first spouse at the time of the second marriage. Robinson, 6 Ga. App. 696 (1) (65 S. E. 792). 

Five years absence rule. If the first spouse has not been absent and unheard of for five years or more, the party marrying again within that period is guilty of bigamy, notwithstanding the fact that he honestly believed at the time of the second marriage that the first spouse was dead. Parnell, 126 Ga. 103, 104 (54 S. E. 804); Herrin, 27 Ga. App. 189, 190 (107 S. E. 779).

Presumptions. Presumption of validity of second marriage is stronger than presumption of life. Murchison, 128 Ga. 339 (2) (57 

S. E. 709).

Presumption of law as to marriage from cohabitation and reputation will not prevail over a subsequent marriage in fact. Brown, 16 Ga. App. 603, 605 (85 S. E. 951).

All the presumptions necessary to make a marriage valid attach on proof of a formal ceremony of marriage and cohabitation by the parties under the belief that they were lawfully married; and the burden is on those who attack the validity of the marriage, to show its invalidity by clear, distinct, positive, and satisfactory proof. 

There is in such case a presumption that the parties had capacity to contract a marriage; and this presumption prevails until overcome by proof. In a prosecution for bigamy the State makes out a prima facie case by proving the first marriage, and that while the first spouse was living the defendant contracted a second marriage, knowing that the first marriage had not been dissolved by death or divorce; and the knowledge need not be shown by direct evidence, but may be inferred from circumstances. Fanning, 46 Ga. App. 716 (1) (2) (169 S. E. 60). 

Venue. Under the laws of Georgia, the venue in bigamy cases is fixed by the place where the second marriage contract was entered into, and not where cohabitation took place. McBride, 16 Ga. App. 

240 (3) (85 S. E. 86).

Statute of limitations. Absence from the State may suspend the statute of limitations. Hulsey, 11 Ga. App. 258 (74 S. E. 1099); 

Pitts, 147 Ga. 801 (95 S. E. 706). 

Subsequent cohabitation will not change statute. Pitts, 147 Ga. 

801 (95 S. E. 706). 

Second wife as witness. 

The second wife is no wife at law and therefore a competent witness. Murphy, 122 Ga. 149 (50 S. E. 48); 

Johnson, 61 Ga. 305.

Defenses. Belief that the other spouse is dead no excuse if second marriage is contracted within five years. Parnell, 126 Ga. 103, 104 (54 S. E. 804). 

Where reasonable effort was made to ascertain about divorce, and jury believed that defendant thought bona fide to be divorced, this might be a good defense, and the jury authorized to acquit. Robinson, 6 Ga. App. 696 (65 S. E. 792).

Where former divorce is invalid, it is no defense in case of bigamy. 

Goolsby, 24 Ga. App. 377 (100 S. E. 788).

Conditional divorce is no defense. son, 21 Ga. App. 823 (95 S. E. 631). 

Divorce must be final. Jack 

The fact that the other party has a lawful husband or wife living, is no defense. Allen, 17 Ga. App. 431 (87 S. E. 681).

Evidence. On trial for bigamy the prior marriage may be established by admission of accused. Murphy, 122 Ga. 149 (3) (50 S. E. 

48); Oliver, 7 Ga. App. 695 (67 S. E. 886).

Direct evidence of knowledge that first husband or wife alive is not essential. Circumstances sufficient. Robinson, 6 Ga. App. 696, 700 (65 S. E. 792); Oliver, 7 Ga. App. 695 (67 S. E. 886). 

First wife not a competent witness. Williams, 67 Ga. 260.

Certified copy of a divorce proceeding brought by the alleged wife against the defendant, upon which service has been acknowledged by defendant, and to which defendant filed an answer not denying the marriage-admissible, where second marriage was entered into before divorce granted in the first one. Oliver, 7 Ga. App. 695 (4) (67 S. E. 886).

Where a person is on trial for the offense of bigamy, it is erroneous to admit, over his objection, evidence tending to show that about seven years prior to the second marriage, while he was still living with his first wife, he had been arrested on a charge of cruelty to his wife. Nor should evidence tending to show that defendant mistreated and neglected his family be admitted. Robinson, 6 Ga. 

App. 696 (5) (65 S. E. 792).

Modes of proving marriage in criminal cases: by proof of general reputation in the family; by proof of general reputation in the community; by proof of the fact that the man or woman, as the case may be, lives together with a person of the opposite sex as his or her spouse, with general recognition in the community of their being married to each other. Plummer, 27 Ga. App. 185 (108 S. E. 128). 

But see: Arnold, 53 Ga. 574 for conflicting rule.

§§ 26-1801, 26-1802.

Bank in favor of the said.......----------, and did compel the said..................against his will to write a certain paper in which he agreed not to notify and not cause to be notified the....... .Bank not to pay the check above described, all being done by the said. ..with intent to extort money from the said...... -------, con- trary, etc. .. (Approved: Chunn, 125 Ga. 789 (54 S. E. 751).) See also indictment: Beard, 36 Ga. App. 266 (136 S. E. 333).

Threatening letters. 

did knowingly send and deliver a letter and writing threatening to accuse, one......………………………...of the crime of ..with intent to extort money, goods and chattels from him, the said of the value of...... ..Dollars, contrary, etc. ..

General. This charge can only be preferred by indictment. Jurisdiction of Court or lack of jurisdiction can not be waived in advance of indictment. Wright, 16 Ga. App. 216 (84 S. E. 975). Where indictment charges that the defendant verbally made some accusations with the intent of extorting money, and evidence shows that this was done in writing, conviction will be set aside. Beard, 36 Ga. App. 266 (136 S. E. 333). 

Where evidence shows that defendant, a constable, arrested and charged various persons with misconducts, although no such misconducts were committed, for the purpose of extorting money, the offense is blackmail. Bulfin, 38 Ga. App. 358 (144 S. E. 15).

Where circumstantial evidence of sending threatening letters is insufficient. O'Neal, 33 Ga. App. 582, 583 (126 S. E. 863). "Wound," as used in this section, does not necessarily import the breaking of the skin, but includes injuries of every kind which affect the body. Gatlin, 18 Ga. App. 9 (3) (89 S. E. 345). One who knowingly sends to a married woman a letter threatening to make her

husband give her a "good buggy-whipping" is guilty of threatening to "wound" her, within the meaning of this section. (Id.) 

Where one falsely and fraudulently represents himself to be a United States officer, arrests, and threatens to prosecute for a crime unless money is paid to settle the offense, and the person arrested, being in fear of the prosecution, pays the money, but it is not alleged that the prosecutor believed or relied on any statement made, the offense is not cheating and swindling, but blackmail. Jackson, 118 

Ga. 125 (44 S. E. 833).

For full discussion of the subject of blackmail see: Cook, 22 Ga. 

App. 770 (97 S. E. 264). Also for indictment.

It is not incumbent upon the State to show that the person sought to be blackmailed was not guilty of an offense or a crime, but it is only necessary for the State to show that the person who was attempting to blackmail was threatening to accuse another of a crime. 

The statute provides that the offense of blackmail is consummated if one accuses another of a crime or threatens to do so, with the intent to extort money from the victim. Baker, 47 Ga. App. 205, 207 (170 

S. E. 209).

It is not necessary that the threats be communicated to a third person. Blackmail is essentially a secretive offense, hidden from all but the victim. The perpetrators expect to extort money from him because they are relying upon his fears of having his alleged misdeeds or crimes exposed to third persons-the general public. In order for a blackmailer to succeed in his scheme, his accusations or threats must be kept secret from all persons save the victim. Baker, 47 Ga. App. 205, 209 (170 S. E. 209).

For other forms of indictments see: Taylor, 44 Ga. App. 64 (160 

S. E. 667); Martin, 44 Ga. App. 276 (161 S. E. 371); Turner, 43 Ga. 

App. 799, 800 (160 S. E. 509).

Indictment for bribery charging receiving money for procuring certain action by city council and influencing official behavior of accused councilman, held sufficient, though not expressly alleging criminal intent. While intent is an essential element to the commission of a crime, and there can be no crime without "a union or joint operation of act and intention or criminal negligence," yet where the indictment alleges an "offense," and names and describes the offense in terms of the penal statute, and alleges that it was "unlawfully" committed, and that it was "contrary to the laws" of the

State, and employs language from which it must necessarily be inferred that the criminal intent existed, it is not void because it fails to expressly allege the criminal intent. York, 42 Ga. App. 453, 461 (156 S. E. 733); Shehany, 170 Ga. 70 (152 S. E. 114).

Indictment for bribery charging receiving money for procuring acceptance by city council of proposal for lease of certain property held not subject to demurrer on ground that contract with city was void because it was for more than a year, and therefore indictment was void also. The subject of investigation before the trial court was not the validity of the contract. The issue formed in the criminal trial was whether the accused received a bribe for procuring the acceptance by the council of the proposal in question. An official act need not be lawful to render the officer liable, but need only be official in form, and done under color of his office. Thus it is not necessary, in order to constitute bribery, that the vote of the public official bribed shall be on a measure which can be enforced. York, 42 Ga. App. 453, 461, 462 (156 S. E. 733); Turner, 43 Ga. App. 799, 802 (160 S. E. 509).

Counts of indictment, charging member of general council of city with bribery, held not subject to demurrer because failing to set out in what respect official behavior was to be influenced by payment of money and what official act was to be performed or not performed. The law does not require that the evidence should be set out in the indictment. Saunders, 43 Ga. App. 59, 60, 61 (158 S. E. 433).

Counts of indictment, charging member of general council of city with bribery, not subject to demurrer because failing to allege to whom offense was unknown until after stated date. Saunders, 43 

Ga. App. 59, 61 (158 S. E. 433). Nor because failing to allege that matter depending before general council was matter over which said council had jurisdiction or that such matter was lawfully depending before that body. (Id.)

Since all who aid and abet commission of misdemeanor are regarded as principals, and may be indicted as such, indictment of two persons, one of whom was councilman, for bribery, not subject to demurrer because of failure to allege that other defendant was officer of city, or that he aided, abetted, or conspired with said councilman in commission of offense, or for any other reason assigned. 

White, 43 Ga. App. 748 (1) (159 S. E. 897).

General. For detailed discussion of the subject of bribery and statute of limitations in bribery, see Taylor, 44 Ga. App. 64 (160 S. 

E. 667).

SPECIFIC CRIMES 

327 Policeman of the City of Atlanta is an officer within the meaning of this section. Payne, 29 Ga. App. 156, 157 (114 S. E. 226).

Where there is no case lawfully pending before officer, offense of bribery can not be committed. Newman, 97 Ga. 367 (23 S. E. 831).

A person can not be bribed to do something outside his official duties. Taylor, 42 Ga. App. 443 (156 S. E. 623). Therefore indictment against clerk of city council charging that he received money as reward for securing passage of ordinance does not charge bribery, and a demurrer should be sustained. (Id.) But see: Taylor, 44 Ga. App. 387 (161 S. E. 793). § 26-4101 defining bribery, covers any governmental or judicial office in State and does not exclude councilman of city. York, 42 

Ga. App. 453, 462 (156 S. E. 733); Saunders, 43 Ga. App. 59 (158 

S. E. 433); Turner, 43 Ga. App. 799 (160 S. E. 509).

As an abstract matter of law it is not unlawful for one, not an official of the government (city), to receive money to influence city council, but it becomes unlawful if the one who received it aided, counseled, abetted, or conspired with an official of the city, and if the crime of bribery was committed. White, 43 Ga. App. 748, 749 

In bribery prosecution, admission of check, signed in name of company by defendant councilman as president, and check signed in name of same company by co-defendant as treasurer, held proper as showing close and intimate association of defendant and co-defendant. York, 42 Ga. App. 453, 456 (156 S. E. 733).

In prosecution of councilman for bribery, evidence that money was paid him for procuring sale of trucks to city admissible to show intent and motive, though transaction was not included in indictment. York, 42 Ga. App. 453, 458 (156 S. E. 733).

Where councilman and co-defendant, not councilman, were charged with receiving money to influence former's official conduct relative to selling trucks to city, co-defendant's participation being proved, and it being shown that neither of the defendants were truck salesmen, evidence that regular salesman of vendor of trucks received his commission, tends to show that money paid defendants was not commission due salesman, but was bribe to influence official conduct of councilman, and is admissible. White, 43 Ga. App. 748 

Where prior to the expiration of the statutory period in which an indictment for the offense in question could have been found and filed, the offense was known to one whose special duty it was to report it, such knowledge, being imputable to the State and being

knowledge of the State in legal contemplation, will operate the statute of limitations in favor of the accused, and a special presentment, found after the expiration of the statutory period, is barred. Taylor, 44 Ga. App. 64, 65 (2) (160 S. E. 667). (See dissenting opinion.) (In this case it was held that the statute of limitations operates in favor of defendant, notwithstanding that party, whose knowledge is imputable to the State was the party to whom bribe was offered, he being also member of police committee of city council, and sworn as a policeman, also deputy sheriff and grand juror, and it being his duty to report the offense.)

In prosecution of councilman for bribery in that he received reward to influence his official behavior in procuring from city order for repairing motor trucks, testimony that he procured mechanic from municipal garage to work on his private automobile, and procured parts from that garage for his automobile, was admissible in rebuttal of his statement as to honest dealings with fellowmen, testimony complained of indicating that defendant, who was chairman of municipal garage committee, procured free work and free municipal garage. Turner, 43 Ga. App. 799, 800 (160 S. E. 509).

For indictment charging burglary of house where valuable goods were stored and kept, see: Bethune, 48 Ga. 505.

The occupier rather than the legal owner should be named in drawing an accusation for burglary. Accusation naming a certain person as the owner of the house is not sustained by evidence that the person owned the building, a hotel, in fee simple, but that another rented and conducted the same, and the party burglarized was the guest of the other. Trice, 116 Ga. 602, 603 (42 S. E. 1008). 

Ownership laid in administrator. Herndon, 45 Ga. App. 360 (164) 

S. E. 478).

Possession by agent raises presumption of ownership by principal. 

Hall, 7 Ga. App. 115 (66 S. E. 390). 

Indictment need not allege that owner is a corporation. Allegation that bank building, which was burglarized, was owned by corporation, chartered under the laws of Georgia, is surplusage and need not be proved. Moore, 25 Ga. App. 251 (2) (102 S. E. 916); 

Crawford, 68 Ga. 822.

Where one person rents a house and uses it as a dwelling, but allows a room therein to be occupied by a boarder or lodger, and this room is burglarized, the ownership of the house, in an indictment for burglary, may be alleged either in the general or in the special occupant. Boyd, 4 Ga. App. 273 (61 S. E. 134).

Title should be laid in husband, if possession and custody in him, though legal title is in wife. Kidd, 101 Ga. 528 (28 S. E. 990); Oglethree, 7 Ga. App. 523 (67 S. E. 126).

The ownership of the personal property may be laid in the person having actual lawful possession of the same, although he may be holding it as agent or bailee of another. Bradley, 2 Ga. App. 622 (58 S. E. 1064); Jackson, 15 Ga. App. 179 (1) (82 S. E. 771).

In a prosecution for burglary, where the house alleged to have been entered was not a "dwelling, mansion, or storehouse" it must be alleged in the indictment that the house was a place of business where valuable goods were contained and stored. Moody, 36 Ga. 

App. 284 (136 S. E. 464).

It is not essential that the house alleged to have been broken and entered should be expressly denominated in the indictment as a "place of business" if descriptive words are used sufficient to show that the house was used as a place of business of another. It is essential, however, that it should appear from the indictment that the place charged to have been broken and entered was used as a place of business. The mere fact that valuable goods were contained or stored therein is not alone sufficient to make the house a place of business, within the meaning of the statute. (Id.)

Indictment describing house as cotton seed warehouse where valuable goods were stored, but no allegation that the warehouse was used as a place of business-bad. (Same held for church.) Jones, 12 Ga. App. 813, 814 (78 S. E. 474); Moody, 36 Ga. App. 284, 285 (136 S. E. 464); McElreath, 55 Ga. 562.

Where a place of business is broken and entered, and that place of business is not also a dwelling, mansion, or storehouse, then it must be alleged and proved that articles of value were stored and contained in the place of business. Lee, 56 Ga. 478; Lanier, 76 Ga. 

304; Jones, 12 Ga. App. 813, 814 (78 S. E. 474).

Where indictment charges burglary to have been committed in the outhouse contiguous to and within the curtilage, it is not necessary to allege that the same was committed in the dwelling house, nor that the outhouse was part of the dwelling house. Hutchins, 3 

Ga. App. 300 (59 S. E. 848).

Indictment need not allege whether burglary was committed in the day time or at night. Ashton, 68 Ga. 25.

Indictment is not demurrable for charging burglary and larceny from the house in same count. Sirmans, 28 Ga. App. 122 (110 S. E. 622).

It is not essential in an indictment for burglary that larceny be charged. But where so alleged, it must be proved. Walker, 5 Ga. 

App. 430 (63 S. E. 534); Jones, 12 Ga. App. 813, 814 (78 S. E. 474).
