331 Where indictment for burglary charges, as the purpose of the breaking, the intent to commit a larceny, no description, value, or ownership of any goods intended to be stolen need be alleged. Boyd, 4 Ga. App. 273 (61 S. E. 134); Farm, 24 Ga. App. 114 (2) (100 S. E. 36).

Indictment alleging breaking, entering and stealing-defective. 

Must allege intent. Wood, 46 Ga. 322 (1).

Indictment must specify the felony which the defendant intended to commit. Lockhart, 24 Ga. 420 (cited in Cook, 161 Ga. 551, 555 (131 S. E. 288)).

Where intent to steal is charged, it is necessary to describe the goods, etc., or to allege their value. Lanier, 76 Ga. 304 (1-a); Farm, 24 Ga. App. 114 (2) (100 S. E. 36).

Indictment may charge a larceny after the breaking and entering, as illustrative of the intent with which the burglary was committed. 

In such cases the defendant may be convicted of the larceny, though not guilty of the burglary. Hutchins, 3 Ga. App. 300 (59 S. E. 848); 

Berry, 124 Ga. 825 (53 S. E. 316).

Indictment designating burglary as misdemeanor - not fatal, where no timely objection made. Moore, 34 Ga. App. 182 (1) (129 

S. E. 6).

Where indictment is defective in charging accessory after the fact, it may still be good for receiving stolen goods. McKissick, 11 

Ga. App. 721 (76 S. E. 71). General.

Venue. The venue of the offense is satisfactorily proved and the jurisdiction of the Court shown if the house burglarized was within the jurisdiction of the Court. The venue and jurisdiction are not affected by the fact that the defendant was found in possession of the stolen goods outside of the jurisdiction of the Court. Peterson, 6 Ga. App. 491 (1-b) (65 S. E. 311).

House defined. All outhouses contiguous to or within the curtilage or protection of the mansion or dwelling house shall be considered as part of the same. A hired room or apartment in a public tavern, inn or boarding house shall be considered as the dwelling house of the person occupying the same. Hutchins, 3 Ga. App. 300 (1) (59 S. E. 848). The use of the phrase "within the protection of the dwelling house" is recognized by the Supreme Court as an enlargement of the term "curtilage," and it is held that if the house is within the protection of the dwelling house or mansion, although not strictly within the curtilage as understood at common law, it

will be protected as part of the dwelling house. Wright, 12 Ga. App. 

514, 518 (77 S. E. 657).

A barn or a cornerib is not the subject matter of burglary, unless it be proved that it is within the curtilage of a dwelling house, or used as a place of business. Hutchins, 3 Ga. App. 300 (3) (59 S.

E. 848). Where a barn is disconnected from the dwelling house by a separate fence, it is not a subject of burglary. (Id.) 

Gear house held dwelling house under conditions stated. Bryant, 60 Ga. 358.

Cornerib held part of dwelling house under circumstances stated. 

Parks, 22 Ga. App. 621 (1) (96 S. E. 1050).

Smokehouse held part of dwelling house under circumstances stated. Moore, 34 Ga. App. 182 (2) (129 S. E. 6). 

Chicken house held part of dwelling house. King, 99 Ga. 52 (25 

S. E. 613).

Outhouse, some distance from the dwelling, held not subject to burglary. Wright, 12 Ga. App. 514 (77 S. E. 657).

Railroad car used exclusively for habitation is a dwelling house within the meaning of this section and can be subject of burglary. 

Gibbs, 8 Ga. App. 107 (1) (68 S. E. 742).

Place of business. The words "place of business," as used in the statute defining burglary, mean any house occupied as a place of business by another, in which valuable goods are contained, and this is so regardless whether such place of business be located in a private or public building. Davenport, 27 Ga. App. 284 (108 S. E. 

131); Goodbread, 29 Ga. App. 195, 196 (115 S. E. 44).

Includes any house used as a place of business by another, whether it is a storehouse or not. But the indictment must allege and the evidence must prove it to be a place of business, although it is not necessary that it shall be designated with these words. 

Keenan, 10 Ga. App. 792, 793 (74 S. E. 297); Jones, 12 Ga. App. 813, 814 (78 S. E. 474). 

For historical review see Hutchins, 3 Ga. App. 300 (59 S. E. 848).

Railway depot is a place of business within the meaning of this section. Stokes, 84 Ga. 258 (10 S. E. 740).

Sheriff's office is a place of business. (In the courthouse.) Davenport, 27 Ga. App. 284 (108 S. E. 131).

Burglary may be committed in a house, which is the place of business of another where valuable goods, ware or produce, or other articles of value are contained or stored, although that "business" may not be of the kind which is carried on in conducting a "storehouse." Bethune, 48 Ga. 505.

SPECIFIC CRIMES 

333 Conviction authorized, although the business done in the house be not carried on with or in the articles or goods stolen. (Id.) 

An incomplete building, which carpenters are engaged in finishing, and where they have deposited their tools, protecting the building by closing the doors and fastening the windows-is subject to burglary. Grimes, 77 Ga. 762.

A person may break and enter into a storehouse or other place, etc., where wheat is contained or stored, with intent to commit rape or murder, or steal money of whatever value may be therein, and be guilty of burglary. Bethune, 48 Ga. 505, 511 (3).

If the house is partly or wholly open to the public, the slightest force in breaking another room or part of the building is burglary. 

Jones, 75 Ga. 825; Daniels, 78 Ga. 98. Aliter in dwelling. Lockhart, If one should enter a house 

through an open window, he would not be guilty of burglary merely because he unlocked a door, after entering, for the purpose of stealing property from another room. Strickland, 12 Ga. App. 640, 641 (77 S. E. 1070).

Conflict. So much of § 26-2401 as makes it a felony to break and enter a "storehouse, or other place of business of another, where valuable goods, ware, produce, or any other articles of value are contained or stored," with intent to commit a larceny, is in conflict with, and prohibits the application of § 26-2633, in so far as it purports to make it a misdemeanor to break and enter a house of the character above mentioned, with intent to steal, where the offender, being detected, is prevented from carrying the intent to steal into effect. Evans, 146 Ga. 98 (1) (90 S. E. 743).

Breaking and entering. To maintain a conviction for the offense of burglary, it is absolutely essential that proof of the breaking and entering be made. Lester, 106 Ga. 371, 372 (32 S. E. 335); Strickland, 12 Ga. App. 640 (77 S. E. 1070); Shaneyfelt, 24 Ga. App. 555 (101 S. E. 592); Mosley, 49 Ga. App. 147 (174 S. E. 543).

Court should charge jury that breaking is an essential element of the crime of burglary. Strickland, 12 Ga. App. 640 (77 S. E. 1070).

Where breaking and entering is shown, the law of larceny from the house is not involved. Stevens, 49 Ga. App. 248 (3) (174 S. E. 718). 

Breaking out, after entry through open door and committing larceny is not burglary. Lockhart, 3 Ga. App. 480 (60 S. E. 215); 

White, 51 Ga. 285.

The necessary breaking requisite in statutory burglary is accomplished when a person who has no business in a factory effects an

entrance by turning the door knob, thereby withdrawing the bolt used in the daytime to keep the door closed, the same being done early in the morning after the door was unlocked, but before it had come into general use for the day by the public or even by the employees of the establishment. Kent, 84 Ga. 438 (11 S. E. 355).

The opening of a door, though it may not be latched or fastened by bolts or locks, or the breaking of a pane of glass, or hoisting a window and effecting an entrance thereby, is a breaking within the meaning of this section. Grimes, 77 Ga. 762, Bloodworth, 9 Ga. App. 

161 (70 S. E. 892); Simmons, 18 Ga. App. 104 (88 S. E. 904).

If the house was closed with blind-shutters and fastened or closed, and they were prized open and the window raised out of its place, that would be sufficient breaking. Dean, 93 Ga. 184, 186 (18 S. E. 

557). But raising blind does not constitute sufficient breaking, unless blinds were closed. Williams, 52 Ga. 580; Tremble, 24 Ga. App. 

26 (99 S. E. 544).

Unlawfully unlocking the door with the owner's key is sufficient breaking. Colbert, 91 Ga. 705, 709 (17 S. E. 840); Pritchett, 92 Ga. 

33, 35 (3) (18 S. E. 350).

Though outer door open, forcing inner door in order to enter apartment-breaking. Daniels, 78 Ga. 98 (1). 

Opening window from the outside-breaking. Cooper, 69 Ga. 761; 

White, 7 Ga. App. 596 (67 S. E. 705).

Intent. Neither larceny nor the intent to steal is an essential element in the crime of burglary. The crime of burglary is complete whenever a house which is the subject matter of burglary is broken and entered with the intent to commit a felony or a larceny. Jones, 12 Ga. App. 813, 814 (78 S. E. 474). 

Question of intent is for the jury. Woodward, 54 Ga. 106.

Time. Immaterial whether burglary was committed in the daytime or at night. Ashton, 68 Ga. 25.

Lawful entry. "Had the accused made an entry on some other business, and whilst in the house had committed a larceny, the offense would not have been burglary, but only larceny from the house." (Dictum by Chief Justice Bleckley.) Kent, 84 Ga. 438, 440 (11 S. E. 355).

Evidence. 

Corpus delicti. In a trial for burglary, proof that the house which may be subject of a burglary was entered by breaking a window closed by a screen and that articles of value were stolen therefrom

SPECIFIC CRIMES 

335 after the breaking, is sufficient to establish the corpus delicti. Simmons, 18 Ga. App. 104 (2) (88 S. E. 904).

Breaking. Where there is evidence that an article which was in the room when room was locked in the afternoon was missing when the room was opened the next morning, and evidence is that the only way the room could have been entered was by opening door with a key, evidence of breaking and entering is sufficient. Sirmans, 28 Ga. 

Proof that door is ordinarily kept locked-admissible on question of breaking. Pritchett, 92 Ga. 33 (18 S. E. 350); Shaneyfelt, 24 Ga. 

App. 555 (101 S. E. 592).

Conviction upheld though no physical evidence of breaking. 

Shaneyfelt, 24 Ga. App. 555 (101 S. E. 592); Humphries, 149 Ga. 

480 (100 S. E. 637).

Entering. Partial entering sufficient, though lower limbs were still outside when arrested. White, 7 Ga. App. 596 (67 S. E. 705); 

Evans, 19 Ga. App. 68 (90 S. E. 1025).

Intent. Where indictment charges breaking and entering with intent to murder a certain person, evidence must show such intent. 

Fagan, 39 Ga. App. 537 (147 S. E. 786).

Where indictment charges that defendant entered a certain house with the intent to steal a certain article, and the proof fails to show either that the article was in the house or that the accused had any reason to believe that it was, conviction is not authorized. Rush, 114 Ga. 113 (39 S. E. 941).

Possession of stolen goods. The recent, absolute, and unexplained possession of property stolen from a house proved to have been burglarized, may be sufficient to authorize a conviction for burglary, but the presumption of guilt arising from such facts is not one of law. Cuthbert, 3 Ga. App. 600 (60 S. E. 322); Scott, 14 Ga. App. 

806 (6) (82 S. E. 376).

Recent possession of stolen property, unexplained, is a strong circumstance to be considered. Murray, 28 Ga. App. 101 (110 S. E. 418).

Possession of stolen goods, shortly after burglary, and unaccounted, affords presumption of guilt. Hobbs, 38 Ga. App. 205 (1) (143 S. E. 509).

The Court should avoid charging the jury that recent possession of the stolen goods raised a presumption of the defendant's guilt, and the judge should avoid the word "presumption" in this connection, and use some such expression as "the law permits the jury to

infer guilt from the fact of recent possession unaccounted for," thus bringing out the idea that such possession authorizes the verdict of guilty, but does not require it. Cook, 49 Ga. App. 86, 88 (174 S. E. 195).

Coincidence of goods lost corresponding in quantity, variety, and brand, with other evidence, sufficient identification. Hobbs, 38 Ga. 

App. 205 (3) (143 S. E. 509).

The failure to give satisfactory explanation for the recent possession of the goods stolen from the house which is alleged to have been burglarized, authorized conviction. Jordan, 119 Ga. 443, 444 (46 S. E. 679).

Presumption from possession of stolen goods does not apply unless proven that goods were actually stolen, and that possession was recently afterwards. King, 99 Ga. 686 (1) (26 S. E. 480).

Where the guilt of the defendant depends upon the possession of the article alleged to have been contained in the house burglarized, the identity of the article found in the defendant's possession with the article which is alleged to have been stolen must be established beyond a reasonable doubt. Rayfield, 5 Ga. App. 816 (63 S. E. 920); 

Davis, 17 Ga. App. 820, 824 (88 S. E. 706); Williams, 33 Ga. App. 

347 (2) (126 S. E. 267); Daniel, 39 Ga. App. 818 (148 S. E. 601); 

Williamson, 38 Ga. App. 267 (143 S. E. 795).

Recent possession of stolen goods is not sufficient to convict of burglary without proof of breaking and entering. Lester, 106 Ga. 

371 (32 S. E. 335).

The time elapsed between the alleged burglary and the possession of the stolen goods is an important element, and the Court should so charge. Tarver, 95 Ga. 222, 223 (21 S. E. 381). 

Where possession is not recent, the evidence is not conclusive. 

Cuthbert, 3 Ga. App. 600 (60 S. E. 322).

In charging possession of stolen goods, judge should use the word "recent," but omission not error where it appears that it must have been recent. Posey, 36 Ga. App. 115 (135 S. E. 520).

Where recent possession is explained and the State depends solely upon such possession for conviction, verdict is contrary to evidence. 

Hampton, 6 Ga. App. 778 (65 S. E. 842); Gibbs, 8 Ga. App. 107 (68 

S. E. 742); Mayfield, 17 Ga. App. 115 (86 S. E. 284); Willis, 33 Ga. 

App. 352 (126 S. E. 303).

Charge of the Court that the defendant must make "an honest and satisfactory accounting for his recent possession of stolen property" is not erroneous. Davidson, 104 Ga. 761 (30 S. E. 946).

Burden of proof that defendant came into possession of the stolen

SPECIFIC CRIMES 

337 goods is not upon defendant, and it is error to so charge the jury. 

Johnson, 22 Ga. App. 639 (96 S. E. 1045).

It is not necessary for the defendant to show that he obtained the goods honestly. It is only necessary to show that he came into custody in any other way than by burglary. Williams, 125 Ga. 268, 269 (54 S. E. 166).

Even though three months elapsed between burglary and finding of stolen goods in defendant's possession, question of guilt is for the jury. Coe, 37 Ga. App. 82 (138 S. E. 919).

Recent possession of article stolen from the house at the time of the burglary may be shown by evidence, though article is not mentioned in indictment. Scott, 14 Ga. App. 806 (5) (82 S. E. 376).

When house in which stolen goods were found was in possession of defendant jointly with others, Court should charge that such possession should not be treated as that of defendant unless exclusively his, but that the fact of joint possession was a circumstance to be considered before the jury. Moncrief, 99 Ga. 295 (25 S. E. 735).

That stolen goods were found in the house occupied by defendant and his mother, does not authorize charge on possession of stolen goods. Sparks, 111 Ga. 830 (35 S. E. 654).

On a trial for burglary, the fact that the goods were found in a room occupied by two or more persons, is not conclusive evidence that the goods were in possession of any one of them. Shropshire, 69 Ga. 273. (But see Young, 95 Ga. 456 (20 S. E. 270).)

Whether explanation of possession of stolen goods is sufficientis a question for the jury. Hobbs, 38 Ga. App. 205 (2) (143 S. E. 

509); Huff, 38 Ga. App. 665 (145 S. E. 99). Failure to charge jury (132 S. E. 261). to this effect-error. Gay, 35 Ga. App. 165

The sufficiency of the identification of the article found in defendant's possession is for the jury. McCoy, 18 Ga. App. 698 (90 S. E. 355).

Although the indictment charged burglary with intent to commit a felony (intent to steal not being charged) evidence of recent possession of the goods stolen-admissible. Walker, 5 Ga. App. 430 (2) (63 S. E. 534).

The nearer the possession to the time of the larceny, the stronger is the inference of guilt. Brown, 38 Ga. App. 196, 199 (143 S. E. 457).

Evidence as to possession by wife of property similar to that stolen, shortly after alleged theft occurred, admissible against accused as a circumstance, the probative value of which is for the

jury. Buckine, 121 Ga. 337 (49 S. E. 257); Jenkins, 2 Ga. App. 684 (2) (58 S. E. 1115). 

Jury authorized to find that possession of the wife of goods recently stolen was constructive possession of the husband. Jenkins, 2 Ga. App. 684 (2) (58 S. E. 1115).

Fact that stolen property was found in possession of someone and that this possession was not satisfactorily explained, raises no inference that accused was the thief. Wilkes, 11 Ga. App. 384 (1) (75 

S. E. 443).

Where State's evidence shows that watch was taken from prosecutor, and that accused and a certain woman were very intimate, no error to admit evidence showing the watch to have been in possession of the woman the morning after the burglary or robbery. Clay, 122 Ga. 136 (2) (50 S. E. 56). 

Conviction unauthorized where defendant had in possession a pair of shoes of the same kind as those stolen, but without identification marks, and of such make as was sold by other merchants in the vicinity, and State depended on recent possession of stolen goods for conviction. Cannon, 12 Ga. App. 637 (77 S. E. 920).

Evidence that scarf pin was found within a few feet from the house which was burglarized is not admissible, where pin was not shown to be the property of the accused. Field, 126 Ga. 571 (55 S. 

E. 502).

Owner's declaration, claiming goods, not in presence of the accused-hearsay. Brooks, 96 Ga. 353 (23 S. E. 413).

Illegal evidence. Evidence obtained by search of the prisoner arrested on charge of burglary is admissible, where the arrest was legal and the search lawful. Thompson, 4 Ga. App. 649 (62 S. E. 99).

Where arrest was unlawful, and defendant compelled to disclose evidence-inadmissible. Scott, 14 Ga. App. 806 (4) (82 S. E. 376).

Evidence that sheriff took prisoner, while in his custody, to the house where the burglary was committed, and placed him in a position at the window through which the burglar entered, and that witness then identified him, although not before-inadmissible. Aiken, 16 Ga. App. 848 (2) (86 S. E. 1076).

Larceny. Where burglary and larceny are charged in the same indictment and defendant is convicted of burglary, immaterial whether larceny is proved or not. Tabor, 17 Ga. App. 754 (1) (88 

S. E. 410).

Ownership of building. Ownership of building laid in corporation, or partnership, judgment not void for want of proof of such

SPECIFIC CRIMES 

339 allegation. Hammontree, 25 Ga. App. 544 (1) (103 S. E. 738); Lawrence, 26 Ga. App. 607 (1) (107 S. E. 621).

Evidence of ownership of house burglarized not necessary by titledeed. Evidence of possession is sufficient. Hall, 7 Ga. App. 115 (66 

S. E. 390).

Value. It is essential that the article stolen be proved to be of some value. Purchase price is sufficient evidence of value. Peterson, 6 Ga. App. 491 (1-a) (65 S. E. 311). Verdicts.

Defendant may be convicted of larceny from the house, if larceny sufficiently charged, and evidence justifies such verdict. Polite, 78 

Ga. 347 (1); Thomas, 18 Ga. App. 101 (3) (88 S. E. 917); Butts, 26

On an indictment for burglary, which contains elements of larceny from the house and simple larceny, a general verdict of guilty of misdemeanor can not be upheld, and motion to arrest judgment should be sustained. Smith, 117 Ga. 16, 17 (2) (43 S. E. 440).

Where evidence shows breaking, larceny from the house is not involved. Tarver, 95 Ga. 222 (3) (21 S. E. 381); Jones, 12 Ga. App. 813, 814 (78 S. E. 474). 

Possessing burglary tools.

One is presumed to intend the natural consequences of his acts, and therefore where defendant was in possession of tools commonly used for the commission of burglary and safe-cracking, and only the intent had to be inferred, the trial judge was not required to charge the law of circumstantial evidence. McNabb, 44 Ga. App. 306 (161 

S. E. 369).

Burglary of Railroad Car. 

Indictment must allege ownership of car. Cooper, 89 Ga. 222 (15 

S. E. 291). "In custody and control of the...... (named) R. R. Co." sufficient allegation of ownership. Gilbert, 116 Ga. 819 (43 S. E. 47).

Possession of carrier supports allegation of ownership of goods. 

Hall, 7 Ga. App. 115, 119 (4) (66 S. E. 390).

The offense being the breaking and entering of a railroad freight car with intent to steal, and the car being described in the indictment as "marked 'Frisco' No. 130476" and there being no evidence that the car referred to in the testimony at the trial, as the car which was broken and entered, was marked "Frisco," the verdict of

guilty was unauthorized. Youngblood, 40 Ga. App. 514 (150 S. E. 457).

Evidence of possession of goods held insufficient to warrant conviction for breaking and entering railroad car. Williams, 11 Ga. 

App. 723 (75 S. E. 1135). 

14. CARRYING CONCEALED WEAPONS. 

Indictment. § 26-5101. charge and accuse.. ..with the offense of on the day of a misdemeanor, for that the said.......... .19...., in the county of........ did unlawfully have and carry about his person concealed and not in an open manner and fully exposed to view a.......... (pistol) (or metal knucks) (or dirk) (or bowie knife) (or a knife manufactured and sold for the purpose of offense and defense), contrary, etc. ...

This charge may be joined with one for carrying pistol without license. Butler, 18 Ga. App. 201 (2) (89 S. E. 178); Fanning, 39 Ga. 

App. 531 (147 S. E. 788); Young, 43 Ga. App. 398 (158 S. E. 922).

Indictment charging one with carrying pistol in the presence of A on given date, and another charging carrying pistol in the presence of B on a different date, prima facie charges different offenses and the accused can be convicted on both, unless the evidence shows that the same transaction was involved. Morgan, 119 Ga. 964 (1) (47 S. E. 567).

Indictment for carrying metal knucks need not allege that it was manufactured for the purpose of offense and defense. Words qualify knives only. Nixon, 121 Ga. 144 (2) (48 S. E. 966). 

General. Constitutionality of act upheld. Cunningham, 128 Ga. 

55 (57 S. E. 90).

One who carries pistol concealed from shop where it has been repaired, guilty under this section, though he does so solely for the purpose of delivering it to the owner and at the latter's request. 

Goldsmith, 99 Ga. 253 (25 S. E. 624).

The following has been held sufficient concealment: Carrying pistol in satchel. Willis, 105 Ga. 633 (32 S. E. 155); wrapped in a bundle. Edwards, 126 Ga. 89 (54 S. E. 409); on horseback. Puryear, 44 

Ga. 221; in pocket. Brown, 2 Ga. App. 417 (58 S. E. 549); Sanders, 122 Ga. 143 (50 S. E. 66); basket or bag upon arm, if concealed, guilty; if not concealed, not guilty. Boles, 86 Ga. 255 (12 S. E. 361); 

Sullivan, 6 Ga. App. 533 (65 S. E. 354); in sack under arm. Warren, 6 Ga. App. 18 (64 S. E. 111).

SPECIFIC CRIMES 

341 Violation of this section even to carry pistol concealed in one's own house. Brown, 114 Ga. 60 (39 S. E. 873).

It is immaterial that pistol is broken and useless. Williams, 61 

Ga. 417; Crawford, 94 Ga. 772 (21 S. E. 922).

Carrying pistol to shop for repair, violation of this section, if concealed. Crawford, 94 Ga. 772 (21 S. E. 922). 

One is guilty though he carries weapon for another. Saylor, 25 

Ga. App. 174 (102 S. E. 924). 

If the weapon is concealed for a moment, offense complete. Brinson, 75 Ga. 882.

Where one having a pistol concealed about his person in one county was legally arrested by an officer in that county and by the latter carried into another county, where the concealed weapon was discovered, the person thus having the concealed weapon and who was arrested and carried into another county could not be prosecuted and convicted in the latter county for the offense of carrying a concealed weapon. James, 153 Ga. 556 (112 S. E. 889).

Pistol found on the seat of an automobile where the defendant was sitting, but was not covered or concealed, did not authorize conviction. Sanders, 24 Ga. App. 329 (100 S. E. 748).

Carrying pistol to church is a different offense from carrying concealed weapon, and conviction for the former is no defense in prosecution for the latter. Veasy, 4 Ga. App. 845 (62 S. E. 561).

Pistol was not concealed if sufficiently exposed to enable witness to recognize it as a pistol. Stripling, 114 Ga. 538 (3) (40 S. E. 733).

Carrying pistol in such manner that those standing in full view can not see it, violates this section. Brown, 2 Ga. App. 417 (1) (58 

S. E. 549).

Error to charge that pistol must be carried in such open manner and so fully exposed to view that a person meeting the one with the weapon would readily see and know that he had a pistol about his person. Stripling, 114 Ga. 538 (1) (40 S. E. 733).

Though weapon carried as a matter of precaution for self-defense, after life was threatened, no excuse. Brown, 72 Ga. 211.

Evidence. Officer with possessory warrant (for other things) may testify as to pistol taken from accused. Hill, 8 Ga. App. 77 (68 S. E. 614).

Not admissible that it was defendant's habit not to carry pistol concealed. Oliver, 106 Ga. 142 (32 S. E. 18).

Testimony that witness saw accused with a pistol hid in his pocket, and saw him take it out at a stated time and place other than his home or place of business, sufficient to convict. It makes

out a prima facie case for the State. Fanning, 39 Ga. App. 531 (147

S. E. 788). 

Evidence showing that accused had possession of a pistol only momentarily and not showing that he intended to convey it to some place other than that at which he received it is not sufficient to sustain a verdict of guilty. Barnes, 23 Ga. App. 6 (97 S. E. 410).

Evidence that just prior to search one had given another a concealed weapon to hold for him-admissible. Warren, 6 Ga. App. 

18 (64 S. E. 111).

Evidence that defendant approached witness with a pistol, that he concealed it in his pocket until he was almost within witness' presence, when he took it from his pocket, warranted conviction. 

Bailey, 8 Ga. App. 32, 33 (68 S. E. 457).

Evidence that concealed weapon was exposed to view by reason of the defendant's leaning over so as to disclose it in the bosom of his overalls, supported conviction. Williams, 7 Ga. App. 33 (65 S. E. 1097). 

15. CARRYING DEADLY WEAPONS AT COURT, ETC. 

Indictment. to and while at a.. § 26-5102. (Misdemeanor.) did carry about his person a certain pistol, ...court of justice, then in session in the .........th district G. M., to wit: the justice court in and for said district, contrary, etc. . . . (Approved: Harrison, 100 Ga. 264 (28 S. 

E. 38)); also: Hill, 53 Ga. 472. "Mayor's court in and for the City of.......'' rison, 100 Ga. 264 (1) (28 S. E. 38). Church. charge and accuse. misdemeanor, for that the said... approved. Har- .with the offense of a .did on the.....day of ....19...., in the county aforesaid, carry about his person a (pistol) to a place of public worship, to wit, ...... Church, contrary, etc.... (Approved: Amorous, 1 Ga. App. 313 (57 S. E. 999).) 

Indictment need not allege that the accused is not an officer of the class excepted in the section. Kitchens, 116 Ga. 847 (43 S. E. 256). 

General. The term "a place of public worship," as it appears in this section, ex vi termini imports the gathering and presence of persons for religious worship, whether it be at a place usually de-

SPECIFIC CRIMES 

343 voted to that purpose or not. Amorous, 1 Ga. App. 313 (57 S. E. 999).

A holiday barbecue at which a great number of persons are assembled is a "public gathering" within the meaning of this section. 

Wynne, 123 Ga. 566 (51 S. E. 636).

Having a license to carry a pistol is no defense in an indictment under this section. Sockwell, 27 Ga. 576 (109 S. E. 531).

One, who after arriving at a “public gathering," there comes into possession of a pistol, does not render himself liable to prosecution under this section. Modesette, 115 Ga. 582 (41 S. E. 992). Coming into possession of a pistol while at a place of worship is not carrying pistol to a place of worship. Culberson, 119 Ga. 805 (47 S. E. 175); 

Cosper, 13 Ga. App. 301, 306 (79 S. E. 94).

Where a person knowing that a public gathering would occur at a certain time and place, shortly beforehand carried a deadly weapon to a place nearby in order to have accessible when the gathering occurred, and while it was in progress went to the place of deposit, obtained actual possession of the weapon, and carried it about his person to the gathering and into the crowd, he was guilty. 

Wynne, 123 Ga. 566 (51 S. E. 636).

One who comes into possession of a pistol at a spring so near to the church as to be in legal contemplation a part of the church, can not be convicted under this section. Culberson, 119 Ga. 805 (47 S. 

E. 175).

This offense distinguished from carrying concealed weapon. One who carries concealed weapon to public gathering commits two offenses. Veasy, 4 Ga. App. 845 (62 S. E. 561). 

16. CARRYING PISTOL WITHOUT LICENSE. 

§§ 26-5103 to 26-5106. (Misdemeanor.) Indictment. did have and carry about his person and did carry around with him on his person and did have in his manual possession outside of his own home and place of business a pistol, without first taking out a license from the ordinary of said county, contrary, etc. Indictment is fatally defective where it does not allege the carrying of the pistol without first obtaining a license. It must also allege that it was carried outside of the home or place of business of the accused. Hansford, 14 Ga. App. 810 (82 S. E. 375); Smith, 14 

Ga. App. 823 (82 S. E. 355).

Violation of this section, to wit, carrying pistol without license, and carrying concealed weapon may be charged in same indictment, and conviction had on both charges. Butler, 18 Ga. App. 201 (89 

S. E. 178); Fanning, 39 Ga. App. 531 (147 S. E. 788).

The proviso relating to officers is no part of the definition of the offense, and need not be negatived in the indictment. It is a matter of defense. Blocker, 12 Ga. App. 81 (1) (2) (76 S. E. 784).

General. This statute should receive a reasonable construction. 

Melton, 41 Ga. App. 501 (153 S. E. 377).

Corpus delicti. The carrying of the pistol is the corpus delicti of the statutory offense of unlawfully carrying a pistol without a license. Proof of the corpus delicti is essential to authorize a conviction of crime. Melton, 41 Ga. App. 501 (153 S. E. 377).

Purpose of act. The purpose of the act in question was to prevent the evil of carrying pistols or revolvers on the person, or having them in manual possession while going from place to place, outside of one's home or place of business. Brown, 15 Ga. App. 484 (83 

S. E. 890); Melton, 41 Ga. App. 501, 503 (153 S. E. 377); Amos, 13 

Ga. App. 140, 141 (78 S. E. 866); Cheney, 10 Ga. App. 451 (73 S. E. 617).

Prima facie case. The State makes out a prima facie case where it shows that the accused carried a pistol on his person, or had manual possession of a pistol, not at his home, or place of business, and the burden is upon the accused to show that he had a license as prescribed by law. Fanning, 39 Ga. App. 531, 532 (147 S. E. 788); 

Young, 43 Ga. App. 398, 399 (158 S. E. 922). 

The State need not affirmatively negative license. Harden, 17 

Ga. App. 322 (86 S. E. 736); Green, 23 Ga. App. 519 (98 S. E. 553).

A prima facie case is made out where it is proved that the defendant had pistol in his hand, though another grabbed it when it was discharged, no proof being had who brought the pistol to the place; and where defendant's statement that he examined pistol for the purpose of purchase was rebutted. Alexander, 25 Ga. App. 

388 (103 S. E. 684). 

Ordinary's jurisdiction. Where defendant purchased license in the county of his residence, and carried pistol openly in another county, he is not guilty. Rogers, 19 Ga. App. 751 (92 S. E. 230).

Pistol. One has a right to carry only identical pistol described in license. Donalson, 24 Ga. App. 73 (1) (2) (100 S. E. 40).

Where one carries a broken and temporarily inefficient pistol to

SPECIFIC CRIMES 

345 the owner, but uses it in demonstrating and threatening, he is guilty of violation of this act. Morris, 17 Ga. App. 271 (86 S. E. 462).

Ownership. Ownership of pistol is immaterial except to illustrate the guilt or innocence of the accused. Gates, 12 Ga. App. 706 (78 

S. E. 270). 

Minors. A minor under eighteen years of age can not carry pistol either with or without license. Glenn, 10 Ga. App. 128 (72 

S. E. 927).

Home or place of business. Verdict of guilty under this section is unauthorized, where it appears that the defendant was a single man, and used his brother's place of residence as his own home about four or five times a week, kept his clothes there with the permission of his brother, although without the consent of his brother's landlord, and where there was no other evidence except that he was seen with a pistol in the yard of the house occupied by his brother. Smith, 14 Ga. App. 823 (82 S. E. 375).

The plantation is the home and place of business of the overseer and farmer. Coker, 12 Ga. App. 425 (76 S. E. 103); Idellett, 14 Ga. 

App. 501 (81 S. E. 379).

Farm laborer is exempt where carrying pistol on farm where he is employed. Miller, 12 Ga. App. 479 (77 S. E. 653); Franklin, 12 

Ga. App. 483 (77 S. E. 653).

Premises rented to a tenant are not a place of business of the landlord. Reagan, 16 Ga. App. 369 (85 S. E. 353).

License required to carry pistol in public road, though road runs through farm where defendant works. Leigh, 26 Ga. App. 637, 638 (107 S. E. 284).

License required to carry pistol in public road though defendant owns land on both sides. Foy, 33 Ga. App. 676 (127 S. E. 619).

Lack of time to secure license-no excuse. Williams, 15 Ga. App. 

311 (82 S. E. 817). 

Temporary possession-no excuse. Cheney, 10 Ga. App. 451 (73 

S. E. 617).

Although the evidence shows that the defendant, on the occasion in question, was carrying the pistol for the purpose of transportation, he would still be guilty. Dunlap, 11 Ga. App. 722 (75 S. E. 

1135); Cheney, 10 Ga. App. 451 (73 S. E. 617); Foy, 33 Ga. App. 

676 (127 S. E. 619).

A person may carry a pistol home from the place of purchase. 

Or where he found it in the road and carried it home for the purpose of safekeeping. Cosper, 13 Ga. App. 301 (79 S. E. 94). Or

where a person examines a pistol for the purpose of buying it and is called away a distance of about twenty feet. Jackson, 12 Ga. 

App. 427 (77 S. E. 371). But where the accused carried the pistol for several miles for the purpose of storing it, this would be no excuse. Usry, 17 Ga. App. 268 (86 S. E. 417). Or where the owner of the pistol left it at the house of the accused, and accused delivered it to him, carrying it over the highway, no excuse. Cheney, 10 Ga. App. 451 (73 S. E. 617). 

Sudden emergency. Sudden emergency, self-defense, defense of property, the prevention of consummation of adultery with one's wife, may be proved as a matter of defense. Harris, 15 Ga. App. 

315 (85 S. E. 813). But there must be an imminent and pressing danger. Where there is time to take out a license, such matters of defense are of no avail. Williams, 15 Ga. App. 311 (82 S. E. 817); 

Harden, 17 Ga. App. 322 (86 S. E. 736).

Where person comes to a place where one is rooming, making threats to kill, and roomer takes the pistol of the house owner in self-defense, he is not guilty. Amos, 13 Ga. App. 140 (78 S. E. 866).

Holdup. Where two persons, acting together and in concert, holdup and rob another, one of the robbers having a pistol in his hand, and the other robber having no pistol, but being present and assisting in the holdup and robbery, and the scene of the robbery being outside of the home and place of business of the one carrying the pistol, and he being without a license to carry it, both of them are guilty of the offense of carrying a pistol without first having secured a license therefor. This is so because in misdemeanors all persons who are present at the scene of the crime, aiding and abetting the actual perpetrator thereof, are guilty as principals. Vinson, 45 Ga. App. 220 (1) (164 S. E. 209).

Evidence. Evidence as to place at which defendant was seen with pistol in his automobile was too indefinite to authorize conviction of carrying pistol without license outside of his home or place of business. Edwards, 36 Ga. App. 655 (137 S. E. 790). 

Evidence that defendant shot a snake with a pistol at a place neither his home nor his place of business, and put pistol in his bosom and drove off, authorized conviction where there was no evidence that he had a license. Long, 39 Ga. App. 572 (147 S. E. 728).

Testimony that witness saw accused with a pistol hid in his pocket, and saw him take it out at a stated time and place other than his home or place of business, is sufficient to authorize conviction. Fanning, 39 Ga. App. 531 (147 S. E. 788).

SPECIFIC CRIMES 

347 Where one man got into an automobile belonging to and operated by another, and placed his pistol on the seat, and getting out left it inadvertently in the car, the owner of the car having been found with the pistol later, although he covered it up with his hand when the officer threw a flashlight into the car, the corpus delicti was not proved. Melton, 41 Ga. App. 501, 502 (153 S. E. 377).

Where the first count of an indictment charges a defendant with carrying a pistol without having first procured a license, and the other count of the indictment charges him with carrying a concealed pistol, and the jury finds the defendant guilty "on count one and count two," and the evidence sustains the jury's finding as to count one, but fails to do so to count two, the verdict is not supported by the evidence and can not stand. Sanders, 42 Ga. App. 

387 (156 S. E. 285).

Proof that the defendant had a pistol in his possession may be shown by circumstantial evidence as well as direct evidence. Williams, 12 Ga. App. 84 (76 S. E. 785).

Circumstantial evidence not excluding every other reasonable hypothesis than that of guilt is insufficient. Miller, 36 Ga. App. 

304 (136 S. E. 539).

The burden is on the defendant to show that he has obtained a license from the ordinary of his own county. Vinson, 45 Ga. App. 

220, 221 (4) (164 S. E. 209).

a. USING FICTITIOUS NAMES. 

Indictment. . . charge and accuse. ......with the offense of drawing fictitious bill of exchange, for the said.....on the day of...19..., in the county aforesaid did unlawfully, feloniously, and fraudulently make and draw a certain bill of exchange in the fictitious name of................., as cashier of the… 

Company, of..., being in form and substance as follows, to wit, (here set out the bill of exchange) said act being done with intent to defraud, contrary, etc. . . (Approved: Nissenbaum, 38 Ga. 

App. 253 (143 S. E. 776).) In an indictment under this section it is not necessary to allege that the act was done with intent to defraud. Phillips, 17 Ga. 459. 

For indictment see: Saffold, 11 Ga. App. 329 (75 S. E. 338).

Indictment under this section and for forgery may be joined. 

Lascelles, 90 Ga. 347 (4) (16 S. E. 945).

General. This section is not void on the ground that it is unreasonable and uncertain. Constitutionality upheld. Nissenbaum, 167 Ga. 495 (146 S. E. 189).

When a man assumes not only a name which is not his own, but the relationship of son to another who has no such son, and in that name draws a bill of exchange and passes it for value to a person who believes he is dealing with the genuine and not a fictitious son of the alleged parent, the offense is under this section. Lascelles, 90 Ga. 347, 348 (7) (16 S. E. 945).

A check is not a bill of exchange within the meaning of this section. Townsend, 92 Ga. 732, 735 (19 S. E. 55). Check and bill (43 S. E. 260), of exchange distinguished. In Brazil, 117 Ga. 32 the Supreme Court held that our penal laws fail to provide a punishment for uttering a bank check drawn in a fictitious name. the Court of Appeals distinguished this when the indictment was But

349 drawn in accordance with § 26-3916 and another drawn under § 26-3918. § 26-3918 held to be broad enough to include bank checks.

Banker's, or cashier's check distinguished from an ordinary bank check, and held that it will support a conviction under this section.

Indictment must allege intent to defraud. Where indictment does not allege intent to defraud, it is absolutely void. Sims, 37 

Ga. App. 819 (142 S. E. 464).

When money obtained by check forged in fictitious name, indictment should be under this section and not under § 26-7410. Sharp, 7 Ga. App. 605 (67 S. E. 699). 

For approved indictment see also Carey, 112 Ga. 226 (37 S. E. 

405). Also: Saffold, 11 Ga. App. 329 (75 S. E. 338). 

General. Constitutionality of this act upheld. Gray, 6 Ga. App. 

428 (2-a) (65 S. E. 191). 

Violation of this section is a felony. Gray, 6 Ga. App. 428, 431 (65 S. E. 191).

An intent to defraud is not presumed by law, but is a matter of fact to be determined by the jury. A single act or representation, in many cases, would not be decisive, especially where the accused has sustained a previous good character. But when it is shown. that he made similar representations, about the same time, to other persons, and by means of such representations obtained goods, all of which were false, the presumption is greatly strengthened that he intended to defraud. Saffold, 11 Ga. App. 329 (3) (75 S. E. 338).

Check drawn under fictitious name is a "writing" within the meaning of this section and one may be convicted for obtaining money on such check. Saffold, 11 Ga. App. 329, 333 (75 S. E. 338);

Townsend, 92 Ga. 732 (19 S. E. 55); Saffold, 139 Ga. 119, 121 (76) 

S. E. 858). 

Forgery not embraced in this section. Hoskins, 11 Ga. 92, 100.

Designation of offense as forgery, even if inaccurate, immaterial. 

Aiken, 90 Ga. 452 (16 S. E. 206).

Writing must be in the name of another or fictitious. Court must so charge. Sessions, 3 Ga. App. 13, 14 (2) (59 S. E. 196).

If two persons have the same name, and one signs a note with the fraudulent intent that the note may be used, in trade, as that of the other, the offense is forgery, and not under this section. Barfield, 29 Ga. 127; Barron, 12 Ga. App. 342, 348 (77 S. E. 214).

Where a bank check was issued payable to an association and was endorsed in the name of the payee "by J. L. Cotton, secretary,' the purported secretary's name so used being fictitious and the endorsement wholly unauthorized, the counterfeit endorsement became a "writing" within the meaning of this section. 351 Indictment alleging false representations, upheld, though it was silent as to certain true representations which formed a material part of the inducement. Hathcock, 88 Ga. 91 (3) (13 S. E. 959).

Indictment for obtaining money through false representations should state ownership of money and name of person defrauded, and proof must be in strict conformity. O'Neal, 10 Ga. App. 474 (73 S. E. 696).

Allegations in indictment that defendant obtained from prosecutor "groceries, consisting of meats and other groceries, of value of $1.10" are not sufficient against a special demurrer. Barker, 6 

Ga. App. 443 (65 S. E. 57). 

Indictment need not specifically state ownership of property, but must charge that person defrauded was deceived by defendant's misrepresentations, and thereby suffered loss. McLendon, 16 Ga.

Indictment charging that defendant obtained prosecutor to sign note not subject to special demurrer on ground that it does not appear whether note was signed as principal or as security, nor whether money or anything of value was received by defendant on said note, nor that money, if any was obtained, was not paid to prosecutor. Moye, 19 Ga. App. 440 (1) (91 S. E. 941).

Where indictment sufficiently set forth offense under the first division of § 26-7401, it is immaterial whether the facts alleged constitute an offense under § 61-9901 or § 26-7410. Burns, 20 Ga. App.

Failure to allege in indictment to whom representations were made was not such defect that could be reached by general demurrer. Mathews, 27 Ga. App. 798 (1) (110 S. E. 33).

General. This section applies where corporation was defrauded. 

Livingston, 17 Ga. App. 136 (86 S. E. 449).

False representation to be the basis of a prosecution under this section must relate either to the past or to the present. No promise or statement as to what may occur in the future, however false, will serve as a basis for such prosecution. Dickerson, 113 Ga. 1035 (39 

S. E. 426); Vaughan, 36 Ga. App. 675 (137 S. E. 854).

Where promise was made at the time of the misrepresentation,

the false pretense may exist apart from the promise. Hansford, 7 

Ga. App. 196 (66 S. E. 400).

Alleged statement of defendant that he would execute mortgage on a certain mule merely constituted a future promise and is not indictable. Moye, 19 Ga. App. 440 (1) (91 S. E. 941). 

False promise to give mortgage on personalty, as security for loan, and false pretense as to ownership of such personalty constituted offense of cheating and swindling. Hansford, 7 Ga. App. 

196 (66 S. E. 400).

Accused must be shown to have had knowledge of falsity of representation. Such knowledge may be shown either by direct or circumstantial evidence, but it must be proved. Hester, 8 Ga. App. 

380 (1) (69 S. E. 31).

Unless it appears beyond a reasonable doubt that defendant knew at the time he made representations that they were false, he can not be convicted, although representations were in fact false. Formby, 14 Ga. App. 596 (1) (81 S. E. 799).

Where alleged representation of defendant was confined solely to ownership of a certain mule, prosecution was based upon § 267410 and not upon § 26-7401. Williams, 13 Ga. App. 338, 344 (79 S. 

E. 207).

Representation as to solvency is representation as to respectability and wealth. Hathcock, 88 Ga. 91 (1) (13 S. E. 959); Hathcock, 8 Ga. App. 371, 372 (2) (69 S. E. 29).

Representations may be made by signs and symbols, or may be implied from misleading silence. Ricks, 8 Ga. App. 449 (69 S. E. 576).

Loss as well as misrepresentation and extension of credit must be shown. McGee, 97 Ga. 199 (22 S. E. 589); Berry, 97 Ga. 202 (23 S. E. 833); Ganey, 10 Ga. App. 777 (74 S. E. 286).

This section was held violated by the misstatement of the following facts: Solvency. Hathcock, 88 Ga. 91 (13 S. E. 959). Employment. Branham, 96 Ga. 307 (2) (22 S. E. 957). Official position and power. Jackson, 118 Ga. 125 (44 S. E. 833). Ownership of property. Williams, 105 Ga. 606 (31 S. E. 546); McLendon, 16 

Ga. App. 262 (85 S. E. 200).

But violation was not indictable where goods so obtained were paid for. Broznack, 109 Ga. 514 (35 S. E. 123). But where payment was made after the commission of the offense and arrest, this will be no defense. Williams, 105 Ga. 606 (31 S. E. 546)..

This section is not violated by merely giving a check, though

395 (73 S. E. 242).

False statement to a commercial agency, for the purpose of obtaining favorable credit rating is binding only for limited time. 

Treadwell, 99 Ga. 779 (27 S. E. 785).

Wealth is a relative term. It may be a small amount. Branham, 96 Ga. 307, 309 (22 S. E. 957).

Injury to party defrauded is sufficiently shown by proof that security taken for debt was of less value than if representation had been true. Rucker, 114 Ga. 13 (4) (39 S. E. 902).

Where defendant represented that he was working for one railroad company where in fact he was working for another, equally solvent, conviction set aside. Ratteree, 77 Ga. 774, 779. 

False statements as to financial condition as basis for credit do not apply to credit extended at subsequent period, unless debtor reaffirms statement or knows or has reason to believe that latter credit is extended solely on faith of previous statement. Broznack, 109 Ga. 514 (2) (35 S. E. 123).

Representation of accused that he was purchaser and owner of valuable property, if false, supported conviction. Williams, 105 

Ga. 606 (1) (31 S. E. 546).

Where payment was actually made for goods obtained on credit by false representations as to financial standing, charge of cheating and swindling not sustained, though subsequent credit, based upon first false representations, has never been repaid. Broznack, 109 Ga. 514 (2) (35 S. E. 123).

If sole purpose of defendant in making false representation was to obtain credit at time, and it was reasonable for him to believe that subsequent credit was extended because of partial payment, subsequent investigation, and subsequent arrangements, he would not be guilty. Formby, 14 Ga. App. 596 (3) (81 S. E. 799).

If defendant made representations not acted on until some time thereafter, and subsequent statement by letter had been cause of contract, original representation would not be foundation for prosecution for cheating and swindling, unless defendant knew that he obtained credit on faith of original representation. Formby, 14 

Ga. App. 596 (2) (81 S. E. 799).

That defendant did not knowingly make false representations as to ownership of property, and that such representations were true when made, was defense to prosecution under this section. Mc-

Where false representations pertained to ownership of property, no excuse that defendant owned other property of much less value.

Charge. Where judge charged substantially as to elements of offense, if precise words of statute were desired for instruction, timely written request should have been presented. Townsend, 27 

Ga. App. 328 (5) (108 S. E. 252). 

Judge inadvertently reading § 26-7410 to jury, stating that defendant was being tried under that section at the beginning of charge, will not demand new trial where conviction under § 267401 was demanded and judge specifically called jury's attention to various allegations in accusation and instructed them that all averments must be proved by the State beyond a reasonable doubt. 

Townsend, 27 Ga. App. 328 (4) (108 S. E. 252).

Venue. The venue of prosecution under this section is in the county in which the owner of money or goods was deprived of his property. Davis, 20 Ga. App. 72 (92 S. E. 552).

Evidence. Testimony as to transaction which had no connection with the one under investigation is not admissible to show good faith on part of accused. McNulty, 21 Ga. App. 783 (95 S. E. 304).

Where defendant was charged with falsely representing contents of writing, it is no objection to witness' testifying as to what representation was made, that writing itself is the best and highest evidence of its contents. Hester, 8 Ga. App. 380 (2) (69 S. E. 31).

Where defendant was charged with false representations as to ownership of property, claim, affidavit, etc., filed by third persons when such property levied upon,—not admissible. Kinard, 1 Ga. 

App. 146 (3) (58 S. E. 263).

Where newly discovered evidence touched only part of the defendants representations which were alleged to be false, new trial refused. Gaddis, 91 Ga. 148 (16 S. E. 936).

Where accusation specifically charges that defendant knew that representations were false, allegation as to knowledge must be supported by evidence. McLendon, 16 Ga. App. 262 (3), 263 (85 S. 

E. 200).

Evidence failed to sustain conviction of false pretenses in connection with execution of mortgage, though accused failed to comply with promise to deliver mortgaged hogs to officer to enable him to levy mortgage fi. fa. Hammond, 15 Ga. App. 471 (83 S. E.

Variance. Where defendant was accused of obtaining credit by representation that he owned bay mule named "Jim" which was unincumbered, error to admit in evidence purchase money note in which title to "one black horse mule known as the 'Hill mule'"' was retained in seller. e. DEFRAUDING HOTELS AND BOARDING HOUSES. 

For indictment see: Smith, 14 Ga. App. 427 (81 S. E. 361). 

Constitutionality of this section upheld. Smith, 14 Ga. App. 427 (81 S. E. 361); Smith, 141 Ga. 482 (81 S. E. 220).

This section denounces fraudulent practices upon the part of persons received as guests in hotels or boarding houses. It does not punish for the mere non-payment of debts. Smith, 141 Ga. 482 (81 S. E. 220). Also 14 Ga. App. 427 (81 S. E. 361).

For accusation see: Neeley, 42 Ga. App. 367 (156 S. E. 306).

Proof that the defendant owed more than he said he owed might establish the element of false representation as to his solvency, but would not establish the element of his insolvency, in the absence of testimony showing how much or how little property he owned.

g. FALSE INFORMATION AS TO LIENS. 

For general discussion of indictment under this section, see: 

Jacobs, 4 Ga. App. 509 (61 S. E. 924).

This section is designed solely for the protection of landlord's liens. Jacobs, 4 Ga. App. 509 (61 S. E. 924).

The operation of this section of the Code is expressly confined to those who are about to give liens, and who, upon being interrogated as to the existence, ownership, and amount of any prior liens, give false information. A concealment of the existence of any lien, when disclosure of the facts is in the proper manner required, is criminal only when the new lien given is a landlord's lien. (Id.) (1). 

An indictment under this section is defective unless it avers that the information alleged to be false was given in response to inquiry, and unless it appears, from the accusation, that the lien taken in pursuance of such false information was a lien arising by operation of § 61-202. (Id.) (1-b).

Accusation under this section must also allege such facts as show that the prior lien alleged to have been given by the accused was in fact a valid, subsisting lien upon the same property upon which the subsequent lien was given. (Id.) (1-c).

As against a proper demurrer, an accusation charging a violation of this section by means of false representations must allege specifically: (a) knowledge of the existence of a prior lien; (b) knowledge of the falsity of said representations; (c) that the representations alleged to have been made were with intent to deceive and

SPECIFIC CRIMES 

357 defraud, and (d) that they did deceive and defraud. Each of these allegations is material in a prosecution for cheating and swindling by false representations; and a demurrer pointing out the absence of any one of them should be sustained. (Id.) (2).

This section does not apply to voluntary statements without solicitation or interrogation. Williams, 13 Ga. App. 338, 344 (79 S. E. 207).

Obtaining money on recorded mortgage or bill of sale, by false statements may be a violation of this section or § 26-7410. Brown, 6 Ga. App. 329 (64 S. E. 1001).

Statute of limitations begins to run when offense discovered. 

Brown, 6 Ga. App. 329 (1) (64 S. E. 1001).

For detailed discussion of this section as compared with § 267410 see: Sims, 34 Ga. App. 683, 685 (131 S. E. 101); Williams, 13 Ga. App. 338, 344 (79 S. E. 207).

i. PROCURING MONEY ON CONTRACT FOR SERVICES FRAUDULENTLY. 

Indictment. . . charge and accuse. .with the offense of cheating and swindling (or misdemeanor), for the said.................on the day of...19..., in the county aforesaid did contract with.................to perform for him service as a farm laborer as cropper for the said.................for the year 19...., with intent then and there to procure money or other things of value thereby, to wit, ........dollars in money, of the value of................dollars, and with the intent then and there not to perform such service so contracted to be done, to the loss and damage of the said......... in the sum of................dollars, and after having so contracted, did procure from the said.. the sum of................dollars in cash, with intent not to perform said service, to the loss and damage of said hirer in the sum of.......... dollars, contrary to, etc. . . . (Approved: Johnson, 125 Ga. 243, 244 (54 S. E. 184).) Note: Indictment should state where defendant was to perform labor. Better practice to specify particular farm. 

Accusation alleging contract with intent to defraud in one count, and fraudulent acts resulting in another, sustained against objection of duplicity. Johnson, 125 Ga. 243 (1) (54 S. E. 184).

SPECIFIC CRIMES 

359 Indictment is fatally defective where terms of contract are not fully shown. Watson, 124 Ga. 454 (52 S. E. 751).

Two offenses are created by this Act. First includes those who contract to perform services with intent to procure money or other things of value and do not intend to perform the services. The second includes those who, after having made a contract procure money or other things of value, with fraudulent intent not to perform the services. Indictment must inform defendant plainly of which offense he stands accused. Patterson, 1 Ga. App. 782 (3) (57 

S. E. 1028).

Indictment which charges procuring advances other than money must contain allegation that defendant did not return things so advanced, or pay for them. Accusation which charges procuring of both, goods and money, but which alleges failure to return or repay only the money, is valid only as to the money charged, and the statements as to the goods are treated as surplusage. Long, 4 

Ga. App. 571 (61 S. E. 1053).

Indictment including in one count various sums making up aggregate charged to have been falsely procured does not charge separate offenses. Young, 4 Ga. App. 827 (62 S. E. 558).

Indictment need not allege expiration of term of service. Millinder, 124 Ga. 452 (1) (52 S. E. 760). 

For approved indictment see: Ashley, 22 Ga. App. 626 (1) (97 

S. E. 82). 

Accusation alleging that defendant procured "advances," or received "value," without specifying the "advances" or "value"" subject to demurrer. Campbell, 121 Ga. 167 (48 S. E. 920); Oglesby, 123 Ga. 506 (51 S. E. 505); Barker, 6 Ga. App. 443 (65 S. E. 57).

Contract must be alleged and fully described in indictment. 

Where contract set out in indictment was too indefinite to be the basis of prosecution as place upon which work was to be performed was not set out with sufficient particularity, demurrer should be sustained. Gatlin, 16 Ga. App. 232, 233 (3) (84 S. E. 973).

Indictment must allege terms of contract including terms of service. Mason, 3 Ga. App. 348, 349 (60 S. E. 4); Gatlin, 16 Ga. 

App. 232 (84 S. E. 973); and it must be sufficiently alleged to put defendant on notice as to the contract. Thorn, 13 Ga. App. 10 (1) (78 S. E. 853).

Indictment not alleging that failure to perform contract, or to repay advances, was without good and sufficient cause, fatally defective. Mason, 3 Ga. App. 348 (1-c) (60 S. E. 4).

Indictment alleging that wages were to be half of crop made by defendant as a cropper, but not alleging the kind or extent of the crop to be planted and failing to locate and identify the particular parcel of land to be cultivated-demurrable. Thorn, 13 Ga. App. 

10 (1) (78 S. E. 853); Solomon, 14 Ga. App. 115 (80 S. E. 215); 

Hurt, 18 Ga. App. 144 (1) (88 S. E. 921).

Where indictment charges contract with Mrs. M. E. Drake, and evidence shows contract with M. E. Drake, and loss and damage to him, variance fatal. Williams, 124 Ga. 136 (52 S. E. 156).

Where indictment charges that defendant was a laborer and evidence shows that contract was of a different nature, variance fatal. 

Jackson, 4 Ga. App. 461 (3) (61 S. E. 862).

Accusation showing that hirer sustained no damage-demurrable. 

Braughner, 125 Ga. 629 (54 S. E. 653).

As § 26-7408 creates two separate offenses, the indictment must fully apprise the accused of offense or offenses charged. Patterson, 1 Ga. App. 782 (3) (58 S. E. 284).

General. §§ 26-7408 and 26-7409 held constitutional. Wilson, 138 Ga. 489 (75 S. E. 619); Latson, 136 Ga. 681 (71 S. E. 1052); 

Townsend, 124 Ga. 69, 70 (52 S. E. 293). 

26-7409 is merely rule of evidence. Wilson, 138 Ga. 489 (95 

S. E. 619).

These sections must be very strictly construed. Ferguson, 18 Ga. 

App. 730 (90 S. E. 371).

These sections are not designed to punish a mere failure to comply with an obligation, but for the procuring of property with a fraudulent intent. Wilson, 138 Ga. 489 (1) (2) (3) (75 S. E. 619); 

Mitchell, 15 Ga. App. 803 (84 S. E. 205).

These sections are not intended to furnish means for an annual accounting between laborers and croppers. Patterson, 1 Ga. App. 

782 (58 S. E. 284); Kirkland, 6 Ga. App. 774 (65 S. E. 963).

Purpose of this act is not to create a remedy or machinery for collection of debts, but to provide punishment for fraudulent and successful intent to cheat. Mitchell, 15 Ga. App. 803, 804 (6) (84 

S. E. 205); Mobley, 13 Ga. App. 728 (2) (79 S. E. 906).

State must prove contract to perform services as alleged, and also that defendant, at the time he procured thing of value upon contract, did not intend to perform services which he contracted for, but then and there had the intent to defraud. Stuckey, 19 

Ga. App. 441 (1) (91 S. E. 784).

SPECIFIC CRIMES 

361 Where State is required to elect between distinct transactions. 

Patterson, 1 Ga. App. 782 (2) (58 S. E. 284).

This section has no application to landlords and tenants. Young, 124 Ga. 788 (53 S. E. 101).

Cropper, who is himself to perform services and labor in making crop is within this section. Vinson, 124 Ga. 19 (1) (52 S. E. 79).

To authorize conviction of violation of these sections, the evidence must show the procurement of money, or other things of value, on a contract to perform services by the accused, with the intent to defraud, the failure to perform such services, or the failure to return the money or other things of value, without good and sufficient cause, and loss and damage to the employer; but it is for the jury to find, from all the evidence in the case, whether or not these facts have been sufficiently established. Mitchell, 15 Ga. App. 803 (1) (84 S. E. 205).

Fraudulent intent. In the absence of fraudulent intent no offense is committed. Hankinson, 6 Ga. App. 793 (65 S. E. 837); 

Ferguson, 19 Ga. App. 739 (90 S. E. 371). 

Fraudulent intent essential element of this offense. Johnson, 13 Ga. App. 586 (1) (79 S. E. 524). It is the paramount, controlling, and ever-essential element which determines the guilt of the defendant. Redwine, 17 Ga. App. 560 (1) (87 S. E. 829); Simmons, 18 Ga. 

App. 65 (1) (88 S. E. 800).

Intent to defraud co-existing with making the contract is an essential element of this offense. Johnson, 13 Ga. App. 586 (1) (79 

S. E. 524); Swilley, 14 Ga. App. 15, 16 (80 S. E. 31); Redwine, 17

Ga. App. 560 (1) (87 S. E. 829). 

Where evidence was insufficient to support inference of present fraudulent intent to defraud at the time of the advancement, conviction was unauthorized. Hudson, 14 Ga. App. 490 (3) (81 S. E. 

362); Mack, 16 Ga. App. 410 (2) (85 S. E. 615).

Where circumstances illustrating intent authorized two equally reasonable theories, one consistent with innocence and other with guilt, jury must adopt that theory consistent with innocence. Redwine, 17 Ga. App. 560 (1) (87 S. E. 829).

Where mortgage is given for the same debt, fraudulent intent is rebutted. Hogan, 12 Ga. App. 227 (76 S. E. 1081).

Evidence not showing intent to defraud at the time money has been received is insufficient to authorize conviction. Grant, 40 Ga. 

App. 136 (149 S. E. 150).

Evidence that defendant made a false affidavit at the time he

made the contract in question that he was not under any other contract of services at the time of the advancement made for him by the prosecutor, the making of which would subject him to prosecution under § 26-7410, is insufficient to show fraudulent intent or to authorize conviction under this section. Johnson, 13 Ga. App. 586 

Charge that intent to defraud must have been existing at the time money was advanced, must be given even in absence of request. Mulkey, 1 Ga. App. 521 (4) (57 S. E. 1022); Porter, 6 Ga. 

App. 770 (2) (65 S. E. 814). Failure to so charge is reversible error. Shepherd, 8 Ga. App. 114 (1) (68 S. E. 652); Simmons, 18 

Ga. App. 65 (88 S. E. 800).

Court should charge, even without request, that, if defendant worked under the contract for such length of time as to render it unreasonable that he obtained advance with fraudulent intent, jury need not presume fraudulent intent from mere fact that he failed to continue work under contract. Raffield, 7 Ga. App. 422 (1), 424 (67 S. E. 109). 

Where defendant was beaten by prosecutor and thereafter left his employment, regardless whether or not he provoked the difficulty by opprobrious words, the only question involved on trial under this section is whether defendant left employment on account of the beating or on account of preconceived fraudulent intent. 

Coleman, 6 Ga. App. 398 (2) (65 S. E. 32); Sterling, 126 Ga. 92 

Evidence that accused formed fraudulent intent after advances were made did not authorize conviction. Redwine, 17 Ga. App. 560 

Presumption of fraudulent intent. Proof of facts stated in this section are presumptive evidence of intent to defraud, to be submitted to the jury. Fuller, 10 Ga. App. 117 (72 S. E. 718). But this presumption is rebuttable, where evidence shows want of fraudulent intent. Paschal, 16 Ga. App. 370 (3) (85 S. E. 358).

State must prove the following elements, before presumption of fraudulent intent arises: (1) Contract. (2) Procurement of money thereon, or other things of value. (3) Failure to perform services. (4) Failure to return money or thing of value in time. (5) Want of good and sufficient excuse. (6) Loss to hirer. Tennyson, 16 

Ga. App. 214 (84 S. E. 988).

The State must prove all elements which create a presumption

363 of fraudulent intent under these sections. Mitchell, 15 Ga. App. 

803 (84 S. E. 205).

Failure without good cause to perform contract or to return loan advanced may be presumptive evidence of fraudulent intent. Johnson, 13 Ga. App. 586 (1) (79 S. E. 524). But mere failure to perform contract does not raise presumption that accused failed to carry out contract without good and sufficient reason. 

It is presumed that accused had a good and sufficient excuse. Thorn, 13 

Ga. App. 10 (2) (78 S. E. 853); Beeman, 17 Ga. App. 752 (88 S.

Instruction that § 26-7409 creates a conclusive presumption is reversible error. Paschal, 16 Ga. App. 370 (3) (85 S. E. 358).

Evidence that defendant after breach of contract and expiration of time within which labor was to be performed, offered to return money advanced will not rebut presumption of intent to defraud. 

Lewis, 15 Ga. App. 405, 406 (2) (83 S. E. 439).

Where evidence showed that defendant reported under contract for more than two months, and hence presumptively entertained no intent to defraud at the time of contracting nearly seven months before work was to commence,-conviction was unauthorized. Swilley, 14 Ga. App. 15 (80 S. E. 31).

Contract. Evidence must show contract for services, distinct and definite as to all essential terms, such as to time when contract is to commence and terminate, the amount of wages, whether laborer is to work by the day, by the month, by the week or year, where he is to work and character of the work to be performed. Sheffield, 13 Ga. App. 78 (1) (78 S. E. 828). Bennett, 37 Ga. App. 20 (138 

S. E. 671); Mason, 3 Ga. App. 348, 349 (60 S. E. 4).

Verbal contract made in March, 1912, by which the laborer agreed to work for the prosecutor from January 1, 1913, at $20.00 per month, is too indefinite to be the basis of prosecution under these sections. Sheffield, 13 Ga. App. 78 (2) (78 S. E. 828).

Writing containing promise to labor, which does not describe work to be performed, too indefinite to be the basis of prosecution under this section. Small, 14 Ga. App. 15 (1) (79 S. E. 1134).

Where one contracts to work as a farm laborer for another for a period of six months, from a day named to another day named, at a fixed number of dollars per month, on a farm "tended" by the employer, "on lands owned by" another person named, in a named county of the State of Georgia, not only is the place where the contract is to be performed sufficiently indicated for all pur-

poses, but the contract is sufficiently certain and definite as a whole to support a prosecution under the "labor contract act." Lewis, 15 Ga. App. 405 (1) (83 S. E. 439).

Terms of the contract must be proven as alleged in the indictment. 

Sheffield, 13 Ga. App. 78 (78 S. E. 828).

Labor contract to be performed during turpentine season at a definite rate, held sufficient. Peacock, 10 Ga. App. 402 (73 S. E. 

404); Golden, 40 Ga. App. 538, 539 (150 S. E. 452).

Where note was given for money advanced, and an agreement that labor was to be performed was conditional upon defendant's failure to pay note at maturity, such contract will not support a charge under these sections, and conviction was illegal. Moore, 8 Ga. App. 695 (70 S. E. 46).

Contract for services in lieu for pre-existing debts will not support charge under these sections. Bridges, 126 Ga. 91 (24 S. E. 916).

Where one makes a contract to purchase of another an article of merchandise, and agrees to pay therefor a sum of money, and, after the contract is completed, agrees that if the purchase price is not paid at the time stipulated, service of labor to the value of such purchase price will be performed for the other contracting party, he is not, upon failure to pay the purchase price or perform the service referred to in lieu thereof, indictable under these sections. 

Calhoun, 119 Ga. 312 (46 S. E. 428).

Conviction not authorized where evidence merely shows that defendant, upon comparison of accounts with hirer, is indebted to latter for unpaid balance of account. Patterson, 1 Ga. App. 782 (2) (4) (58 S. E. 284). 

Where there was a novation of the original contract and the hirer failed to live up to his part of the contract, defendant was justified in leaving. Williams, 7 Ga. App. 467 (67 S. E. 118).

Implied contract can not be the basis of prosecution under this section. Sanders, 7 Ga. App. 46 (65 S. E. 1042).

Contract is sufficient as to duration where it contains words "beginning to work Jan. 1, 1907, and continue to work thereafter until $62.00 have been worked out at $11.00 per month." Mosely, 2 Ga. 

App. 189, 191 (58 S. E. 298). 

Contract without consideration is void. Mason, 3 Ga. App. 348 (1) (60 S. E. 4). 

Note given by employer by which he promises to pay at a future date a pre-existing debt of employe is not an advance, unless payee expressly agreed to take it in payment. Coleman, 6 Ga. App. 298 (3) (65 S. E. 46).

365 Though contract be within the statute of frauds and civilly unenforceable, conviction for fraudulent procurement of money may still be had. Brown, 8 Ga. App. 211 (1) (68 S. E. 865).

Contract made on Sunday will not support charge under these sections. Bendross, 5 Ga. App. 175 (1) (2) (62 S. E. 728).

Contract to furnish and pay labor does not come within these sections. Accused must have contracted to do service himself, and failed to do so. Johnson, 125 Ga. 243 (3) (54 S. E. 184); Hankinson, 6 Ga. App. 793 (1) (65 S. E. 837); Coleman, 6 Ga. App. 398 (4) (65 

S. E. 46).

Burden of proof is on the prosecution to show not only that services contracted for have not been performed, but also that advances with interest thereon had not been repaid at or before time fixed for commencement of services. Johnson, 13 Ga. App. 

586 (1) (79 S. E. 524).

Excuse. Burden of proof is on the State to show that accused did not have a good excuse for failure to perform the contract or repay advancement. Johnson, 13 Ga. App. 586 (2) (79 S. E. 524); 

Johnson, 18 Ga. App. 700 (90 S. E. 355); Allen, 22 Ga. App. 274 (95 

S. E. 872); Ashley, 22 Ga. App. 626 (97 S. E. 82).

The burden of proving that the accused did not have a good cause for quitting the hirer rests upon the State. Thorn, 13 Ga. 

App. 10 (2) (78 S. E. 853); Jones, 15 Ga. App. 642 

Beeman, 17 Ga. App. 752 (88 S. E. 408). (84 S. E. 88);

This essential proof is not furnished by the hirer's testimony that the accused "did not have any reason for not returning the money or picking the cotton." Cofer, 34 Ga. App. 220 (129 S. E. 110); 

Miller, 34 Ga. App. 140 (128 S. E. 588).

A conviction is unauthorized where the State fails to prove that the accused did not have any good reason for failure to perform contract or return the advance. Such essentials are not supplied by statements of the hirer, that he knew of no reason why the laborer did not work for him. Such statements are conclusion of opinion and worthless unless supported by facts. Barlow, 42 Ga. 

App. 437 (156 S. E. 641). 

Mere failure to perform contract does not raise presumption that accused failed to carry out contract without good and sufficient reason or excuse. It is presumed that he had a good and sufficient reason. Thorn, 13 Ga. App. 10 (2) (78 S. E. 853); Beeman, 17 Ga. 

App. 752 (88 S. E. 408).

Defense. Performance of service or repayment of advancement with interest is a complete defense. Johnson, 13 Ga. App. 586 (1) (79 S. E. 524).

Payment to be effectual as a defense must be made on or before the first day of term of service. Barnes, 3 Ga. App. 333 (3) (59 

S. E. 937); Harwell, 2 Ga. App. 613 (1) (58 S. E. 1111). 

Where defendant was arrested and placed in jail before the date for commencement of labor, at the instance of the prosecutor, conviction illegal. Kemp, 12 Ga. App. 80 (76 S. E. 752).

It is no defense that defendant was under contract to work for another during period covered by promise under which he obtained advances. Paschal, 16 Ga. App. 370 (1) (85 S. E. 358).

Dissolution of partnership prior to time of performance is a good defense, where defendant promised to work for partnership and not for individual partner. Reese, 12 Ga. App. 647 (77 S. E. 922).

Tender. Offense is not committed if valid tender is made before the time of performance. Starling, 5 Ga. App. 171, 174 (62 S. E. 993). 

Effect of tender by a third party is for the jury. Paschal, 16 

Ga. App. 370 (85 S. E. 358).

Rule that tender shall be for the exact amount admitted to be due does not apply to provisions of these sections. (Id.) (2). 

Whether present offer to pay instanter whatever amount had been advanced was equivalent to return of money, was question for the jury. (Id.) 

Loss or damage. In order to sustain conviction, loss or damage must result to hirer, and State must prove such loss or damage. 

Mobley, 13 Ga. App. 728 (79 S. E. 906); Jones, 16 Ga. App. 264 (85 S. E. 204).

Loss or damage must be capable of definite computation. Mobley, 13 Ga. App. 728 (1) (79 S. E. 906).

Prosecution under this section will not lie for injuries to anyone except hirer. Patterson, 1 Ga. App. 782 (2) (58 S. E. 284).

Fact that prosecutor under this section is other than the employer who suffered damages, is immaterial. Mitchell, 15 Ga. App. 

803, 804 (3) (84 S. E. 205).

Minor. A minor who arrived at the age of criminal responsibility may be convicted under these sections, though the contract can not be enforced civilly against him. Anthony, 126 Ga. 632 (55 S. E. 

479); Vinson, 124 Ga. 19 (2) (52 S. E. 79).

Orders from parents that minor return home rebuts fraudulent
