367 intent. Howard, 126 Ga. 538 (55 S. E. 239); Jackson, 12 Ga. App. 

693 (78 S. E. 53).

Where minor broke contract at the command of a stranger, he is guilty. Anthony, 126 Ga. 632 (2) (55 S. E. 479).

Evidence. The evidence as a whole must justify conviction. 

Mulkey, 1 Ga. App. 521 (2) (57 S. E. 1022).

Where evidence showed that the accused quit work for prosecutor after first day, and went to work for other employer to whom he had previously hired, it was inferable that he could have performed contract for prosecutor. Mosely, 2 Ga. App. 189, 191 (58 

S. E. 298).

Parol evidence admissible to establish the common and customary meaning of words "turpentine season." Peacock, 10 Ga. App. 402 (4) (73 S. E. 404).

Evidence that on previous occasion defendant had fraudulently obtained money independently of the transaction involved-is inadmissible. Denham, 5 Ga. App. 303 (1) (63 S. E. 62).

Evidence that defendant secured $2.00 from prosecutor upon promise to cut cord of wood on following Monday or Tuesday, that he did not cut it on those dates or any other time, and that he told prosecutor that he did not cut wood because he had to take his brother to hospital-sufficient to convict. Lloyd, 26 Ga. App. 81 (105 S. E. 384). 

Variance. Where accusation alleged that contract was made by accused with named individual, and evidence showed that contract was made, not with such individual in his individual capacity, but as superintendent of county farm, and that money and provisions advanced were the property, not of the individual, but of the county, variance is material. Roberts, 6 Ga. App. 574 (65 S. E. 359).

Where indictment charged advancement of $1.00 and proof showed advancement of two plugs of tobacco, worth fifteen cents each, in addition to $1.00, such variance is not fatal. Mitchell, 15 Ga. App. 

803, 804 (4) (84 S. E. 205). 

Variance as to date of contract is fatal. Green, 6 Ga. App. 324 

Venue. In prosecution under these sections venue is the county where the advances were received. Dyas, 126 Ga. 556 (55 S. E. 

488); Davis, 16 Ga. App. 162 (84 S. E. 596). j. TRAMPS. Indictment. charge and accuse. .with a misdemeanor, for that the said…………………………….. on the....day of................

19...., did falsely and fraudulently conceal himself from the conductor and train authorities, by hiding in a box car upon a train of the...... Railroad Company, for the purpose of avoiding the payment of fare and stealing a ride thereon, contrary, etc. . . . (Approved: Mack, 119 Ga. 352, 353 (3) (46 S. E. 437).)

Accusation under this section discussed. Dixon, 27 Ga. App. 228 (1) (107 S. E. 777). 

General. Openly entering and remaining in car with no intent to pay fare, will not render one guilty under this section. Concealment in car for the purpose other than to avoid payment of fare, will not render one guilty under this section. If one conceals himself in car to avoid paying fare and is removed before journey begins, he is guilty of attempting to steal ride. If he remains in car until after the commencement of journey, he is guilty of stealing ride. Mack, 119 Ga. 352 (1-3) (46 S. E. 437).

Constitutionality of this section upheld. Pressly, 118 Ga. 315 (45 S. E. 395). 

Where conductor ordered one without fare or ticket to leave train, and such person, after opportunity to comply concealed himself in the car and continued his journey, he is guilty under this section. Intoxication is no excuse. Brazzell, 119 Ga. 559 (1) (2) (46 S. E. 837).

Evidence failing to show that accused was concealed in box-car, or that he was therein for purpose of stealing a ride, or to escape paying his fare, or that he concealed himself from conductor or train authorities, or that he was riding on train without their knowledge and consent, conviction unauthorized. Dixon, 27 Ga. App. 228 (2) (107 S. E. 777). 

The gist of the offense punished by this section is the fraudulent concealing of himself by a person in a car of a railroad company for the purpose of stealing a ride and to escape payment of fare therefor. Dixon, 27 Ga. App. 228 (107 S. E. 777).

No violation occurs where the car belongs to a circus of which defendant is an employe. Dixon, 27 Ga. App. 228 (107 S. E. 777).

For approved indictment charging the offense of attempt to cheat and swindle, see: Norris, 40 Ga. App. 232 (149 S. E. 158).

Allegation in indictment that the defendant knew that the representations made by him as to ownership of property were false, is material allegation, and must be supported by proof. Carlisle, 2 

Ga. App. 651 (58 S. E. 1068).

Indictment failing to allege facts showing actual pecuniary loss is fatally defective. Busby, 120 Ga. 858 (48 S. E. 314); Ganey, 10 

Ga. App. 777 (74 S. E. 286); Albert, 11 Ga. App. 93 (74 S. E. 714).

Where indictment alleges making of false statement which relates. to number of different facts, it need not allege that loss resulted from each and all of these statements; loss from any one is sufficient. 

Whitaker, 11 Ga. App. 208 (6) (75 S. E. 258).

Indictment charges intent to defraud sufficiently by averment that representations were fraudulently made, though not specifically alleging intent to defraud. Crawford, 4 Ga. App. 789 (3-a) (62 

S. E. 501); Isaacs, 7 Ga. App. 799 (2) (68 S. E. 338); Sadler, 9 

Ga. App. 201 (1) (70 S. E. 969).

Accusation will not be quashed because, instead of charging defendant of being a cheat and swindler, it charges him with cheating and swindling. Crawford, 4 Ga. App. 789 (2) (52 S. E. 501).

For indictment charging fraudulent sale of stock certificates, see: Clarke, 44 Ga. App. 341, 342 (161 S. E. 674).

For indictment charging false and fraudulent sale of property not belonging to defendant, see: Ray, 44 Ga. App. 763 (162 S. E. 861).

Indictment alleging that defendant bought property in one county and paid for it with check on bank in another county, falsely representing that check would be paid, but afterwards stopping payment, sufficient. Garner, 100 Ga. 257 (28 S. E. 24).

An indictment for cheating and swindling may be predicated on a false representation relating partly to matters of fact and partly to matters of opinion, where it is alleged that the loss to the prosecutor ensued through his acting upon the false representation as to the fact. Whitaker, 11 Ga. App. 208 (3) (75 S. E. 258).

Accusation must show how fraudulent representation as to value of property damaged prosecutor. Goddard, 27 Ga. App. 226 (2) (107 

S. E. 888).

By demurrer accused can compel the State to show whether fraudulent representations were in writing or parol. Goddard, 27 

Where indictment is sufficient to charge offense under § 26-7401, it is immaterial whether facts alleged constituted offense under § 

26-7410. Burns, 20 Ga. App. 77 (1) (92 S. E. 548). 

Indictment alleging that defendant cheated prosecutor and defrauded him in named sum, sufficiently alleges loss. Such allegation implies loss. Cheek, 14 Ga. App. 536 (1) (81 S. E. 641). 

Indictment should state name of person defrauded. 

Ga. App. 452 (2) (83 S. E. 641). 

Oliver, 15 

An indictment should allege ownership of property. Variance between allegation and proof of ownership of property and name of person defrauded-fatal. Oliver, 15 Ga. App. 452 (2) (83 S. E. 641).

Where offense falls within specific statute, indictment should not be under this section. Sharp, 7 Ga. App. 605, 606 (67 S. E. 699). General.

Scope. This section is very broad and enlarges the common law offense of cheating and swindling. Crawford, 2 Ga. App. 185, 187 (58 S. E. 301).

It is broad enough to include real estate or any interest therein. 

Morse, 9 Ga. App. 424 (71 S. E. 699); Holton, 109 Ga. 127 (2) (34 

S. E. 358).

Where offense falls within specific statute, indictment should not be under this section. Sharp, 7 Ga. App. 605, 606 (67 S. E. 699).

Any deceitful means and artful practices by which an individual is defrauded and cheated is within the terms of this section. It is

SPECIFIC CRIMES 

371 for the jury to determine whether the means used were deceitful or artful. Crawford, 2 Ga. App. 185, 188 (58 S. E. 544).

Elements. The elements of the crime of cheating and swindling by false representations are: (a) That representations were made; (b) that they were knowingly and designedly false; (c) that they were made with intent to deceive and defraud; (d) that they did deceive and defraud; (e) that they related to existing fact or present event; (f) that party relying on representation was thereby induced to part with his property. It is incumbent upon the 

State to prove all of these elements, and if any one is lacking, conviction is unauthorized. Goddard, 2 Ga. App. 154 (58 S. E. 

304); Jacobs, 4 Ga. App. 509 (2) (61 S. E. 924).

Representation. Representations indictable under this section are: (1) False and made with intent to defraud; (2) true, yet used artfully and deceitfully with intent to defraud. Crawford, 2 Ga. App. 185, 188 (58 S. E. 544).

Representations relating to the future can not be basis of prosecution under this section; they must relate to present or past. 

Foster, 8 Ga. App. 119 (1) (68 S. E. 739); Edge, 114 Ga. 113 (1) (39 S. E. 889).

Promise relating to future can not be basis of prosecution, but promise coupled with false pretense may be basis, if the one defrauded would not have acted on the promise without the pretense. 

Holton, 109 Ga. 127 (1) (34 S. E. 358).

Statement that the accused intended to do thereafter a certain thing, made in connection with false statement as to past fact, will not prevent conviction, though representation as to such intention was part of the inducement to part with money. Smith, 116 Ga. 587 (42 S. E. 766).

No promise relating to future will serve as a basis for a prosecution under this section. Fennel, 16 Ga. App. 173 (94 S. E. 721). 

But false pretense may be segregated from promise. Holton, 109 

Ga. 127 (34 S. E. 358). Where person who is alleged to have been defrauded acted solely on promise, prosecution will not lie, although accused might have been guilty of false pretense also. 

Meachan, 7 Ga. App. 713 (2) (68 S. E. 52); Foster, 8 Ga. App. 119 (1) (68 S. E. 739). 

Representation of title. Obtaining money by false statement as to title or interest in real estate is indictable under this section, although the truth of the statement might have been ascertained

by inspection of the clerk's records. Crawford, 117 Ga. 247 (1) (43 S. E. 762); Phillips, 40 Ga. App. 141 (149 S. E. 157).

False statement that one's title is good is not an expression of opinion, but statement of fact, and prosecution will lie. Holton, 109 

Ga. 127, 130 (2) (34 S. E. 358).

Obtaining money on mortgage or bill of sale of personalty by fraudulent statement as to existence of liens may be offense under § 61-9901 or under this section, though liens may be recorded. 

Brown, 6 Ga. App. 329 (1) (64 S. E. 1001).

Giving second mortgage on personalty without disclosing prior mortgage is no offense where no representation made as to nonexistence of first mortgage. Griffin, 3 Ga. App. 476, 477 (3) (60 

S. E. 216).

One may be defrauded by representations the truth or falsity of which has not been investigated. Crawford, 4 Ga. App. 789 (3-b) (62 S. E. 501).

A representation by one that he has title to a certain lot of lumber, made for the purpose of inducing another to purchase it, if false within the knowledge of him who makes the representation,is within this section. James, 43 Ga. App. 324 (1) (158 S. E. 644).

Where one represented ownership of property in himself, and contracted for sale and future delivery, prosecutor paying for the same at the time of the contract, and defendant failed to deliver, conviction not authorized where evidence failed to show affirmatively that representation of ownership was false and fraudulent. Ray, 44 Ga. App. 763 (162 S. E. 861).

Falsity of representation. Where defendant represented blind horse as sound for the purpose of trade, proof of defendant's knowledge of the defect is essential; mere suspicion is not enough. Ricks, 15 Ga. App. 645 (2) (84 S. E. 86).

While jury on trial of one charged with making false representations as to soundness of horse, would be authorized to find from circumstances that knowledge of defect existed at the time when representations were made, defendant's knowledge of such defect, as a fact, must be proved in some way before conviction is authorized. Waterman, 114 Ga. 262 (2) (40 S. E. 262).

Intent to defraud. The gist of the offense of cheating and swindling is the existence of fraudulent intent. Moore, 11 Ga. App. 813 (76 S. E. 368); Foster, 8 Ga. App. 119 (68 S. E. 739).

Where defendants estimated that they picked 1000 pounds of cotton, and received pay for picking that much, with understand-

SPECIFIC CRIMES 

373 ing that if amount paid was too much they would work out excess, and if too little prosecutor would make it good, and amount proved to be 750 pounds, fraudulent intent was not shown and conviction not warranted. (One dissenting.) Bowles, 12 Ga. App. 14 (76 S. 

E. 594).

Purpose to deceive must exist when representation made to induce trade, or agreement. After formed fraudulent intent will be no basis for conviction. Garner, 100 Ga. 257 (28 S. E. 24); Crawford, 2 Ga. App. 185, 188 (58 S. E. 301).

Belief of seller that he is giving full value is immaterial, where he, either by false representations or by fraudulent concealment of material facts, deceives prospective purchasers and induces them to purchase, to their damage, what they otherwise would not have purchased. Crawford, 4 Ga. App. 789, 790 (12) (62 S. E. 501).

If defendant honestly thought that bank stock was a good investment, and in good faith recommended purchase of this stock, there was no intent to defraud and he was not guilty of cheating and swindling. Whitaker, 11 Ga. App. 208 (1) (75 S. E. 258).

In case of cheating and swindling, to give in charge to the jury the section of the Code pertaining to this crime, without more, is not a sufficient compliance with a written request to charge that "intention is an essential ingredient, and it must be proved beyond a reasonable doubt, and, before you will be authorized to convict, it must appear that it was the intention of the defendant at the time to cheat and defraud the prosecutor." Ager, 2 Ga. App. 158, 159 (2) (58 S. E. 374). 

Where defendant represented that mule was "all right as far as he knew" such evidence will not warrant conviction in the absence of evidence that the defendant knew the mule to be defective. 

Webb, 12 Ga. App. 519 (77 S. E. 670).

Deceitful means and artful practices. Possession of property obtained from owner by deceitful means and artful practices, whereby he is defrauded, sufficient to convict. Morse, 9 Ga. App. 424 (2) (71 S. E. 699); Jones, 93 Ga. 547 (19 S. E. 250).

Silence may be deceitful means or artful practice. Crawford, 117 Ga. 247 (2) (43 S. E. 762).

One who writes a promissory note for an illiterate person, and fraudulently inserts amount larger than that stipulated for,-is guilty under this section. Wells, 89 Ga. 788 (15 S. E. 679).

Inducement to part with property need not be constituted solely of deceitful means and artful practices alleged in the indictment.

Proof that they were relied on and constituted in part such inducement will authorize conviction, though there may have been other contributing inducements. Braxton, 117 Ga. 703 (45 S. E. 64); 

Thomas, 90 Ga. 437 (16 S. E. 94).

Concealment of material fact is not an offense under this section, unless fraudulent and intended to deceive, and was resorted to to obtain money or other thing of value from one actually deceived thereby. Crawford, 117 Ga.. 247 (3) (43 S. E. 762).

Assignment of wages or other personal property by laborer, and his subsequent collection of such wages or other personal property, without knowledge of assignee, will not render laborer guilty under this section. (One dissenting.) Meacham, 7 Ga. App. 713, 714 (3) (68 S. E. 52). 

Representations did deceive. One can not be deceived by false representations which he knows to be false. But it will not be presumed, in favor of defendant, that the party to whom false representations were made knew them to be untrue. Crawford, 4 Ga. 

App. 789, 790 (12) (62 S. E. 501).

The person to whom the representation was made must in fact be cheated and defrauded thereby. Albert, 11 Ga. App. 93 (74 S. E. 714). 

Where blind horse was represented as sound, but the defect was not only patent but actually discovered by the prosecutor before the trade was concluded, conviction illegal. Ricks, 15 Ga. App. 

645 (84 S. E. 86); Rainey, 94 Ga. 599 (19 S. E. 892); Odum, 10 Ga. 

App. 27 (72 S. E. 511).

The burden is upon the State to prove among other things that the one charged to have been cheated and defrauded relied upon. the alleged false and fraudulent representations, and was thereby induced to part with his property. Davis, 27 Ga. App. 195 (107 

S. E. 883).

Existing fact or present event. Representation as to future milk yielding capacity of cow not indictable under this section. Miller, 99 Ga. 207, 208 (2) (25 S. E. 169). Distinguishing Parks, 94 Ga. 

601 (20 S. E. 430), where misrepresentation referred to present milk yielding capacity of cow. 

Loss or damage. Actual pecuniary loss is an essential ingredient of the offense and must be proved. Hay, 7 Ga. App. 407 (66 S. E. 

984); Busby, 120 Ga. 858 (48 S. E. 314). 

But the accused need not be benefited. Foss, 15 Ga. App. 478

375 The offense described in this section is complete as soon as the owner is deprived of his property. Oliver, 15 Ga. App. 452 (1) (83 S. E. 641).

Check obtained, though not presented, is sufficient to warrant conviction, if obtained with fraudulent intent. Parker, 29 Ga. App. 

26 (113 S. E. 218).

If by deceitful means or artful practice one is induced to give another his negotiable note promising to pay a given sum at a named date, whether as a matter of fact the maker is or is not insolvent, he is nevertheless defrauded and cheated. Holton, 109 Ga. 

127 (2) (34 S. E. 358); James, 43 Ga. App. 324 (2) (158 S. E. 644). 

Counterfeit money or possession thereof is not a thing of value.

Person can not swindle another by representing that if he will go to a certain expense he can procure a designated amount of counterfeit money. Foster, 8 Ga. App. 119 (2) (68 S. E. 739). 

For opinion discussing the question of damages, see: Bolton, 43 

Ga. App. 759 (159 S. E. 910).

Instances where this section held violated. Misstating position and power. Jackson, 118 Ga. 125 (44 S. E. 833); Ryan, 104 Ga. 78 (30 S. E. 678). Weight of load of hay misstated. Jones, 99 Ga. 46 (25 S. E. 617). Change for one dollar returned for twenty dollar coin. Jones, 97 Ga. 430 (25 S. E. 319). Distinguishing Crofton, 79 

Ga. 584 (4 S. E. 333). Execution of note by false assumption of authority may be violation of this section. Barron, 12 Ga. App. 

342 (7) (77 S. E. 314). Misstating amount of note to illiterate maker. Wells, 89 Ga. 788 (15 S. E. 679). Vendor representing ownership of land. Holton, 109 Ga. 127 (34 S. E. 358). Money obtained on bill of sale on personalty subject to lien. Brown, 6 Ga. 

App. 329 (64 S. E. 1001). Blind horse represented as sound. Tatum, 58 Ga. 408, 409; Ricks, 15 Ga. App. 645 (84 S. E. 86); Bryan, 3 

Ga. App. 26, 29 (59 S. E. 185).

Instances where this section held not violated. Defendant promising to work in future to pay advances. Oliver, 6 Ga. App. 791 (65 

S. E. 943); Ryan, 45 Ga. 128. Defendant representing that spurious money can be obtained at a certain place. Foster, 8 Ga. App. 119 (68 S. E. 739). Defendant representing to surgeon that expenses would be paid, where surgeon intended to perform operation regardless of representation. Davis, 27 Ga. App. 195 (107 S. E. 883).

Miscellaneous. One may be guilty of this offense where false pretense was made in reference to his official power and influence

if the party defrauded relied on such statement. Jackson, 118 Ga. 

125 (44 S. E. 833).

Acceptance of money not to institute prosecution for crime is no offense under this section. Franklin, 2 Ga. App. 385 (58 S. E. 491).

Fraudulent sale of worthless bank stock is indictable under this section. Whitaker, 11 Ga. App. 208 (1) (75 S. E. 258).

When a person gave to a merchant a ten dollar bill to get change and take out $1.90, price of goods bought, and merchant fraudulently gives him $3.10 instead of $8.10 change, falsely pretending that it was a five dollar bill, he is guilty of larceny and not of cheating and swindling, or larceny after trust. Finkelstein, 105 Ga. 617 (31 

S. E. 589); Hecox, 105 Ga. 625 (31 S. E. 592).

While ignorance of law can not be pleaded as an excuse for a crime, yet knowledge of law for all intents and purposes will not be imputed to every person. Where prosecutor in pending warrant or indictment, knowingly and with intent to defraud, falsely pretends to the wife of accused that he has power to compromise the crime against her husband, and thereby deceives her, and by promise to settle the prosecution obtains money from her, and there is a breach of promise, such prosecutor is guilty under this section. 

Ryan, 104 Ga. 78 (30 S. E. 678).

Cheating and swindling distinguished from blackmail, where one falsely and fraudulently represented himself to be United. 

States officer and obtained money to settle prosecution for offense. 

Jackson, 118 Ga. 125 (44 S. E. 833).

One may as a matter of law cheat and defraud another the second or third time by the same false representations with reference to the same matter. False representation that the defendant has chipped over entire crop of turpentine boxes were made at different times as to several chippings of the same crop of boxes. 

Williams, 8 Ga. App. 583 (70 S. E. 47).

Illegal transaction may be the basis of prosecution under this section. A person may be guilty of cheating and swindling in transaction in which both parties knew that they violated or were about to violate the law, provided one cheats the other out of something of value. Foster, 8 Ga. App. 119 (2) (68 S. E. 739).

Fraudulent conversion of vendor after sale of personal property may be larceny, but is not cheating and swindling, unless artful practices induced purchaser to buy what vendor could not sell. 

Meacham, 7 Ga. App. 713, 714 (3) (68 S. E. 52).

Forged draft or check made in the name of any person or in

SPECIFIC CRIMES 

377 fictitious name, if defendant obtained money thereon, will not support prosecution under this section, but under § 26-3918. Sharp, 7 

Ga. App. 605 (67 S. E. 699). .

Where one executes a paper purported to be executed by him as agent, he is not guilty of forgery, though he had no authority to execute it. Where false writing is not intended to be received as other than it purports to be, maker may be guilty of cheating and swindling, but not of forgery. Barron, 12 Ga. App. 342 (7) (77 

S. E. 214).

Where defendant bought property and paid for it with check, falsely representing that check would be paid, but afterwards stopped payment on check, offense may be under this section. Garner, 100 Ga. 257 (28 S. E. 24).

In trial of landlord for cheating and swindling cropper, weak evidence supported conviction. Pullen, 26 Ga. App. 181 (2) (105 

S. E. 866).

Defense. Subsequent repentance and restitution by the wrongdoer will be no bar to a prosecution against him. Lowe, 111 Ga. 

650 (36 S. E. 856).

The fact that the party defrauded did not exercise reasonable diligence affords no defense to the accused. Crawford, 4 Ga. App. 

789 (3-b) (62 S. E. 501). See also (Id.) (11).

No defense that person defrauded could, by making independent investigation, have ascertained that representations were false. 

Whitaker, 11 Ga. App. 208 (4) (75 S. E. 258).

Venue. A prosecution for cheating and swindling must be had in the county in which the owner of money or goods is deprived of his property. Davis, 20 Ga. App. 72 (92 S. E. 552).

Where defendant bought property in one county and paid for it with check on bank in another county, falsely representing that check would be paid, but afterwards stopping payment, venue was properly laid in former county, the intent to stop payment having existed at the time of purchase. If intent had not been formed until accused was in latter county, he would not have been subject to indictment in county where purchase was made. Garner, 100 

Ga. 257 (28 S. E. 24).

Limitations. The statute of limitations does not begin to run until after the offense is known to the prosecutor, or someone interested in the prosecution or injured by the offense. The indictment should so allege. Brown, 6 Ga. App. 329 (64 S. E. 1001).

Evidence. Conviction of defendant sustained by evidence that manager of aid society received telephone message purporting to be spoken by third party, stating that defendant wanted to borrow $5.00, and that speaker would see that defendant paid it on a named day, that in a few minutes defendant appeared and said that he had come for the money telephoned about, that manager let him have $5.00 of the money of the society, requiring him to execute a mortgage, that levy under mortgage was met by a claim of homestead, that third party denied giving the message, and refused to pay. Braxton, 117 Ga. 703 (2) (45 S. E. 64).

Draft for $10.00 which accused procured from prosecutor and had cashed, admissible on trial of accusation charging fraudulent procurement of $10.00. McCoy, 124 Ga. 218 (2) (52 S. E. 434).

Answer of defendant filed in receivership proceedings involving solvency of alleged banking corporation, if relevant, admissible. 

Whitaker, 11 Ga. App. 208 (14) (75 S. E. 258).

Original record of petition in bankruptcy in United States court and original schedules attached are not admissible in trial of action in State courts. Duly certified copy is best and highest evidence. Whitaker, 11 Ga. App. 208 (15) (75 S. E. 258).

The fact that no charter has been granted to banking corporation must be established by some person who has examined the records in the office of the Secretary of State. Whitaker, 11 Ga. 

App. 208 (12) (75 S. E. 258).

In trial of landlord for cheating and defrauding cropper, written statement of account identified by cropper, although vague and indefinite, but showing balance due cropper,-admissible. Pullen, 26 Ga. App. 181 (105 S. E. 866).

Variance. Where the indictment alleges that representations were made to A, and the proof showed that they were made directly to B, but in A's presence and hearing and for the purpose of having A to act upon them, and that at the same time the one who made the representations handed to A a fraudulent bill, directly connected with the fraudulent representations, and that A, acting upon the representations, made in his presence and hearing, had B to "O. K." the bill, it was held that this did not constitute a material variance between the allegations in the indictment and the proof. 

Foss, 15 Ga. App. 478 (4) (83 S. E. 880).

Accusation charging cheating and swindling by averring that accused represented that he owned a "certain horse mule, named 'Jim'," and that said mule was unincumbered, when in fact the

SPECIFIC CRIMES 

379 mule did not belong to him, it was error to allow the State to introduce instruments showing title in certain parties to a mule described therein as "black horse mule known as 'Hill mule'." 

Williams, 13 Ga. App. 338 (2) (79 S. E. 207). 

Indictment should allege ownership of property. Variance between allegation and proof of ownership of property and name of person defrauded-fatal. Oliver, 15 Ga. App. 452 (2) (83 S. E. 641). 

Evidence that title to mule described in note was in third party did not support indictment alleging that person accepting such note was defrauded by representations that mule was received by defendant in swap. Fennell, 16 Ga. App. 173 (84 S. E. 721).

Sentence. Where the sentence provides for a penalty "and in addition to said fine making restitution to" the defrauded party, last proviso is without legal force and should be ignored, and sentence executed as if it did not appear therein. Ray, 40 Ga. App. 

145 (149 S. E. 64).

Passing worthless checks. If any person shall buy any of the products mentioned in the preceding section (fruits, melons, vegetables, butter, eggs, poultry, or other farm, orchard, and dairy products), either for himself or others, and give a draft, check, or order in payment of such products, and the payment of the draft, check, or order is refused by the drawee, by which the seller sustains loss, such buyer shall be guilty of a misdemeanor. § 5-9916.

Any person who, with intent to defraud, shall make, or draw, or utter, or deliver any check, draft or order for the payment of money upon any bank, or other depository, knowing at the time of such making, drawing, uttering or delivering that the maker or drawer has not sufficient funds in or credit with such bank or depository, for the payment of such check, draft or order upon its presentation, shall be guilty of a misdemeanor. The making, drawing, uttering, or delivering of such check, draft, or order as aforesaid shall be prima facie evidence of intent to defraud. The word "credit" as used herein shall be construed to mean an arrangement or understanding with the bank or depository for the payment of such check, draft or order. § 13-9933. Indictment: charge and accuse. with the offense of a misdemeanor, for that the said..............., in the county of. on the day of...19..., with force and arms, did then and there unlawfully draw and utter a certain draft upon........... of the following tenor and effect, to wit: (here set out the

and did thereby obtain from draft, or check).... ..... And having drawn said draft, as aforesaid, ....endorsed same on the back thereof as follows: ....., the following property to wit, (here set out the property obtained)......... he, the said .not then and there having in the hands of.................sufficient funds to pay said draft, and did not then and there within thirty days thereafter deposit with...funds sufficient to pay said draft, contrary, etc. . . . (Approved: Persons, 44 Ga. App. 300 (161 S. E. 167).) 

Giving check on bank where there is no fund there is no offense under this section, unless accompanied by false representations. 

Williams, 10 Ga. App. 395 (73 S. E. 424); Berry, 153 Ga. 169, 175 (111 S. E. 669). 

Pecuniary loss necessary. Busby, 120 Ga. 858 (48 S. E. 314); 

Berry, 153 Ga. 169, 175 (111 S. E. 669).

This charge can not be prosecuted on a postdated check. Neidlinger, 17 Ga. App. 811 (88 S. E. 687); Strickland, 27 Ga. App. 772 (110 S. E. 39).

Where it appears that the transaction amounted merely to a promise to pay in the future, the defendant can not be convicted. 

Highsmith, 38 Ga. App. 192 (143 S. E. 445).

If the check is given solely for a past due loan, the accused must be acquitted. By giving such check the defendant does not obtain from the payee any money, property or other thing of value. He does not deprive the other party of any right. Bank checks are not payment until themselves paid. The acceptance of such check is not a novation. Berry, 153 Ga. 169 (111 S. E. 669); Driskell, 47 Ga. 

App. 741, 743 (171 S. E. 389).

The gravamen of this offense is the "intent to defraud." The means of effecting this intent to defraud is by making, drawing, uttering, or delivering any check, draft, or order for the payment of money upon any bank or depository, knowing at the time of such making, drawing, uttering, or delivering that the maker has not sufficient funds in, or credit with, such bank, or other depository, for the payment of such check, draft, or order in full upon presentation. 

The State makes out a case by proving the following facts: (1) The making, drawing, uttering, or delivering any check, draft, or order for the payment of money upon any bank or depository; and (2) knowledge on the part of the defendant that at that time he did not have sufficient funds in, or credit with, such bank or depository for the payment of such instrument, in full upon its presentation. Berry, 153 Ga. 169, 173 (111 S. E. 669).

Allegation in indictment that defendant "did sell and dispose of all the cotton and cotton seed grown on three acres of cotton planted on Mrs. J's farm" did not sufficiently describe and specify the property and a demurrer should be sustained. Miller, 18 Ga. App. 

487 (89 S. E. 607).

Accusation charging fraudulent sale is sufficient which alleges that defendant executed mortgage covering, with other property, a certain described mule, and defendant, without consent of mortgagee, and with intent to defraud him, disposed of mule, to the damage of mortgagee in the sum of $160.00. It is not necessary to allege more specifically "how or in what manner" mule was disposed of, or to whom it was sold, or "how and in what way" loss of $160.00 was sustained by mortgagee. Description of mortgaged property as "12 acres of cotton," without more, insufficient. Hampton, 124 Ga. 3 (2) (52 S. E. 19).

Substitution of the word "of" in mortgage set out in accusation for word "to" in certified copy, not material variance. Conley, 85 Ga. 348 (5) (11 S. E. 659).

There was no fatal variance between the judgment alleged in the accusation, which was for a certain amount and costs, and the judgment shown by the evidence, which made no mention of costs; the execution for costs having issued additionally, and being, in effect, a part of the judgment. Conley, 85 Ga. 348 (8) (11 S. E. 659). 

General. Constitutionality of this act upheld. Conley, 85 Ga. 

348 (14) (11 S. E. 659).

Bill of sale to secure debt is in the same class as mortgage in reference to these sections. See Acts of 1921, p. 123. § 67-9901. 

Farmer, 18 Ga. App. 307 (89 S. E. 382).

By § 61-9903 this law has been extended to protect liens and advances on crops. Robinson, 10 Ga. App. 791 (74 S. E. 92).

The elements of the offense inhibited by § 67-9901 consist of a fraudulent sale, without the consent of the mortgagee, with intent to defraud the mortgagee, and loss to the mortgagee. Farmer, 18 

Ga. App. 307 (3) (89 S. E. 382); Wright, 9 Ga. App. 442 (71 S. E.

One aiding in sale of such property is principal. Wyatt, 16 Ga.

Fraudulent intent required by this section will be implied where proof shows clear violation of § 61-9903 by sale of crop without landlord's consent. Smith, 17 Ga. App. 554 (4) (87 S. E. 829). (See also: Wrongful sale of property under lien.)

In absence of evidence showing that turning over cotton to landlord by tenant in settlement of claim for rent and supplies was collusive or was fraudulently done, tenant not criminally liable.

Where charge of Court made no reference to intent to defraud,error. Davis, 7 Ga. App. 332 (66 S. E. 960); Reece, 5 Ga. App.

The loss mentioned in this section does not necessarily refer to a loss of the debt, or any part of it, nor will the solvency of the mortgaged property, of itself, prevent such a sale or disposition from being a violation of the law. Coleman, 79 Ga. 637 (3) (5 S. E. 204). 

Where the prosecutor testified that he lost "$50.00 the value of the cow sold by the defendant," this was a statement of fact and

383 showed the loss as contemplated by this section. Farmer, 18 Ga. 

App. 307 (4) (89 S. E. 382).

But such a loss is not shown by a general statement of the prosecutor that he lost valuable time, and employed a lawyer to foreclose mortgage. Denney, 2 Ga. App. 146 (58 S. E. 318).

Proof that defendant killed and ate calf was sufficient to warrant conviction. Killing and eating is included in "otherwise disposing." Linder, 17 Ga. App. 520 (87 S. E. 703). But the Linder case has been overruled in Stenson, 43 Ga. App. 582 (158 S. E. 

778), where the Court of Appeals held that the words "otherwise dispose of" must be construed to mean a disposition of the property in the nature of a sale and not in any other manner. Citing: 

Conley, 85 Ga. 348 (11) (11 S. E. 659); Scott, 6 Ga. App. 332, 334 (64 S. E. 1005).

Where the defendant had nothing to do with the sale made by the sheriff, a conviction under this section is unauthorized. Tatom, 27 Ga. App. 779 (109 S. E. 917); Lord, 114 Ga. 30 (39 S. E. 948).

Crop of cotton mortgaged in May and sold in November is, when sold, personal property under mortgage. Hamilton, 94 Ga. 770 (21 

S. E. 995). But see also: Williams, 25 Ga. App. 138, 140 (102 S. E. 

870); Barnesville Bank, 34 Ga. App. 269, 270 (129 S. E. 112).

Where mortgage was given on crop which was planted at date of mortgage, but which was destroyed by storm, and a new crop was planted, lien of mortgage not attached to any part of new crop. 

Conviction could not be predicated on the sale of any part of crop planted subsequently to date of mortgage. Hall, 2 Ga. App. 739 (1) (2) (59 S. E. 26). The old rule was that a valid mortgage could not be made of a crop which has no actual or potential existence at the date of the mortgage. A conviction under §§ 67-9901 and 67-9903 can not be predicated on a sale of any part of the crop planted subsequently to the date of the mortgage, but such conviction, to be lawful, must be based on the fraudulent sale of the crop planted before the date of the mortgage. (Id.) But under the provisions of § 671101 a crop mortgage may be given before the crop is actually planted, where it is executed, and the mortgage so stipulates, to secure advances for the purpose of making and gathering the crop. 

A mortgage on crops not in esse or in potential existence is still invalid where not given to secure advances for the purpose of making and gathering such crops, or where it is not so stipulated in the mortgage. Dawson National Bank v. Bank of Dawson, 42 

Ga. App. 300, 302 (155 S. E. 791).

Cropper whose contract stipulated that he was to receive one-half of the crops left after enough had been sold to pay expenses of cultivation and who gave a mortgage to third person covering onehalf of cotton, does not violate this section by delivering cotton to landlord to be sold and the proceeds to be credited on expense account. Cody, 69 Ga. 743.

Evidence. The evidence must show with sufficient particularity that the property sold was the mortgaged property. Gibson, 16 Ga. 

App. 265 (85 S. E. 191).

Some evidence showing sale of portion of mortgaged property, without consent, and with intent to defraud, and that loss sustained, supported conviction. Hays, 25 Ga. App. 591 (2) (103 S. E. 730).

Evidence of other transactions which tend to establish the existence of the fraudulent intent which is the gist of the offense is admissible in illustration of his intent and motives in the transaction under investigation. Wyatt, 16 Ga. App. 817 (81 S. E. 802).

Where execution of mortgage not denied, but it was denied that mortgage included certain cotton seed alleged to have been sold, charge that the record of the mortgage was prima facie evidence of genuineness thereof, and that party signing mortgage knew and understood what he was doing, but that prima facie presumption might be overcome by proof, and if defendant did not know he had given a mortgage and sold the seeds so believing, he could not do it with intention to defraud and would not be guilty,-approved. 

Cammon, 20 Ga. App. 175 (2) (92 S. E. 957).

Description of property covered by chattel mortgage as mortgagor's entire interest in all crops grown by him and his croppers on certain land, consisting of about one hundred acres in cotton, was too indefinite to be foundation of prosecution for selling mortgaged property. Wyatt, 16 Ga. App. 817 (2) (81 S. E. 802).

The record of a deed properly executed is prima facie evidence of its delivery, and becomes conclusive evidence if it is not rebutted by proof. Where property alleged to have been illegally disposed of is described in mortgage as "my crop of cotton seed raised for this year, 1916, on the G. farm, Polk County, Georgia," and parol evidence, before introducing mortgage, described property more fully, mortgage admissible. Cammon, 20 Ga. App. 175, 176 (1) (3) 

Proof that tenant pawned part of crop will not support indictment charging merely that he did "sell" it. Gilbert, 16 Ga. App. 249 (1) (85 S. E. 86).

Punishment. Fine, double the amount of debt, not excessive. 

Conley, 85 Ga. 348 (3) (11 S. E. 659).

Venue. The venue is fixed by the place of sale, and not by the place of the execution of the mortgage. Ham, 7 Ga. App. 57 (2) (66 S. E. 22); Davis, 7 Ga. App. 332 (66 S. E. 960); Dudley, 28 

Ga. App. 711 (113 S. E. 24). 

Venue not proven, new trial should have been granted. Smith, 121 Ga. 196 (48 S. E. 912).

Charge fixing venue at the place of execution of mortgagé instead of place of sale, erroneous. Davis, 7 Ga. App. 332 (66 S. E. 960). 

Accessories. All persons who participate in the offense of selling mortgaged personal property by aiding and abetting in its commission are principals. Sirmans, 48 Ga. App. 159 (1) (172 S. 

E. 93). 

m. SALE OF PROPERTY UNDER LIEN. 

Indictment. . . . charge and accuse.. ..with the offense of in the county of...State .19...., did then and there a misdemeanor, for the said... of Georgia, on the.................day of.. unlawfully and with force and arms, for that he unlawfully, wrongfully and fraudulently, after having made a rent contract for the year....... ..with one.. on which rent contract he was due $....... for rent and advances made upon the crops grown upon said rented land, for which he was due the said landlord, on a landlord's lien, sell and otherwise dispose the said..

of. .bushels of.. .and...------------.bushels of.. and bales of....

, grown on said rented premises before the of............ --, payment of the landlord's lien, without the consent of, and with the intent to defraud, said the landlord, and loss was in the sum aforesaid, contrary, sustained by the said... 

etc.... (Approved: Holt, 5 Ga. App. 184 (62 S. E. 992).) 

For approved indictment see also: Sims, 43 Ga. App. 438 (158 

S. E. 913).

Indictment charging that defendant sold a bale of cotton subject to lien, and weighing five hundred and eighty-two pounds, and evidence showing that it weighed five hundred and eighty-eight pounds, variance immaterial. Sims, 43 Ga. App. 438 (158 S. E. 913).

General: In order to render penal the sale by a tenant of personalty which is subject to landlord's lien for rent and advances, three necessary facts must appear: (1) that such sale was made without the consent of the landlord; (2) that it was made with intent to defraud the landlord; and (3) that, in consequence of the sale, the landlord sustained loss. Reece, 5 Ga. App. 663 (63 S. E. 

670); White, 24 Ga. App. 74 (1) (100 S. E. 39).

On the trial of an accusation against a tenant, charging him with selling and otherwise disposing of his crop before the repayment of the advances made to him by the landlord, it is necessary to show the existence of this relationship; that the tenant did sell or otherwise disposed of a portion of his crop before the payment to the landlord, and without the landlord's consent, with intention to defraud the landlord; and that the landlord suffered loss by the illegal disposition of the crop by the tenant. Thompson, 12 Ga. App. 201 (2) (76 S. E. 1072).

Relationship of landlord and tenant must be shown. (Id.) 

Where contract created the relationship of vendor and vendee and not that of landlord and tenant, conviction under this section unauthorized. Brundridge, 10 Ga. App. 816 (74 S. E. 298).

It must be shown that the accused was the tenant of the landlord in whose favor the lien existed. It is not sufficient to show merely that accused cultivated the crop, when it also appears that another person had rented the premises and given obligation for the payment of rent, although other person may have been defendant's wife. Hackney, 101 Ga. 512 (10) (28 S. E. 1007).

Title to crop is in the tenant, and landlord has only a lien for rent. 

Where tenant disposes of crop, it is not larceny, but a violation of this section. Landlord can not acquire title to crops by simply taking possession of them. Teel, 7 Ga. App. 600 (67 S. E. 699).

SPECIFIC CRIMES 

387 Landlord has no lien for supplies furnished for prior year to that in which crop in question was raised. Where tenant has paid rent in full and has delivered to landlord money and produce enough to pay for supplies advanced to him in making crop for the particular year in question, he can not be convicted under this section. Robinson, 10 Ga. App. 791 (74 S. E. 92).

The fact that landlord consented to selling crop is no defense under indictment for selling other crop, except that it may be shown to rebut intent to defraud. Smith, 17 Ga. App. 554 (3) (87 S. E. 829). 

Cotenant who disposes of crop or part thereof before landlord has been settled with, without landlord's consent and to his damage, is guilty, whether other cotenants participated in sale or not. Smith, 17 Ga. App. 554 (2) (87 S. E. 829). 

Sale. This section includes sales of any nature. Bell, 14 Ga. 

App. 425 (2) (81 S. E. 253).

Sale for future delivery of crops subject to landlord's lien is crime, in violation of this section. Bell, 14 Ga. App. 425 (2) (81 S. 

E. 253).

Loan of part of crop under lien for rents and advances was violation of this section, if made with intent to defraud and with resulting loss. Bugg, 17 Ga. App. 211 (1) (86 S. E. 405).

Evidence that defendant loaned crop which was subject to landlord's lien, did not support indictment charging sale thereof. Indictment should have charged that defendant "disposed" of property. Bugg, 17 Ga. App. 211 (86 S. E. 405).

Proof that defendant pawned part of crop which was subject to landlord's lien, did not support indictment charging sale thereof. 

Gilbert, 16 Ga. App. 249 (1) (85 S. E. 86).

Tenant's transfer of rent notes, taken from sub-tenant, and payable to himself in cotton, subject to landlord's lien, is crime, when made without landlord's consent. Bell, 14 Ga. App. 425 (2) (81 S. 

E. 253).

Bona fide purchaser is protected against landlord's lien. Thornton, 80 Ga. 397 (6 S. E. 915).

Intent to defraud. Intent to defraud and loss to defrauded person is necessary element of this crime, and must be charged. Charge not referring to intent to defraud is erroneous. Reece, 5 Ga. App. 

663 (63 S. E. 670); Thompson, 12 Ga. App. 201 (2) (76 S. E. 1072); 

Morrison, 111 Ga. 642 (36 S. E. 902).

Where evidence did not show intent to defraud, conviction was unauthorized. Kellam, 2 Ga. App. 479 (58 S. E. 695).

Where landlord had lien on crop, and defendant sold the same, without criminal intent, he would not be guilty, regardless whether or not landlord gave his consent. Thompson, 12 Ga. App. 201 (3) (76 S. E. 1072).

Fraudulent intent required by this section will be implied where proof shows clear violation of this section by sale of crop without landlord's consent. Smith, 17 Ga. App. 554 (4) (87 S. E. 829).

Failure to charge that if defendant loaned cotton with intention to repossess it and deliver it to satisfy lien, he would not be guilty, was not error. Bugg, 17 Ga. App. 211, 212 (7) (86 S. E. 405).

Judge need not charge specifically that fraudulent intent is essential element of selling crop without consent of landlord, where this and the preceding sections have been fully read to jury. Smith, 17 

Ga. App. 554 (4) (87 S. E. 829). 

n. SELLING OR ENCUMBERING PERSONAL PROPERTY HELD UNDER CONDITIONAL PURCHASE. 

No offense has been committed where accused was ignorant of the fact that title had been reserved. Miley, 118 Ga. 274 (45 S. E. 245).

No offense has been committed where title has not been retained. 

Shirley, 13 Ga. App. 676 (79 S. E. 752).

No offense has been committed where the contract reserving title was void. Singleton, 14 Ga. App. 527 (81 S. E. 596).

No offense has been committed under this section where vendor gave permission to sell under express condition that proceeds will be accounted for, and defendant has not accounted for the same. 

Dempsey, 94 Ga. 766 (22 S. E. 57).

Where one holds personal property under conditional sale, and where by the terms of purchase title is retained in vendor until payment of purchase price, and where holder, without consent or approval of vendor, encumbers the property to the injury of vendor, crime is complete. Bernolak, 18 Ga. App. 7 (1) (89 S. E. 302).

The offense is complete when the property is encumbered and is not affected by a subsequent contract between the parties. Bernolak, 18 Ga. App. 7 (1) (89 S. E. 302).

Disposition of property otherwise than by selling or encumbering not punishable under this act. Dempsey, 94 Ga. 766 (1) (22 S. E. 57). 

Intent to defraud must be shown. Miley, 118 Ga. 274 (45 S. E. 245).

SPECIFIC CRIMES 

389 This section includes selling in the nature of barter or exchange. 

Sale, or exchange, is a transmutation of property from one man to another, in consideration of some price or recompense in value. 

Though often used in more limited sense, embracing only those contracts which are founded upon a money consideration, a "sale," in its broadest sense, comprehends any contract for the transfer of property from one person to another for a valuable consideration, and the word "sell," as used in this section is to be construed in its broad sense. McDuffie, 19 Ga. App. 39 (90 S. E. 740).

Written contract of conditional sale is competent evidence and should be admitted. Bernolak, 18 Ga. App. 7 (1) (89 S. E. 302). 

Vendor is under no duty to record contract. Chambers, 85 Ga. 

220 (11 S. E. 653).

Court did not err in excluding testimony offered to show that mule to which title was retained by vendor and which defendant traded off was not suitable for particular purpose for which defendant had purchased it, defendant not having offered to show that mule was totally worthless or that he paid full value thereof, to show that vendor suffered no damage. McDuffie, 19 Ga. App. 39, 40 (3) (90 S. E. 740).

Where peddler without a license sells watch under contract reserving title, he is guilty of a misdemeanor, contract reserving title is a nullity, and act of buyer in selling watch is not crime in violation of this section. Singleton, 14 Ga. App. 527, 528 (3) (81 S. E. 

596). Under the provisions of § 84-2002, a corporation can not be licensed as a peddler. And the fact that a corporation has paid the fee required by law does not authorize an employe, servant, or agent of the corporation, to peddle without personal compliance with the requirements of that section. (Id.) (2). § 67-9907 referring to settlement of cases where amount due, and cost of prosecution, have been paid, has reference only to prosecution for offense declared in § 67-9906. Sanders, 145 Ga. 507, 508 (2) (89 S. E. 484).

Indictment charging sale of "one bay horse" is not supported by evidence that property sold was "Texas pony," without any evidence touching color or sex of animal; but where it can be fairly inferred that the Texas pony was a bay horse, there could be a conviction as far as this element is concerned. Dempsey, 94 Ga. 766 (4) (22 S. E. 57).

18. COMPOUNDING CRIMES AND MISDEMEANORS. 

§§ 26-4603, 26-4604. 

Punishment. Compounding felonies. § 26-4603. Not less than one nor more than five years in the penitentiary.

Compounding misdemeanors. § 26-4604. (Misdemeanor.) 

For full discussion of the subject see: 

Sheppard, 151 Ga. 27 (105 S. E. 601). charge and accuse.. ..with the offense of with Indictment. compounding a felony (or misdemeanor), for that the said... on the................day of---------------, 19., in the county of----force and arms, did, after prosecuting under pretense of the penal law one....... ..for the offense of.. ---, compound with the offender, the said....., for the consideration of the sum of.. dollars in money, of the value of dollars, paid to the said by him, the said..... did direct the information to dis- 

continue, and did compound with him the said offender, the said for the consideration of the said sum of.............dollars, not to prosecute said...for the offense of..... and did by threats of a prosecution against the said. to pay to the said...the sum of.. cute the said........ ..for the offense of. .cause the said.. dollars not to proseas aforesaid, and, after so compounding with the said.. as aforesaid, did fail and refuse to prosecute the said..................for the offense of....………………. as aforesaid, contrary, etc. . . . (Approved: Sheppard, 151 Ga. 27 (105 S. E. 601).)

It is not necessary to allege the essential element of the pretended. offense, the compounding of which is the basis of the prosecution. 

Sheppard, 151 Ga. 27 (105 S. E. 601).

General. An actual commission of the preceding crime is essential to the offense of compounding the same, and has to be proved. 

Hays, 15 Ga. App. 386 (83 S. E. 502).

There could be no compounding of a crime unless there was a crime to compound. Hays, 142 Ga. 592, 594 (83 S. E. 236). 

Good faith is immaterial. Hays, 15 Ga. App. 386 (4) (83 S. E. 502).

Statutes against compounding offenses must be strictly construed. 

Hays, 142 Ga. 592, 593 (83 S. E. 236); Sheppard, 151 Ga. 27, 30 (105 

S. E. 601).

Elements of the offense of compounding a crime are: (1) a crime, punishable by death or imprisonment in the penitentiary; (2) taking or receiving any money, goods, chattels, lands, or other reward, on promise to compound the crime; (3) compounding the crime, for any cause. Hays, 142 Ga. 592, 593 (83 S. E. 236).

SPECIFIC CRIMES 

391 Benefit to the compounder is not necessary. Consideration may accrue to another. Hays, 15 Ga. App. 386 (2) (83 S. E. 502).

Parol evidence admissible to show the actual agreement to compound where written contract does not set forth the facts. Hays, 15 Ga. App. 386 (1) (83 S. E. 502).

Venue. If the parties entered into a negotiation in Alabama, looking to the compounding of a felony, and, in furtherance of the agreement, proceeded to Georgia and signed a written agreement purporting and intended to carry into effect the previous parol understanding, this would be such a compounding in Georgia as would render the offender indictable in the State of Georgia. Hays, 15 Ga. 

App. 386 (83 S. E. 502). 

19. CONCEALMENT OF DEATH OF BASTARD CHILD. 

§ 26-1106. Indictment. (Misdemeanor.) charge and accuse.. .with the offense of on concealing the death of her bastard child, for the said.... the day of .19...., in the county aforesaid, being then and there pregnant with a bastard child to which she gave birth, and having been delivered of said bastard child alive, the said child then and there died, and the said then and there unlawfully and willfully concealed (or attempted to conceal) its death, so that it might not come to light whether it was murdered or not, contrary, etc. (Approved: McLoud, 122 Ga. 393, 394 (50 S. E. 145).)

General. This section contemplates and seeks to prevent the concealment of the death of such infants as, having been illegitimately begotten, arrived at the stage where they are ordinarily called "quick," and would, in the usual course of events, probably be born alive. McLoud, 122 Ga. 393 (1) (50 S. E. 145). §§ 26-1101, 26-1103 and 26-1105 are to be considered with this section. (Id.) 

See also: Foeticide, Homicide, Abortion. 

20. CRUELTY TO ANIMALS. 

§ 26-7902. (Misdemeanor.) 

Indictment. . . . did willfully shoot a dog, the property of...... whereby unjustifiable physical pain and suffering and death was

caused to said dog, contrary, etc. . . . (Approved: Moore, 121 Ga. 

194 (48 S. E. 919).) . . . did unlawfully and willfully turn out, to go at large, a certain....... .(horse) belonging to him, and omitted and neglected to feed and take care of said... .(horse), whereby unjustifiable physical pain and suffering and death were caused, and permitted to be occasioned to the said................ (horse), contrary, etc. (Approved: Griffith, 116 Ga. 835, 836 (43 S. E. 251).)

Definition. Cruelty to animals, as defined by our law, includes any willful act of omission or neglect whereby unjustifiable physical pain and suffering or death is caused or permitted to a domestic animal, and the omission or neglect to furnish an animal food sufficient for its sustenance, by its owner or keeper, which is willful, is a violation of the statute. Griffith, 116 Ga. 835 (1) (43 S. E. 251).

The gist of the offense is cruelty to a domestic animal. The identity or ownership of the animal is not involved. James, 1 Ga. App. 

779 (57 S. E. 959). 

Domestic animals. Dog, May, 120 Ga. 497 (48 S. E. 153); Rudulph, 27 Ga. App. 588 (110 S. E. 503); Horse, Griffith, 116 Ga. 835 (43 S. E. 251); Clary, 8 Ga. App. 92 (4) (68 S. E. 615); Cow, James, 1 Ga. App. 779 (57 S. E. 959); Bull, Stonecypher, 17 Ga. App. 818 (88 S. E. 719).

General. Where cruelty shown, person in possession of the animal is presumed to be guilty of causing the same. This presumption can be rebutted. Tally, 5 Ga. App. 480 (63 S. E. 543). (See Judge 

Russell's poem.)

Driving automobile over a dog on the highway, where there is a reasonable opportunity to avoid it, cruelty. Rudulph, 27 Ga. App. 

588 (110 S. E. 503).

A dog, which makes a practice of killing or injuring sheep is a nuisance. The owner of such sheep may, without liability to prosecution, cause it to be killed, even after it had escaped from the place where it has attacked the sheep. Miller, 5 Ga. App. 463 (1) (63 S. 

E. 571).

A person may violate the statute by cruelty to his own dog. But he also may kill his dog by some swift and comparatively painless method, without liability to prosecution. One who has the owner's consent to kill the dog stands upon the same footing. Miller, 5 Ga. 

App. 463 (2) (63 S. E. 571).

SPECIFIC CRIMES 

393 Common law rule that a man has a right to kill a dog which is in the habit of injuring his chickens has not been changed in Georgia, and is still the law, regardless of the comparative values of the dog and the chickens. Johnston, 32 Ga. App. 348, 350 (123 S. E. 222).

Value. Evidence of value of horse before alleged cruelty, together with extent to which value was impaired, admissible to throw light upon extent of cruelty. McKinne, 81 Ga. 164 (2) (9 S. E. 1091). 

Venue. On trial of an indictment for cruelly beating and maltreating a horse, evidence showing that said horse was driven in different counties, excessively and in such manner that the horse was weak and staggering in the evening, had marks of the whip upon him, and shortly afterwards died, but which failed to show in which county the alleged crime was committed, was insufficient to show venue., Smith, 69 Ga. 768.

Evidence. For discussion of rules of evidence establishing dangerous character of the animal (bull), where defense was that the shooting of the animal was necessary in order to save self and members of defendant's family, see: Stonecypher, 17 Ga. App. 818 (88 

S. E. 719).

KILLING OR MAIMING HORSE, CATTLE OR HOG. § 26-7901. 

Indictment. etc. (Misdemeanor) . . did willfully and maliciously maim (kill) a (horse, cattle, or hog), the property of…............... ........, contrary, Indictment need not set out the evidence nor negative want of malice. Barnes, 17 Ga. App. 266 (86 S. E. 461); Arnold, 70 Ga. 723.

Indictment need not allege the name of the owner of the animal, or the person in whose possession it was, unless such allegation is necessary to identify the animal in question. Stokes, 14 Ga. App. 

522 (81 S. E. 595).

Indictment charging malicious mischief under this section which charged the commission of the offense in a certain year without naming either a day or month was defective, and should be quashed on special demurrer before arraignment. Bailey, 65 Ga. 410 (1).

General. Animals upon which this crime can be committed are those enumerated in the code-section. Patton, 93 Ga. 111, 114 (19) 

S. E. 734).

Shooting of cow is not a violation of this section, but only the kill-

ing and maiming. Bailey, 65 Ga. 410 (2). The word "maim," as used in this section, implies the infliction of some injury, which deprives the animal of or renders useless or partially useless, some useful organ or member-an organ or member useful to its own locomotion or defense, or useful to its owner in the way in which the animal was employed. Spaulding, 25 Ga. App. 194 (3) (102 S. E. 907). 

Such injury must be permanent. (Id.)

Malice. Malice may be inferred where the act is wanton or reckless. Stokes, 14 Ga. App. 522 (81 S. E. 595); Mosely, 28 Ga. 190.

The rule being that in stock law counties the land lines supply the place of the statutory fence, malice is not shown where the only evidence from which it was contended malice could be inferred was that the accused did not have a fence at least four and a half feet high around his crop. Crowder, 10 Ga. App. 355 (73 S. E. 424).

Malice may be implied where the killing or maiming of an animal is done wantonly and recklessly, or under circumstances which bespeak a mind disposed to the commission of mischief, whether the act was influenced by an intent to injure the owner or not. Stokes, 14 Ga. App. 522 (3) (81 S. E. 595).

Fence. In a county where the no fence law is operative, the provisions of the Code which define lawful fences have no application or pertinence in a trial under this section. Stokes, 14 Ga. App. 522 (2) (81 S. E. 595).

But where the alleged malicious killing or maiming was done in a county where the no fence law is not operative, the accused can not avail himself of the defense that the killing or maiming was done to prevent injury to his crop or other property, unless it be made clearly to appear that the crop or the other property was protected by a substantial fence not less than four and a half feet high. (Id.) 

Defense. Protecting one's crop. Wright, 30 Ga. 325.

It is the duty of the Court to explain the whole section to the jury. 

Arnold, 70 Ga. 723, 724 (3).

In view of the provisions of § 62-802 the owner of the enclosure is not permitted to kill or injure any domestic animal for the first breaking, or until after notice is given to the owner of the animal or his agent, if possible. Where the evidence or the accused's statement did not show that the breaking was not the first breaking, or that any notice was given to the owner as required by law, conviction was demanded by the evidence. Barnes, 17 Ga. App. 266 (4) (86 S. E. 461).

21. CRUELTY TO CHILDREN. 

§ 26-8001. 

(Misdemeanor.) 

did cruelly, unreasonably, and maliciously beat a child, contrary, etc. did unlawfully deprive of necessary sustenance one.. a child five and a half years old, the said.......... failing and refusing to provide said child with necessary sustenance, the said............. being the father of said child, contrary, etc. . (Approved: Justice, 116 Ga. 605 (42 S. E. 1013).) General. This section was intended only to protect children who because of immaturity are unable to protect themselves, and not to a youth of eighteen years of age. Collins, 97 Ga. 433, 434 (25 S. E. 325). 

A girl fourteen years of age is presumptively a "child" within the meaning of this section. Stone, 1 Ga. App. 292 (57 S. E. 992).

Whether a girl fourteen years of age is a child is a matter for the jury. Stone, 1 Ga. App. 292, 294 (57 S. E. 992).

Evidence that father, on account of religious belief, refuses to supply medicine to sick child, does not authorize conviction under this section. Justice, 116 Ga. 605 (42 S. E. 1913).

The element of unreasonableness should not be omitted from the charge under this section. Gary, 118 Ga. 17 (44 S. E. 817). 

22. DISTURBING THE DIVINE WORSHIP, ETC. 

Indictment. 

§§ 26-6901, 26-6902. 

(Misdemeanor.) charge and accuse.. .with the offense of ....on the............ disturbing the divine worship, for the said..

day of……………………………………., 19..., in the county aforesaid, by cursing and using profane and obscene language, and by being intoxicated, and by fighting, and by loud talking, and by then and there otherwise indecently acting, did interrupt and disturb a congregation of persons then and there lawfully assembled for divine service a…………… church, a Primitive Baptist Church, contrary, etc. . . . (Approved: 

Minter, 104 Ga. 743, 744 (30 S. E. 989).)

Precise language constituting disturbance need not be alleged in indictment. Minter, 104 Ga. 743 (1) (30 S. E. 989).

Joint indictment against two must apply to the same transaction. 

Where there were two disturbances, one at twelve o'clock, and the other at one o'clock, and there was no concert or connection between the two, indictment not supported by evidence. Jackson, 87 

Ga. 432 (13 S. E. 689).

Charge that "the defendant did then and there in a tumultuous and boisterous manner, and by indecently acting, disturb a congregation of persons lawfully assembled for divine service at the... church" and "that they attempted to prevent the administration of the holy sacrament of the Lord's supper, at the.....church in " is in the absence of a special demurrer for want of averments sufficient to charge the offense. Any attempt to do such disturbance is indecent. Hicks, 60 Ga. 464; Folds, 123 Ga. 167, 170 (51 

S. E. 305).

Although indictment is against four, one may be convicted if evidence warrants such verdict. Stewart, 31 Ga. 232.

General. In order to authorize the conviction of one charged in an indictment with having disturbed a congregation of persons lawfully assembled for divine service, by cursing, by using profane and obscene language, and by being intoxicated, it is necessary to show that there was a lawful assembly of persons engaged in divine service as alleged in the indictment, and that, in the manner charged, some person of the congregation was actually disturbed. Hill, 24 

Ga. App. 711 (101 S. E. 915).

It is not necessary for the defendant charged with this offense to go into the church to disturb it, or even to go on the church grounds to disturb the congregation. If either in the church or outside of it he is guilty of any of the conducts defined in this section, which actually does disturb any of the congregation from the very beginning of their assembling until they are finally dispersed, any member of the congregation, whether one, two, ten, five hundred, or a thousand, if he is guilty of such conduct as disturbs people who are assembled to worship, then this offense is made out. Daniel, 4 Ga. App. 844 (62 S. E. 567).

The protection of the law extends to congregation-dinner on the church ground or near thereto, where service was to be continued afterwards, and anyone disturbing the congregation at such times and places violates this act. Minter, 104 Ga. 743 (3) (30 S. E. 989); 

Folds, 123 Ga. 167 (5) (51 S. E. 305).

Where single member of the congregation is disturbed, it is a violation of the law. Nichols, 103 Ga. 61 (1) (29 S. E. 431); Daniel,

SPECIFIC CRIMES 

397 

4 Ga. App. 844 (62 S. E. 567); Taylor, 7 Ga. App. 603 (1) (67 S. E. 648).

This section protects every member of the congregation from disturbance by any indecent acting. Nichols, 103 Ga. 61, 63 (29 S. E. 431).

Protection extends until congregation leaves the church grounds. 

Steele, 24 Ga. App. 276 (100 S. E. 656); Brown, 14 Ga. App. 21 (80 

S. E. 26).

Accused taking possession of doorsteps of church and by curses and threats prevents congregation from assembling for divine worship, violates this section. Tanner, 126 Ga. 77 (54 S. E. 914).

Where indictment charged defendant with disturbing the divine worship in church, and evidence showed that it happened on the church ground, evidence supported the charge. Brown, 14 Ga. App. 

21 (80 S. E. 26).

The expression "religious service" is synonymous with "divine service." McDaniel, 5 Ga. App. 831 (63 S. E. 919).

Proof that a congregation was assembled at a church, at which there was preaching and the taking up of a collection, is sufficient to show that there was "a congregation of persons lawfully assembled for divine worship." McDaniel, 5 Ga. App. 831 (2) (63 S. E. 919). 

Where proof showed that defendants made indecent and vulgar noises during service, and indictment charged that they talked loudly, used profane and vulgar language, smoked pipes, struck matches, and otherwise indecently acted, conviction warranted. 

Taffe, 90 Ga. 459 (16 S. E. 204).

Indecently acting must be taken in its comprehensive sense and embraces all improper conduct which interrupts and disturbs a congregation of persons lawfully assembled for divine worship. Folds, 123 Ga. 167 (4) (51 S. E. 305).

Where majority of church disturbed the minority, and there was doubt whether the meeting was for the purpose of divine service, upon which the evidence conflicted, conviction upheld. McCluskey, 37 Ga. App. 324 (140 S. E. 391).

Although defendant, at a former trial, was acquitted of another charge of being intoxicated at church, evidence of such intoxication is admissible on trial for disturbing the divine worship. Rowland, 34 Ga. App. 689 (131 S. E. 96).

Minister not guilty under this section because he preached on occasion when he bona fide claimed right to do so, thereby preventing

another from occupying same pulpit. Woodall, 4 Ga. App. 783 (2) (62 S. E. 485); Jackson, 21 Ga. App. 779, 782 (95 S. E. 302).

Where one shoots in self-defense, though it happens to be near a church and actually disturbs divine worship, he is not guilty under this section. Cummings, 8 Ga. App. 534 (69 S. E. 918). But cursing and fighting upon trivial provocation is a violation of this section. 

Brown, 14 Ga. App. 21 (4) (80 S. E. 26).

Talking and whispering, so as to disturb others is "indecently acting." Nichols, 103 Ga. 61 (2) (29 S. E. 431).

Talk outside of church, not shown to be loud enough to disturb congregation is not "indecently acting." Taylor, 1 Ga. App. 539 (57 S. E. 1049); Taylor, 7 Ga. App. 603 (67 S. E. 684). Indictment. 

23. DISTURBING SCHOOL. 

§ 26-6913. (Misdemeanor.) did unlawfully and with force and arms willfully interrupt and disturb a congregation of persons assembled at a public school at schoolhouse in said county, then and there lawfully and peaceably held for scientific, literary and social improvement, by then and there being intoxicated, and by cursing, and by loud and boisterous discourse, contrary, etc. . . . (Approved : 

Gazaway, 9 Ga. App. 194, 195 (70 S. E. 978).) 

See also: Huffman, 95 Ga. 469 (20 S. E. 216).

Indictment should state the exact nature of the disturbance, and also the exact nature of the school-assemblage which the accused is charged with interrupting. Failure to demur, however, is waiver of this right, and can not be taken advantage of by motion to arrest judgment. Gazaway, 9 Ga. App. 194 (70 S. E. 978). 

For approved indictments see: Manning, 16 Ga. App. 654 (85 S. 

E. 930); Henderson, 24 Ga. App. 702 (101 S. E. 916).

General. Disturbing school play is violation of this section, although at the time there was no formal or ordinary school session. 

Henderson, 24 Ga. App. 702 (101 S. E. 916).

Courts will take judicial cognizance that a meeting of a public school for the purpose of holding commencement exercises is a meeting of the school for the purpose of literary and social improvement. 

Manning, 16 Ga. App. 654 (2) (85 S. E. 930).

Where there is no evidence that anyone present was disturbed, conviction not authorized. (Id.) 

A person, who, by loud talking and laughing, disturbs a "sleight-

SPECIFIC CRIMES 

399 of-hand" performance conducted by a traveling performer at a schoolhouse, under an arrangement with the trustees whereby the performer is to pay the trustees 10 per cent. of the door receipts for the use of the schoolhouse, is not guilty under this section. Harwell, 10 Ga. App. 115 (72 S. E. 936). 

Disturbing divine worship, and disturbing a Sunday school, are two distinct and separate offenses. Clay, 4 Ga. App. 142 (3) (62 S. 

E. 1028).

Statute protects visitors lawfully present at school celebration. 

Gazaway, 9 Ga. App. 194, 197 (70 S. E. 978). 

24. EMBEZZLEMENT. 

§§ 26-2801 to 26-2804, 13-9920. 

Punishment. Embezzlement by public officers, agents, etc. § 26-2801. Not less than two nor more than seven years in the penitentiary. 

Embezzlement by bank or other corporate officers, servants, or stockholders. § 26-2803. Not less than two nor more than seven years in the penitentiary. 

Embezzlement of county money. § 26-2804. Not less than two nor more than twenty years in the penitentiary, and removal from office. 

Embezzlement by officers of a bank. § 13-9920. Not less than one nor more than ten years in a penitentiary. (All of these felonies are reducible.) Indictment.
