See also: Denmark, 44 Ga. App. 157 (161 S. E. 286).

Where indictment alleged that the funds embezzled belonged to two named eleemosynary or beneficial corporations, allegation as to corporate character was material, and, there being no proof of incorporation, a verdict would not be sustained. Roberson, 12 Ga. 

App. 102 (1) (76 S. E. 752).

Where indictment alleged that the defendant did steal certain money, it was not demurrable on the ground that it failed to allege that the money was taken with the intent to steal the same. Cason, 16 Ga. App. 820 (1) (86 S. E. 644).

A bill of particulars is not necessarily a part of the indictment nor need money received and embezzled be specified particularly in the indictment. Camp, 31 Ga. App. 737 (2-f) (122 S. E. 249).

Neither the nature nor the place of the employment nor from whom the accused received the money alleged to have been embezzled need be stated in the indictment. Hays, 114 Ga. 25 (40 S. E. 13). 

Where the accused makes a false report to his employer, it is not necessary to state the nature and character of such report. Hays, 114 Ga. 25 (40 S. E. 13); Jackson, 76 Ga. 551.

Where the amount embezzled is a trust fund, a statement of the amount and of the facts constituting the trust is sufficient. Camp, 31 Ga. App. 737 (2-e) (122 S. E. 249); Trueheart, 13 Ga. App. 661 (79 S. E. 755).

Where indictment charges embezzlement by a public officer, it should charge defendant to be an officer or person employed in a public department, station or office of the government of this State. 

Hoyt, 50 Ga. 314 (5).

Indictment against county school commissioner, alleging. that the money belonged to the County of Floyd, not supported by evidence that it belonged to the City of Rome. Bridges, 103 Ga. 21 (4) (29 S. 

E. 859). General.

Real estate. The law of embezzlement does not apply to real estate. Manning, 175 Ga. 875 (166 S. E. 658).

Embezzlement by public officers.

Definition. The definition of the word "embezzle," according to 

Webster's International Dictionary, is as follows: "To appropriate fraudulently to one's own use, as property entrusted to one's care; to apply to one's private use by a breach of trust; as, to embezzle money held in trust.' United States Fidelity and Guaranty Co., 134 Ga. 56, 59 (67 S. E. 649). 

Under the definition of the offense of embezzlement given in our Code, it seems that it is necessary that the appropriation shall be made of property belonging to another, or, in case of a public officer, to the public, which rightfully came into the possession of the person charged with its appropriation, and that such person can not be convicted unless it be shown that the money has been fraudulently appropriated by the officer to his own use. The words of the statute constituting the offense afford no reason why, like other crimes, a guilty intent is not necessary to be shown. Some conflict seems to exist in the adjudicated cases on the question, whether a mere neglect to pay over money which has come into the hands of an officer is sufficient evidence to make out the fact of a guilty misappropriation. Some of the textbooks lay down the proposition that a neglect or refusal to pay over the funds is sufficient evidence of misappropriation to sustain a conviction, and a number of cases are cited to sustain the text. An examination of some of these cases will convince that the rule thus laid down is not only unsound, but not supported as a general proposition by the authorities. . . . Failure to pay over money or the refusal to do so, is not sufficient to convict of embezzlement. Robinson, 109 Ga. 564 (35 S. E. 57).

Larceny distinguished. Embezzlement is distinguished from larceny in that for larceny the property must be taken from the actual or constructive possession of the owner, while for embezzlement the offense may be committed though the owner has never come into possession of his property. It was an instance of this sort where a person escaped punishment because his act was not larceny, that led to the enactment of this statute in England defining such offense as a distinct crime. Robinson, 109 Ga. 564, 565 (35 S. E. 57).

An ordinary who is guilty of embezzlement may be convicted as accessory before the fact of larceny of county property in his charge, if the evidence warrants it. Groves, 76 Ga. 808.

Venue. Unless affirmatively shown to the contrary, the county in which the accused is an officer will be taken as the place of venue. 

Robson, 83 Ga. 166, 167 (8) (9 S. E. 610).

SPECIFIC CRIMES 

403 Instances of embezzlement. Destruction of public document by ordinary. Groves, 76 Ga. 806, 812.

Personal custody of tax collector of money collected officially. 

Robson, 83 Ga. 166 (9 S. E. 610).

Personal disposition of the money received officially by a clerk of the county board of road commissioners. Cooper, 101 Ga. 783 (29 S. E. 22).

One can not be convicted of embezzlement when it appears that all moneys collected by him in his fiduciary capacity have been fully paid to the person, firm, or corporation, or department of government, to which the funds should have been paid. The case is not altered if the payments are made on the wrong account. Gibson, 13 

Ga. App. 459 (1) (79 S. E. 354).

Deposits of public funds of the County of Fayette, in the Bank of Fayetteville as the "depositary and distributing agent" of said funds under the Act of 1915 (Acts 1915, p. 233), creating a depositary and distributing agent of the public funds of the county, were general deposits, title to which became vested in the bank upon being deposited; and neither the depository nor its officers can be indicted for embezzlement of such funds as the property of the county. 

Blalock, 166 Ga. 465 (143 S. E. 426).

Tax collector using the money he has collected in any way, whatever, for his own profit is guilty of embezzlement. Fuller, 73 Ga. 408. 

Reimbursement. Although officer reimbursed his sureties, he is not freed from criminal liability. Robson, 83 Ga. 166, 167 (7) (9 S. 

E. 610).

Evidence. Receipts signed by the accused after date alleged in the indictment-admissible, but it is subject to parol explanation. 

Bridges, 103 Ga. 21, 22 (5) (29 S. E. 859).

The proof required to convict under the law of embezzlement is the establishment of all elements necessary to constitute the offense, particularly the fraudulent appropriation of public funds which went into the hands of the accused as an officer. The appropriation may be proved by inference from all the circumstances. Robinson, 109 Ga. 564 (35 S. E. 57).

Where a school commissioner is on trial for embezzlement conclusions reached by the Board of Education as to his guilt are not admissible for or against him. Bridges, 110 Ga. 246 (1) (34 S. E. 1037).

Transcripts from the books of the treasurer and comptroller general are admissible on the trial of the collector. Shivers, 53 Ga. 149, 152. 

Evidence that the accused was pressed for money and resorted to illegal practices admissible to explain his conduct and to show motive. Bridges, 103 Ga. 21 (3) (29 S. E. 859). 

Embezzlement by bank and other corporate officers. 

Note: § 26-2803, insofar as it relates to bank officers is super seded by the Banking Act of 1919. Ga. L. 1919, p. 216, Art. XX, 

Camp, 31 Ga. App. 737 (122 § 20, as incorporated in § 13-9920. 

S. E. 248). 

§ 13-9920 (Acts 1919, p. 216, Art. XX, § 20) is broader than 

§ 26-2803, and includes willful misappropriation as well as embezzlement. Hendricks, 32 Ga. App. 546, 547 (123 S. E. 925). It is not retroactive. 

The above stated act, being penal, must be strictly construed. 

Johnson, 166 Ga. 755 (144 S. E. 283).

Definition. In order to constitute embezzlement there must be both, a wrongful conversion and a fraudulent intent. Mangham, 11 Ga. App. 427 (75 S. E. 512). 

The word "steal" implies taking and carrying away and criminal conversion. Cason, 16 Ga. App. 820 (2) (86 S. E. 461). 

Constitutionality upheld. Cason, 16 Ga. App. 820 (3), 824 (86 

S. E. 644); Carter, 143 Ga. 632 (1) (85 S. E. 884).

Corporations. State law of embezzlement applies to protect corporations chartered by this State and doing business here from fraud of its own officers. Cory, 55 Ga. 236, 237, 238; Cook, 8 Ga. 

App. 522, 527 (70 S. E. 31).

State law of embezzlement does not apply to corporations which do not operate under franchises granted by this State. It is only for domestic corporations which by virtue of this section stand on a footing with the departments of the government. In this respect the statute must be strictly construed. Cory, 55 Ga. 236. Statute does not apply to a corporation incorporated by an Act of Congress of the United States. (Id.)

An officer or agent of a corporation can not take money of the corporation entrusted to him, or in his possession by virtue of his official relation or agency, and use it, even temporarily, for his private benefit, and avoid criminal responsibility by calling it a loan. Denmark, 44 Ga. App. 157 (2-d) (161 S. E. 286).

SPECIFIC CRIMES 

405 On a trial for embezzlement it is not necessary in order to convict, to prove that the defendant was actually rendering service as an officer of the corporation at the time of the alleged wrongful conversion. Proof that he was an officer is sufficient. Denmark, 44 Ga. 

Officers. The stealing of money from a bank by a former officer after the severance of his connection with the bank can not constitute embezzlement under this section, although it is an indictable offense. Camp, 31 Ga. App. 737 (4-a) (122 S. E. 248).

Only corporate officers can be principals in the first degree, but others disconnected therewith may be principals in the sceond degree or accessories. Bishop, 118 Ga. 799 (45 S. E. 614). 

Venue. Where treasurer of a corporation discounted notes and deposited the proceeds in banks out of the county and failed to account for them, venue was in the county of the principal offices and place of business of the corporation. Mangham, 11 Ga. App. 427 (2) (75 S. E. 512).

Where the president of a bank, by reason of his official position with it, embezzles its funds by drawing them by checks issued in another county, venue of the crime is properly laid in the county in which the bank is situated. Weathers, 24 Ga. App. 363 (1) (100 

S. E. 768).

Presumptions. False entries unexplained are sufficient to raise presumption of guilt against the officer making them. Holder, 28 

Ga. App. 21 (110 S. E. 762).

Where, in an indictment for embezzlement, the name of the organization of which the accused was financial secretary imports a corporation, the presumption is that it is a corporation, and, in the absence of affirmative proof by the accused that no such corporation existed, and where there is no allegation in the indictment that it was a corporation, it is not necessary for the State to prove the fact of incorporation. Vaughn, 17 Ga. App. 268 (1) (86 S. E. 461).

Substitution. Where a corporate officer substitutes certain stocks of less value for other stocks of more value, deposited as collateral security, with intent to defraud, he is guilty of embezzlement. Wilkins, 36 Ga. App. 743 (138 S. E. 253).

Restoration. An intent to restore the money used privately which is never consummated avails nothing. Nor does the denomination by the accused of the money as a loan. Such transactions are called

by law a wrongful conversion from which the fraudulent intent is inferred. Mangham, 11 Ga. App. 427 (75 S. E. 512).

Funds. The word "funds' includes all the available assets of the bank. Johnson, 37 Ga. App. 129 (139 S. E. 118). This ruling was reversed by the Supreme Court, holding that where an indictment charged that the defendant embezzled the "moneys and funds" of a bank, these words do not include notes and securities, or credits. 

Johnson, 166 Ga. 755 (144 S. E. 283).

Evidence. On the trial of a cashier for embezzlement it is not error to prove embezzling of certain money alleged to have been squandered upon women. Green, 26 Ga. App. 109, 110 (105 S. E. 634).

Evidence that the husband of the woman on whom the defendant squandered money, and husband's parents were people of limited financial standing-admissible. Green, 26 Ga. App. 109 (12) (105 

S. E. 634).

Evidence that the receiver of the defendant's effects took possession of certain personal property found in possession of a woman jointly indicted with the defendant-admissible to show conspiracy. 

Green, 26 Ga. App. 109 (6) (105 S. E. 634).

Where State contended that the defendant embezzled money to squander it on a woman, conversation between the defendant and a dry goods dealer with reference to the payment of a bill for articles purchased by the woman in question-admissible. Green, 26 Ga. 

App. 109 (7) (105 S. E. 634).

Where State contended that the defendant embezzled money to squander it on a woman, love letters from the defendant to the woman found in her furniture are-admissible. Green, 26 Ga. App. 

109 (11) (105 S. E. 634).

Evidence of false entries to conceal conversion-admissible. Jackson, 76 Ga. 551 (8).

Evidence of defendant's strained circumstances, showing necessity for large sum of money,-admissible. Bulloch, 10 Ga. 46. 

This case distinguished in Haupt, 108 Ga. 53, 62 (33 S. E. 829), where it was held that such evidence is admissible only where it connects the defendant directly with the crime. 

Conversation between the accused and the bank examiner with reference to the shortage, in which conversation the accused made damaging admissions-admissible. Green, 26 Ga. App. 109 (10) (105 S. E. 634).

Acts of embezzlement during a period of time some of which

SPECIFIC CRIMES 

407 are barred by the statute of limitations, may be alleged and proved, even those barred, for the purpose of showing fraudulent intent. 

Mangham, 11 Ga. App. 427 (3) (75 S. E. 512).

It is not incumbent upon the State to show full amount charged in indictment. Either full amount, or any part would be sufficient. 

Hetrick, 27 Ga. App. 671 (4) (109 S. E. 528).

Where there are several acts alleged in the indictment in one count as making up the offense, State need not prove all, or elect upon which it will rely. Jackson, 76 Ga. 551, 552 (7) (10).

Where the indictment charged that the defendant was in the employ of the State council of a fraternal order, and embezzled funds belonging to the State council, it is immaterial that the proof showed that he was financial secretary of the local council, his duty as such agent being to turn over the funds to the proper officer of the State council. Cook, 8 Ga. App. 522 (70 S. E. 31).

It is not essential for the State to prove specifically that the accused appropriated any of the money by purchasing with it any particular article. Trueheart, 13 Ga. App. 661, 662 (6) (79 S. E. 755). 

Admission in evidence of a copy of written demand, served on the defendant, for the return of the money which he was charged with embezzling no error. Vaughn, 17 Ga. App. 268, 269 (86 S. 

E. 461).

Evidence of a receipt of the defendant for money collected for the corporation named in the indictment, admissible, though the indictment did not relate to that money. Hamilton, 18 Ga. App. 

295 (6) (89 S. E. 449). In the absence of written request the

Court need not charge the jury that such receipt is admitted only to show motive. (Id.)

Charge of Court. Where the Court charged that, to convict, the jury must be satisfied beyond a reasonable doubt, that the defendant did embezzle, steal, and take away the money described in the indictment, failure to charge that money must have been taken with intent to steal-no error. Cason, 16 Ga. App. 820 (2) (86 

S. E. 644).

Court need not charge, in the absence of appropriate, timely, written request, that mere neglect by the defendant to pay over money of the corporation to the corporation would not be sufficient to convict. Hamilton, 18 Ga. App. 295 (4) (89 S. E. 449).

In the absence of timely, appropriate, written request the Court need not charge the jury that, in order to convict the accused, it was necessary to show not only the receiving of the money, but

also attempt to conceal, flight, falsification of accounts, or evasion; where this proposition was otherwise sufficiently covered by the general charge. Hamilton, 18 Ga. App. 295 (5) (89 S. E. 449).

It is no error to charge the jury that if the defendant falsified his account, this would be a circumstance to be considered by the jury in passing upon the question of criminal intent. Trueheart, 13 Ga. 

App. 661, 662 (5) (79 S. E. 755).

Ingredients of crime: (1) Contract, parol or in writing. (2) En ticing away. (3) Knowledge that servant was employed under contract. (4) Servant has actually left employment. Hudgins, 126

At common law there were three classes of servants recognized: 

First, menial servants; second, apprentices; third, laborers. The general definition of servants in these sections include all three classes. Bryan, 44 Ga. 328, 335. "Employment” not synonymous with "hiring." Hightower, 72 

Ga. 482.

A contract providing for the division of the crop between the grower, laborer, and third party furnishing laborers, is not such a contract as is contemplated in this section. Bryan, 44 Ga. 328, 334.

One who is employed to bring hands and superintend them is not a servant. Bryan, 44 Ga. 328.

Indictment for escape need not allege where the Court which convicted the defendant was located, or that it had jurisdiction of the offense. Daniel, 114 Ga. 533 (2) (40 S. E. 805).

The allegation that the defendant unlawfully escaped is sufficient allegation that the chain-gang was a lawful place of confinement. 

Daniel, 114 Ga. 533 (3) (40 S. E. 805).

Indictment need not set out the names of the individuals constituting the posse, and evidence that defendant obstructed one of the posse while the prisoner was attempting to escape is sufficient, though the name of the man obstructed is not alleged in the indictment. Perry, 63 Ga. 402.

General. United States convict confined in Georgia State jail is not amenable. Statute strictly construed. It refers to prisoners who were convicted in the Georgia State courts only. Brandon, 37 

Ga. App. 495 (141 S. E. 63).

Rescue and escape distinguished. Robinson, 82 Ga. 535, 544 (9 

S. E. 528).

To constitute the crime of assisting to escape from custody, the evidence must show that the prisoner was in the act of escaping, and that the accused knowingly assisted him. Harvey, 8 Ga. App. 

660 (4) (70 S. E. 141); Robinson, 82 Ga. App. 535 (9 S. E. 528).

Impediment while the prisoner is still in sight is violation of this section. Perry, 63 Ga. 402 (3).

The word "escape" as used in this section may be construed to include escape from constructive confinement. Smith, 8 Ga. App. 

297, 298 (68 S. E. 1071).

This section applies to a "trusty" allowed some measure of liberty. Johnson, 122 Ga. 172 (1) (50 S. E. 65).

This section is not applicable to one whose confinement is for safekeeping only, and was not a part of the court sentence. Welch, 4 Ga. App. 388 (61 S. E. 496).

It is not a penal offense to liberate one from unlawful custody, although he may have submitted to such custody without resistance. 

Adams, 121 Ga. 163 (48 S. E. 910).

A chain-gang controlled by private persons is not a legal place of confinement, and one escaping therefrom can not be convicted under this section. Daniel, 114 Ga. 533 (6) (40 S. E. 805).

Escape from place of confinement provided by municipal authorities for violations of municipal ordinances punishable under these sections. Collins, 120 Ga. 849 (48 S. E. 319). See also § 77-619. 

Crime of escape is continuous until convict captured. Smith, 8 

Ga. App. 297, 298 (68 S. E. 1071). 

Escape from personal custody of officer, and escape from place of confinement distinguished. Smith, 8 Ga. App. 297 (63 S. E. 402).

The legal character of the custody must have been known to the defendant in order to be guilty under these sections, but no positive knowledge is required. Good reason for belief will be sufficient. 

Habersham, 56 Ga. 62 (7).

Question of legality of custody is for the jury. Habersham, 56 

Ga. 62 (4).

If original court issuing warrant had legal right to do so, it is no defense that there was no charge pending against defendant. 

Craig, 45 Ga. App. 226 (164 S. E. 101).

Custody by a private person after a legal arrest without warrant, becomes illegal if protracted for an unreasonable time, and

SPECIFIC CRIMES 

413 whether the time was reasonable or unreasonable is a question for the jury. Habersham, 56 Ga. 62 (4),

Custody voluntarily assumed by a private person without warrant, may be lawfully terminated with his consent, by turning the prisoner loose, especially if the latter be not guilty. Habersham, 56 Ga. 62 (6).

Aiding escape from the custody of a de facto officer is a violation of these sections. Robinson, 82 Ga. 535, 547 (9 S. E. 528).

Anyone who knowingly aids a convict or attempts to aid him, either to get away or to stay away, is guilty under this section. 

Smith, 8 Ga. App. 297, 298 (68 S. E. 1071).

One who assists escaped convict to remove shackles by furnishing. ax,-is guilty. Smith, 8 Ga. App. 297 (68 S. E. 1071).

No defense that defendant left chain-gang to escape unmerited punishment. Johnson, 122 Ga. 172 (3) (50 S. E. 65).

No defense that several months after his escape defendant paid his fine to the sheriff. Johnson, 122 Ga. 172 (2) (50 S. E. 65).

Arrest of an escaped misdemeanor convict may be effected by any peace officer without a warrant. Williford, 121 Ga. 173 (1) 

Solicitor-general is entitled to pay from penitentiary fund for the prosecution of an escape or for any crime committed by penitentiary convict while serving there. Campbell, 162 Ga. 221 (133 S. 

E. 468).

The fact that the person accused of a crime voluntarily surrendered to the sheriff and made no attempt to escape can not be proved by him in his own behalf. Register, 10 Ga. App. 623 (74 S. E. 429); 

Lingerfelt, 125 Ga. 4 (53 S. E. 803).

An officer has no right to shoot one whom he is attempting to arrest for the violation of a municipal ordinance, or a misdemeanor, in order to prevent his escape, even though the offender can not be taken otherwise. Holmes, 5 Ga. App. 166 (12) (62 S. E. 716). 

27. EXTORTION. 

$$ 89-9909 to 89-9912.

Punishment. Misdemeanor. Dismissal from office. 

Attorney-general taking fees. § 89-9901. Not less than two nor more than twenty years in the penitentiary, removal from office and disqualification, forever, from holding office. 

Indictment. . . for that the said. in the county aforesaid, on the.................day o...................19...., with force and arms, being

then and there a lawful constable in and for the...... th district, G. M., of................County, Georgia, did, by color of his office as such constable, unlawfully take.... ...Dollars in money from which was not due him, said money of the value of Dollars, and the property of................, contrary, etc. (Approved: Dean, 9 Ga. App. 303, 305 (71 S. E. 597).)

The indictment need not set out the evidence, but only such words are necessary as set out the offense in the language of the Code, and so plainly that the nature of the offense can be easily understood by the jury. Dean, 9 Ga. App. 303 (71 S. E. 597); Saunders, 43 Ga. App. 59, 61 (158 S. E. 433).

General. The offense of extortion consists of the oppressive misuse of official power by the exaction of money. Where deputy sheriff was instructed to arrest certain parties, but consented to accept a cash bond, which he reported to his superior officers at once, but declined to deliver the cash bond to them,—although he had no right to take such bonds, there was no such criminal intent as would be included in this section. Holt, 11 Ga. App. 34, 36 (74 S. E. 560); White, 56 Ga. 385.

Under the Code only public officers can be convicted of the offense of extortion. Either de jure or de facto officers. White, 56 Ga. 385.

In order to throw light upon the question of guilty intention, the officer's experience or lack of experience may be shown. Parol evidence is admissible. White, 56 Ga. 385.

The specification of conduct constituting the crime of extortion is sufficient allegation of official misbehavior. Lancaster, 136 Ga. 

405 (71 S. E. 731).

Where defendant extorted about $200.00 in installments, some received more than two years before indictment found, but some less than two years before that date, conviction warranted. Hurst, 44 Ga. App. 289 (3) (161 S. E. 278).

It is not lawful to collect any cost in a peace-warrant case until after the same shall have been returned to and passed upon by the Superior Court. Where a constable, by color of his office, took from another costs alleged to be due to a magistrate and to himself upon a peace warrant, before the bond required thereon had been returned to the Superior Court, such constable is guilty of the offense of extortion. Levar, 103 Ga. 42 (1) (2) (29 S. E. 467).

Ignorance of the law is no defense in charge of extortion. Levar, 103 Ga. 42 (3) (29 S. E. 467).

SPECIFIC CRIMES 

415 If money is voluntarily paid to accused to settle prosecution, and bona fide so received by him, and such money is not a bribe, defendant is not guilty of extortion. White, 56 Ga. 385.

Where indictment charged defendant, a notary public who was ex officio justice of the peace, with drawing and issuing a warrant not for the purpose of prosecution but for pecuniary gain to himself, thus extorting money from the accused, there being a local act authorizing such officer to charge for his services in a proper case, such indictment is subject to demurrer where there was no allegation that the affidavit upon which such warrant was founded was improper or that the issuing of the warrant was otherwise irregular. Hohenstein, 126 Ga. 536 (55 S. E. 238).

It is official misbehavior, amounting to extortion, for a constable to knowingly make an illegal levy with the purpose of oppressing one against whom he is illegally executing the process. Lancaster, 136 Ga. 405 (6) (71 S. E. 731). 

28. FALSE IMPRISONMENT. 

§§ 26-1501 to 26-1504.

Indictment. charge and accuse. false imprisonment, for that the said. of................19...., in the county of .with the offense of on the........day in and upon one. in the peace of God and said State, then and there being, did make an assault on him, the said......... ..., then and there did beat, wound, and ill treat and then and there did violate the personal liberty of him, the said. will of said....... unlawfully and injuriously and against the and against the laws of said State, and without sufficient legal authority, confining and detaining in confinement him, the said for a long space of time, to wit, for the space (Cobb.) ..with the offense ...................hours, then next following, contrary, etc. .

(Camp- General. If a person be arrested as a fugitive from justice from another State by a private person without a warrant, he must be carried, without delay, before the most convenient officer qualified to receive an affidavit and issue a warrant and if he be detained beyond a reasonable time without being carried before such officer, the person arresting and detaining him commits the offense of false imprisonment, especially if the person arrested and detained be not the alleged fugitive, but an innocent man, and his detention. be accompanied with maltreatment, such as force and chains. 

Lavina, 63 Ga. 513 (2). Defendant in this case held the prisoner over night.

Although an arrest without a warrant be justifiable, yet to detain a prisoner longer than a reasonable time for suing out a warrant is false imprisonment. Potter, 77 Ga. 419, 422, 423 (3 S. E. 94).

An officer transporting a prisoner from another State to this State, on the governor's order, is not guilty of false imprisonment, if he proceeds without undue delay. Pettus, 42 Ga. 358.

The law does not presume malice against a judicial officer because he renders an illegal judgment, or because, in the discharge of his official functions, he does an illegal act. Campbell, 48 Ga. 353, 354 (5).

A justice of the peace indicted for false imprisonment under color of legal process, is not entitled to the right of appearance and being heard before the grand jury at the time the true bill is found. Campbell, 48 Ga. 353, 354 (4).

Venue is in the county where the illegal imprisonment took place and also in the county where the prisoner was illegally detained. 

Lavina, 63 Ga. 513 (1).

Arrest by policeman without warrant, on request of a sheriff of another county, when no offense has been committed in the policeman's presence, is an illegal arrest, and subsequent imprisonment constitutes offense under this section. Gordon et al., 114 Ga. 354 (40 S. E. 229). 

False imprisonment consists in the unlawful detention of the per-

SPECIFIC CRIMES 

417 son of another, for any length of time, whereby he is deprived of his personal liberty. Waters, 142 Ga. 133 (82 S. E. 535).

Arrest of owner of property for cutting down telephone poles wrongfully placed on his property, without warrant, constitutes false imprisonment. Holliday et al., 12 Ga. App. 779, 780 (78 S. E. 482).

A police officer of a municipality has no authority as such to serve a warrant in a county outside of the municipality. If he does so, and arrests another he is guilty of the offense of false imprisonment. Coker, 14 Ga. App. 606 (1) (2) (81 S. E. 818).

Where a policeman arrests a person, without a warrant, for an alleged violation of the law providing punishment for the disturbing and interrupting a military parade, it is incumbent upon the officer, in order to justify his act in making the arrest, to show affirmatively that the parade was in compliance with the law. Otherwise the officer is guilty of false imprisonment. White, 99 Ga. 16 (26 

S. E. 742).

If authority for the arrest is shown, the presumption is that it was made legally and for a lawful purpose, and the burden of proof is upon the person asserting the contrary. Piedmont Hotel Company, 9 Ga. App. 672 (3) (72 S. E. 51).

Where illegal detention is shown it makes no difference what person is restrained illegally of their personal liberty. It would be equally false imprisonment whether the party be a good woman or a bad woman, a rich woman or a poor woman, an old woman or a young woman. Every person, regardless of character, sex, wealth, condition, or anything else, is entitled to their personal liberty; and if illegally restrained of that liberty, then there is a violation of the law of Georgia. Seals, 33 Ga. App. 818 (2) (128 S. E. 224).

It must also appear, in order to justify a detention, that it was done by legal authority. It is on the accused to show his warrant and authority. An officer has no more right than any other man if he has no warrant for the arrest of a person unless the crime be committed in his presence. Seals, 33 Ga. App. 818 (8) (128 S. E. 224).

a. FORGING OFFICIAL CERTIFICATES, ETC. 

Indictment. . . . charge and accuse. ..with the offense of in the County of………………………………….. forgery, for the said. on the ………..day of…………………………......19...., did wrongfully, falsely, and fraudulently make, sign, and forge the name of...on and to a certain deed, the same being in form and substance as follows, to wit: ; and said acts were done with intent to defraud.. who is the present owner of said land, (under the will of............ ..) the grantee from.. and the acts herein complained of were and are contrary, etc. . . . (Approved: Davis, 25 Ga. App. 532, 536 (103 S. E. 819).)

Indictment charging forgery of will should be drawn under § 

26-3901 and not under § 26-3914. Beall, 21 Ga. App. 73 (1) (94 

S. E. 74). 

Indictment charging forgery of will must allege that forgery was done with intent to defraud State or some person. Indictment without such averment is fatally defective, and verdict of guilty is nullity. Beall, 21 Ga. App. 73 (1-a) (94 S. E. 74).

Indictment based on this section and charging the forging of an order for a thing not money is fatally defective and will not support a conviction if it fails to allege that the thing in question was of some value. Johnson, 109 Ga. 268 (34 S. E. 573); Battle, 122 Ga. 575 (50 S. E. 342); Smith, 35 Ga. App. 366 (133 S. E. 284); 

McCombs, 109 Ga. 500 (34 S. E. 1023). 

Indictment for forgery of deed need not aver ownership of land. 

Davis, 25 Ga. App. 532 (1-e) (103 S. E. 819).

Where forgery indictment contains two counts, first being complete within itself, including copy of instrument alleged to have been forged and uttered, which is set out in full, and in second count express reference to instrument is made, thereby purporting to incorporate it into second count, and thus charging all substantial elements of the offense in second count, failure to set out alleged forged instrument in second count will not render that count subject to demurrer. Pope, 42 Ga. App. 680 (2) (157 S. E. 211); Pope, 41 Ga. App. 653 (154 S. E. 194); Durden, 152 Ga. 441 (110 S. E. 283).

Where indictment does not allege intent to defraud remedy after verdict is motion in arrest of judgment. Gibson, 79 Ga. 344 (2) (5 S. E. 76).

Indictment may charge allegations as to forging and uttering forged instrument in same count. Thomas, 59 Ga. 784 (3); Blount, 11 Ga. App. 239 (1-a) (74 S. E. 1099); Nalley, 11 Ga. App. 15 (1) (74 S. E. 567).

Indictment need not allege extrinsic facts to show writing to be efficient means of consummating fraud; such facts are matters of evidence. Travis, 83 Ga. 372 (9 S. E. 1063); Shope, 106 Ga. 226 (1) (32 S. E. 140); McLean, 3 Ga. App. 660 (1) (60 S. E. 332); 

Davis, 25 Ga. App. 532 (1-e) (103 S. E. 819). 

Where the word "fraudulently" is omitted before the word "forge" in the indictment, the defect is cured by the charge that the filling in of the blanks and the signing of the name was fraudulently done. Barron, 12 Ga. App. 342 (1-a) (77 S. E. 214).

It is not necessary to allege in the indictment what was the connection, if any, between the person whose name was alleged to have been forged and the person defrauded; these facts may be shown by evidence. Barron, 12 Ga. App. 342 (1-d) (77 S. E. 214).

It is not necessary to allege and prove that actual loss resulted from the forgery. Barron, 12 Ga. App. 342 (1-e) (77 S. E. 214).

Averment in the indictment that name of grantor was forged is equivalent to averment that deed was forged. Davis, 25 Ga. App. 

Indictment charging one person's name forged with intent to defraud another, sufficient. Davis, 25 Ga. App. 532 (1-c) (103 S. E. 819).

Indictment charging two persons jointly of the offense of forgery need not allege what particular part each played. Davis, 25 Ga.

Indictment averring certain acts, naming them, "were done with intent to defraud" certain party, naming him, sufficient. Davis, 25 Ga. App. 532 (1-e) (103 S. E. 819). 

Averment in indictment that grantor's name was "falsely and fraudulently" signed to deed sufficiently shows that such signing was done without grantor's knowledge or consent. Davis, 26 Ga. 

App. 467 (1-b) (106 S. E. 317).

Indictment need not allege in what manner and by what means intent was consummated. Davis, 25 Ga. App. 532 (1-e) (103 S. E. 819).

SPECIFIC CRIMES 

421 General. Forgery is a felony, although the word felony is not used in the statute defining it, punishment being within legal definition of felony. Gray, 6 Ga. App. 428 (2-a) (65 S. E. 191).

The intent of the accused to defraud is the essence of the offense and must be proved by affirmative proof beyond a reasonable doubt. 

Chambers, 22 Ga. App. 748 (750 S. E. 256); Harrison, 13 Ga. App. 

31 (78 S. E. 686).

Forgery may be committed of any writing which, if genuine, would operate as a foundation of another man's liability or the evidence of his right. It is sufficient if the instrument forged, supposing it to be genuine, might have been prejudicial. If the writing purports to have legal efficacy it may be the subject of forgery. Chambers, 22 Ga. App. 748, 750 (97 S. E. 256).

Any writing in such form as to be the means of defrauding another, may be the subject of forgery, or alteration in the nature of forgery. Berrisford, 66 Ga. 53; Chambers, 22 Ga. App. 748, 751 (97 S. E. 256).

Instrument need not be negotiable in order to be subject of forgery. Wilson, 7 Ga. App. 583 (2) (67 S. E. 705). 

To prove that instrument is a promissory note, it must show that it is for a fixed sum, payable absolutely, unconditionally, and at all events. Corbett, 24 Ga. 287.

Making of immaterial alteration whereby no damage could accrue to any person will not constitute forgery. Jackson, 72 Ga. 28.

An immaterial alteration of a paper whereby no damage would result to anyone will not constitute forgery. Alteration of order to pay for fifty-four pounds of lint cotton at eight and one-half cents per pound by inserting the figure three before the marginal figures so as to make the figures in the margin 354 did not change the value of the order and did not constitute forgery. Jackson, 72 

Ga. 28; McIntosh, 23 Ga. App. 513 (98 S. E. 555). 

Figures in check, following words in body thereof denoting sum called for, are not material part of the instrument, words being controlling in determining legal effect. McIntosh, 23 Ga. App. 513 (98 S. E. 555).

It is held that clause (7) of this section applies, notwithstanding that the forged instrument was composed of two parts, the other part not coming within this section being treated as surplusage. Johnson, 36 Ga. App. 310 (136 S. E. 329).

Misspelling name of ostensible signer will not prevent act from being forgery. Essence of crime, making false writing with in-

tent that it shall be received as act of another than party signing it. Hale, 120 Ga. 183 (1) (47 S. E. 531).

Order without date to pay "this man" certain sum supported conviction. Thomas, 59 Ga. 784 (1).

Signing of name of an illiterate person to note with his consent is not forgery, though accused falsely and fraudulently inserted too large an amount and read over the note as though it contained true amount. Wells, 89 Ga. 788 (15 S. E. 679).

If there are two persons with the same name and one of them signs that name to notes with intention that the notes be used in trade as the notes of the other, he commits forgery. Barfield, 29 

Ga. 127 (1); Barron, 12 Ga. App. 342, 343, 348 (7) (77 S. E. 214).

Teacher's license not embraced by this section, the certificates. mentioned referring to such as relate to money, property or other things of value. Maddox, 87 Ga. 429 (13 S. E. 559). But see § 32-9905. 

Form of salary assignment construed as order for money within. the meaning of § 26-3901. Johnson, 36 Ga. App. 310, 311 (136 S. 

E. 329). 

Where the signature to the paper alleged to be forged is affixed by one who claims to be an agent, and the paper is then signed by this person as agent, paper can not be made the basis of a conviction for forgery, although, in truth and in fact, there was no agency. Barron, 12 Ga. App. 342, 344 (77 S. E. 214). 

Ambiguity in forged instrument is properly left to jury. Hagar, 71 Ga. 164; McGarr, 75 Ga. 155.

Crudeness of forgery being such as to cause its immediate detection-no defense. Wilson, 7 Ga. App. 583 (1) (67 S. E. 705).

Deed is subject of forgery if it contains warranty of title, specifies valuable consideration and the names of vendor and vendee, though there be no formal words of conveyance. Allgood, 87 Ga. 668 (7) (13 S. E. 569).

Order addressed to treasurer of county to pay to certain person stated sum of money for services rendered as bailiff at stated term of Superior Court for specified number of days, and signed by sheriff, was subject of forgery. Chambers, 22 Ga. App. 748, 751, 752 (97 S. E. 256).

Forgery may be committed by forging paper not formally signed, if it is shown that person intended to be considered as writer. 

Curtis, 16 Ga. App. 678 (1) (85 S. E. 980).

SPECIFIC CRIMES 

423 Charge. An intent to defraud is an essential element of the offense of forgery. Failure to so charge is reversible error. Blount, 11 Ga. App. 239 (2) (74 S. E. 1099).

Indictment containing two counts, one charging forgery and the other uttering forged instrument as true, and the undisputed evidence being clear, both as to the actual forgery and the uttering forged instrument as true, charge that if jury found accused guilty on one count they would necessarily find him guilty on both counts. was not erroneous inasmuch as the evidence demanded a verdict of guilty on both counts. Sellers, 12 Ga. App. 687 (2) (78 S. E. 196).

It was not error to charge in the trial of one for forging a railroad pass that it would be forgery for a person to take a piece of paper on which another has witten his name and fraudulently write above it a promissory note, the charge being a correct law, and properly used for the purpose of illustration. Roberts, 92 Ga. 451 (2) (17 S. E. 262). 

Evidence. Evidence being introduced that the alleged forged deed purported to have been made in 1852 was written on form not in use in this country until several decades later, it is not error to allow witness to show similarity or difference between alleged forged deed and genuine deed on similar form made in 1847. Davis, 25 Ga. App. 532 (8) (103 S. E. 819).

Not error to admit letter, body and signature of which was typewritten, which accomplice testified was received from defendant in due course of mail, and with which was enclosed a check for his share of proceeds of forgery, it appearing that the letter disclosed some peculiarities of writing machine as other letters written by defendant and that letter was found in accomplice's room long before his confession. Davis, 25 Ga. App. 532 (11) (103 S. E. 819).

Where intent to defraud was alleged as being directed against two persons, proof of intent to defraud either is sufficient to convict. McGarr, 75 Ga. 155, 159.

Endorsement of forged draft, made payable to defendant, is sufficient to show intent to defraud. Timmons, 80 Ga. 216 (4 S. E. 

766); Jordan, 127 Ga. 278 (5) (56 S. E. 422).

Intent to defraud is conclusively shown by proof that defendant knowingly passed forged instrument as genuine. Jordan, 127 

Ga. 278 (4) (56 S. E. 422).

Goods, similar to those delivered to unidentified person upon forged order, found in possession of accused, not sufficient to prove

that accused wrote the order. McCombs, 109 Ga. 496 (34 S. E. 1021). 

Handwriting may be identified as that of the accused, by the introduction of writing which he acknowledged. Thomas, 59 Ga. 784 (5). 

Evidence as to sale of instrument admissible, after proof of its alteration, to show fraudulent intention. Berrisford, 66 Ga. 53.

Forging of deed established by proof that signatures of maker and witnesses were forged and were in the handwriting of the accused, who presented the instrument for record, and that maker and witnesses have not authorized such acts. Allgood, 87 Ga. 668 

Evidence that forged instrument was uttered together with testimony pointing directly to accused as the author and sole beneficiary of the forgery supported a verdict against him for the forgery, there being no evidence that the forgery was done by another. Womble, 107 Ga. 666 (4) (33 S. E. 630).

Evidence that accused, without money before forgery, had money after the crime, admissible on trial therefor. Walker, 127 Ga. 48 

Where the existence and contents of a writing are material in a forgery case, and the writing is in possession of the accused, secondary evidence is admissible, the writing being inaccessible because accused can not be compelled to produce it. Sellers, 12 Ga. 

App. 687 (1) (78 S. E. 196); Nalley, 11 Ga. App. 15 (5) (74 S. E. 567).

From evidence that those whose names were signed to notes did not sign them or authorize anyone else to do so, and that defendant had promised bank to send it notes of these parties as collaterals, and that the notes were mailed to the bank by some one, the jury could infer that the defendant either by himself or by an agent, mailed the notes. Fryer, 12 Ga. App. 533 (3) (77 S. E. 830).

Evidence that grantee named in alleged forged deed never returned property for taxation during period of purported ownership under deed was admissible. Davis, 25 Ga. App. 532, 535 (12) (103 S. E. 819). 

Variance. To forge the name of the acceptor is not the same as to forge the name of the endorser. Where indictment charged that a certain person was endorser, and evidence showed that he was acceptor,-variance fatal. Morel, 74 Ga. 17.

Indictment charging that instrument was an order for goods,

SPECIFIC CRIMES 

425 and evidence showing that it was recommendation for credit, conviction still upheld. Johnson, 62 Ga. 299 (2).

Indictment for forgery need set out only material parts of the instrument, but when minute descriptive matter is alleged in the indictment, the instrument is not admissible in evidence unless it conforms to the description given. Haupt, 108 Ga. 53 (2) (34 S. E. 313). 

A written instrument set forth according to its tenor in an indictment must be proved as alleged, hence where an indictment for forgery of a note gave a copy of the note, including the date, and it was not charged that the forgery extended to the change of the date of the note, it was error to admit into evidence a note bearing a date different from that alleged in the indictment. Perkins, 29 

Ga. App. 278 (115 S. E. 27). 

b. UTTERING FORGED CERTIFICATES. 

Indictment. Indictment approved. Curtis, 16 Ga. App. 678 (2) 

Indictment not demurrable, though paper alleged to have been forged was addressed to person without indicating his initial or given name. Curtis, 16 Ga. App. 678 (3) (85 S. E. 980).

Where indictment indicates that the goods received on forged instrument were of value, failure to specifically so allege is no ground for demurrer. Battle, 122 Ga. 575 (50 S. E. 342). 

Indictment need not show that property described in forged deed is or ever was in existence. Davis, 26 Ga. App. 467 (1-c) (106 S. 

E. 317). 

Indictment may allege intent to defraud two or more persons, and allegation is sufficiently established by proof of intent to defraud any one or more of them. Davis, 26 Ga. App. 467 (1-d) (106 S. E. 317).

General. Essential elements of crime are knowingly and fraudulently publishing forged paper as true with intent to injure another. Couch, 28 Ga. 367; Stephens, 56 Ga. 604; Sims, 37 Ga. 

App. 819, 820 (142 S. E. 464).

Intent to defraud is essential element of uttering and publishing a forgery and Court should instruct jury that this intent must be shown. Blount, 11 Ga. App. 239 (2) (74 S. E. 1099). 

Filing forged deed for record with clerk is uttering and publishing deed. Davis, 26 Ga. App. 467 (1-c) (106 S. E. 317).

Forged paper must not only be published as true when party

knows it to be forgery, but also with intent to injure some one. 

Raper, 16 Ga. App. 121 (1) (2) (84 S. E. 560).

It is error to charge jury that defendant is guilty if by reasonable inquiry he could have ascertained that check was forgery. 

Putnam, 25 Ga. App. 322 (2) (103 S. E. 191).

Where evidence is circumstantial only, Court should charge law of circumstantial evidence, without request. Davis, 26 Ga. App. 

467 (2) (106 S. E. 317).

Verdict finding defendant guilty of uttering and publishing a forged paper is void unless it also finds that he uttered it as true. 

Stephens, 56 Ga. 604; Ezzard, 11 Ga. App. 30 (1) (74 S. E. 551).

Conviction of defendant on second count of indictment charging uttering and publishing forged will, held not repugnant to or inconsistent with his acquittal on first count charging forgery of will. 

Pope, 42 Ga. App. 680 (157 S. E. 211). 

i. FORGING BANK CHECK OR DRAFT. 

An indictment charging that the accused did "make and forge the following check for money, to wit: 

No. 26. 

Marietta, Ga., July 17, 1894.

The First National Bank pay to the order of Mrs. 

Anna Lyons twenty-five dollars 00-100. $25.00/100. 

E. C. Henderson. meaning C. E. Henderson of the firm of Henderson and Austin,' etc., is not a good indictment for forgery. It does not charge the forgery of the name of any person alleged to be actually in existence, but at most only charges a mere intention to forge the name of a real person bearing the name of C. E. Henderson, and shows on its face that this intention failed of accomplishment. Hicken, 96 Ga. 759 (22 S. E. 297).

Indictment containing two counts, one charging forgery, the other the uttering the forged instrument as true, and the undisputed evidence being clear, both as to the actual forgery and the act of uttering the instrument as true, charge that if jury found the accused guilty on one count they would necessarily find him guilty on the other, was not erroneous inasmch as the evidence demanded the verdict of guilty on both counts. Sellers, 12 Ga. App. 

687 (2) (78 S. E. 196).

While in an indictment for forgery only the material parts of the instrument, as a contract, are required to be set out, yet when, as descriptive of the instrument charged to have been forged, minute particulars, such as the number of the check, are set forth.

SPECIFIC CRIMES 

427 in the bill, those particulars must be proved as laid; and when bill of indictment charges the alteration of a check which is in part described as bearing a specified number, a check of similar import as that described but bearing another number is not admissible as being the original check alleged to have been altered. 

Haupt, 108 Ga. 53 (2) (34 S. E. 313); Martin, 43 Ga. App. 287, 291, 292 (158 S. E. 635).

Where check, drawn on bank, chartered in this State, by person whose named signed thereto is endorsed by other than payee, it has apparent "legal efficacy" and will support indictment for forgery, and felonious uttering of such check. Brazil, 117 Ga. 32 (1) (43 

S. E. 460). 

Check payable to "order of cash" is payable to bearer. If such a check is forged it is not so imperfect that no one could be defrauded by it. Hale, 120 Ga. 138 (47 S. E. 547). 

Payee not named, but check payable to..........., execution so imperfect that no one could have been defrauded and indictment should be quashed on demurrer. Williams, 51 Ga. 535; Brazil, 117 Ga. 32, 34 (43 S. E. 460).

Where checks charged to have been forged were in court, they should have been introduced; if not, verdict of guilty unauthorized. Richard, 127 Ga. 42 (55 S. E. 1044). 

k. KNOWINGLY UTTERING AND PASSING ALTERED BANK NOTES. 

Indictment approved. Brazil, 117 Ga. 32 (43 S. E. 460).

Indictment need not charge that there was intent to defraud any particular person. Dukes, 94 Ga. 393 (21 S. E. 54); Brazil, 117 

Ga. 32 (1) (43 S. E. 460); Howell, 25 Ga. App. 547, 548 (103 S. E. 799).

It was competent for the State to prove that at or about the time at which, it was alleged, the crime in question was committed, the accused committed with another a similar crime. Bates, 18 

Ga. App. 718 (1) (90 S. E. 481). 

In order to render testimony admissible as to handwriting, it is not necessary for the witness to state that he is an expert on handwriting. Any witness is competent to testify as to his belief, who will swear that he knows or recognizes the handwriting; the weight, force, and credit to be given to such evidence is a matter entirely for the jury. Bates, 18 Ga. App. 718 (2) (90 S. E. 481).

A witness claiming to be an expert on handwriting, who stated, with reference to the handwriting on several papers, that "the

same party wrote all of them," did not state a conclusion, but simply gave an opinion on a question of fact, based upon expert knowledge. Bates, 18 Ga. App. 718 (3) (90 S. E. 481).

Though the defendant be indicted in different counts for the three grades of forgery set forth in §§ 26-3901, 26-3910 and 26-3911, namely, the making, uttering, and the possessing of the forged instrument, yet the failure of the judge to give in charge to the jury, so far as applicable, § 26-3901, defining the offense of forgery proper, affords no ground of complaint to the defendant, when the judge does give in charge §§ 26-3910 and 26-3911, defining the other two grades of the offense, and confines the consideration of the defendant's guilt by the jury to those latter two sections, there being no evidence to authorize a conviction under the count of forgery. 

Jordan, 127 Ga. 278 (6) (56 S. E. 422).

Charge of Court as to what would constitute offense of uttering forged check, which was complained of as not instructing jury that intent to defraud must be proved, held not cause for new trial. 

Fincher, 42 Ga. App. 250 (155 S. E. 344). 

1. POSSESSING FORGED BANK NOTES, INTENDING TO PASS THEM. 

This section has reference to a check only upon a bank of this State or an incorporated bank whose notes or bills are in circulation in this State. The section is in pari materia with § 26-3907. Therefore an indictment under this section must allege that the check was on a bank of this State or on an incorporated bank whose notes and bills are in circulation in this State. Grover, 27 Ga. App. 105 (1) (107 S. E. 547). Where indictment fails to so allege, defect is fatal. (Id.) 

Where indictment was founded on §§ 26-3901, 26-3910 and 26-3911, and there was no evidence to authorize a conviction under count for forgery as that offense is described in § 26-3901, the Court properly restricted charge to the grades of the offense defined in 

§§ 26-3910 and 26-3911. Jordan, 127 Ga. 278 (6) (56 S. E. 422). 

Charge that jury could convict although description of check in second count of indictment did not refer to indorsement and check in evidence was indorsed, if check in evidence corresponded in all other particulars with check described in the indictment-not error. 

Jackson, 26 Ga. App. 424 (106 S. E. 924).

The law is well and definitely settled that the word "utter" and "uttering" mean substantially to offer. If a person offers another a thing, as, for instance, a forged instrument, or a piece of counter-

SPECIFIC CRIMES 

429 feit coin which he intends to pass as good,—that is an "uttering,' whether the thing offered be accepted or not; and it is said that the offer need not go so far as to be in law a tender. But to constitute an uttering there must be a complete attempt to do the particular thing which the law forbids; though there may be a complete conditional uttering as well as any other, which will be criminal. It has been expressly adjudicated that the allegation of uttering and publishing is proved by evidence that the prisoner offered to pass the instrument to another person, declaring or asserting, directly or indirectly, by words or action, that it was good. . . . Since the offense of uttering is an attempt, it is completed when the forged instrument is offered; and acceptance of it is unnecessary. . . . To complete the offense, there must be a representation of genuineness, but ordinarily this is implied in the act of uttering. To utter and publish a document is to offer directly or indirectly, by words or actions, such document as good. Walker, 127 Ga. 48, 49, 50 (56 S. 

E. 113).

The allegation that the defendant did "utter and publish" a certain forged check is supported by evidence that he offered to pass said check to another person as a genuine instrument, though the offer was not accepted and the defendant did not exhibit the forged instrument to the witness, there being other evidence from which the jury might find that the check has been forged by the defendant and was in his possession at the time said offer was made. Walker, 127 Ga. 48 (1) (56 S. E. 113).

Indictment charging attorney with altering a genuine answer to a summons of garnishment and with publishing the false, altered and counterfeited answer as true, was not subject to demurrer on the ground that it joined in one count two separate offenses, or upon the ground that it did not appear that paper might be used to defraud. The alleged indictment was in this case in effect an order for money, and the amount thereof was stated, but in an indictment un-

Indictment under this section held fatally defective which does not name any person, firm or corporation that defendant intended to defraud. Howell, 25 Ga. App. 547 (103 S. E. 799).

An indictment founded on § 26-3905, must allege that the forged paper was uttered and published as true, but in an indictment. founded on § 26-3914 this allegation is not required, for, under the latter section, the crime of uttering consists in publishing or tendering a paper, knowing the writing to be forged. General. Where character of instrument is in question, this section may be given in charge. Thomas, 59 Ga. 784 (7).

Forged option to buy land is included in this section. Description sufficient if property can be identified by parol evidence. McLean, 3 Ga. App. 660 (2) (3) (60 S. E. 332).

Writing need not be of any particular form or character, if only it may be the means of defrauding another. Travis, 83 Ga. 376 (9

By this section it was the intent of the legislature to embrace every species of writing that could be used or written in a form and with a view of defrauding another. Travis, 83 Ga. 372 (9 S. E. 1063).

Where one to whom certificate of stock is issued altered the same by raising the figures as to number of shares for which it purported to be issued, and signed his name to the blank for transfer of the certificate and negotiated the same with a bank, he was guilty of uttering a forged instrument, though the date and name of the transferee were not inserted. Smith, 13 Ga. App. 663, 664 (79 S. E. 764). 

There need be no signature to constitute a forgery. Curtis, 16 Ga.

431 to be issued, and signed his name to the blank for transfer of the certificate and negotiated the same with a bank, instruction to convict if paper was uttered with intent to defraud any person was not erroneous where charge as a whole predicated conviction on an intent to defraud the bank. q. CONVEYING LAND BY FORGED TITLE. 

§ 26-3921 defines two offenses: (1) Selling, leasing, renting, or otherwise conveying to another land or the timber thereon, the title of which is forged, or the grant of any deed or conveyance whereof is forged, knowing the same to be forged; (2) or taking possession of or occupying or exercising any acts of ownership over any land. or timber thereon under any grant, deed, bond, lease or other conveyance which is forged, or any part of the title whereof is forged, knowing the same to be forged. Davis, 20 Ga. App. 68 (1) (92 S. E. 550).

To "take possession of" any land or timber thereon, as used in the second clause of § 26-3921, implies the actual possession of the whole or some part of the land or timber. It is a corporeal act, as distinguished from title or ownership. Possession is a species of property, distinguished from title or ownership. It may be partially actual and partially ideal. To "occupy" any land or timber thereon, as used in the clause of the section named, implies the actual and corporeal possession of the whole or a portion of the land or timber. Occupancy is always actual, as distinguished from possession, which may be actual or constructive. Occupancy is never constructive, save in the sense that land may be occupied through the actual possession of another. The "acts of ownership" over any land or the timber thereon, as used in this clause of the Code section, implies and is to be interpreted as acts differing from a mere verbal claim of ownership, of like character to taking possession of or occupying lands or timber, or some part thereof. Davis, 20 Ga. App. 68 (2) (92 S. E. 550).

The indictment need not charge an intent to defraud or injure anyone. Watson, 78 Ga. 349 (1).

Indictment need give only substantial description of title. Watson, 78 Ga. 349 (2).

Record of genuine grant does not charge defendant with knowledge that grant he uttered was spurious; constructive notice is no substitute for actual notice in establishing criminal intent. Pearson, 55 Ga. 659, 660.

The bar of the statute of limitations applies only as to occupancy actually outside of the four-year period prescribed in the statute,

for occupancy is in the nature of a continuing act and each day's occupancy is, in legal contemplation, a new and independent act of occupation. Coker, 115 Ga. 210 (1) (41 S. E. 684).

a. GAMING. 

Indictment. Indictment need not set out the name of the game. 

Slade, 125 Ga. 788 (1) (54 S. E. 750). 

Indictment need not allege with whom game was played. Hinton, 68 Ga. 322; Brand, 112 Ga. 25, 26 (37 S. E. 100). 

The words "wagering," "playing," "gaming," and "betting," though each having a meaning more or less different from the other, are often used one for the other. Thrower, 117 Ga. 753, 756 (45 S. 

E. 126).

Allegation that the accused "did play and bet for money and other things of value at a game played with cards" is sufficient,

SPECIFIC CRIMES 

433 though there be no allegation as to what "other things of value" were. Brand, 112 Ga. 25 (37 S. E. 100); Woody, 113 Ga. 927 (2) (39 

S. E. 297); Slade, 125 Ga. 788 (1) (54 S. E. 750).

Where several persons are charged by name under joint indictment, and it is not alleged that other unknown persons participated, conviction of one of the named persons is not authorized by evidence which does not disclose that any of those jointly indicted with him were connected with the transaction. Hubbard, 123 Ga. 17 (3) (51 

S. E. 11); Pullen, 116 Ga. 555 (42 S. E. 774); Woody, 113 Ga. 927 (39 S. E. 297). Note: It seems that it is a better practice to bring several indictments in gaming. 

Indictment may charge in one count conjunctively that the defendant played and bet at a game played with cards, dice and balls, without being subject to demurrer. Hubbard, 123 Ga. 17 (1) (51

S. E. 11). At the trial the offense can be established by evidence of playing and betting at a game played with either cards, dice or balls. (One dissenting.) (Id.)

An indictment charging, in alternative, playing and betting for money or other things of value, at a game of cards, bad on special demurrer. Haley, 124 Ga. 216 (52 S. E. 159); Cooper, 9 Ga. App. 

877 (72 S. E. 436); Hubbard, 123 Ga. 17, 18 (51 S. E. 11). But such charge in alternative must be objected to by special demurrer. Indictment is not void if no special demurrer filed. Pulliam, 140 Ga. 

864 (2) (80 S. E. 315).

The accusation need not identify the players, nor the particular game played. Hicks, 16 Ga. App. 228 (1) (84 S. E. 837).

An accusation may be more restricted, but it can not be broader, than the affidavit on which it is based. Where an affidavit sets out that the defendant was guilty of the general offense of gaming, accusation can allege that he was guilty of any specific act included within the definition of gaming. Glass, 119 Ga. 299 (46 S. E. 435); 

Murphy, 119 Ga. 300 (46 S. E. 450). 

The word "playing" is used as a generic term. To "shoot" craps is to "play" craps. Sims, 1 Ga. App. 776 (57 S. E. 1029).

General. Playing and betting several games by the same person at the same time is but one offense. Wingard, 13 Ga. 396.

Gambling means the playing of a game of chance or skill for stakes, or the betting on the result of the game, or gaming or playing for money. Fleming, 125 Ga. 17, 18 (53 S. E. 579).

The law of gaming was designed to prevent gambling of any nature. The game may be one of chance or skill for stakes. Fleming, 125 Ga. 17, 18 (53 S. E. 579).

Games. Chuckluck. Archer, 69 Ga. 767 (2). Craps. Sims, 1 Ga.

Keeping, maintaining, or carrying on lottery, scheme or device, is gaming. Sable, 48 Ga. App. 174 (1) (172 S. E. 236).

Checks or chips which represent money and are payable in money are things of value. Robinson, 77 Ga. 101 (1); Porter, 51 Ga. 300.

Pool playing under agreement between the players that the loser should pay for the use of the table is gambling within this statute.

Money is judicially recognized as a thing of value. It is not necessary to allege or to prove that the money bet was of any value. 

Grant, 89 Ga. 393 (15 S. E. 488).

It is immaterial whose money the defendant bet, or who put up the money with which he played. Kincaid, 13 Ga. App. 683 (2) (79

It is not necessary that money be at stake. The statute penalizes also playing for anything of value. Alexander, 13 Ga. App. 354, 355 (79 S. E. 177).

Illegal arrest. Whether the defendant was arrested by a lawful officer, or not, and whether arrest was legal or illegal, is immaterial on a trial for gambling. Mitchell, 126 Ga. 84 (9) (54 S. E. 931).

435 Bystanders. Bystanders are guilty of playing and betting, if they bet on the result of the game. Parmer, 91 Ga. 152 (2) (16. S. E. 937);

Conviction may be warranted, though the accused had no cards in his hands when found and arrested, where another shuffled the cards. Frost, 120 Ga. 311 (47 S. E. 901).

Evidence. Neither defendant's presence, nor his flight is sufficient to convict, without more. Griffin, 2 Ga. App. 534 (58 S. E.

It is not necessary to show who won and who lost. Arnold, 117

Evidence that several men were sitting or lying in a circle, playing a game with cards, or dice, and that they fled upon the arrival of an officer, and that money was found on the place,-sufficient to convict of gambling. Evidence showing that a number of persons were playing cards, that each contributed enough money to pay for the number of milkshakes necessary to furnish each with one of the beverages, and that, at the time they were playing, this money has been collected and paid over to the owner of the house with the understanding that the man winning would take it and set up the crowd to the milkshakes, not sufficient to convict. In such case each one of the crowd was paying for his own milk-shake and nobody was winner and nobody loser. Simmons, 106 Ga. 355 (1) (32 S. E. 339).

Where on trial of one accused of gaming, the evidence shows the presence of the defendant at the time and place of the gambling, but there is no evidence, direct or circumstantial, to show actual participation by the defendant in the game played, and the evidence for the State is consistent with the defendant's contention that he was merely an onlooker, the evidence is not sufficient to authorize conviction. Freeman, 21 Ga. App. 494 (94 S. E. 588).

Finding the defendant on his knees with ten negroes around a table with a deck of cards and one dollar and five cents on it, defendant and the others fleeing on the approach of officers, authorized conviction. Roberts, 26 Ga. App. 66 (105 S. E. 707); Schley, 25 Ga. App. 549 (103 S. E. 799).

While gaming is one of the offenses which ordinarily must be

proved by circumstantial evidence, such circumstantial evidence which does not exclude all reasonable hypothesis save guilt is insufficient. Griffin, 2 Ga. App. 534 (58 S. E. 781). 

Where money was heard rattling, and cards playing, without more, the law presumes that the defendant was a spectator. Cox, 7 Ga. App. 22 (65 S. E. 1062).

Possession of either cards or money by one present at card game sufficient to authorize inference that he participated in the game. 

Griffin, 5 Ga. App. 43 (1) (62 S. E. 685).

Statement of witness that "this gambling took place on the same night he (named person) was killed at that (named) place"-inadmissible, unless it appears that such statement is intended to show when the alleged gambling occurred. Fleming, 125 Ga. 17 (53 S. 

E. 579).

Where several persons are charged by name under joint indictment, and it is not alleged that other unknown persons participated, conviction of one of the named persons is not authorized by evidence which does not disclose that any one of those jointly indicted with him were connected with the transaction. Hubbard, 123 Ga. 17 (3) (51 S. E. 11); Pullen, 116 Ga. 555 (42 S. E. 774); Woody, 113 Ga. 

927 (39 S. E. 297). 

Indictment charging that the defendants played and bet with "each other" sustained by evidence that they played and bet at the same game against the one who presided. Archer, 69 Ga. 767.

Where the defendant is not charged with having engaged in any particular game, proof that he played at cards or dice for money or other things of value will warrant conviction. Evidence in such case, that the defendant played or bet for money or other things of value at a certain game will warrant conviction, although it does not appear in which of the games he was engaged. Alford, 15 Ga. App. 

426 (1) (83 S. E. 444).

Where the game played is specified in the indictment, it must be proved as alleged. Alford, 15 Ga. App. 426 (1) (83 S. E. 444). The burden is upon the State to show that the particular game charged was played. Hicks, 16 Ga. App. 228 (84 S. E. 837).

Where the indictment specifies game played or bet at, evidence is restricted to that particular game. Hicks, 16 Ga. App. 228 (84 S. E. 837).

Implements seized in gaming house are admissible in evidence before the grand jury. Kneeland, 70 Ga. 424.
