437 that the defendant was, as a gaming room,-admissible. Pritchett, 20 Ga. App. 189 (2) (92 S. E. 948).

Testimony of flight of defendant when he saw chief of police in neighboring city some months after the gambling charged-admissible. Grant, 122 Ga. 740 (1) (2) (50 S. E. 946).

Declaration of one of the gamblers during the progress of the game is part of the res gestae of the game. Glover, 89 Ga. 391 (15) 

S. E. 496). Verdict.

Accusation containing two counts charging gaming with cards and with dice charges but one offense and a general verdict of "guilty" upheld. Colquitt, 6 Ga. App. 109 (64 S. E. 281); 

Tooke, 4 Ga. App. 495 (61 S. E. 917).

Former jeopardy. Plea of former acquittal good if defendant was convicted on a general indictment. Not so if time, place, players, etc., be alleged, and different. McCoy, 121 Ga. 359 (49 S. E. 294). 

Municipal ordinances. Quietly playing and betting for money, while an offense under the statutes of the State, does not constitute disorderly conduct in violation of a municipal ordinance. Kahn, 95 Ga. 419 (22 S. E. 641); Sheppard, 11 Ga. App. 811 (76 S. E. 367).

Municipal ordinance forbidding the assembling of two or more persons for the purpose of gaming is not covered by State law, and is valid. Ward, 25 Ga. App. 320 (1) (103 S. E. 191). 

b. GAMING HOUSES. 

Indictment. Description of the house in the indictment, as to location, need not be more definite than that it is in the county. 

Dohme, 68 Ga. 339 (1).

The indictment need not state the tenant's name. Bashinski, 123 

Ga. 508 (51 S. E. 499). 

For indictment charging dealing in futures see: Layton, 165 Ga. 

265 (140 S. E. 847).

The Code, (making penal the keeping of a gaming house or renting a house to be used for gaming), defines a single offense, which may be committed in any of the three ways therein designated. 

Therefore an indictment containing two counts, one charging the defendant with maintaining a gaming house, and the other with knowingly renting the house with the view and expectation of the same being used for gaming, is not open to demurrer on the ground of misjoinder of separate and distinct offenses. Bashinski, 123 Ga. 508 (1) (51 S. E. 499).

General. 

99 

Gambling and gaming distinguished. The words, "wagering, "playing," "gaming," and "betting," though each having a meaning more or less different from the other, are often used one for the other. The statute in prohibiting gaming does not intend to prohibit amusement, sport, recreation, or diversion, but is aimed at the hazarding of money on certain prohibited games and devices. In prohibiting a gaming house it is intended to prevent the maintenance of a place (italics by the Court) at which persons come together for the purpose of hazarding and betting money, whether the subject matter of a single bet is or is not made penal. There is a difference between gambling and gaming. In defining gaming contracts the Code refers to contracts in which money has been wagered, although there may be no sport, no skill, no element of contest between those betting; and therefore, while some few courts rule that betting on a horse race is not even gaming, most others decide it to be gaming, and our own courts have held that "betting on a horse race is gaming in the sense of the Code." It may not be gambling, but it is gaming. Thrower, 117 Ga. 753, 756 (45 

S. E. 126).

Common law. Keeping a gaming house was an offense at common law, though no form of gambling was then punishable, and gaming contracts were enforced by the courts. Prior to the first

Penal Code this common law offense was punished in Georgia. 

Thrower, 117 Ga. 753 (1) (2) (45 S. E. 126).

Gist of the offense. The gist of the offense of knowingly renting a house for the practice of gaming is knowledge on the part of the landlord that the house is to be used for that purpose. Knowledge may be proved by circumstances. Bashinski, 123 Ga. 508 (51 S. E. 499).

One permitting others to assemble in a house or room in his control and play a game of chance in which a thing of value is hazarded, is guilty of keeping a gaming house, regardless of his purpose in permitting the game. Alexander, 13 Ga. App. 354 (1) (79 

S. E. 177).

Evidence of a single instance of gaming will not warrant conviction of maintaining gaming house. White, 115 Ga. 570, 571 (41 S. 

E. 986); Bell, 92 Ga. 49 (18 S. E. 186).

A single instance of gaming, without more, will not constitute the house in which it occurs a gaming house, but it is sufficient to show a single occasion when one permits persons with his knowledge to

SPECIFIC CRIMES 

439 come together and play for money. The permission may be inferred from the other circumstances and surroundings tending to show that the house or room was a gaming house. Bluhakis, 18 Ga. App. 

112 (88 S. E. 911). While a single act or instance of gaming in a house or room will not constitute the place a gaming house or room, yet such an act together with all the attendant circumstances and surrounding indications may be sufficient evidence to show that the house or room is really one of that character. Bell, 92 Ga. 49, 51 (18 S. E. 186); Atterberry, 4 Ga. App. 336 (61 S. E. 296).

In prohibiting gaming houses or gaming places the legislature intended to prevent the maintenance of a place at which persons gather for the purpose of hazarding and betting money, whether the subject matter of a single bet is or is not made penal. Gullatt, 169 Ga. 538 (2) (150 S. E. 825).

Proof of the commission of the offense in any one of the three ways designated by this section will support a general verdict of guilty. Bluhakis, 18 Ga. App. 112 (88 S. E. 911).

To maintain a place of any character where persons are allowed to bet, offer to bet, place an order for a bet, or telegraph or telephone bets on races of any sort, is an act prohibited by the Code. 

Thrower, 124 Ga. 1 (52 S. E. 76).

It is a criminal offense under this section to rent premises to be used as gambling house. Proof of defendant's mental state may be inferred. Rivers, 118 Ga. 42, 45 (44 S. E. 859). As where the circumstances would place the ordinary man on guard. Bashinski, 122 

Ga. 164 (50 S. E. 54); Bashinski, 123 Ga. 508, 510 (51 S. E. 499).

If accused did not have knowledge that the room or house was to be used for gaming, when the rent contract was made, he is not under obligation to use ordinary diligence to discover the use, though jury may infer the knowledge if the circumstances or the conduct of the business are such as to give notice. Bashinski, 123 

Ga. 508 (6) (51 S. E. 499).

One who maintains a house or a place for the purpose of permitting gaming on dog races is guilty of keeping gaming house or place. 

Gullatt, 169 Ga. 538 (2) (150 S. E. 825). The fact that the operator of the place advised the public that upon personal request he will give any one a profit-sharing coupon which would entitle him to share in the profits in case he selected the winning dog in advance of the race, did not take the place out of the gaming house or gaming place class. (Id.) (4-a.)

The fact that the gaming was conducted in orderly and quiet manner is no defense. (Id.) (4-b.)

440. 

Place where futures are bought and sold on margin is a gaming house. And this is true though the contracts are telegraphed out of the State, if actual wagering takes place and the settlement of the wagers takes place within the State. A statement in each transaction that actual delivery is contemplated will not prevent such place from being a gaming house, if, as a matter of fact, the customers do not make tender, or accept actual delivery, but settle their winnings and losses in money. Anderson, 2 Ga. App. 1 (4) (4-a) (4-c) (58 S. E. 401); see also: Layton, 165 Ga. 265 (140 S. E. 847).

Aiding and abetting. Any act done in connection with maintaining or keeping gaming house is an offense under this section. White, 127 Ga. 273 (1) (56 S. E. 425); Rosenthal, 126 Ga. 558 (3) (55 S. E. 497).

This section extends to all participants who keep and maintain the house. Bryan, 120 Ga. 201 (3) (47 S. E. 574); White, 127 Ga. 

273 (56 S. E. 425).

If the State shows on the trial for keeping and maintaining a gaming house that the accused was criminally connected by act and intent with the commission of the offense, it is sufficient to convict, as all concerned in the commission of a misdemeanor are in fact principals. Ponder, 18 Ga. App. 703 (1) (90 S. E. 365).

Lease of the house by the defendant to another is immaterial, it appearing that he, the defendant, was in possession. Scott, 29 Ga. 

263; Stevenson, 83 Ga. 575, 580 (10 S. E. 234).

Lending money to conduct a gaming house, and visiting the house, and doing anything towards keeping and maintaining it, sufficient to warrant conviction. Groves, 123 Ga. 570 (1) (51 S. E. 627).

If the accused aided in maintaining gaming room, that would be sufficient to convict. It is not necessary that the accused should have been wholly in control of the place. If anything was done by defendant as part of something connected with keeping and maintaining room, that would be sufficient to sustain conviction. Ponder, 18 Ga. App. 703, 704 (5) (90 S. E. 365).

Social club. Where gambling was carried on in a social club, the officer collecting a portion of the losses for the club's benefit, the offense is under this section. Cochran, 102 Ga. 631 (29 S. E. 438).

Horse races. Betting on a horse race is gaming within the meaning of the Code. One who maintains a house for the purpose of betting on horse races, keeps a gaming house, even though such betting were not prohibited by statute and though race is run in a different

SPECIFIC CRIMES 

441 

State. Thrower, 117 Ga. 753 (4) (5) (45 S. E. 126); Jones, 120 Ga. 

185 (47 S. E. 561).

Husband and wife. Where husband and wife live together, the husband is the head of the house and it is his duty affirmatively to interfere with gaming; when both are present, it is the husband's duty, not the wife's, to prevent unlawful gaming therein, and in order to hold her liable, criminally, for permitting such gaming, it must appear affirmatively that she was active in the granting of permission, not merely passive in the matter and took no measure to hinder or prevent the game. Bell, 92 Ga. 49 (4) (18 S. E. 186). 

Keeping and maintaining. "Keep" and "maintain," frequently used as synonymous, have different meanings under this section. 

The offense may be committed by keeping or maintaining, or by keeping and maintaining. Proof that the defendant had been guilty of either of the prohibited acts would sustain a charge that he had kept and maintained. Bryan, 120 Ga. 201 (47 S. E. 574); Thomas, 118 Ga. 774 (45 S. E. 622).

The house need not be kept during any period of time. It is sufficient to show that it was kept at any time within the statute of limitations. Bryan, 120 Ga. 201 (2) (47 S. E. 574).

Reputation. The general reputation of the place, as well as the reputation of those who frequented it,-admissible. Dudley, 18 Ga. App. 509 (1) (89 S. E. 599). 

Evidence that persons known by common repute as gamblers had been often seen to enter and leave the building, portion only of which was owned or controlled by the defendant, though never seen in defendant's room, did not establish the character of the defendant's place or room. Phillips, 19 Ga. App. 143 (1) (91 S. E. 234). 

Evidence. Testimony that the accused was "gambling" is conclusion of the witness. Fleming, 125 Ga. 17, 18 (53 S. E. 579).

Testimony of one witness is sufficient. Pyles, 3 Ga. App. 29 (59 

S. E. 193).

Evidence merely that game played with cards and poker chips. was in progress when the police entered, but not showing that either money or other thing of value was placed as hazard, insufficient to support conviction. Phillips, 19 Ga. App. 143 (1) (91 S. E. 234).

Circumstantial evidence may show the purpose for which the house has been leased. Rivers, 118 Ga. 42 (2) (44 S. E. 859).

Knowledge of the accused that the house was to be used for gaming may be shown by any competent evidence. Bashinski, 122 Ga. 

264 (50 S. E. 54); Bashinski, 123 Ga. 508 (3) (51 S. E. 499).

Long established reputation of the room in which the gaming was conducted, means and access thereto through connecting door of defendant's room in the hotel, and other circumstances may warrant conviction of keeping a gaming house. Dudley, 18 Ga. App. 509, 510 (3) (89 S. E. 599). 

A special presentment against one for keeping a gaming house is not evidence of his guilt, but is a public charge to the effect, calculated to put one on inquiry; and such presentment is admissible with a view of establishing the reputation of the person to whom the house is rented. Rivers, 118 Ga. 42 (4) (44 S. E. 859).

Where defendant kept his sleeping apartment with doors "blanketed" in fit condition for privately gaming therein, and had a table suitable for gaming, several packs of cards and boxes of chips, and a memorandum book with names and numbers entered in it, and his guests hid under the bed on being surprised by the police, verdict of guilty warranted. Pacetti, 82 Ga. 297 (7 S. E. 867); Hicks, 1 Ga. App. 722 (57 S. E. 958).

Charge of Court. Where accusation charged that the accused did keep and maintain a gaming house, and that he did in a certain room, occupied by him, permit persons, with his knowledge, to play for money at certain game for hazarding money, specified in the indictment, the Court need not charge, without timely written request, that a single act of gaming, without more, would not constitute a house in which it occurred a gaming house, but that it was sufficient to show a single occasion when one permits persons with his knowledge to come together and play for money. Bell, 92 Ga. 49 (18 S. E. 

186); Bluhakis, 18 Ga. App. 112, 113 (3) (88 S. E. 911).

Verdict. A general verdict of guilty is sufficient under an indictment for keeping and also for renting a gaming house, without specifying on which count it rested. Dohme, 68 Ga. 339. 

Municipal ordinance. Municipal ordinance making it a penal offense to maintain a place for betting on races is invalid. Thrower, 124 Ga. 1 (52 S. E. 76). 

c. GAMING TABLES. 

The indictment need not allege that things of value were bet. 

Simms, 60 Ga. 145 (3).

The words in this section "other table of like character" embrace any table on which visible, material, or mechanical means are employed to dispose of money or other articles of value, by chance, under conditions of risk, and with the result of profit to one of the participants and loss to the other. The question as to the species of

SPECIFIC CRIMES 

443 tables, whether of "like character" or not, is one of law for determination by the Court, but the question whether the particular table is of that species is one of fact for the jury. Mims, 88 Ga. 458 (14 

S. E. 712); Brown, 40 Ga. 689.

Implements of crime may be seized as evidence before grand jury under warrant for the keeper himself. Kneeland, 70 Ga. 424.

The fact that the State imposes a specific tax on the keeper of pool tables does not affect the guilt or innocence of one charged with gambling. Hopkins, 122 Ga. 583 (50 S. E. 351). 

d. LOTTERY TICKETS. 

Indictment. Indictment need not allege the manner of operation of the slot machine. Kolshorn, 97 Ga. 343 (1) (23 S. E. 829).

General. Slot machine, into which, if one dropped a nickel, he either lost it or won fifteen cents, comes within this section. Kolshorn, 97 Ga. 343 (2) (23 S. E. 829). 

Suit club with membership fee of one dollar per week, holding weekly drawings, as a result of which the member holding the lucky number received a suit of clothes, and then ceased to be a member, constitutes lottery scheme. De Florin, 121 Ga. 593 (49 S. E. 699).

Slot machine operated whereby person depositing money may, by chance, get articles worth more than the money deposited, is in violation of this act. Brockett, 33 Ga. App. 57 (125 S. E. 513). 

A gift enterprise is a sporting artifice, by which, for example, a merchant or tradesman sells his wares for their market value, but, by way of inducement, gives to each purchaser a ticket which entitles him to a chance to win certain prizes, to be determined after the manner of a lottery. Russell, 129 Ga. 154, 161 (58 S. E. 881); 

Meyer, 112 Ga. 20, 23 (37 S. E. 96); Whitley, 133 Ga. 738 (1) (66 S. 

E. 933). in Where a number of persons are entitled to a certain amount, any event, though not the same amount in each case, and all can not be paid at one time, determination by lot of what portion of that number shall be paid at different times, will not make the transaction a lottery. It is when the amount to be paid, or the value of the article to be delivered, is itself to be determined, in whole or in part, by chance, that elements of lottery are present. Equitable 

Loan Co., 117 Ga. 599 (15), 600 (45 S. E. 320).

Keeping of lottery was not criminal at common law, although lotteries have ever been deemed as contrary to public policy. Roney, 135 Ga. 1, 3 (68 S. E. 701).

Punchboard is gambling device. Hobbs, 35 Ga. App. 226, 230 (132

S. E. 775). 

Operator of slot machine so arranged that when a person inserted five cents in coin and pulled lever package of candy worth five cents was ejected, and sometimes, but not always, small metal tokens were also ejected, which could be used by inserting them in the machine. and thereby securing horoscopic message or pretended fortune, held guilty of operating a gambling device, although the metal tokens were plainly marked "for amusement only," and had no redemption value in money or merchandise. Jenner, 173 Ga. 86 (159 S. E. 564); 

Jenner, 43 Ga. App. 747 (160 S. E. 115).

Cash sale inaugurated by a merchant under regulations whereby any person who traded $1, paying cash, received a ticket, one trading $10 received ten tickets, etc., such tickets being numbered, and one holding number drawn from sealed box to be given absolutely free an automobile, constituted gift enterprise scheme, which is contrary to public policy. Standridge, 148 Ga. 283 (96 S. E. 498).

Chance, as here used, refers to that chance which is employed in connection with lottery schemes, where the attempt is to attain certain ends, not by skill or any known or fixed rules, but by the happening of a subsequent event, incapable of ascertainment or accomplishment by means of human foresight or ingenuity. If the result in a given transaction could be accomplished or foretold by the exercise of skill or foresight, its ascertainment would not be attributed to chance, but to the exercise of skill and foresight, and consequently to design. Chance and design are exactly opposite, and the presence of either will exclude the other. Russell, 129 Ga. 154, 161 (58 S. E. 881).

Lottery. Definitions: "A scheme for distributing prizes by chance or lot, where a valuable consideration is given for the chance of drawing a prize; especially where such chances are allotted by sale of tickets."—"A scheme by which a result is reached by some action or means taken, in which result man's choice or will has no part, and which human reason, foresight, sagacity, or design can not enable him to know or determine, until the same has been accomplished." "Where a pecuniary consideration is paid, and it is determined by lot or chance, according to some scheme held out to the public, what and how much he who pays the money is to have for it.""Any scheme for the disposal or distribution of property by chance among persons who have paid, or promised, or agreed to pay, any valuable consideration for the chance of obtaining such property, or a portion of it, or for any share of or interest in such prop-

SPECIFIC CRIMES 

445 erty, upon any agreement, understanding, or expectation that it is to be distributed or disposed of by lot or chance, whether called a 'lottery,' a 'raffle,' or a 'gift enterprise,' or by whatever name the same may be known." Equitable Loan Co., 117 Ga. 599, 658 (44 S. E. 320). 

The essentials of lottery are: Consideration, prize, chance. Russell, 129 Ga. 154, 161 (58 S. E. 881); Equitable Loan Co., 117 Ga. 599 (14) (44 S. E. 320).

The sale and not the purchase of lottery tickets is made penal. 

Roney, 135 Ga. 1 (2) (68 S. E. 701).

Similar schemes. "Similar schemes" as used in this section necessarily refers to schemes like lotteries or gift enterprises, and consequently the element of chance is essential to their existence. Russell, 129 Ga. 154, 161 (58 S. E. 881).

Construction. §§ 26-6501 and 26-6502 of the Code should be con strued together. Russell, 129 Ga. 154 (58 S. E. 881). 

Constitutionality. Upheld. Evans, 68 Ga. 826. 

Acts 1916, p. 155, forbidding popularity contests held in conflict with the Constitution. Commercial Security Co., 148 Ga. 597 (1) (97 S. E. 516). 

City ordinance. City ordinance prohibiting gaming is-void. 

Alexander, 13 Ga. App. 354 (1) (79 S. E. 177). 

Principals. All participants are principals. Agents and clerks are principals. Claim that one is not regularly employed but served temporarily in another's place is no defense. Thomas, 118 Ga. 774 (45 S. E. 622); Henderson, 95 Ga. 326, 327 (22 S. E. 537).

Evidence. Evidence that the defendant was found in control of what he admitted was a "policy shop," with the paraphernalia used in drawings exposed to view therein, and when arrested, stated that he did not run the place, but was waiting in the place of another, was sufficient to support conviction. Thomas, 118 Ga. 774 (3) (45 

S. E. 622).

Indictment charging the defendant with keeping, maintaining, and operating a scheme for the hazarding of money, known as a "policy lottery," proof that he kept and maintained such scheme is sufficient to warrant a conviction, without showing a drawing. 

Thomas, 118 Ga. 774 (1) (45 S. E. 622).

Verdict. Where indictment contains two counts, one count charging the carrying on a "lottery," and the other charging the carrying on of "a scheme and device other than lottery", (italics by the Court), for the hazarding of money, and where the evidence

showed one scheme and device only, a general verdict of "guilty" (meaning guilty on both counts) is contrary to law and the evidence. B'Gos, 43 Ga. App. 379 (159 S. E. 137). 

e. WITNESSES. 

§ 26-6407, providing that players shall be competent and compellable witnesses, and also providing that nothing then said by such witness shall at any time be received or given in evidence against him in any prosecution, except on an indictment for perjury, in any matter in which he might have testified, does not violate the Constitution, regulating the right of a person to refuse to give incriminating evidence. Kneeland, 62 Ga. 395, 396 (3).

A witness who has participated in the game and is testifying under this section can not criminate himself, for by provisions of this section such testimony can not be used against him. Therefore such witness is compellable. Wheatley, 114 Ga. 175 (39 S. E. 877); Kneeland, 62 Ga. 395, 396. Note: In the Wheatley case this rule is criticised but followed.

The protection of the statute does not extend to cases where the witness voluntarily testified. It applies only to such witnesses who are compelled to give evidence. Moore, 97 Ga. 759, 761 (25 S. E. 

362). The Court need not charge this section where the witness voluntarily testified. (Id.)

This section (§ 26-6502) does not apply to the offense of carrying on lotteries. Henderson, 95 Ga. 326 (22 S. E. 537).

The indictment need not allege that the accused was of sound mind and discretion, or that the person killed was a human being, or was in the peace of the State. Barnes, 24 Ga. App. 372 (1) (100 

S. E. 788).

Indictment charging murder is not demurrable because it does not allege that the killing of the deceased by the defendant was unlawful. Davis, 153 Ga. 669 (1) (113 S. E. 11).

An indictment which elaborates the details of the particular charge of murder, by alleging that the accused shot at one person with the intent to murder him, but missed and murdered another, is not demurrable for duplicity. Grier, 158 Ga. 321 (1) (123 S. 

E. 210).

An indictment for murder alleging that the defendant ran over and killed a named person, sufficiently charged the offense of involuntary manslaughter. Reams, 24 Ga. App. 135 (1-a) (100 S. E. 230). 

Where indictment charges the defendant with murder, in that he killed and murdered a said person in a described manner, it is not demurrable on the ground that it wholly omits to disclose the death of the alleged victim. Rafe, 24 Ga. App. 334 (1) (100 S. E. 793).

An indictment which charges the offense of involuntary manslaughter, in that the homicide was committed without any intention to do so on the part of the slayer, but while he was engaged in the commission of an unlawful act, is sufficient, although it does not expressly allege that the homicide was without malice. 

Hayes, 11 Ga. App. 371 (7) (75 S. E. 523).

SPECIFIC CRIMES 

449 Indictment charging the defendant with involuntary manslaughter in the commission of a lawful act, by negligently permitting the. administration of chloroform by an assistant not qualified to administer it, should state the name of the person who is alleged to have administered the chloroform, so as to enable the defendant to properly prepare for trial. Roughlin, 17 Ga. App. 205 (86 S. E. 452).

An allegation in an indictment for involuntary manslaughter that an act which of itself is intrinsically lawful was done unlawfully, unless by explanatory statements it is specially pointed out in what manner the act was done unlawfully, is not a statement of fact, but a mere conclusion of the pleader, and not sufficient to inform the accused of the nature of the alleged offense. Roughlin, 17 Ga. 

App. 205 (1) (86 S. E. 452).

Indictment charging involuntary manslaughter in that the defendant killed a human being while engaged in violation of a municipal ordinance prohibiting the sale of condemned milk, is not void, nor demurrable for failure to allege the penal offense. Leontas, 166 Ga. 266 (142 S. E. 891).

In an indictment for homicide it is not necessary to allege that the defendant was a person of sound mind and discretion. Brown, 13 Ga. App. 437 (3) (79 S. E. 231); Green, 172 Ga. 635 (2) (158 

S. E. 285).

The indictment for murder need not specifically state that the deceased was a human being. The name of the deceased implies these facts. Sutherland, 121 Ga. 591 (49 S. E. 781); Green, 172

Where an indictment alleged that the accused "did kill and murder" the deceased on a stated day, it need not charge that the victim died on the same day. "If killed on that day, he died on that day." Reed, 148 Ga. 18 (2) (95 S. E. 692).

The date on which the death occurred need not be stated. An indictment for murder may be found at any time after the death of the person killed. Black, 14 Ga. App. 534 (3) (81 S. E. 588).

An indictment is not demurrable on the ground that it does not describe the place of the homicide other than the county. Walker, 141 Ga. 525 (1-a) (81 S. E. 442).

An indictment for murder by choking, beating and drowning is not demurrable on the ground that it did not describe the mode of choking, beating and drowning. Walker, 141 Ga. 525 (1) (81 S. 

E. 442).

An indictment charging murder by shooting "with a certain pistol and with a certain rifle," is not demurrable on the ground that the homicide was charged as committed with two different instruments alleged conjunctively, and that it is physically impossible to kill a person with a gun and a pistol at the same time, and that one of them alone must have produced the death. Knight, 148 Ga. 

40 (1) (95 S. E. 679).

In an indictment for murder, which charges that the accused did kill and murder a named person by shooting him with a gun, from the effects of which shooting he died, it is not necessary to allege that the gun was loaded with powder and leaden balls. Green, 172 Ga. 635 (2) (158 S. E. 285); Cook, 119 Ga. 108 (1) (46 S. E. 

64); Brown, 13 Ga. App. 437 (2) (79 S. E. 231). Nor is it a valid objection that the weapon was not alleged with sufficient particularity or the manner in which it was loaded, or that it was aimed and pointed at the deceased, or that the weapon used was one likely to produce death. Brown, 13 Ga. App. 437 (2) (79 S. E. 231); 

Waller, 164 Ga. 128 (138 S. E. 67).

Indictment charging defendant with having killed the deceased by stabbing him "with a certain knife and with other sharp instruments to the grand jury unknown" is not subject to demurrer on the ground that this allegation is too general to put the defendant upon proper notice as to what instrument is alleged to have been used by him, or that the weapon is not particularly set forth. Hall, 133 Ga. 177 (1) (65 S. E. 400).

An indictment for murder embraces lesser grades of homicide. 

Davis, 14 Ga. App. 764 (82 S. E. 297).

Principals in first and second degree. No distinction need be made in the indictment between a principal in the first and second degree. Jones, 130 Ga. 274 (6) (60 S. E. 840).

Where two persons are jointly indicted for murder, and the indictment charges that both of the accused did kill and murder the deceased with a certain gun which the defendants then and there held, the indictment is not subject to demurrer, on the trial of one of the accused, (1) because it does not allege which one of the defendants named in the indictment held the gun when the shot was fired, (2) because the indictment does not allege which one of the defendants named in the indictment fired the shot claimed to have been fired. Brannon, 140 Ga. 787 (80 S. E. 7).

Indictment charging two persons with murder alleged to have been committed with an automobile driven by them is not sub-

SPECIFIC CRIMES 

451 ject to demurrer on the ground that it did not show which one was actually driving, nor was there any allegation of a conspiracy or joint action or common intent to violate the law. Moreland, 37 Ga. 

App. 180 (139 S. E. 361).

General. 

Word "homicide."

The word "homicide" does not imply criminality on the part of the accused. Hanks, 48 Ga. App. 832 (2) (174 S. E. 151).

Corpus delicti. State must prove, first, that the person alleged in the indictment to have been killed is actually dead, and second that the death was caused or accompanied by violence, or other direct criminal agency of some other human being, that is, it was not accidental, nor due to natural causes, nor to an act of the deceased; and third that the accused caused the death by one or more of the means charged. Warren, 153 Ga. 354 (2) (112 S. E. 283).

Where there is no evidence that the deceased died from the wounds inflicted by the defendant, he could at most be convicted only of the offense of assault with intent to murder. Pope, 13 Ga. 

App. 711 (2) (79 S. E. 909). 

Where one shoots another with a pistol, inflicting a wound which causes a disease from which the wounded person dies, on his trial for murder assault with intent to murder is not involved. Clements, 141 Ga. 667 (4) (81 S. E. 1117).

Reasonable doubt. It is a reasonable doubt of the guilt of the accused on the trial which will furnish a ground of acquittal, not merely any doubt as to which of two men did the killing. Hunter, 133 Ga. 78 (3) (65 S. E. 154). 

Venue. Where the evidence indicates that the deceased was killed at the place where his body was found, and the evidence showed that the body was found in Burke County, combined with other evidence of the case, the venue was sufficiently proved. Moore, 130 

Ga. 322, 334 (6) (60 S. E. 544).

Evidence that the defendant lived in Gilmer County, together with evidence that the physician found the deceased about one hundred and twenty-five yards from defendant's house, not sufficient to prove venue. Holden, 144 Ga. 338 (1) (87 S. E. 27).

Where the evidence is conflicting the question of venue is for the jury. Strange, 9 Ga. App. 204 (1) (70 S. E. 968).

The county where the defendant inflicted the mortal wound on the

deceased establishes the venue. Fitzgerald, 136 Ga. 163 (5) (71 

S. E. 128). 

Assaulting one and killing another. Where the accused shot at one, and hit and killed another, but would not have been justified. in shooting the former, and would have been guilty of murderhe is guilty of murder. Holleman, 171 Ga. 200 (4) (154 S. E. 906); 

Adams, 168 Ga. 530 (3), 537 (148 S. E. 386); Hamilton, 129 Ga. 747 (2) (59 S. E. 803); Godbee, 141 Ga. 515, 521 (81 S. E. 876). 

Where the accused deliberately shot at one sitting in an automobile but missed him, and killed another on the other side of the automobile, conviction for murder authorized. Grant, 152 Ga. 252 (4) (109 S. E. 502). 

Cause of death. If one willfully, unlawfully, and with malice aforethought shoots another with a pistol, inflicting a wound which, though not necessarily mortal, is the primary cause of a disease which brings about the death of the wounded person, he is guilty of murder. Downing, 114 Ga. 30 (39 S. E. 927); Clements, 141 Ga. 667, 668 (81 S. E. 1117); Lochamy, 152 Ga. 235 (4) (109 S. E. 497).

When one inflicts upon another a wound with a weapon likely to produce death, and the person wounded actually dies in consequence of the wound, the quality of the act of the slayer can not be affected by a lack of skill and care upon the part of those who treat or attempt to treat the wound and administer remedies therefor. Perdue, 135 Ga. 277 (69 S. E. 184); Allen, 133 Ga. 260 (65 S. E. 431). Nor will it be affected by the fact that no competent physician could be procured to render timely medical aid. Bonner, 125 Ga. 237 (54 S. E. 143).

Where a person, in violation of the statute, administers morphine to another in such quantity as to cause death, he commits an unlawful act, and a conviction of involuntary manslaughter, in the commission of an unlawful act, would be authorized. It would be no defense that in the administration of the drug the intent was not to cause death, but to alleviate pain. Silver, 13 Ga. App. 722 

Self-destruction.

Homicide does not include intentional or accidental self-destruction. Jones, 130 Ga. 274, 289 (60 S. E. 840).

MURDER. 

General. Whenever one deliberately makes up his mind unlawfully to kill another and executes his intention, then that killing is

SPECIFIC CRIMES 

453 with express malice and is murder. Watson, 150 Ga. 627 (104 S. E. 

572); DuPre, 153 Ga. 798 (3) (113 S. E. 428).

Where an involuntary killing happens in the commission of an unlawful act which, in its consequences, naturally tends to destroy the life of a human being, the offense is deemed to be murder. 

Gadsden, 134 Ga. 785 (2) (68 S. E. 497); Ashford, 144 Ga. 832 (3) (88 S. E. 205).

If defendant, engaged in a quarrel, and hearing another party approaching from behind, throws his knife behind him with such force that it kills the party so approaching, the offense is murder, notwithstanding the absence of intent to kill. Harris, 119 Ga. 114, 116 (45 S. E. 973).

Shooting one charged with a misdemeanor, who attempts to escape, murder if death ensues. Maughon, 7 Ga. App. 660, 665 (67 

S. E. 842).

Where the defendant has set out to rob the deceased, and did rob or attempt to rob him, and the deceased was thereby killed, by the defendant, in the manner set forth in the indictment, and if the killing was a natural, reasonable, and probable consequence of such robbery, or attempt at robbery, the offense is murder. Bigger, 171 Ga. 596, 600 (4) (156 S. E. 201).

Death penalty. It can never be said that the death penalty is demanded by the evidence. After the offense of murder is established, it is solely within the province of the jury whether the accused shall be recommended to the mercy of the court. This discretion is not controlled by any rule of law, and it is error to charge the jury in such manner as would suggest any criterion for the determination of a recommendation for mercy. Hill, 72 Ga. 131; Glover, 128 Ga. 

1,7 (57 S. E. 101); Morrow, 168 Ga. 575, 591 (148 S. E. 500). But see 

Meyers, 169 Ga. 468, 482 (151 S. E. 31). Presumptions.

Deadly weapons. Homicide resulting from the use of deadly weapons is presumed to be felonious until the contrary appears from the circumstances or excuse. McBride, 150 Ga. 92 (2) (102 

S. E. 865).

Where the weapon was a knife and the defendant stabbed the deceased in the neck with it, and death resulted, intent to kill may be presumed. Charlton, 157 Ga. 373 (2) (121 S. E. 334).

If a deadly weapon be used in the commission of a homicide, in the usual and natural manner which weapon would produce death,

the presumption of intent to kill would arise. But a weapon may be used in a manner not naturally calculated to produce death; and in such cases the question of intention to kill is one of fact. 

Delk, 135 Ga. 312, 313 (3) (69 S. E. 541).

Killing. Where the State proved that the accused killed the deceased, in the county and in the manner described in the indictment, a prima facie case of murder is made out, and the burden is. on the accused to set up a defense. Rickerson, 10 Ga. App. 464, 465 (73 S. E. 681).

When evidence of killing by the defendant has been submitted, the presumption of innocence is overcome, and the burden shifts to the defendant to show that the killing was justifiable homicide, or not murder, or any other grade of homicide. Although the above rule is not quite accurate, where it has been charged to the jury, the verdict will not be reversed where there is no evidence to mitigate the killing. Tuggle, 119 Ga. 969 (1) (47 S. E. 577).

Where the defendant admits the killing, the law puts upon him the burden to satisfy the jury that he was justified under some rule of law, unless the admission, together with the evidence in the case against him, or the statement of the defendant, shows justification. or mitigation. Gay, 173 Ga. 793 (161 S. E. 603).

Where the killing is proven to be the act of the defendant, the presumption of innocence with which he enters upon the trial is removed from him, and the burden is then upon him to justify or mitigate the homicide. Elliott, 132 Ga. 758 (64 S. E. 1090).

Where on the trial for murder the accused admitted the killing, but coupled such admission with declarations which, if believed, showed justification, no presumption that the homicide was murder arose from such admission. Perkins, 124 Ga. 6 (52 S. E. 17).

Where the killing is proved the law presumes that every person intends the natural consequences of his acts. Chelsey, 121 Ga. 340 (2) (49 S. E. 258). 

All men are presumed to intend the natural and proximate consequences of their acts. Where a man kills another by use of means appropriate to that end, he is presumed to have intended that end. 

Kinsey, 24 Ga. App. 342 (1) (100 S. E. 770); Fallon, 5 Ga. App. 659 (1-a) (63 S. E. 806). 

The law presumes an intentional homicide to the malicious until the contrary is shown by circumstances of alleviation, excuse or justification; and it is incumbent on the defendant to make out such circumstances, to the satisfaction of the jury, unless the State's

SPECIFIC CRIMES 

455 evidence shows it. Robertson, 162 Ga. 1, 5 (132 S. E. 418); Greer, 159 Ga. 85 (3) (125 S. E. 52).

Presumption of malice arises by proof of the homicide, committed by the defendant as laid in the indictment. The burden then shifts to the defendant to show justification. Peek, 155 Ga. 49 (6) (116 

S. E. 629).

Where the evidence relied upon by the State to establish the fact of the homicide discloses circumstances of mitigation or justification, such evidence does not raise a presumption of malice. Surles, 148 

Ga. 537 (97 S. E. 538).

The presumption of malice is rebuttable. Harrell, 22 Ga. App. 

104 (95 S. E. 537).

The jury, in case of homicide, would not be authorized to find the defendant guilty of murder on the bare presumption raised by proof of the killing, if such presumption had been fully rebutted by positive and direct testimony, reasonable in its character and given by a credible witness. Edwards, 7 Ga. App. 623, 624 (67 S. E. 701).

Malice will be implied in every case where no considerable provocation occurs and all circumstances of the killing show abandoned and malignant heart. Shepherd, 150 Ga. 799, 800 (3) (105 S. E. 485).

The law presumes every homicide to be felonious, until the contrary appears, and it is incumbent upon the accused to show cir cumstances of alleviation. Elrod, 27 Ga. App. 265 (2) (108 S. E. 

67).

Malice. Malice is a state of mind, an intention to kill under such circumstances as the law would not justify nor in any way excuse. Goosby, 153 Ga. 496, 497 (4) (112 S. E. 467).

Malice involves intention and sometimes more besides. Williams, 13 Ga. App. 83, 85 (78 S. E. 854).

Malice does not necessarily mean that there shall be entertained any hatred by the slayer, or ill will, or ill feeling or anything of that character toward the person killed. It means intention on part of the slayer to take human life. Crawford, 149 Ga. 485 (2) (100 S. E. 693); Warren, 163 Ga. 176, 178 (11) (135 S. E. 735). 

There can be no murder without malice. Slocumb, 157 Ga. 131, 133 (8) (121 S. E. 116).

Malice may be implied in a killing by reckless driving. Wright, 166 Ga. 1 (1) (2) (145 S. E. 452). 

Malice may be implied where no considerable provocation appears, and where all circumstances of the killing show abandoned

and malignant heart. An abandoned and malignant heart, in the sense of law, is commonly held to be evidenced by weapons likely to produce death and brutal and bloodthirsty use of the same. It is for the jury to determine whether the wound, and the weapon, used in an ordinary way, was a weapon likely to produce death, and whether there was a brutal and bloodthirsty use of such weapon. 

Reed, 168 Ga. 731, 732 (10) (149 S. E. 23).

Malice, as an ingredient of the crime of murder, imports an unlawful killing. Nail, 142 Ga. 595 (83 S. E. 226).

Malice need not have existed any length of time previous to the infliction of the mortal wound. If it existed but a moment before the homicide, it is sufficient. Mills, 133 Ga. 155 (1) (65 S. E. 368); 

Godbee, 141 Ga. 515, 521 (81 S. E. 876).

If the instrument, used in the manner in which it was used on the occasion, was a weapon likely to produce death, and from the use of such weapon in such manner death ensues, the law, from the use of such weapon in such manner, implies malice and the intent to kill. Donalson, 40 Ga. App. 360, 362 (3) (149 S. E. 429).

External circumstances, capable of proof, such as preparation to commit the offense, threats, previous difficulties, etc., indicate express malice. Henderson, 120 Ga. 504, 506 (2) (48 S. E. 167); 

Mann, 124 Ga. 760 (53 S. E. 324).

If a man feloniously and recklessly fires a loaded weapon into a crowd and kills a member of the crowd, he is guilty of murder, regardless whether he intended to kill any individual member of the crowd, or not. Smith, 124 Ga. 213, 214 (52 S. E. 329); Hamilton, 129 Ga. 747 (2) (59 S. E. 803).

Where the evidence is conflicting, the question of malice is for the jury. Delk, 135 Ga. 312 (1) (69 S. E. 541); Boyd, 136 Ga. 340 (4-a) (71 S. E. 416).

It is the absence of malice which differentiates manslaughter from murder. If at the time of the killing the circumstances are such as to exclude malice, then the homicide can not be murder. Mize, 135 Ga. 291, 298 (69 S. E. 173); Mills, 133 Ga. 155 (1) (65 S. E. 

368); Nail, 142 Ga. 595 (83 S. E. 226).

Where one voluntarily fired a loaded pistol at another without excuse or justification and kills the person, it is no defense that the accused only intended to wound, or maim the deceased. Stovall, 106 Ga. 443 (3) (32 S. E. 586); Scott, 132 Ga. 357 (1) (64 S. E. 272). 

Duels. If two parties intentionally agree to fight with deadly weapons and in such fight one kills the other, the person killing is

SPECIFIC CRIMES 

457 guilty of murder or voluntary manslaughter. Daniels, 157 Ga. 780 

If two persons deliberately agree to fight with deadly weapons on a subsequent day at a definite time and place, and both being armed, they meet by chance near the appointed place and near the appointed time, and without any fresh cause of quarrel or other altercation one slays the other without justification, the crime is murder and not voluntary manslaughter. Bundrick, 125 Ga. 753 (2) (54 S. E. 638).

Defense. 

Killing in revenge for past wrong. The law never justifies a killing for a past injury, nor will a person be deprived of the right of self-defense solely because he may have been guilty in the past of some wrongful act. Brown, 135 Ga. 656, 659 (70 S. E. 329).

Justification can not be based on a deadly assault which has been completely ended, unless the assailant has some further apparent ability to continue it. Cochran, 9 Ga. App. 824, 825 (72 S. E. 281).

If the parent deliberately slays one who has debauched his daughter, in revenge of the wrong, the killing is murder. The law does not justify killing for deliberate revenge, however grievous the past wrong may have been. The law does not trust the punishment to individual vengeance. Mize, 135 Ga. 291, 297 (69 S. E. 173); 

Patterson, 134 Ga. 264, 265 (67 S. E. 816).

While a husband may be justified in killing another man, if necessary to prevent the latter from committing rape on the wife of the former, he will not be justified at a later day in killing the other person in revenge for a previous attempt to commit rape upon his wife. Ellison, 137 Ga. 193 (4) (73 S. E. 255).

Where a wife had been suspected by her husband of infidelity, and she later admitted that she had been guilty of adultery, and also stated that she will see her paramour again, this did not justify the killing of the wife by her husband, nor did it reduce the homicide from murder to manslaughter, and the question of voluntary manslaughter was not involved. Stevens, 137 Ga. 520 (73 S. E. 737).

While a father may not lawfully kill one merely because he has had unlawful sexual intercourse with his daughter, still he may justify the homicide by showing that it was necessary in order to prevent further acts of fornication. And there is no qualification to this rule as to time and place. Miller, 9 Ga. App. 599 (1) (71 S. 

E. 1021).

Neither the fact that the person who was assaulted made grave charges against his own wife, who was the defendant's sister, nor the fact that he did not believe these charges to be true when he made them, would justify the defendant in shooting him, or reduce the homicide from murder to manslaughter. Renfoe, 8 Ga. 

App. 676 (70 S. E. 70).

Killing deliberately after reason has had time to resume its sway can not be justifiable homicide. Ward, 25 Ga. App. 296 (1) (103 

S. E. 726). 

Drunkenness. Voluntary drunkenness is no defense. Bonner, 26 

Ga. App. 185 (4) (105 S. E. 863); Peek, 155 Ga. 49 (7) (116 S. E. 

629). But if voluntary drunkenness causes permanent insanity, the defense of insanity applies. Peek, 155 Ga. 49 (7) (116 S. E. 629).

General denial. In a homicide trial the defendant may avail himself of both defenses,-that he did not kill the deceased, and that if he killed him it was justifiable. Green, 7 Ga. App. 803 (68 

S. E. 318). 

Defendant's plea of "not guilty" puts in issue every material allegation in the indictment, charging him with the offense of murder. Phillips, 131 Ga. 426 (62 S. E. 239).

Self-defense. Every person has a right to take human life when it becomes necessary to do so in order to save his own life, or in defense of his person against one manifestly intending or endeavoring, by violence or surprise, to commit a felony on him. Phinazee, 27 Ga. App. 610 (3) (109 S. E. 691).

While one is attempting, without provocation, to commit a felony on another, the latter will not be justified in killing the former, unless there is a necessity to do so to prevent the commission of a felony, or the circumstances are such as to excite the fears of a reasonable man that such necessity exists, and the slayer really acts under the influence of such fears in killing his assailant. Jones, 147 Ga. 356 (4) (94 S. E. 248). § 26-1014 providing that the danger must be urgent and pressing to justify the killing, does not qualify or limit the law of justifiable homicide as laid down in §§ 26-1011 and 26-1012. White, 24 

Ga. App. 122 (100 S. E. 9). 

Where self-defense is relied on, § 26-1016, providing for all other instances which stand upon the same footing of reason and justice, -not applicable. Ward, 25 Ga. App. 296 (3) (103 S. E. 726).

If a person kill another in his defense, it must appear that the danger was so urgent and pressing at the time of the killing that

SPECIFIC CRIMES 

459 in order to save his own life the killing of the other was absolutely necessary, and it must appear also that the person killed was the assailant or that the slayer had really and in good faith endeavored to decline any further struggle before the mortal blow was given. 

Hill, 164 Ga. 298, 299 (4) (138 S. E. 299).

It is voluntary manslaughter to kill to prevent trespass to one's person, family, or property,—less than a felony. Gaillard, 149 Ga. 

190 (3) (99 S. E. 629); Robertson, 162 Ga. 1 (132 S. E. 418); Bozeman, 150 Ga. 667 (104 S. E. 640).

One can not create an emergency which rendered it necessary for another to defend himself, and then take advantage of the effort of such other person to do so. Pryer, 128 Ga. 28 (3) (57 S. 

E. 93); Price, 137 Ga. 71 (5) (72 S. E. 908); Short, 140 Ga. 780, 

One does not forfeit his right to defend himself against an assault solely because he may have been guilty of a wrongful act in the past. Brown, 135 Ga. 656 (70 S. E. 329).

Where one provokes a difficulty and makes no effort to decline it, but kills his adversary in the contest, it is not justifiable homicide, but if a person provokes a difficulty and the provocation amounts to no more than a trespass merely, it would not put him in the wrong in resisting or defending himself against a felonious attack on account of such provocation. Bennett, 19 Ga. App. 442 (2) (91 S. E. 889).

One who provokes a difficulty may yet defend himself against violence on the part of the one provoked, if the violence be disproportionate to the seriousness of the provocation or greater in degree than the law recognizes as justifiable under the circumstances. 

Sams, 124 Ga. 25 (52 S. E. 18); Bennett, 19 Ga. App. 442, 445 (91 

S. E. 889).

If the defendant made a felonious assault upon the son of the deceased, such as to justify the father in protecting the person of his son, the defendant could not claim the deceased was the aggressor, in defending the felonious assault upon his son. Mize, 135 

Ga. 291, 296 (69 S. E. 173).

On the trial for murder one can derive no benefit from the principles of self-defense, if it appears that he himself provoked the difficulty and himself created the necessity to defend. Riley, 3 Ga. 

App. 534 (4) (60 S. E. 274). 

An actual assault is unnecessary. Fallon, 5 Ga. App. 659 (2) (63 

S. E. 806).

Generally it is immaterial how a threat was communicated; the question of importance is, was it actually received by the party against whom it was directed? Thurman, 14 Ga. App. 543 (1) (81 

S. E. 796).

It is well settled that where one in repelling a mere assault commits a homicide, he is at least guilty of voluntary manslaughter. 

Franklin, 15 Ga. App. 349, 351 (83 S. E. 196); Sinyard, 17 Ga. App. 285 (1) (86 S. E. 657). 

Defense of family. Parents and children may mutually protect each other and justify the defense of the person and reputation of each other. § 26-1015. Chisholm, 162 Ga. 13, 14 (2) (132 S. E. 388).

Brothers have the same right to defend each other as they have to defend themselves. Curtis, 2 Ga. App. 224, 226 (7) (58 S. E. 291); 

Mattox, 9 Ga. App. 292, 294 (70 S. E. 1120); Warnack, 3 Ga. App. 

590 (3) (60 S. E. 288).

The right which the law gives to a brother to defend a brother when in peril, and if need be to take life in such defense, does not necessarily depend on whether the brother himself is blameless or at fault. If the brother who interposes is himself blameless in connection with such attack, his right to interpose may be justified by a real or apparent necessity presented by the facts and circumstances as they appear to him at the moment of his interposition in behalf of his brother. Warnack, 3 Ga. App. 590 (4) (60 S. E. 288). 

If the defendant shot while acting under the fears of a reasonable man that the life of his sister was in danger, or that a felony was being attempted upon her person, he is not guilty of any offense. Whittemore, 26 Ga. App. 273, 275 (106 S. E. 16).

If the deceased was endeavoring to take the life of the defendant or his brother, who was present and did the actual shooting, or was endeavoring to commit a felony on either, and if there was a command to shoot by the defendant to his brother, the killing was justifiable. Lawhorn, 158 Ga. 473 (3) (123 S. E. 808).

It is voluntary manslaughter to kill to prevent a trespass to one's person, family, or property,-less than a felony. Gaillard, 149 Ga. 190 (3) (99 S. E. 629); Robertson, 162 Ga. 1 (132 S. E. 

418); Bozeman, 150 Ga. 667 (2) (104 S. E. 640).

The right of mutual protection does not extend to a brother in law. Gillis, 8 Ga. App. 696 (2) (70 S. E. 53).

Reasonable fear. The doctrine of reasonable fear does not apply to any case of homicide where the danger apprehended is not ur-

SPECIFIC CRIMES 

461 gent and pressing, or apparently so, at the time of the killing. 

Short, 140 Ga. 780 (3) (80 S. E. 8).

A bare fear of any of those offenses, stated in the Code, to prevent which the homicide is alleged to have been committed, shall not be sufficient to justify the killing. It must appear that the circumstances were sufficient to excite the fears of a reasonable man, and that the party killing really acted under the influence of those fears, and not in a spirit of revenge. Nunn, 14 Ga. App. 695 (82 S. E. 56); Worley, 136 Ga. 231, 233 (71 S. E. 153). § 26-1012.

Under § 26-1012 circumstances sufficient to excite the fears of a reasonable man, and acting under the influence of such fears, and not in spirit of revenge, take the place of proof of an actual endeavor on the part of the person slain to commit such act. Worley, 136 Ga. 231, 234 (71 S. E. 153).

The Code does not undertake to define what circumstances shall or shall not be sufficient to excite the fears of a reasonable man. It is true that in order to justify a homicide, there must be something more than mere verbal threats. There must be an appearance of imminent danger. The means of inflicting the threatened injury must apparently be at hand, and there must be some manifestation of the intention to inflict an injury presently; but it is not essential that there should be an actual assault. Mere threats or menaces may, under some circumstances, be sufficient. Rossi, 7 Ga. App. 732, 734 (68 S. E. 56); McCray, 134 Ga. 416, 430 (68 S. E. 62).

The expression "the fears of a reasonable man," as used in the Code, is identical in meaning with the expression, "fears of a reasonably courageous man." Cochran, 9 Ga. App. 824 (3) (72 S. E. 281).

A bare fear of injury can never be regarded as sufficient to justify a homicide. The doctrine of reasonable fears as a defense does not apply to any case of homicide where the danger apprehended is not urgent and pressing, or apparently so, at the time of the killing. 

Ellison, 137. Ga. 193 (1) (73 S. E. 255); Williams, 120 Ga. 870, 873 (48 S. E. 368); Tolbirt, 124 Ga. 767 (4) (53 S. E. 327); Martin, 36 

Ga. App. 288, 291 (136 S. E. 324).

Absolute necessity to kill is not the only test by which to determine whether a homicide was justifiable, and it is error for the Court to confuse the defenses stated in §§ 26-1011, 26-1012 and 

26-1014. McCray, 134 Ga. 416 (68 S. E. 62).

The word "felony" as used in § 26-1011 means an offense for which the offender, on conviction, shall be punished by death or

imprisonment in the penitentiary, and not otherwise. Freeman, 1 

Ga. App. 276 (2), 277 (57 S. E. 924).

The idea of prevention or defense against an impending or progressing wrong must enter into all cases of justifiable homicide. 

Mize, 135 Ga. 291 (3) (69 S. E. 173).

The words "acting under the fears of a reasonable man" embrace, in substance, both actual and apparent necessity. Edwards, 7 Ga. 

App. 623, 626 (67 S. E. 701). 

Sufficiency of reasonableness of fear is for the jury. Dorsey, 2 Ga. App. 228, 231 (58 S. E. 477).

Where the evidence in a murder trial showed that the defendant was attacked by the deceased, her husband, with a garden fencepaling, and in order to save her life, or in fear of her life, she cut him with a knife, thereby causing his death, it was held that she was justified and a verdict finding her guilty of manslaughter was reversed. Lewis, 4 Ga. App. 219 (60 S. E. 1068).

A bare fear that the life of the accused, or his limb, or person, was in danger at the time he took the life of the deceased, will not justify the killing. It must appear that the circumstances were such as would excite the fears of a reasonable man. Roseboro, 127 

Ga. 826 (3) (56 S. E. 991); Rooks, 42 Ga. App. 474 (2) (156 S. E. 479). 

If the defendant shot the deceased under the fears of a reasonable person that some bodily harm was about to be done him amounting to a felony,-not a misdemeanor, and he really acted under the influence of those fears and not in a spirit of revenge, then he was justified, and the seeming necessity, when acted upon in good faith, is the equivalent of real necessity. McKie, 165 Ga. 

210 (7) (140 S. E. 625).

If the accused was only justified in believing that the deceased attempted the offense of stabbing on his person, he was not justified in shooting the deceased. Martin, 28 Ga. App. 723, 726 (f) (113 

S. E. 27).

The doctrine of reasonable fear applies only where the danger is urgent and pressing, or apparently so, at the time of the killing. 

Ingram, 26 Ga. App. 233 (4) (105 S. E. 727); Elrod, 27 Ga. App. 

265 (1) (108 S. E. 67).

Adultery, fornication, seduction, rape. A husband may be justified in killing another man, if necessary to prevent the latter from committing rape upon the wife of the former. Ellison, 137 Ga. 193 (73 S. E. 255).

SPECIFIC CRIMES 

463 A husband may attack another for intimacy with his wife in his presence, raising a well founded belief that the criminal act is "just over or about to begin," and the adulterer, though in danger, has no right to defend himself by using a deadly weapon. Wilkerson, 91 Ga. 729, 734 (17 S. E. 990); Drysdale, 83 Ga. 744 (10 S. E. 

358); Daniels, 162 Ga. 366, 369 (133 S. E. 855); Redding, 25 Ga.

"Just over or about to begin" is used with reference to the state of facts and circumstances which left doubtful in the mind of the husband the stage of the proceedings which his arrival interrupted. 

In other words, if the situation as disclosed to the husband was such that he was unable to determine whether the adulterous act was just over or about to begin, he would be justified in killing the adulterer. Brown, 135 Ga. 656, 658 (70 S. E. 329).

While it is true that the jury may acquit the slayer of all crimes if they find that the killing was necessary, or apparently so, either to prevent the commission of the sexual intercourse or the completion of the same, yet, if the circumstances were not such as to impress a rational mind that it was necessary to take human life to prevent sexual intercourse, and if the jury should find that the slayer killed the deceased under a violent and sudden impulse of passion, engendered by the circumstances, the homicide would be manslaughter. Patterson, 134 Ga. 264, 266 (67 S. E. 816).

If a man takes the life of another who attempts the seduction of his wife, under circumstances of direct and gross aggravation, it is for the jury to find whether the case stands upon the same footing of reason and justice as other instances of justifiable homicide enumerated in the Code. Rossi, 7 Ga. App. 732 (2) (68 S. E. 56).

A husband has a right to kill to prevent the seduction of his daughter or adultery of his wife, where the jury is authorized to infer that the killing stands upon the same footing of reason and justice as self-defense. Coart, 156 Ga. 536, 538 (119 S. E. 723).

It can not be justifiable homicide for the slayer to kill his wife's paramour after the act of adultery. O'Shields, 125 Ga. 310, 312 (54) 

S. E. 120).

Where the deceased committed assault upon defendant's wife, verdict of guilty of voluntary manslaughter upheld. Evans, 32 Ga. 

App. 36 (1) (122 S. E. 623).

A parent may protect his minor daughter from debauchery to the same extent that the husband may defend the chastity and virtue of his wife. Gossett, 123 Ga. 431 (1) (51 S. E. 394).

Where the accused found the deceased in the act of intimacy with the accused's wife, a conviction of involuntary manslaughter is unauthorized. Gibson, 44 Ga. App. 264 (161 S. E. 158).

Communications made to husband by wife after the homicide, in regard to improper proposals made to her by the deceased would not justify the killing. Best, 26 Ga. App. 671 (9) (107 S. E. 266).

Defense of property. It is justifiable homicide to kill to prevent a felony upon one's habitation or property or under such circumstances as would arouse the fears of a reasonable man that a felony was about to be committed. Hughes, 159 Ga. 828 (2) (127 S. E. 113).

A person may be justified in killing to prevent his habitation from being entered through violence or surprise by persons attempting to enter in a riotous manner, even though they have no actual or apparent intention to commit a felony therein, but intend merely to commit a misdemeanor upon the slayer or some person dwelling in the habitation. Brown, 8 Ga. App. 382 (5) (69 S. E. 45).

One who may rightfully eject another from his house has the right to use whatever force is necessary to accomplish that purpose. 

If request, persuasion, and remonstrance have proven fruitless, and the right to the possession of one's home and the protection of his family require the eviction of the intruder, the degree of force which may be employed is limited only by the necessity for its Even life itself may be taken if a lesser degree of force is unavailing. Rossi, 7 Ga. App. 732 (68 S. E. 56). use.

A killing to prevent a taking of slight moment or importance can not be justified, though the taking may technically amount to robbery. Bennett, 19 Ga. App. 442, 446 (91 S. E. 889).

If one steals the property of another, and flees, and the owner, upon learning later of the theft, pursues and overtakes him, at a distance from the place where the larceny was committed, without any effort to retake possession by peaceable means, and without any necessity to take life, fires upon the thief and kills him, such killing is not justifiable, though the theft be a felony. Drew, 136 Ga. 658 (3) (71 S. E. 1108).

If the owner of property is authorized to use reasonable force for its protection, or recapture from a fleeing thief, and does no more, and such thief resists the owner with force, his conduct may be such as to place him in the position of the aggressor, and to authorize the owner to defend himself by the use of further reasonable force. Drew, 136 Ga. 658 (2) (71 S. E. 1108).

SPECIFIC CRIMES 

465 

The words "a serious injury" in § 26-1013 are not limited to a felony. Freeney, 129 Ga. 759 (4) (59 S. E. 788). But the injury herein referred to must be such as in its nature, character, or effect is "traveling to a felony." Bennett, 19 Ga. App. 442, 446 (91

S. E. 889). 

Provocation. Words, threats, menaces, or contemptuous gestures alone are insufficient to reduce the homicide from murder to manslaughter. Jackson, 160 Ga. 565 (128 S. E. 579); Elrod, 27 Ga. 

App. 265 (4) (108 S. E. 67); Coleman, 149 Ga. 186 (99 S. E. 627). 

Provocation by words, threats, menaces or contemptuous gestures might amount to a complete justification if the jury should determine that they were sufficient, under the circumstances, to excite the fears of a reasonable man that a felony was about to be committed upon him. Griggs, 17 Ga. App. 301 (7) (86 S. E. 726); 

Rouse, 136 Ga. 356, 359, 360 (71 S. E. 667); Vernon, 146 Ga. 709, 714 (92 S. E. 76).

If the provocation given by the deceased to the defendant, and the only provocation given him, was to advance and place his hand upon his collar, and the conduct was justified, then that conduct of the deceased would not avail the defendant for the purpose of reducing the offense from murder to voluntary manslaughter. Slocumb, 157 Ga. 131, 132 (7) (121 S. E. 116).

While it is true that "provocation," in one sense of the word, is an "action or mode of conduct that excites resentment or vindictive feeling; a cause of anger" (Standard Dictionary), and, as used in the Code it has been so construed by the Supreme Court, it is nevertheless also understood and defined in the broader sense of "an incitement to action" (Standard Dictionary), "that which arouses and moves" (Webster's International Dictionary); "provoke" is defined as "to call forth, cause, occasion" (Century 

Dictionary). Manson, 14 Ga. App. 837, 838 (82 S. E. 763).

Whether in a particular case words, threats, or menaces are sufficient to arouse in the mind of the person to whom they are directed a reasonable fear that his life is in imminent danger, or that a felony is about to be committed on his person,-is a question for the jury. Manson, 14 Ga. App. 837, 838 (82 S. E. 763).

Malice is excluded if the intention to kill grows out of hot blood produced by provocation other than that produced by mere words, threats, menaces, or contemptuous gestures. Robertson, 162 Ga. 1, 6 (132 S. E. 418).

Arrest. One upon whom an arrest unlawfully and without a warrant is attempted to be made has a right to resist force with force proportionate to that being used in detaining him. The mere fact of unlawful arrest will not alone authorize the killing of the officer making it. But if, in the progress of the transaction, the officer is about to commit a felony upon the other party, and so acts, and makes such a show of violence, as to excite in the person sought to be arrested the fears of a reasonable man that a felony is about to be committed upon him, and such a person acts under the influence of those fears, and not in the spirit of revenge, he may protect himself, although it may be necessary to slay the officer for the purpose. In some cases, where the circumstances are not such as to justify the killing of the officer, they may be sufficient to reduce the killing from murder to manslaughter. Perdue, 135 Ga. 277, 284 (69 S. E. 184); Norton, 137 Ga. 842 (3) (74 S. E. 759); Reed, 163 Ga. 206, 208 (135 S. E. 748); Howell, 162 Ga. 14, 16 (6-b) (132 

S. E. 59); Giddens, 154 Ga. 54 (3) (113 S. E. 386); Wall, 153 Ga. 

309, 310 (11) (112 S. E. 142).

Generally to slay a person who without authority of law is seeking to make an arrest for a misdemeanor, where the motive of the slayer is merely to avoid an arrest, is manslaughter. Plemmons, 43 

Ga. App. 344 (158 S. E. 630).

The killing of an officer while resisting a legal arrest is murder. 

Alexander, 160 Ga. 769, 770 (129 S. E. 102).

That the attempted arrest is illegal will not alone authorize the killing of the officer making it. Howell, 162 Ga. 14, 16 (6-a) (132 

S. E. 59); Wall, 153 Ga. 309 (11), 310 (112 S. E. 142).

If an unauthorized person seeks to make an arrest, but does nothing to put the other in real or apparent danger of life, and if the mere assault is met by drawing and firing a deadly weapon upon the person making the arrest, the latter, not having forfeited his right to live, and not having created a legal necessity for such deadly resistance, may defend himself against the excessive and unjustifiable counter-assault. Coleman, 121 Ga. 594 (49 S. E. 716).

If the defendant began the unlawful arrest with an intent to kill if necessary to make it effective, and by a show of deadly weapons put the deceased in the fear of his life, and the latter thereupon drew, and fired, the defendant, having provoked and created a necessity, could not meet the same, but would be guilty of murder if under such circumstances he took the life of the party legally resisting the illegal arrest. Coleman, 121 Ga. 594 (5) (49 S. E. 716).

SPECIFIC CRIMES 

467 Where a deputy sheriff was murdered while attempting to arrest the defendant at his still, when he was in the act of operating it, the law relative to the right of a person to resist an illegal arrest is inapplicable, the offense being a felony, and the officer having a right to make an arrest with or without a warrant. Williams, 148 Ga. 310 (1) (96 S. E. 385).

While to slay one who, without a warrant, is seeking to arrest another for a misdemeanor, to avoid arrest, is manslaughter, it is murder to kill an officer to prevent the latter from arresting the slayer. Glaze, 156 Ga. 807 (2-a) (120 S. E. 530).

Whether arrest is legal or illegal, if the deceased was loading a pistol, and said to, the defendant: "When I get my pistol loaded, I am going to kill you," and the defendant believed his life in danger, defendant shot in self-defense, and the homicide was justifiable. Paramore, 161 Ga. 166, 167 (129 S. E. 772).

If an escaped convict, whether felony or misdemeanor, kills an officer to prevent his capture, it is murder. Williford, 121 Ga. 173 (1) (48 S. E. 962). 

A fugitive from justice, accused of a felony and knowing that he is liable to be arrested on that charge, may nevertheless resist with such force as may be necessary an unlawful attempt to commit a crime upon him, whether such attempt is made by an official armed with a warrant for his arrest or by a private citizen under circumstances authorizing him to make an arrest, and this is true although the fugitive may have known he was liable to be arrested by the person making the attempt. It is one thing to resist a lawful arrest, and quite a different thing to resist an assault or other crime upon the person of the party liable to be arrested; and the latter can not be deprived of his right of self-defense, either because the other party could lawfully have arrested him, or because he knew that this was so. Smalls, 99 Ga. 25, 26 (4) (5) (25 S. E. 614). Abortion. Indictment. charge and accuse. ..with the offense of murder, for that the said.. ......., in the county aforesaid, did on theday of 

19...., then and there unlawfully and with force and arms, and without any intention to do so, but in the commission of an unlawful act which in its consequences naturally tends to destroy the life of a human being, did unlawfully, feloniously, and willfully kill and murder............ the said................being at the time a pregnant woman, by then and there using and employing an instrument and instruments to the jurors unknown,

which instrument and instruments by the said.. were used and employed for the purpose and with the intent to thereby produce a miscarriage and abortion of the said.................. and by the use of said instrument and instruments on the person of said...………………………….. did thereby cause and produce the miscarriage and abortion and thereby kill the said. ... the employment and use of the said instrument and instruments to the grand jurors unknown not being then and there necessary to preserve the life of the said....... and not having been advised by two physicians as necessary for that purpose; and the said................in the manner and form aforesaid the said.................did unlawfully, feloniously, and willfully kill and murder.. contrary, etc. . . . (Approved: Herndon, 38 

Ga. App. 117 (2), 118 (142 S. E. 695); Wilbanks, 41 Ga. App. 268, 269 (152 S. E. 619).)

Murder can be charged, where death ensues, and facts do not come under provisions of §§ 26-1101 or 26-1102. Summerlin, 150 

Ga. 173, 175 (103 S. E. 461).

State need not show that foetus was living. Wilbanks, 41 Ga.
