MANSLAUGHTER. 

VOLUNTARY MANSLAUGHTER. 

Intent. To constitute voluntary manslaughter the killing must be intentional. Alexander, 160 Ga. 769 (3) (129 S. E. 102).

Shooting at one and killing another. If a person shoots at another under such circumstances that if death ensued the offense would be reduced from murder to voluntary manslaughter, and by accident. the shot hits and kills another person standing by, for whom the shot was not intended, the offense would be voluntary manslaughter. 

McLendon, 172 Ga. 267 (157 S. E. 475); Strickland, 9 Ga. App. 552 (1) (72 S. E. 919); Hart, 135 Ga. 356 (69 S. E. 530).

Definition. Whenever a homicide is neither justifiable nor malicious it is manslaughter. Conley, 21 Ga. App. 134 (5) (94 S. 

E. 261).

In all cases of voluntary manslaughter there must be both such provocation as the statute provides, and passion. The provocation must come from an assault or an attempt to commit a serious personal injury, or from circumstances which are equivalent to an assault or an attempt to commit a serious personal injury, and

SPECIFIC CRIMES 

469 there must be an absence of all deliberation or malice, either express or implied. Harris, 2 Ga. App. 487, 488 (58 S. E. 680).

It is not every blow which will, as a matter of law, reduce a homicide from murder to voluntary manslaughter. It is a question for the jury whether the provocation is sufficient to justify the excitement of passion and to exclude all idea of deliberation or malice, express or implied. Reese, 3 Ga. App. 610, 613 (60 S. E. 284).

A homicide to be voluntary manslaughter must be the result of that sudden, violent impulse of passion supposed to be irresistible and justly aroused. For if there should have been an interval between the assault or provocation and the homicide, sufficient for the voice of reason and humanity to be heard, the killing is attributed to deliberate revenge and is murder. Williams, 130 Ga. 

400, 406 (60 S. E. 1053). 

Where the defendant shot the deceased, not in fear of a felonious assault, but because a minor assault sufficient to justify the excitement and passion, voluntary manslaughter was involved. Johnson, 39 Ga. App. 836 (2) (148 S. E. 610). 

Provocation. Words, threats, menaces, and contemptuous gestures on the part of the deceased are not, unless they amount to an assault, effectual to mitigate a homicide from murder into manslaughter, though they may create such an apparent danger as to justify a homicide. Brantley, 5 Ga. App. 458 (63 S. E. 519).

If the killing was the result of a sudden heat of passion, it is immaterial who provoked the difficulty, or how justifiable the passion may have been, on a conviction of manslaughter. Anderson, 14 Ga. 

App. 607 (2) (81 S. E. 802); Gann, 30 Ga. 67.

The provocation may be a single act or fresh provocation may extend the initial provocation to the time of the homicide, so as to excite a sudden and uncontrollable passion. Mize, 135 Ga. 291, 298 (69 S. E. 173).

The fact that the person slain may himself have been actuated by violent passion, in the absence of any demonstration by him against the slayer, has no bearing upon the grade of the homicide. Rentfrow, 123 Ga. 539 (51 S. E. 596).

The question of provocation, heat, uncontrollable passion, are for the jury. Mattox, 9 Ga. App. 292, 294 (70 S. E. 1120).

Equivalent circumstances. The law does not specifically declare what circumstances shall be deemed "equivalent." It furnishes a standard, and leaves the jury in each case to make a comparison ·

and determine whether the facts of the case before them come up to the standard or not. Findley, 125 Ga. 579 (4) (54 S. E. 106).

The law does not require "other equivalent circumstances, referred to in § 26-1007, as reducing the killing from murder to voluntary manslaughter, to be in the nature of an assault or an attempt to commit a serious personal injury by the deceased. The "other equivalent circumstances" must be such as would as much exclude all idea of deliberation or malice and justify the excitement of passion as would an assault, or an attempt to commit a serious personal injury. Battle, 133 Ga. 182 (65 S. E. 382); Land, 11 Ga. App. 761 (4) (76 S. E. 78).

In order to reduce a homicide from the grade of murder to that of voluntary manslaughter, where there was neither an actual assault upon the slayer nor an attempt to commit upon him a serious bodily injury, it is not necessary that the proof should show that the circumstances of the killing were in the nature of an assault or an attempt to seriously injure his person, but only that the circumstances were such as would as much justify the excitement of passion as would an actual assault or attempt to commit a serious personal injury. Rumsey, 126 Ga. 419 (2) (55 S. E. 167).

As brothers have a right of mutual protection under the law, an actual assault by the person killed upon the brother of the person killing, or an attempt by the person killed to commit a serious personal injury upon the brother of the person killing is included in the above provision-"other equivalent circumstances." Sheffield, 16 Ga. App. 287 (85 S. E. 253); Armistead, 18 Ga. 704, 708.

Cooling time. If there should have been an interval between the assault or provocation given and the homicide, sufficient for the voice of reason and humanity to be heard, the killing shall be attributed to deliberate revenge, and be punished as murder. Williams, 130 Ga. 400, 406 (60 S. E. 1053); Harris, 2 Ga. App. 487, 489 (58 S. E. 680); Nixon, 14 Ga. App. 261, 263 (80 S. E. 513).

The question of "cooling time" is for the jury. Williams, 130 

Ga. 400 (60 S. E. 1053); Mize, 135 Ga. 291, 298 (69 S. E. 173); Mc- 

Phearson, 19 Ga. App. 232, 233 (91 S. E. 336).

Accomplices. One may be convicted as principal in the second degree of the offense of voluntary manslaughter. Pope, 13 Ga. App. 

711 (1) (79 S. E. 909); Maughon, 9 Ga. App. 559 (71 S. E. 922).

But not as an accessory before the fact to voluntary manslaughter, because the existence of an accessory presupposes premeditation and preparation. Maughon, 9 Ga. App. 559, 567 (71 S. E. 922).

SPECIFIC CRIMES 

471 Convicts. The law which provides for reducing a homicide from murder to voluntary manslaughter makes no exception of a convict, but contemplates that no homicide by any person shall be classed as murder where there is an absence of malice, and that there may be an absence of malice on the part of the slayer if the homicide is the result of irresistible passion produced by an assault or some similar act. Westbrook, 133 Ga. 578, 585 (66 S. E. 788).

Adultery, fornication. If the parent deliberately slays one who has debauched his daughter, in revenge of the wrong, the killing is murder; but the defilement of a daughter is more likely to arouse the resentment of a father than an actual assault upon his own person. If, upon discovery of a wrong inflicted upon his daughter, and under circumstances sufficient to arouse an uncontrollable passion and to exclude all idea of revenge, the parent suddenly kills the person who has debauched her, the homicide is manslaughter. 

Mize, 135 Ga. 291, 297 (69 S. E. 173).

Where a husband finds his wife at night in company with a man, and the wife then and there discloses to the husband that she is guilty of acts of infidelity, and that the man in whose company she is is her paramour, and that she intends to continue her acts of infidelity, and lascivious intercourse with the man in whose company she is found, and the husband, in the heat of passion excited by the words and conduct of the wife, shoots and kills her, on the trial of the husband under an indictment charging him with the offense of murder, the jury would be authorized to find him guilty of manslaughter. The killing of the wife by the husband under such circumstances could not be justifiable homicide. Jackson, 135 

Ga. 684 (2). (2-a) (70 S. E. 245).

The fact that the deceased, the wife of the slayer, may have been unchaste, would not in itself amount to justification of the homicide, nor would it, in the absence of sudden heat of passion, be sufficient to reduce the homicide from murder to manslaughter. Rogers, 128 Ga. 67 (57 S. E. 227).

Mutual combat. Mutual combat exists where there is a fight and both parties are willing to fight. Slocumb, 157 Ga. 132 (3-a) (121 

S. E. 116).

Mutual combat appears sufficiently where mutual intent by the accused and the deceased to fight is shown, and one or more shots are fired, or one or more blows struck. Daniels, 157 Ga. 780, 781 (4) (122 S. E. 223). Bailey, 148 Ga. 401 (96 S. E. 862).

Mutual intent to fight may exist where there is a mutual intention to fight, though only one blow be struck. Rutland, 28 Ga. App. 

145, 146 (110 S. E. 634).

Mutual intent to fight may be inferred by the jury from the conduct of the parties. Sapp, 2 Ga. App. 449 (58 S. E. 667). 

Mutual blows are not always necessary. Hollis, 17 Ga. App. 77 (86 S. E. 95); Findley, 125 Ga. 579, 583 (54 S. E. 106).

Where there is no evidence of mutual combat, nor is it shown in the defendant's statement, it is error to charge that section. Lamp, 164 Ga. 57 (137 S. E. 765).

Doctrine of seeming or apparent necessity does not apply to case of mutual intent to fight. Shepherd, 150 Ga. 799 (1) (105 S. E. 485).

Although there may be a mutual intention to fight, and agreement to that effect, yet if one of the disputants kill the other with malice, it is murder. Cargile, 137 Ga. 775 (74 S. E. 621). 

Where two men suddenly fall out and quarrel, and draw knives. and fight, and one kills the other by stabbing him, the offense is voluntary manslaughter. Johnson, 4 Ga. App. 59 (60 S. E. 813).

No matter who struck the first blow, if there is a mutual intent to fight, and this intent is put into effect, if one of the fighters is killed, the killing is voluntary manslaughter. Gann, 30 Ga. 67; 

Sapp, 2 Ga. App. 449 (58 S. E. 667). 

Where the accused fired two shots, one before the deceased drew any weapon, and the other after he drew it, the jury was authorized to find that mutual combat existed and find the accused guilty of voluntary manslaughter. Smith, 8 Ga. App. 680, 681 (70 S. E. 42).

If the defendant shot the deceased after he had ceased to fight, and because the deceased had shortly before struck him with brass knucks, the killing would be voluntary manslaughter, if the defendant's shot was influenced by the heat of ungovernable passion. 

Webb, 8 Ga. App. 430, 432 (69 S. E. 601).

Where bad blood existed between the accused and the deceased on the night of the homicide, and both of them were armed with deadly weapons, and they intended to settle their differences by the use of these weapons, and the defendant killed the deceased under these circumstances, voluntary manslaughter is involved. 

Andrews, 38 Ga. App. 701 (2) (145 S. E. 499).

Reasonable fear. The doctrine of reasonable fear has no connection with voluntary manslaughter. Rawls, 160 Ga. 605, 606 (2) (128 S. E. 747).

SPECIFIC CRIMES 

473 

INVOLUNTARY MANSLAUGHTER. 

General. If the killing is caused by an unavoidable accident, then the defendant should be acquitted. Lyles, 130 Ga. 294, 304, 305 (60 S. E. 578); Allen, 134 Ga. 380 (1) (67 S. E. 1038).

There can be no conviction of the offense of involuntary manslaughter, either in the commission of an unlawful act, or in the commission of a lawful act without due caution and circumspection, where the homicide is directly due to an independent intervening cause, in which the accused did not participate and could not foresee. Garbo, 4 Ga. App. 583 (1) (62 S. E. 140).

Where one voluntarily shoots another and the shot kills, the homicide can not be involuntary. Conley, 21 Ga. App. 134, 315 (5) (94 S. E. 261).

Where the defendant pointed a pistol at the deceased, not intending to kill him, and pulled the trigger and fired, the result of such conduct, under the law, would not be accidental. Baker, 12 Ga. 

App. 553 (3) (77 S. E. 884).

In the commission of a lawful act. The essential elements of the offense of involuntary manslaughter in the commission of a lawful act, which must be charged and proved, are: (1) the killing of a human being; (2) without any intention to do so; (3) in the commission of a lawful act; (4) which might probably produce death; (5) in a manner not justified by law. Roughlin, 17 Ga. App. 205, 208 (86 S. E. 452).

The gist of the offense of involuntary manslaughter in the commission of a lawful act consists in the unlawful manner in which the act was done. In other words, if the act charged was not done in an unlawful manner, no offense was committed. Roughlin, 17 

Ga. App. 205, 209 (86 S. E. 452). 

Criminal negligence will support conviction. Flannigan, 136 Ga. 

132 (1) (70 S. E. 1107).

The law of misadventure or accident expressly excludes culpable neglect. So that, if a homicide be committed without evil design or intention, but with culpable neglect, it can not be said to have been the result of misfortune or accident. Allen, 134 Ga. 380, 381 (1) (67 S. E. 1038); Baker, 12 Ga. App. 553, 554 (77 S. E. 884).

In the commission of an unlawful act. The charge of involuntary manslaughter in the commission of an unlawful act can be based upon an act malum prohibitum as well as upon an act of malum in se. Silver, 13 Ga. App. 722 (4) (79 S. E. 919).

An act is not unlawful, within the purview of the statute defining

involuntary manslaughter, unless it is prohibited by some valid law of the State. Hayes, 11 Ga. App. 371 (75 S. E. 523).

Where a person, in violation of the statute, administers morphine. to another in such quantity as to cause death, he commits an unlawful act, and a conviction of involuntary manslaughter in the commission of an unlawful act would be authorized. It would be no defense that in the administration of the drug the intent was not to cause death, but to alleviate pain. Silver, 13 Ga. App. 722 (79

S. E. 919). 

Where one, without lawful justification, kicks another in the stomach, and, in consequence, his intestines are ruptured, and death. results, a verdict finding the slayer guilty of involuntary manslaughter in the commission of an unlawful act is authorized. Smith, 12 Ga. App. 13 (1) (76 S. E. 647).

Where death results to one from the discharge of a gun in the hands of another, who had no intention to kill, the discharge being caused by the reckless manner in which the gun was handled, the slayer is guilty of involuntary manslaughter. Leonard, 133 Ga. 435 (66 S. E. 251); Clonts, 18 Ga. App. 707 (90 S. E. 373); Baker, 12 

Ga. App. 553 (77 S. E. 884); Gray, 12 Ga. App. 634 (77 S. E. 916).

Automobiles. Where one operates an automobile upon a public street or highway at a rate of speed penalized by statute, or while under the influence of intoxicating liquors, and, in consequence thereof, he kills a human being without any intention to do so, he is, under the view of the case most favorable to him, guilty of involuntary manslaughter. Black, 34 Ga. App. 449 (2) (130 S. E. 

591); Hudson, 26 Ga. App. 596 (3) (107 S. E. 94); Herrington, 31 

Ga. App. 167 (120 S. E. 554).

In the prosecution for the killing of a person while operating an automobile and while in intoxicated condition, it is not necessary for the State to show that the accused was drunk, but it is sufficient if the State shows, beyond a reasonable doubt, that the accused was under the influence of some intoxicant, as charged, to any extent whatsoever, whether drunk or not. Chapman, 40 Ga. App. 

725 (2) (151 S. E. 410).

A chauffeur colliding with another while driving on the wrong side of the road and at an excessive speed, resulting in the death of the occupant of the other car, conviction of the owner, who was riding in the car with the chauffeur and who attempted to escape immediately afterwards, of involuntary manslaughter, authorized. 

This decision is based on the contention that the owner of the car

SPECIFIC CRIMES 

475 ET T. is liable for the illegal driving of his servant, unless it appears that the owner attempted to prevent such illegal driving, and the same was done against his will. Moreland, 164 Ga. 467, 468 (139 S. E. 77).

Where an automobile was driven at an excessive rate of speed by the defendant, striking and killing a child, after which he slowed up and continued on his way, conviction for involuntary manslaughter in the commission of an unlawful act is authorized. White, 26 Ga. 

App. 431 (106 S. E. 304). 

Convict guards. A conviction of involuntary manslaughter in the commission of an unlawful act was authorized by the evidence, from which it appeared that the deceased, a convict, working in the sun on a public highway on a very hot day, "gave out" and fell from the "wheeler" he was driving, and that the defendant, who was a convict guard, and another guard, made him get up and walk to a telephone pole and handcuffed him to it, and that in a few minutes he slumped down apparently unconscious and was taken to a camp, where he soon died of sunstroke. The jury were authorized to find, under the evidence and the defendant's statement, that the defendant was guilty of an assault and battery on the deceased, which contributed to and accelerated the death, and were its proximate cause, without any intention so to kill. Wells, 46 Ga. App. 412 (167 S. E. 709).

Abortion. 

Indictment. 

For the said. aforesaid, on the................day of.. in the county and State with force and arms, and without any intention to do so, but in the commission of an unlawful act, did unlawfully, feloniously, and willfully kill........ the said.. .....being at the time a pregnant woman, by then and there using and employing an instrument and instruments (to the grand jurors unknown) which said instrument and instruments. were by the said...................used and employed for the purpose and with the intent thereby to produce the miscarriage and abortion of the said, and by the use and employment of said instrument and instruments on the person of the said...did thereby cause and produce the miscarriage and abortion of the said... and did thereby kill the said................., the use and employment of said instrument and instruments not being then and there necessary to preserve the life of said... , and not having been advised by two physicians to be necessary for that purpose; said in the manner and form aforesaid, the said.................did un-

lawfully, feloniously, and willfully kill, . 

Summerlin, 25 Ga.

App. 565, 566 (103 S. E. 830). (Approved: Summerlin, 150 Ga. 173 

(103 S. E. 46).)

Involuntary manslaughter can be charged, where death ensues, and facts do not come under provisions of §§ 26-1101 or 26-1102. 

Summerlin, 150 Ga. 173, 175 (103 S. E. 46). 

See also: Abortion, Foeticide, Murder, Voluntary Manslaughter, Assault With Intent to Murder.

MISCELLANEOUS. 

Conspiracy. Mere presence and participation in the general transaction in which a homicide is committed is not conclusive evidence of consent and concurrence in the perpetration of the crime by a defendant sought to be responsible for the homicide as aiding and abetting the actual perpetrator, unless such defendant participated in the felonious design of the person killing. Futch, 137 Ga. 75 

Where the defendant and his half-brother have conspired to take the life of the deceased, the jury need not believe beyond a reasonable doubt that the defendant fired the shot that killed the deceased, -to authorize conviction. Ammons, 26 Ga. App. 652 (1) (106 S. 

E. 796).

Where one is jointly indicted with another for murder, and the evidence shows that the other party alone did the act which resulted in the death of the person alleged to have been murdered, and that the accused, although with the slayer at the time of the homicide, did nothing to assist or encourage its commission, and there being no evidence of conspiracy between the accused and the actual perpetrator of the offense, the verdict finding the accused guilty is illegal. Walker, 118 Ga. 10 (43 S. E. 586); Futch, 148 Ga. 

149 (95 S. E. 980).

Where several persons conspire to rob a merchant in his store, and one of the conspirators remains in his automobile in front of the store, with the engine running, in order that they may speedily escape from the scene of the robbery, while the others enter the store, and, in furtherance of the common design to rob, kill the merchant intended to be robbed, such killing is the probable consequence of the unlawful design to rob, and all the conspirators are guilty of murder, including the one in the automobile. It is not necessary that the crime of murder should be part of the original design; but it is enough if it be one of the incidental probable consequences of the execution of their design, and should appear at the moment to

SPECIFIC CRIMES 

477 one of the participants to be expedient for the common purpose. 

Gore, 162 Ga. 267 (1-a) (134 S. E. 36). 

See also: Accomplices.

Evidence. 

Motive. On the trial of one charged with murder the defendant's motive is always relevant. Boone, 145 Ga. 37 (1) (88 S. E. 

558); Helms, 138 Ga. 826, 830 (76 S. E. 353).

Acts of gross ill-treatment and cruelty on the part of the husband toward his wife, not too remote from the time of the alleged homicide of the latter by the former, or a continued line of misconduct extending near the time of the homicide,-admissible to show malice or motive. Roberts, 123 Ga. 146 (5) (51 S. E. 374); Campbell, 123 

Ga. 533 (2) (51 S. E. 644).

On the trial of one for the murder of his wife, evidence that while the accused was in custody by virtue of a warrant sworn out by his wife, the witness exhibited to him the warrant and a petition for habeas corpus for the custody of their minor child-admissible, to show motive, it further appearing that the homicide was committed a few hours thereafter. Lindsey, 145 Ga. 9 (88 S. E. 202).

Evidence that the deceased testified against the accused,-admissible to show motive. Hayes, 126 Ga. 95 (54 S. E. 809).

In homicide prosecution indictment against the defendant and others, charging them with larceny after trust,-admissible, there being some evidence to show that the deceased had been instrumental in procuring such indictment, and the Court instructing the jury that the indictment was admitted merely to show motive, and that the jury would not be interested in, nor concerned with any other question that might be illustrated by the indictment. Lance, 166 Ga. 15, 18 (14) (142 S. E. 105).

Evidence to show that the accused had made complaints as to the deceased having employed a laborer who was under contract of employment to the accused-inadmissible. Little, 164 Ga. 509 (139 

S. E. 37).

Where accused is charged with the murder of his father by assassination, evidence that before the homicide he has spoken of his father's having insurance on his life, and shortly after the killing he asked a witness to assist him in collecting the insurance money, -admissible. Johnson, 130 Ga. 22 (60 S. E. 158).

Evidence that the accused knew that the deceased carried insurance on his life, and that the accused was, or believed himself to be, the beneficiary-admissible. Johnson, 128 Ga. 71, 72 (57 S. E. 84).

Where the accused is charged with the homicide, and the motive assigned to the charge is that the deceased carried an insurance policy on his life, with the accused beneficiary thereon, the policy is admissible. Canady, 171 Ga. 11, 12 (2) (154 S. E. 332); Powers, 172 Ga. 1 (12) (157 S. E. 195).

Where the defendant is accused with murdering his father, whose heir at law he was, it is competent to show that the defendant has spoken of money that his father was supposed to have deposited in a bank, such evidence tending to show motive. But it is error to admit evidence to show the financial condition of the accused, and that he was in very indigent circumstances. Johnson, 128 Ga. 71 (57 S. E. 84).

Unchaste conduct of a wife or daughter, known to a husband or father prior to the homicide, by him claimed to have been committed to prevent a seduction or criminal intimacy with her, may throw light on his motives or acts. Gossett, 123 Ga. 431, 441 (51 

S. E. 394).

Corpus delicti. Where one is charged with a homicide, proof that the homicide, as charged, was actually committed must be clear and unequivocal. Such proof can be furnished by direct or circumstantial evidence. Brown, 10 Ga. App. 216 (73 S. E. 33).

The proof of the corpus delicti must not only show that the person has been killed, but must also identify the person shown to have been killed as the one whose death is the subject of inquiry. These elements must appear from some form of proof other than extrajudicial confessions or admissions alone; but if the defendant in his statement made on the trial of the case admits them, the State is not required to make further proof of them. Wall, 5 Ga. App. 

305 (63 S. E. 27).

Failure to prove the identity of the deceased as laid in indictment. -fatal. Holden, 144 Ga. 338 (3) (87 S. E. 27).

Where the dead body of a human being, partially destroyed by fire, was found in the debris of the burned residence of the defendant, with the head, arms, and legs truncated, no remains of these parts being found, but the remainder of the charred body was taken. out, this was sufficient evidence to prove the corpus delicti. Sligh, 171 Ga. 92, 93 (3) (154 S. E. 799).

Res gestae. Testimony describing wounds inflicted upon a person killed at the same time as the person with whose murder the accused is charged,-admissible, where such evidence is part of the res gestae. Westberry, 175 Ga. 115 (3) (164 S. E. 905).

SPECIFIC CRIMES 

479 The accused being on trial for the murder of his wife, the testimony of an eye-witness to the effect that he shot another woman just before shooting his wife, the two acts being performed so nearly in point of time as to make the first shooting a part of the res gestae of the act for which the accused was indicted,-admissible. 

Besides the evidence would show the animus of the defendant. 

Lampkin, 145 Ga. 40 (88 S. E. 563).

Evidence that the defendant was cursing and fighting at the time he was arrested-admissible to show animus of the accused on the occasion of the homicide. Scrutchens, 146 Ga. 189 (91 S. E. 25).

Surrounding circumstances. In a trial for murder the actions, intentions, and motives of both parties to the affray, and all the circumstances making up the res gestae, may be proved. Robinson, 118 Ga. 198 (44 S. E. 985).

In determining whether a killing is murder, voluntary manslaughter, or justifiable, all the facts and circumstances that preceded and led up to the killing are proper matter for the consideration of the jury, to determine the sufficiency of the provocation, cooling time, etc. Nixon, 14 Ga. App. 261, 263 (80 S. E. 513).

Evidence that upon an application for bail the judge had released the accused, charged with murder, upon a bond of a small amountirrelevant to the issue. Greason, 118 Ga. 808 (45 S. E. 615).

Where a witness testified that he had left the accused and the deceased a few minutes before the homicide in a friendly conversation, and upon hearing the shot, returned to the store, where the homicide occurred, and found the body of the deceased on the floor, and his hat resting partly on the floor and partly up against the chair, and his pipe on the floor, and fresh tobacco poured out, and a match between his fingers, it was not error to permit the witness further to testify that the "deceased generally laid his hat aside when he sat down for a conversation, and lit his pipe to smoke," and that he generally laid his hat down in the fashion in which it was found after the homicide. Butler, 142 Ga. 286 (82 

S. E. 654).

Evidence for the defendant that immediately after the shooting defendant went to the husband of the deceased and called him down to the scene of the shooting-not admissible. Gibbons, 137 Ga. 786 (74 S. E. 549).

Where two are jointly indicted for murder, and the tracks of two persons are shown as leading from a road to the place where the body of the deceased was found, evidence tending to identify the

tracks as having been made by both defendants admissible on the separate trial of one of them. Thomas, 143 Ga. 268 (84 S. E. 587).

Identification of the accused as the slayer. In a murder case the identification of the accused as the person who did the killing, is of paramount importance, and should be established beyond a reasonable doubt. Patton, 117 Ga. 230 (43 S. E. 533).

Coroner's inquest. Where defendants, suspected with murder, were brought before the coroner's jury summoned to hold an inquest on the body of the deceased, and, without being informed that they were not compelled to testify, were sworn and examined as witnesses, not on their own motion but on that of the coroner or the jury, in regard to the homicide and their connection with it, on a subsequent trial under an indictment charging them with murder, confessions or inculpatory statements elicited on their examination before the coroner's jury were not admissible against them. Adams, 129 Ga. 248 (58 S. E. 822).

Character of defendant. Where the defendant, a woman, has not put her character in issue, evidence of sexual intercourse between her and another man, not her husband, is inadmissible, where it was not part of the res gestae, nor had causal connection with the crime. 

Hightower, 14 Ga. App. 246 (80 S. E. 684).

Certificate of honorable discharge from the United States Army is not admissible to establish the good character of the accused for peaceableness, nor to establish his good character generally. Taylor, 120 Ga. 857 (3) (48 S. E. 361).

Where on the trial for homicide a witness had testified that the character of the defendant for peaceableness was good, evidence that the accused had been drunk on occasions prior to the time of the alleged homicide, or that he habitually used intoxicants-not admissible. Dunn, 16 Ga. App. 9 (84 S. E. 488).

Character of the deceased. In the trial of a criminal case, it is the privilege of the defendant under certain circumstances to put in issue the character of the deceased. But until the defendant has done so the State can not put into issue the character of the deceased for peaceableness. Worley, 138 Ga. 336, 340 (75 S. E. 240); Crawley, 137 Ga. 777 (1), 778 (74 S. E. 537).

But where the defendant takes the initiative by his own statement or other evidence, the State may rebut this by evidence to show the character of the deceased as to peaceableness. Crawley, 137 Ga. 777 (1) (74 S. E. 537). 

Specific acts to show the character of the deceased-not admis-

SPECIFIC CRIMES 

481 sible. Andrews, 118 Ga. 1, 2, 3 (43 S. E. 852); Vernon, 146 Ga. 

709 (4) (92 S. E. 76); Warrick, 125 Ga. 133 (6) (53 S. E. 1027).

The evidence of the violent character must be confined to general reputation. Alexander, 8 Ga. App. 531 (5) (69 S.. E. 917).

Record of former conviction of the deceased not admissible to show bad character. Alexander, 8 Ga. App. 531 (3) (69 S. E. 917).

Evidence that the deceased had the reputation of carrying firearms and deadly weapons on his person-inadmissible, unless there is evidence to show that this was known to the accused. Warrick, 125 Ga. 133 (5) (53 S. E. 1027); Futch, 137 Ga. 75 (5) (72 S. E. 911). 

Where on the trial of one charged with murder it appears that the character of the deceased for peaceableness has not been put in issue, the following questions propounded to a witness for the State by counsel for the defendant on cross-examination are not admissible: "Did you ever hear of his (the deceased) being in acts of violence or crime?" "Do you know of his killing a negro down the branch?" Hawkins, 141 Ga. 212 (5) (80 S. E. 711).

Where a father was on trial for the murder of his daughter, and no attack had been made on the character of the daughter for chastity, there was no error in excluding evidence that a physician made an examination of the body of the deceased and found her to be a virgin. Bullard, 127 Ga. 289 (56 S. E. 429).

Where nothing other than the statement of the accused tended to show that the deceased was the aggressor and was making an attack on the accused, testimony offered by him, in a murder prosecution, to prove that the deceased was a man of violent character was —inadmissible. Luffman, 166 Ga. 296 (3) (143 S. E. 371).

Proof of the violent and turbulent character of the deceased is admissible only when it is shown prima facie that the deceased. was the assailant, that the accused was assailed, and that the defendant was honestly seeking to defend himself. But if the defendant was the aggressor and attacked the deceased without provocation from him, then the bad character of the deceased would not be an excuse; for it is the same offense to kill a bad person as it is to kill a good person. Crawley, 137 Ga. 777 (74 S. E. 537).

On the trial of one charged with murder the exclusion of testimony, offered in his behalf, that the person killed had a violent character, was proper, in the absence of evidence that the defendant knew of that character. The foundation for the introduction of such testimony could not be laid in the defendant's statement to the jury. Wiggins, 16 Ga. App. 477 (85 S. E. 674).

Evidence that the deceased had bought whiskey, two or three months prior to the homicide, inadmissible to show character for drunkenness. Perdue, 135 Ga. 277 (69 S. E. 184). Nor is evidence that the police raided the home of the deceased and charged her with selling whiskey. Lucas, 146 Ga. 315 (1) (91 S. E. 72).

Evidence that the deceased was lascivious or lewd not admissible, nor specific acts of lewdnes. Chewning, 18 Ga. App. 11 (5) (88 

S. E. 904).

Threats by the accused. Evidence as to difficulties between the accused and the deceased shortly before the homicide, and of threats made by the accused on the occasion of the difficulty-admissible. 

Cason, 148 Ga. 477 (1) (97 S. E. 74).

Conversation of the accused and another person, some days before the commission of the homicide, in which the former expressed angry and threatening sentiments toward the deceased,-admissible to show state of mind of the accused toward the person whom he killed. Strickland, 137 Ga. 115 (3) (72 S. E. 922).

Where a threat is made to kill some stated person and that person is afterward murdered, evidence of such threat is admissible. against the person making it, upon his trial for such murder. 

Hixon, 130 Ga. 479 (3) (61 S. E. 14).

Evidence that the accused was greasing his pistol and said that he was going to get a man before the sun went down-admissible. 

Crumbly, 141 Ga. 17 (80 S. E. 281).

Threat is admissible although it was made in a conditional form. 

Golatt, 130 Ga. 18 (60 S. E. 107).

Threat is admissible although it has not been communicated to the deceased. McCray, 134 Ga. 416 (5) (68 S. E. 62).

Threat to prosecute the father of the deceased admissible to show accused's state of mind. Brooks, 134 Ga. 784 (68 S. E. 504).

Remoteness of time when threat was made no objection to the admissibility of such threats. Hixon, 130 Ga. 479, 482 (61 S. E. 

14); Willingham, 169 Ga. 142, 143 (5) (149 S. E. 23); McDaniel, 100 Ga. 67 (27 S. E. 158).

Threats by the deceased. Uncommunicated threats by the deceased toward the defendant are not generally admissible, unless there is evidence tending to show that the deceased was the assailant, or some overt act showing his intention to carry out his threat. 

The foundation must be laid by some evidence, but the defendant's statement is insufficient. Rouse, 135 Ga. 227 (69 S. E. 180); Pride, 133 Ga. 438, 439 (66 S. E. 259).

SPECIFIC CRIMES 

483 Where evidence of threats by the deceased is introduced, declaration of peaceful intention by the deceased admissible in rebuttal. 

Taylor, 121 Ga. 348 (3) (49 S. E. 303).

Evidence of threats by the deceased toward the accused admissible for the consideration of the jury, in passing upon the question of reasonable fear, if such threats were communicated to the accused. Taylor, 131 Ga. 765, 769 (63 S. E. 296).

In prosecution for homicide, in which the defendant contended that the deceased was approaching him with a knife when he struck the deceased, the Court did not err in refusing to allow a witness to testify that in April preceding the killing, which occurred in November, the deceased was trying to cut the defendant with a knife, which the witness took away from him, although defendant claimed that the deceased attacked him with a knife at the time of the homicide. Gibson, 42 Ga. App. 285 (155 S. E. 922).

Ill feelings. Evidence of previous difficulties and ill feeling between the defendant and the deceased-admissible. Cason, 148 Ga. 

477 (97 S. E. 74); Coleman, 141 Ga. 737 (82 S. E. 227).

Evidence that the deceased made an unprovoked attack with a deadly weapon upon the defendant some months before the homicide and that about six weeks before the homicide he cursed the accused and threatened to whip him-admissible. Baker, 142 Ga. 

619 (83 S. E. 531).

Evidence of bad feeling on the part of the deceased toward the defendant is inadmissible, unless defendant knew about it. Sasser, 129 Ga. 541 (4) (59 S. E. 255).

Ill feelings, and quarrels between the deceased and his wife about the defendant-not admissible, unless the defendant knew of it. Sasser, 129 Ga. 541 (5) (59 S. E. 255).

Declarations and admissions. Where a homicide is admitted and the accused seeks to justify it upon the ground that he was actuated by the fears of a reasonable man, the conduct and condition of the deceased in his presence, shortly before the final encounter, and the influence of his conduct or condition upon the mind of the accused, are relevant as being illustrative not only of the reasonableness of his fears, but also as indicating the quo animo of the deceased, although the previous difficulty may have been between the deceased and a third party. Dunn, 16 Ga. App. 9 (1) (84 S. E. 488).

Declaration of the deceased, made as he fell from the fatal wound: "O, Lord, my poor wife and children!"-admissible in evidence. (One dissenting.) Goodman, 122 Ga. 111 (49 S. E. 922).

Self-serving declarations are not admissible. Williams, 123 Ga. 

138 (2), 141 (51 S. E. 322).

Conversation between the accused and a witness prior to the homicide, that "if Mrs. Moore (the wife of the deceased) had been a man, me or her would have to die"-inadmissible, as it is irrelevant and prejudicial. Conversation, which had no immediate connection with the homicide, and was with another person than the deceased, merely indicating the state of feeling of the accused toward the wife of the deceased, inadmissible, as irrelevant and prejudicial. Darby, 16 Ga. App. 171 (84 S. E. 724).

It is no valid ground of objection to the admission in evidence of an incriminatory statement or confession made by the defendant in a criminal case that the language indicated that the accused had committed also another and separate offense. Watts, 8 Ga. App. 

694 (70 S. E. 46).

The admission of the killing by the defendant may be proved, although in the same connection he offered exculpatory statement showing that the killing was justifiable, if such statement was freely and voluntarily made. Such evidence is admitted to show the killing but can not be considered by the jury as an admission of guilt, or confession. Brannon, 140 Ga. 787 (2) (80 S. E. 7).

Any statement or conduct of a person which indicates a consciousness of his being guilty of a crime which has been committed, where at the time or thereafter he is charged with or suspected of the crime, is admissible on his trial for having committed it. Hixon, 130 Ga. 479 (61 S. E. 14).

Declarations by the accused showing malice on his part-admissible against him. Campbell, 123 Ga. 533 (51 S. E. 644).

On the trial of one for murder, declaration by his wife, on being informed by him that he had killed the deceased, that "I begged you never to do that," to which the accused made no response, is admissible in evidence as tending to show malice, under the principle that silence, when the circumstances require an answer or denial, may amount to an admission. Nunn, 143 Ga. 451 (85 S. E. 346).

Original evidence, not in rebuttal, by the defense, that a few moments after the killing defendant went to the sheriff and admitted the killing and surrendered-not admissible. Jones, 132 

Ga. 340 (63 S. E. 1114).

Dying declarations. Dying declarations of one with whose murder the defendant is not charged in the case on trial, not admissible,

SPECIFIC CRIMES 

485 though declarant was killed at the same time, in the same transaction, and allegedly by the same person, who killed the other person whose death is the subject of the investigation. Westberry, 175 Ga. 

115 (1) (164 S. E. 905). 

See also: Dying Declarations.

Flight. On the trial of one charged with a crime, the fact of his flight may be given in evidence, to be considered by the jury; but at most it is only a circumstance to be considered on the issue of the guilt of the accused. Kettles, 145 Ga. 6 (88 S. E. 197); Barnett, 136 Ga. 65 (3) (70 S. E. 868).

The accused may explain his flight and show that it was entirely consistent with his innocence; and in like manner the State may introduce evidence of circumstances connected with the flight, which will strengthen its probative value as tending to show the guilt of the accused. Johnson, 120 Ga. 135, 136 (47 S. E. 510).

Testimony that one, who is incarcerated in jail on a specific charge, broke jail and fled, is admissible on his trial for that charge as a circumstance to be considered by the jury in determining his guilt. 

Flannigan, 136 Ga. 132 (2) (70 S. E. 1107).

Evidence that the accused did not flee after the homicide, although he had full opportunity of flight,-not admissible. Flannigan, 135 Ga. 221 (3) (69 S. E. 171).

Weapons. Whether or not the deceased had a license to carry a pistol-irrelevant. Williams, 145 Ga. 177 (4) (88 S. E. 958).

Weapon used in committing homicide, if identified, admissible. 

Roberts, 123 Ga. 146 (3) (4) (51 S. E. 374).

Where one of the theories of the State is that the defendant and another jointly indicted with him, but not on trial, were acting in concert to effect the killing, it is relevant to prove that the other person indicted was, prior to the killing, possessed of a pistol of calibre corresponding to the size of empty cartridge shells found at the scene of the homicide immediately after the occurrence. 

It is also relevant to prove that the defendant on trial, charged with homicide, committed through the instrumentality of a pistol, was seen prior to the killing, possessed of a pistol of a calibre corresponding to the size of the bullet found in the body of the dead man. 

Garner, 6 Ga. App. 788, 789 (4) (65 S. E. 842).

Evidence that the accused habitually and customarily carried a pistol-admissible, to rebut the State's contention that he carried the pistol on the occasion in question as a part of the preparation for the homicide. Little, 164 Ga. 509 (138 S. E. 37).

Intoxication. The bottle of whiskey, which the testimony showed had been taken from the person of the accused shortly after the homicide, admissible, especially if there is some evidence from which the jury may legitimately infer that the defendant, at the time of the killing, was partially under the influence of intoxicating liquors. Chewning, 18 Ga. App. 11 (3) (88 S. E. 904).

Evidence that when the accused was carried to jail, shortly after the homicide, he exhibited signs of being under the influence of intoxicating liquors-admissible. Robinson, 130 Ga. 361 (60 S. E. 

1005); Mulligan, 18 Ga. App. 464 (89 S. E. 541).

Exhibits. A photograph of the scene of the homicide, in which a person was made to represent the position of the deceased as found immediately after he was shot, is admissible, in connection with the testimony which tended to show that the body of the deceased was found in the position of the person as represented in the photograph, as illustrative of the surroundings at the time of the homicide. Butler, 142 Ga. 286 (9) (82 S. E. 654).

Articles of wearing apparel, claimed by the accused to have been worn by him at the time of the difficulty, and evidencing by their physical condition that an assault has been made upon the accused by the deceased, are not admissible in evidence in behalf of the accused when their identification rests solely upon his statement to the jury. Proof of genuineness and identification must be made by relevant testimony, as a condition precedent to their introduction. in evidence. Register, 10 Ga. App. 623 (3) (74 S. E. 429). 

Opinion evidence. Testimony that the defendant appeared excited on a certain occasion is not opinion evidence, and is admissible. 

Roberts, 123 Ga. 146 (6) (51 S. E. 374).

A witness may state what his intention was and it is not opinion evidence. Alexander, 118 Ga. 26 (44 S. E. 857).

Where evidence has been introduced as to the physical and mental condition of the accused at the time of the homicide, question of physician as to his opinion of how long the accused would probably live is illegal. Bullard, 127 Ga. 289 (2) (56 S. E. 429).

Where the physical evidence is before the jury, testimony in the nature of opinion evidence founded on such data as are before the jury, from which they are as competent to draw conclusions as the witness, inadmissible. Thus, upon a trial for murder, where the mortal wound was inflicted with a knife, the blade of which was broken in making the blow, and where the knife with part of the broken blade as well as the part which was broken off were before

SPECIFIC CRIMES 

487 the jury, evidence as to the length of the part broken off was inadmissible. Williams, 145 Ga. 177 (88 S. E. 958). 

Hearsay. Where the question whether or not the deceased had a knife in his hand at the time when he was shot becomes material in a trial for murder, evidence that the witness asked the deceased some time before the homicide for his knife, and the deceased told him that he did not have a knife,-hearsay, and not admissible. 

Roberts, 145 Ga. 78 (88 S. E. 559).

Where the defendant was on trial for murder, allegedly committed in killing a police officer who attempted to arrest him, evidence that the defendant's daughter, almost immediately after she had gone from the house of the accused to next door neighbors, telephoned police officers, urging them to come to the house of the defendant, stating that the accused was drunk and trying to kill his own family-admissible; this evidence tended to explain the conduct of the officer, and to show the legality of the attempted arrest. Pryor, 168 Ga. 136 (4) (147 S. E. 97). Further testimony that the wife of the accused told the deceased police officer that her husband "was all out of whack, and to go and quiet him or put him up,"-admissible for the same purpose. (Id.) (5). 

Fugitive from justice. In a prosecution for the homicide of an arresting officer, evidence which tends to show that the purpose of the deceased was to effect an arrest, and that the slayer was a fugitive from justice,-competent. Harper, 129 Ga. 770 (1) (59 S. E. 792). 

Other crimes. In a prosecution for the murder of a young girl while attempting to have unnatural sexual relation with her, evidence in regard to other improper transactions with women, in which the accused took part, occurring at the same place not a great while before the homicide,-admissible as showing motive and design, and as tending to show identity of the criminal. Frank, 141 

Ga. 243 (80 S. E. 1016).

Where a witness testified for the State that the accused fired the fatal shot, indictment charging witness with the homicide not admissible for any purpose except to discredit him. Hayes, 126 Ga. 

95 (2) (54 S. E. 809).

Indictment charging another with the same homicide not admissible, where the same is still undisposed of. Weldon, 21 Ga. App. 

330 (94 S. E. 326).

Relationship. In a case in which the defense urged that the killing of the deceased was necessary to save the life of another per-

son, the relationship existing between the slayer and the person alleged to have been defended, whether the tie be one of affinity, consanguinity, or close friendship, or even the defenselessness of the person whose life was in danger, may be considered by the jury in connection with all the facts and circumstances of the case, in determining whether the homicide stands upon a like footing of reason and justice with homicide in self-defense. Gillis, 8 Ga. App. 696 (3) (70 S. E. 53).

Secondary evidence. Where the defendant has the original insurance policies, and does not produce them at the trial, the contents of the same are admissible by parol without first giving the defendant notice to produce them. Moore, 130 Ga. 322 (60 S. E. 544).

Miscellaneous. Where one contention of the defendant was that the person slain went to the place of the homicide for the purpose of having difficulty with him, it was neither hearsay nor irrelevant to allow the mother of the deceased to testify that she had asked her son to do something for her, the performance of which would require him to go to the place where the homicide occurred. Ricketson, 134 Ga. 306 (3) (67 S. E. 881).

Evidence that at the time of the homicide the deceased was in an advanced and apparent state of pregnancy is admissible, as bearing upon the enormity of the offense and furnishing ground for the consideration of the jury in determining whether or not a recommendation for life imprisonment would be proper. Withrow, 136 Ga. 337 

Where one tried for murder is convicted of voluntary manslaughter, such conviction amounts to acquittal of murder, and erroneous admissions of evidence tending to show that the homicide was murder will not be cause for new trial. French, 43 Ga. App. 97 (157 

S. E. 902).

Testimony by wife of the deceased that the night before the shooting of the deceased one of the co-defendants shot her in the handadmissible. Henderson, 170 Ga. 843 (2) (154 S. E. 232). 

Variance. Where the indictment alleged that the murder was committed by hitting and striking the deceased on the head with a certain soda-water bottle, evidence that the killing was done, not with a soda-water bottle, but with another instrument of similar nature-a blunt instrument which inflicted a wound of a similar character-harmless variance. Watson, 21 Ga. App. 637 (94 S. E. 857).

SPECIFIC CRIMES 

489 

Charge of Court.

Manslaughter. Instruction on the law of voluntary manslaughter and justifiable homicide should be independent of each other. White, 147 Ga. 377 (4) (94 S. E. 222). Where the charge commingles the law of justifiable homicide with the law of voluntary manslaughter, it will require a new trial. Mills, 133 Ga. 155 (65 S. E. 368).

If there is anything deducible from the evidence, or from the defendant's statement at the trial, which would tend to show manslaughter, voluntary or involuntary, it is the duty of the Court to instruct the jury fully on the law of manslaughter. (Italics by the 

Court.) Griffin, 18 Ga. App. 462 (5-a) (89 S. E. 537).

Where there is evidence, independently of the defendant's statement, sufficient to raise the theory of voluntary manslaughter, it is the duty of the Court to charge the law upon that subject, even without request, and his failure to do so is a ground for a new trial. 

McLendon, 172 Ga. 267 (5) (157 S. E. 475).

Where there is evidence authorizing a verdict of involuntary manslaughter, it is the duty of the Court to charge the law upon that subject and his failure to do so is a reversible error. Kelly, 145 Ga. 

210 (3) (88 S. E. 822).

Where there is evidence sufficient to raise doubt, however slight, upon the question whether the homicide was murder or manslaughter, voluntary or involuntary, it is the duty of the Court to charge on all these grades of homicide. Jackson, 43 Ga. App. 468 (159 S. E. 293).

A charge on voluntary manslaughter should not be given unless it is authorized by the evidence. Kelly, 145 Ga. 210, 212 (88 S. E. 

822); Griggs, 148 Ga. 211 (96 S. E. 262).

Where the question of manslaughter was raised by the prisoner's statement alone, and it is in conflict with the evidence, the Court is not bound to give in charge the law of involuntary manslaughter in the absence of timely and pertinent written request. Reed, 148 Ga. 

18 (95 S. E. 692). Note: The above rule has been stated in Cargile, 136 Ga. 55 (70 S. E. 873). This decision was overruled in Smith, 147 

Ga. 682 (1-b) (95 S. E. 223). However the old rule is stated again in Vincent, 153 Ga. 278, 298 (9) (112 S. E. 120); Griggs, 148 Ga. 211, 214 (96 S. E. 262); Reed, 148 Ga. 18 (95 S. E. 692); Carter, 171 Ga. 

406, 410 (115 S. E. 670).

Where the evidence is conflicting, and the jury would be authorized to find a verdict for voluntary manslaughter, or murder, it is error not to charge the jury on voluntary manslaughter. Jackson, 132 Ga. 570 (64 S. E. 656). 27

Where the State's evidence shows murder, and the defendant's statement, if wholly believed, justifiable homicide, but if believed in part only, voluntary manslaughter, charge on manslaughter proper and conviction on that sustained. Grimes, 123 Ga. 754 (1) (51 S. E. 

721). In such case it is error to refuse a timely and appropriate written request to charge the law upon voluntary manslaughter. 

Northfoot, 142 Ga. 714 (83 S. E. 655).

Where any fact or circumstance tends to show mutual combat or intention on the part of the accused and the deceased to fight, the Court should charge the law of voluntary manslaughter. Cash, 18 

Ga. App. 486 (4) (89 S. E. 603).

Where the evidence and the statement of the accused, taken together or separately, raise a doubt, although slight, as to the intention to kill, the law of involuntary manslaughter should be given in charge. And where the act from which death results may or may not be lawful under the facts, both grades of the law of involuntary manslaughter should be given in charge. Warnack, 3 Ga. App. 590 (60 S. E. 288).

Where neither the evidence nor the defendant's statement warrants a conviction of involuntary manslaughter, it is error to charge the jury that they may convict the defendant of that offense. Jordan, 117 Ga. 405 (43 S. E. 743); Segar, 12 Ga. App. 685 (78 S. E. 51). 

Where the weapon used was not a deadly one, or the manner in which it was used was not such as would ordinarily cause death, the law of involuntary manslaughter should be charged. See the following instances: Glass pitcher: Lyman, 89 Ga. 337 (15 S. E. 467); 

Brake stick: Warnack, 3 Ga. App. 590 (60 S. E. 288); Beer bottle: 

Farmer, 112 Ga. 80 (37 S. E. 120); Billiard cue: Dorsey, 126 Ga. 633 (55 S. E. 479). But Cox, 21 Ga. App. 238, 241 (94 S. E. 47), holds that an ordinary farm hoe is a deadly weapon. Higgins, 172 Ga. 221 (151 S. E. 643) holds that a baseball bat is a deadly weapon. (One dissenting.)

Where a person is on trial for murder, a correct charge on the law of manslaughter, even if not authorized by the evidence, is not cause for a new trial, where the defendant is convicted of murder. Clark, 142 Ga. 601 (3) (83 S. E. 223); Glasco, 137 Ga. 336 (73 S. E. 578).

Where the defendant is convicted of manslaughter, he can not complain of an alleged error committed by the Court in charging the law of murder. Faison, 13 Ga. App. 180 (79 S. E. 39); Horton, 43 Ga. App. 324, 325 (6) (158 S. E. 629).

Nor can the defendant complain of an alleged error in charging the law of murder or voluntary manslaughter where he is convicted

SPECIFIC CRIMES 

491 1 of involuntary manslaughter. Gray, 12 Ga. App. 634 (1) (77 S. 

E. 916); Goss, 14 Ga. App. 402 (81 S. E. 247).

Where under the evidence the real issue is whether the defendant was guilty of murder or justified, it is error to give the law of manslaughter in charge. Tolbirt, 119 Ga. 970 (47 S. E. 544).

Only that part of the law of homicide need be given in charge which is applicable by the facts to the case. Farris, 35 Ga. 241 (2).

In case of doubt the Court should define all possible grades and let the jury find which grade has been committed. Crawford, 12 

Ga. 142 (6).

Where the evidence for the State demands a verdict for murder, and the defendant's statement a verdict of not guilty on account of accident or misfortune, the law of involuntary manslaughter is not involved. Goodwin, 148 Ga. 33 (95 S. E. 674).

A charge that a homicide is presumed to be murder and the burden is upon the defendant to show a lesser degree of crime or none at all, is error, where the defendant denied any guilt. Such error is not cured by an additional charge: "When you reach the conclusion that a murder has been committed, the question then remains whether the defendant is the one who committed the murder.' 

Beach, 138 Ga. 265, 266 (4) (75 S. E. 139).

Evidence that the deceased circulated reports that he was in the habit of having adulterous intercourse with the wife of the defendant whenever he desired, and it was doubtful whether her youngest child was his or the defendant's, is not sufficient to authorize a charge on voluntary manslaughter. Plymel, 164 Ga. 677, 678 (2) 

Admission of counsel.

Counsel for the defendant admitted directly to the Court that voluntary manslaughter was not involved in the case; consequently it was held that the Court did not err in failing to charge the law of voluntary manslaughter as applicable to the case, or in defining what was cooling time. Riggins, 169 Ga. 

583 (2) (151 S. E. 15).

Where the counsel for the defendant argued before the jury the law of voluntary manslaughter and stated to the Court that he thought the case, under the evidence, involved every grade of homicide, the judge did not err in instructing the jury on the law of manslaughter. Jeffords, 41 Ga. App. 618 (2) (154 S. E. 201).

Where the evidence demands a charge on manslaughter, the fact that defendant's counsel argued to the jury that no question of manslaughter is involved did not waive defendant's right to such

charge, and the Court should charge the law of manslaughter. Horton, 120 Ga. 307 (47 S. E. 969); Andrews, 134 Ga. 71 (67 S. E. 422).

Where the evidence requires a charge on voluntary manslaughter the Court should so charge, although defendant's counsel insists, in a conference with the Court, that no such law is involved. Tanner, 145 Ga. 71 (88 S. E. 554); Hill, 147 Ga. 650 (95 S. E. 213).

Where counsel for the State and the defendant agreed in open court with the approval of the Court, before arguing to the jury, that there was no lower grade of homicide involved in the case, and that verdict should be rendered either for murder or acquittal, the Court did not err in failing to charge the law on either grades of manslaughter. O'Neal, 172 Ga. 526 (6), 527 (158 S. E. 51).

Note: Attention is called to the apparent conflict in the above cited cases.

Fear. It is not error to charge that bare fear of any offense to prevent which the homicide was alleged to have been committed, shall not be sufficient to justify the killing, and that it must appear that the circumstances were sufficient to excite the fears of a reasonable man, and that the party killing really acted under the influence of those fears and not in spirit of revenge. Rooks, 42 Ga. App. 

474 (2) (156 S. E. 479).

Mutual protection. The Court should charge that parents may protect their children when evidence involved this defense. Such charge should be given, even without request. Parker, 37 Ga. App. 

84 (139 S. E. 94).

Burden of proof. On the trial of one charged with murder, where the defense relied upon was justifiable homicide in self-defense, it is erroneous to instruct the jury to the effect that the burden was upon the accused to establish this defense to the satisfaction of the jury and beyond a reasonable doubt. This placed the burden on the accused, while the law placed it on the State. McDonald, 12 Ga. 

App. 526 (77 S. E. 655).

Flight. It is error for the Court to charge that flight unexplained is a circumstance pointing to defendant's guilt, as this amounts to an expression of opinion. Kettles, 145 Ga. 6 (88 S. E. 197).

Intoxication. Where the evidence showed that the accused was drunk at the time he committed the offense, an instruction to the jury that "voluntary drunkenness is no excuse for crime" is not an expression of opinion on the facts of the case. Brown, 13 Ga. App. 

370 (79 S. E. 177).

SPECIFIC CRIMES 

493 Threats. To instruct the jury that "threats are of very little importance as evidence in guiding the jury" is illegal. The jury and not the judge must weigh the evidence. Dorsey, 2 Ga. App. 228 (58 

S. E. 477).

Where there was uncontradicted evidence that the accused made threats to take the life of the deceased, the following charge was approved: "There is some evidence here as to threats. I charge you that threats alone, while they may tend to show malice and intention, are not sufficient of themselves to authorize a conviction, but threats connected with other facts and circumstances may or may not be sufficient to authorize a conviction, as the jury may, from all the evidence, determine in the case." Humphrey, 141 Ga. 671 (4) (81 S. E. 1034).

Waiver. The Court may charge the jury as to every lawful defense raised by the accused, notwithstanding the fact that in his written request the accused stated that he relied on one or more specific defenses only, and not upon another defense named. Mc- 

Phearson, 19 Ga. App. 232 (2) (91 S. E. 336). But if the Court, upon such request omits to charge on the defense so waived by the accused, he can not be heard to complain. (Id.)

Insanity. Where evidence as to the insanity of the defendant is introduced under a general plea of not guilty, it is the duty of the Court to instruct the jury upon the subject of insanity as a defense. 

In the absence of evidence that the defendant acted under the influence of an overmastering delusion, there is no error in not presenting the theory of partial or temporary insanity, without special timely and written request. Carter, 2 Ga. App. 254 (58 S. E. 532).

Character of the deceased. When the accused desires a special charge on the character of the deceased for violence, he should make a pertinent and timely request in writing. Moon, 22 Ga. App. 617 (2) (97 S. E. 81). Verdicts.

Under an indictment for murder the accused may be convicted of a lesser offense, if the latter is involved in the homicide, and sufficiently charged in the indictment. Reams, 24 Ga. App. 135 (1) (100 

S. E. 230); Watson, 116 Ga. 607 (4) (43 S. E. 32).

An indictment for murder embraces the minor offense of assault with intent to murder, as the whole embraces all of its parts. Cox, 33 Ga. App. 144 (126 S. E. 288).

Conviction of shooting at another is lawful where the indictment

for murder charged killing by shooting the deceased with a certain pistol. Jackson, 25 Ga. App. 748 (1) (2) (105 S. E. 162).

If the jury is not convinced of the defendant's guilt of murder, but is satisfied of his guilt of manslaughter, they should convict of that offense. Best, 26 Ga. App. 671 (7-a) (107 S. E. 266).

Where the evidence for the State shows murder, and that for the defendant justification, or the defendant denies the homicide, and there is no evidence authorizing manslaughter, a verdict of guilty of manslaughter is illegal. Spence, 7 Ga. App. 825, 834 (68 S. E. 443).

On the trial for murder the jury may convict of a lesser offense, if the evidence warrants it, although the Court did not charge the jury on that lesser offense. Spence, 7 Ga. App. 825 (68 S. E. 443).

Whenever in the trial of one charged with murder there is any evidence, or anything in the defendant's statement, tending to show that the homicide was voluntary manslaughter, a verdict finding defendant guilty of that offense is authorized. Plemmons, 43 Ga. App. 344 (2) (158 S. E. 630). 

Where the evidence, as a whole, tended to support two theories, and only two: one that the defendant shot the deceased in the back without legal justification or excuse, and was therefore guilty of murder; and the other that he shot solely to protect the life of his sister from the deceased, who had already fired a shotgun in close range at and toward her, verdict of guilty of manslaughter unauthorized. Lewis, 16 Ga. App. 154 (1) (84 S. E. 609).

Verdict of guilty of manslaughter will not be sustained, when the evidence and the statement of the defendant present only the issue whether the defendant was guilty of murder or was justifiable. 

Berry, 122 Ga. 429 (50 S. E. 345); Herrington, 125 Ga. 745 (54 S. E. 749).

A verdict of guilty of manslaughter will not be sustained, when the testimony of witnesses and the statement of the defendant present only the issue whether the defendant was guilty of murder, or the homicide was due to accident or misfortune. Robinson, 124 Ga. 

787 (53 S. E. 99).

A verdict that the defendant is guilty of involuntary manslaughter will be referred to the highest grade of that offense, and be treated as equivalent to a finding that he was guilty of involuntary manslaughter in the commission of an unlawful act. Thomas, 121 Ga. 331 (49 S. E. 273). 

Where two persons, who, without concert of action, shot another who is killed, are under indictment for murder, a verdict of guilty

SPECIFIC CRIMES 

495 5 1 of shooting at another is valid if sufficiently charged in the indictment. Wood, 30 Ga. App. 665 (1) (118 S. E. 763).

A verdict of voluntary manslaughter is authorized where the defendant participated in the act of killing committed by another, but did not participate in the latter's intent to kill. Mills, 24 Ga. App. 

68 (2) (100 S. E. 32). This case lays down the rule that where the accused committed an assault on the deceased, and intended only to participate in an assault and battery, not intending to kill, he is guilty of manslaughter only. (Id.) (1-a.)

Where murder or manslaughter was the only proper verdict, conviction for manslaughter will not be reversed, although the Court committed minor errors in charging the jury. O'Shields, 125 Ga. 

310 (54 S. E. 120). 

33. INCEST. 

§§ 53-105, 26-5701, 26-5702.

Punishment. Not less than one nor longer than twenty years in the penitentiary. (Reducible.)

Incestuous marriage: Not less than one nor more than three years in the penitentiary. (Reducible.) with the offense of 

Indictment. ... charge and accuse.. incest, for the said. being a married man, in the county aforesaid, on the……………………………………..day of……………………………......19…….., and on divers other days and times, before and after that day, did, then and there, (and on said other days and times) commit divers acts of incestuous adultery, by cohabiting and having sexual intercourse with one..... an unmarried woman; she, the said.. the................(daughter) of him, the said.. (Approved: Cook, 11 Ga. 53, 54.) ..., being then and there, ......contrary, etc. . . 

See also: Lipham, 125 Ga. 52 (1) (53 S. E. 817).

It is not the name but the description of the crime, which characterizes the offense charged. Indictment in the language of the Code section is sufficient. Lipham, 125 Ga. 52 (1) (53 S. E. 817); Cook, 11 Ga. 53.

General. Incest is sexual intercourse between a man and a woman who, because of relationship by either consanguinity or affinity, can not lawfully contract a marriage. Taylor, 110 Ga. 150, 152 (35 S. E. 161); Lipham, 125 Ga. 52 (53 S. E. 817).

The elements of the offense of incestuous adultery are, marriage of defendant, sexual intercourse, and the relation of the parties within the levitical degrees. Cook, 11 Ga. 53, 56.

Incestuous sexual intercourse under this section is indictable

either as fornication, or as adultery, according to whether the person indicted is single or married, without regard to the condition, in this respect, of the other person participating in the criminal act, and this section does not create any such offense as incestuous fornication and adultery. Kedrick, 100 Ga. 360, 362 (28 S. E. 120). 

But see Nephew, 5 Ga. App. 841 (2) (63 S. E. 930).

Incestuous adultery or fornication is not a joint offense, and one person may be indicted and found guilty thereof. Powers, 44 Ga. 209 (1). 

A woman who consents to an act of incestuous intercourse is an accomplice of the man, and this is true though some coercion was used to obtain her consent. Whidby, 121 Ga. 588 (1) (49 S. E. 811); 

Solomon, 113 Ga. 192 (38 S. E. 332); Brown, 18 Ga. App. 30 (88 S. 

E. 710). Corroboration necessary. Yother, 120 Ga. 204 (47 S. E. 

555). It is error to charge that if there was sufficient coercion to make the case almost a rape, then it is a question for the jury whether or not the woman is an accomplice. Such case is either rape or adultery or fornication, and if the woman consented, no matter on what ground, she is an accomplice. Whidby, 121 Ga. 588 (1) (2) (49 S. E. 811). In the crime of incest there may be a certain force or power exerted, resulting from the age, relationship or circumstances of the parties, which overcomes the objections of the female, without amounting to that violence which would constitute rape. Raiford, 68 Ga. 672.

For proof of marriage by admission and other evidence, see 

Adultery and Fornication, also Cook, 11 Ga. 53.

Sexual intercourse with stepdaughter is incestuous. Taylor, 110 

Ga. 150 (1) (35 S. E. 161).

A man who marries the mother of an illegitimate daughter becomes the stepfather of such child within the meaning of this section. Lipham, 125 Ga. 52 (53 S. E. 817); Nephew, 5 Ga. App. 841, 843 (63 S. E. 930).

Evidence. Acts and declarations of accused manifesting solicitude concerning the pregnancy of the woman are admissible and may be sufficient corroboration of her testimony. Taylor, 110 Ga. 

150 (7) (35 S. E. 161). Woman may testify that she has never had any sexual intercourse with any other man than accused. (Id.) See also: Jennings, 13 Ga. App. 678 (79 S. E. 756).

Facts of previous criminal intercourse allowed in evidence, though barred by statute of limitations, to throw light on the relations existing between the parties. Taylor, 110 Ga. 150 (35 S. E. 161); Lip-

34. KIDNAPPING. (Abduction.) §§ 26-1601 to 26-1605. 

Punishment. Kidnapping: Not less than four nor more than seven years in the penitentiary.

Kidnapping for ransom: Not less than four nor more than twenty years in the penitentiary. § 26-1603. 

(Reducible felonies.)

Enticing children from Industrial Home. (Misdemeanor.) § 26-1604. 

Harboring absconding children. Indictment. 

(Misdemeanor.) § 26-1605. 

charge and accuse. kidnapping, for that the said. with the offense of on the……………………………………..day of……………………………….. 1 19., in the county aforesaid, did maliciously, feloniously, fraudulently lead, take, carry away, decoy, entice away one....... being a child under eighteen years of age, from her parents, etc. she and.. --------, against their will and without their consent, contrary, (Approved: Dowda, 74 Ga. 12, 13.) See also: Arrington, 3 Ga. App. 30 (59 S. E. 207). A count in an indictment for kidnapping, framed under § 26-1602, charging that the accused forcibly, maliciously, and fraudulently took and enticed away a child under eighteen years of age, against its will and without its consent, was fatally defective, when it failed to allege that the child had no parent or guardian. Sutton, 122 Ga. 

158 (50 S. E. 60); Blair, 26 Ga. App. 618 (107 S. E. 278).

Consent of a guardian need not be negatived in an indictment where both parents are alive and named in the indictment. Where both the parents of a minor are in life, the legal presumption is that the control of such minor has not passed to a guardian. If in any manner the parental authority had been lost and vested in a guardian and the abduction took place with the consent of the guardian, such facts may be shown by way of defense. Pruitt, 102 Ga. 688 (29 S. E. 610).

The indictment need not allege the names of the parents. Arrington, 3 Ga. App. 30 (1) (59 S. E. 207).

One can not lawfully be convicted under a count in an indictment for kidnapping, based upon § 26-1602, which charges that the accused forcibly, maliciously, and fraudulently enticed away a child under 18 years of age, against its will and without its consent, where the evidence shows that the child had a parent or guardian. However, where the conviction is under a count, based upon § 26-1601,

which charges the accused with forcibly abducting a named person, without lawful authority or warrant, from a named county, and conveying such person beyond the limits of the county, against his will, the conviction is not contrary to law or the evidence for the reason that the evidence disclosed that the person alleged to have been kidnapped was a child under the age of 18 years, and that such child had a parent or guardian. Blair, 26 Ga. App. 618 (107 S. 

E. 278).

An indictment properly charging the completed offense of kidnapping is sufficient to support the verdict for an attempt, without specifically alleging some overt act done towards the commission of the crime. Arrington, 48 Ga. App. 70 (171 S. E. 878).

Indictment against a father for the offense of kidnapping is nullity where it appears that he has not parted with his parental control. Hunt, 94 Ga. 257 (21 S. E. 515).

Indictment need not allege from what place child was taken nor where carried. Dowda, 74 Ga. 12 (2), 13. 

General. 'Any person" means man, woman, or child of any age. 

Sutton, 122 Ga. 158, 159 (50 S. E. 60). § 26-1602 provides for two offenses: one where the child kidnapped has a parent or guardian, and the other, where it has neither. 

In the latter case, it must be forcibly, maliciously or fraudulently led, taken or carried, or decoyed, or enticed away against its own will, and without its consent; in the former, if these things shall be done against the will and without the consent of the parent, irrespective of that of the child, this alone would complete the offense. 

Gravett, 74 Ga. 191 (1); Thweatt, 74 Ga. 821 (2); Bryant, 21 Ga. 

App. 668, 669 (94 S. E. 856); Sutton, 122 Ga. 158, 159 (50 S. E. 60); 

Arrington, 3 Ga. App. 30 (59 S. E. 207); Taylor, 25 Ga. App. 500 (113 S. E. 740); Blair, 26 Ga. App. 618 (107 S. E. 278).

The object of § 26-1602 is to protect the rights of parents and guardians, and of children. Bryant, 21 Ga. App. 668, 670 (94 S. E. 856). 

To "decoy" means to lead into danger by artifice, to allure into a net, to snare, to entrap, to ensnare, to allure, entice. Arrington, 3 Ga. App. 30, 33 (59 S. E. 207).

It is an offense under § 26-1602 for a married man to entice a female under the age of eighteen to leave her parents' home without their consent, under a false and fraudulent promise of marriage, for the purpose of sexual intercourse with her, though she is not taken beyond the limits of the county, and though she leaves willingly. Carter, 14 Ga. App. 51 (80 S. E. 206).

SPECIFIC CRIMES 

499 1 1 

If one without force or fraud persuades a girl of fourteen to accompany him for the bona fide purpose of marriage, and he marries her, he can not be convicted of kidnapping. Cochran, 91 Ga. 763 (18 S. E. 16). 

Force and malice. Force and malice need not appear. Decoying or enticing away without consent of the parents or guardian completes the offense. Arrington, 3 Ga. App. 30 (2) (59 S. E. 207); 

Taylor, 25 Ga. App. 500 (1) (103 S. E. 740).

Inveigling children is kidnapping, just as much as forcible abduction of a person under § 26-1601. Dowda, 74 Ga. 12 (1).

Upon the trial of one for kidnapping, under § 26-1602, if it be shown that the child was fraudulently decoyed or enticed away from its parent without the consent or against the will of the parent, it is not necessary to show that either force or malice entered into the transaction. Rowell, 41 Ga. App. 499 (153 S. E. 371). 

Defense. It is no defense, that the girl, sixteen or seventeen years of age, consented to leave the parents and go to another county. 

Thweatt, 74 Ga. 821.

Bad character of child. Bad character of the child kidnappedimmaterial. Hunt, 8 Ga. App. 374, 376 (69 S. E. 42).

Conspiracy. It is conspiracy for the accused and others to assemble to aid girl under fourteen in escaping from her parents for the purpose of marriage. Handley, 115 Ga. 584, 585 (41 S. E. 992). 

Where a girl under eighteen years of age was enticed away by one person, and another conspired with him, both are guilty. Taylor, 25 Ga. App. 500 (2) (103 S. E. 740).

Parental control and consent. Parental control of the child is not lost by father's temporary willingness to allow her to live apart from his home and retain her earnings, she having returned home at the time the alleged crime has been committed. Hunt, 8 Ga. App. 

374, 376 (69 S. E. 42).

Notice of the father's unwillingness to relinquish dominion over his child is not essential to the guilt of the defendant. Gravett, 74 

Ga. 191, 192 (3-a). 

Testimony of the father of prosecutrix that he did not agree that she should go away with the defendant sufficient to establish the fact that prosecutrix went away without the consent of her parents. 

Carter, 14 Ga. App. 51 (80 S. E. 206). 

In Arrington, 48 Ga. App. 64, 69, 70 (171 S. E. 874) it was held that the fact that the child's father was present and consented to the attempt to kidnap the child, was no defense.

Age. The fact that the accused was ignorant of the girl's age, and that he believed, in good faith, and had good grounds to believe that she was more than eighteen years of age is no defense. Smiley, 34 Ga. App. 513 (1) (130 S. E. 359).

Evidence. Evidence of harsh treatment by parents-not admissible. Gravett, 74 Ga. 191, 192 (5).

Evidence must show that the accused either "forcibly, maliciously, or fraudulently" enticed the child away. Where the child alleged to have been inveigled is above the age of discretion, though under the age of eighteen, these elements are not sufficiently made out by showing that the child went away in company with the defendant, especially where the State's own evidence shows that the child went on its free will and accord, and not as a result of any inveigling on the defendant's part. Hendon, 10 Ga. App. 78 (72 S. E. 522).

Where the indictment, based upon § 26-1602, charges that the accused forcibly, maliciously, and fraudulently enticed away a child under 18 years of age, against its will and without its consent and the evidence showed that the child had a parent or a guardian, conviction illegal. Blair, 26 Ga. App. 618 (107 S. E. 278).

Evidence that the defendant had sexual intercourse with the prosecutrix is admissible, as it illustrates the purpose of the accused in inducing the prosecutrix to go away with him. Carter, 14 Ga. App. 

51, 52 (80 S. E. 206).
