General. Any greater larceny than simple larceny must necessarily include the latter. Brown, 90 Ga. 454 (16 S. E. 204); Kelly, 24 Ga. App. 155, 156 (100 S. E. 23).

In indictments for compound larceny, the allegations in reference to the aggravating fact serve to individualize the transaction, and a more general description of the property is permissible in such cases than would be permitted in an indictment for simple larceny. Blackmon, 24 Ga. App. 384 (1) (100 S. E. 730).

a. SIMPLE LARCENY. 

Indictment. charge and accuse. ..with the offense of simple larceny, for that the said, on the 

19...., in the county aforesaid, with force and arms.. of the personal goods of....... day of, (describe and of the the property).………………….. value of $…………….. unlawfully, wrongfully, and fraudulently did take and carry away, with intent to steal the same, contrary, (Approved: Johnson, 119 Ga. 257 (45 S. E. 960).)

Indictment must allege ownership of the property stolen, or that the owner is unknown. Thomas, 96 Ga. 311 (22 S. E. 956). etc. 

Where indictment is brought for simple larceny, ownership of the property must be specifically alleged. The owner must be identified. Where the indictment is brought for larceny from the person, the owner need not be identified by name. Hugo, 110 Ga. 768 (36 S. E. 60); Hanson, 13 Ga. App. 372, 373 (79 S. E. 176).

Where property belongs to partnership, indictment must allege the names of the partners. Buffington, 124 Ga. 24 (52 S. E. 19).

Carrier has such ownership in goods in transportation as will support allegation of ownership. Hall, 7 Ga. App. 115, 116 (4) (66 S. 

E. 390). 

Ownership may be laid in gratuitous bailee. Wimbish, 89 Ga. 294 (15 S. E. 325).

Where ownership is laid in a name which imports a corporation, it is presumed that it is the name of a corporation, and the indictment need not allege the fact of incorporation. Mattox, 115 Ga. 212, 213 (7) (41 S. E. 709). 

Value of property stolen must be alleged and proved. Smith, 95 

Ga. 460 (21 S. E. 45).

Description of the property stolen must be sufficiently definite to enable the accused to know the exact transaction he is charged with. 

Gibson, 13 Ga. App. 67 (78 S. E. 829); Carson, 22 Ga. App. 551 (1) (96 S. E. 500).

Where the accusation described the goods stolen as "two and onehalf gallons of syrup," of stated value, and the property of a named person, the description is insufficient on special demurrer. Mathis, 27 Ga. App. 229 (107 S. E. 629).

Description of the goods stolen as "five twenty dollar bills, and three ten dollar bills, of the value of $130"-sufficient. McNatt, 27 

Ga. App. 642 (3) (109 S. E. 514).

An indictment for simple larceny must accurately describe the property. But where not demurred to, a witness may describe it,

SPECIFIC CRIMES 

503 although the indictment may be silent. Roberts, 83 Ga. 369 (9 S. E. 675).

Description of the stolen property should be simple such as, in connection with other allegations, will affirmatively show the defendant guilty, will reasonably inform him of the instance meant, and put him in a position to prepare for his defense. Ayers, 3 Ga. 

App. 305 (1) (59 S. E. 924).

Insufficient description of the property stolen is a good ground for a demurrer, but can not be taken advantage of by motion to quash the indictment. King, 117 Ga. 39 (1) (43 S. E. 426).

The description must identify the stolen article. Brown, 116 Ga. 

559 (2) (42 S. E. 795). But where some of the words consisted of technical terms requiring explanation by expert evidence, the description is not defective. Wrenn, 12 Ga. App. 694 (2) (78 S. E. 202).

The following description was held sufficient: "Lot of cord wood." Walthour, 114 Ga. 75 (39 S. E. 872). "100 pounds of seed cotton of the value of $10.00, the property of a named person. 

Bright, 10 Ga. App. 17 (72 S. E. 519). 92 It is not necessary to allege in the indictment the location of the property stolen, where the indictment is for simple larceny, or the place from which it was taken and carried away, further than to state that it was in the county in which the Court had jurisdiction, unless a statement of the location is a descriptive averment essential to the identification of the property. Gibson, 13 Ga. App. 67, 68 (78 S. E. 829).

Accusation is not fatally defective where it does not allege that the taking of the property was either unlawful or wrongful, or fraudulent, where it is charged that the taking was "with intent to steal the same." McCall, 40 Ga. App. 543 (150 S. E. 469).

In an indictment for larceny the ownership of the property may be laid in the agent having lawful possession of the property for another. But it is not properly laid in a servant having the mere custody or control of the goods for his master. Jackson, 21 Ga. App. 

146 (94 S. E. 55). Where husband has charge of a plantation as the agent of his wife, ownership of the property stolen is properly laid in the husband. But it would be improper to allege ownership in superintendent of the plantation. (Id.)

An allegation of ownership of the property stolen in one who had possession thereof is sufficient, though the legal title might be in another. Thomas, 27 Ga. App. 38 (2) (107 S. E. 418).

Where ownership is laid in an agent, the indictment need not al-

lege the agency or bailment. Bennett, 28 Ga. App. 235 (110 S. E. 756).

Where a boat conveying liquors in violation of the prohibition laws of this State was seized by United States officials in one county, and after the removal of the liquor from the boat it was turned over to the sheriff of another county, his possession of the boat would give him such special property in the boat as would authorize prosecution for larceny, in which the ownership was laid in said sheriff. 

Goldberg, 150 Ga. 59 (1) (2) (103 S. E. 90); Goldberg, 25 Ga. App. 

197 (103 S. E. 90).

Where a constable levied on certain wood, as the property of the accused, and the accused was charged with simple larceny by stealing the same wood from the constable, the ownership of the property was properly laid in the constable, although he had no other interest in the same than the levy. Gladden, 43 Ga. App. 236 (3) (158 S. E. 338).

Where title to the property stolen was laid in the levying officer, conviction unauthorized on showing that no legal levy was made by such officer. Russell, 13 Ga. App. 561 (2) (79 S. E. 495). General,

Venue. Where the stolen property was brought into the county of the trial, it is immaterial in what county it was stolen. The venue is established. Barnes, 25 Ga. App. 555, 557 (103 S. E. 857).

The venue of the offense of simple larceny is in either county, where property is stolen and removed to another county. But this rule refers to simple larceny only, and not to compound offenses although simple larceny may be a component part of such offenses. 

Thus, where the charge is larceny from the house, larceny from the car, larceny from the person, etc., the venue must be laid and proved in the county where the actual entering and stealing occurred. Williams, 105 Ga. 743, 745 (31 S. E. 749).

Where property is stolen in one county and removed to another, the larceny is considered as having been committed in each county, and is punishable in either. Green, 114 Ga. 918, 920 (41 S. E. 642); 

Morton, 118 Ga. 306 (45 S. E. 395); McCoy, 123 Ga. 143, 145 (51 S. 

E. 279).

Where the accused committed a larceny in another State and brought the stolen goods into this State, larceny in this State was not committed. Golden, 2 Ga. App. 440 (2) (58 S. E. 557); Lee, 64 

Ga. 203.

SPECIFIC CRIMES 

505 Elements. Larceny from the house and simple larceny distinguished. For the former to exist one must make a theft from the house of another, but stealing cotton from in front of a warehouse is not larceny from the house. Middleton, 53 Ga. 248, 249.

Wrongful and fraudulent taking with intent to steal then and there formed is a necessary element of simple larceny and distinguishes it from larceny after trust. Pittman, 13 Ga. App. 705 (79 

S. E. 915).

Intent to steal is a necessary ingredient of the offense of simple larceny. Though it may be established by exceedingly weak and unsatisfactory circumstantial evidence, it must be established before a person can be convicted. Jackson, 116 Ga. 578, 579 (42 S. E. 750); 

Kelley, 24 Ga. App. 155, 156 (100 S. E. 23).

Conviction of simple larceny is illegal unless there is evidence that the defendant took the goods fraudulently and wrongfully and with intent to steal the same. Pittman, 13 Ga. App. 705 (79 S. E. 

915); Wright, 18 Ga. App. 337 (1) (89 S. E. 432). And the Court must so charge the jury. Russell, 13 Ga. App. 561 (2) (79 S. E. 

495); Belmas, 15 Ga. App. 288 (2) (82 S. E. 819).

If defendant got possession of the property through plan, scheme, device or fraud, with intent to steal the same, and carried it away under such circumstances, larceny has been committed and he is guilty of simple larceny. Barnes, 25 Ga. App. 555, 557 (103 S. E. 857).

The question of intent is for the jury, where the taking is shown. 

Johnson, 9 Ga. App. 409 (3) (71 S. E. 507); Adams, 12 Ga. App. 808 (78 S. E. 473).

Borrowing property and carrying it away with intent to steal is larceny. Rice, 6 Ga. App. 160 (1) (64 S. E. 575). But where there is no intent to steal at the time of the borrowing, and the intent is formed afterwards, the offense is not simple larceny. Abrams, 121 

Ga. 170 (4) (48 S. E. 965).

Taking and carrying. If the goods were moved at all by the defendant, it is a sufficient asportation. Wallace, 25 Ga. App. 759, 761 (105 S. E. 57). 

Where one with intent to steal takes actual possession of the property of another, and removes it to any distance whatever, he is guilty of larceny. Mitchell, 21 Ga. App. 77 (1) (93 S. E. 1022).

Asportation is sufficient where there is the slightest change in location whereby dominion of the property is transferred from the owner to the wrongdoer. Johnson, 9 Ga. App. 409 (2) (71 S. E. 507).

Selling goods of another without taking possession of them is not

sufficient taking to constitute larceny, but where buyer in good faith takes possession of the property and removes it, the seller is guilty. 

Smith, 15 Ga. App. 400 (83 S. E. 437).

Lost property. Finding and retaining lost property for the purpose of converting it, when the owner of the same is known, constitutes simple larceny. Slaughter, 113 Ga. 284 (38 S. E. 854); Sheffield, 26 Ga. App. 72, 73 (105 S. E. 376); Flemister, 121 Ga. 146 (48) 

S. E. 910).

One who persuades another, who has found lost money belonging to person whom they knew, and who is on his way to return the lost money, to let him have part of the money, promising to return it later with 10% interest, which he never does, is guilty of simple larceny. Sheffield, 26 Ga. App. 72 (105 S. E. 376).

Making change. Where money is delivered to another either for the purpose of making change or to pay for the goods and return the balance, and money is converted, the offense is stealing. Walker, 9 Ga. App. 863 (1) (72 S. E. 446); Fitzgerald, 118 Ga. 855 (45 S. E. 

666); Finkelstein, 105 Ga. 617 (1) (31 S. E. 589).

Fraud. Where one fraudulently represents himself to be another's agent to buy goods, and thereby comes into possession of goods for delivery for his alleged principal, and converts goods to his own use, he is guilty of simple larceny. Harris, 81 Ga. 758 (7 

S. E. 689).

Where sale on credit is induced by false representations, delivery being unconditional, with intent to pass title, no larceny committed. 

Foster, 117 Ga. 39 (43 S. E. 421).

Where one obtains possession of money by trick and fraud with intent to appropriate the same to his own use, and the owner intends to part with the possession only and not with the property, possession of money is obtained unlawfully, and subsequent appropriation of it in pursuance of original intent warrants conviction of simple larceny. McNatt, 27 Ga. App. 642 (2) (109 S. E. 514).

Where one fraudulently intends to get possession of money of another, and by false representation induces owner to deliver money to him for the purpose of being applied to the owner's use, and then appropriates it in pursuance of original fraudulent intent, he may be convicted of simple larceny. Johnson, 27 Ga. App. 635 (1) (109 

S. E. 535).

Where defendant borrowed the coat of another, the coat to be returned the same day, and he never returned it, intent to steal may be inferred. Maxwell, 25 Ga. App. 306 (103 S. E. 178).

SPECIFIC CRIMES 

507 

Claim of right. Intent to steal is negatived by taking under bona fide claim of right. Publicity of taking is strong evidence of good faith. Causey, 79 Ga. 564 (5 S. E. 121); Cleveland, 114 Ga. 110 (2) (39 S. E. 941).

The bona fides of the taker's claim is for the jury. Lee, 102 Ga. 

221 (29 S. E. 264). 

Bailment. Falsely acquiring possession of property under a pretended bailment, with intent to convert the same, is simple larceny. 

Kelley, 24 Ga. App. 155 (2), 156 (100 S. E. 23). 

Entrapping thief. Owner of goods may entrap the accused by furnishing opportunity to steal. Varner, 72 Ga. 745. But he may not do so by solicitation. Williams, 55 Ga. 391.

Drunkenness. Voluntary drunkenness is no excuse, though intent to steal was caused by drunkenness. But drunkenness may be circumstance from which lack of intent to steal may be inferred. 

Walker, 9 Ga. App. 863 (2) (72 S. E. 446).

Restitution. Restitution made after the commission of the offense-no defense. Coleman, 43 Ga. App. 586 (1) (159 S. E. 605).

Property under levy. Person who steals his own property from officer who has seized it under a levy is guilty of larceny. Seizure of personalty and not the official entry constitutes the levy. Ayers, 

Crops. Tenant disposing of crops grown on rented land, to the injury of the landlord, is not guilty of larceny. Teel, 7 Ga. App. 600 (2) (3) (67 S. E. 699). 

A cropper converting part of the crop to his own use is not guilty of larceny. Indictment must be under § 61-9904. Lane, 113 Ga. 1040 

Gambling. If the defendant took the money in a gambling game, before it was completed and before the winner was determined, with intent to steal the same, he is guilty of simple larceny. Barnes, 25 

Ga. App. 555, 557 (103 S. E. 857). 

Vendor. Where a vendor fraudulently converts the property he has sold to his own use, he is guilty of simple larceny. Meacham, 7 Ga. App. 713 (68 S. E. 52).

Fiduciary relation. Larceny after trust distinguished. If one obtains possession of personal property by trick or fraud or under false pretense of a bailment, with intent to appropriate it to his own use, and subsequently, while in the custody thereof by virtue of a fiduciary relation, appropriates it, he may be convicted of simple

larceny. But if, during the existence of the fiduciary relation, the owner of the property voluntarily intrusts the possession thereof to his servant or agent, who has not obtained possession by any fraud or false pretense, and who thereafter converts the chattel to his own use, the offense is not simple larceny but larceny after trust. Where no fiduciary relation exists between the parties, and therefore consent to the possession of the chattels can not be implied, one temporarily intrusted therewith, who converts it to his own use, may be convicted of simple larceny. Lanier, 17 Ga. App. 261, 262 (2-a) (86 

S. E. 417).

One can not be convicted of simple larceny unless it appears that he took the goods described in the indictment wrongfully and fraudulently, with intent then and there entertained to steal the same. If possession of the goods be delivered by the owner to another under an agreement by the latter to sell them for the benefit of the owner and to return to the owner either the proceeds arising from the sale or the goods themselves if unsold, and the goods are subsequently converted, the conversion is larceny after trust delegated, and the person thus guilty of the conversion can not be convicted of simple larceny, unless there is some proof that he fraudulently induced the owner to surrender possession of the goods, intending at the time to appropriate them to his own use. Pittman, 13 Ga. App. 705 (79 

S. E. 915).

Accomplice. Where two persons agree to commit a larceny and to divide the stolen property, and one of them actually commits the larceny, and the other stands conveniently nearby, and then receives his portion of the property stolen, both are guilty as principals. 

Folsom, 11 Ga. App. 199 (3) (74 S. E. 939); Morris, 26 Ga. App. 60 (105 S. E. 380).

Larceny and trespass distinguished. goods of another without his consent. goods of another with intent to steal. Evidence. 

Trespass is the taking the 

Larceny is the taking the 

Beall, 68 Ga. 820.

Corpus delicti. Where corpus delicti is not proved, the conviction is illegal. Williams, 17 Ga. App. 196 (86 S. E. 413).

The corpus delicti of a larceny may be proved by circumstantial evidence. Patterson, 17 Ga. App. 341 (3) (86 S. E. 782).

Value. The fact that the defendant sold the stolen goods sufficiently shows that they were of some value. Greenfield, 14 Ga. App. 

603 (2) (81 S. E. 814); Tolver, 10 Ga. App. 33 (2) (72 S. E. 516).

SPECIFIC CRIMES 

509 

Value may be inferred from the purchase price. Peterson, 6 Ga.

Evidence of trivial value, such as five cents, will support conviction. Taylor, 139 Ga. 578 (1) (77 S. E. 373).

Where value of property is not shown, or that it had some value, conviction is illegal. Lane, 113 Ga. 1040 (39 S. E. 463); Portwood, 124 Ga. 783 (1) (53 S. E. 99). 

The value of the property stolen may be shown inferentially. Matthews, 26 Ga. App. 41 (2) (105 S. E. 383).

Recent possession. Where it is shown that the property stolen was found shortly thereafter in defendant's possession, and that particular articles had been missing from the merchandise of the owner, and that their absence had been noted for different periods of time, and the goods in question had never been sold by the owner, conviction warranted. McDuffie, 17 Ga. App. 342 (1) (86 S. E. 821).

Where on the trial of one charged with larceny it is shown by the evidence that recently after the commission of the offense the stolen goods were found in the possession of the defendant, that fact will authorize the jury to infer that the accused was guilty, unless he explained his possession to their satisfaction. There is a wide difference between resting the result of a trial upon facts which legally constitute the offense charged, and making it turn upon other facts which are not evidence of the constituent facts. (Italics by the 

Court.) Morris, 47 Ga. App. 792 (171 S. E. 555).

Evidence that the prosecutor missed yellow bolt of homespun and that defendant about that time asked another if he would buy a bolt of yellow homespun,-insufficient to convict. Starke, 25 Ga. 

App. 766 (104 S. E. 918).

Where the guilt of one charged with simple larceny depends wholly upon inference arising from the possession of the article alleged to have been stolen, which possession was shown by uncontradicted and unimpeached testimony to be consistent with innocence, conviction is illegal, although defendant may be guilty of receiving stolen goods. Slaughter, 24 Ga. App. 428 (100 S. E. 774). 

See also: Burglary.

Variance. Where accusation laid the ownership of the property stolen in a named person, and such property was under levy, and evidence showed that the title to the property was not in the person as laid, but that the property, when stolen, was in the lawful possession of the person so alleged to be the owner, who was the levying

officer, there was no variance. Cosby, 28 Ga. App. 550 (1) (112 S. 

E. 154); Gladden, 43 Ga. App. 236 (158 S. E. 338).

Where indictment described the property stolen as bills of various denominations, it meant bank bills. Where evidence did not show such bills to be bank bills, conviction not warranted. Johnson, 119 

Ga. 257 (2) (45 S. E. 960).

Where the indictment alleges that certain amount of money was stolen, the State need not prove the theft of the precise amount stated in the indictment. Martin, 17 Ga. App. 612 (2) (87 S. E. 844).

Where the indictment alleges the ownership of the property stolen. in one person, and the evidence shows that he held the property for another as an agent or bailee, there is no variance. Bennett, 28 Ga. 

App. 235 (110 S. E. 756).

Where the accusation charged that the goods stolen belonged to three named persons, and were in possession of one of them, and the evidence showed that they belonged jointly to the one in possession and two others of different names than those alleged, the variance is fatal. Horton, 21 Ga. App. 120 (3) (93 S. E. 1012). 

Indictment for larceny of "one set of single black-leather buggy harness" not sustained by proof not showing harness to be of leather or black in color. Moore, 13 Ga. App. 15 (78 S. E. 772).

In prosecution for simple larceny description of the stolen property must be proved as alleged, whenever the failure of the evidence. to conform to the averments would tend to put the accused again in jeopardy for the same offense. Moore, 13 Ga. App. 15, 16 (2) (78 

S. E. 772).

Miscellaneous. Proof of corpus delicti, venue, and the recent possession of the stolen property, and its sale by the defendant,-sufficient to make out prima facie case. Gilliard, 17 Ga. App. 364 (86 

S. E. 939).

Proof that the defendant was a farm hand, that as such he was directed to haul wood to the house, and, after hauling wood, to put up the team and do some other work, and that after hauling wood the defendant took the team and drove it from Monroe County to Macon, and tried to sell the mules, and finally did sell them, shows simple larceny and not larceny after trust. White, 24 Ga. App. 336 (100 S. E. 756).

Proof that the defendant took cotton seed from landlord, with the consent and in the presence of landlord's agent, intrusted with its custody, will not support conviction of simple larceny. Smith, 14 

Ga. App. 17 (2) (80 S. E. 22).

SPECIFIC CRIMES 

511 Where accused picked up some money on the street, alleged to have been stolen, and the owner demanded it from the accused, and there was evidence authorizing inference, that the accused knew at the time the owner demanded the money that it belonged to the person so demanding, and the accused refused to deliver it, inference that the accused appropriated the money with intent to steal the same is authorized. Pierce, 18 Ga. App. 432 (89 S. E. 430).

Where the accused was charged with larceny of a boat seized by officers of the law while being used to transport liquors, petition of the solicitor-general filed on proceedings to condemn the boat, and judgment thereunder―irrelevant and incompetent evidence. Goldberg, 150 Ga. 59 (5) (103 S. E. 90).

Illegal arrest. Although the arrest may be illegal, evidence discovered by search of the defendant's person with his consent, tending to point to defendant as the thief,—is admissible. Byrd, 10 Ga. 

App. 214 (2) (73 S. E. 34).

Verdicts. Although the defendant was indicted for larceny after trust, he may still be convicted for simple larceny, where evidence shows that at the time he induced the owner to intrust him with the property, he had intended to steal. Bryant, 8 Ga. App. 389 (2) (69 

S. E. 121).

The verdict of guilty of simple larceny is not contrary to law, although the evidence showed that the defendant was guilty also of larceny from the person and robbery by sudden snatching,—all in the same transaction. Hall, 41 Ga. App. 368 (153 S. E. 199).

The same transaction may constitute both simple larceny and larceny after trust. In such cases there may be conviction of either offense. Kelley, 24 Ga. App. 155 (1) (100 S. E. 23).

Simple larceny is involved in a charge of larceny from the house. 

Conviction for simple larceny may be had under a charge for larceny from the house, where the evidence warrants it. Blandford, 115 Ga. 824 (42 S. E. 207). 

b. HORSE STEALING. 

Indictment. charge and accuse. simple larceny, for that the said.. ...with the offense of on the........ ...day of did wrongfully, fraudu- .19...., in the county of...………….. lently and privately take, steal and carry away with intent to steal the same, one sorrel horse mule (and wagon), of the value of............ dollars, contrary, etc. . . . (Approved: Kelley, 24 Ga. App. 155, 157 (100 S. E. 23).)

Note: Describe animal fully.

The offense must be charged as simple larceny, but the indictment must designate the nature, character and sex of the animal, and give some other description by which its identity might be ascertained. § 26-2605.

The word "horse" is a generic term, which includes horse as a species, mule and ass. Horse, as a species, may again be subdivided into stallion, ridgeling, gelding, and mare, and the same subdivision may be made as to a mule and an ass. Brown, 86 Ga. 633 (13 S. 

E. 20). 

Indictment charging theft of "one dark bay horse with one white spot on the end of his nose, and one small white spot on his forehead" is insufficient. Brown, 86 Ga. 633 (13 S. E. 20), distinguishing Taylor, 44 Ga. 263. See also: Tucker, 114 Ga. 61 (39 S. E. 

926); Kelley, 24 Ga. App. 155, 157 (100 S. E. 23). (Concurring opinion.)

The expression "mare" for a female horse, "mare mule" for a female mule, and "jenny" for a female ass are sufficient descriptions. Teal, 119 Ga. 102, 104 (45 S. E. 964).

An indictment charging the theft of "one horse of the female sex, said animal being a dark bay mare," with other description,-sufficient. Teal, 119 Ga. 102, 104 (45 S. E. 964). 

General. Where larceny of the horse has been committed in another State, and the horse was brought into Georgia, the offense of larceny has not been committed in Georgia. Lee, 64 Ga. 203. 

c. CATTLE STEALING. 

Indictment. . . charge and accuse. simple larceny, for that the said. ..19..., in the county of... ....with the offense of on the........day of one animal of the....... sex and of the species known as cattle, ..............in color, marked of the personal goods of……………….. and branded.............. and of the value of...Dollars, unlawfully, wrongfully and fraudulently, did take and carry away with intent to steal the same, contrary, etc. . . . (Approved: Nightengale, 94 Ga. 395 (21 S. E. 

221).)

Description of the animal alleged to have been stolen as a certain black and white milk cow of a stated value, of the personal goods of a named person-sufficient. Wheeler, 18 Ga. App. 15 (1) (88 S. E. 712); Sowell, 28 Ga. App. 478 (1) (111 S. E. 689). 

Indictment charging that the cow was "blue and white speckled" and evidence showing that it was "black and white speckled”variance immaterial. Graham, 16 Ga. App. 221, 225 (84 S. E. 981).

SPECIFIC CRIMES 

513 Indictment for cattle stealing is sufficient where it is in the language of the Code, though it names offense as "larceny." Sneed, 16 Ga. App. 351 (1) (85 S. E. 354).

Although needlessly minute or comprehensive description must be proved as alleged, the superfluous elements need not be established with the same degree of certainty as the essentials of the case. 

Nightengale, 94 Ga. 395 (2) (21 S. E. 221).

Sex of the animal is not a necessary allegation in indictment for cattle stealing. Burch, 4 Ga. App. 384 (1-a) (61 S. E. 503). Horse stealing distinguished. Gibson, 7 Ga. App. 692, 693 (67 S. E. 838).

General. It is a matter of common knowledge, and the courts will take judicial cognizance, that a cow is a female animal, is a horned animal, and has cloven hoofs, and that the larceny of a cow is therefore within § 26-2607. It is also a matter of common knowledge that a heifer is a young cow. Adams, 22 Ga. App. 786 (97 S. 

E. 201); Sowell, 28 Ga. App. 478 (111 S. E. 689).

Venue. Where accused took the cattle in a certain county with intent to steal, the larceny was committed in that county, and the venue was properly laid there, regardless where the accused disposed of the cattle. Clanton, 17 Ga. App. 474, 475 (2) (87 S. E. 691).

Where the accused took the cattle in one county with intent to drive them without the permission of the owner, and formed the intent to steal them when he reached another county, or another State, the crime was committed in the place where such intent to steal was formed. Clanton, 17 Ga. App. 474, 475 (2) (87 S. E. 691).

The venue may be proved by circumstantial evidence. Graham, 16 Ga. App. 221 (84 S. E. 981); McCoy, 123 Ga. 143, 145 (51 S. E. 

279); Livingston, 18 Ga. App. 679 (1) (90 S. E. 287).

Intent to steal. Killing of an animal, not with intent to steal it, is not larceny. If animus furandi entered defendant's mind after the animal was killed, he would not be guilty of cattle stealing. 

Nightengale, 94 Ga. 395 (3) (21 S. E. 221).

Restitution. No defense. Coleman, 43 Ga. App. 586 (159 S. E. 

605).

Former adjudication. Acquittal of larceny of a cow is bar to subsequent prosecution for the same larceny in which the animal stolen is described as a steer. Burch, 4 Ga. App. 384 (1-b) (61 S. 

E. 503).

Where several articles belonging to different persons are stolen

at one time, only one larceny is committed, and one indicted may be charged with the larceny of all of the articles, alleging ownership according to the facts. But after indictment and conviction of larceny of any one of the articles, the prosecution is exhausted, and the thief can not be subsequently indicted and convicted of the larceny of any one of the articles embraced in the same larceny, although that particular article was omitted from the former indictment. Dean, 9 Ga. App. 571 (71 S. E. 932).

Beef. Evidence of finding beef at the home of the defendant is not sufficient to convict of cattle stealing, the beef not being identified as part of the animal stolen, and the evidence being entirely circumstantial. Taylor, 29 Ga. App. 34 (113 S. E. 93). 

d. HOG STEALING. 

Indictment. charge and accuse.. .with the offense of simple larceny, for that the said............., on the............ day of............. 

19..., in the county of one animal of the. of the species known as hog, sex and (describe the animal fully). of the personal goods of.............., and of the value of

Dollars, unlawfully, wrongfully and fraudulently, did take and carry away with intent to steal the same, contrary, etc.

Where indictment describes property as "one red and black spotted sow hog of the value of $10, one white and black spotted sow hog of the value of $10, one red and black spotted male hog of the value of $10, one dark red male hog of the value of $10, and two white and black spotted sow hogs of the value of $10 each, description is sufficient. Knight, 25 Ga. App. 765 (1) (105 S. E. 

248); Geiger, 21 Ga. App. 75 (1) (93 S. E. 1027). 

Earmark need not be alleged. But where it is alleged, it must be proved. Robertson, 97 Ga. 206 (2) (22 S. E. 974). Where there. was a material variance between earmark as charged, and as proved, conviction was illegal. Crenshaw, 64 Ga. 449. 

Where indictment described the hog as "barrow hog, color white and black spotted" and evidence showed that the hog stolen was "black and white spotted" hog, the variance was fatal. Paulk, 5 

Ga. App. 567 (63 S. E. 659).

Variance between allegation and evidence as to sex of hogs,fatal. Green, 95 Ga. 463 (22 S. E. 289). 

General. Where the ownership of several hogs is in different persons, the stealing of the hogs, all at the same time and place,

SPECIFIC CRIMES 

515 is but one offense. Lowe, 57 Ga. 171; Dean, 9 Ga. App. 571 (71 S. 

E. 932).

The taking of a dead hog is larceny if the taking is with an intent to steal; but to constitute the offense of hog-stealing the animal must be alive when the thief forms the intent to steal and proceeds to take the hog into possession. Paulk, 5 Ga. App. 567, 572 (63 S. E. 659); Smith, 11 Ga. App. 385 (75 S. E. 447). 

Where defendant shot the hog with intent to steal it, but was surprised and discovered, conviction for attempt to steal hog was authorized. Tinker, 125 Ga. 743 (54 S. E. 662). 

Bona fide claim. Intent to steal negatived by evidence that the defendant claimed the hog in good faith. Smith, 11 Ga. App. 385 (75 S. E. 447); Lee, 102 Ga. 221 (1) (29 S. E. 264).

Evidence. Sufficient evidence that the deceased hog, some of whose remains were found in prisoner's possession, was the identical hog stolen, warrants conviction. Stevens, 77 Ga. 310 (2 S. E. 684).

Evidence that the sow was killed to prevent her from recognizing the stolen pigs, upon the trial of a possessory warrant for the same pigs, admissible. Crowell, 74 Ga. 396.

Evidence as to changing of marks on the stolen hog-admissible. 

Finley, 26 Ga. App. 9, 11 (105 S. E. 497). 

Bail trover proceedings against the prosecutor to recover hogs alleged to have been stolen-not admissible. Finley, 26 Ga. App. 

9, 12 (9) (105 S. E. 497).

Evidence that the defendant carried the hog alleged to have been stolen in his buggy to the home of certain persons, to whom he said that he had more hogs than he could feed, that he left the hog with such persons, and that the prosecutor found it at such person's house, and that before his arrest defendant asked prosecutor what he would take to compromise the case, offering a certain sum, sufficient to convict. Cotton, 21 Ga. App. 507 (94 S. E. 589).

Evidence that the hog was heard to squeal, that witness ran to him, that defendant ran off from him, that hog was dead, being knocked in the head,-enough to show taking and carrying away with intent to steal. Cross, 64 Ga. 443 (1).

Charge. It is reversible error for the Court to refuse to charge the jury, on the trial of one charged with hog-stealing, that they could recommend, if they saw fit, that the defendant be punished as for a misdemeanor. Moore, 150 Ga. 679, 680 (2) (104 S. E. 907); 

Moore, 26 Ga. App. 21 (2) (105 S. E. 621).

Felony. The quality of the crime of hog-stealing can not be reduced from felony to misdemeanor, though the punishment may be as for a misdemeanor, if the jury recommends it and the judge approves. Wells, 116 Ga. 87, 88 (42 S. E. 390). 

e. OTHER DOMESTIC ANIMALS. 

Dog comes within the terms of this section. Patton, 93 Ga. 111, 114 (19 S. E. 734). 

Sheep. Clark, 19 Ga. App. 145 (91 S. E. 231). 

f. ALTERING BRANDS AND MARKS. 

Indictment. charge and accuse.... ........with the offense of a felony, for that the said.. -------------, on the... ...day of... 

19..., in the county of...did then and there unlawfully and feloniously mark........ the property of..............by cutting off (describe the alteration)................, and by then and there altering and changing the mark on said... .....with the intention to claim and appropriate said...to his, the said, use, and to prevent identification by the said owner of said........... 

contrary, etc. . . . (Approved: Lawrence, 10 Ga. App. 786 (74 S. E. 

300).)

General. Word "marks" means only artificial marks or brands placed upon stock. Churchill, 108 Ga. 265, 269 (33 S. E. 972).

It is not necessary, to support conviction under an indictment for altering brands and marks, that it should appear that at the time the criminal act was committed the accused knew who was the owner of the animal. As to this matter it is sufficient if it appear that the animal was not the property of the accused and that he marked or branded it in the manner described in the indictment, with an intention to appropriate it to his own use, or to prevent identification by the true owner. Lawrence, 10 Ga. App. 786 (74 S. E. 300). 

g. LARCENY OF DEEDS AND PAPERS. 

Ownership in prosecution under § 26-2615 is a matter of description and is not an element of the crime. Hence it need not be alleged in detail as it must be in simple larceny. Hanson, 13 Ga. 

App. 372 (79 S. E. 176). 

h. LARCENY OF BONDS. 

Federal government currency comes within the category of "bank bills," named in § 26-2616. Johnson, 119 Ga. 257, 260 (45 S. E. 960).

SPECIFIC CRIMES 

517 1 Warehouse receipt is a subject matter of larceny. Currie, 3 Ga. 

App. 309 (59 S. E. 926). 

j. LARCENY OF THINGS SAVORING OF THE REALTY. 

Anything detached from the realty becomes personalty instantly on being so detached, and may be subject matter of larceny, even by the person wrongfully detaching it. § 26-2619.

Coffin removed from the grave becomes personalty and can be subject matter of larceny, provided the coffin is the property of the party who bought it and buried the dead. Ware, 31 Ga. App. 

554, 555 (121 S. E. 251). 

k. LARCENY FROM THE PERSON. 

Indictment. charge and accuse. with the offense of the (the prop- of larceny from the person, for that the said............., on the………………………….. day of.................19...., in the county aforesaid, did then and there unlawfully, wrongfully, and fraudulently take..... value of......... Dollars, from the person of.. erty of...), privately and without the knowledge with intent to steal the same, contrary, etc. proved: Hugo, 110 Ga. 768 (36 S. E. 60); Powell, 88 Ga. 32 (13 S. 

E. 829).) of said (Ap- Ownership of the property taken need not be alleged in an indictment for larceny from the person. Hugo, 110 Ga. 768 (36 S. 

E. 60); Hanson, 13 Ga. App. 372, 373 (79 S. E. 176).

Description of the stolen property as "one watch and chain of the value of seventy-five dollars, and the property of a named person" sufficient. Powell, 88 Ga. 32 (13 S. E. 829).

Indictment need not allege that the crime was committed without the possessor's knowledge. Chislon, 19 Ga. App. 609 (91 S. E. 923). 

General. Larceny from the person is distinguished from robbery by the presence of force or intimidation as an essential element of robbery. Fanning, 66 Ga. 167; Moran, 125 Ga. 33, 34 (53 S. E. 806).

Attempted larceny may become robbery when force and violence are used to complete the unlawful act. Where thief's hand is caught in the pocket of another and a struggle ensues and money is taken violently and by infliction of physical injuries, the offense is robbery, and not larceny from the person. Carter, 3 Ga. App. 477 (2) (60 S. E. 216). 

Larceny from the person varies from simple larceny in that the taking must be privately and without the knowledge of the person

from whom it is taken. Jackson, 116 Ga. 578, 579 (42 S. E. 750);

Moye, 65 Ga. 754. To constitute a larceny from the person it must appear that some article of value was wrongfully and fraudulently taken from the person of another privately and without his knowledge, with intent to steal the same. (Id.)

Where owner has knowledge that the property is being taken, larceny from the person is not committed. Moye, 65 Ga. 754 (2); 

Jackson, 116 Ga. 578 (42 S. E. 750); Stewart, 10 Ga. App. 442 (73 

S. E. 602).

The force which distinguishes robbery from larceny from the person, where the property is taken without the knowledge of the owner, may be no more than is used to break a watch chain, in detaching a watch from the person. Bowen, 16 Ga. App. 110, 111 (2) (84 S. E. 730).

Larceny from the person and robbery are offenses of different character and can not be joined in the indictment. Robbery involves force, larceny does not. Doyle, 77 Ga. 513.

Bank notes are subject of larceny from the person. The common law is changed in that respect. Thomasson, 22 Ga. 499, 505.

Where possession of the property is given voluntarily for a lawful purpose, though the defendant received the property with a fraudulent intent, the crime can not be larceny from the person. 

It may be simple larceny. Hecox, 105 Ga. 625 (31 S. E. 592).

The offense of larceny from the person may be committed although the person from whom the property is taken may be, or becomes almost contemporaneously with the larceny, aware that the larceny has been committed; and the judge may so instruct the jury. Watts, 8 Ga. App. 205 (4) (68 S. E. 863).

For the offense of larceny from the person to be punishable as for a felony, there must be proof that the value of the thing stolen exceeds fifty dollars, where indictment so charges. Powell, 88 Ga. 

32 (2) (13 S. E. 829).

Under indictment charging larceny from the person conviction of simple larceny may be had as the latter is included in the former. 

Lavender, 107 Ga. 707 (33 S. E. 420). 

1. LARCENY FROM THE HOUSE. 

Indictment. . . charge and accuse.. larceny from the house, for that the said.. day of................19...., in the county of........... ..with the offense of on the........... did then and there unlawfully, after entering the dwelling house of...

, privately

SPECIFIC CRIMES 

519 steal therefrom.... etc. of the value of.......... Dollars, contrary, (Approved: Jefferson, 117 Ga. 710 (45 S. E. 61).) charge and accuse.. the house, for that the said. and with the offense of larceny from ..., in the county of...... day of19., with force 

State of Georgia, on the........ and arms, did from the office and place of business of…………………………-----, said office and place of business being a house in said State and county, wrongfully, fraudulently, and privately take, steal, and carry away, with intent to steal the same, of the value of... 

Dollars, and the property of, contrary, etc. . . . (Approved: 

Blackmon, 24 Ga. App. 384 (100 S. E. 730).) 

For other approved indictments see: Glaze, 2 Ga. App. 704, 705 (58 S. E. 1126); Heard, 120 Ga. 848, 849 (48 S. E. 311).

Indictment charging the accused with entering a dwelling house and stealing therefrom valuable goods is a good indictment, though the word "privately" is omitted. Jenkins, 13 Ga. App. 695 (1) (79 S. E. 861); Kimbrough, 101 Ga. 583 (29 S. E. 39).

Where the larceny of several articles is charged in one bill of indictment, it is better practice to set out the value of each article; but the indictment is good if it alleges merely the aggregate value of the articles charged to have been stolen. Bone, 120 Ga. 866 (3) (48 S. E. 356). 

Animus furandi must be alleged and proved. Musgrove, 5 Ga. App. 467 (1) (63 S. E. 538). 

Ownership of the property should be laid in the occupant, though title may be in another. Indictment charging ownership in one, and evidence showing occupation in another,-variance fatal. Lindsey, 9 Ga. App. 299 (2) (70 S. E. 1114); Trice, 116 Ga. 602 (42 S. 

E. 1008).

Where the goods stolen belonged to a partnership, and one of the partners has custody thereof, indictment alleging such partner as owner-upheld. Goode, 70 Ga. 752.

Title to property alleged in husband is supported by proof of title in wife, both living in the same house. Thomas, 125 Ga. 286 (54 S. E. 182).

Where indictment charged ownership in one, and evidence shows him to be a lodger in the house, and that theft was committed in his room, indictment upheld. Farlinger, 110 Ga. 313 (1) (35 S. E. 152). 

Ownership of the house and of the goods can properly be laid in a person who had possession of the house and the goods at the time

of the theft as the owner's agent. Jackson, 15 Ga. App. 179 (1) (82 S. E. 771). 

Where accusation alleges that the ownership was in a named church, and the proof showed that the property belonged to the conference with possession in the named church as bailee, the variation was not fatal. Chambers, 40 Ga. App. 644 (150 S. E. 864).

As larceny from the house is not an offense against the habitation, but against the property, as contradistinguished from the building, the ownership of the house is immaterial. Simmons, 73 

Ga. 609, 615. 

See also: Burglary. General.

Larceny from the house is a larceny of a compound nature. Blackmon, 24 Ga. App. 384 (1-a) (100 S. E. 730).

Larceny from the house is a crime involving moral turpitude. 

Jenkins, 14 Ga. App. 276 (3) (80 S. E. 688).

Classifications. There are four classifications of the offense of larceny from the house: (1) Breaking any house with intent to steal; (2) entering any house with intent to steal; (3) stealing from any house after having broken in the same; (4) stealing from the house after having entered it. Heard, 120 Ga. 848 (1) (48 S. E. 

311); Jones, 146 Ga. 187, 188 (91 S. E. 67).

House. The language of § 26-2630 is very broad, and a punishment is prescribed for a larceny from any building whatever. Williams, 105 Ga. 814, 815 (32 S. E. 129).

Theft of goods from a warehouse platform, used for the purpose of carrying goods into the warehouse and removing them therefrom, as well as for temporary deposit of goods, is larceny from the house. Suddeth, 24 Ga. App. 591 (1) (101 S. E. 763); Wilson, 9 

Ga. App. 297 (1) (70 S. E. 1125).

A structure having a roof and lateral enclosure of some sort in which persons live or work, animals are confined or property is stored or contained,-is a house within the meaning of the law of larceny from the house. McCabe, 1 Ga. App. 719 (58 S. E. 277).

To steal articles of value from the porch of a restaurant, the porch being also used as a part of the restaurant,-is larceny from the house. Johnson, 2 Ga. App. 405 (58 S. E. 684).

The front porch of a dwelling house, covered by a roof, is a part of the dwelling house, and a larceny from the porch of such dwelling house comes within the law of larceny from the house. Downer, 10 Ga. App. 827 (1) (74 S. E. 301); Burge, 62 Ga. 170, 171.

SPECIFIC CRIMES 

521 A wharf, or landing place, covered with roof but unenclosed, is not a house or building as contemplated in the law of larceny from the house. McCabe, 1 Ga. App. 719 (58 S. E. 277).

Pigeon, or chicken house is subject of larceny from the house. 

Williams, 105 Ga. 814 (32 S. E. 129); Gardner, 105 Ga. 662 (31 S. 

E. 577); Carter, 106 Ga. 372 (32 S. E. 345).

The offense of larceny from the house of valuable goods can be committed in or upon any house and is not limited to houses in which burglary may be committed. Williams, 46 Ga. 212, 217; 

Stanley, 58 Ga. 430; Bearden, 95 Ga. 459 (20 S. E. 11).

Kind of house is immaterial. Accordingly, theft from cotton. house has been held to be larceny from the house. Stanley, 58 Ga. 430, 432. 

Valuable goods. "Value" does not necessarily mean money value or market value. Gates, 20 Ga. App. 171 (5) (92 S. E. 974).

Intoxicating liquors, although prohibited, are things of value and subject of larceny. Gates, 20 Ga. App. 171 (5) (92 S. E. 974); 

August, 11 Ga. App. 798 (1) (76 S. E. 164). "Anything" that has any intrinsic value, however small, can be the subject matter of larceny from the house. Edmondson, 18 Ga. 

App. 233, 239 (89 S. E. 189).

Warehouse receipt of cotton is subject matter of larceny. Currie, 3 Ga. App. 309 (2) (59 S. E. 926).

Asportation. The distance of the asportation is immaterial. Glaze, 2 Ga. App. 704, 707 (58 S. E. 1126).

Private taking. In order to constitute larceny from the house the theft must have been privately committed. Jones, 146 Ga. 187 (91 S. E. 67); Jenkins, 13 Ga. App. 695, 697 (79 S. E. 861).

Entrance. Where all other elements of the offense of larceny from the house are present, manner of entrance in the house need not be proved. Parks, 66 Ga. 192, 194.

Punishment. Formerly it was held that § 26-2629 provides no punishment but merely creates a crime, and therefore this crime is not punishable. Jenkins, 13 Ga. App. 695 (2) (79 S. E. 861); 

Jenkins, 14 Ga. App. 276 (1) (80 S. E. 688). But later it was held that larceny from the house as defined in § 26-2629 is punishable as prescribed in §§ 26-2631, 26-2632 and 26-2633. Jones, 146 Ga. 

187 (2) (91 S. E. 67); Jones, 19 Ga. App. 67 (1) (90 S. E. 981).

Conflicts. The law of larceny from the house is not in conflict with the law of burglary. Evans, 146 Ga. 98 (2) (90 S. E. 743).

So much of § 26-2401 as makes it a felony to break and enter a "storehouse, or other place of business of another, where valuable goods, wares, produce, or any other articles of value are contained or stored," with intent to commit a larceny, is in conflict with, and prohibits the application of § 26-2633 insofar as it purports to make it a misdemeanor to break and enter a house of the character above described, with intent to steal, where the offender, being detected, is prevented from carrying his intent into effect. There is no conflict between the other sections. Evans, 146 Ga. 98 (1) (90 S. E. 743). 

Burglary distinguished. Larceny from the house may be, in this 

State, breaking a house with intent to steal, or entering a house with intent to steal, and it is very true that burglary, to wit, breaking and entering with intent to steal, does, in the very nature of things, include breaking with intent to steal, or entering with intent to steal. But there is an ingredient in larceny from the house. that does not exist in burglary. In burglary, if one break and enter with intent to steal, he is guilty of the offense. But he is not guilty of larceny from the house if, after breaking and entering with intent to steal, he, of his own motion, change that intent. To make out the crime of larceny from the house, when there is no theft or taking, there must be a breaking or entering with intent to steal, and the offender must be prevented by detection. The crime of actual larceny from the house is imputed, because it exists in fact because of its having been prevented by another. But burglary, to wit, breaking and entering with intent to steal, is complete as soon as the breaking and entering is complete, with intent to steal. 

No amount of after repentance will help. Williams, 46 Ga. 212, 215. 

Where the indictment for burglary charges that the breaking and entering of the dwelling house was with intent to commit. larceny, and the evidence shows breaking, the offense of larceny from the house is not involved, and a conviction would be illegal. 

Tarver, 95 Ga. 222, 227 (3) (21 S. E. 381).

Larceny after trust. Where one voluntarily, and without being induced by the fraud of another, delivers property into the possession of another, for the purpose of holding and keeping it for him and for his benefit, and the person so receiving such possession wrongfully and fraudulently converts the property to his own use, such conversion is larceny after trust, without the element of simple

SPECIFIC CRIMES 

523 larceny, and a conviction of larceny from the house is illegal. 

Wright, 18 Ga. App. 337 (1) (89 S. E. 432).

Forgery. The fact that forgery was committed in accomplishing larceny from the house is no defense to a charge of larceny. 

Currie, 3 Ga. App. 309 (1) (59 S. E. 926).

Consent. Where the property is taken with the consent of the owner or his authorized agent, there can be no larceny. Watson, 6 Ga. App. 801 (65 S. E. 1126).

Where one employs another to steal an article from the owner, he is not guilty of larceny where the person so employed and taking the article from the owner acts with the owner's consent and as his agent. Edmondson, 18 Ga. App. 233 (89 S. E. 189). 

Restitution. The fact that the no loss or recovered the same is 

309 (3) (59 S. E. 926). owner of the property suffered immaterial. Currie, 3 Ga. App. 

Intent. Where want of intent is the sole defense, Court should charge fully the law thereon. Glaze, 2 Ga. App. 704 (58 S. E. 1126).

Duress. Where the sale of the property was under duress, the vendor can not be convicted of larceny for subsequently removing the property. Love, 78 Ga. 66 (3 S. E. 893).

Verdicts. Where an indictment for burglary charges that the breaking and entering of the dwelling house was with intent to commit a larceny and the larceny is particularly set out, there may be a conviction of larceny from the house. Ray, 121 Ga. 189 (1) (48 S. E. 903); Thomas, 18 Ga. App. 101 (88 S. E. 917).

Where the evidence makes out both charges, burglary and larceny from the house, and both are properly charged in the indictment, a conviction for either is lawful. Green, 119 Ga. 120 (1) (45 

S. E. 990); Lockhart, 3 Ga. App. 480 (3) (60 S. E. 215); Butts, 26 

Ga. App. 40 (1) (105 S. E. 372).

Upon a charge of larceny from the house conviction may be had for simple larceny, if the evidence warrants it. Patterson, 122 Ga. 

587 (2) (50 S. E. 489); Blandford, 115 Gå. 824 (1) (42 S. E. 207).

Larceny from the house involves the lesser offense of simple larceny.

Evidence. Where the evidence shows that the value of the property stolen is less than fifty dollars, accomplice need not be corroborated, although the indictment charges the value to be more than fifty dollars. Wall, 75 Ga. 474 (3).

Description of the property stolen must be supported by evidence,

though indictment described it with unnecessary details, and though description was unnecessarily minute. McLendon, 121 Ga. 158 (48 S. E. 902). 

Evidence of the prosecutrix that she saw money in the house immediately prior to the time the defendant went into the house, that she missed the money after the accused left, that no one else went into the house, and that immediately after missing the money she went to the defendant and he had money in his pocket folded up like prosecutrix had her money folded-warrants conviction. 

Hill, 26 Ga. App. 422 (106 S. E. 306).

Where the only circumstance against the defendant was a letter found in the house where the theft was alleged to have been committed, such letter being addressed to the defendant, which letter defendant admitted to belong to him, verdict of guilty not authorized. Culp, 21 Ga. App. 786 (2) (95 S. E. 268). 

Variance. Where indictment charged entering and stealing, and evidence showed entering with intent to steal, variance fatal. Hicks, 101 Ga. 581 (28 S. E. 917). 

Indictment alleging house to be "storehouse" and evidence showing it to be "warehouse" where goods are stored, there is no variance. Martin, 95 Ga. 478 (3) (20 S. E. 271).

Where indictment alleges that the article was stolen from a wagon shed and evidence showed that it was stolen from under a buggy shed house, variance fatal. Thompson, 92 Ga. 448 (17 S. E. 265). 

p. BREAKING AND ENTERING CAR. 

Indictment. charge and accuse... .with the offense of larceny, for that the said................., on the...... on the……………………………………..day of 

19...., in the county of... did break and enter a railroad car of the……………………………………..Ry Co., with intent to steal the goods, wares, and freight therein contained, and, after so breaking and entering, did steal therefrom...... of the value of 

Dollars, contrary, -" etc. . . . (Approved: Berry, 124 Ga. 825 (53 S. E. 316).) 

For approved indictment see also: Farm, 24 Ga. App. 114 (1) (3) (100 S. E. 36).

When an indictment under this section alleges that the accused "did then and there, unlawfully and with force and arms, break and enter a railroad car with intent to steal goods, wares, and freight in said car being," no description, value or ownership of any goods. intended to be stolen need be alleged. Farm, 24 Ga. App. 114 (100 

S. E. 36).

Allegation that the railroad car was in possession of a named

SPECIFIC CRIMES 

525 railroad company sufficiently states the ownership. Farm, 24 Ga. 

App. 114 (100 S. E. 36).

General. This section embraces two offenses. The one is committed when the railroad car is broken and entered with intent to steal, though that intent may not be carried into effect; and the other is where there has been a breaking and entering of the car, and an actual stealing therefrom. The indictment charging the first offense must allege that the breaking and entering was with the intent to steal, and this intent to steal may be alleged by an averment that, after breaking and entering, the accused did steal. 

Berry, 124 Ga. 825, 826 (53 S. E. 316). 

Ownership. Allegation of ownership of car in certain railroad company is supported by evidence that possession and control of the car was in the company. Adkins, 115 Ga. 582 (41 S. E. 987).

Venue. It must appear that the larceny from the car was actually committed in the county of the trial. Williams, 105 Ga. 743, 745 (31 S. E. 749).

Larceny from the house. If, in the commission of the offense of larceny from railroad car, or breaking and entering a railroad car, the greater offense of larceny from the house, involving an amount of fifty dollars or more, is committed, as where the car is within a house, the State may elect to prosecute for the offense of larceny from the house. Bone, 121 Ga. 147 (48 S. E. 986). 

r. STEALING BALED COTTON. 

Indictment. charge and accuse. simple larceny, for that the said.... .19...., in the county of.......... .with the offense of on the day of .....bales of lint cotton, did, unlawfully, wrongfully and fraudulently, take and carry away…..... of the aggregate weight of................pounds, and of the value of the property of... was stored, contrary, etc. from........ where the same

No locality except that for venue, that is within the county, need be charged. Hall, 120 Ga. 142 (47 S. E. 519).

Place of storage need not be charged, where the indictment is for simple larceny, for the words "from any place where the same may be stored" simply mean any place where the same may be placed or located. Mosely, 74 Ga. 404; Morris, 84 Ga. 7, 8 (10 S. 

E. 368).

Indictment need not give the exact weight of cotton. Green, 114 

Ga. 918 (41 S. E. 55).

General. The purpose of this section is to make the stealing of baled cotton a felony, regardless of the value thereof, or the place where it was stored. Hall, 120 Ga. 142 (47 S. E. 519).

Where cotton was stolen in one county and carried into another, venue was in either. Green, 114 Ga. 918 (2) (41 S. E. 55).

Substantial proof of the weight of the cotton as alleged-is sufficient. Green, 114 Ga. 918 (1) (41 S. E. 55).

One who assists another in removing cotton, believing it to belong to the latter, but who being informed that the cotton was stolen, yet continues to assist, is guilty as principal. Green, 114 

S. LARCENY OF AUTOMOBILES. 

By 26-2603 the larceny of an automobile was made a felony; and any person convicted of this offense is punishable by imprisonment in the penitentiary for a time not less than one nor more than five years. By § 27-2511 any person, upon second conviction of larceny of an automobile, is punishable by imprisonment in the penitentiary for five years, which punishment is different from that imposed by § 26-2603 for the first conviction of larceny of an automobile, and this being so, the indictment for the second offense must allege the indictment and the conviction of the accused for the first offense, and proof of such allegation must be made, before the accused can be subjected to the punishment provided in § 272511, the latter punishment being the maximum provided under the above stated act. Tribble, 168 Ga. 699 (148 S. E. 593).

The rule found in § 26-2602, allowing the thief in simple larceny to be indicted in any county into which he has carried the property is applicable to thefts of automobiles, even though such theft be made a felony by § 26-2603. Lanier, 25 Ga. App. 489 (2) (103 S. 

E. 730).

Evidence as to the condition of the stolen automobile at the time it was recovered-admissible. Gilbert, 27 Ga. App. 604 (2) (109 

S. E. 697).

The accused contending that he bought the automobile in question from two unknown men dressed as soldiers, testimony of witnesses that two soldiers attempted to sell them an automobile about the same time defendant claims to have bought the automobile alleged to have been stolen,-admissible, although they are unable to identify the automobile alleged to have been stolen as the same automobile that the soldiers tried to sell them. Stringer, 26 Ga. 

App. 491 (106 S. E. 300).

u. LARCENY AFTER TRUST BY BAILEE. 

Indictment. with the offense of on the........day then and there unlaw- ..., the owner thereof, Dollars, for of charge and accuse. larceny after trust, for that the said.. of…---------------19.--., in the county aforesaid, did fully, after having been intrusted by......

with........... in paper money, of the value the purpose of holding, keeping said...... the said..……………………………………., did fraudulently convert said. use and did otherwise dispose of said..... of said…………………….. said. for said….......…………………., he, ..to his own .without the consent the owner thereof, and to the injury of him, the and without paying the said.--------------- the said.…………………………………. or the full market value thereof, on demand, which demand was made, all of which was contrary, etc. (Approved: Cody, 100 

Ga. 105 (28 S. E. 106).) Indictment need not allege other disposition of the property than its fraudulent conversion by the bailee to his own use. Cody, 100 

Ga. 105 (1) (28 S. E. 106).

Indictment charging that defendant fraudulently converted goods to his own use, need not charge that the same was done without the consent of the owner, and to his injury, and without paying on demand full value. These clauses apply to other disposition of the goods than to fraudulent conversion to his own use. Alderman, 57 Ga. 367 (1). 

Indictment charging disposition of the property in alternativedefective. Sanders, 86 Ga. 717 (12 S. E. 1058); Cody, 100 Ga. 105, 109 (28 S. E. 106).

The description of the property stolen in the indictment for larceny after trust need not meet the standard set for indictments for simple larceny. Cody, 100 Ga. 105, 110 (28 S. E. 106); Sanders, 86 

Ga. 716, 723 (12 S. E. 1058).

Where delegated trust is charged, sufficient ground must be shown for such delegated trust. Rice, 6 Ga. App. 160, 161 (64 S. E. 575).

Indictment for larceny after trust charging offense under § 262806 with consent of the owner is bad on demurrer. Cory, 55 Ga. 236. 

Indictment under § 26-2806 is fatally defective unless it charges that the delivery of the property intrusted to the accused was for some purpose in which bailor or some person other than the accused had interest. Barksdale, 28 Ga. App. 535 (1) (112 S. E. 165).

Under first clause of § 26-2806 indictment need not set out demand for payment, nor is proof thereof essential. Innes, 19 Ga. App.

271, 272 (5) (91 S. E. 339); Sewell, 23 Ga. App. 765 (2) (99 S. E. 

320); Alderman, 57 Ga. 367; Keys, 112 Ga. 392 (37 S. E. 762).

Indictment is not defective because it describes, as owner of the property, one who at the time it was intrusted to the defendant, was lawfully in actual possession, and who at the time of the conversion was entitled to such possession. Waters, 15 Ga. App. 342 

Ownership of the goods stolen may be laid in bailee, including common carrier, from whom they were stolen. Waters, 15 Ga. App. 342 (1) (83 S. E. 200). 

Where one of joint owners is in possession of the goods or money when it is stolen, indictment naming such joint owner alone as owner is good. Waters, 15 Ga. App. 342 (2) (83 S. E. 200).

Though the offenses described in § 26-2806 (defining larceny by bailee) and § 26-2809 (defining larceny by any other person) are distinct offenses, they are kindred offenses, and may be charged in separate counts of the same indictment. Innes, 19 Ga. App. 271 (2) (91 S. E. 339); Sewell, 23 Ga. App. 765 (2) (99 S. E. 320). 

General. § 26-2806 makes two kinds of offenses criminal: (1)

That in which the party fraudulently converts to his own use money or article intrusted to him; (2) that in which he otherwise disposes of the same without the consent of the owner or bailor, and to his injury, and without paying to such bailor or owner on demand the full market value or market price thereof. In the first kind the crime is complete as soon as the party fraudulently converts the property to his own use. McCoy, 15 Ga. 205, 211. In the second class the crime is complete (the other elements being present) when demand is made and the full market value and price is not there upon paid. Raiden, 1 Ga. App. 532 (57 S. E. 989). The venue lies in the county where the crime becomes completed in one or the other methods shown in § 26-2806. Raiden, 1 Ga. App. 532 (57 

S. E. 989); Innes, 19 Ga. App. 271 (2) (91 S. E. 339).

Under the second clause of § 26-2806 the refusal to pay, upon demand, or the property converted, is an ingredient of the offense, which must be charged and proved. Soule, 71 Ga. 267, 270; Cody, 100 Ga. 105, 107 (28 S. E. 106); Whitaker, 9 Ga. App. 213, 217 (70) 

S. E. 990).

Joint owners. While joint owners of property can not be guilty of larceny if either merely takes the property to his exclusive use, unless the person from whom it was taken had the right to its exclusive possession at the time, yet one joint owner may be guilty

SPECIFIC CRIMES 

529 of larceny if he takes the entire property with felonious intention to deprive the other joint owner of his share. Therefore, where A and B are joint owners of a promissory note and A collects the entire amount of the note, with felonious intention to deprive B of his share of the proceeds, and actually does so deprive him, A is guilty of larceny. Sewell, 23 Ga. App. 765 (3) (99 S..E. 320).

Bailee. "Any other bailee" means any bailee, whether of the classes enumerated in the Code or not, with whom money or other things of value may be deposited. Belt, 103 Ga. 12 (1) (29 S. E. 

451); McCrory, 11 Ga. App. 787 (1) (76 S. E. 163).

The word "bailee" as used in § 26-2806 is broadly construed to include every person to whom the possession of property is delivered by another, but the use here contemplates more than a loan solely for the benefit of the borrower. Rice, 6 Ga. App. 160, 161 (64 S. E. 575). 

Temporary loan of property, without hire, or other benefit, is not such bailment as would make the conversion larceny after trust. 

Rice, 6 Ga. App. 160 (2) (64 S. E. 575). 

Fraudulent conversion. Fraudulent conversion is deception deliberately practiced in order to gain an undue and unfair advantage. 

Etheridge, 78 Ga. 340.

To constitute the offense of larceny after trust there must be a specific intent to fraudulently convert to the use of the bailee the property intrusted to him, or otherwise fraudulently to dispose of the property. Culpable negligence can not be an ingredient of larceny after trust. Rucker, 12 Ga. App. 632 (77 S. E. 1129).

Where one voluntarily and without being induced by fraud of another delivers property into the possession of another, for the purpose of holding and keeping it for him and for his benefit, and the person so receiving possession wrongfully and fraudulently converts the property to his own use, such conversion is larceny after trust, without an element of simple larceny. Wright, 18 Ga.

App. 337 (1) (89 S. E. 432). 

Mere use of the article does not show fraudulent conversion unless such use was fraudulent. There must be circumstances indicating the purpose to deprive the owner of his property. Snell, 50 

Ga. 219.

Swapping mule which had been intrusted to the defendant with a view of his purchasing it and refusing to pay purchase price on demand is fraudulent conversion. Aiken, 73 Ga. 812.

Where, during a fiduciary relation, the owner of the property,

which another has procured by fraud, voluntarily intrusts possession of the property to the other, who thereafter converts it to his own use, the offense is larceny after trust. Lanier, 17 Ga. App. 261, 262 (2) (86 S. E. 417).

Simple larceny distinguished. The offense of larceny after trust differs from simple larceny in that the taking occurs after lawfully acquiring possession of the property converted. But where one induces another to hire property to him, and he thereupon steals it, he may be convicted either of simple larceny or of larceny after trust. 

Bryant, 8 Ga. App. 389 (69 S. E. 121); Martin, 123 Ga. 478 (51 S. E. 

334); Rice, 6 Ga. App. 160 (64 S. E. 575); Pittman, 13 Ga. App. 705 (79 S. E. 915).

The same transaction may constitute larceny after trust and simple larceny. In such a case there may be conviction of either offense. Kelley, 24 Ga. App. 155 (1) (100 S. E. 23).

Acquiescence. Acquiescence of prosecutor in larceny after trust will not destroy criminal element. Waters, 15 Ga. App. 342 (3) (83 S. E. 200).

Making change. Where buyer handed money to seller for the purpose of making change, and seller appropriated it with intent. to steal, he is guilty of simple larceny and not of larceny after trust. Finkelstein, 105 Ga. 617, 620 (31 S. E. 589); Hecox, 105 Ga. 625 (2) (31 S. E. 592). 

Evidence. In prosecution of pawnbroker for larceny after trust in conversion of watch and ring, pawn ticket, similar to that given for watch and ring, and representing the same article, was admissible on the question of intent. Wilensky, 15 Ga. App. 360 (3) (83 

S. E. 276).

Similar transactions in which the accused by similar means procured money from other persons and converted it, admissible in evidence. McCrory, 11 Ga. App. 787 (5) (76 S. E. 163).

In order to convict of larceny after trust, the exact trust substantially as alleged in the indictment must be proved. To allege one trust and to prove another would be fatal. Clack, 47 Ga. App. 

323 (2) (170 S. E. 398); Anthony, 47 Ga. App. 187 (170 S. E. 202).

Venue. Where the jury, under the evidence, were authorized to find that the defendant in Fulton County was intrusted by the prosecutor with the personal property in question, to be taken to Upson County for exhibition and then returned to the owner in Fulton County, and that the bailee took it to Bibb County and there pawned it, and where the jury were authorized to find that

SPECIFIC CRIMES 

531 the defendant had conceived in Fulton County the intention of fraudulently converting the property to his own use, and that in furtherance of that intention he took the same to Bibb County for the purpose of unlawfully and fraudulently disposing of it, the venue could be laid in Fulton County. Maynard, 47 Ga. App. 221 (3) (170 

S. E. 265). 

w. LARCENY AFTER TRUST "BY ANY OTHER PERSON." 

Indictment. charge and accuse. larceny after trust, for that the said. of. de- .with the offense of on the......day dạy 19., in the county of... having been intrusted by one.. as administratrix of the estate of... ceased, with certain money, to wit................dollars, of the value of ....dollars, the property of said administratrix, for the purpose of applying the same for the use and benefit of said owner by safe-keeping the same and delivering the same over to said owner, did then and there fraudulently convert the same to his own use, contrary, etc. . . . Goodman, 2 Ga. App. 438 (1) (58 S. E. 558); 

Keys, 112 Ga. 392 (1) (2) (37 S. E. 762).

Where it is sought to charge the violation of a trust, in that the accused failed to apply the property to the use and benefit of the person delivering it, it is not necessary that the indictment should allege the ownership of the property, nor is it necessary that the ownership be established by evidence. Grier, 18 Ga. App. 738 (2) (90 S. E. 490). Indictment is void if it fails to charge that the conversion was fraudulent. Rambo, 25 Ga. App. 390 (103 S. E. 494). 

Indictment for larceny after trust is fatally defective unless it charges that the delivery of the property to the accused was for some purpose in which the bailor or some person other than the accused had an interest. Barksdale, 28 Ga. App. 536 (1) (112 S. E. 165).

Under § 26-2809 it is not necessary to allege and prove demand. 

Where indictment so alleges, it is surplusage and need not be proved. 

Lewis, 17 Ga. App. 667 (1) (87 S. E. 1087); Turner, 18 Ga. App. 

653 (5) (90 S. E. 225).

Description of the property as "two bales of lint cotton, weighing about five hundred pounds each, and of the value of sixty dollars each",-sufficient. White, 19 Ga. App. 230 (1) (91 S. E. 280).

Where the indictment charges that the accused failed to apply the property to the use or benefit of one other than the person delivering it, ownership of the property should be alleged. Norfleet,

9 Ga. App. 853 (72 S. E. 447); Hamilton, 11 Ga. App. 41, 43 (74 

S. E. 446); Guyton, 12 Ga. App. 562 (77 S. E. 830).

The words "fraudulent conversion" and "taking with intent to steal" are synonymous, and impart the intent. Hagood, 5 Ga. App. 

80 (5) (62 S. E. 641).

Under § 26-2809 only the bailment, the purpose thereof and the fraudulent conversion must be alleged and proved. But where there is no other evidence of conversion, demand and refusal may be alleged and shown for the purpose of establishing the fraudulent conversion. Bowen, 16 Ga. App. 179 (1) (84 S. E. 793); Lewis, 17 

Ga. App. 667 (1) (87 S. E. 1087); Turner, 18 Ga. App. 653 (5) (90 

S. E. 225).

The offenses defined in §§ 26-2809 and 26-2806 are kindred offenses and may be charged in separate counts in the same indictment. Innes, 19 Ga. App. 271 (2) (91 S. E. 339); Sewell, 23 Ga. 

App. 765 (2) (99 S. E. 320).

The character of the bailment and the purpose thereof must be alleged. Carter, 53 Ga. 326, 328. 

Note: It has been held in Norfleet, 9 Ga. App. 853, 855 (72 S. E. 

447); Guyton, 12 Ga. App. 562 (77 S. E. 830) that the indictment must allege ownership in the bailor or someone other than the accused. But see: Grier, 18 Ga. App. 738 (2) (90 S. E. 490).

Since the amendment of 1910 (Acts 1910, p. 60) no indictment is required where the property converted does not exceed $50.00 in value. As in such cases the offense is. a misdemeanor, an accusation is sufficient. (Note: This amendment was not incorporated in the Penal Code of 1910, but is incorporated in § 26-2809.) 

General. There are three essential elements of the crime of larceny after trust under § 26-2809,-(1) the bailment; (2) the purpose of the bailment; (3) the fraudulent conversion. The crime is complete when the fraudulent conversion takes place. Birt, 1 Ga. 

App. 150 (57 S. E. 965); Goodman, 2 Ga. App. 438 (1) (58 S. E. 

558); Bowen, 16 Ga. App. 179 (1) (84 S. E. 793).

The fraudulent conversion of the property of another is the gravamen of the offense of larceny after trust. Lewis, 17 Ga. App. 667 (1-b) (87 S. E. 1087).

Simple larceny. Where property was acquired from the owner by trick and fraud, and subsequently converted, the offense is simple larceny. To constitute the offense of larceny after trust there must be first a trust. Finkelstein, 105 Ga. 617 (31 S. E. 589); Lanier,

SPECIFIC CRIMES 

533 

17 Ga. App. 261 (2-a) (86 S. E. 417); Kelley, 24 Ga. App. 155 (100 

S. E. 23).

Fraudulent conversion. If a person, fraudulently intending to get possession of money and appropriate it to his own use, by false representations induces the owner to deliver the money to him for the purpose of being applied for the owner's benefit, and then appropriates it in pursuance of the original intent, he is guilty of both larceny after trust and simple larceny, and may be convicted of either offense. Martin, 123 Ga. 478 (51 S. E. 334).

Where one intrusted with money by another fraudulently converts it, he is guilty of larceny after trust, though he may have fraudulently induced the delegation of trust with intent to so convert the money. Walker, 117 Ga. 260 (43 S. E. 701).

Where one is intrusted with timber to be sawed into lumber, he is bailee of the timber and lumber, and may be convicted under an indictment charging that he was intrusted with lumber. Chaffin, 5 Ga. App. 368 (63 S. E. 230).

Contractor engaged to build house and receiving price in advance, though never intending to perform contract, is not guilty of larceny after trust. Wylie, 97 Ga. 207 (22 S. E. 954).

Cropper who converts to his own use part of his crop after it had been set aside to the landlord and intrusted to the cropper's charge, is guilty of larceny after trust, although he may be guilty of other offense. Smith, 7 Ga. App. 468 (67 S. E. 202).

Where accused was intrusted with a ring for the purpose of pawning it, and returning the proceeds to the owner, but he fraudulently converted the proceeds to his own use, he was guilty of larceny after trust. Birt, 1 Ga. App. 150 (1) (57 S. E. 965).

Where master intrusted bill to servant for the purpose of making change, and servant did not return either bill or change, he was guilty of larceny after trust. Mobley, 114 Ga. 544 (40 S. E. 728); 

Basley, 10 Ga. App. 470 (73 S. E. 624).

Restitution. If there was a fraudulent intent at the time of the conversion, subsequent offer to pay back the amount converted will not affect the crime. McCoy, 19 Ga. App. 32 (4) (90 S. E. 737).

Venue. Evidence that accused was intrusted with certain money in a particular county, and thereafter converted it, sustained finding that conversion took place in that county, where there is no evidence to the contrary. Bowen, 16 Ga. App. 179 (2) (84 S. E. 

793); McCoy, 19 Ga. App. 32 (2) (90 S. E. 737); Keys, 112 Ga. 

392 (6) (37 S. E. 762).

Evidence. Jury is authorized to infer fraudulent conversion from proof of failure and refusal of defendant to return money intrusted to him. Lewis, 17 Ga. App. 667 (1-a) (87 S. E. 1087).

Variance. Where it is alleged that trust was delegated to defendant by one person and evidence shows that such trust was delegated to him by another, variance fatal. McCrary, 81 Ga. 334 (6 S. E. 588); McNish, 88 Ga. 499 (14 S. E. 865); Rucker, 95 Ga. 

465 (20 S. E. 269).

Where indictment alleges that defendant was intrusted with money by "A," and proof shows that defendant was intrusted with money by "B" and "A" acting as "B's" agent in handing the money to defendant-the variance is fatal. McCrary, 81 Ga. 

334 (6 S. E. 588).

Conviction is not authorized where proof shows that the purpose of the trust was different from that alleged in the indictment. 

White, 19 Ga. App. 230 (3) (91 S. E. 280); Carty, 26 Ga. App. 249 

Punishment. Provision that where the thing converted does not exceed fifty dollars in value, punishment shall be as for a misdemeanor, is not applicable where money is delivered in installments as parts of a large sum under single agreement, and more than fifty dollars so delivered were fraudulently converted, although no single installment exceeds fifty dollars. McCoy, 19 Ga. 

App. 32 (3) (90 S. E. 737). 

x. CONVERSION WHEN INTRUSTED FOR COLLECTION. 

An allegation of the value intrusted for collection must be made in the indictment. An indictment alleging that the defendant was intrusted with promissory notes for stated sums of money, for the purpose of collecting money which was due thereon, is subject to special demurrer, where there is no allegation that the notes were of value. Henderson, 24 Ga. App. 353 (100 S. E. 731). 

y. CONVERSION WHEN INTRUSTED FOR SELLING. 

Indictment. An indictment under § 26-2811, otherwise sufficient, will not fail though it does not in express terms allege that the proceeds of the sale were to be paid to the prosecutor. Boyd, 111 

Ga. 804 (35 S. E. 675); Keys, 112 Ga. 392 (37 S. E. 762).

Where it is sought to charge a violation of a trust, in that the accused failed to apply the property to the use or benefit of one other than the person delivering it, indictment should allege ownership. Norfleet, 9 Ga. App. 853 (72 S. E. 447).

SPECIFIC CRIMES 

535 General. The offense defined in § 26-2811 is not committed when one uses part of the purchase price obtained from the property intrusted to him for selling to reimburse himself for the expenses in maintaining the property while in his custody. Etheridge, 78 Ga. 

340, 341.

If possession of goods be delivered by the owner to another under an agreement that the latter will sell it for the owner's benefit, and will return to the owner either the proceeds or the goods themselves, if unsold, and the goods are subsequently converted by the party so intrusted, the offense is larceny after trust and not simple larceny, in the absence of proof that the owner was fraudulently induced by the accused to surrender possession of the goods. Pittman, 13 Ga. App. 705 (79 S. E. 915). 

36. LEWDNESS AND DISORDERLY HOUSES.
