Indictment. charge and accuse.. a misdemeanor, for the said....... .with the offense of on the.. 

............day of............. 

19...., in the county aforesaid, did keep and maintain a common, illgoverned, and disorderly house to the encouragement of idleness, drinking, and other misbehavior, contrary, etc. . . 

Jones, 2 Ga. App. 433 (3) (58 S. E. 559).) charge and accuse..... 

.19...., ...with the offense of public indecency, for the said.......... on the................day of.. i.................county did commit the offense of open lewdness and did commit an act of public indecency consisting of the exposure of his private parts in a public place, where he and the said exposure of his private parts might have been seen by many persons, and where he was in fact seen by....... ..persons, to wit, .and.. said act tending to debauch the morals of the public, contrary, etc. 

Gilmore, 118 Ga. 299 (2) (45 S. E. 226). But see: Hobgood, 24

Maintaining and keeping a lewd house is an entirely distinct and separate offense from that of open lewdness or any notorious act of public indecency tending to debauch the morals. These two of

fenses can not be joined in the same accusation. (One dissenting.) 

Lasseter, 17 Ga. App. 323 (1) (86 S. E. 743).

An accusation of public indecency which charged that the offense was committed by exposure of the private parts in a public place where the accused might have been seen by many persons, and was seen by named persons, was defective in not showing that the exposure itself was or might have been seen. Hobgood, 24 Ga. 

App. 196 (100 S. E. 228).

The omission of the words "tending to debauch the morals" in an accusation for public indecency is not such a defect as could be reached by oral motion to quash. Gilmore, 118 Ga. 299 (2) (45 

S. E. 226). 

Indictment charging divers specific vices conjunctively sustained by proof of any one of such vices. Heard, 113 Ga. 444 (3) (39 S. E. 118).

The offense of keeping and maintaining a lewd house, and the offense of keeping a common, ill-governed, and disorderly house may be joined in the same indictment in different counts. Jones, 2 Ga. 

App. 433 (2) (58 S. E. 559).

General. To render an act notorious and public under § 26-6101 it must have been committed at a place where it might have been seen by more than one person. Morris, 109 Ga. 351 (34 S. E. 577); 

Lockhart, 116 Ga. 557 (1) (42 S. E. 787).

House of ill-fame means lewd house or place for the practice of adultery and fornication. Cotton, 10 Ga. App. 397 (3) (73 S. E. 683). 

To constitute a house a disorderly house in law, the noises, etc., must be ordinary and usual, or common, and the disturbance must be general and not of only one person in a thickly settled neighborhood. (Italics by the Court.) Heard, 113 Ga. 444, 448 (39 S. E. 

118); Palfus, 36 Ga. 280.

To sustain an indictment under § 26-6103, it must appear that the house was in fact a "common, ill-governed, and disorderly" establishment, and that the keeping and maintenance of it encouraged idleness, or gaming, or drinking, or other misbehavior; or that the house was kept and maintained in such manner as to cause "common disturbance of the neighborhood of orderly citizens. Fanning, 17 Ga. App. 316, 317 (2) (86 S. E. 731). 

A house may be lewd house, though devoted chiefly to some other vocation, if lewd women are accustomed to frequent there and

SPECIFIC CRIMES 

537 carry on their practices therein. Fitzgerald, 10 Ga. App. 70 (1) (72 S. E. 541).

A wife living with her husband in the house alleged to be of ill fame, may be guilty of keeping lewd house. Hudson, 134 Ga. 373 

It need not be shown that the house was kept for profit. Scarborough, 46 Ga. 26.

Principals. One who aids in maintaining, directly or indirectly, a lewd house by contributing to its maintenance, is guilty as a principal. Clifton, 53 Ga. 241; Brannan, 43 Ga. App. 231, 235 (158 

S. E. 355).

Maintaining a lewd house is a misdemeanor, and any person aiding or abetting therein is guilty as principal. Ward, 22 Ga. App. 786 (1) (97 S. E. 198). 

Indecency. What is decent and what is indecent is determined by the sensibilities and the moral standard of the people, as evolved from generation to generation along with their civilization. What is decent in one period may be indecent in another and vice versa. 

Redd, 7 Ga. App. 575 (2), 576 (67 S. E. 709).

The word "indecency" has a somewhat narrower meaning in the criminal law than in ordinary speech, yet it is broader in meaning than the phrase "exposure of the person." A criminal public indecency may be committed without any improper exposure of the human body. Redd, 7 Ga. App. 575 (1) (67 S. E. 709).

Whether an act is decent or indecent depends upon the time, the place, and all the circumstances surrounding its commission, including the intention, actual or implied, of the actor. Redd, 7 Ga. 

App. 575, 576 (3) (67 S. E. 709).

A public or intentional, or wanton violation of the dictates of decency by unnecessary intruding upon the attention of the other the sexual act and all other things directly suggestive of it, is an act of public indecency within the purview of § 26-6101. Redd, 7 

Ga. App. 575 (5), 576 (67 S. E. 709).

For a man intentionally to cause a bull and a cow to engage in a sexual intercourse near a public highway and in full view of it, knowing that a woman and a number of children were so situated that they could hardly fail to see the spectacle, and that they would likely be offended by it, is an act of criminal, notorious public indecency. Redd, 7 Ga. App. 575, 576 (6) (67 S. E. 709).

Disorderly house. A disorderly house is a house in which the people abide, or to which they resort, to the disturbance of the

neighborhood, or for purposes which are injurious to public morals, health, convenience or safety, while disorderly conduct may consist of noise disturbing one person only. Fanning, 17 Ga. App. 

316, 317, 318 (86 S. E. 731).

Fact that several persons as well as intoxicating liquors were found in a house, without showing disturbance, not sufficient to convict of keeping a disorderly house. Fanning, 17 Ga. App. 316, 317 (3) (86 S. E. 731).

Evidence showing shooting, dancing, cursing and loud noises at ice cream festivals given twice a week for two years resulting in disturbance of neighbors, sufficient to convict. Wilder, 3 Ga. App. 

443, 444 (60 S. E. 112).

Gaming. Gaming is a separate and independent offense from keeping a house to the encouragement of gaming. Thrower, 117 Ga. 

753, 755 (45 S. E. 126).

Sale. A person making a bona fide sale of real estate does not stand in such accessorial relation with the buyer as to be indictable for maintaining a lewd house, if the property be put to such use. Bennett, 20 Ga. App. 170 (1) (92 S. E. 943).

If a person, in possession of a house, makes an executory sale thereof to a lewd woman to be conducted as a lewd house, and she thereupon occupies it and devotes it to that purpose, he stands in such an accessorial relationship to her act as to be indicted. Kinard, 10 Ga. App. 133 (72 S. E. 715).

Husband and wife. Where a husband and wife live together, the husband is presumed to own everything in the house, and to be the head of the house. When husband and wife are present, it is his duty, not hers, to prevent disorder in the house. In order to hold the wife criminally liable for permitting disorder, it should be shown that she took active part in the running of the house and in the allowance of the disorder. Durham, 49 Ga. App. 374 (175 S. 

E. 542).

Landlord and tenant. Leasing house to be used as a lewd house, or permitting it to be so used, is a violation of § 26-6102, and all participants are principals. Kessler, 119 Ga. 301 (46 S. E. 408).

In order to convict an innkeeper of maintaining a lewd house, on the theory that, along with other guests, he allows lewd women to stop at his inn and ply their vocation, it is necessary to show that the innkeeper had knowledge, actual or implied, of the unlawful practices that were going on. Such knowledge may be

SPECIFIC CRIMES 

539 shown directly or circumstantially. Fitzgerald, 10 Ga. App. 70 (2) (72 S. E. 541).

When a landlord aids and abets a tenant in the unlawful enterprise, or by some affirmative act gives his consent and appropriation to the tenant's maintaining a lewd house, he shares the tenant's guilt. But if the house is leased for a lawful purpose, the mere non-interference of the landlord with the illegal traffic of the tenant, after having notice of it, does not involve him in the tenant's guilt. Kessler, 126 Ga. 725, 727 (55 S. E. 963).

Charge to the jury was erroneous, where Court stated that the jury were authorized to convict the defendant if lewd people were housed by him, and plied their immoral vocation with defendant's knowledge, without stating that the lewd acts of adultery or fornication must have been committed in the particular house. 

Jones, 14 Ga. App. 811, 812 (7) (82 S. E. 470). 

No law prohibits a landlord from boarding or housing lewd women, and the house where they may be so maintained will not be a lewd house, unless acts of fornication or adultery are therein committed. This is true, although the landlord might have knowledge that the inmates commit adultery or fornication away from the domicile. Jones, 14 Ga. App. 811, 812 (7) (82 ˚S. E. 470).

Reputation. Proof of defendant's reputation for lewdness is not admissible, unless put in issue by the defendant. Ward, 14 Ga. App. 

110 (2) (80 S. E. 295); Ward, 22 Ga. App. 257 (2) (95 S. E. 872).

Reputation that the house is kept and maintained as a lewd house -admissible. Ward, 14 Ga. App. 110 (1) (80 S. E. 295); Ward, 22 

Ga. App. 257 (2) (95 S. E. 872).

Evidence of reputation for lewdness of inmates of the house, other than the accused,-admissible. Ward, 14 Ga. App. 110 (2) (80 S. E. 295).

To authorize conviction, it is not enough to prove the general reputation of the house, or of its inmates, or both. Ward, 14 Ga. 

App. 110 (1) (80 S. E. 295).

Reputation of house as a lewd house is admissible, but insufficient to convict if not corroborated. Smith, 13 Ga. App. 241 (79 S. E. 

51); Ward, 14 Ga. App. 110 (80 S. E. 295).

The circumstances corroborative of reputation for lewdness, that would authorize a conviction for the offense of maintaining a lewd. house, must be such circumstances as tend to show lewd and lascivious conduct at such house, and from which it might be rea-

sonably inferred that fornication or adultery took place there. 

Wilkes, 23 Ga. App. 727, 728 (99 S. E. 390).

General reputation of the house, or of persons, as to lewdness, may be shown, although witness does not remember who stated them. Fitzgerald, 10 Ga. App. 70 (3) (72 S. E. 541).

Evidence of the general reputation for chastity of the women. frequenting and boarding in the house is admissible. McCain, 57 

Ga. 390.

Where reputation of the house as a lewd house is being shown, proof may run back more than two years to show long established reputation; the jury being cautioned that certain act must be proved within the statutory period. Hogan, 76 Ga. 82 (4).

Reputation of the defendant as a lewd woman, and of the house as a place of prostitution together with evidence that men frequented the place night and day, and that defendant, her niece and daughter lived there together, sufficient to convict. Mimbs, 2 Ga. App. 387 (1) (58 S. E. 499). 

Fact that women of notoriously lewd reputation room at the hotel, and that hotel had the reputation in the community of being a place. where adultery and fornication is commonly committed, would be sufficient to authorize finding that the hotel was a lewd house, and that the proprietor knew, or should have known, that he was maintaining a lewd house. Basil, 22 Ga. App. 765 (1-a) (97 S. E. 259).

Evidence. Evidence that the officer was urged by others to make an arrest on account of the reputation of the house-inadmissible. Jones, 14 Ga. App. 811 (1) (82 S. E. 470).

Evidence that man and woman were found in bed in night-clothes in defendant's house on the grounds of a club, and that the defendant had told another that he could bring a woman out to his house after the club members have left, is not sufficient to authorize conviction. Cummings, 25 Ga. App. 319 (103 S. E. 193).

It is not necessary that the State should show any particular act of fornication or adultery to have been committed, if the evidence, either directly or circumstantially, is such that it satisfied the jury that the house was kept and maintained as a lewd house. Fitzgerald, 10 Ga. App. 70, 71 (5) (72 S. E. 541).

Jurisdiction. City ordinances prohibiting the same offense as the State laws, and inflicting punishment,-invalid. Cotton, 10 Ga. 

App. 397 (73 S. E. 683).

Recorder of Macon has no jurisdiction to try defendant for the

SPECIFIC CRIMES 

541 offense of maintaining a lewd house. Griggs, 154 Ga. 519 (2) (114 

S. E. 899). 

37. LIBEL. 

§§ 26-2101 to 26-2104. 

(Misdemeanor.) 

Indictment. 

charge and accuse.. ..with the offense of a misdemeanor, for that the said... on the.......day of 

19., in the county aforesaid, did, with force and arms, wickedly and maliciously express, print and publish, and cause and procure to be expressed, printed and published, a certain false, scandalous, malicious and defamatory libel, in the form of an advertisement, in the columns of a newspaper, published in the City of in the county aforesaid, known by the name of the "tending to blacken the honesty, virtue, integrity and reputation of the said...…….. .........., and thereby to expose him to public hatred, ridicule and contempt, in which said false, scandalous, malicious and defamatory libel, there were and are contained certain false, scandalous, malicious, defamatory and libelous matter, of and concerning the character, honesty, virtue, integrity and reputation of the said........ ---, to wit: (here set out the libel) 66 ," to the great damage, scandal and disgrace of the said and contrary, etc. . . . Taylor, 4 Ga. 14, 15.

In an indictment for libel, placed in a situation where it might have been seen and read it is unnecessary to aver or prove that it was read or seen. Giles, 6 Ga. 276 (1).

An indictment alleging that a defamatory matter, signed by another, was published by the accused, need not allege that it was written by the person who signed it. Taylor, 4 Ga. 15 (1).

It is no ground of demurrer that the indictment uses the word "express" instead of "publish," where the libel is set out in full. 

Graham, 6 Ga. App. 436 (1) (65 S. E. 167).

General. Publication and circulation of handbills containing statements concerning the Knights of Columbus, and a purported oath of that order, which was false, constitute the crime of libel. 

Alumbaugh, 40 Ga. App. 15 (148 S. E. 622).

Libel per se. Where a communication does not charge a criminal offense on its face, and it is a question for the jury whether such offense is charged by innuendo, it is error for the Court to charge the jury that the communication is libelous per se. Such fact is question for the jury. Baker, 97 Ga. 452 (7) (25 S. E. 341).

To charge one in a publication that he is a drunkard, a cuckold, and a tory is libelous. Giles, 6 Ga. 276 (3).

To charge a real estate agent in a newspaper statement that he had discriminated against negroes on account of their race, and that he had caused a negro tenant to lose a certain location and sell out his business at a loss and advising colored people to rent from another agent and "leave the old skunk to stink himself to death" -is libelous. Pledger, 77 Ga. 242 (1) (3 S. E. 320).

Where the language alleged to be libelous imports a felony or a misdemeanor, it is libelous per se, as a matter of law; but in all other cases it is a question of fact for the jury. Baker, 97 Ga. 452 (25 S. E. 341).

Truth of publication. The truth of the publication must be established by evidence before it can be given in charge to the jury as a defense. Pledger, 77 Ga. 242 (3 S. E. 320).

Author. A person who is proved to have written the libel, which is afterwards published, is presumed to be the author thereof, unless he shows another to be the same. Giles, 6 Ga. 276 (4).

Publication. Publication is sufficiently shown by proof of sending only one copy of the newspaper in question into the county without showing that the newspaper had a general circulation therein. 

Baker, 97 Ga. 452 (6). 

Privileged communication. If made in good faith, communication to secret society in investigation and trial of a member for the violation of the by-laws,-privileged. Graham, 6 Ga. App. 436 (2) (65 S. E. 167); Graham, 7 Ga. App. 407 (66 S. E. 1038).

Practice. Libel should not be read to the jury until after the defendant had an opportunity of cross-examining the witness by whom publication was proved. Taylor, 4 Ga. 14 (4).

Joint defendants. Where two persons are tried for libel one may be convicted, although the other is acquitted. Baker, 97 Ga. 452 (4) (25 S. E. 341).

Publisher. The proprietor or publisher of a newspaper, containing defamatory matter, is a competent witness, and if he refuses to testify in the case, or state the real name of the author of the publication, he is to be considered as the author himself, and is liable to indictment and punishment as such. Moreover he might be punished for contempt as any other witness. Pledger, 77 Ga. 242, 243 (6) (3 

S. E. 320).

Venue. The venue in a prosecution for criminal libel may be laid in any jurisdiction where the libelous article was published or cir-

SPECIFIC CRIMES 

543 culated, irrespective of where such article was written or printed. 

Leavy, 45 Ga. App. 574, 575 (7) (165 S. E. 470). 

38. LIQUORS. 

88 58-101 to 58-612.

Note: The Acts of 1935 have made radical changes in the laws of 

Georgia, pertaining to intoxicating liquors. After the elections held in accordance with these Acts there is considerable uncertainty in reference to the status of the liquor laws in the State, and several test cases were presented to the courts. At the time this book was sent to the press none of these cases were decided. For this reason the law pertaining to intoxicating liquors is presented as it stood before the Acts of 1935 were passed and the new Act is herein reprinted. A full study of the changes will be presented in our first supplement.

General. Courts will not take judicial cognizance that "home brew" is a prohibited beverage. Thompson, 42 Ga. App. 249 (155 

S. E. 354).

Constitutionality of prohibition act upheld. Young, 167 Ga. 165 (5) (6) (7) (144 S. E. 726).

The word "liquor" means "intoxicating liquor" in this law, where nothing to the contrary appears. Humphrey, 39 Ga. App. 

406 (1) (147 S. E. 402); Weston, 42 Ga. App. 414 (156 S. E. 321).

Courts will not take judicial cognizance of the fact that a liquor, not otherwise denominated than "beer" is intoxicating. Bledsoe, 16 Ga. App. 479 (1) (85 S. E. 676); Lumpkin, 9 Ga. App. 470 (71 S. 

E. 755). Nor "near beer." Abbott, 11 Ga. App. 43 (1) (74 S. E. 621).

Whiskey is, as a matter of law, an intoxicant and this fact need not be proved in a prosecution for the violating of the prohibition act. Gordon, 25 Ga. App. 189 (3) (103 S. E. 38).

Under the State prohibition act it is unlawful to possess any liquors, beverages, or drinks made in imitation of or intended as substitute for alcoholic or spirituous, vinous, or malt liquors, including those liquors and beverages commonly known and called "near beer," whether such liquors and beverages are or are not intoxicating. Green, 43 Ga. App. 578 (159 S. E. 778); Watters, 42 Ga. App. 

292 (155 S. E. 780). 

The Eighteenth Amendment to the Constitution of the United

States and the National Prohibition Act, commonly known as the "Volstead Act" did not supersede or abrogate the State prohibition act. Jones, 150 Ga. 657 (104 S. E. 771); Neville, 152 Ga. 414 (1) (110 S. E. 180).

Conviction under the National Prohibition Act is no bar to prosecution in the State courts. Cooley, 152 Ga. 469 (110 S. E. 449); 

Bryson, 27 Ga. App. 230 (1) (2) (108 S. E. 63).

Conviction for manufacturing liquors is no defense to a charge of possessing liquor, though both grew out of the same transaction. 

Morgan, 28 Ga. App. 358 (1) (111 S. E. 72).

Evidence, if otherwise competent, admissible, though obtained by illegal search and seizure. Brooks, 19 Ga. App. 3 (12) (90 S. E. 989).

Prohibition act should receive a reasonable construction, equally removed, on the one hand, from that extreme strictness, which would make it unpopular or ridiculous and difficult of enforcement, and, on the other, from the latitude which would render it ineffective. Roberts, 4 Ga. App. 207 (2) (60 S. E. 1082). "Intoxicating liquors or mixture thereof" mean liquors which will intoxicate, and which are commonly used for such purpose, and such mixtures of the same as may be used as beverages and become

SPECIFIC CRIMES 

545 substitute for ordinary intoxicating drinks. Roberts, 4 Ga. App. 

207, 208 (7-d) (60 S. E. 1082).

In the absence of evidence to the contrary, corn liquor is presumed to be intoxicating. Wilburn, 8 Ga. App. 28 (2) (68 S. E. 460).

In the absence of evidence to the contrary peach brandy is presumed to be intoxicating. Howard, 7 Ga. App. 61 (2) (65 S. E. 1076). 

Name "bolo" prefixed to the word "gin" in accusation charging offense under the prohibition act, will not be considered to indicate that something other than gin was sold, but will be regarded merely as signifying particular kind of gin referred to. Norris, 15 Ga. App. 

511, 512 (6) (83 S. E. 866).

Unreasonable explanation is worse than no explanation at all. 

Davis, 4 Ga. App. 274 (61 S. E. 132).

Husband and wife. Husband is not liable for wife's offenses unless he aids, procures or acquiesces in their commission. Lumpkin, 9 Ga. App. 470 (71 S. E. 755).

The husband is recognized as the head of the family, and, where he and his wife reside together, the legal presumption is, that the house and all the household effects, including any intoxicating liquors, belong to the husband. Black, 41 Ga. App. 349 (2) (152 S. 

E. 922).

Expert. A witness who has drunk of the liquor is competent to testify that the liquor is intoxicating, though he does not profess to be an expert, where he has drunk of the liquor and experienced its effect. Wilcox, 8 Ga. App. 536 (1) (69 S. E. 1086). Scienter.

Scienter is not an element of the offenses created by the State prohibition law. That the defendant thought in good faith that liquor was not intoxicating,-no defense. 

578 (65 S. E. 333). 

a. SELLING, BARTERING, ETC. 

charge and accuse.. 

Ware, 6 Ga. App. ..with the offense of Indictment. selling liquor, for that the said................., in the county of............ on the................day of………………………. .19...., did sell and barter, for a valuable consideration, alcoholic, spirituous, malt, and intoxicating liquors, intoxicating bitters, and drinks which, if drunk to excess, will produce intoxication, contrary, etc. . . . (Approved: Howe, 10 

Ga. App. 215 (1) (2) (73 S. E. 34).) 

See also: Brown, 8 Ga. App. 691 (1) (70 S. E. 49); Hall, 8 Ga. 

App. 747 (1-a) (1-b) (70 S. E. 211).

Manufacture and sale of liquor may be charged in one count.

Proof of either will warrant a general verdict of guilty. Jones, 12 

Ga. App. 564 (2) (77 S. E. 892). 

Indictment need not negative exceptions which allow sale of pure alcohol under certain conditions. McAdams, 9 Ga. App. 166 (2) (70 

S. E. 893). 

Indictment need not name the purchaser. Pines, 15 Ga. App. 348 (83 S. E. 198). Nor state the amount of liquor sold, nor state the consideration paid for it, but where so stated, such allegation becomes material. Hall, 8 Ga. App. 747 (2) (70 S. E. 211); Finch, 6 

Ga. App. 338 (2) (64 S. E. 1007). Indictment need not specify the kind of liquor sold. Snell, 7 Ga. App. 751 (1) (67 S. E. 1045).

Indictment need not state the precise locality at which the alleged sale of intoxicating liquors was consummated, provided it showed that the Court had jurisdiction. Pines, 15 Ga. App. 348 (1-a) (83 

S. E. 198).

The date of the offense should be shown on the accusation, to enable the defendant properly to prepare for his defense. An accusation charging the violation of an ordinance prohibiting the keeping of liquors for sale should show the date of the offense. Norris, 15 

Ga. App. 511, 512 (5) (83 S. E. 866).

Where indictment charges keeping liquor in a public place, it should specify what public place is referred to. Hall, 8 Ga. App. 

747, 748 (2) (70 S. E. 211).

Where indictment charges keeping liquor in the place of business, it need only allege that place of business was in the county and further description is unnecessary. Hall, 8 Ga. App. 747, 748 (2) (70 

S. E. 211).

General. Keeping liquor on hand is the criminal act. The purpose is immaterial. (One dissenting.) Cohen, 7 Ga. App. 5 (1) (65 

S. E. 1096); Nowell, 18 Ga. App. 143 (4) (88 S. E. 909).

The word "liquor" is collective and its significance includes singular as well as plural. Wilburn, 8 Ga. App. 28 (2) (68 S. E. 460).

Medicinal, toilet, and culinary preparations, not intended to be used as intoxicating beverages, and not reasonably capable of being so used, are not embraced in the prohibition statute. Roberts, 4 Ga. 

App. 207, 208 (7-c) (9) (60 S. E. 1082).

An indictment may charge the violation of the prohibition law in all the separate ways mentioned in the statute in a single count, and proof of violation in any one way will warrant conviction. But only one punishment may be imposed. Hall, 8 Ga. App. 747 (1-a) (1-b) (70 S. E. 211).

SPECIFIC CRIMES 

547 Constitutionality. Upheld, even where interstate sale was made from Georgia. Whitley, 134 Ga. 758 (68 S. E. 716); Cureton, 135 

Ga. 660 (70 S. E. 332); Cureton, 136 Ga. 91 (70 S. E. 786).

Sale. A single sale is sufficient to constitute the illegal act. Lambert, 11 Ga. App. 764 (76 S. E. 73); Cooper, 13 Ga. App. 169 (1) (78 

S. E. 1097).

If the witness sold whiskey to the accused, and latter sold it back to the witness, the accused is guilty. Cumby, 11 Ga. App. 410, 411 (75 S. E. 443).

A sale on credit is a complete sale, whether subsequently paid for or not. Subsequent cancellation of the deal is no defense. Finch, 6 Ga. App. 338 (1) (64 S. E. 1007); Lupo, 118 Ga. 759 (45 S. E. 602).

Where one gets intoxicating liquor and leaves some money in a place accessible to the person furnishing the liquor, the sale may be presumed. Rucker, 12 Ga. App. 632 (77 S. E. 1129); Flood, 12 Ga. 

App. 702, 704 (78 S. E. 268).

Where the accused refused to accept money for the liquor, and there is no evidence that he later appropriated the money to his own use, conviction of illegal sale is unauthorized. Flood, 12 Ga. App. 

702 (78 S. E. 268).

The ownership of the liquor is immaterial. One may sell illegally the property of another. Fitts, 17 Ga. App. 836 (1) (88 S. E. 712).

Evidence that money passed to one accused of illegal sale of whiskey and whiskey was delivered by him as a single transaction is sufficient to support a finding that the transaction was a sale. Cowart, 18 Ga. App. 677 (1) (90 S. E. 286).

Inference created by proof that the accused received money from another person, accompanied by a request to procure whiskey for the latter, that he went off, and returned, and delivered whiskey to the person paying him the money, is not rebutted by uncorroborated statement of the accused that he bought the whiskey from a third person and paid him for it. Dawson, 16 Ga. App. 249 (3) (85 S. E. 82).

Where defendant, upon being asked as to where whiskey could be obtained, pointed out a negro, from whom he thought some could be obtained, and the inquirer gave defendant some money with which to get some whiskey from such negro, and defendant shortly thereafter told the inquirer that the whiskey could be found in a certain place where the inquirer did find it, the jury were authorized to infer that the defendant himself made the sale, or assisted the negro to make it, and did not act purely as the agent of the purchaser. 

Bragg, 23 Ga. App. 138 (1) (99 S. E. 310).

Proof that the accused delivered liquor and received money for it is prima facie evidence of selling. Burden of proof that he was the agent for the buyer is upon the accused if he avails himself of that defense. Braswell, 9 Ga. App. 879 (72 S. E. 445); Jones, 12 Ga.

One may be guilty of sale or barter of liquor "for a valuable consideration" though the consideration be only a stolen article, to which no title passes as against the person from whom it was stolen. 

Turner, 18 Ga. App. 393 (89 S. E. 538).

Agency. The middleman in an illegal sale of intoxicating liquors is guilty, unless he acts solely as the agent of the buyer. Sessions, 6 Ga. App. 336 (3) (64 S. E. 1101).

If the accused induced the sale, or acted as agent for both buyer and seller, or if he had profit in the transaction, he is guilty. Guilford, 11 Ga. App. 768 (1) (76 S. E. 103).

Where the accused is charged with selling liquor and his defense is that he had no interest in the sale whatever, but acted solely as the buyer's agent, he must show when, how, and from whom he bought the liquor for the buyer. Fletcher, 12 Ga. App. 809 (1) (78 

S. E. 478); Myers, 16 Ga. App. 266 (1) (85 S. E. 206); Scott, 18 Ga.

App. 309 (1) (89 S. E. 349). 

Evidence that one behind the counter of a "near beer" saloon sold whiskey without protest of the proprietor placed the burden on the proprietor to show that the seller was not his agent. Bragg, 15 Ga. App. 623, 624 (8) (84 S. E. 82).

Presumption of guilt raised by showing that the accused procured intoxicant is successfully rebutted by testimony of the accused and another unimpeached witness that he bought the liquor from a third person. Cowart, 14 Ga. App. 763 (82 S. E. 313).

Whether the defendant in receiving money and delivering intoxicating liquor was the agent of the seller or of the buyer-is a question for the jury. Pitts, 17 Ga. App. 836 (1) (88 S. E. 712).

The employer is liable for the illegal sale of intoxicating liquor by a clerk where he fails to show that the sale was unauthorized. 

Rooney, 117 Ga. 709 (3) (45 S. E. 72).

It is no defense that the accused sold the liquor as an employe of a social club to the members thereof. Rothschild, 12 Ga. App. 728, 729 (4) (78 S. E. 201).

In misdemeanor cases all who participate are principals. Ownership of the liquor is immaterial. If the accused sold it as an agent of another, he is still guilty. Roberts, 8 Ga. App. 476 (69 S. E. 585); 

Brown, 11 Ga. App. 813 (2) (76 S. E. 360).

SPECIFIC CRIMES 

549 Buyer. The purchaser of intoxicating liquors is not an accomplice of the seller. Gamble, 4 Ga. App. 845 (1) (62 S. E. 544).

Place of business. "Place of business" means public place of business, where people are expressly or impliedly invited to transact business. Roberts, 4 Ga. App. 207 (4) (60 S. E. 1082).

Storage room from which the public is excluded is not a place of business. Roberts, 4 Ga. App. 207 (5) (60 S. E. 1082).

Residence used for business included in "place of business.” 

Stewart, 8 Ga. App. 118 (68 S. E. 624); Tooke, 4 Ga. App. 495, 497 (4-c) (61 S. E. 917).

Private operating room of a practicing dentist, prima facie, is not a public place of business. Cantrell, 8 Ga. App. 725 (70 S. E. 96).

Kitchen of a public restaurant is a place of business. Hall, 8 Ga. 

App. 747, 748 (4) (70 S. E. 211).

Where one works for another, no matter in what capacity, the employer's place of business may become the place of business of the employe, within the meaning of this section. Toles, 10 Ga. App. 

444 (3) (73 S. E. 597).

If one lives at or near his place of business and keeps on hand prohibited liquors, and said dwelling is used in connection with his business as part of the place, such dwelling house is in law a part of the place of business, within the meaning of the prohibition law. 

Flahive, 10 Ga. App. 401 (3) (73 S. E. 536).

All parts of a place of business are included therein within the meaning of the prohibition law. Rooms, stairs, courts, yards, closets, etc. Flahive, 10 Ga. App. 401 (4) (73 S. E. 536).

Place of business is within the State where agent of nonresident principal had on storage in this State liquors, which he sent out in Alabama and Tennessee to customers who sent their orders to the office of the principal in Tennessee. To punish such sale is a valid exercise of police power and not in violation of the interstate commerce clause of the Federal Constitution. Cureton, 136 Ga. 91 (70 

S. E. 786).

Place of business does not cease to be place of business on Sunday. 

Landreth, 10 Ga. App. 399, 401 (73 S. E. 349).

Where evidence showed that a third person brought the liquor to the place of business of the accused, and hid it there without the knowledge of the owner, conviction of the owner illegal. Smith, 5 

Ga. App. 834 (63 S. E. 928); Sewell, 11 Ga. App. 754 (75 S. E. 1135).

Where accusation charged keeping liquor at a place of business, it is no defense that the liquor has not been sold by the accused, and

evidence negativing such sale is irrelevant. Smith, 11 Ga. App. 89 (3) (74 S. E. 711).

Public place. The phrase "public place," as used in the prohibition act, is to be given a relative meaning; and a place may be public during some hours of the day and private during others. The phrase "public place," by a broad, general, and not wholly exhaustive definition, includes any place which, from its public character, members of the general public frequent, or where they may be expected to congregate at any time as a matter of common right; also any place at which, even though it is privately owned and controlled, a number of persons have assembled, through common usage or by general or indiscriminate invitation, express or implied; it excludes those places which, though publicly owned, are devoted to a private use and are not open to the access of the public; also those places privately owned or controlled from which the indiscriminate public is generally excluded; notwithstanding that at a particular time in question a number of persons may have congregated there, if the congregation is the result of special invitation for that occasion alone. Tooke, 4 Ga. App. 495, 496 (4) (61 S. E. 917).

It is immaterial whether a public place was for business, amusement, literary culture, physical training or worship. Gary, 7 Ga. 

App. 501, 504 (67 S. E. 207).

A town guard-house is not a public place relative to prisoners. 

Tooke, 4 Ga. App. 495, 496 (4-b) (61 S. E. 917).

A person's residence primarily is not a public place, but it may become so through the use to which the owner devotes it. Tooke, 4 Ga. App. 495, 497 (4-c) (61 S. E. 917).

Evidence. Evidence obtained by officers who arrested the accused without warrant on suspicion, and held him illegally, by taking from his pocket his keys to his safe, against his consent and against his resistance, and unlocking the same and discovering therein intoxicating liquors, inadmissible, because obtained by violation of the Constitution. Underwood, 13 Ga. App. 206 (78 S. E. 1103).

Where contents of valise were voluntarily disclosed by the accused, valise and its contents admissible in evidence. Weatherington, 13 Ga. App. 408 (2) (79 S. E. 240).

Evidence of liquor found in place admissible, though such evidence has been obtained by unlawful seizure. Taylor, 5 Ga. App. 

237, 238 (5) (62 S. E. 1048).

On the trial for the sale of intoxicating liquors, a certified copy from the records of the Internal Revenue Collector of the United

SPECIFIC CRIMES 

551 States, showing that the accused paid a special license tax as a retail liquor dealer-admissible. Daniel, 11 Ga. App. 799, 800 (2) (76 S. 

E. 162); Huckabee, 7 Ga. App. 677 (1) (67 S. E. 837).

Possession of internal revenue special tax receipt is prima facie evidence of guilt, though rebuttable. Allen, 11 Ga. App. 245 (75 S. 

E. 11); Cassidy, 10 Ga. App. 123 (4) (72 S. E. 939).

Where an employe is on trial charged with selling liquor in the presence of his employer, Federal License to sell liquor, or certified copy of the Collector of Internal Revenue-admissible to show guilt, though license was granted to the employer. Christian, 9 Ga. App. 61 (1) (70 S. E. 258). 

Where in one count indictment charges the accused with selling liquor, and in the other count with possessing it, evidence tending to establish guilt under one count is admissible, though it might be entirely irrelevant as to the other. Reddick, 15 Ga. App. 437 (1) (83 S. E. 675).

Evidence that six or seven bottles of the beer sold by the accused and purchased by the witness would make him drunk sustained finding that it was intoxicating. Bledsoe, 16 Ga. App. 479 (1) (85 S. E. 676). 

Where evidence shows that the buyer asked for "liquor" (which in ordinary parlance imports intoxicating liquor), and the clear liquid is furnished without comment by the seller, the jury is authorized to find that it was intoxicating liquor. Gates, 18 Ga. App. 

94 (3) (88 S. E. 910). 

Where the accused delivered to another something in a bottle, which he said was whiskey, and for which he accepted money, a conviction is authorized, though the accused denied that it was whiskey, and said at the trial that it was ginger ale, and the buyer did not know on account of drunkenness at the time of the transaction. 

Lewis, 6 Ga. App. 779 (65 S. E. 842).

Testimony that various persons were seen to go, at different intervals at night, into the house of the accused, shut the door, and remain some time, not admissible, where no evidence is offered that liquor was sold in that house on that occasion. Holmes, 12 Ga. App. 359 (1) (77 S. E. 187). 

Evidence that large quantity of whiskey contained in pint bottles had been claimed by the accused and delivered to him,-admissible on the trial for selling intoxicating liquors. Webb, 13 Ga. App. 733, 734 (5) (80 S. E. 14).

Secretive methods employed by the accused, in prosecution for selling intoxicating liquors, and the circumstances surrounding the

transaction, in connection with the fact that unusual number of persons were seen to go into his house and sometimes return with packages, warrants inference that he brought liquor into the place for the purpose of illegal sale, though no sale was shown. Meeks, 13 

Ga. App. 79 (78 S. E. 777).

Circumstances apparently indicating sale of intoxicating liquorsadmissible, though there was no direct evidence of defendant's presence at the house, occupied by him and under his control, where unusual quantities of liquor were found. Gales, 14 Ga. App. 450 (1) (81 S. E. 364).

Receipt of unusual quantities of liquor is a circumstance of more or less probative value, for the consideration of the jury. Hayes, 18 Ga. App. 68, 69 (2) (88 S. E. 752); Dunn, 18 Ga. App. 95 (1) (89 

S. E. 170).

Evidence that one accused of conducting blind tiger has never been engaged in any business since he left his last employment,admissible. Borders, 18 Ga. App. 333, 335 (24) (89 S. E. 451).

Evidence that the defendant and another person, as barbers, jointly occupied room where whiskey was found, but that their business was entirely separate, was not sufficient to justify conviction, there being no direct evidence that whiskey belonged to the defendant, or that it did not belong to the other barber. Lunceford, 17 Ga. App. 730 (2) (88 S. E. 212).

Where the question is involved whether the liquor was intoxicating, and the State introduces the liquor in evidence, it is proper for the jury to inspect it personally, apply their own senses to it, look at it, taste of it, smell of it, and thereby determine whether or not it is intoxicating. Morse, 10 Ga. App. 61 (3) (72 S. E. 534). 

Where the indictment charged the sale of "alcoholic, spirituous, malt, or intoxicating" liquors, proof that the liquor sold belonged to either of the general classes puts the burden upon the accused to show that it was not intoxicating when drunk to excess, or was not a beverage or reasonable of being used so. Stoner, 5 Ga. App. 716, 717 (2) (63 S. E. 602).

Proof that the defendant sold "liquors is sufficient to show that he sold intoxicating liquors, especially where the evidence showed. that it looked like rye whiskey." Carswell, 7 Ga. App. 198 (1) (66 S. 

E. 488).

In order to convict of selling beer, beer must be proved to belong in the class of liquors prohibited. Lumpkin, 9 Ga. App. 470 (71 S. 

E. 755).

Evidence that the accused had near-beer license from State,

SPECIFIC CRIMES 

553 county and municipality is-irrelevant. Abott, 11 Ga. App. 43 (3) (74 S. E. 621).

Where accused is charged with sale of intoxicating liquors, evidence that numerous empty bottles were found on his premises, which had contained whiskey, and other bottles and jugs containing whiskey at the time of the raid,-admissible. Smith, 12 Ga. App. 482 (77 

S. E. 651); Craig, 9 Ga. App. 233 (1) (70 S. E. 974). 

Evidence that a year before the alleged transaction empty whiskey bottles were found on the premises of the accused—not admissible. Jackson, 12 Ga. App. 480 (77 S. E. 651).

In prosecution for selling intoxicating liquors, testimony that the witness saw in the depot, in the town of the trial, several barrels marked with the name of the accused and labeled "whiskey"-admissible. Daniel, 11 Ga. App. 799 (5), 800 (76 S. E. 162).

Keeping liquor for illegal sale may be shown by direct or circumstantial evidence. Butler, 11 Ga. App. 133 (74 S. E. 858).

Former adjudication. Evidence of acquittal of the accused of keeping liquor for the purpose of sale, immaterial on the trial for selling liquor. One may sell liquor which he does not keep for sale. 

Taylor, 5 Ga. App. 237, 238 (3) (62 S. E. 1048).

Acquittal of one charged with possessing liquor is no bar to charge of selling liquor. Phillips, 27 Ga. App. 1 (107 S. E. 343).

Selling and possessing. Where sale of intoxicating liquor was shown by the evidence possession will be presumed. Leggett, 36 Ga. 

App. 661 (137 S. E. 789).

Where a person is accused in one count on a charge of misdemeanor, alleging that on May 18, 1918, the defendant did sell spirituous liquors, etc., and in another count of the same accusation it is alleged that the defendant on the same day did have, control, and possess spirituous liquors, etc., and the same evidence is relied on to convict under both counts, a verdict finding the defendant guilty on the first count and not guilty on the second count is void for repugnancy. Kuck, 149 Ga. 191, 193 (99 S. E. 622); Davis, 43 Ga. App. 

122 (157 S. E. 888). 

c. CONTRACTING TO SELL, ETC. 

Indictment. charge and accuse. .with the offense of a misdemeanor, for that the said.. in................County, on the ............day of... .19...., did contract to sell, take orders for, and solicit personally and by agent, and by and through the United 

States mails, and by and through the..................Company, the sale of

spirituous liquor, malt liquor, and intoxicating liquor, contrary, etc. (Approved: Cashin, 18 Ga. App. 87 (1) (88 S. E. 996).)

Accusation may charge the sale of intoxicating liquor in one count and solicitation in another, and a general verdict of "guilty" is sufficient. Williams, 107 Ga. 693 (2) (33 S. E. 641).

General. Constitutionality upheld, against allegation that this act is in violation of the interstate commerce clause of the Federal 

Constitution. Kirkpatrick, 138 Ga. 794 (2) (76 S. E. 53).

It is an offense to solicit orders for intoxicating liquors, whether the accused acted as the agent of the seller, or as principal. Loeb, 115 Ga. 241 (2) (41 S. E. 575).

Nonresident in another State soliciting orders for the sale and delivery of intoxicating liquors by the United States mail from persons living in this State does not violate any law of the State of Georgia, and indictment setting out these facts is demurrable. R. 

M. Rose Co., 133 Ga. 353 (65 S. E. 770).

Where resident agent solicits orders for nonresident principal for delivery of intoxicating liquors, personally giving away samples, he violates the State law of Georgia. Kirkpatrick, 12 Ga. App. 252 (2) (77 S. E. 104); Kirkpatrick, 138 Ga. 794 (76 S. E. 53).

Where witness asked the accused where he could get some liquor, and accused stated that another, living in accused's home, could get it for him, evidence did not show solicitation in the absence of voluntary offer to procure the liquor. Wardlaw, 12 Ga. App. 361 (77 S. E. 205).

Printed circulars received by witness, through the United States mail, offering intoxicating liquors, with price stated, and bearing defendant's name, street address, number of post-office box, telephone number, etc., corresponding with defendant's address,-admissible, where it is shown that intoxicating liquors were delivered upon. orders sent in response to such circulars. (One dissenting.) Cashin, 18 Ga. App. 87 (2) (88 S. E. 996). 

i. DRUNKENNESS IN PUBLIC PLACES. 

Indictment. charge and accuse.. ..., ......with the offense of a misdemeanor, for that the said... in the county of.............. on the........day of... 19..., was and appeared upon a certain highway, to wit: the same being a public highway, (dedicated to, by………………………..), in an intoxicated condition, which drunkenness and intoxication was caused by the excessive use of intoxicating wines, beers, liquors and opiates, and which intoxication was made manifest by boisterousness, by indecent condi-

SPECIFIC CRIMES 

555 tion and acting, and by vulgar, profane and unbecoming language, and loud and violent discourse of the defendant, while so intoxicated, contrary, etc. . . (Anderson, 27 Ga. App. 318 (108 S. E. 259).) charge and accuse. with the offense of a misdemeanor, for that the said................., in the county of---------, on the…………………………………….. day of... .19...., unlawfully and with force and arms was and appeared in a drunken and intoxicated condition within the curtilage of the private residence occupied by Mrs.......... and.. and................., said private residence not being in the defendant's exclusive possession; which drunken and intoxicated condition was caused by the excessive use of intoxicating wines, beers, liquors, and opiates, and was made manifest by boisterousness, by indecent condition and acting, by vulgar, profane and unbecoming language, and by violent discourse, contrary, etc. . . . (Fletcher, 28 Ga. App. 344 (111 S. E. 585).)

Indictment must designate particular highway on which accused appeared in intoxicated condition. It is not sufficient to state in general terms of the statute. Burkes, 7 Ga. App. 39 (65 S. E. 1091).

Description of road as public road passing residences of two named landowners and citizens-sufficient. Mathis, 11 Ga. App. 95 (74 S. E. 713). General.

Proof that the road was commonly and largely used by the general public for a number of years, without more, will not support an allegation that such was a "public" highway or a "public" road. 

Johnson, 1 Ga. App. 195 (2-a) (58 S. E. 265).

The words "public highway" denote a generic term. The words "a public road," when used in an indictment based upon the act of 1905 (Acts 1905, p. 114), are descriptive of a species whose identity and characteristics are fixed by law, and are material; and allegations must be sustained by proof. (Id.) (2-b.)

The terms “public highway" and "public road" are not synonymous. The word "road" refers to the piece or strip of land taken; "way" in legal parlance, merely denotes ah easement, and that the land has been subjected to servitude. "Highway" is also a generic term which includes other uses besides the right of ordinary locomotion over land which had been subjected to public use. (Id.) (3.) 

Where the defendant is charged with being intoxicated on a public highway, State must show that the road was in fact a public highway. Hutchinson, 8 Ga. App. 684, 685 (70 S. E. 63).

Burden of showing that the road was a public highway is not carried by showing that it was used by the public for several years. 

Johnson, 1 Ga. App. 195 (2-a) (58 S. E. 265).

A road may be shown to have become a public highway by (1) legislative enactment, (2) by an action of the proper authorities, (3) by dedication, (4) by prescription. Johnson, 1 Ga. App. 195 (4) (5) (6) (7) (58 S. E. 265); Davis, 9 Ga. App. 430 (1) (71 S. E. 

603); Lovett, 13 Ga. App. 71 (1) (78 S. E. 857). 

Judicial notice taken that "Federal Highway No. 1" in Jefferson

County, Georgia, is a public highway. Moye, 46 Ga. App. 727 (169 

S. E. 59).

Where road is not a public highway, and indictment charges drunkenness on a public highway, conviction is not authorized. 

Where the misconduct occurred on a little road leading into a public highway, three or four hundred yards therefrom, it did not occur in legal contemplation on the highway. Anderson, 27 Ga. App. 318 (108 S. E. 259). Nor in a store near the highway. Hutchinson, 8 

Ga. App. 684 (2) (70 S. E. 63).

Where prescription is depended upon to show road to be a public highway, twenty years' use must affirmatively be shown. Johnson, 1 Ga. App. 195 (58 S. E. 265).

Indecency. A man, while intoxicated, can be on a public highway without violating the law. In order to convict of drunkenness, it must be manifested by conduct specified in the statute. 

Mere presence of one, who is intoxicated, on the public highway or within curtilage of a private residence, is not a violation of this statute. Coleman, 3 Ga. App. 298 (59 S. E. 829); Dixon, 28 Ga. 

App. 559 (2) (112 S. E. 159). 

Using profane language is sufficient to convict. Brinson, 28 Ga. 

App. 482 (111 S. E. 738); Barrentine, 18 Ga. App. 726 (90 S. E. 372). 

Question as to what constitutes boisterousness or indecent conduct or acting, -for the jury. Haines, 8 Ga. App. 627 (5) (70 S. E. 

84); Sullivan, 17 Ga. App. 122 (1) (86 S. E. 287).

The word "boisterous" is defined in the Standard Dictionary as "vociferous and unrestrained, noisy, uproarious." Morris, 18 Ga. 

App. 684, 688 (90 S. E. 361).

To vomit on one's person and clothing, although involuntary, is such an "indecent condition" as will authorize conviction, upon proof of drunkenness of the accused. Lovett, 13 Ga. App. 71, 72 

---

SPECIFIC CRIMES 

557 Reckless driving can not be properly included in "indecent condition and acting." Peterson, 13 Ga. App. 766 (2) (79 S. E. 927); 

Davis, 14 Ga. App. 569 (81 S. E. 906).

A condition is "indecent" that is offensive to the public propriety, offending against delicacy, unfit to be seen, gross or immodest. 

Howell, 14 Ga. App. 414 (81 S. E. 247).

One who lies prone and helpless on his back across a public highway while in the state of intoxication, thereby partly blocking the road, is guilty under this act. Howell, 14 Ga. App. 414 (1) (81 

S. E. 247).

Private residence. Drunkenness within the curtilage of the pri vate residence of another warrants conviction. Fletcher, 28 Ga. 

App. 344 (111 S. E. 585).

Evidence. In prosecution for intoxication on a highway and within the curtilage of a private residence, it is not error to admit testimony of defendant's conduct at the residence, though not on the public highway. Evidence of defendant's conduct while going from the residence to the highway-admissible, as tending to show his condition at the time charged. Riggins, 15 Ga. App. 398 (83 

S. E. 503).

Evidence of disorderly conduct adjacent to the highway at or about the same time when the accused is alleged to have been drunk on a highway-admissible. Davis, 9 Ga. App. 430 (5) (71 S. E. 603).

Charge. Where the indictment alleges that the defendant was drunk on a public highway, evidence must show that the highway was in fact public. It must show that the highway became public in any one of the four ways provided by law. Therefore, it is error for the Court to charge the jury, that it is immaterial whether or not the road was maintained by the public or county authorities. as a public highway, but that if the jury finds that the road was used by the public for a number of years, as a means of ingress or egress to and from their homes, and that the crime was committed on said road by the defendant, the jury should convict. Johnson, 1 

Ga. App. 195 (6) (7) (58 S. E. 265).

Driving while under influence of liquor. On the trial of one charged with operating an automobile on a public highway while under the influence of intoxicating liquor, it is not necessary for the State, in order to secure a conviction, to show that the accused was drunk, but it is sufficient if the State shows, beyond a reasonable doubt, that the accused (while driving the car) was under the

influence of some intoxicant as charged, to any extent whatsoever, whether drunk or not. Moye, 46 Ga. App. 727 (169 S. E. 59). 

k. FURNISHING LIQUOR TO MINORS. 

Indictment. charge and accuse. of a misdemeanor, for that the said. on the.. ..day of........ intoxicating, and malt liquors to..... securing the written authority of the with the offense in the county of .19...., did furnish spirituous, a minor, without first parent and guardian of said minor, contrary, etc. . . . (Ross, 13 Ga. App. 659 (1) (79 S. E. 746).) 

Where indictment negatives authority from mother only, and does not allege that she was the sole parent, or that father was dead, or that there was no guardian,-it is bad on demurrer. Newman, 63 Ga. 533. But if there is no demurrer, and the evidence shows the facts necessary, a conviction will be upheld. Reich, 63 

Ga. 616.

General. Corporation may be indicted and convicted of the offense of furnishing liquor to minors, if transaction occurred in the course of the corporation's business, by its agents, or by another with consent of the agent. Southern Express Co., 1 Ga. App. 700 (58 S. E. 67).

A common carrier may be guilty of this offense. Southern Express Co., 6 Ga. App. 31 (2) (64 S. E. 341). 

The word "furnish" has the same meaning as the word "deliver" under the prohibition law. Southern Express Co., 1 Ga. App. 700 (3) (58 S. E. 67).

This act contemplates furnishing liquor for the use of a minor or for some use to which he applies his own will. Where liquor was furnished to a minor upon an order from his parent, and the liquor was actually delivered to the parent, the seller is not guilty under this section. Dixon, 89 Ga. 785 (15 S. E. 684).

Leaving whiskey in the virtual control of a minor during the temporary absence of the accused amounts to criminal negligence, legally equivalent to actual intention to furnish whiskey, where the accused had reason to believe that the minor desired the whiskey. 

Ayers, 16 Ga. App. 278 (2) (85 S. E. 201).

Where the minor acted in good faith as the agent of a buyer, the seller is not guilty of furnishing liquor to a minor, by delivering it to the minor, if he knew of the agency, and if the liquor was actually delivered to the buyer. Harley, 127 Ga. 308 (56 S. E. 1006).

SPECIFIC CRIMES 

559 Agent who negotiates for his principal a sale of liquor to a minor is equally guilty with his principal. Hardu, 10 Ga. App. 47 (2) 

Age of minor. Defendant must show special diligence in ascertaining age of the minor. Such diligence is not shown by inquiry of the minor as to his age. Unless, after inquiry, defendant was honestly mistaken as to the minor's age, single sale is sufficient to convict. Reich, 63 Ga. 616 (4).

Question whether the accused was negligent in finding out the age of the minor or was mistaken-for the jury. Askew, 4 Ga. App. 

446 (61 S. E. 737).

Where one sells intoxicating liquor in another county upon an order received through the mail, he ships at his peril to an unknown customer. Ignorance of age is no excuse. Newsome, 1 

Ga. App. 790 (58 S. E. 71).

Whether accused believed he was dealing with an adult-for the jury. Nobles, 14 Ga. App. 480, 481 (81 S. E. 370); Smith, 17 Ga. 

App. 118 (2) (86 S. E. 283).

Authority from parent. The burden to show written authority from parent or guardian of the minor is upon the accused. Graham, 121 Ga. 590 (2) (49 S. E. 678).

Authority from parent or guardian must be special for each occasion. A general permit is insufficient. Gill, 86 Ga. 751 (13 S. E. 86).

Delivery of liquor on verbal order to minor to carry it to parent places the burden of proving that the order was sent on the accused, and also that this order was the basis of the transaction, and also that the minor carried the liquor intact to the parent. 

Dixon, 89 Ga. 785 (15 S. E. 684).

It is no justification that the parents of the minor are both dead, and that he has no guardian. Blair, 81 Ga. 628 (7 S. E. 855).

Agent. It is no defense that the accused did not make the sale himself, but through a clerk. Snider, 81 Ga. 753 (3) (7 S. E. 631).

Conviction. Indictment charging sale to three minors, conviction upheld on evidence showing sale to one. Southern Express Co., 1 Ga. App. 700 (3) (58 S. E. 67).

Indictment charging furnishing of several kinds of liquors, conviction upheld on evidence showing sale of one. Southern Express 

Co., 1 Ga. App. 700 (4) (58 S. E. 67).

p. CARRYING, RECEIVING OR POSSESSING LIQUORS. 

Indictment. . . . charge and accuse. .........with the offense of possessing intoxicating liquors, for that the said, in the County of…………………….. on the day of……….. .19..., did have, control, and possess spirituous and intoxicating liquor, to wit, 2 gallons of corn whiskey, contrary, etc. . . . Vismore, 41 Ga. App. 

544 (1) (153 S. E. 776); Page, 23 Ga. App. 548 (1) (99 S. E. 55). charge and accuse........with the offense of a misdemeanor, for that the said.........., on the... on the day of...19..., in the county aforesaid, did have, control and possess a certain beverage commonly known and called............ same being in imitation of or intended as a substitute for beer, ale, wine or whiskey, and other alcoholic, malt, spirituous or vinous liquors, contrary, etc. . (See: Watters, 42 Ga. App. 292 (2) (155 S. E. 780).) (See also: 

Thomas, 49 Ga. App. 484, 485 (176 S. E. 155).)

For indictment against common carrier see: 

Co., 23 Ga. App. 67 (1) (97 S. E. 550). 

Southern Express

Prohibition extends to all malted or fermented beverages, and therefore indictment is not demurrable because it does not set out that liquors are intoxicating or alcoholic. Young, 167 Ga. 165 (2) (144 S. E. 726). 

Indictment need not negative sacramental wine, or that the liquor was for medicinal purposes. Shaw, 35 Ga. App. 664 (134 S. E. 328).

Indictment need not set out the amount of liquor found in defendant's possession. Harris, 21 Ga. App. 796 (95 S. E. 321). 

General. Constitutionality upheld. Jackson, 148 Ga. 351 (96 

S. E. 1001); Saddler, 148 Ga. 462 (97 S. E. 79).

Possession. Volstead Act did not prohibit possession of liquor for personal purposes, but Georgia State law does. Abbott, 33 Ga. 

App. 146 (125 S. E. 723).

One may be guilty of possessing liquor though he only passed it to another to take a drink. Tuten, 36 Ga. App. 662 (137 S. E. 853). 

Temporary taking and drinking from bottle is not possession of liquor within the meaning of the prohibition law. Robinson, 40 

Ga. App. 662, 665 (150 S. E. 919); Grace, 33 Ga. App. 75 (125 S. 

E. 728); Graham, 150 Ga. 411 (104 S. E. 248).

The accused would be guilty of possessing liquor, if he knowingly has in his possession any quantity thereof, even a spoonful. Black, 41 Ga. App. 349 (3) (152 S. E. 922).

SPECIFIC CRIMES 

561 Where the defendant, tried for possessing liquor, perfected a sale for whiskey, there would be a presumption that he had the whiskey in his possession. Leggett, 36 Ga. App. 661 (137 S. E. 789).

Common carriers are included in the prohibition act. Seaboard 

Air Line, 23 Ga. App. 72, 74 (97 S. E. 549).

Under some circumstances a person could be guilty of manufacturing liquors without having the liquors in his possession and control. Morgan, 28 Ga. App. 358 (1) (111 S. E. 72).

Where indictment charges that the defendant had, controlled and possessed intoxicating liquor, evidence of any one of them is sufficient to convict. Barbour, 21 Ga. App. 243 (1) (94 S. E. 272).

There is no independent crime of keeping intoxicating liquors for sale distinct from having, controlling and possessing. Corley, 23 Ga. App. 480 (1) (98 S. E. 401). 

One sending another into another county for liquor is guilty of possessing liquor in any county in which the agent carried the liquor. Jackson, 154 Ga. 544 (114 S. E. 811).

There is no law in this State which makes the transportation of intoxicating liquor on a through bill of lading in interstate commerce illegal on an interstate railway, where shipment is from one State to another, merely passing through Georgia. Such law would be invalid and void because of a conflict with the interstate commerce clause of the Federal Constitution. Gaines & Co., 154 Ga. 

344 (114 S. E. 327).

Knowledge. If the defendant had no knowledge of the liquor being in his car, he can not be convicted of transporting liquor, and the Court should so charge the jury. Harvill, 29 Ga. App. 68 

Where defendant knew that liquor was in the car he was driving, although the owner was along, a finding that he aided and abetted in transporting and possessing the liquor was authorized. Ingram, 37 Ga. App. 374 (140 S. E. 528). .

Lawful purpose. A common carrier is authorized to transport and deliver to a practicing physician, who is the sole proprietor of a drug store, pure alcohol for medicinal purposes, under certain conditions specified in the prohibition law, from one point within the State to another point within the State of Georgia. Southern 

Express Co., 149 Ga. 489 (1) (100 S. E. 709); Southern Express Co., 24 Ga. App. 307 (100 S. E. 791). (Overruling Southern Express 

Co., 23 Ga. App. 376 (1) (2) (98 S. E. 272).)

Intoxicating liquors being subject to the police power of the

State, even when such liquors are acquired lawfully, they are taken. with their inherent infirmities, and subject to such legislation as the State may enact under its police power. Barbour, 146 Ga. 667 (1) (92 S. E. 70).

Where liquor was delivered for a lawful purpose and the statute was complied with, this, if properly pleaded, would be a good defense, if the defendant did not know, or by the exercise of ordinary diligence could not have discovered that the affidavit was false. 

Southern Express Co., 23 Ga. App. 67, 70 (97 S. E. 550).

Where the defendant came into possession of intoxicating liquors innocently, as a common carrier, not knowing that it contained intoxicating liquors, and, after receiving information, still continued. to deliver it, conviction warranted. Seaboard Air Line Railway, 23 Ga. App. 72, 75 (97 S. E. 549).

Husband and wife. In this State the husband is the head of the family, and where he and his wife reside together, the legal presumption is that the house and all the household effects, including intoxicating liquors, belong to the husband as the head of the family. This presumption is, however, rebuttable. George, 37 Ga. 

App. 513 (140 S. E. 903); Black, 41 Ga. App. 349 (2) (152 S. E. 

922); Isom, 32 Ga. App. 75 (122 S. E. 722).

In this State the husband is the head of the family, and where intoxicating liquors are kept in the house occupied by himself and family, he is guilty of aiding and abetting in the commission of a misdemeanor, if he knowingly allows such liquors to remain there, irrespective of who owns the liquors or put them there. Williamson, 40 Ga. App. 496 (150 S. E. 464).

Unless the husband knowingly possessed liquor, he could not be convicted. But the husband is presumed by law to possess everything on the premises. Clark, 37 Ga. App. 496, 498 (140 S. E. 783).

In this State a married woman can not legally have, control, or possess intoxicating liquor, though it be owned by her husband. 

Harris, 38 Ga. App. 83 (142 S. E. 746). (Note: Attention is called to the fact that, although the above citation is taken verbatim from the reports, there is apparently an error therein. It is suggested that the word "can" was intended in place of "can not.")

Ownership. It is a violation of the law for anyone to take actual possession and control of intoxicating liquors of any amount, regardless of ownership. Smith, 34 Ga. App. 776 (131 S. E. 185).

Joint defendants. Under indictment against two persons charging them with having, possessing and controlling certain intoxicating

SPECIFIC CRIMES 

563 liquors, either one or both of them may be convicted, according as evidence may show either one or both guilty. Possessing liquor is not a joint offense in such cases, but joint and several. Page, 23 

Ga. App. 548 (1) (99 S. E. 55).

Where the accused and another occupied the house jointly where liquor was found, and the other had key to it, and control similar to the defendant's, and there was no evidence that the other did not own the liquor found, conviction, without more, unauthorized. 

Cummings, 25 Ga. App. 427 (103 S. E. 687).

Defendant's absence. Where liquor was found in defendant's residence, it is not necessarily a complete defense that the defendant was not at the place of his residence at the time the liquor was found there and had not been there since the time the liquor was placed there. One may have possession and control of liquor without actual presence. Hendrix, 24 Ga. App. 56 (1) (100 S. E. 55).

Repugnant verdicts. Conviction for transporting liquor is repugnant to acquittal of possessing liquor, based on the same transaction, at the same trial. Davis, 43 Ga. App. 122 (157 S. E. 888).

Where indictment in one count charges selling and in another possessing liquor, the accused can not be convicted of selling liquor without being also convicted of possessing. Where in such case the evidence authorizes conviction of possessing, but not of selling liquor, a general verdict of guilty is illegal. Simmons, 162 Ga. 316 (134 S. E. 54).

Evidence. Where indictment charges that defendant had corn whiskey, and evidence only shows that he had liquor, the variance is fatal. Vismore, 41 Ga. App. 544 (3) (153 S. E. 776).

Evidence that the accused permitted another to bring intoxicating liquor to his premises and that the accused assisted another to pour out the liquor upon approach of officers, authorized conviction of possessing liquor. Robinson, 40 Ga. App. 662 (1) (150 S. E. 919). 

Evidence that the defendant was found drunk sitting under the steering wheel of an automobile, and no other person was in the car with him, and there was a jug about three-fourths full of whiskey in the car, supported conviction of possessing liquor. Fussell, 40 

Ga. App. 224 (2) (149 S. E. 154).

On the trial of one charged with having had on a given date in 1918 unlawful possession of twenty-five gallons of corn whiskey, evidence that about two or three months before that time he had in his possession a flask containing corn whiskey-admissible. 

Autrey, 23 Ga. App. 763 (99 S. E. 389).

On the trial of one charged with the offense of possessing whiskey, evidence that a large quantity of whiskey was found in defendant's place of business about two months after the date of the offense charged-admissible. Johnson, 37 Ga. App. 331 (140 S. E. 422).

Where on the trial of a case for possessing intoxicating liquor the defendant put his character in issue, and a witness for the State, on direct examination, testified, that the accused had the reputation of being a bootlegger, and that he had been told that the defendant was selling whiskey, on cross-examination the accused was entitled to know whom the witness had heard to say that the accused was a bootlegger or was selling whiskey; and it was no excuse for the witness to withhold this information that he has promised to do so. Ogden, 41 Ga. App. 360 (1) (153 S. E. 94).

Previous accusations of possessing whiskey, to which the defendant pleaded guilty-admissible. Ealey, 40 Ga. App. 730 (151 S. E. 

400, 401).

Testimony of police officer, in prosecution for possessing and transporting intoxicating liquors, that he had been to defendant's place a number of times, raiding for whiskey,-admissible. Hoffman, 42 Ga. App. 370 (156 S. E. 282).

Conviction authorized on evidence that whiskey was found in defendant's kitchen, and defendant stated that it belonged to another person staying with him. Ray, 42 Ga. App. 420 (156 S. E. 646).

Conviction of possessing liquor unauthorized when circumstantial evidence shows that it was found in defendant's barn, which was unlocked and was used by other persons. Eads, 42 Ga. App. 

473 (156 S. E. 647).

In prosecution for possessing intoxicating liquors evidence that a case of new empty bottles was found in the home of the accused, at the time when whiskey was also found-admissible. Dyson, 43 

Ga. App. 414 (159 S. E. 143).

Where the only evidence was that there was some jug of whiskey buried in the ground about seventy-five yards from defendant's house, no witness swore that it belonged to the defendant, and the evidence showed that other people lived close there, conviction of possessing liquor unauthorized. Pruett, 36 Ga. App. 625 (137 

S. E. 788).

Evidence of whiskey being found in a hole under defendant's residence authorizes conviction, although defendant denied knowl- 1

SPECIFIC CRIMES 

565 edge of it, and insisted that it has been planted there by others. 

Rowland, 38 Ga. App. 664 (1) (145 S. E. 100).

Testimony of sole witness that he found the smell of whiskey and a broken bottle in a car driven by the defendant, does not authorize conviction. Tutt, 39 Ga. App. 533 (145 S. E. 785).

Where one is on trial for having intoxicating liquors in his possession in a described automobile at a certain place at a certain time, evidence that he had such whiskey at another place shortly before, admissible, as a circumstance pointing to his guilt. Grayson, 39 Ga. App. 673 (148 S. E. 309).

Evidence as to the finding of two bottles of whiskey buried in the chicken yard of the premises occupied by the accused and a man who rented rooms from her, will not authorize conviction. 

Arnold, 40 Ga. App. 621 (151 S. E. 48).

Evidence that the defendant's house was searched subsequently to the day on which the alleged sale was made, and liquor was found there—admissible. Hayes, 36 Ga. App. 668 (1-c) (137 S.

E. 860). 

Evidence of liquor found in defendant's residence, upon search, authorizes conviction. Meyer, 21 Ga. App. 670 (94 S. E. 839).

Evidence that liquor was found in defendant's possession on the day of the trial-admissible, where the charge is predicated on possession at a previous time. Hayes, 36 Ga. App. 668 (1-b) (137

S. E. 860). 

Evidence on the trial of one for possessing intoxicating liquor that police officers arrested him for being drunk and disorderly is relevant for the purpose of showing that his arrest was legal and, therefore, that the evidence as to the finding of whiskey on his person was legal. Gatlin, 27 Ga. App. 627 (1) (109 S. E. 522).

Evidence that the sheriff found a jug of whiskey hidden by the side of the road, that the defendant drove by and stopped, came back, climbed a fence, and started digging in the vines where the jug was, and that on seeing the sheriff he walked off, is insufficient to authorize conviction. Mathis, 28 Ga. App. 65 (110 S. E. 342).

Finding of two quarts of whiskey concealed in a piano in defendant's room in a house in which other persons occupied rooms, insufficient to convict of possessing intoxicating liquors. Harris, 28 Ga. App. 463 (111 S. E. 686). 

q. POSSESSING APPARATUS. 

Indictment. charge and accuse. a misdemeanor, for that the said.……………………….... ....with the offense of in the county of.. 77777274

on the............ day of 

19..., did knowingly permit and allow and did have and possess and locate on his premises apparatus for the distilling and manufacturing of spirituous, vinous, malted, fermented, and intoxicating liquors and prohibited liquors and beverages, contrary, etc. 

(Approved: Edwards, 25 Ga. App. 179 

(102 S. E. 847).) 

For approved indictment see also: Johnson, 152 Ga. 270 (3) (109 

S. E. 673); McRae, 23 Ga. App. 13 (97 S. E. 410).

Where indictment charges that complete still was found on the premises of the accused, such allegation becomes material and must be proved. Davis, 24 Ga. App. 319 (100 S. E. 782).

Accusation alleging that defendant allowed "some persons" whose identity is unknown to have apparatus on the premises, sustained against demurrer. Johnson, 152 Ga. 270 (1) (109 S. E. 673).

In a charge of permitting apparatus to be located on the premises, no locality except venue need be alleged in the indictment, and if alleged, it is surplusage, and need not be proved. Howell, 29 Ga. 

App. 174 (114 S. E. 717).

The indictment need not describe the premises on which it is alleged that the apparatus was located. Edwards, 25 Ga. App. 179 (102 S. E. 847); McRae, 23 Ga. App. 13 (97 S. E. 410).

The nature and kind of apparatus need not be described. Edwards, 25 Ga. App. 179 (102 S. E. 847); McRae, 23 Ga. App. 13 (97 

S. E. 410).

General. The accused may be guilty, although he kept the apparatus on the premises himself, and did not allow anyone else to do so. Edwards, 25 Ga. App. 179 (102 S. E. 847).

If a person knows that a still is on his premises and does not undertake to have it removed, his consent is implied. Hester, 28 

Ga. App. 118 (110 S. E. 318).

It is not necessary to show that a complete apparatus was found on the premises of the accused, unless it is so charged in the indictment. Strickland, 27 Ga. App. 321 (2) (108 S. E. 124); Clark, 32 

Ga. App. 78 (1) (122 S. E. 626).

Where any apparatus used to make whiskey, or any part of such apparatus, is found in a person's possession or control upon his premises, he may be lawfully convicted of possessing apparatus. 

Brown, 28 Ga. App. 442 (1) (111 S. E. 696). 

Neither "mash" nor "mobby" is part of the "apparatus for the distilling or manufacturing" of liquors, referred to in the Code. 

Davis, 24 Ga. App. 319 (1) (100 S. E. 782).

SPECIFIC CRIMES 

567 Where an apparatus was found in a pasture, rented by the defendant, and some distance from his house, although the evidence is weak, conviction is upheld. Oswalt, 26 Ga. App. 677 (107 S. E. 

169); Alexander, 25 Ga. App. 236 (102 S. E. 880).

Where a still is located on defendant's premises, it is prima facie evidence that it was with his permission, and the burden of proof that he had no knowledge of it, is upon the defendant. Neville, 29 

Ga. App. 232 (1) (114 S. E. 720); Strickland, 27 Ga. App. 321 (1) 

Knowledge of the existence of the apparatus is for the jury. 

Malcom, 28 Ga. App. 627 (1) (112 S. E. 651); Johnson, 38 Ga. App. 

369 (143 S. E. 905).

Incomplete apparatus is sufficient to convict. Strickland, 25 Ga. 

App. 1 (102 S. E. 383).

Where there is no evidence that the land upon which the apparatus was found was owned, controlled or possessed by the defendant, conviction illegal. Alexander, 25 Ga. App. 175 (102 S. 

E. 878).

When evidence for the State shows that an apparatus for distilling or manufacturing of whiskey was found upon defendant's premises, and that defendant was in actual possession of the premises, such evidence is, by the express terms of the statute, prima facie evidence that the defendant had knowledge of the fact that the apparatus was located upon his premises, and the burden of proof is then upon the accused to show that he had no such knowl edge. Carter, 21 Ga. App. 493 (1) (94 S. E. 630); Thomas, 38 Ga. 

App. 173 (143 S. E. 599).

In the absence of timely written request the Court need not explain to the jury what the term "premises" means. Carter, 21 

Ga. App. 493 (3) (94 S. E. 630).

Evidence. Evidence that the witness found an old automobile gas tank, and pieces of pipe, covered up, on defendant's premises, apparently used for making whiskey, insufficient to convict, although one of the witnesses swear that whiskey could be manufactured in them. Walker, 26 Ga. App. 184 (105 S. E. 707).

Illegally obtained evidence, without search warrant, is nevertheless admissible. Johnson, 30 Ga. App. 639 (118 S. E. 702). 

r. MAKING LIQUOR. 

Indictment. charge and accuse. of manufacturing whiskey, for that the said.... of............. on the.................day of…………………………….. ...with the offense , in the county .19...., did unlawfully

and with force and arms distill, manufacture, and make alcoholic liquors, spiritous liquors, whiskey, and rum, contrary, etc. . (Approved: Thomas, 25 Ga. App. 558 (103 S. E. 859).) 

General. Constitutionality upheld. Yaughan, 148 Ga. 517, 518 

It is against the laws of this State for any one to distill, manufacture, or make alcoholic, spirituous, vinous, and mixed liquors and beverages part of which are alcoholic. Faulkner, 43 Ga. App. 

763, 768 (160 S. E. 117).

A private person as well as an officer, has a right to make an arrest for making liquor with or without a warrant. Williams, 148 Ga. 310 (1) (96 S. E. 385).

The greater offense of making liquor can not be merged into the lesser offense of possessing liquor. Ussery, 37 Ga. App. 345 (140 

S. E. 427). Therefore, upon the trial of one charged with manufacturing whiskey a plea that the accused was convicted a few months previously of possessing whiskey and that the former conviction was based on the same facts and grew out of the same transaction is not a good plea of autrefois convict. (Id.) 

Under some circumstances a person could be guilty of making liquor without having the liquor in his possession and control. 

Morgan, 28 Ga. App. 358 (1) (111 S. E. 72).

Evidence. Presence of a person at a distillery when whiskey is actually being made and his flight therefrom on seeing the officer approaching may, when not satisfactorily explained, authorize a jury to find him guilty of manufacturing liquor. Strickland, 43 

Ga. App. 578 (2) (159 S. E. 756).

A conviction of making intoxicating liquor is not authorized by evidence as to the defendant's presence with others at a still where such liquor was being made, and that after the officers appeared on the scene and arrested one of the party the defendant "jumped up and started off," "trying to walk away," and that the officer twice told him to stop, and pulled him back. Burchfield, 40 Ga. 

App. 506 (150 S. E. 459).

Evidence that the accused was seen by the sheriff at a spring washing a copper still 50 or 75 yards from where there were a still furnace and two barrels of beer, without showing that the accused had anything to do with the preparation of the beer or was going to use the still to make beer,-insufficient to convict of attempt to manufacture intoxicating liquor. Foster, 37 Ga. App. 498 (140 S. E. 775).

SPECIFIC CRIMES 

569 Presence at still and flight, without more, insufficient to convict. 

Thomas, 25 Ga. App. 558 (3) (103 S. E. 859).

Evidence of finding still and mash three-quarters of mile from defendant's house-admissible. Whittemore, 36 Ga. App. 299 (136 

S. E. 806).

Where evidence did not show that whiskey found at a still was made there, or that beer found there by officers was intoxicating, conviction of manufacturing intoxicating liquors unauthorized. 

Phillips, 37 Ga. App. 505 (141 S. E. 64).

Whether defendant's explanation of his presence at the still was reasonable and satisfactory,-question for the jury. Chapman, 38 

Ga. App. 345 (143 S. E. 923); Strickland, 43 Ga. App. 578 (2) (159 

S. E. 756).

AMENDMENTS OF 1935. 

Be it enacted by the General Assembly of Georgia, and it is hereby enacted by the authority of the same, that: 

Section 1. Title: This Act may be cited as "The Alcoholic Beverage Control Act." 

Sec. 2.
