Death, unless the defendant is recommended to mercy by the jury, in which case the punishment is the same as for an assault with intent to commit rape. (Not less than one nor more than twenty years (Not reducible.) in the penitentiary.)

Violation of § 26-1303 by having sexual intercourse with female under fourteen is a reducible felony. 

Publishing name of the female assaulted or raped. Indictment. charge and accuse. 

(Misdemeanor.) 

.with the offense of rape, for the said on the...day of..........19...., in the county aforesaid, did make an assault upon the person of………………………….. and did strike, beat, and wound her, and did have carnal knowledge of and sexual intercourse with said... ..., a female, forcibly and against her will, contrary, etc. . . . Annunciatio, 176 Ga. 787 (169

S. E. 3). 

Where, in an indictment for rape, the defendant is charged to have had carnal knowledge of the female forcibly and against her will, the allegation is sufficiently full without specifying the particular manner in which such carnal knowledge was had. McMath, 55 

Ga. 303, 304 (6).

An indictment for rape is sufficient if it shows the sex of the assaulted party without using the word "female." Joice, 53 Ga. 50. General.

Carnal knowledge. To constitute the crime of rape, there must have been an actual carnal knowledge of the female, an actual penetration of her body. Very slight penetration is sufficient. The vagina may remain intact and not penetrated in the least. The mere entering of the vulva is sufficient. Morris, 54 Ga. 440; Brown, 76 

Ga. 623.

It is essential to show, either by direct or indirect evidence, that actual carnal knowledge or carnal sexual intercourse was had; but slight penetration is necessary. Ravenel, 153 Ga. 130 (2) (111 S. E. 

643); Wesley, 65 Ga. 731.

There is a carnal knowledge if there is the slightest penetration of the sexual organ of the female by the sexual organ of the male. It is not necessary that the vagina be entered or that the hymen be ruptured; the entering of the vulva or labia is sufficient. Hall, 29 

Ga. App. 383 (1-a) (115 S. E. 278).

On the issue of whether the defendant had sexual intercourse with the child, testimony of a physician that about seven months prior to

SPECIFIC CRIMES 

601 the alleged crime he treated the accused for a venereal disease-relevant and admissible, in connection with evidence tending to show that the child developed such disease within about seven days after the alleged criminal act; that the alleged disease is usually communicated from one person to another by sexual intercourse, and that when so communicated it usually manifests itself within a period of three to ten days after the act. This is true although another physician testified that shortly after the alleged crime he examined the accused and in his opinion the accused was not infected with such disease. Riley, 153 Ga. 182 (1) (111 S. E. 729).

Force and lack of consent. Force and lack of consent are the essential elements of the crime of rape. Morrow, 13 Ga. App. 189, 194 (79 S. E. 63).

A reluctance on the part of the female to submit will not make the act rape on the part of the man. Taylor, 110 Ga. 150 (35 S. E. 161).

If the female consent to the sexual intercourse, the offense is not rape. There must be such a lack of consent as to make the act "forcibly and against her will." She may express her consent by her conduct at the time of the intercourse, and even though she may verbally proclaim unwillingness, consent may be implied from her action. A mixed resistance or a merely equivocal submission will not do. There may be a slight physical resistance even though there is a mental willingness to submit. Davis, 152 Ga. 320, 329 (110 S. E. 18).

Though physical force is used, where the female finally consented, the offense of rape was not committed. Mathews, 101 Ga. 547 (1) (29 S. E. 424).

If the woman gave any kind of consent, the offense would not be rape. It matters not how this consent was obtained, or how reluctantly that consent might be given, if there was the least part of consent on the part of the woman during the transaction, then a person charged with rape could not be convicted of rape. Avery, 12 

Ga. App. 562 (4) (77 S. E. 892). 

Although a woman never said "yes," nay more, although she constantly said "no," and kept up a decent show of resistance to the last, it may still be that she more than half consented to the ravishment. Davis, 152 Ga. 320, 331 (110 S. E. 18).

It is not required that the female shall do more, in resisting, than her age, strength and the attendant circumstances make it reasonable for her to do. But it must appear beyond a reasonable doubt that there was an actual resistance, or that resistance was prevented

by violence or restrained by fear. Davis, 152 Ga. 320, 330, 331 (110 

S. E. 18).

Resistance must not be mere pretext, but must be up to the point where it is overpowered by actual force. Morrow, 13 Ga. App. 189, 194 (79 S. E. 63).

Evidence that the assaulted female was under the age of consent, is conclusive that the act was done forcibly and against her will. 

Stephen, 11 Ga. 225 (15); Gosha, 56 Ga. 36.

Sexual intercourse with a woman incapable of consent is rape, though she does not resist. But the mere fact that the woman is weak minded does not disable her from giving consent if she can control her personal actions. Morrow, 13 Ga. App. 189, 198 (2) (79 

S. E. 63). 

Female over 14 years of age is presumed by law to be capable of consent. The test of capacity to consent after the age of 14 is mental capacity to understand the sexual act and to given an intelligent consent. Morrow, 13 Ga. App. 189, 198 (2) (79 S. E. 63).

Evidence of female's physical development is relevant only to illustrate her mental capacity. Morrow, 13 Ga. App. 189 (79 S. E. 63).

In prosecution for rape "against her will" is synonymous with "without her consent." Gore, 119 Ga. 418, 419 (46 S. E. 671); 

Brown, 138 Ga. 814 (1) (76 S. E. 379).

A consent induced by fear of bodily harm or personal violence is not consent; and though a man lay no hands on a woman, yet if by array of physical force he so overpowers her mind that she dares not resist, he is guilty of rape. Vanderford, 126 Ga. 753 (5), 759 (55 S. 

E. 1025).

A female over 14 years of age is presumed to possess sufficient mental capacity to intelligently assent to or dissent from act of sexual intercourse; and where in a rape case the contention of the State is that a woman above that age did not possess such intelligence, the burden rests upon the State to establish this fact. Smith, 161 Ga. 

421 (2-a) (131 S. E. 163).

A man who has sexual intercourse with an imbecile female, who is mentally incapable of expressing any intelligent assent or dissent, or of exercising any judgment in the matter, is guilty of rape, though no more force is used than is necessary to accomplish the carnal act, and though the woman offer no resistance. Smith, 161 

Ga. 421 (2) (131 S. E. 163).

Where the defendant assaulted the female, and she fainted, not having consented, nor given the accused any reason to believe that

SPECIFIC CRIMES 

603 she consented, the offense was rape. Lancaster, 168 Ga. 470, 477 

Where a consent is finally given, notwithstanding the use of force, the crime is not rape. Wade, 37 Ga. App. 121 (138 S. E. 921).

Carnal knowledge of a woman while she is asleep may constitute rape. Brown, 138 Ga. 814 (76 S. E. 379).

Where the evidence showed that the girl, alleged to have been assaulted, resisted and screamed and told her sister to scream and tell her brother to come and make the accused leave, but also showed from the girl's testimony that the accused was on her half an hour, and that she had a watch in her hand and timed him from the time the intercourse commenced until he desisted, in order to see how long it took a man to do that way to a woman, the evidence did not support a charge of rape, although the latter part of the testimony was elicited from the witness on cross-examination, and in monosyllabic answers. Cheney, 109 Ga. 503 (35 S. E. 153).

The resistance on the part of the female must be actual, and it must have been prevented by violence or restrained by fear. Simmons, 99 Ga. 699, 700 (26 S. E. 484).

Force is necessary to the commission of the crime of rape. Lack of consent is insufficient. Lancaster, 168 Ga. 470 (9) (148 S. E. 139).

Identification. On trial for rape, the identification of the accused as the person who committed the offense is of paramount importance and should be established beyond a reasonable doubt. Harris, 155 

Ga. 405 (5) (117 S. E. 460).

Where it was shown that the offense of rape had been committed, and the question was as to the identity of the criminal on trial, it was incumbent on the State to make out the case beyond a reasonable doubt; but it was not necessary to show that it was impossible for the offense to have been committed by anybody else, or that it might not, by bare possibility, have been done by another. It is sufficient to show to a moral certainty that it was the prisoner. Johnson, 73 Ga. 107.

Lord Hale's doctrine. The crime of rape is one which is easily charged, hard to prove, and harder still to be defended by the accused, be he ever so innocent.. It is proper argument to the jury, but not for the Court to charge. Black, 119 Ga. 746 (3) (47 S. E. 370). 

Assaulted female as witness. "The rules of evidence in indictments for rape are different from what they are in ordinary cases. 

The offense is peculiar. This accusation is easily made, hard to be

proved and harder to be defended by the party accused, notwithstanding his innocence. The defendant, in consideration of these things, is let in, in his defense, to some privileges which are not always allowed to persons accused of crimes." The consideration which is given for the rule is that the crime is generally in secret, and there is a consequent absence of direct testimony. The evidence of the prosecutrix is admitted, while that of the defendant is excluded. Men are, therefore, put in the power of abandoned and vindictive women to a great extent. Innis, 42 Ga. 473, 481.

The injured female is usually a competent witness, but it is generally laid down that the degree of credit to be given to her evidence depends, more or less, upon the concurrence of circumstances with her testimony; for instance, if she be of good fame, if she presently discovered the offense, made pursuit after the offender, and showed circumstances and signs of the injury, if the place where the fact was done was remote from people, inhabitants, or passengers, or if the offender fled,-these and the like are concurring evidences which give greater probability to her evidence when proved by others than by herself. But if she concealed the injury for any considerable length of time after she had an opportunity to complain, if the place where the fact was supposed to be committed were near to inhabitants or places of common recourse or passage, and she made no outcry when the fact was supposed to be done, when and where it is probable that she might be heard by others, these and like circumstances carry a strong presumption that her testimony is false or feigned. Smith, 77 Ga. 705, 706 (2-a).

The defendant can not be convicted on the uncorroborated testimony of the female. Hamilton, 143 Ga. 265 (3) (84 S. E. 583).

Corroboration of evidence of female alleged to have been raped, essential to conviction. (Two dissenting.) Davis, 120 Ga. 433, 435 (48 S. E. 180). This decision criticised but followed: Fields, 2 Ga. 

App. 41, 42 (58 S. E. 327); Lancaster, 168 Ga. 470, 476 (7) (148 S. 

E. 139). (One dissenting.)

The accused should not be convicted upon the woman's testimony alone, no matter how positive it may be, unless she made some outcry or told of the injury promptly, or her clothing were torn or disarranged, or her person showed signs of violence, or there were other circumstances which tend to corroborate her story. Davis, 120 Ga. 

433, 435 (48 S. E. 180); Vanderford, 126 Ga. 753, 759 (55 S. E. 1025).

Corroboration of the female not required where the charge is assault with intent to rape. Fields, 2 Ga. App. 41 (58 S. E. 327); 

Moore, 37 Ga. App. 829 (142 S. E. 202).

605 The presence in the adjoining room of a woman who was the aunt of the female and the wife of the defendant, the failure to make an outery, repetition of the sexual intercourse at the same place, and under the same circumstances, failure to make a complaint, and the birth of a child in due season, were all circumstances tending to negative the claim of the female that the offense was rape. Avery, 12 

Ga. App. 562 (2) (77 S. E. 892).

Before the jury were authorized to convict, testimony of the female should be corroborated by other evidence tending to show the commission of the crime charged, such as evidence that the female made some outery or told of her alleged injury promptly, or her clothes were torn or dismantled, or that her person showed signs of violence, or that there were other circumstances tending to corroborate her story. All of which the jury are the judges, and the Court may so charge. Hamilton, 169 Ga. 826 (1) (151 S. E. 805). 

Corroboration. Testimony that female child, under 14 years of age, was asked why she had not been home, and that she said that she had been out with some boys and that they would not let her home, admissible on trial for rape. Getting, 166 Ga. 160 (1) (142 

S. E. 685). 

Testimony of girl's mother that when she went to make up her bed, she found blood on the linen, and also blood was found on child's underclothing, which were in the bathroom, admissible as testimony of facts tending to corroborate her statement. Pierce, 167 

Ga. 376, 377 (2) (3) (145 S. E. 450).

Evidence as to the conduct of the prosecutrix when she came to the house to which her children of tender age had fled, immediately after the commission of the crime,-admissible, such evidence tending to show her mental condition, and corroborate her testimony. 

Loyd, 150 Ga. 803 (1) (105 S. E. 465).

Evidence that the children of the prosecutrix came through the darkness to the witness's house-admissible, where under the circumstances testified to by the prosecutrix, the conduct of the children threw some light upon the transaction. Loyd, 150 Ga. 803 (105) 

S. E. 465).

In a case where the record discloses that an old man, who had theretofore borne an unblemished character, was, upon an indictment for rape upon a child of tender years, convicted of an assault, and where a careful study of the evidence for the State leads to the conclusion that, at most, a weak and unsatisfactory case against the accused was made out, the Supreme Court will not affirm the judgment of the lower court if there is any good reason for apprehend-

ing that the trial was not in all respects absolutely fair. Seymour, 102 Ga. 803 (30 S. E. 363).

Delay in making complaint of assault and in instituting prosecution ordinarily affords ground for discrediting female, but may be explained to the jury. Bennett, 102 Ga. 656 (1) (29 S. E. 918); Lancaster, 168 Ga. 470, 476 (8) (148 S. E. 139).

Corpus delicti. The corpus delicti can not be proved by the complaint of the female. Huey, 7 Ga. App. 398 (66 S. E. 1023).

Res gestae. Hearsay statements, even where admissible as part of the res gestae, are not sufficient to convict, unless the corpus delicti is established by other evidence. Williams, 11 Ga. App. 662 (75 

S. E. 988).

Complaint by the female assaulted at the first opportunity after the alleged offense,-admissible, but the particulars can not be stated. Lowe, 97 Ga. 792 (1) (25 S. E. 676).

Statement of an infant to her mother immediately after the alleged offense upon the child-admissible. McMath, 55 Ga. 303.

The particulars of the complaint by the injured female are not admissible by the State, unless part of the res gestae. The fact that she made a complaint is admissible to rebut consent. Huey, 7 Ga. 

App. 398 (1) (3) (66 S. E. 1023). The corpus delicti, venue, place, time, explanation as to condition of clothing, bruises are such particulars, and inadmissible. Huey, 7 Ga. App. 398 (2) (66 S. E. 

1023); Thomas, 144 Ga. 298, 299 (4) (87 S. E. 8).

The particulars may be inquired into by the defendant on crossexamination. Jackson, 20 Ga. App. 721 (93 S. E. 230).

Particulars are admitted where they lead to the arrest of the defendant, and to explain such arrest. Stephen, 11 Ga. 225, 226 (8). 

On trial for rape the condition of the clothing of the female within short time after the alleged commission of the crime-admissible. 

Chambers, 141 Ga. 652 (1) (81 S. E. 880).

Where there is evidence that the assaulted female made a complaint the rule that the particulars of the complaint are inadmissible does not apply where it was made in defendant's presence and immediately after the offense. Williams, 15 Ga. App. 306 (82 S. E. 938).

The complaint of the female three days after the alleged assault is not admissible as part of the res gestae, where it appears that she had frequent opportunities for making complaint to relatives and friends, and no reason is shown for her delay and silence. Huey, 7 

Ga. App. 398 (66 S. E. 1023).

Character of the injured female. It is no defense that the woman be lewd or unchaste. The crime of rape may be committed on the most abandoned and depraved strumpet. On the trial of a father for raping his daughter, letters from the accused to the daughter, written while incarcerated on that charge, stating that his freedom depended on her action, and pleading for the withdrawal of her charges against him, and which contained no protestation of his innocence, or denial of the charge, tended to corroborate the daughter, and were admissible. Testimony on the trial of one for rape to the effect that the defendant's father admitted that the defendant had treated the alleged injured female "wrong," and that the father had attempted to settle the case for money, not admissible, though introduced only for the purpose of impeaching the testimony of the father. Females under 14 years of age. Child under 14 years is legally incapable of consenting to sexual intercourse. Todd, 25 Ga. App.

As a result, even though the age of the female is not mentioned in the indictment, no reference is made to this act, and the offense is alleged to be "forcibly and against her will," thus clearly falling within § 26-1301, it is lawful for the Court to charge this act if the evidence warrants it, and a conviction under the same can be had. Echols, 153 Ga. 857, 859 (113 S. E. 170). (One dissenting.) § 26-1303 has no application where the child is over 14 years of age. Davis, 152 Ga. 320, 325 (110 S. E. 18).

Atkins, 154 Ga. 540 (114 S. E. 878).

Where charge on evidence of previous unchaste character of the alleged victim of rape is required, to the effect that such evidence should be weighed as independently bearing on the question whether or not she consented to the alleged sexual intercourse, and as illustrating the issue of consent on her part,-timely and pertinent written request should be presented. Where consummation of the intercourse is shown, the Court need not charge law of Assault With Intent to Rape. Berry, 87 Ga. 579 

Verdict. On a trial for rape, where the evidence justifies conviction for assault with intent to rape, such conviction may be had, and the Court should so charge the jury. Bailey, 153 Ga. 413 (1) (112 

S. E. 647).

Under an indictment for rape the accused can not be convicted of assault with intent to rape, if the evidence affirmatively shows that the offense was actually committed. But where the evidence is conflicting, and does not demand a finding that the defendant had committed rape, conviction for assault with intent to rape will be upheld. 

Byrd, 28 Ga. App. 504 (111 S. E. 924.)

Where the evidence is conclusive that the carnal knowledge was realized, a verdict finding the prisoner guilty of assault with intent

to rape is contrary to law. Kelsey, 62 Ga. 558; Rich, 160 Ga. 513, 514 (128 S. E. 666).

On an indictment for rape the accused can be convicted of assault with intent to rape, although the indictment does not contain an allegation of an assault. Harris, 21 Ga. App. 75 (1) (94 S. E. 75).

Conviction for assault, assault and battery, or assault with intent to rape may be founded on an indictment for rape. Sills, 36 Ga. 

App. 103 (135 S. E. 758).

Conviction for assault and battery, upon an indictment for assault with intent to rape, can only stand where assault and battery is charged in the indictment. Davis, 41 Ga. App. 466 (153 S. E. 436).

To sustain a verdict for assault with intent to rape, the evidence should be as clear as to convict of rape, so that a verdict of assault in a prosecution for rape is not sustained by evidence of improper exposure of female patient's person by her physician, under false statements of the necessity thereof. Nichols, 72 Ga. 191 (1).

Where two are jointly indicted for rape, and the evidence shows that the principal in the first degree is guilty of rape and the other is guilty as principal in the second degree, jury would not be authorized to find principal in the second degree guilty of assault with intent to rape, though there was evidence tending to show guilt of the latter offense as a separate and distinct crime from that for which the two defendants were jointly indicted. Bailey, 153 Ga. 413 (2) (112 S. E. 647).

Upon an indictment for rape a verdict for assault, assault and battery, or assault with intent to rape may be had, where the evidence warrants it, and such offenses are sufficiently charged in the indictment. Moore, 151 Ga. 648, 662 (108 S. E. 47).

A verdict of fornication, adultery or seduction can not be found upon an indictment for rape. Davis, 152 Ga. 320, 326 (110 S. E. 18).

Such verdict is null and void, and should be arrested on motion. 

Holland, 161 Ga. 492 (131 S. E. 503); Speer, 60 Ga. 381.

Where evidence, if credible, proves the offense of rape, failure of the judge, without request, to charge on assault and battery is not cause for a new trial, though the jury would have been authorized to convict of the lesser offense, in view of defendant's statement. 

Moore, 151 Ga. 648 (5) (108 S. E. 47).

43. RECEIVING STOLEN GOODS. 

§§ 26-2620 to 26-2623. 

Punishment. The same punishment as would be inflicted on the person convicted of having stolen or feloniously taken the property. (Reducible.) See: Accessories. The said the principal thief, has plead guilty (or was convicted) at the........... .term of......…………….. .......court to an indictment for simple larceny, charging him with stealing said property, contrary, etc. . . . Where principal is unknown. charge and accuse.. with the offense of receiving stolen goods, for that the said......... on the day of…………………………19, in the county aforesaid, did then and there unlawfully buy and receive from some person, to the grand jury unknown (so that he might be taken and prosecuted to conviction), (here describe the property), of the value of $.........., the same being the property of……………………………………….., the same having been feloniously stolen by some party unknown, said stealing of said............. being from.......... (a railroad car), after said thief or thieves have broken open the same, said.. ....being located he, the said................, knowing said goods were stolen when he so bought and received them from said thief, contrary, etc. (Approved: Licette, 75 Ga. 253.) 

For approved indictment see also McKissick, 11 Ga. App. 721 (76 S. E. 71).

Indictment for receiving stolen goods knowing them to be stolen must allege that the principal thief has been indicted and convicted. 

Whitehead, 41 Ga. App. 466 (153 S. E. 428); Ford, 35 Ga. App. 655 (8) (134 S. E. 353). (Where principal thief is unknown, or can not be found, indictment may so allege. See: Indictments.)

Indictment not alleging trial and conviction of principal thief should be quashed on motion. But it is not ground for motion in arrest of judgment. Martin, 95 Ga. 478 (1) (20 S. E. 271).

The rule that indictment should charge that the principal thief has been indicted and convicted, or that he can not be found, does not apply to misdemeanor. Tinch, 11 Ga. App. 158 (1) (74 S. E. 1003). 

Indictment need not allege that sentence had been imposed on the principal thief. Fowler, 25 Ga. App. 297 (103 S. E. 264).

Joinder. Principal and accessory after the fact can not be jointly indicted where prosecution of accessory is for receiving stolen goods knowing them to be stolen. Smiley, 23 Ga. App. 317 (98 S. E. 125).

Count for receiving stolen goods, knowing them to be stolen, may be joined in an indictment with a count for simple larceny. Johnson, 61 Ga. 212 (1).

Description. 

Indictment for receiving stolen goods, knowing them to be stolen, must be as full and particular, as to descriptive averments of the crime, as if the accused were charged as principal. 

Wright, 1 Ga. App. 158 (5) (57 S. E. 1050).

The stolen goods must be sufficiently described in the indictment to identify the articles. Brown, 116 Ga. 559 (2) (42 S. E. 795). "One sack of nitrate of soda, weighing about 200 lbs. of the value of $10.00" is sufficient. Fowler, 25 Ga. App. 297 (1) (103 S. E. 264). General.

Though law of receiver of stolen goods classifies one who receives stolen goods as an accessory after the fact to the larceny, yet the offender is not technically an accessory, and is guilty of a distinct offense, the gist of which is the felonious knowledge that the goods. were stolen. Springer, 102 Ga. 447, 452 (30 S. E. 971); Tinch, 11 

Ga. App. 158 (74 S. E. 1003); Ford, 162 Ga. 422 (2) (134 S. E. 95).

The conviction of the principal is not an element in the crime of receiving stolen goods, knowing them to be stolen, but is a regulation which affects the time when, and the manner in which, a person indicted of this offense can be tried. Ford, 162 Ga. 422 (2) (134 S. E. 95).

Infant. Where one receives stolen goods from an infant, and the infant is acquitted because of his tender years, the receiver of the goods can not be convicted as an accessory after the fact. He is guilty as a principal. Edwards, 80 Ga. 127 (1) (4 S. E. 268).

SPECIFIC CRIMES 

613 Knowledge. The person receiving stolen goods must have knowledge that they were stolen, at the time of receiving them. Where the accused received stolen goods, not knowing at the time that they had been stolen, but, upon being informed of the larceny, secreted the goods and retained the possession thereof, he was not guilty of receiving stolen goods knowing them to be stolen. Pat, 116 Ga. 92 (2) (42 S. E. 389).

Principal thief. One of the material facts which the State must prove, where the offense charged is that of receiving stolen goods, is the guilt of the principal thief. Belton, 21 Ga. App. 792, 793 (1) (95 S. E. 299).

The accessory could waive the conviction of the principal and go to trial on the charge preferred against him. Ford, 162 Ga. 422 

Where an accusation for knowingly receiving stolen goods alleged that the principal thief had been indicted and convicted, but where upon the trial of the accessory it appeared from the evidence that the principal thief had been convicted after the issuance of the accusation, and where the accessory was convicted of the offense charged, a motion to set aside and vacate the verdict and judgment, upon the ground that the accusation, verdict, and judgment were fatally defective and void, was properly overruled. Perry, 41 Ga. 

App. 651 (1) (154 S. E. 211). The reason for this rule is explained by referring to the principle that the accessory can waive the conviction of the principal, and when he elects to go on trial knowing that the principal's conviction is subject to attack, he has impliedly waived his right. Also, because the requirement that the indictment and conviction of the principal must be alleged and proved is not an element of the crime, but a regulation for the protection of the accused. It merely prevents one from being convicted as accessory where the principal might be acquitted. It seems immaterial when the principal was convicted, as long as his conviction took place before the trial of the accessory. Ford, 162 Ga. 422 (134 

S. E. 95).

Where the conviction of the principal has been reversed by the higher courts, and a new trial granted, knowledge of these facts on the part of the accused, who is charged as a receiver of stolen goods, without proper objection, will be considered as waiver of his right to be tried after conviction of the principal. Ford, 162 

Ga. 422 (134 S. E. 95).

Where the principal thief pleads guilty, such plea stands upon.

the same footing as a conviction. Belton, 21 Ga. App. 792, 793 (1) (95 S. E. 299).

Jurisdiction. One whom the evidence shows to have been accessory to the commission of a felony can not be legally convicted in any court with jurisdiction limited to misdemeanors, although the principal may have been convicted of a misdemeanor. Snow, 5 Ga. 

App. 608 (1) (63 S. E. 651).

Upon the trial of one for knowingly receiving stolen goods, where the indictment charges that the principal thief is unknown to the grand jurors, so that he can not be apprehended and convicted, it is not necessary for the State to show that the theft occurred in the county of the trial. It is sufficient if it be shown that the "knowingly receiving" was done in that county. 

App. 160 (5) (99 S. E. 891). 

O'Neal, 24 Ga.

The old rule was that one can not be punished for receiving goods stolen in another State, and brought into this State, for the goods must have been stolen in the jurisdiction in which it was sought to punish for the receiving. Golden, 2 Ga. App. 440 (2) (58 S. E. 557). Since the passage of the act relative to bringing stolen property into the State (Acts 1918, p. 272), § 26-2622, it is not necessary to show that the property was stolen in this State. 

O'Neal, 24 Ga. App. 160 (5-a) (99 S. E. 891).

Punishment. Same punishment as the principal may mean that the sentence of the principal shall be the measure of that imposed upon the accessory. But the better construction probably is, that the latter should not exceed the maximum of what the former might have been. Anderson, 63 Ga. 675, 678. Evidence.

Knowledge. Knowledge that the goods were stolen is an essential element and must be established; but it may be inferred from circumstances, sufficient to excite the suspicion of an ordinarily prudent man. Where one is found in possession of the stolen goods immediately after the theft, the burden to prove that his was not a guilty possession rests upon him. Williams, 16 Ga. App. 697 (6), 698 (85 S. E. 976).

Value. Proof of the value of the goods stolen is indispensable in order to support indictment. Courts will not take judicial notice that cotton is a thing of value. Wright, 1 Ga. App. 158 (3) (5) (57 S. E. 1050).

SPECIFIC CRIMES 

615 Evidence that the thief pawned a ring worth $1600 to defendant for $1, that he did not tell him where he got the ring, and that defendant later got uneasy about the ring and sold it to another for $2 giving thief $1, warrants conviction. Pharr, 26 Ga. App. 433 (106 S. E. 306).

In order to convict receiver of stolen goods, the ownership and the larceny of the goods must be proven as charged with reasonable certainty. O'Connell, 55 Ga. 296.

Accomplice. The thief is not an accomplice of the receiver of stolen goods, and the receiver may be convicted upon the uncorroborated evidence of the thief. Springer, 102 Ga. 447 (30 S. E. 971).

Conviction of principal thief. The evidence should show that the principal was convicted or pleaded guilty before the trial of the receiver of stolen goods, unless the principal is unknown and that fact is alleged in the indictment. Belton, 21 Ga. App. 792, 793 (1) (95 S. E. 299). 

Parol evidence of the trial and conviction of the principal is sufficient to show these facts, if not objected to. Martin, 95 Ga. 478, 479 (20 S. E. 271).

Where the principal thief waived indictment and entered a plea of "guilty," accusation and plea are admissible in evidence against the accused on trial for the offense of receiving stolen goods. Belton, 21 Ga. App. 792, 794 (6) (95 S. E. 299).

The record of the conviction of the principal thief is conclusive evidence of his conviction; but is merely prima facie evidence of his guilt. The introduction of such record in evidence by the State places the onus upon the accessory of disproving the guilt of the principal. Ford, 162 Ga. 422 (3) (134 S. E. 95).

Where the principal thief is unknown, every fact, including the time of the theft, essential to the conviction of the principal, must be proved, as well as that the party on trial received the stolen goods, within the statute of limitations, with knowledge that they were stolen. Belton, 21 Ga. App. 792, 793 (1) (95 S. E. 299).

Where the principal thief has been convicted or has pleaded "guilty" before the trial of the receiver of the stolen goods, it is not essential, in order to sustain conviction, to prove the exact date or term of court when the principal entered a plea of "guilty." 

Belton, 21 Ga. App. 792, 793 (1) (95 S. E. 299); Licette, 75 Ga. 

253; Wright, 1 Ga. App. 158 (57 S. E. 1050).

44. RIOT. 

§ 26-5302. (Misdemeanor.) charge and accuse.... and...... and and........ on the...day of with the offense of a misdemeanor, for that the said and.. .19..., in the county aforesaid, with force and arms, did commit an unlawful act of violence, to wit, did then and there, acting with a common intent, make an unlawful assault on one..... and one..... and did then and there attempt to commit a personal injury on said.. ……….., and…………………………….., contrary, etc. proved: Lock, 122 Ga. 730, 731 (50 S. E. 932); Carter, 7 Ga. App. 

44 (2) (65 S. E. 1072).) (Ap- 

For other approved indictment see: Green, 109 Ga. 536 (1) (35 S. E. 97).

In its nature riot is a joint offense, for which one person alone can not be indicted. In order to constitute the crime of riot, there must be at least two persons; one alone can not be indicted. Robinson, 84 Ga. 674, 680 (11 S. E. 544).

Indictment for riot by two named persons "together with others," not named in the indictment, and not alleged to be unknown to the grand jury, subject to special demurrer. Martin, 115 Ga. 255 (41 S. E. 576).

Participants, whose names are unknown, may be included in the indictment, but it must be alleged that their names are unknown. 

Lewis, 5 Ga. App. 496, 497 (63 S. E. 570).

General. Riot is doing, by two or more persons, either with or without a common cause of quarrel, an unlawful act of violence, or any other act in a violent and tumultuous manner. Carnes, 28 Ga. 192, 193.

To warrant conviction of riot, joint action of two or more persons must appear. Tripp, 109 Ga. 489 (34 S. E. 1021).

The defendants need not have been engaged in an unlawful act, where they acted in a violent and tumultuous manner. This is true, although the indictment charged that they acted "unlawfully and violently." Taylor, 8 Ga. App. 241 (1) (68 S. E. 945).

In order to constitute riot, where the act is lawful, there must be violence and tumultuousness, or where the act is unlawful there must be at least violence. Taylor, 8 Ga. App. 241 (68 S. E. 945); 

Rachels, 51 Ga. 374.

SPECIFIC CRIMES 

617 1 1 Violence. In the absence of violence, making noise and behaving in a tumultuous manner does not constitute riot. Coney, 113 

Ga. 1060, 1061 (39 S. E. 425); Barron, 74 Ga. 833.

Common intent and concert of action. All persons connected with and sharing in the common purpose of the assembly are guilty of riot, whether their conduct is violent and tumultuous or not. 

O'Quinn, 39 Ga. App. 829, 830 (148 S. E. 618).

Though common intent and concert of action must be shown, yet it is not necessary for the evidence to show any previous plot or conspiracy. Both, the intent and the concert of action may be inferred from the manner in which the unlawful act of violence is committed. Grier, 11 Ga. App. 767 (1) (76 S. E. 70); Walker, 17 Ga. App. 525 (1) (87 S. E. 711).

Common intent and concert of action is sufficiently shown where two brothers went to the home of their father, and used violent, profane, and abusive language accompanied by threats to kill their father, declaring to each other and to their father that they were armed and prepared to execute their threats. Oglesby, 12 Ga. App. 684 (1) (78 S. E. 134). 

Evidence that two persons, under circumstances indicating a previous combination to use violence, committed such an assault upon the person of the prosecutor as amounted to an act of illegal violence, warranted conviction. Stafford, 93 Ga. 207 (19 S. E. 50).

Removal of prisoner from jail. Mob gathering to prevent removal of prisoner from jail guilty of riot. All sharing in the common purpose are guilty, whether the conduct is violent and tumultuous or not. Green, 109 Ga. 536 (2) (35 S. E. 97).

Effort to release prisoner in a violent and tumultuous manneris riot. Fisher, 78 Ga. 258.

Threats. Where three men gathered in front of the house of one at night, and cursed and threatened him in loud voices, and frightened him and the members of his family by repeatedly firing a gun, they were guilty of riot. Lewis, 2 Ga. App. 659 (1) (58 S. 

E. 1070); Walker, 17 Ga. App. 525 (87 S. E. 711); Kilcrease, 21 Ga. 

App. 803 (95 S. E. 271).

Verdicts. When severance is granted, the acquittal of one does not operate as an acquittal of the other. Rachels, 51 Ga. 374.

Conviction of one of two rioters upheld, though the other be acquitted, if the evidence shows that any other person capable of committing the crime participated with the person convicted in the

criminal act, charged in the indictment. Martin, 115 Ga. 255 (41

S. E. 576). 

Where four defendants were convicted of riot, and petition for certiorari assigned error on the ground that the verdict was without evidence to support it, it was error to grant a new trial to three of the defendants and to deny a new trial to the fourth, because one person can not commit riot. Lewis, 5 Ga. App. 496 (1) (63 S. E. 570).

Judge may set aside verdict, in proper case, as to two defendants, and leave it standing as to two. Sims, 87 Ga. 569 (14. S. E. 122). 

45. ROBBERY. 

§§ 26-2501 to 26-2503.

Punishment. Robbery by open force: Not less than four nor more than twenty years in the penitentiary.

Robbery by intimidation: Not less than two nor more than twenty years in the penitentiary. (Reducible.) 

Note: Compare with larceny from the person, and sudden snatching. §§ 26-2626, 26-2628. Indictment. charge and accuse. .with the offense of robbery, for that the said on the..................day of……………………….. 

19..., in the county aforesaid, did wrongfully, fraudulently, and violently, by force and intimidation, take from the person of............, without his consent and with intent to steal the same, the property of............... and of the value of... contrary, etc.... (Approved: Carson, 22 Ga. App. 743, 744 (97 S. E. 202).) -" charge and accuse. 

..with the offense of robbery, for that the said............ on the...............day of... .19...., in the county aforesaid, did suddenly snatch and suddenly carry away from the person of..., and with intent to steal the same, and without the consent of the said.. (here describe the property).............. of the value of.. dollars and of the personal goods of..................and in the possession, and control of the said ..., contrary, etc. . . . (Hickey, 125 Ga. 145 (53 S. E. 1026).) 

Robbery by force and by intimidation may be charged in the same indictment, either in one count or in separate counts. Harris, 1 Ga. App. 136 (1) (57 S. E. 937); Lampkin, 87 Ga. 516 (2) (13 

S. E. 523).

Indictment describing property as "five dollars in money, of the

SPECIFIC CRIMES 

619 value of five dollars"-sufficient as to the description of the stolen property. Humphries, 100 Ga. 260 (1) (28 S. E. 25).

Indictment may not charge robbery and assault and battery even in separate counts. Davis, 57 Ga. 66.

Robbery, larceny from the person, and cheating and swindling can not be charged in the same indictment. Doyle, 77 Ga. 515 (1).

In an indictment for robbery the ownership of the personal property stolen may be laid in the person having actual lawful possession of the property, although he may be holding it merely as the agent or bailee of another; and it is not necessary to set forth in the indictment the fact that the person in whom the ownership was laid is holding the property merely as an agent or bailee of the owner. 

Where under such indictment the evidence discloses that the prosecutor held the property as an agent or bailee of the true owner, there is no material variance between the indictment and the proof. 

Jones, 42 Ga. App. 290 (6) (155 S. E. 797).

An indictment for robbery must negative the owner's consent. 

Where it alleges that the taking was with the consent of the owner, it sets forth no offense, and a conviction based upon such indictment is illegal. Scott, 25 Ga. App. 553 (103 S. E. 732).

Indictment is not void for failure to allege that the taking was without the consent of the owner of the property, where it charges. that the act was done with force and arms, wrongfully, fraudulently and violently, by force and intimidation. Shehany, 170 Ga. 70 (152 

S. E. 114).

Indictment failing to charge that the property was taken from the person of another, by the defendant, is fatally defective. Steager, 39 Ga. 583. General.

Robbery by intimidation is the same as "putting in fear" at common law, and is constructive force, as where a person through fear is induced to part with his property. Robbery by actual force implies violence. If there is any injury done to the person, or if there is a struggle to retain possession of the property before it is taken, it is the force referred to in our Code. Robbery by sudden snatching is where no other force is used than is necessary for the thief to obtain the possession of the property from the owner, who is off his guard, where there is no resistance by the owner or injury to his person. Rivers, 46 Ga. App. 778 (2) (169 S. E. 260).

Robbery by force and robbery by intimidation are not two of

fenses, but different grades of the same offense. Lampkin, 87 Ga.

516 (2) (13 S. E. 523). 

In order to constitute robbery there must be force or intimidation, or a sudden snatching. Where the evidence failed to show that any force or intimidation was used, or that there was a sudden snatching, taking, or carrying away, conviction of robbery unauthorized. 

Davis, 24 Ga. App. 327 (100 S. E. 767).

To constitute robbery it is not essential that the victim be conscious. Bowen, 16 Ga. App. 110 (1) (84 S. E. 730); Hines, 16 Ga. 

App. 411, 413, 414 (85 S. E. 452).

Loser of money at cards, compelling the winner to surrender his winnings, is not guilty of robbery. But if he compelled the winner to surrender other money besides his winnings, the defendant is guilty. Gant, 115 Ga. 205, 206 (2) (41 S. E. 696).

Intent to steal. The intent to steal is a substantive element of robbery. Judge should so instruct the jury. Failure to so instruct is error. Sledge, 99 Ga. 684 (2) (26 S. E. 756); Blackshear, 20 Ga.

Force. Where according to the evidence for the State the accused was guilty of robbery by force, and according to the evidence for accused he was not guilty of any offense, verdict of guilty of robbery by intimidation was unauthorized. Story, 12 Ga. App. 644 (77 S. 

E. 914).

Force consists in personal violence or that degree of force that is necessary to remove articles attached to the person or clothing as to create a resistance, however slight. Barksdale, 24 Ga. App. 115 (2) (100 S. E. 45).

Actual force implies personal violence. If there is any injury done to the person, or if there is a struggle to retain possession of the property, before it is taken, the force is sufficient. Tanner, 24 Ga. 

App. 132 (2) (100 S. E. 44).

The force sufficient to break a watch-chain will be sufficient violence under the law of robbery. Bowen, 16 Ga. App. 110 (2) (84 

S. E. 730).

Where the element of force, which was necessary to constitute robbery, was present, it is no defense that the person robbed made no resistance. McIntyre, 41 Ga. App. 352 (1-a) (152 S. E. 914).

Intimidation. If the delivery of the property is from fear of injury to the person, property, or character, though it seems voluntary, the crime is robbery. Long, 12 Ga. 293, 294 (10) (11).

Intimidation means putting in fear. A person is regarded in fear

SPECIFIC CRIMES 

621 if the circumstances are such as in common experience are likely to create an apprehension of danger. Johnson, 1 Ga. App. 729, 730 (57

S. E. 1056). 

If the stealing be attended with such circumstances of terrorsuch threatening by words or gesture, as in common experience are likely to create an apprehension of danger and induce a man to part with his property for the safety of his person,-it is robbery. Johnson, 1 Ga. App. 729, 730 (57 S. E. 1056); Jordan, 135 Ga. 434, 436 (69 S. E. 562); Long, 12 Ga. 293, 321 (12).

Intimidation is the same as "putting in fear" at common law and is constructive force. Tanner, 24 Ga. App. 132 (2-a) (100 S. E. 44).

A person is guilty of robbery by intimidation who has obtained possession of a pistol under the pretense of examination with a view of purchasing it, and then, by using it to put the owner to fear, carried it away. Grant, 125 Ga. 259 (1) (54 S. E. 191).

Robbery by intimidation was committed where the defendants arrested another without a warrant, carried him to an adjoining county, and, by exciting fear, induced him to consent to their taking part of his money. Sweat, 90 Ga. 315 (1) (17 S. E. 273).

Evidence that the defendant held a pistol in a threatening and intimidating manner over the victim of an alleged robbery, while his confederates ran their hands through the pockets of the victim, and without violence relieved the latter of his money and other loose valuables unattached to his person or clothing, authorizes conviction of robbery by intimidation, but not of robbery by force, the robbery having been accomplished without force. Barksdale, 24 Ga. 

App. 115 (3) (100 S. E. 45).

The threat necessary for the offense of robbery by intimidation may be made by a county officer. Sweat, 90 Ga. 316 (17 S. E. 273).

Sudden snatching. The act of the General Assembly approved 

August 6, 1903 (Acts 1903, p. 43), § 26-2501, defining robbery, by adding to that section "or the sudden snatching, taking or carrying away any money, goods, chattels, or anything of value from the owner or person in possession or control thereof, without the consent of the owner or person in possession or control thereof," did not create an independent and new statutory offense, nor abolish the distinctive element which differentiates the crime of robbery from larceny, i.e., violence. Robbery which is committed by sudden. snatching, as described in the amending act, is robbery by force, and is punishable as prescribed in § 26-2502. Pride, 125 Ga. 748 (54 S.

E. 686); Pride, 125 Ga. 750 (2) (54 S. E. 688); Jones, 18 Ga. App. 8 (2) (89 S. E. 342).

The snatching involves an element of force, and must be charged to the jury, where the law is applicable. Moore, 20 Ga. App. 190 (2) (92 S. E. 963). 

Where one demanded an article in the hands of another, and, upon refusal to deliver, forcibly snatched it and ran off with it, against the consent of the person in possession of it, the offense was robbery if there was an intent to steal. McDow, 110 Ga. 293 (34 S. E. 1019).

Where a purse was secured by a steel chain to the owner's finger, and the defendant suddenly snatched it with force sufficient to break the chain and injure the owner's finger, with intent to steal, the crime was robbery. Smith, 117 Ga. 320 (43 S. E. 736). 

Robbery and larceny distinguished. Robbery and larceny from the person are distinguished by the use of force and violence. Moran, 125 Ga. 33, 34 (53 S. E. 806). Or intimidation. Morris, 125 Ga. 36 (53 S. E. 564); Pride, 125 Ga. 748, 749 (54 S. E. 686).

Only difference between robbery by sudden snatching and larceny from the person is that in the latter case the property is taken without the knowledge of the possessor. Williams, 9 Ga. App. 170 (1) (70 S. E. 890).

In order to constitute robbery by sudden snatching, an element of force is necessary. In order to constitute the offense of larceny from the person, the property must be wrongfully, fraudulently and privately taken and carried away. Moore, 20 Ga. App. 190 (2) (92 

S. E. 963). Prior to the act of 1903 (Ga. L. 1903, p. 43), § 26-2501, amending the former definition of robbery, "violence of some kind was an indispensable essential of the offense of robbery. Without violence there could be no robbery." Since the amendment, violence is not an essential element of that offense, but "robbery, by sudden taking and carrying away the property of another without his consent, can be committed without violence of any kind. "The only difference now between robbery of this class and larceny from the person is that in the latter case the property is abstracted without the knowledge of its possessor; but if the possessor becomes conscious, even in the taking, that his property is being taken away from him, and this knowledge is obtained before the taking is complete, the offense of robbery is complete." Williams, 9 Ga. App. 170 (70 S. E. 

890); Hall, 41 Ga. App. 368 (153 S. E. 199).

Proof of struggle to retain property may be sufficient evidence of force. Long, 12 Ga. 293, 294 (9); Burke, 74 Ga. 372.

SPECIFIC CRIMES 

623 Injury to the person inflicted in the taking of the property may authorize inference of force. Long, 12 Ga. 293, 294 (9).

Asportation. The slightest change of location sufficient. Permanent appropriation not necessary. Rivers, 46 Ga. App. 778 (3) (169 S. E. 260). 

From the person of another. It is not necessary that the property be taken directly from the person. It is sufficient if taken while in his possession or immediate presence. Crawford, 90 Ga. 701 (2) (17 

S. E. 628); Clements, 84 Ga. 660 (1) (11 S. E. 505). 

Where the prosecutor was in his smokehouse within fifteen steps. of his dwelling house, and he was prevented by threats and intimidation of the defendants, from leaving the smokehouse and returning to the dwelling house, until some of them entered and stole the property, the offense was robbery. Clements, 84 Ga. 660 (1) (11 S. 

E. 505).

The words "from the person of another" include property under the personal protection of one, though not actually from the physical body. Clements, 84 Ga. 660 (1), 665 (11 S. E. 505); Jackson, 114 Ga. 826, 827 (40 S. E. 1001).

There is a distinction between custody and possession. The owner of goods by delivering them to another may give such other person the mere custody or charge of the goods, the technical possession remaining in himself, or he may by such delivery divest himself of the possession of the goods. Rivers, 46 Ga. App. 778 (4) (169 S. E. 260).

Conspiracy. Where the evidence shows that the defendants had a common intent to rob, all are guilty, though some may not have actually participated. Ferguson, 32 Ga. 658.

Where the victim was robbed by two men, one pointing a pistol and the other holding and searching him, both are guilty of both grades, robbery by force and robbery by intimidation. Harris, 1 

Ga. App. 136 (2) (57 S. E. 937).

Want of consent. Want of consent of the person alleged to have been robbed is an essential element of the offense of robbery. Shehany, 170 Ga. 70 (152 S. E. 114).

Description of property. "Greenback" judicially recognized as a species of currency of the United States. Jones, 10 Ga. App. 59 (72 S. E. 518). "Dollar" judicially recognized as money of the 

United States of the value of one hundred cents. Maxwell, 9 Ga. 

App. 875 (72 S. E. 445).

Venue. Where the defendant arrested the prosecutor in one county and took him into another, and there got possession of his money, the venue was in the latter county, and not where the arrest was made. Sweat, 90 Ga. 315 (1) (17 S. E. 273). 

Bona fide claim of ownership. To constitute robbery there must. be force or intimidation, asportation without the consent of the owner, and the intent to steal. A person taking the property from another under a bona fide claim of right and with the purpose of applying it to the payment of a debt from the latter to himself, is not guilty of robbery, the animus furandi being absent. It is otherwise if the claim of right is a mere pretense. Crawford, 90 Ga. 701 (1) (17 S. E. 628). 

Evidence. Where the indictment charges ownership of the property stolen in a third person, it must be proved, although such allegation is not necessary. Staples, 114 Ga. 256 (40 S. E. 264).

Evidence that the stolen property was found the next morning in the possession of a woman with whom the accused was intimate, relevant. Clay, 122 Ga. 136 (2) (50 S. E. 56).

There is no force required beyond the effort of the robber to obtain possession of the property, but if the owner makes some degree of resistance, while the act may be robbery by force, it is also robbery by sudden snatching. Where all the elements of robbery by snatching are proved, it is no variance from the indictment for such robbery that the proof should disclose a superadded element of force, which would have authorized indictment and conviction for robbery by force. Hickey, 125 Ga. 145 (53 S. E. 1026). 

Charge. Indictment charging robbery by force and robbery by intimidation, conviction may be had for both grades or either, as may be shown by the evidence, and the Court may so charge the jury. Carter, 3 Ga. App. 477 (1) (60 S. E. 216). 

Where one is charged with the offense of robbery by force and intimidation, it is error to charge the jury that sudden snatching is also robbery. Pride, 124 Ga. 791 (53 S. E. 192). 

Where only robbery by force and robbery by intimidation are. charged, the Court need not charge the law of robbery by sudden snatching. Clay, 122 Ga. 136 (50 S. E. 56).

Restoration. Robbery is not purged by the re-delivery of the stolen property, even after short time. McGinty, 97 Ga. 368 (1) (23 

S. E. 824).
