46. SEDUCTION. 

§§ 26-6001 to 26-6003. 

Punishment. Not less than two nor more than twenty years in the penitentiary. (Not reducible.) with the offense of 

Indictment. .. charge and accuse...... seduction, for that the said......... on the................day of…............. 

19...., in the county aforesaid, did by persuasion and promise of marriage seduce a virtuous unmarried female, to wit,, and by such persuasion and promise of marriage induced her to yield to his lustful embraces, contrary, etc. . . . (Approved: Wooten, 150 Ga. 

40 (102 S. E. 352).)

Indictment charging other fraudulent means in addition to persuasion and promises, demurrable for not stating what other fraudulent means used. McGouldrick, 20 Ga. App. 185 (1) (92 S. E. 953); 

Langston, 109 Ga. 153 (35 S. E. 166).

Indictment which sets out means other than persuasion and promise of marriage by falsely and fraudulently representing to the female as follows: "I won't hurt you, you needn't be afraid of any trouble, nothing will happen to you, you can trust me," thereby inducing the girl to have sexual intercourse with the defendant, is subject to special demurrer. McGouldrick, 20 Ga. App. 185 (2) (92

S. E. 953). 

Indictment need not charge that the promise of marriage was false and fraudulent. Wooten, 150 Ga. 40 (102 S. E. 352).

General. 

Yielding to gratify passion is no seduction. Keller, 102 Ga.

506 

If the defendant did have carnal knowledge of the prosecutrix, and if she was virtuous and permitted the defendant to have carnal knowledge of her, by reason of her love for him, and persuasion and promise of marriage, the defendant is guilty of seduction. Odum, 21 Ga. App. 310 (4) (94 S. E. 257). 

Seduction and fornication. Seduction is based on confidence and affection which engagement has engendered, whereas an intercourse upon the mere prospect of an engagement or promise to marry is mere fornication. Morris, 14 Ga. App. 395, 398 (81 S. E. 257).

Under an indictment for seduction it is competent for the jury to find the defendant guilty of fornication, if the evidence justifies it; seduction is the higher offense and necessarily includes fornication,

if both parties are single. Kiser, 43 Ga. App. 156 (158 S. E. 346); 

Kiser, 172 Ga. 488 (157 S. E. 681).

Law of fornication should be charged even without request, where applicable. Kiser, 172 Ga. 488 (157 S. E. 681). But it was held in 

Hembree, 17 Ga. App. 117 (2) (86 S. E. 286) that the failure to define fornication is not error in the absence of timely written request.

Law of fornication is not involved and should not be given in charge on trial for seduction where the evidence for the State makes case of seduction and the defense of the accused is that he never had sexual intercourse with the person alleged to have been seduced. 

Kiser, 41 Ga. App. 568 (1) (153 S. E. 620).

Adultery as well as fornication are embraced in a charge of seduction. Disharoon, 95 Ga. 351, 356 (22 S. E. 698); Boggs, 11 Ga. App. 

92 (1) (74 S. E. 716). 

Character of female.

Evidence as to the character of the female is not competent except in rebuttal impeaching her chastity, or veracity as a witness. Lewis, 89 Ga. 396 (1) (15 S. E. 489).

Character of female can not be proved by hearsay of third person. 

McTyier, 91 Ga. 254 (2) (18 S. E. 140).

Passionate nature of the woman is no defense, if she keeps her chastity and surrenders it because of persuasion and promises. Keller, 102 Ga. 506 (8) (31 S. E. 92).

A woman is a virtuous female if her body is pure, though her mind and heart be impure. Hays, 16 Ga. App. 20, 21 (7) (84 S. E. 

497). She may be virtuous within the meaning of the law, if she has never had sexual intercourse, though men might have taken liberties with her, such as hugging and kissing. (Id.) 

A woman who has never been married and never had sexual intercourse is virtuous within the meaning of the law, and may be the victim of seduction. Keller, 102 Ga. 506 (8) (31 S. E. 92).

The word "virtuous" means physical purity and not purity of mind. Any virgin is virtuous within the meaning of the law, and every woman is presumed to be virtuous. Woodard, 5 Ga. App. 447 (1) (2) (63 S. E. 573). 

Every virgin is virtuous. Generally if a woman parts with her virginity, before wedlock, and by her consent, she is not virtuous. 

O'Neill, 85 Ga. 383 (1) (11 S. E. 856). 

Physical chastity, not moral or intellectual chastity, is the test to determine whether the woman is virtuous, at the time of the seduc-

SPECIFIC CRIMES 

627 tion. Washington, 124 Ga. 423 (3) (52 S. E. 910); Lanier, 25 Ga. 

App. 545 (1) (103 S. E. 731).

On a trial for seduction it is for the Court to construe the meaning of the word "virtuous," as used in the statute. Woodard, 5 Ga. 

App. 447 (1) (63 S. E. 573). It is not a question for the jury. Mc- 

Tyier, 91 Ga. 254 (5) (18 S. E. 140); O'Neill, 85 Ga. 383 (1) (11 S. 

E. 856).

On the question whether a woman is virtuous, jury may consider evidence of debauched mind and apply their knowledge of human nature and the customs of society in determining such questions. 

Lanier, 25 Ga. App. 545 (103 S. E. 731); O'Neill, 85 Ga. 383 (2) (11 

S. E. 856).

A virtuous woman upon whom the crime of rape has been committed, does not thereby lose her virtue, and if unmarried, she may become the victim of seduction. Jones, 90 Ga. 616, 628 (16 S. E. 380).

Evidence of lewd and lascivious nature of the woman- -admissible. 

Keller, 102 Ga. 506 (5) (31 S. E. 92).

Evidence of subsequent intercourse with other men-inadmissible. 

Keller, 102 Ga. 506, 507 (7) (31 S. E. 92).

Where the defendant attacked the character of the prosecutrix, testimony showing that her conduct was good. offered by the State in rebuttal,-admissible. Champion, 21 Ga. App. 656 (1) (94 S. E. 828).

It is not a reversible error to admit testimony as to the general character of two female associates of the prosecutrix, where such testimony is tending to contradict evidence showing intemperate, loose, and careless behavior on part of the prosecutrix when in company with these persons and defendant. Thomas, 19 Ga. App. 104, 105 (3) (91 S. E. 247).

It is not competent in trial for seduction for the accused to prove acts of sexual intercourse between the woman charged to have been seduced, and any person or persons other than himself, occurring after the time when the alleged seduction took place. Daniel, 41 

Ga. App. 608 (2) (154 S. E. 204). 

Virtuous engagement to marry. Where testimony showed bona fide existing and virtuous engagement to marry, jury were authorized to infer that illicit intercourse was not purely meretricious transaction, notwithstanding further testimony of the prosecutrix that: "He told me he would marry me if I got into any trouble, and that he loved me, and I told him that I loved him," and "I agreed to

it because I loved him and thought he loved me, and because he said if he got me a baby that he would marry me." Durrance, 20 Ga. 

App. 192, 193 (1) (92 S. E. 962).

To accomplish sexual intercourse with a virtuous woman pending virtuous engagement to marry may be seduction though consent be obtained without persuasion other than that which is implied (considering past courtship and present relations of the parties) in proposing intercourse and repeating promise of marriage. Daniel, 41 

Ga. App. 608 (1) (154 S. E. 204).

Promise of marriage alone is not sufficient persuasion. O'Neill, 85 Ga. 383 (11 S. E. 856). This rule is true, although promise was made on account of pregnancy. Cherry, 112 Ga. 871 (1) (38 S. E. 341).

If a single woman allowed a single man to have sexual intercourse with her, solely because of promise to marry her in the event she became pregnant, it was purely a meretricious transaction, and not seduction. Woodall, 7 Ga. App. 245, 247 (66 S. E. 619).

It need not be shown that the time for the marriage has been definitely fixed. Woodall, 7 Ga. App. 245, 246 (66 S. E. 627).

Evidence that invitations to the wedding were sent out and other preparations made,-admissible as a circumstance evidencing the existence of an engagement to marry. Parker, 11 Ga. App. 251 (1) (75 S. E. 437).

Promise of marriage need not be valid and binding, provided that the woman believed in it, and consented to sexual intercourse in reliance on it. Mercer, 42 Ga. App. 416 (2) (156 S. E. 321).

As the statutes do not limit punishment of seduction to cases in which seduction is accomplished solely upon promise of marriage, it is not essential that promise be absolute; it may be conditional upon some other event than intercourse, provided that the woman believed in the promise, and yielded because of it. Mercer, 42 Ga. App. 416 (2) (156 S. E. 321). 

Infants. An infant may be guilty of seduction under a promise to marry, if he has reached the age of puberty, although his promise is not binding because of his infancy, and although he has not reached the age at which he can contract marriage. Mercer, 42 Ga. 

App. 416 (2) (156 S. E. 321). 

Offer to marry. Offer to marry can only be made before arraignment at first trial. Parker, 17 Ga. App. 252 (2) (87 S. E. 705); 

Jinks, 114 Ga. 430, 431 (3) (40 S. E. 320).

Ending of prosecution for seduction by offer to marry, with bond

SPECIFIC CRIMES 

629 and license, bars indictment for fornication. Banks, 150 Ga. 73 (102 

S. E. 519); Banks, 25 Ga. App. 169 (102 S. E. 843).

Where prosecution is suspended by marriage, defendant is not justified in abandoning his wife within the statutory period of five years because he suspected that she has been unfaithful. Arnold, 15 Ga. App. 347 (1) (83 S. E. 155).

Accomplice. The woman is not an accomplice in the crime of her own seduction, and her testimony needs no corroboration. Keller, 102 Ga. 506 (4) (31 S. E. 92); Washington, 124 Ga. 423 (1) (52 S. 

E. 910).

Marriage of female to another. The fact that the female alleged to have been seduced subsequently married another was no bar to prosecution. Morris, 14 Ga. App. 395 (1) (81 S. E. 257).

Rape. If evidence shows rape, conviction of seduction is illegal. 

However, slight resistance does not support a charge of rape. Jones, 90 Ga. 616 (16 S. E. 380).

Venue. Where the female had sexual intercourse at various times and places with the same man, and she consented to each act of sexual intercourse because of persuasion and promises of marriage, she was seduced on the occasion of the first sexual intercourse, and the venue was in the county where the first sexual intercourse took place. Davis, 28 Ga. App. 372 (110 S. E. 922).

Evidence. Evidence that the female alleged to have been seduced had a living child, and that the defendant attempted to persuade her to take medicine to cause an abortion-admissible to show sexual intercourse. Parker, 11 Ga. App. 251 (2) (75 S. E. 437); Odum, 21 Ga. App. 310 (2) (94 S. E. 257).

Where the indictment does not charge that the female is unmarried, evidence thereof is unnecessary, but admissible. Jordan, 120 

Ga. 864 (4) (48 S. E. 342); Boggs, 11 Ga. App. 92 (1) (74 S. E. 716).

Evidence that the defendant was unmarried is admissible although not charged in the indictment. Boggs, 11 Ga. App. 92 (1) (74 S. E. 716). 

Evidence of good character of the girl's parents-inadmissible. 

Lewis, 89 Ga. 396 (1) (15 S. E. 489).

Woman's testimony that her yielding to the accused was due to love-admissible. Washington, 124 Ga. 423, 424 (8) (52 S. E. 910). 

Evidence of the death of the girl's mother-admissible. Pike, 121 

Ga. 604 (1) (49 S. E. 680).

Where there was evidence that original letter written by the prosecutrix to the defendant was in defendant's possession, and he

could not lawfully be compelled to produce it, secondary evidence admissible. Thomas, 19 Ga. App. 104 (1) (91 S. E. 247).

Weeping of woman at the trial of a man for seduction is no ground for a new trial, where no objection was made at the time. 

Washington, 124 Ga. 423, 424 (10) (52 S. E. 910).

One charged with seduction and convicted of fornication, will not be heard to complain to rulings which could have been prejudicial to him only in the event of his having been convicted of seduction. 

Moulton, 18 Ga. App. 285, 286 (3) (89 S. E. 341).

Argument of counsel. Maintenance, education and legitimacy of the child which may have been the result of illicit connection are not involved in the trial for seduction, and it is error for the Court to permit the State to urge the jury to convict the defendant in order that the child might have a legitimate father. Parker, 11 Ga. App. 

251, 252 (5) (75 S. E. 437).

Charge of the Court. It is error for the Court to charge that it is not lawful defense for the accused to blacken the character of his alleged victim. Thomas, 146 Ga. 346 (1) (91 S. E. 109).

It is not a reversible error for the Court to charge the full section of the Code defining the offense of seduction, although the indictment charged the offense to have been committed by persuasion and promises of marriage, where the Court also instructed the jury, that the State relied for conviction upon proof of persuasion and promises of marriage and not by other false and fraudulent means. 

Thomas, 19 Ga. App. 104, 105 (5) (91 S. E. 247); Thomas, 146 Ga. 

346, 347 (3) (91 S. E. 109). But where the Court, in a similar case, failed to charge the jury that the State relied for conviction upon proof of persuasion and promises of marriage and not by other false and fraudulent means, the charge was held to be confusing, and the judgment reversed. Joiner, 37 Ga. App. 487 (140 S. E. 799).

The Court need not define the word "virtuous" without special request. Helton, 45 Ga. App. 348, 350 (164 S. E. 686).

Presumption. A presumption of law is that the female alleged to have been seduced was virtuous, and the presumption remains until removed by evidence. Moon, 49 Ga. App. 9 (2) (174 S. E. 176). 

Essential elements.

An essential element in the offense of seduction is that the person seduced was an unmarried, as well as a virtuous, female. It follows that upon a prosecution for that offense, the burden is on the State to affirmatively show that the female

SPECIFIC CRIMES 

631 charged to have been seduced, was an unmarried woman at the time of the alleged offense. Where the State fails to establish these facts, a conviction is unauthorized. Crumpler, 46 Ga. App. 58 (166

S. E. 457). 

47. SODOMY AND BESTIALITY. 

§§ 26-5901 to 26-5905. 

Punishment. Sodomy. Imprisonment in the penitentiary for life. (Not reducible.) § 26-5902.

Bestiality. Not less than five nor more than twenty years in the penitentiary. § 26-5904. (Reducible. But see Stephens, 51 Ga. 236.)

Attempt of sodomy or bestiality. (Misdemeanor.) § 26-5905. 

SODOMY. Indictment, charge and accuse... .with the offense of day of...19...., in sodomy, for the said....………..on the………………………………………..day of…………….:..... the county aforesaid, did unlawfully and with force and arms, being then and there a man, have carnal knowledge and connection against the order of nature with one... who was then and there a man, by then and there taking into his mouth the male organ of said.. and thus said carnal knowledge and connection against the order of nature was had by said.....…………………………………., a man, with said............, who was then and there a man, contrary, etc. . (Approved: Jones, 17 Ga. App. 825, 826 (88 S. E. 712).) For approved and complete indictment charging the offense of sodomy between man and woman, see: Comer, 21 Ga. App. 306 (3) 

General. Sodomy committed in jail between inmates. Mobley, 44 Ga. App. 793 (163 S. E. 309).

Sodomy as defined in this section is a crime which may be committed otherwise than per anum. Herring, 119 Ga. 709 (2) (46 S. 

E. 876); Jones, 17 Ga. App. 825 (88 S. E. 712); Comer, 21 Ga. App. 

306 (94 S. E. 314).

There is no limitation as to the means by which this crime may be committed. Jones, 17 Ga. App. 825 (88 S. E. 712); Herring, 119 Ga. 

709, 721 (46 S. E. 876); White, 136 Ga. 158 (71 S. E. 135).

In this section the words "the same unnatural manner" refer to the words "against the order of nature," and should be so construed. (Divers ways in which such crime may be committed discussed.) Comer, 21 Ga. App. 306 (2-a) (94 S. E. 314).

Where a man and a woman voluntarily have carnal knowledge and a connection against the order of nature with each other, they

are both guilty of sodomy, whether the offense be committed by the mouth of the woman or the mouth of the man. Comer, 21 Ga. App. 

306 (94 S. E. 314).

Where crime has been committed by two men, both are guilty. 

Jones, 17 Ga. App. 825 (88 S. E. 712).

The indictment being for sodomy, and the question of guilt depending upon the opinion of two physicians, one of whom testified that he did not know whether there was a penetration or not, and the other, although he had not examined the party, testified that from the evidence, which he heard, he was of the opinion that there was no penetration, conviction for sodomy was unauthorized. 

Hodges, 94 Ga. 593 (19 S. E. 758).

Where there was no penetration, defendant may still be guilty of attempt to commit sodomy. Hodges, 94 Ga. 593 (19 S. E. 758). 

Or assault with intent to commit sodomy. (Id.) 

Evidence that defendant approached prosecutor at night on the street, asking him if certain people were coming that way, put one hand on prosecutor's shoulder, and putting other hand down on prosecutor's breeches and over his private parts, said "Let's go down on the alley yonder," and ran when prosecutor's friends approached, was not sufficient to sustain charge of "then and there" making an assault with intent to commit sodomy upon the person of the prosecutor. Bennett, 21 Ga. App. 505 (94 S. E. 626).

BESTIALITY. 

Verdict of guilty is not illegal because it contains a recommendation of the defendant to mercy. The penalty being fixed by law, it is not within the power of either the jury or the Court to change it. 

Stephens, 51 Ga. 236.

In a case of bestiality, penetration may be proved by circumstances, and need not necessarily be shown by an actual eye witness thereof. Circumstantial evidence, if convincing beyond a reasonable doubt, will authorize a jury to convict and the Court to uphold the conviction. Collins, 73 Ga. 76. 

48. TRESPASS. 

§§ 26-3001, 26-3002, 45-401, 91-107, 91-9901, 91-9902. (Misdemeanor.) Indictment. charge and accuse. .with the offense of trespass, for that the said... on the................day of............... 

19.

, in the county aforesaid, did then and there unlawfully and

SPECIFIC CRIMES 

633 with force and arms squat and settle and remain on the inclosed lands of (describe the lands), with no to wit: bona fide claim of title thereto and without the consent of the contrary, etc. . Baker, 9 Ga. App. 423 (71 owner, S. E. 594). In an indictment brought under § 45-401 of the Code, prohibiting illegal hunting and fishing, it should be alleged that the notice against hunting and fishing had been posted by the landowner in two or more places on each tract of land owned; that the landowner had registered his name in "the register for posting lands," after first having stated that the two or more notices had been posted, and that at the time of the registering he gave a description of the lands as provided by law, including lot number and district, and sufficient to put the public on notice. Hardaway, 1 Ga. App. 150 (58 

S. E. 141).

In an indictment brought under § 26-3002 the description of the land on which the alleged trespass occurred must be definite. 

Mitchell, 12 Ga. App. 557 (77 S. E. 889); Baker, 19 Ga. App. 84, 85 (90 S. E. 983); Heard, 4 Ga. App. 572 (61 S. E. 1055).

Indictment charging defendant with felling timber upon the land of "A," in X District G. M., is subject to special demurrer for indefiniteness of description of the land, though previous statements in the indictment located the land in the county of the prosecution. "A" might have owned several tracts of land in that district. Morrow, 17 Ga. App. 116 (1) (86 S. E. 280).

Under § 26-3001 the indictment need not allege that the act of trespass was "willfully" committed. Wilcher, 118 Ga. 196 (1) (44 

S. E. 995). General.

Simple larceny and trespass are not the same offense. In trespass there is no animus furandi, in larceny there is. One indicted for trespass can not be convicted where evidence shows that he is guilty of larceny. Beall, 68 Ga. 820 (3); Sevy, 71 Ga. 361.

The Willfulness is the ingredient of the offense of trespass. word "willful," as used in this statute, means "intentionally, malevolently, with a bad purpose, an evil purpose, without ground for believing the act to be lawful." Black, 3 Ga. App. 297 (59 S. 

E. 823).

Passing over inclosed lands of another, after being forbidden to do so, is not a violation of this statute, unless the act was willful. 

Poole, 17 Ga. App. 738 (1) (88 S. E. 411).

Where indictment need not allege that the act was done willfully, conviction still can not be had where the act done was without criminal intent. Shrouder, 121 Ga. 615 (3) (49 S. E. 702).

Dispute of title. The law of criminal trespass was not designed to try disputed land titles, but to punish those who willfully, and without claim of right, commit acts of trespass on the lands of others. Hately, 118 Ga. 79, 81 (44 S. E. 852). Title in accusedadmissible evidence. (Id.) § 26-3002 does not apply to one who bona fide claims to be the true owner and entitled to the possession of the land, nor, likewise, to an agent who bona fide believes his principal, by whose direction he goes upon the land, is the owner thereof. Wiggins, 119 Ga. 216 (1) (2) (46 S. E. 86); Shrouder, 121 Ga. 615 (3) (49 S. E. 702).

Tenant who in good faith claims possession under one who bona fide claims title and right of possession, can not be convicted of trespass. Claim of right in good faith is a perfect defense. Hayes, 13 Ga. App. 647 (79 S. E. 761).

Squatter. A squatter may be defined to be a person who settles or locates on land, inclosed or uninclosed, with no bona fide claim. or color of title, and without the consent of the owner. Baker, 9 

Ga. App. 423 (1) (71 S. E. 594).

Crawling under the house, without more, does not amount to squatting. Baker, 9 Ga. App. 423 (71 S. E. 594).

Cropper. The law of criminal trespass does not cover the conversion by a cropper of a portion of his crop, though he may be prosecuted under another section. Lane, 113 Ga. 1040, 1041 (39 

S. E. 463). 

Cultivated and inclosed lands. The words "cultivated lands" as used in § 26-3002 are not intended to apply to such land only as at the time has growing crops upon it. "Cultivated lands" applies also to land actually prepared for a crop, and to land which has been used for growing crops, and which the owner intends again to devote; in due season, to such use. Bryce, 113 Ga. 705 (39 S. E. 

282); Horsely, 16 Ga. App. 136 (84 S. E. 600). "Cultivated lands" does not apply to uncultivated real estate. 

Wiggins, 119 Ga. 216 (3) (46 S. E. 86).

A house situated on inclosed land is necessarily included within the inclosure, and comes within the provision of § 26-3002. Poole, 17 Ga. App. 738 (2) (88 S. E. 411). § 26-3002, prohibiting willful trespass on a field, orchard, garden, or other inclosed or cultivated land of another, after being per-

SPECIFIC CRIMES 

635 sonally forbidden so to do, applies even to visitors to tenants who do not journey over the roadway, but instead proceed across cultivated lands. Horsely, 16 Ga. App. 136 (2) (84 S. E. 600).

Notice. Any one of the three classes named in the statute may give the requisite notice: The owner, the person entitled to the possession for the time being, or the authorized agent; and an owner's daughter, left in possession of the premises in the owner's absence, is such an agent who may give notice. Bryce, 113 Ga. 705, 706 (39 S. E. 282).

The notice given to trespassers by the owner of the land must be explicit. Murphey, 115 Ga. 201 (41 S. E. 685).

The tenant in possession is authorized to forbid trespass upon the land. Bryce, 113 Ga. 705 (1) (39 S. E. 282).

The landlord has no right to forbid third persons to go on the rented premises for lawful purposes with the permission of the tenant. Mitchell, 12 Ga. App. 557 (2) (77 S. E. 889).

Larceny. Applying the rule of ejusdem generis sub-section (2) of the law of criminal trespass does not include the theft of personal goods from the house, with the knowledge but without the consent of the owner. Grier, 103 Ga. 428, 429 (30 S. E. 255).

Under sub-section (2) of the law of criminal trespass, it is necessary that the article taken have some value. Such value must be alleged and proved. While this act defines trespass, it creates, in effect, a species of larceny, and denominates the offense a trespass. 

Gilreath, 96 Ga. 303, 305 (22 S. E. 907).

Evidence. Evidence from which it could reasonably be inferred that the defendant knowingly and willfully cut down trees on the land of another authorizes conviction, though it may not be conclusively shown that he acted willfully and knowingly. Black, 17 

Ga. App. 294 (1) (86 S. E. 659).

Where the indictment charges that the defendant moved a certain dwelling house from a described land of a certain person, and the evidence, while showing that the dwelling house was removed by the accused from some land belonging to the person alleged in the indictment, but failing to show that the house was taken from the particular land described in the indictment,-conviction not legal. Kennedy, 19 Ga. App. 448 (91 S. E. 878).

Evidence that about ten days after the prosecutor bought the land and, after showing defendant's hands his lines, twenty pieces of timber were cut on prosecutor's land, that prosecutor did not give or sell the timber to the defendant, and that the defendant

told the prosecutor that he had a lease covering that land and that he had a right to cut the timber, although weak, authorizes conviction. Bennett, 25 Ga. App. 504 (103 S. E. 858).

Where the indictment alleged that the accused entered the lands of "A," the person entitled to the possession of the place, and the evidence showed that "A" had no title, but was in possession merely as an agent of "B," the variance was fatal. Jackson, 124 

Ga. 135 (52 S. E. 155). 

49. VAGRANCY. 

§§ 26-7001, 26-7002. 

(Misdemeanor.) 

Indictment. charge and accuse.. a misdemeanor, for that the said. ..with the offense of on the.......... ...day of 

19., in the county aforesaid, did then and there, unlawfully, and with force and arms, wander and stroll about in idleness, being then and there able to work and having no property to support him, the said... .........., and did then and there lead an idle, immoral, and profligate life, having no property to support him and being then and there able to work and not working, and being then and there able to work and having no property to support him did not have any visible and known means of a fair, honest, and reputable livelihood, contrary, etc. (Approved: Cody, 118 Ga. 784 

In order to convict a minor, between the ages of sixteen and twenty-one, of vagrancy, the indictment or accusation must affirmatively allege and the evidence show that the parents of the accused can not support him, and that he is not attending an educational institution. Rogers, 4 Ga. App. 392 (61 S. E. 496).

Where an indictment alleges that the defendant's parents can not support him, and that he is not attending an educational institution, such allegation is material, and must be proved. Jacobs, 1 

Ga. App. 519, 520 (57 S. E. 1063).

An indictment for vagrancy is not defective because it charges in one count several ways in which this statute has been violated, and the State is not required to elect for which act it will ask conviction. Cody, 118 Ga. 784 (1) (2) (45 S. E. 622). General.

The law enumerating the various instances of vagrancy was enacted to prevent men from becoming drones, thieves, or charges

SPECIFIC CRIMES 

637 upon the public. Hartman, 119 Ga. 427, 429 (46 S. E. 638); Daniel, 110 Ga. 915, 916 (36 S. E. 293).

Under the law of vagrancy the gist of the offense is the failure or refusal to work when work is necessary to support self and family. Simmons, 126 Ga. 632 (55 S. E. 479); Hartman, 119 Ga. 427 (46 

S. E. 638).

Small income. Small income which is sufficient to maintain the defendant, no matter in what meager style, is a good defense. 

Leonard, 5 Ga. App. 494 (63 S. E. 530).

Sufficiency of earnings. Labor sufficient to furnish livelihood is reasonably continuous employment. Lewis, 3 Ga. App. 322, 323 (59 S. E. 933).

Now, what would be "reasonably continuous employment" is difficult to determine. Keeping in mind the mischief to be remedied. and the purpose of the law, any work or labor which is sufficient to furnish the means of livelihood to the laborer, if he has no family, and to prevent him from wandering about in idleness, would be "reasonably continuous employment," as defined by the statute. 

The public is not concerned in the length of the labor or the proceeds of the labor. Its only object is to protect itself from the idler and the result of idleness. The solicitous inquiry of society, which the penal statute requires to be answered is that of the Master of the vineyard: "Why stand ye here all the day idle?" Lewis, 3 

Ga. App. 322, 323 (59 S. E. 933).

Occasionally earning money, which is insufficient to one's support, is no defense where the charge is vagrancy. Welborn, 119 

Ga. 429 (3) (46 S. E. 645); Cody, 118 Ga. 784 (5) (45 S. E. 622).

Fact that one may work one or two days in a week and remain idle during the remainder of the week, will not constitute him a vagrant, if his earnings are sufficient to support him. Hawks, 3 

Ga. App. 447 (1) (60 S. E. 207).

The length of time in which one may become a vagrant is immaterial, it being a question for the jury to determine, not how long it may take one to become a vagrant, but whether in fact the defendant has become and is a vagrant. Hawks, 3 Ga. App. 447 (60 

S. E. 207).

Verdict of guilty is unsupported where it is not shown that the accused did not have means ample for his support. Elders, 17 Ga. 

App. 742 (88 S. E. 414).

Ability to work. A conviction of vagrancy is unwarranted where there is no evidence that the accused was able to work. Bryant, 34

Ga. App. 523 (130 S. E. 352); Elders, 17 Ga. App. 742 (88 S. E. 414).

Abode. A habitual loafer, who is able to work, has no property, no reasonably continuous employment, and no regular income, is properly convicted, although he has a fixed place of abode, where he usually lodges. Carter, 126 Ga. 570 (55 S. E. 477).

Evidence. Where the evidence showed that for two years the accused had been able to work, but had not worked, and that he had no property to support him, conviction was authorized. Price, 67 

Ga. 723.

Evidence that the accused had not done any work for some time is not objectionable, in a prosecution for keeping intoxicating liquors at a public place, as virtually placing the accused on trial for vagrancy, where there was no evidence that he had no property or means of support and was able to work. Griffin, 15 Ga. App. 

552 (3) (83 S. E. 871).

Evidence that the accused had no visible means of support, was able to work, and lived an idle, immoral, and profligate life, was sufficient to convict.. Cody, 118 Ga. 784 (4) (45 S. E. 622).

Conviction was unwarranted where the evidence that the defendant was seen at time not to work was opposed by positive testimony that he worked. Miller, 4 Ga. App. 392 (61 S. E. 494); 

Leonard, 5 Ga. App. 494 (63 S. E. 530).

Preacher. Where a preacher had no regular church but obtained voluntary contributions, and evidence showed that he was in good standing and there was no evidence of his idleness, conviction was not warranted. Hicks, 76 Ga. 326. 

Minors. Children under sixteen years of age can not be lawfully convicted of vagrancy. Johnson, 124 Ga. 421 (52 S. E. 737).

Where there is no evidence that the defendant is under the age of sixteen, the Court need not charge the jury that the State must show the defendant to be over sixteen years of age before he can be convicted. Shank, 36 Ga. App. 301 (136 S. E. 332).

Conviction is unwarranted, where the minor is over sixteen years of age, and the evidence does not show affirmatively that the parents of the minor are unable to support him. Braswell, 119 Ga. 72 (45 

S. E. 963); Rogers, 4 Ga. App. 392 (61 S. E. 496); Collins, 125 Ga. 

15 (53 S. E. 809).

Where the evidence does not show inability of the parents of the accused to support him, or unwillingness to do so, conviction is illegal. Henderson, 112 Ga. 19 (37 S. E. 98); Turner, 2 Ga. App.

SPECIFIC CRIMES 

639 

386 (58 S. E. 492); Braswell, 119 Ga. 72 (45 S. E. 963); Collins, 125 

Ga. 15 (53 S. E. 809).

Married women. A married woman, whose husband is not shown to be unable to support her, can not be convicted of vagrancy upon proof alone that she is able to work and does not work; this is true, though she and her husband may be living in a state of separation. 

Brown, 14 Ga. App. 25 (79 S. E. 1133).

Women. Women, whose livelihood depends solely upon immoral practices are, in the eyes of the law, without means of support. 

Smith, 22 Ga. App. 45 (1) (95 S. E. 470).

Proof of immoral conduct will not warrant conviction of vagrancy. 

Hartman, 119 Ga. 427, 429 (46 S. E. 628).

Evidence that woman, 25 years old, was of lewd reputation, that she never worked, that she was an addict of morphine, that she was arrested on the complaint of her mother, and that she was able to work and had no property, although weak, sufficient to convict. Arwood, 25 Ga. App. 482 (103 S. E. 726).

Evidence that grown woman, able to work, without means of reputable livelihood, was a street-walker, who loitered around saloons and did not work,-sufficient to convict. Welborn, 119 

Ga. 429 (3) (46 S. E. 645). 

Municipal ordinances. Municipal ordinances punishing "idling, loitering, or loafing upon the streets,' not void as an effort to punish for the same acts which are State offenses. To convict under such ordinance, it is not necessary to prove that the accused is without property or means of support. Taylor, 118 Ga. 63 (2)
